intel_2026.whatItMeans: This group covers incidental support services for marine and freshwater fishing and aquaculture, such as feeding, harvesting, auction preparation, sorting, grading, and quality testing. It also includes post-harvest handling and preservation like chilling fish to maintain freshness before sale, as well as protecting fish from predators, fisheries control and surveillance, and maritime ecosystem restoration.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: **PMA (Foreign Investment):** Open — up to 100% foreign ownership.
intel_2026.whatChanged: New code in KBLI 2025 — no direct equivalent in KBLI 2020.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Jasa Penunjang Kegiatan Penangkapan Dan (03300)? This is classified as Unknown risk with PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through the requirements.
intel_2026.baliContext: Bali's fishing and aquaculture sector is centered around Jimbaran, Kedonganan, and the north coast (Singaraja area). Marine aquaculture — particularly seaweed, lobster, and ornamental fish — has foreign investment potential. Freshwater aquaculture thrives in Tabanan and Gianyar.

editorial.headline: The Fisheries Support Code With a Bali Scope Test
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 03300 covers practical support around catching and aquaculture, nationally open to PMA, but Bali registration depends on the exact declared activity risk.
editorial.body:
KBLI 03300 is not the act of fishing itself, nor the later business of turning fish into a finished product. Its centre of gravity is the operational support that sits around capture and aquaculture: feeding services, harvesting assistance, auction preparation, sorting, grading, quality testing, and the handling needed before sale. The record also brings in preservation before the market, such as chilling fish to keep it fresh, along with fish protection, fisheries control or fish-guard work, and maritime ecosystem restoration.

That breadth matters. This is a service code for the infrastructure of fisheries activity, used by operators whose role is to make the catch or cultivation process workable, orderly, safer, or more market-ready before the product moves onward. It can fit small, practical service businesses as well as larger operators, because the record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. The scope is therefore not only a technical classification; it is a statement about where the business sits in the fisheries chain: close to production, before downstream distribution or processing, and tied to support rather than ownership of the fishery activity itself.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a pma_max_asing of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In ordinary language, that means the record treats the code as nationally open to foreign ownership up to 100%. There is no foreign-share cap below full ownership in the supplied data, so the editorial conclusion should not invent one. For founders comparing structures, the national rule is the easier part of the story: this code is open on the national investment list, and it is open across all stated business scales.

Bali is more exacting. The record does not mark the code as outright blocked in Bali, but it does assign Blocked (scope-dependent) and gives a clear warning: the OSS risk at Besar scale is low on some scopes and higher on others, so PMA registration in Bali is possible only by declaring the higher-risk scope and verifying live OSS against the exact activity. That sits against the province-wide moratorium rule blocking Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The honest reading is therefore neither panic nor comfort: KBLI 03300 is nationally open, but in Bali a foreign-owned setup must be scoped with care, because the registration outcome turns on the declared activity rather than the title alone.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 03300 is nationally open, but in Bali the registration outcome turns on the declared activity rather than the title alone.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)

editorial.headline: Coal Mining, Open Nationally and Not Stopped by Bali’s PMA Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: This code covers coal extraction and on-site coal preparation, with all business scales open and a national PMA ceiling recorded at 100%.
editorial.body:
**Coal mining under this activity code is not a decorative category.** The slim record defines it as the mining of coal by underground or surface methods, including mining by liquefaction methods. Its operational core is extraction, but the scope also reaches the immediate handling that makes mined coal usable, classifiable, movable, and storable: cleaning, measuring, grouping, crushing, and compacting coal to classify it, improve quality, or make transport and storage easier. It also covers the recovery of coal from mine-waste piles, which keeps the activity tied to coal that comes from the mining environment itself.

That makes this a code for operators whose business substance is coal mining and direct coal preparation, not a loose energy, trading, support, or processing label. The record itself also flags mining-authorisation language connected to this field, including Izin Usaha Pertambangan Khusus (IUPK) Eksplorasi and Perpanjangan IUP Tahap Operasi Produksi. Those names should be read carefully: the slim record identifies them, but it does not give thresholds, timelines, capital rules, or procedural steps. For a founder, the important classification point is narrower and more useful: the activity is about extracting coal and carrying out the immediate preparation work that belongs with that extraction.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It says the activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In plain English, the classification is not reserved in the record for one enterprise size; the record places every scale on the open side. For foreign investment, the national PMA position is also clear: the status is TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing recorded as 100. That means the national foreign-ownership ceiling shown in the record is 100%, and there is no foreign-stake cap below full ownership in the data provided here. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

The Bali picture is the part that needs precision. Across Bali, the record's moratorium permanently blocks PMA for every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. This coal-mining code is not marked as blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, with the Bali status recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason given is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. The honest reading is therefore not that Bali is casually easy, and not that a foreigner is barred. It is that, based only on this slim record, the code is nationally open to PMA up to 100% and is not stopped by Bali’s Low and Medium-Low risk PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Coal Upgrading, After the Mine and Before the Market
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the standalone processing that cleans, sorts, crushes, compacts, and grades coal to improve quality, calories, transport, or storage.
editorial.body:
Coal beneficiation under this activity is not the extraction of coal. It sits after the mining act and before the coal is treated as a more usable commercial material: cleaned, measured, grouped, crushed, compacted, and otherwise prepared so its quality or calorific value can be classified or improved. The practical centre of the activity is physical upgrading. It makes coal easier to sort, move, store, and present according to quality, but it must be carried out separately from the coal mining process itself.

That distinction matters for founders because the business being registered is a processing and quality-improvement activity, not a mining concession. A company using this activity would be built around facilities, handling systems, grading procedures, crushing or compaction capability, storage flow, and quality classification. The record opens it across every business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth does not make the activity informal; it simply means the classification is not restricted to one company size. The real question is whether the applicant’s actual operations match the standalone beneficiation scope, rather than drifting into extraction.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clean. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with foreign ownership allowed up to 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain terms, the record does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership. editorial.headline: Lignite Mining, Clearly Open but Still Address-Sensitive in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 05200 covers the extraction and basic preparation of lignite, with national PMA access open across all business scales and no Bali moratorium block on the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 05200 is a mining classification for lignite, the younger form of coal. Its scope is not merely the act of taking material from the ground; it covers underground and surface extraction, including mining by liquefaction methods, and the immediate physical handling that makes lignite usable, movable, and storable. The record brings together excavation, crushing, washing, screening, blending, and compaction when these activities are part of improving quality or easing transport and storage. In plain English, this is the code for operators whose business is the extraction and primary preparation of lignite itself.

That distinction matters because the activity is industrial in character, but the slim record keeps the scale door wide. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses. A small domestic operator and a large enterprise may sit under the same activity code if the actual activity remains within the lignite mining and basic preparation scope described above. The important editorial point is to read the code through what it does, not through the size of the company: the defining feature is lignite extraction and its direct preparation, not a downstream product, a support service, or a separate construction activity.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clean. Sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, the record categorises the activity as TERBUKA and places pma_max_asing at 100. That means the record gives no foreign-share cap below full ownership. For a PMA analysis, the plain reading is therefore that foreign ownership may reach 100% at the national level, subject only to facts and procedures not stated in this slim record. Nothing in this record supports adding a minimum capital figure, a special licence summary, a tax treatment, or a timeline, so those should not be smuggled into the classification note.

Bali is the more practical reading, and here the answer is still not a ban. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason says medium-high/high risk is not blocked by the moratorium, with verification per address. The province-wide moratorium in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, but this activity is recorded as outside that block. The honest conclusion is narrow but useful: KBLI 05200 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali moratorium does not block it on this record; the remaining caution is location-specific verification, not a disguised provincial prohibition.

editorial.headline: Crude Oil Mining, Without the Bali Moratorium Trap
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers crude oil extraction, condensate production, and related bituminous or shale-oil mining, open nationally to PMA at full foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 06100 is the upstream oil activity itself.** Its scope is the mining of crude petroleum: searching for oil content, drilling, extraction, separation, containment, and the production of crude oil and condensate. The record also places within this activity the processing steps needed to obtain crude oil through containment, filtering, drying, stabilization, and similar handling. It is not written as a light trading or advisory activity. It is the industrial act of bringing crude petroleum, condensate, bituminous sands, shale oil, and tar sands into usable crude form when those processes are tied to the mining operation.

That breadth matters for registration. The activity is open across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practice, the substance of the scope reads as heavy upstream extraction, but the slim record does not restrict the code to one scale only. A registrant choosing it is describing a business whose center of gravity is petroleum mining and the directly connected production of crude oil or condensate, including the physical processes of excavation, drilling, crushing, washing, filtering, mixing, and storage where those processes belong to the mining operation.

For foreign ownership, the national signal is unusually clear. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the recorded foreign ownership ceiling is **100%**. That means the record does not show a foreign-share cap below full ownership. The source given for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, so the editorial reading should stay narrow: nationally, this activity is foreign-open at the stated ceiling, and no additional capital threshold, licence, timeline, or sectoral condition can be added unless it appears in the source record.

The Bali picture is also clear, but in the opposite way from many low-risk activities. The Bali moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, yet this record marks the Bali status as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK** and says it is **not blocked** because the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. So the honest conclusion is not that Bali is closed to this PMA registration today. On the slim record provided, the activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and is not caught by Bali's PMA moratorium. The real caution is precision: this conclusion rests only on the registered activity described here, not on any neighbouring support, exploration, refining, or downstream activity outside the record.

editorial.headline: Natural Gas Mining With a Clean Bali Registration Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 06201 covers the integrated search, drilling, mining, separation and storage of natural gas, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 06201 is a natural-gas mining classification, not a general energy trading label or a broad industrial-gas bucket. Its scope is built around the upstream physical chain: searching for gas deposits, drilling, mining, separating the gas, and holding it in storage as part of one connected activity. The record expressly includes natural hydrogen and other forms of natural gas, and it also brings coalbed methane into the same activity frame. In plain English, this is the code for operators whose business is finding and extracting natural gas resources, then handling the immediate separation and containment that belong to that extraction sequence.

The scope also reaches into petroleum-and-gas work areas where the activity is exploration, exploitation, and carbon capture, storage, or utilisation. It can include temporary gas seismic survey activity when the survey is not permanently established and lasts less than 30 days. That matters because the code is not written only for the moment of production; it can also sit at the investigative and field-development stages of a gas project. The common thread is still the same: the activity must remain tied to natural gas resources and the upstream operational chain described in the record.

On scale, the code is open across Besar, Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah. That is unusually broad for a technically heavy activity, but the editorial point is not that every scale looks commercially realistic; it is that the slim record lists all four as open. For foreign investment, the national status is TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100. Stated plainly, the record allows full foreign ownership nationally under the cited PMA basis. There is no foreign-share cap below full ownership in the data provided here, so a foreign-owned setup is not constrained by a minority ceiling on the face of this record.

The Bali picture is also clean, but for a specific reason. The province’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. This code is not marked as blocked in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the reason given is that the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which means it is not caught by that moratorium. The honest conclusion is therefore not a hidden warning; it is that KBLI 06201 is foreign-open nationally and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the supplied Bali screening record.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)

editorial.headline: Geothermal Undertaking With a Clear PMA Path in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This geothermal activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and is not caught by Bali’s PMA moratorium at the higher-risk large-scale level.
editorial.body:
**Pengusahaan Tenaga Panas Bumi** is the upstream business of geothermal energy. Its scope is not simply desk research or a broad energy label: it covers the search for geothermal resources, geothermal drilling, and related work that carries the resource through to the place where it will be used. The record is explicit that the activity may include locations in forest areas, and it also includes the separation of associated minerals arising from geothermal undertaking. Just as importantly, the boundary is clear: this activity stops before the conversion of geothermal energy into electricity.

That makes this a code for operators working in the exploration, exploitation, or utilization stages of geothermal resources, rather than a generic renewable-energy registration. The practical profile is field-heavy and resource-linked: identifying a geothermal prospect, drilling it, developing the geothermal undertaking around it, and handling the mineral by-products that come from that undertaking. It is therefore a serious industrial activity, but the scale gate in the record is broad. Micro, small, medium, and large businesses are all listed as open scales, so the registration pathway is not reserved only for large companies in the national classification itself.

National rules leave the foreign-investment position unambiguous. The PMA status is open, and the foreign ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain English, the record supports a fully foreign-owned PMA structure for this activity at the national level, subject to the normal reading of the cited PMA source. There is no ownership cap below full control in the slim record, so this is not a case where a foreign investor must stop at a minority or joint-venture threshold based on the data provided here.

The Bali picture is also unusually clean, but for a different reason. Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA across the province on a permanent, island-wide basis. This activity is not marked as blocked: its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason given is that the OSS risk at large scale is Medium-High/High, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. The honest conclusion is therefore not that Bali is closed to this PMA activity. Based only on this record, a foreigner can register this geothermal undertaking in Bali today, with the important caveat that its higher-risk character is exactly why it falls outside the moratorium rather than inside it.

kewajiban:
Pemegang Izin Pertambangan Rakyat (IPR) :

  1. Melakukan kegiatan Penambangan dalam jangka waktu paling lambat 3 (tiga) bulan setelah IPR diterbitkan;
  2. Menyusun rencana Penambangan berdasarkan dokumen pengelolaan WPR yang disusun oleh Menteri, yang meliputi: metode Penambangan, peralatan dan perlengkapan yang digunakan, jadwal kerja, kebutuhan personil; dan biaya atau permodalan;
  3. Mematuhi persyaratan teknis pertambangan antara lain:
    1. Tidak menggunakan bahan peledak;
    2. Tidak menggunakan bahan berbahaya beracun yang dilarang sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
    3. Tidak melakukan kegiatan Penambangan dengan menggunakan metode Penambangan bawah tanah bagi orang perseorangan; dan
  4. Menerapkan kaidah teknis Pertambangan yang baik khususnya pengelolaan lingkungan dan keselamatan Pertambangan.

Pemegang IUP/IUPK/IUPK Sebagai Kelanjutan Operasi Kontrak/Perjanjuan:

  1. Menempatkan jaminan kesungguhan Eksplorasi;
  2. Membayar pendapatan negara dan pendapatan daerah termasuk kewajiban iuran tetap dan iuran produksi;
  3. Menyusun dan menyerahkan rencana Reklamasi dan/atau rencana Pascatambang;
  4. Menyediakan dan menempatkan dana jaminan Reklamasi dan/atau dana jaminan Pascatambang;
  5. Melaksanakan Reklamasi dan Pascatambang;
  6. Menyusun dokumen lingkungan;
  7. Melaksanakan pengembangan dan pemberdayaan masyarakat;
  8. Menggunakan jalan Pertambangan;
  9. Melaksanakan penerapan kaidah teknik Pertambangan yang baik, yaitu:
    1. Ketentuan keselamatan Pertambangan;
    2. Pengelolaan dan pemantauan lingkungan Pertambangan, termasuk kegiatan Reklamasi dan/atau Pascatambang;
    3. Upaya konservasi Mineral dan Batubara; dan
    4. Pengelolaan sisa tambang dari suatu kegiatan Usaha Pertambangan dalam bentuk padat, cair, atau gas sampai memenuhi standar baku mutu lingkungan sebelum dilepas ke media lingkungan;
  10. Memenuhi ketentuan penetapan jumlah produksi dan penjualan nasional;
  11. Mengutamakan pemanfaatan tenaga kerja setempat, barang, dan jasa dalam negeri sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
  12. Melakukan divestasi saham bagi PMA sesuai ketentuan perundang-undangan;
  13. Pada tahap kegiatan Operasi Produksi wajib menyediakan dana ketahanan cadangan Mineral dan Batubara;
  14. Menggunakan perusahaan Jasa Pertambangan lokal dan/atau nasional;
  15. Menyelesaikan hak atas tanah;
  16. Melakukan peningkatan nilai tambah melalui kegiatan pengolahan dan/atau pemurnian; dan
  17. Melaksanakan kewajiban lainnya sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.

persyaratan:
Bentuk Perizinan Izin Pertambangan Rakyat (IPR)

  1. Orang perseorangan:
    1. Surat permohonan;
    2. Nomor Induk Berusaha;
    3. Salinan Kartu Tanda Penduduk;
    4. Surat keterangan dari kelurahan/desa setempat yang menyatakan pemohon merupakan penduduk setempat;
    5. Surat pernyataan untuk mematuhi ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang lingkungan hidup serta keselamatan Pertambangan; dan
    6. Surat keterangan fiskal sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang perpajakan.
  2. Koperasi:
    1. Surat permohonan;
    2. Nomor Induk Berusaha;
    3. Salinan Kartu Tanda Penduduk pengurus Koperasi;
    4. Surat keterangan dari kelurahan/desa setempat yang menyatakan seluruh pengurus Koperasi merupakan penduduk setempat;
    5. Surat pernyataan kesanggupan pengelolaan lingkungan serta keselamatan Pertambangan; dan
    6. Surat keterangan fiskal sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang perpajakan.

  1. Teknis: Surat pernyataan dari tenaga ahli Pertambangan dan/atau geologi yang berpengalaman paling singkat 3 (tiga) tahun; atau
  2. Lingkungan: Berupa surat pernyataan kesanggupan untuk mematuhi ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang perlindungan dan pengelolaan lingkungan hidup.
  3. Finansial:
    1. Bukti penempatan jaminan kesungguhan pelaksanaan kegiatan Eksplorasi;
    2. Bukti pembayaran harga nilai kompensasi data informasi hasil lelang sesuai dengan nilai penawaran lelang;
    3. Surat keterangan fiskal sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang perpajakan.

Permohonan Izin Usaha Khusus (IUPK):

  1. Teknis: Berupa surat pernyataan dari ahli Pertambangan dan/atau geologi yang berpengalaman paling singkat 3 (tiga) tahun.
  2. Lingkungan: Berupa surat pernyataan kesanggupan untuk mematuhi ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang perlindungan dan pengelolaan lingkungan hidup.
  3. Finansial:
    1. Bukti penempatan jaminan kesungguhan pelaksanaan kegiatan Eksplorasi;
    2. Surat keterangan fiskal sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang perpajakan; dan
    3. Bukti pembayaran nilai kompensasi data informasi.

  1. Administartif:
    1. Surat permohonan;
    2. Nomor Induk Berusaha; dan
    3. Susunan pengurus, daftar pemegang saham, dan daftar pemilik manfaat Badan Usaha dari pemegang KK atau PKP2B.
  2. Teknis:
    1. Rencana pengembangan seluruh wilayah yang telah disetujui yang memuat paling sedikit peta dan batas koordinat wilayah;
    2. Rencana Pengembangan dan/atau Pemanfaatan Batubara yang telah disetujui bagi pemegang PKP2B;
    3. Neraca sumber daya dan cadangan; dan d. Rencana pembangunan sarana dan prasarana penunjang kegiatan Operasi Produksi yang berada dalam WIUPK atau di luar WIUPK.
  3. Lingkungan:
    1. Persetujuan dokumen lingkungan hidup yang diterbitkan oleh instansi yang berwenang sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan; dan
    2. Dokumen rencana Reklamasi dan rencana Pascatambang.
  4. Finansial:
    1. Laporan keuangan 3 (tiga) tahun terakhir yang telah diaudit oleh akuntan publik;
    2. Bukti pelunasan iuran tetap dan iuran produksi 3 (tiga) tahun terakhir; dan

editorial.headline: Iron Sand Mining With a Clear Bali Registration Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 07101 covers iron sand mining and its immediate handling steps, open nationally to all business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 07101 is the activity code for **iron sand mining**. Its recorded scope is narrow but material: the mining of iron sand, including the sorting, separation, and cleaning activities that sit directly around that mining activity. In plain English, this is not a general trading, processing, or construction classification. It is a mining classification for extracting iron sand and handling it through the first operational steps described in the record.

The slim record also names the regulatory instruments attached to this activity: an **Izin Usaha Pertambangan Khusus (IUPK) Eksplorasi** and an **extension of an IUP for the production-operation stage**. Those phrases matter because they keep the code anchored in the mining-permit universe rather than in ordinary commercial registration. The record does not give timelines, technical thresholds, land conditions, tax treatment, capital figures, or operational obligations beyond those named instruments, so the clean reading is disciplined: this code describes the activity and its listed permit context, but it does not by itself supply the full licensing route.

Nationally, the investment signal is clear. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. That means the record treats this activity as open to foreign investment nationally, without a foreign-equity cap below full ownership. The code is also open across every business scale in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. For founders reading this as a market-entry signal, the important point is that the national classification does not reserve the activity only for a single scale or close it to PMA by ownership percentage.

The Bali picture is also unusually direct. The Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the activity is **not blocked** for PMA registration in Bali. The reason given is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not caught by Bali’s moratorium on Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. That does not turn the code into a simple business, and it does not add any extra permission beyond what the record says. It simply means the honest Bali lede is not a prohibition: for this recorded activity, the island-wide PMA moratorium does not block registration today.

editorial.headline: Iron Ore Mining With a Clean National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers iron ore extraction, upgrading, and agglomeration, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the slim record.
editorial.body:
**Iron ore mining is a primary extractive activity, not a trading label or a downstream manufacturing shortcut.** The scope covers the mining of iron ore itself, and it expressly includes work that improves the quality of the ore and agglomerates iron ore and its concentrates. In practical editorial terms, the centre of gravity is the mineral activity: finding, extracting, concentrating, and preparing iron ore material within the boundaries described by the record. The slim record also names Izin Usaha Pertambangan Khusus (IUPK) Eksplorasi and Perpanjangan IUP Tahap Operasi Produksi, so the activity sits in a mining-rights context rather than a general commercial-services context.

The registration profile is broad by scale. The record lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar as open scales, which means the classification is not presented here as reserved only for a large enterprise category. That does not make every real-world project simple; mining is naturally capital-heavy, site-specific, and operationally serious. But those are business realities, not extra legal thresholds supplied by this record. The editorially safe point is narrower and clearer: within the slim record, the activity is open across all four listed scales, from micro through large.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is unambiguous. PMA is classified as TERBUKA, with a 100% foreign ownership ceiling. There is no partial foreign-cap in the record to soften or qualify; the ceiling should be read plainly as full foreign ownership being allowed at the national classification level. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That source line matters because it is the record’s only stated basis for the PMA position, and nothing outside it should be imported into the explanation.

For Bali, the honest picture is also clean: the record does not block this activity for PMA registration under the Bali moratorium. The moratorium rule in the slim record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, but this activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with the reason stating that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi and therefore not blocked by the moratorium. So the national and Bali readings point in the same direction here: foreign-open nationally, and not moratorium-blocked in Bali on the record provided.

editorial.headline: Uranium and Thorium Mining Is Open, but Only at Large Scale
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 07210 covers uranium and thorium ore mining and concentration, with PMA access nationally and no Bali moratorium block at large scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 07210 sits in a narrow and highly specialised part of the mining map: the extraction of ores containing uranium and thorium concentrates. The record names uranium ore, including pitchblende, as an example of the material in scope. It also includes the concentration of uranium and thorium, and the making of yellowcake. In plain English, this is not a general mining category and not a broad mineral-trading label; it is for radioactive mineral mining and the first-stage concentration work that belongs to that activity.

The boundaries matter. The scope does not extend to improving the grade or quality of uranium and thorium ore beyond the activity described here. It also does not cover producing uranium metal from ore, nor further processing such as smelting and refining. The record additionally includes radioactive mineral processing and associated radioactive mineral processing outside the assigned radioactive mineral mining area, as well as radioactive mineral mining and/or processing. Taken together, the code is best read as a large-scale industrial activity around radioactive mineral extraction and concentration, not downstream metallurgy.

For registration, the scale signal is unusually simple: this activity is open only to **Besar** scale. Nationally, the investment status is **TERBUKA**, and the foreign ownership ceiling is **100%** under the cited presidential regulations. That means the national reading is clear: a foreign-owned PMA structure is not capped below full ownership in the slim record. There is no basis here to invent a smaller ceiling, a special timeline, or an additional capital threshold. The record gives one scale, one national status, one foreign-ownership ceiling, and one source.

The Bali picture is also direct, and it is not the common moratorium problem. Bali’s provincial moratorium blocks all low and medium-low risk KBLI for PMA across the island, permanently, according to the cited governor letter. But this record marks the Bali status as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK** and says the OSS risk at **Besar** scale is **Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi**, so it is **not blocked by the moratorium**. The honest conclusion is therefore not that Bali closes this activity to foreign investors today, but that this specific PMA path is nationally open and, on the record provided, not caught by Bali’s low and medium-low risk moratorium.

editorial.headline: Gold and Silver Mining With a Clear Bali Green Light
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 07221 covers the mining, cleaning, and separation of gold and silver ore, with national foreign ownership open up to 100% and no Bali PMA moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 07221 is a mining classification in the most literal sense: it covers the extraction of gold and silver ore, along with the cleaning and separation work that turns mined material into a more defined mineral output. The Indonesian scope is direct and industrial, not ornamental. It is about the activity of taking gold and silver ore from the ground and processing it through the basic cleaning and separation stages named in the record. The same scope also references Izin Usaha Pertambangan Khusus (IUPK) Eksplorasi and Perpanjangan IUP Tahap Operasi Produksi, so the classification sits squarely inside the mining-rights vocabulary used for exploration and production-stage continuation.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That does not turn every mining project into the same kind of business in practice, but it does mean the classification itself is not restricted to one scale band in the slim record. A founder reading this code should therefore separate two questions. First, what does the classification describe? Gold and silver ore mining, cleaning, and separation. Second, at what registered business scales is it open? All four listed scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar.

For foreign ownership, the national signal is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership value given in the record is 100%. In plain English, this record does not show a foreign-shareholding cap below full ownership. Its stated PMA source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the slim record adds a minimum capital number, a special tax treatment, a processing threshold, or a timeline, so none should be read into the classification from this editorial. The defensible conclusion is narrower and stronger: nationally, KBLI 07221 is foreign-open, with the record showing a 100% ceiling.

The Bali position is also clear, and it is not a hidden local veto. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as false and gives the status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which means it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium described in the record. That moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali on a permanent island-wide basis, but this activity is not caught by that block on the facts provided. The honest Bali lede is therefore straightforward: a foreign-owned company can treat this code as nationally open and not blocked by the Bali PMA moratorium, while still staying within the exact mining activity described here.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest Bali lede is therefore straightforward: this foreign-open mining code is not blocked by the Bali PMA moratorium on the facts provided.

Salinan Kartu Tanda Penduduk (KTP) untuk orang perseorangan atau salinan Kartu Tanda Penduduk (KTP) seluruh pengurus beserta susunan pengurus untuk koperasi

  1. Mematuhi ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan dibidang lingkungan hidup serta keselamatan pertambangan. (untuk badan usaha Perseorangan), atau;
  2. Kesanggupan pengelolaan lingkungan dan keselamatan pertambangan (untuk badan usaha Koperasi)
Surat keterangan fiskal sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang perpajakan
Titik koordinat IPR

Titik koordinat IPR

editorial.headline: Platinum-Track Precious Metal Mining, Open Nationally and Viable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers precious metal ore mining beyond gold and silver, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block on the record supplied.
editorial.body:
KBLI 07229 sits in a narrow but consequential corner of the mining economy: the extraction and cleaning of precious metal ores other than gold and silver. The record gives platinum ore as the clear example, so the activity should be read as a specialist precious-metal mining classification rather than a general metals or jewellery trade category. Its centre of gravity is upstream: mineral-bearing ore, the mining work around it, and the cleaning process that prepares that ore within the stated scope.

The scope also names two formal mining-stage references: Izin Usaha Pertambangan Khusus (IUPK) Eksplorasi and Perpanjangan IUP Tahap Operasi Produksi. For an editorial reading, that places the code within both exploration and production-operation continuity, without expanding the record into assumptions about procedures, timing, or eligibility. The practical point is simpler: this is not a retail, craft, or downstream precious-metals activity. It is a mining classification for founders or operators whose business substance is tied to precious metal ore itself.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That does not mean every project looks the same; it means the classification is not confined in the supplied data to one enterprise scale. A small registered operator and a larger mining company may both encounter the same KBLI label if the underlying activity is the mining and cleaning of qualifying precious metal ore. The editorial discipline is to keep the classification tied to the activity, not to the size or ambition of the company using it.

The foreign-investment picture is clean. Nationally, the record marks the PMA status as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali does not reverse that position on the supplied record: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the stated reason is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The moratorium rule still matters as context because Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. But this record does not place KBLI 07229 inside that blocked group. The honest conclusion is therefore direct: on the data supplied, a foreign-owned company can use this KBLI nationally, and the Bali moratorium does not block PMA registration for it today.

Pemegang Izin Pertambangan Rakyat (IPR) :

  1. Melakukan kegiatan Penambangan dalam jangka waktu paling lambat 3 (tiga) bulan setelah IPR diterbitkan;
  2. Menyusun rencana Penambangan berdasarkan dokumen pengelolaan WPR yang disusun oleh Menteri, yang meliputi: metode Penambangan, peralatan dan perlengkapan yang digunakan, jadwal kerja, kebutuhan personil; dan biaya atau permodalan;
  3. Mematuhi persyaratan teknis pertambangan antara lain:
    1. Tidak menggunakan bahan peledak;
    2. Tidak menggunakan bahan berbahaya beracun yang dilarang sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
    3. Tidak melakukan kegiatan Penambangan dengan menggunakan metode Penambangan bawah tanah bagi orang perseorangan; dan
  4. Menerapkan kaidah teknis Pertambangan yang baik khususnya pengelolaan lingkungan dan keselamatan Pertambangan.

editorial.headline: Tin Ore Mining With a Clear PMA Door
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers tin ore mining and preparation, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium rule.
editorial.body:
Tin ore mining under KBLI 07291 is a mineral extraction activity, but the record frames it more narrowly than a general mining label. Its scope covers the mining and preparation of tin ore: the work of taking tin-bearing material from the ground and preparing that ore as the activity’s commercial object. The scope also names two licensing contexts attached to the activity: a Special Mining Business Licence for Exploration, and an extension of a Mining Business Licence at the Production Operation stage. That makes the activity both operational and administrative in character: it is not merely the idea of trading in tin, but the registered mining activity around tin ore itself.

The scale picture is unusually broad in the record. The activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That does not mean every operator will look the same; it means the classification is not confined, in this record, to one business-size lane. A founder reading it should therefore separate the commercial size of the company from the legal character of the activity. The code describes tin ore mining and preparation, while the scale field says the registration lane can exist from micro through large scale. Nothing in the record adds a capital threshold, a timeline, or a separate operational condition, so none should be assumed beyond the named scope and licensing references.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is direct. PMA status is TERBUKA, with a foreign ownership ceiling of 100%, under the cited Perpres framework. In plain English: the national investment classification does not impose a foreign-share cap on this activity. For a foreign-owned company, that is the central national reading of the slim record. It should not be softened into vague encouragement, and it should not be expanded into promises about approvals. The record says open, and it says the ceiling is 100%; it does not say more.

The Bali reading is also clear, and it matters because Bali applies an island-wide PMA moratorium to Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium in the record. The stated reason is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it falls outside the Low and Medium-Low risk group blocked for PMA. The honest conclusion is therefore not a hidden warning but a clean distinction: nationally this activity is foreign-open up to 100%, and in Bali it is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than blocked by the moratorium. The registration question remains serious because tin ore mining is a defined mining activity with named mining-licence contexts, but the Bali moratorium field itself does not close the door.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is therefore not a hidden warning but a clean distinction: nationally this activity is foreign-open up to 100%, and in Bali it is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than blocked by the moratorium.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

editorial.headline: PMA-Open Lead Ore Mining, Cleared for Bali Registration
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 07292 covers lead-ore mining and preparation, open across all business scales, nationally open to full foreign ownership, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 07292 is narrow but not minor. The slim record describes mining and preparation of *bijih timah hitam*, rendered in clear English as lead ore. Its scope is not only extraction: it includes preparation of the ore, and it expressly reaches the production-operation stage when that activity is integrated with processing and/or refining facilities. The record also names IPR cooperative applications, which matters because the code is not written only for one corporate scale or one style of operator.

The registration profile is broad. The code is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the record treats it as a code that can sit from smaller cooperative-context registrations through large operations. The practical reading stays anchored to the actual activity described: mining and preparing lead ore, with the integrated processing and/or refining language where applicable. For PMA, the national status is straightforward: TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100. In ordinary English, the foreign ownership ceiling shown in this record is full foreign ownership, not a lower foreign-stake cap. The legal source given for that national PMA position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

The Bali field is the decisive part of the record. It includes an island-wide, permanent moratorium rule: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. For this activity, however, the Bali field does not say blocked. Its status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the specific reason is that OSS risk at the Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. The point is not that Bali has no moratorium language in the record; the point is that this code's recorded risk position sits outside the low and medium-low moratorium trigger.

The honest conclusion, then, is relatively clean. Nationally, KBLI 07292 is foreign-open up to 100%. In Bali, the record does not impose the PMA moratorium block, because the reason field says the relevant large-scale OSS risk is medium-high/high. A founder reading this code should therefore see it as a mining-and-preparation activity for lead ore, open across all listed scales and PMA-open nationally and in Bali under the record's stated moratorium logic. The substance is industrial and specific, while the registration picture is unusually direct because the record itself does not force a Bali exception.

editorial.headline: Bauxite Ore Mining With a Clear National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 07293 covers bauxite ore mining and holding, open to every business scale and fully open to foreign ownership under the record supplied.
editorial.body:
KBLI 07293 is a mining classification for **bauxite ore**. In plain English, the activity is not trading, processing, or manufacturing aluminium products; it is the extraction and holding of bauxite ore itself. The Indonesian scope is brief but firm: it covers mining activities and the penampungan, or holding and storage, of bauxite ore. The same scope text also names the mining-permit terrain attached to the activity: IUPK Exploration and extension of the IUP Production Operation stage.

The scale profile is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** businesses, so the classification is not confined to one size of operator. A founder reading it should understand the scale line as a registration-access signal, not as a promise that every scale will face the same operational reality. The activity remains mining, and the supplied scope points to a sector where exploration and production-operation status matter because the record itself names them.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is straightforward: the PMA status is **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. There is no partial cap in the record. On the supplied facts, a foreign-owned company is not being told to stop at a minority or capped stake; the classification is open at full foreign ownership under the cited national source, **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**.

The Bali position is also clear, and it is important not to overstate the moratorium. Bali’s rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, but this record says KBLI 07293 is **not blocked** in Bali. The reason given is specific: OSS risk at the Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not caught by that moratorium. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: for this record, Bali is not showing a PMA moratorium block, while the activity remains one that should be read through its mining scope and risk classification rather than through a generic “easy registration” lens.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is therefore clean: for this record, Bali is not showing a PMA moratorium block.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

editorial.headline: Copper Ore Mining, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A clear reading of copper ore mining as a KBLI activity: broad scale access, full foreign ownership nationally, and no Bali moratorium block on the record provided.
editorial.body:
Copper ore mining under this activity is not a generic metals label. The scope points to the extraction of copper ore itself, including chalcocite and rock formations described as a mixture of monticellite and copper skarn. In plain English, this is the mining activity attached to copper-bearing mineral deposits, not downstream trading, fabrication, or general industrial handling. The record also ties the activity to mining-authorisation language: an IUPK Exploration and an extension of an IUP at the production-operation stage. That makes the centre of gravity clear: this is an upstream mining code, with exploration and production-stage continuity sitting inside the official scope.

The registration profile is unusually broad on paper. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, which means the slim record does not limit the code to large operators only. That does not make the activity administratively simple; it simply says the code is available across the listed business scales. The foreign-investment reading is also direct: the national PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no partial foreign cap in the data supplied here. For a foreign-owned company reading the record nationally, the formal signal is full openness under the cited investment-regulation source.

The Bali question is where many activities become more complicated, but this record does not show a current PMA registration block in Bali. The Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record is specific: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. This activity, on the record provided, does not fall into that blocked lane for the stated large-scale risk reading. The honest conclusion is therefore not that Bali is closed to this code; it is that the Bali moratorium does not block it on the data shown.

That distinction matters. Nationally, the activity is foreign-open up to 100% ownership. In Bali, the supplied record says it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium because of the risk level attached at Besar scale. A founder should read that as a narrow but important clearance: the code stands open in the investment classification and is not stopped by the Bali Low and Medium-Low PMA moratorium. The remaining seriousness lies in the activity itself: copper ore mining is a regulated mining activity, and this editorial cannot add obligations, thresholds, timelines, permits, or capital assumptions beyond the slim record. On this record alone, the story is clean: a copper ore mining activity, available across all listed scales, fully open to foreign ownership nationally, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the moratorium described.

editorial.headline: Nickel Ore Mining, Open Nationally and Not Moratorium-Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 07295 covers nickel ore mining and preparation, open across all business scales with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali PMA moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
KBLI 07295 is the activity line for **nickel ore mining and preparation**. The slim record describes it in direct terms: it covers mining activity and the preparation of nickel ore. That makes the code industrial and upstream in character, centred on extracting the ore and readying it within the mining activity itself, rather than describing downstream manufacturing or trading. The record also places the activity beside two mining-business terms: IUPK Exploration and extension of an IUP at the Production Operation stage. Those terms are part of the record’s own scope note, so they should be read as context for the kind of mining activity this classification is designed to hold.

The registration scale picture is unusually broad. The record marks this activity as open to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**. In plain English, it is not reserved in the slim record for one narrow size of operator. A small registered business and a large registered business sit in the same scale list, though the activity itself remains defined by nickel ore mining and preparation. That distinction matters: the scale field tells us who the classification is open to by size category, while the scope field tells us what the classification actually covers. This code should not be stretched beyond that mining-and-preparation perimeter.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clear. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the maximum foreign ownership value is **100%**, with the source stated as **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. There is no foreign share cap below full ownership in the slim record. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national classification data does not impose a reduced foreign-equity ceiling for this activity. The clean reading is therefore simple: at national level, KBLI 07295 is open to PMA, up to full foreign ownership.

The Bali reading is also explicit, and it is important not to overcomplicate it. The record says **l4_bali_blocked** is false and gives the Bali status as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**. The reason is that the OSS risk at **Besar** scale is **Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi**, so it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, permanently; this activity is not captured by that block according to the provided status and reason. The honest conclusion is that KBLI 07295 is nationally foreign-open and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is that KBLI 07295 is nationally foreign-open and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity

moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices

editorial.headline: Manganese Ore Mining With a Clear National and Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 07296 covers manganese ore mining and preparation, open across all business scales and nationally available to foreign ownership up to the recorded ceiling.
editorial.body:
KBLI 07296 is a compact but weighty classification: it covers the mining and preparation of manganese ore. In plain English, this is the activity of extracting manganese-bearing ore and getting it ready within the mining chain. The Indonesian scope is narrow enough to be useful: it does not describe downstream manufacturing, trading, or a broad metals business. It is about the mineral activity itself, and the preparatory work attached to that ore.

The record also names two mining-administration references inside the scope: **Izin Usaha Pertambangan Khusus (IUPK) Eksplorasi** and **Perpanjangan IUP Tahap Operasi Produksi**. Those names matter because they show the classification sitting in a serious regulated-mining context, not a generic small-business category. But the record does not give thresholds, timelines, licence sequencing, capital rules, or technical requirements, so none should be inferred. For founders and investors, the clean reading is simply that this KBLI is for manganese ore mining and preparation, with the listed mining references attached to the activity scope.

On scale, the classification is unusually broad in the slim record: it is open to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**. That means the activity is not presented here as limited to one business-size lane. The practical editorial point is that the scale field should not be confused with the ownership field. A code can be open across scales while still needing a separate reading on foreign ownership and Bali registration status. For KBLI 07296, the national PMA position is clear: the status is **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling recorded as **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. There is no partial cap in the slim record; the recorded ceiling is full foreign ownership.

The Bali reading is also clear, and it is not a hidden block. The Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the record states that it is **not blocked by the moratorium** because the OSS risk at **Besar** scale is **Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi**. That is the decisive distinction. Bali’s provincial moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, but this record places the activity outside that blocked lane. So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is straightforward: nationally, this manganese ore mining activity is open to PMA up to 100%; in Bali, the slim record does not mark it as blocked by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest national-vs-Bali picture is straightforward: nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and not marked as blocked by Bali’s moratorium.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan pertambangan bahan galian lainnya yang tidak mengandung bijih besi yang belum termasuk kelompok 07291 s.d. 07296, seperti bijih seng, platinum, silikon, litium, berilium, magnesium, kalium, kalsium, bismut, molibdenum, raksa, wolfram/tungsten, titanium, vanadium, kromit, antimoni, kobalt, tantalum, kadmium, galium, indium, yitrium, magnetit, niobium, zirkonium, ilmenit, krom, sesium, hafnium, skandium, rutenium, selenium, telurida, strontium, germanium, dan senotim.

Salinan Kartu Tanda Penduduk (KTP) untuk orang perseorangan atau salinan Kartu Tanda Penduduk (KTP) seluruh pengurus beserta susunan pengurus untuk koperasi
Surat keterangan dari kelurahan/desa setempat yang menyatakan seluruh pengurus koperasi atau orang perseorangan pemohon beserta seluruh pekerjanya merupakan penduduk setempat

  1. Mematuhi ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan dibidang lingkungan hidup serta keselamatan pertambangan. (untuk badan usaha Perseorangan), atau;

editorial.headline: KBLI 07299 Covers the Minerals That Sit Outside the Obvious Boxes
editorial.standfirst: A broad mining classification for non-iron-bearing mineral materials, open nationally to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 07299 is a wide, technical home for mining activity involving other non-iron-bearing mineral materials. In plain English, it covers the extraction of minerals that are not iron ore and are not otherwise captured by a more specific mineral-mining classification. The record gives a long mineral field: zinc ore, platinum, silicon, lithium, beryllium, magnesium, potassium, calcium, bismuth, molybdenum, mercury, tungsten, titanium, vanadium, chromite, antimony, cobalt, tantalum, cadmium, gallium, indium, yttrium, magnetite, niobium, zirconium, ilmenite, chromium, cesium, hafnium, scandium, ruthenium, selenium, telluride, strontium, germanium, and xenotime. That list matters because the code is not a generic trading or consultancy label; it is about the mining of named mineral materials with industrial, technological, or strategic uses.

The scope note also names **Izin Usaha Pertambangan Khusus (IUPK) Eksplorasi** and **Perpanjangan IUP Tahap Operasi Produksi**. The editorial point is not to add a licensing theory beyond the record, but to recognise the character of the activity: this is a mining-sector classification, not a light commercial wrapper. A founder choosing it should be describing real mining activity over the covered mineral materials, with the scale and risk profile that such activity naturally carries in the OSS reading reflected by the record.

On scale, the code is unusually broad: it is open to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**. That means the classification is not reserved only for large-scale operators in the record; it can appear across the stated business scales. But the foreign-investment reading is equally important. Nationally, KBLI 07299 is marked **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%** under the cited presidential regulations. There is no partial foreign cap in the record, so the clean national reading is that a PMA structure may use this activity with full foreign ownership.

The Bali picture is also clean, but for a different reason than a casual reader might assume. The Bali moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. This code is **not** blocked in Bali because the OSS risk at **Besar** scale is **Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi**, so it falls outside that moratorium block. The honest conclusion is therefore not “nationally open but Bali blocked”; it is that KBLI 07299 is nationally foreign-open and, on the record provided, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali, while still belonging to a higher-risk mining context rather than a low-risk activity.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 07299 is nationally foreign-open and, on the record provided, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity

Pemegang IPR:

  1. Melakukan kegiatan Penambangan dalam jangka waktu paling lambat 3 (tiga) bulan setelah IPR diterbitkan;
  2. Menyusun rencana Penambangan berdasarkan dokumen pengelolaan WPR yang disusun oleh Menteri, yang meliputi: metode penambangan, peralatan dan perlengkapan yang digunakan, jadwal kerja, kebutuhan personil, dan biaya atau permodalan; 
  3. Mematuhi persyaratan teknis pertambangan, antara lain:
    1. Tidak menggunakan bahan peledak;
    2. Tidak menggunakan bahan berbahaya beracun yang dilarang sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
    3. Tidak melakukan kegiatan penambangan dengan menggunakan metode penambangan bawah tanah bagi orang perseorangan; dan
    4. Menerapkan kaidah teknis pertambangan yang baik khususnya pengelolaan lingkungan dan keselamatan pertambangan

Membayar IPERA

Pemegang IPR:

  1. Melakukan kegiatan Penambangan dalam jangka waktu paling lambat 3 (tiga) bulan setelah IPR diterbitkan;
  2. Menyusun rencana Penambangan berdasarkan dokumen pengelolaan WPR yang disusun oleh Menteri, yang meliputi: metode penambangan, peralatan dan perlengkapan yang digunakan, jadwal kerja, kebutuhan personil, dan biaya atau permodalan; 
  3. Mematuhi persyaratan teknis pertambangan, antara lain:
    1. Tidak menggunakan bahan peledak;
    2. Tidak menggunakan bahan berbahaya beracun yang dilarang sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
    3. Tidak melakukan kegiatan penambangan dengan menggunakan metode penambangan bawah tanah bagi orang perseorangan; dan
    4. Menerapkan kaidah teknis pertambangan yang baik khususnya pengelolaan lingkungan dan keselamatan pertambangan

editorial.headline: Decorative and Building Stone Quarrying, With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 08101 covers quarrying and basic processing of decorative and building stone, open nationally to all business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 08101 is a quarrying classification for decorative stone and building stone. Its scope is not a broad construction label; it is tied to the extraction of named stone materials, including marble, andesite, paras, obsidian, and granite. The record also brings the immediate quarry-side handling into the same frame: breaking, separating, and cleaning the stone are part of the activity as described. In plain English, this is the code for taking these building and ornamental stones from the ground and preparing them at the basic material stage, before they become architectural finishes, structural inputs, or traded stone products.

That scope matters because it gives the code a practical industrial character. A founder using this classification is not simply describing design, retail, contracting, or trading activity. The centre of gravity is extraction, with associated first-stage processing. The Indonesian wording also names the extension of an IUP for the rock production-operation stage and an individual IPR application within the slim record’s scope text. Those references should be read carefully and only as part of the stated record: they signal the mining-administration context around the activity, without turning this editorial into a permit checklist or adding obligations that are not provided here.

Nationally, the code is marked **TERBUKA** for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. That is the clean national reading: foreign investment is not capped below full ownership in the record, and the stated source is **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. The classification is also open across all listed scales: **Mikro**, **Kecil**, **Menengah**, and **Besar**. So the business scale signal is unusually broad in the record. It is not confined to a single small-business category, nor reserved only for larger operators; the slim record lists the full scale range.

The Bali picture is also clear, and it is less restrictive than many founders might expect from the island-wide moratorium rule. Bali’s rule, as stated in the record, blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province on a permanent basis. But this code is not marked as blocked: **l4_bali_blocked** is false, and the Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**. The record’s reason is specific: at **Besar** scale the OSS risk is **Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi**, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. The honest lede, therefore, is not that a foreigner is shut out of Bali. It is that this nationally open, 100% PMA classification remains available in Bali under the record’s stated risk-and-moratorium reading.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest lede is not that a foreigner is shut out of Bali; this nationally open, 100% PMA classification remains available under the record’s stated risk-and-moratorium reading.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices

Pemegang IPR:

  1. Melakukan kegiatan Penambangan dalam jangka waktu paling lambat 3 (tiga) bulan setelah IPR diterbitkan;
  2. Menyusun rencana Penambangan berdasarkan dokumen pengelolaan WPR yang disusun oleh Menteri, yang meliputi: metode penambangan, peralatan dan perlengkapan yang digunakan, jadwal kerja, kebutuhan personil, dan biaya atau permodalan; 
  3. Mematuhi persyaratan teknis pertambangan, antara lain:
    1. Tidak menggunakan bahan peledak;
    2. Tidak menggunakan bahan berbahaya beracun yang dilarang sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
    3. Tidak melakukan kegiatan penambangan dengan menggunakan metode penambangan bawah tanah bagi orang perseorangan; dan
    4. Menerapkan kaidah teknis pertambangan yang baik khususnya pengelolaan lingkungan dan keselamatan pertambangan

  3. Mematuhi persyaratan teknis pertambangan, antara lain:
    1. Tidak menggunakan bahan peledak;
    2. Tidak menggunakan bahan berbahaya beracun yang dilarang sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
    3. Tidak melakukan kegiatan penambangan dengan menggunakan metode penambangan bawah tanah bagi orang perseorangan; dan
    4. Menerapkan kaidah teknis pertambangan yang baik khususnya pengelolaan lingkungan dan keselamatan pertambangan

editorial.headline: Limestone Quarrying With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers limestone extraction and processing, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block under the record’s stated risk position.
editorial.body:
KBLI 08102 is the quarrying activity for limestone, known in Indonesian practice as batu kapur or gamping. Its scope is not limited to taking stone out of the ground. The record includes the immediate preparation work that makes quarried limestone usable: breaking, crushing, screening, and grinding. In plain business terms, this is the activity of extracting limestone and reducing it into workable material, rather than selling a finished construction service or manufacturing a downstream product.

The scope text also identifies extension activity for operation-production stage IUP in rock, and extension activity for operation-production stage IUP in certain non-metallic minerals. Those phrases matter because they place this code inside a quarrying and mineral-material context, not a generic trading or building-material retail category. The editorial point is narrow but important: the code is about the extraction and physical preparation of limestone itself. Anyone registering it should be looking at an upstream quarrying profile, where the core business is the source material and its primary mechanical processing.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, which means the activity is not framed only as a large industrial operation in the slim record. A small quarrying operator and a larger corporate operator both sit inside the same activity description, provided the actual business remains within the recorded scope. Nationally, the foreign-investment position is also clear: PMA status is TERBUKA, and the recorded foreign ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no partial cap to soften or explain; under this record, the national ceiling is full foreign ownership.

The Bali reading is the practical one founders will care about. The province’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this record is not marked as blocked. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: a foreign investor looking at this limestone quarrying activity is not facing the Bali PMA moratorium block on the facts given here. That does not add any licence, timeline, tax, land, or capital assumption; it simply reads the record as written.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is therefore clean: a foreign investor looking at this limestone quarrying activity is not facing the Bali PMA moratorium block on the facts given here.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

Membayar IPERA

Pemegang IPR:

  1. Melakukan kegiatan Penambangan dalam jangka waktu paling lambat 3 (tiga) bulan setelah IPR diterbitkan;
  2. Menyusun rencana Penambangan berdasarkan dokumen pengelolaan WPR yang disusun oleh Menteri, yang meliputi: metode penambangan, peralatan dan perlengkapan yang digunakan, jadwal kerja, kebutuhan personil, dan biaya atau permodalan; 
  3. Mematuhi persyaratan teknis pertambangan, antara lain:
    1. Tidak menggunakan bahan peledak;
    2. Tidak menggunakan bahan berbahaya beracun yang dilarang sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
    3. Tidak melakukan kegiatan penambangan dengan menggunakan metode penambangan bawah tanah bagi orang perseorangan; dan
    4. Menerapkan kaidah teknis pertambangan yang baik khususnya pengelolaan lingkungan dan keselamatan pertambangan

editorial.headline: Gravel Extraction With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers gravel excavation and processing, open across business scales and nationally open to full foreign ownership, without a Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 08103 is a materials activity, not a trading label.** Its scope is the physical work of excavating gravel, then cleaning and separating it so the output can be used as a defined mineral product. The record describes the products in concrete terms: sandstone, hard boulders, and gravelly sand. That makes the code relevant where the business activity is tied to quarrying and preparing these stone materials, rather than simply reselling construction inputs or managing a downstream supply chain.

The record also places the activity in the administrative world of rock-mining operations, with references to an extension of an IUP for the rock production-operation stage and an individual IPR application. Those phrases matter because they show the activity is treated as a regulated extraction field in the source record. They should not be inflated into extra requirements here: the slim record gives the activity labels, the business scales, and the ownership position, but it does not give a separate checklist of permits, timelines, capital levels, tax treatment, or operating thresholds.

For business scale, the opening is unusually broad. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. In plain English, the record does not reserve this activity only for large companies, nor does it limit the classification to small local operators. A founder reading the scale field should understand that the activity can sit at any of those registered sizes, provided the actual business matches the substance of the scope: gravel excavation, cleaning, separation, and the stated stone outputs.

The national foreign-investment picture is also direct. The PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Because the ceiling is not below full ownership, the record does not describe a capped foreign stake. The Bali position is the important second check: the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says it is not blocked because OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. Bali’s moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, but this activity is not caught by that block on the record supplied. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: nationally open to PMA, full foreign ownership indicated, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the supplied Bali moratorium analysis.

editorial.headline: Sand Extraction, Open Nationally and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the excavation, cleaning, and separation of sand, with a national PMA opening that remains usable in Bali under the recorded risk position.
editorial.body:
**Sand extraction under this activity is not a vague trading label.** It is the physical work of digging sand, then cleaning and separating it into usable forms. The record names concrete outputs: concrete sand, masonry sand with only a small soil content, fill sand with a larger soil content, and other sand products. That makes the activity operationally grounded: it is about extracting and preparing material, not merely brokering, storing, or reselling it.

The scope also reaches sand excavation, cleaning, and separation at sea, but only within the boundaries stated in the record. It covers marine locations outside port working areas, port interest areas, special terminals, mining business permit areas, shipping lanes, and the core zones of conservation areas except where conservation-area management is provided for in spatial or zoning plans. The same record also references the extension of a rock production-operation mining business permit stage, so the classification sits in a regulated extraction context rather than in ordinary low-friction commerce.

On who may register it, the national picture is broad. The activity is marked **TERBUKA** for PMA, with a foreign ownership ceiling of **100%**. It is also open across the stated business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In plain English, the slim record does not describe a partial foreign cap here; it records a full foreign-ownership ceiling nationally, and it does not restrict the available registration scale to only large operators.

The Bali position is the important practical nuance. The record does not say this activity is blocked for PMA in Bali. Its Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The moratorium rule itself is still real and island-wide: Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. But this record places the relevant Bali reading outside that blocked bucket. For a foreign-owned setup, the honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: nationally this activity is open to PMA up to 100%, and in Bali it is not recorded as blocked by the moratorium under the supplied risk note.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally this activity is open to PMA up to 100%, and in Bali it is not recorded as blocked by the moratorium under the supplied risk note.
