Kelompok ini juga mencakup kegiatan pengurusan hasil sampingan, seperti produksi kulit dan jangat dari tempat pemotongan hewan dan peternakan/fellmongery, penjemuran tulang, pengolahan sisaan atau kotoran hewan, dan pembersihan lemak. Pemotongan babi yang dilakukan oleh pedagang dimasukkan dalam golongan 462 dan 472.

editorial.headline: Pig Slaughterhouse Operations, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10112 covers pig slaughterhouse work, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali PMA block under the record’s current risk reading.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 10112 is the business of operating a pig slaughterhouse.** The record defines it around the physical slaughterhouse sequence: slaughtering pigs, including wild pigs, then skinning, cleaning, and packing the meat. It is not written as a general meat-trading category or a broad food-service activity. Its centre of gravity is the controlled handling of animals and meat at the slaughter point, plus the immediate preparation that turns the slaughtered animal into packed meat.

The scope also reaches the less visible side of the slaughterhouse: the management of by-products. The record includes the production of hides and skins from slaughterhouses and farms or fellmongery, drying bones, processing animal remnants or waste, and cleaning fat. That matters because this code is not only about the main cut of meat leaving the facility. It captures the full industrial logic of the slaughterhouse floor, including the materials and residues generated by the work itself.

On scale, the record is unusually clear: this activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. In practical editorial terms, the code is not reserved in the record for only one size of enterprise. A small operator and a larger facility both sit within the same activity description, provided the registered business is truly doing the slaughterhouse and associated handling described in the scope. The wording supports a business model built around slaughtering, cleaning, packing, and by-product management, rather than a model that merely buys and sells meat elsewhere.

The national foreign-investment position is also direct. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with `pma_max_asing` at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. So the national reading is full foreign ownership: 100%. The Bali-side picture does not reverse that in this record. The Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`, `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the reason is explicit: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule still matters because Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, but this record does not place KBLI 10112 inside that block. The honest reading is therefore clean: nationally foreign-open, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record’s stated Bali risk rationale.

editorial.headline: Poultry Slaughterhouses With a Clean National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10113 covers the formal slaughter, cleaning, packing, and by-product handling of poultry meat, open nationally to PMA and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10113 is the activity code for a poultry slaughterhouse: the place where poultry is processed into meat through slaughtering, skinning, cleaning, and packing. The scope also reaches the less visible work that keeps the operation complete, including the handling of by-products such as processing poultry remains or droppings, stretching skin, sorting feathers, and cleaning fat. In plain English, this is not a retail description or a trading label; it is the operational classification for the slaughterhouse process itself.

The scale profile is broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the code is not confined to either neighborhood-scale operators or industrial facilities. That matters because the same activity can sit behind very different business models: a smaller local processing operation, a mid-sized supplier, or a larger meat-processing facility. The common thread is the underlying activity, not the commercial polish around it: poultry comes in, slaughterhouse work is performed, meat is cleaned and packed, and the associated by-products are managed as part of the same operational frame.

Nationally, the investment signal is straightforward. The code is marked **TERBUKA** for PMA, with `pma_max_asing` set at 100. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national record allows full foreign ownership, and the source named in the record is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no recorded national cap below full ownership, and no threshold, permit, timeline, tax treatment, or minimum capital figure appears in this slim record. The clean reading is therefore simple: at the national level, the activity is open to foreign investment up to 100%.

Bali does not change that picture into a hidden percentage cap. The Bali status is recorded as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and `l4_bali_blocked` is false. The reason is explicit: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, but this activity is not blocked under that rule. So the honest Bali-side conclusion is not a warning disguised as nuance: KBLI 10113 is nationally open to PMA and, on the record provided, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: A Clear National and Bali Opening for Other Animal Slaughterhouses
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10119 covers a specialised slaughterhouse activity that is nationally foreign-open and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10119 is a narrow but materially important slaughterhouse category. The activity is not about pigs, ruminants, or poultry; it sits with other animals named in the record, such as camels, rabbits, and whales. Its practical scope is the work of turning animals into packed meat: slaughtering, skinning, cleaning, and packing. The record also brings the downstream handling of by-products into view, including hides and skins from slaughterhouses and farms, fellmongery, bone drying, treatment of residues or animal waste, and fat cleaning.

That breadth matters because this is not merely a cutting-room label. It describes a facility and operating model where meat handling and by-product management belong to the same registered activity. A founder looking at this code should read it as an industrial and processing classification, not as a retail or trading shortcut. The record itself separates slaughterhouse activity from slaughtering performed by traders, and the editorial point is simple: this code is for the slaughterhouse operation and its attached handling of meat and by-products.

Nationally, the investment position is clean. The record marks the PMA status as **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. It is also open across the full scale range listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That combination gives this activity a broad national registration posture: small operators and larger industrial setups are both within the scale field, and foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership by the national PMA figure supplied here.

The Bali reading is also unusually direct. The record does **not** mark this activity as blocked for PMA registration in Bali. Its Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the stated reason is: **OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium**. The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this record places KBLI 10119 outside that blocked result. So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is not a contradiction: nationally open, fully foreign-open by the supplied ceiling, and not blocked in Bali on the Bali fields provided.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Meat Preservation at Industrial Breadth
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10120 covers the processing and preservation of meat products, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10120 is the activity code for turning meat into preserved or processed products. Its scope is broad: canning, smoking, salting, freezing, sweetening, irradiation with an irradiator, and similar preservation methods. It also reaches the production of frozen meat as carcasses, cuts, and individual portions, as well as dried, salted, and smoked meat. The record names finished meat products too: sausages, salami, pudding, andouilettes, saveloy, bologna, pates, rillettes, meatballs, and ham. It even includes whale-meat processing carried out on land or on a special vessel.

That breadth matters because this is not merely a retail or kitchen activity. The centre of gravity is transformation and preservation: changing raw meat into stable, packaged, frozen, cured, smoked, or otherwise processed goods. A founder using this code should therefore read it as a manufacturing and processing classification, not as a catch-all for every business that happens to use meat. The slim record also draws a boundary around the code by excluding ready-to-eat food made from meat and poultry, and soups containing meat, without making those excluded activities part of this classification.

On scale, the record is unusually inclusive. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. That means the classification can describe anything from a small processor producing preserved meat products to a larger plant handling frozen carcasses, portioned meat, or packaged processed meats. The record does not add a production threshold, licence condition, capital requirement, facility size, tax rule, or timeline, so none should be inferred. The only safe reading is that all four listed business scales are available under this code.

The national foreign-investment picture is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, so the national record permits full foreign ownership. Bali does not overturn that here. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, l4_bali_blocked is false, and the reason given is: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi -> not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this activity is not marked as blocked. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: nationally it is open, and in Bali it is not blocked for PMA registration on the record provided.

editorial.headline: Salted and Dried Fish Processing, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers preserved finfish and roe products, open across all business scales nationally, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record’s risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10211 is a food-processing activity, not a fishing activity. Its scope is the processing and preservation of finned fish through salting or drying, producing items such as salted tembang, salted anchovies, and plain dried fish. The same record also brings in the processing and preservation of salmon eggs or roes, caviar, and caviar substitutes. In plain English, this is the industrial or business-side treatment of fish and fish roe into preserved products whose identity comes from salt, drying, or comparable preservation within the recorded scope.

The registration picture is broad at the national level. The record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale businesses. That matters because the code is not reserved in the record for one narrow size of operator: it can describe a small producer working with a defined preserved-fish line, a medium processor, or a larger operation dealing in the same category of salted, dried, or roe-based products. The editorial point is discipline: the scale tells us who can register the activity, while the scope tells us what the activity is. It does not turn this code into a wider seafood licence, and it does not add activities that are not named in the record.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, sourced in the record to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For an investor reading only the national layer, this is a foreign-open activity with no lower percentage cap shown in the slim record. The correct national statement is therefore simple: the activity is open for PMA nationally, up to 100% foreign ownership, across the listed business scales.

Bali is the decisive caveat. The record says l4_bali_blocked is true, and gives the reason as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule in the record states that Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest practical reading is that a foreigner cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today, even though the same activity is nationally marked TERBUKA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. That is not a contradiction; it is the national-versus-Bali split this record is asking the reader to notice.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreigner sees a nationally open activity, but in Bali the record’s moratorium turns that opening into a blocked PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Frozen Fish Processing With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the freezing and preservation of finfish, from whole fish to cuts, and is nationally open to foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
This KBLI activity is about industrially preserving finfish through freezing. The record describes a processing activity that turns fish into frozen products such as frozen milkfish, tuna, skipjack, and snapper. It also makes clear that the fish may be frozen whole or after being cut into forms such as fillet, loin, saku, steak, chunk, or brown meat. In plain English, this is not a general seafood-trading label; it is the freezing and preservation of finfish as a food-processing activity.

The boundary matters. The slim record separates this activity from the narrower service of cooling fish with ice merely to keep it fresh. Here, freezing is the defining process, and preservation is the commercial purpose. That distinction gives the code its practical shape: it belongs to operators whose work changes fish into frozen inventory that can be stored, handled, and sold as frozen product, whether the input is a whole fish or a prepared cut.

The registration picture is broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale businesses, so it is not framed only for large processors. A small operator freezing cut fish and a larger facility producing frozen tuna or snapper both sit within the scale range described by the record, provided the actual activity remains the freezing and preservation of finfish. The editorial point is simple: scale affects the business form and operational reality, but the activity definition itself is anchored in the freezing process.

For foreign investors, the national position is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali does not add a separate percentage cap in this record. Just as importantly, the Bali-side status is not blocked: `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the stated reason is “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The honest reading is therefore straightforward: nationally open, fully foreign-open on the record, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the cited moratorium logic.

editorial.headline: Pemindangan Fish Processing Is Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM
editorial.standfirst: This fish-processing activity is open to all business scales, but it is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM — foreign ownership is 0% nationwide — and PMA registration in Bali is separately blocked under the province's low-risk moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the processing and preservation of finfish through **pemindangan**, the Indonesian boiling-and-salting preservation method associated in the record with products such as pindang bandeng or paso, pindang tongkol, pindang cue, pindang naya, pindang lemuru or tembang, pindang layang, and pindang cakalang. In plain English, it is a food-processing classification for businesses that turn finfish into preserved pindang products, not a general seafood-trading label and not a catch-all for every form of fish processing.

The scale picture is broad. The slim record opens the activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** businesses, which means it can describe anything from a very small pindang producer to a larger industrial operation, provided the registered activity is still the pemindangan-based processing and preservation of finfish described above. That matters because the classification is anchored in the production method and the resulting pindang product line. A company using this code should be able to recognise itself in that scope, rather than treating the title as a convenient umbrella for unrelated fish activities.

Nationally, the position is closed to foreign ownership. The record allocates this bidang usaha to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 10/2021 as amended by 49/2021 (Lampiran II, the *dialokasikan* column), which sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 0%. A PT PMA cannot hold this activity anywhere in Indonesia, at any business scale.

Bali adds a second restriction on top of the first. The record marks the activity as blocked in Bali, with the reason “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026”, under the province-wide rule that blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. Both restrictions apply at once, and only the second is provincial: registering in another province would not open the national allocation.

editorial.headline: Fermented Fish Processing, With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10215 covers fermented fish preservation and fish-based condiments, open nationally to all business scales and not blocked for PMA in Bali under the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10215 is a focused food-processing activity: the treatment and preservation of finfish through fermentation. The record names familiar product forms rather than abstract industrial language: fermented fish such as ikan peda and ikan kayu, plus fish sauce and fish terasi. In plain English, this is the category for businesses that turn fish into preserved, fermented products where time, salt, process control, and handling transform the raw material into a stable food ingredient or finished condiment.

That makes the activity broader than one product line but still tightly bounded. It is not a general seafood-trading category and not a catch-all for every marine product. Its centre of gravity is processing and preservation, specifically by fermentation, and specifically for finfish and fish-derived fermented outputs named in the scope. A founder choosing this activity should read the scope as a production classification: the business is making or preserving these fish-based fermented goods, not merely branding them, distributing them, or operating a restaurant that happens to serve them.

The registration picture is unusually clean in the slim record. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the classification is not limited to one enterprise size. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That means the record presents KBLI 10215 as nationally open to foreign ownership up to the full stated ceiling. There is no lower percentage in the record, and there is no separate Bali ownership cap to add on top of it.

editorial.headline: Surimi Processing with a Clear Bali Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10216 covers fish mincing and grinding into minced fish meat or surimi, open across all business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10216 is a narrow but important food-processing activity: the processing and preservation of finned fish through mincing or grinding the fish meat to produce minced fish meat or surimi. Its character is not retail, capture, cold storage, or general seafood trade. The recorded scope points to transformation: fish flesh is worked mechanically into a prepared intermediate or product form, with preservation sitting inside that same processing frame.

That makes the code relevant for operators whose business identity is built around fish meat preparation rather than simply handling fish as a commodity. The record opens the activity to every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practical editorial terms, this means the classification is not reserved only for industrial plants or only for small local processors. A micro or small operator can sit inside the same activity definition as a larger processor, so long as the registered activity remains the processing and preservation of finned fish through mincing or grinding into minced fish meat or surimi.

The national foreign-investment picture is clean. The slim record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower percentage in the record, and there is no special national caveat supplied here. The responsible reading is therefore straightforward: nationally, this activity is open to PMA ownership up to the recorded 100% ceiling.

Bali does not change that into a hidden percentage cap. The Bali-side field is not a second ownership calculation; it is a registration-status screen. Here, l4_bali_blocked is false and the status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason given is specific: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, but this activity is recorded as not blocked by that rule. The honest national-versus-Bali conclusion is therefore unusually simple: KBLI 10216 is nationally foreign-open up to 100%, and the record does not mark it as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Canned Fish Processing Built for Every Scale
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10217 covers airtight canned fish processing, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record supplied.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10217 is a manufacturing code for the processing and preservation of fish through airtight packaging or canning, supported by retort or pasteurisation. In practical terms, the activity is the industrial transformation of fish into shelf-stable canned products such as canned sardines, canned lemuru, canned mackerel, and canned tuna. The record also brings one important boundary into view: a fish-processing vessel belongs here only when it processes and preserves fish in cans without carrying out the catching activity itself.

That makes the code less about fishing as an extraction activity and more about controlled food processing. The defining act is not landing fish, trading fish, or operating a mixed capture-and-processing business. It is the preservation process: airtight containment, thermal treatment, and the production of canned fish goods. For founders, that distinction matters because the business identity sits in the processing line, the packaging method, and the final canned product.

The scale picture is broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the code can describe anything from a small formal processor to a large canning operation, provided the activity remains within the stated scope. Nationally, the PMA position is also clear: the code is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100%. On the supplied record, there is no national foreign-share cap below full ownership.

The Bali reading is equally important, and here the honest conclusion is clean rather than dramatic. In Bali, the record leaves this activity unblocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, while the Bali status remains OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which means it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium described in the record. That moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this record places KBLI 10217 outside that blocked result. For a foreign-owned setup, the national and Bali readings therefore point in the same direction: this canned fish processing activity is nationally open, and the record does not block PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Surimi-Based Fish Processing Is Open Nationally and in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers fish mince and surimi processing into prepared foods, with access across all business scales and no Bali PMA moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10218 is about turning fish-based mince or surimi into further processed products. The slim record defines the activity as processing and preserving fish based on lumatan or surimi, then carrying it into foods such as bakso, nuget, otak-otak, kamaboko, sosis, pempek, siomai, dimsum, cikuwa, and imitation crab sticks. In plain English, this is not a raw-fish trading activity and not a general restaurant category. It sits in the manufacturing space where fish material is shaped, preserved, and transformed into recognizable prepared products.

That scope matters because the commercial profile can range from small prepared-food production to larger industrial processing. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. A founder reading this should therefore treat the code as scale-flexible: it is not written only for a household-size operation, and it is not reserved only for a large factory. The same activity description can support different operating sizes, as long as the registered business is genuinely doing the fish-based processing and preservation described in the record.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the listed maximum foreign ownership is 100%. That means the national record does not impose a foreign-shareholding cap below full foreign ownership for this activity. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 is the record's cited basis for that national position. Nothing in the slim record adds a minimum capital figure, special licence, quota, timeline, or separate approval condition, so those points should not be inferred from the activity code itself.

The Bali reading is also straightforward, but for a different reason. The record marks Bali as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with l4_bali_blocked set to false. Its reason is: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently; this record says the code is not caught by that block. The honest conclusion is therefore simple: on the information provided here, this fish-processing activity is nationally open to PMA and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: The Broad, Practical Edge of Fish Processing
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10219 covers specialised fish processing and preservation methods that sit beyond standard handling, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10219 is for fish processing and preservation work that uses other methods within the record’s stated scope. In plain English, it captures specialised handling of finfish after capture: processing or preserving fish on vessels used only for that purpose, producing fish meal for human consumption or animal feed, making meal and soluble meal from fish that cannot be eaten by humans, preparing fish-meal concentrate, cutting fish into filet, loin, saku, steak, and chunk where freezing is not part of the process, and using radiation through an irradiator as a preservation method.

That makes this activity less about retail seafood and more about industrial transformation. The record points to operations that change the condition, form, or shelf-life of fish before the product moves onward. Some are food-facing, such as non-frozen cuts or fish meal for human consumption. Others are input-facing, such as animal-feed fish meal or products made from fish unsuitable for human consumption. The common thread is not a single product but a processing logic: fish is being preserved, reduced, concentrated, cut, or otherwise prepared through methods covered by this entry.

The registration picture is broad on scale. The slim record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the code is not framed around one size of operator. A small processor cutting finfish without freezing and a larger facility making fish-meal concentrate both sit within the scale range stated in the record, provided the actual activity matches the scope. The important discipline is to stay inside what the code says: this is finfish processing and preservation by the listed or comparable methods, not a general licence for every seafood activity or every frozen-processing workflow.

The national-versus-Bali picture is unusually clean. Nationally, the record marks the PMA status as TERBUKA and gives the foreign-ownership ceiling as 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For Bali, the record does not mark the activity as blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the reason given is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. The moratorium rule itself remains important because Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently; here, however, the slim record’s Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The honest reading is therefore direct: for this activity, the record shows national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block.

editorial.headline: Salted and Dried Aquatic Products, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers salting or drying crustaceans, mollusks, echinoderms, and other aquatic biota, with full national PMA openness but a Bali registration block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10291 is about a specific, traditional form of aquatic-product preservation: processing crustaceans, mollusks, echinoderms, and other aquatic biota by salting or drying. The record’s scope points to products such as salted shrimp, salted squid, ebi, salted jellyfish, salted cuttlefish, dried sea cucumber, and dried cuttlefish. The centre of gravity is not fishing, trading, cold storage, or restaurant service. It is the transformation and preservation of aquatic material through salt or drying into stable products.

For operators, the scale picture is unusually broad. The activity is open to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** scales, so the code can describe anything from a very small producer to a larger processing operation, provided the activity remains within the recorded scope. That breadth matters because the same activity can appear artisanal in one context and industrial in another, yet the KBLI record still frames it by the processing method and product category: salted or dried aquatic biota.

Nationally, the PMA reading is clean. The record marks the activity as **TERBUKA**, with **pma_max_asing** at **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. In plain English, the national classification does not itself cap foreign ownership below full ownership for this activity. A foreign-owned company looking only at the national PMA line would see an activity that is open, not conditional or partially capped.

Bali is the decisive complication. The same record marks **l4_bali_blocked** as true and gives the reason: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks **ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA**, island-wide and permanent. So the honest reading is this: although KBLI 10291 is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, a foreigner cannot register this activity for PMA in Bali today under the Bali-side status recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is that KBLI 10291 is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but blocked for PMA registration in Bali today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Smoked and Roasted Aquatic Biota, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers smoked or roasted non-fish aquatic products, with national PMA openness offset by a Bali PMA block under the provincial risk moratorium.
editorial.body:
This KBLI activity is about a very specific processing craft: preserving and preparing aquatic biota other than ordinary fish through smoking or roasting. The record names crustaceans, molluscs, echinoderms, and other aquatic organisms, with examples such as smoked or roasted squid and smoked or roasted sea cucumber. The commercial identity of the activity is therefore not seafood trading, restaurant service, or general food manufacturing in the abstract. It is the transformation and preservation of aquatic raw material by heat and smoke, producing a finished smoked or roasted product.

That narrowness matters. A founder reading this code should see a processing activity, not a broad licence to operate across the whole seafood chain. The slim record points to production work: taking qualifying aquatic biota and applying smoking or roasting as the preservation method. It also shows that the activity is not reserved to one business size. The scales open to it are Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so the code can describe anything from a small producer to a larger processing operation, as long as the underlying activity stays within the recorded scope.

Nationally, the record is straightforward: PMA status is marked TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100. In plain English, the national investment list treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to 100%, with the cited national source being Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That is the first half of the picture, and it is important because it means the national entry is not the obstacle. On the national record alone, a foreign-owned setup is not capped below full ownership.

Bali is the decisive second half. The Bali-side field says l4_bali_blocked is true, and the reason is stated as: OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026. The moratorium rule in the record is also direct: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent). So the honest conclusion is simple but uncomfortable: a foreigner cannot register this PMA activity in Bali today, even though the same activity is nationally open. The contradiction is not in the scope of the activity; it is in the layer of administration. Nationally open does not mean Bali-registerable when the provincial moratorium blocks the risk class.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreigner cannot register this PMA activity in Bali today, even though the same activity is nationally open.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Frozen Aquatic Biota Processing, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers the freezing and preservation of non-finned aquatic biota, from shrimp and crab to cephalopods and shellfish, across every business scale.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 10293 is a processing activity, not a simple cold-holding activity.** Its centre of gravity is the preservation of crustaceans, molluscs, echinoderms, and other aquatic biota through freezing. The record points to finished frozen products: frozen shrimp, frozen frog legs, frozen cephalopods such as squid, cuttlefish, and octopus, frozen crab and swimming crab, and frozen shellfish. In plain English, this is the industrial freezing of non-finned aquatic biota into commercial frozen goods.

The record also draws an important boundary around the activity. This is not merely a service that keeps aquatic biota fresh with ice. The registered activity is deeper than temporary chilling: it is freezing as a preservation and processing step, producing frozen aquatic products rather than only maintaining freshness in transit or storage. That distinction matters for founders because the business identity should follow the real operating model: a processor preserving aquatic biota by freezing, not a generic cold-service operator.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the activity can describe anything from a small processor handling a focused product line to a larger cold-processing operation working across several types of aquatic biota. The substance remains the same across those scales: the registered activity is tied to freezing and preservation of non-finned aquatic biota, with the scope explicitly covering all industries of cooling or icing aquatic biota other than finned fish.

The national foreign-investment picture is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with the record citing Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the source. Bali does not add a separate ownership percentage in this record, and it would be wrong to invent one. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The moratorium rule still matters as context because Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, but this record says the activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The honest reading is therefore straightforward: nationally foreign-open, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the record provided.

editorial.headline: Boiling and Preserving Other Aquatic Biota Under KBLI 10294
editorial.standfirst: Nationally open to foreign ownership, this aquatic processing activity is still blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the province’s risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10294 covers a specific kind of food-processing activity: the processing and preservation of crustaceans, molluscs, echinoderms, and other aquatic biota through **pemindangan**, the Indonesian preservation method named in the record. It is not a general seafood category. The scope points to an industrial treatment of aquatic organisms other than ordinary fish, with the defining feature being the preservation process itself. For a founder, that makes the code less about retail, trading, or aquaculture, and more about the activity of transforming aquatic raw material into a preserved product.

The national record is straightforward. The activity is marked **TERBUKA**, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is **100%** under **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. The code is also open across the recorded business scales: **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, Besar**. In plain English, the national classification does not reserve this activity only for Indonesian ownership, and it does not confine it to one narrow size band. A small processor and a larger processing operation both sit within the scale range shown in the record, provided the registered activity is genuinely the processing and preservation described in the scope.

The Bali answer is materially different. The record marks the Bali status as **Blocked (risk class)**, with `l4_bali_blocked` set to true. Its stated reason is: **OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026**. The moratorium rule supplied in the record is wider than this one activity: **Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent)**. For this code, the practical editorial conclusion is therefore clear: a foreign-owned company may see a 100% national ceiling, but cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today according to the Bali-side fields in the record.

That distinction matters because the national headline alone would be misleading. KBLI 10294 is nationally open, and the ownership ceiling shown is complete foreign ownership. But Bali’s moratorium is not expressed here as a reduced foreign-share cap, a partnership requirement, or a negotiable local quota. The record gives only a blocked Bali status, a stated risk-class reason, and the governor-letter source. So the honest reading is precise: this is a nationally foreign-open aquatic biota processing code, available across all recorded scales, but blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the province’s Low and Medium-Low risk moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Fermented Aquatic Biota Processing With Full PMA Access
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers fermentation-based processing and preservation of aquatic biota, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 10295 sits in the world of fermentation-led aquatic processing: the transformation and preservation of crustaceans, molluscs, echinoderms, and other water biota into fermented products such as shrimp paste.** Its centre of gravity is not fishing, trading, or restaurant preparation, but the industrial act of processing and preserving aquatic material through fermentation. That makes the scope narrower and more technical than its plain title may first suggest: the defining feature is the method, and the record identifies fermentation as the process that gives the activity its character.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** operators, so it can describe a small producer as well as a larger processing operation, provided the registered business is truly doing the activity captured here. For founders, that matters because scale is not treated as a closed gate in the record. The code is not reserved only for a large factory, nor only for a small traditional producer. What matters is whether the real business activity matches the recorded scope: processing and preserving specified aquatic biota through fermentation, with shrimp paste given as the example product.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the recorded maximum foreign ownership is **100%**. In plain English, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to the full ceiling stated in the record. There is no partial cap in the slim record, and there is no separate condition to invent around it. The stated source is **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**, so the national picture should be read exactly as the record frames it: open, with a one-hundred-percent foreign-ownership ceiling.

The Bali picture is also clear, but it needs to be stated carefully. The record does include a Bali moratorium rule: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, under the cited governor letter. For this activity, however, the Bali block flag is **false** and the Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**. The reason given is precise: **"OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium"**. That means the honest national-vs-Bali reading is not a contradiction. Nationally, the activity is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, this record does not mark it as blocked by the moratorium. The right conclusion is therefore simple and disciplined: this is a fermentation-based aquatic processing activity that is nationally open to PMA, open across all recorded business scales, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali according to the slim record.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is simple: nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership, and not marked as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Milled Seafood Processing with a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10296 covers minced and ground aquatic-biota products, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10296 sits in a practical corner of Indonesia’s seafood-processing economy: the transformation and preservation of aquatic biota through milling or grinding. The record describes crustaceans, molluscs, echinoderms, and other aquatic biota being processed into products such as minced squid, minced shrimp, shrimp balls, squid balls, crab balls, and shrimp kaki naga. In plain English, this is not a fishing activity and not a restaurant category. It is a processing activity: taking aquatic raw material and turning it into shaped, minced, or ground-value products that can move through the food supply chain with a defined industrial identity.

The scale profile is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, which means it can describe anything from a very small formal processor to a larger production setup, as long as the activity remains within the recorded scope. That breadth matters editorially because the code is not limited to a single business size. A founder reading this should focus first on whether the actual activity is truly the milling, grinding, processing, and preservation of the listed aquatic biota products, rather than being distracted by brand format or sales channel.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives a pma_max_asing of 100, so the national reading is that it is foreign-open up to 100%. There is no lesser foreign-ownership ceiling in the slim record, and no additional capital threshold or special operating condition is stated here. The clean conclusion is therefore simple: at the national level, this is a fully open PMA activity according to the cited source field.

The Bali picture is also clean, but for a different reason. The record does not block the activity in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. Its reason is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” That matters because the moratorium rule in the record blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, while this activity is not caught by that block on the record presented. So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is not a hidden contradiction: KBLI 10296 is nationally foreign-open, and Bali is not marked as blocked for PMA registration in this slim record.

data.judul: Pengolahan dan Pengawetan Biota Air Lainnya dengan Pengalengan
data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan pengolahan dan pengawetan krustasea, moluska, ekinodermata, biota air lainnya melalui proses pengemasan kedap udara/airtight atau pengalengan yang disertai proses retort atau pasteurisasi yang menghasilkan produk seperti udang dalam kaleng, kerang dalam kaleng, cumi atau sotong dalam kaleng, dan kepiting atau rajungan dalam kaleng. Kegiatan kapal pengolah yang hanya melakukan pengolahan dan pengawetan biota air dalam kaleng (tanpa melakukan kegiatan penangkapan) termasuk dalam kelompok ini.

editorial.headline: Canned Aquatic Products That Stay Open in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10297 covers airtight, retorted or pasteurised canning of crustaceans, molluscs and other aquatic biota, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10297 is a processing code, not a catching code. Its centre of gravity is the transformation and preservation of aquatic biota through airtight packaging or canning, followed by retort or pasteurisation. The record names crustaceans, molluscs, echinoderms and other aquatic biota, and gives concrete examples: canned shrimp, canned shellfish, canned squid or cuttlefish, and canned crab or swimming crab. A processing vessel can also fall here when it only processes and preserves aquatic biota in cans, without carrying out fishing activity.

That distinction matters because the activity is defined by the method and output: sealed packaging, canning, heat treatment, and a shelf-stable aquatic product. The slim record does not add a separate permit, capital threshold, production quota or timeline, so none should be read into the classification. What it does say is enough to locate the business clearly: this is for operators whose registered activity is the canning and preservation of non-fish aquatic products in the forms described above.

On scale, the code is unusually broad. The record marks it as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. In plain English, the activity is not reserved only for one size of operator in the record: it can describe a small canning operation, a growing medium enterprise, or a large industrial processor, provided the actual activity remains within the recorded scope. The same scope also keeps the line clean for vessels used only as processing platforms, because the record expressly includes those when they do not conduct capture.

The national-vs-Bali picture is clean rather than conflicted. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a pma_max_asing of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For Bali, the record does not mark the activity as blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the stated reason is “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The Bali moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, but this entry is not caught by that block on the supplied record. For a foreign-owned setup, the honest reading is therefore straightforward: this code is nationally open up to the recorded ceiling, and the Bali status supplied here does not block PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Seaweed Processing With a Conditional Bali Gate
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10298 covers processing and preserving seaweed, nationally open to full foreign ownership but requiring careful Bali scope verification before PMA registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10298 is the activity code for processing and preserving seaweed. In plain terms, the record points to work that turns harvested seaweed into a processed form, especially drying it into dry seaweed, and also covers other seaweed-processing outputs within the stated scope. It is not a broad food-manufacturing category. Its editorial importance is more specific: it sits at the point where a raw coastal commodity becomes a tradable processed product.

The code is open across business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar all appear in the record as scales open to registration. That matters because the activity can describe very different operating realities, from small drying and preservation work to larger-scale processing. The scope, however, stays anchored in seaweed treatment and preservation. A founder using this code should therefore describe the actual processing activity precisely, because the Bali-side treatment in the record depends on the exact declared scope rather than on a generic reading of the title.

Nationally, the position is clear. The record marks PMA status as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In practical editorial English, that means the national foreign-ownership ceiling shown in the record is 100%. There is no lower ownership cap in the slim record, and no additional national threshold or capital condition is supplied here. The national story is therefore not the difficult part: this is a foreign-open activity at the national level, according to the data provided.

Bali is more nuanced. The record does not mark this code as outright blocked in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false. But the Bali status is Blocked (scope-dependent), and the reason says that OSS risk at scale Besar is low on some scopes but higher on others, making it registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope and verifying live OSS for the exact activity. That sits against the stated Bali moratorium rule: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest reading is conditional rather than casually open. Nationally, KBLI 10298 is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, the registration outcome depends on the exact seaweed-processing scope and its live OSS risk classification.

editorial.headline: Where Other Aquatic Processing Becomes an Industrial Activity
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10299 covers non-standard processing and preservation of aquatic biota, open nationally to PMA and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10299 sits in a very specific corner of Indonesia’s aquatic-processing economy: the treatment and preservation of crustaceans, molluscs, echinoderms, and other aquatic biota by methods outside the more ordinary named categories. The record gives examples that make the scope concrete rather than abstract: shrimp flour, shellfish flour, frog flour, and processing or preservation of other aquatic biota through radiation using an irradiator. This is not a general seafood-trading activity. It is a production and preservation classification for specialised aquatic inputs, including forms that may be intermediate materials rather than finished consumer products.

The activity is open across every business scale listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the code is not reserved in the record for one narrow enterprise size. A small processor and a larger industrial operator can both find a scale pathway here, provided the actual activity remains within the stated scope: processing and preserving the relevant aquatic biota by the methods described. The clean editorial test is practical: if the business is transforming or preserving those aquatic materials, including into flour-like outputs or by irradiation, this code is plausible; if the business is merely selling, farming, importing, or serving aquatic products, those facts are not supplied by this record and should not be folded into this classification.

Nationally, the PMA picture is straightforward. The record marks the code as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded here is 100%. There is no lower foreign-share cap in the slim record, and none should be invented. For a foreign-owned setup, the important point is that the national investment list does not close this activity to PMA on the information provided here.

Bali is also clear, but for a different reason. The province’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, according to the stated governor-letter source. This code, however, is not marked as blocked in Bali. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. That does not create a separate Bali ownership percentage, partnership rule, or quota. It simply means the record does not block PMA registration in Bali under the moratorium logic supplied here.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the code is foreign-open, and in Bali the record does not block it under the moratorium logic supplied here.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

editorial.headline: Salt-Preserved Fruit and Vegetables, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10301 covers salted fruit and vegetable preservation, from loose to packaged asinan, with a national PMA opening that does not translate into Bali registration today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10301 is a narrow food-processing activity: the preservation of fruit and vegetables through salting. The record points to products such as **asinan kedondong** and **asinan wortel**, and it is careful about form: the activity may be done in packaged or unpackaged products. Its centre of gravity is not general food trading, catering, farming, or broad vegetable processing. It is the act of preserving fruit and vegetables by a salt-based process, then producing the resulting preserved food.

That makes the code relevant for operators who are building a production activity around Indonesian preserved produce rather than merely selling finished goods. The scale access is broad: the record opens it to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**. In practical classification terms, that means the activity is not reserved in the record for one business size. A small local producer, a mid-sized processor, or a larger factory-style operation can all sit within the scale language given here, provided the registered activity is genuinely this salted preservation activity.

Nationally, the PMA picture is simple. The record marks the activity as **TERBUKA**, with `pma_max_asing` at **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. On the national reading alone, this is therefore a foreign-open activity with no lower foreign-equity ceiling shown in the slim record. That is an important distinction: there is no percentage to negotiate downward in the national field, no partial cap stated here, and no separate threshold or licensing condition supplied in the record. The national data says open; the foreign-ownership number says 100%.

Bali is where the analysis changes. The record says `l4_bali_blocked` is **true** and marks the Bali status as **Blocked (risk class)**. The reason is given as: **“OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026”**. The moratorium rule is also explicit: **“Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent)”**. So the honest reading is this: a foreign-owned company may see a nationally open KBLI, but cannot treat that national opening as a Bali registration path today. For Bali PMA purposes, the record blocks the code because of the provincial moratorium logic, not because the national PMA percentage is below 100%.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign-owned company may see a nationally open KBLI, but cannot treat that national opening as a Bali registration path today.

l4_bali.reason: Not among the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026. The low/medium-low risk tier was named only in the Governor's January 2026 request letter (B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP); check the risk tier and zoning on OSS before filing.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This group covers the preservation of fruits and vegetables through a pulping process, whether the final product is packaged or unpackaged. The resulting products include mango jam, marmalade (orange jam), mulberry jelly, fruit and vegetable purees, nut pastes, and ground chili.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Small, Medium**: Low risk. NIB, issued Automatic (instant). Authority: District/City (Bupati/Walikota).
  Obligations: Memiliki bukti penyampaian wajib Data Industri tervalidasi setiap 6 (enam) bulan sekali sesuai perat; Menjamın keamanan dan keselamatan alat, proses, hasil produksi, penyimpanan, serta pengangkutan, ses (+2 more)

editorial.headline: Fruit and Vegetable Pulping With a Clear Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers preserved fruit and vegetable products made through pulping, from jams and jellies to purees, nut pastes, and ground chili.
editorial.body:
This activity is the industrial language for a familiar kind of food work: preserving fruit and vegetables by turning them into pulp-based products. The record names both packaged and unpackaged forms, so the defining feature is not the container but the process. Mango jam, orange marmalade, mulberry jelly, fruit and vegetable purees, nut pastes, and ground chili all sit inside the same practical idea: produce that has been processed into a spread, paste, puree, jelly, or crushed preparation.

That makes the code broader than a single product line, but still quite disciplined. It is not a general food-trading description and it is not every possible fruit or vegetable activity. The centre of gravity is preservation through pulping, with the finished output taking forms that can move from household-style staples to larger prepared-food production. A founder reading this should recognise the activity by asking what actually happens to the raw material. If the business is built around pulping fruit or vegetables into the kinds of products named in the record, this is the relevant commercial shape.

The scale position is unusually open in the record. Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all listed as open, which means the classification is not reserved only for larger industrial operators. A small producer of ground chili, a medium prepared-food operation, or a larger facility producing purees and jams can all sit within the same activity description, provided the underlying work remains the preservation of fruit or vegetables by pulping. The editorial point is simple: the code follows the activity and product form, not the founder's ambition level.

The national-vs-Bali picture is also clean. Nationally, the record marks PMA status as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, so the national reading is foreign-open up to full ownership. Bali does not add a separate ownership percentage in this record. Instead, Bali is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the Bali reason says: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule still matters as context, because Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently, but this record does not mark the activity as blocked. On the slim record alone, the honest conclusion is that this activity is nationally open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Dried Produce Manufacturing With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10303 covers the drying and crisping of fruits, vegetables, and tubers, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 10303 is a processing code, not a trading label.** Its centre of gravity is the preservation of fruits and vegetables by drying, whether the finished goods are packaged or unpackaged. The record names a practical range of outputs: raisins from grapes, dried shallots, dried garlic, dried chillies, dried bamboo shoots, potato flour, dried mashed potato, and dried mushrooms. It also reaches into the production of fruit and vegetable chips, including potato chips and potato snacks, plus freeze-dried fruit and the drying of tubers such as cassava and porang.

That scope matters because it describes an activity built around transformation: fresh agricultural material becomes a shelf-stable product through drying, crisping, freeze-drying, or tuber processing. A founder using this code should therefore be thinking about a production operation whose identity is the preservation and manufacture of dried produce, not simply the buying and selling of fruit, vegetables, or snacks. The examples in the record are deliberately varied, moving from ingredients such as dried garlic to consumer-facing products such as chips, but they all sit inside the same logic of drying-based food processing.

The scale position is broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so it can describe anything from a small dried-produce operation to a larger manufacturing setup, provided the real activity remains inside the stated scope. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the recorded foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Put plainly, the national record treats this as foreign-open, with no partial foreign-share cap stated in the slim record.

The Bali reading is also relatively clean, but it should be stated precisely. The record does not mark this activity as blocked for PMA registration in Bali: `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`. The reason given is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. That matters because the moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali. For this code, the honest national-vs-Bali picture is therefore consistent: nationally open to foreign ownership up to 100%, and not blocked by the Bali moratorium on the basis recorded here.
