editorial.headline: Syrup Manufacturing With a Clear National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10723 covers the standalone conversion of sugar into syrup, open across all business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10723 is a manufacturing activity with a narrow, concrete center of gravity: the processing of sugar into syrup. The record names sugar syrup, syrup, and maple sugar as examples, so this is not a general food-and-beverage trading category or a broad sweetener business. It is about the industrial act of turning sugar into a syrup product, provided the activity can stand as its own registration line rather than disappearing inside an inseparable sugar-factory process.

That practical boundary matters. A founder using this code should be registering a business whose actual activity is syrup production as a distinct operation. The record opens the activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** scales, which means the classification is not reserved only for large plants or only for small producers. Its scale range is broad, but the registered activity should still remain faithful to the described scope: sugar is processed, and the output is syrup or the named syrup-related product.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is **100%**. In plain English, the national record treats this as open to foreign investment, with no lower ownership cap stated in the slim record. The cited source for that national position is **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. There is no basis here to add a hidden permit story, a capital threshold, a tax condition, or a staged approval timeline. The record gives the foreign-ownership answer, and that answer is fully open at the national level.

The Bali picture is also clear, but it has to be read carefully. Bali’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, island-wide and permanent, according to the record. This code, however, is not marked as blocked: `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**. The stated reason is: **OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium**. So the honest conclusion is not that Bali imposes a separate percentage cap, and not that a foreign investor needs an invented local partnership. The conclusion is simpler: for this slim record, KBLI 10723 is nationally open at 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the listed moratorium logic.

editorial.headline: Other Sugar Manufacturing With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10729 covers specialist sugar and sweetener processing, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10729 is not the ordinary headline category of sugar production; it is the quieter industrial space around sugar and sweeteners once they are processed into other forms. The record places rock sugar, liquid sugar, and powdered sugar inside its scope. It also includes the making of sugar substitutes from cane juice, beet, maple, stevia, and palm plants such as coconut and aren. The same scope extends to molasses, sweet non-fruit topping sauces, and brown sugar whose main raw material is not nira.

That makes this activity a manufacturing classification for businesses working with transformed sugar and alternative sweetening materials, rather than a narrow retail or trading label. A founder would look at this code when the substance of the business is processing: turning sugar or sweetener inputs into another product form, or producing the listed substitutes and sweet derivatives. The record is explicit enough to give the activity a practical boundary without adding a licence story that is not present here.

On scale, the code is broadly available. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so it is not reserved for a single size of enterprise. A small producer of powdered sugar and a larger manufacturer of liquid sweetener would still need to match their real operations to the recorded scope, but the scale field itself does not close the door at any one level. That matters because the classification can serve both small production setups and larger industrial plans, provided the activity remains within the described processing field.

The national-vs-Bali picture is unusually clean. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the recorded foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 given as the source. Bali does have an island-wide moratorium rule blocking all Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, but this record does not mark the activity as blocked in Bali. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. In plain terms, the record supports a full-foreign PMA reading nationally, and it does not show a Bali moratorium block for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: The national-vs-Bali picture is unusually clean: the record supports full foreign ownership and does not show a Bali moratorium block.

editorial.headline: Cocoa Processing With a Clear National Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10731 covers the industrial processing of cocoa beans into core cocoa ingredients, with registration open across every listed business scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10731 is the cocoa-processing lane: the transformation of cocoa beans into cocoa powder, cocoa butter, cocoa fat, cocoa oil, cocoa paste, cocoa cake, and other cocoa products. The emphasis is on processing, not merely trading or packaging. It is the activity code for businesses whose economic substance sits inside the conversion of raw cocoa into the intermediate and finished cocoa materials used further along the food and manufacturing chain.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the code is not framed only for large industrial plants. A small producer and a larger processor may both sit within the same activity definition, provided the registered business is genuinely carrying out the cocoa-bean processing described in the scope. That breadth matters because the code follows the activity, not the glamour of the product or the size of the brand around it.

Nationally, the record is direct: the PMA status is TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100. Put simply, foreign ownership may reach the national ceiling of 100%. There is no partial foreign-ownership cap in this slim record, and no additional national condition is stated here. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, so the editorial conclusion must stay narrow: for this record, the national position is open to foreign ownership up to the listed ceiling.

The Bali picture is not a hidden closure. At the Bali level, the record records l4_bali_blocked as false and assigns the status OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. Its reason is precise: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently; this activity is not marked as blocked under that rule. So the honest reading is clean: nationally open, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the data provided.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is clean: nationally open, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the data provided.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Chocolate Manufacturing With a Clear National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10732 covers chocolate products, chocolate-based sweets, spreads, fillings, and chocolate drinks, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 10732 is a manufacturing code for chocolate in several forms.** The record places it around the making of compound chocolate, couverture chocolate, imitation chocolate, white chocolate, and chocolate confectionery. It also includes chocolate-based spreads and fillings, and it reaches into chocolate drinks when they are made in powder or liquid form. In plain English, this is not a retail shelf category or a cafe concept; it is the activity of producing chocolate and chocolate-derived products.

That breadth matters because the code is not limited to one premium or mass-market expression of chocolate. The slim record names both couverture and imitation chocolate, which gives the activity a practical manufacturing range, from ingredients used in further preparation to finished sweets and drink bases. The common thread is the chocolate basis of the output. A founder reading this code should therefore focus on whether the planned activity is the making of those chocolate goods, spreads, fillings, or drinks, rather than on how the product will later be branded, sold, or consumed.

On scale, the record is unusually straightforward. KBLI 10732 is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the activity is not framed, in this slim record, as only a large industrial category or only a small producer category. It can describe a micro operation, a small or medium manufacturer, or a large-scale manufacturer, as long as the underlying activity remains the manufacture of the chocolate products described in the scope. The scale field is important here because it tells the founder that the activity itself can sit across the full range named in the record.

The national foreign-investment picture is also clear. Nationally, the activity's PMA status is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to a 100% ceiling. In practical editorial terms, the national record treats this chocolate manufacturing activity as open to foreign ownership up to the full ceiling stated in the data. Bali does not add a separate percentage in the record, and it should not be read as doing so. The Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with the reason stated as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently; this code is not marked as blocked by that rule. The honest reading is therefore simple: nationally, the code is open up to 100% foreign ownership, and in Bali the slim record does not mark it as blocked for PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is simple: nationally, the code is open up to 100% foreign ownership, and in Bali the slim record does not mark it as blocked for PMA registration.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the business of preserving fruits, nuts, peels, and other plant parts by candying and drying them, whether packaged or not. Examples include candied nutmeg and dried mango sweets.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this activity is open to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Manisan Buah-buahan dan Sayuran Kering (10733)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur who wants to produce branded dried or candied fruit and vegetable snacks, such as dried mango strips or candied tropical nuts, for export or local specialty retail.

editorial.headline: Preserved Fruit and Dried Vegetables, With Bali Still Open
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10733 covers sweetened and dried plant-based preserves, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10733 is a food-processing activity built around preservation by sweetness and dryness. The record describes the work as preserving fruit, nuts, fruit peel, and other parts of plants through sweetening and drying, whether the result is packaged or unpackaged. The examples are concrete: sweetened nutmeg and dried sweetened mango. That gives the code a clear commercial center of gravity: not farming the crop, not retailing the finished snack, but the industrial act of transforming plant material into a preserved fruit or vegetable product.

The scale profile is broad. The record opens this activity to **Mikro**, **Kecil**, **Menengah**, and **Besar** operators, which means the classification can serve very different business shapes, from small production to larger manufacturing. The important editorial point is that the code is defined by the process and product, not by the size of the factory or whether the goods are sold loose or in packaging. A founder reading the scope should therefore focus on the actual activity: sweetening and drying fruit, nuts, peel, or other plant parts into preserved food products.

Nationally, the investment picture is straightforward. The record marks the PMA status as **TERBUKA**, with `pma_max_asing` at **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. In plain English, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to the full stated ceiling. There is no smaller cap in the slim record, and there is no separate national condition listed here beyond the fields provided. For a foreign-owned setup, the national signal is therefore clean: this is not presented as a closed activity in the record.

Bali does not add a blockage on the record supplied here. The Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and `l4_bali_blocked` is false. The reason is specific: **OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium**. That matters because the record also states the moratorium rule: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. This activity, on the supplied record, sits outside that block because of the stated Bali-side risk reasoning. The honest conclusion is narrow but useful: nationally open, full foreign-ownership ceiling in the record, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the Bali moratorium field supplied.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is narrow but useful: nationally open, full foreign-ownership ceiling in the record, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Non-Chocolate Confectionery, With a Clear Path Through Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers other confectionery made without chocolate, from caramel and nougat to chewing gum, cough sweets and pastilles.
editorial.body:
This activity is about the manufacture of confectionery that sits outside chocolate. The record names caramel, cachous, nougat, fondant, marzipan, chewing gum, cough sweets and pastilles, which gives the category a practical breadth: it is not a single sweet, but a production lane for many finished sugar-based products. The important boundary is equally clear. The activity described here is other confectionery **not made from chocolate**, so the editorial focus belongs on non-chocolate sweets and related products rather than on the wider food industry.

For founders, the scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar** operators, meaning it can describe anything from a small formal producer to a larger industrial manufacturer, so long as the activity remains within the stated scope. That matters because the same KBLI heading can support very different business realities: a compact confectionery workshop, a growing packaged-sweets producer, or a larger operation making multiple non-chocolate product lines. The code is therefore best read as a manufacturing classification, not as a retail or distribution label.

Nationally, the investment signal is straightforward. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the foreign-ownership ceiling in the record is **100%**. In plain English, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to full foreign participation. The source given is **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**, so the national position is not being inferred from market custom or general sector logic; it comes from the stated PMA source in the record. There is no basis in the slim record to add a lower cap, a local-partner requirement, a minimum capital figure, or a special threshold.

The Bali picture is also clean, and it should not be made more complicated than the record makes it. Bali’s status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and `l4_bali_blocked` is false. The reason is explicit: **OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium**. The moratorium rule itself is still important context, because Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis, according to **Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP**. But this activity is not marked as blocked in Bali. The honest reading is therefore simple: nationally open, foreign ownership up to 100%, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the Bali-side status recorded here.

editorial.headline: Pasta and Noodle Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Clear for Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10740 covers the making of pasta, noodles, couscous and analog rice, with all business scales open and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10740 is a manufacturing code for the factory-side making of pasta and similar staple products. Its scope is broad but still quite specific: macaroni, noodles, spaghetti, bihun and sohun, whether cooked or uncooked, sit inside it. So do semolina in the form of couscous and analog rice. The center of gravity is production, not restaurant service, retail presentation, or a prepared-meal concept built around pasta.

That distinction matters because this activity is about making the base product itself. A business registered here is positioning itself as a producer of the noodle, pasta, couscous or analog-rice item, rather than as a seller of finished dishes. The slim record also draws the boundary away from processed foods based on pasta or couscous, and away from soups that contain pasta. In plain English, this is the industrial or small-scale manufacturing lane for the product before it becomes part of a more elaborate food preparation.

The scale profile is unusually clean. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar operators. That means the code is not written only for a large factory; it can also fit a smaller producer, provided the real activity remains the manufacture of the covered products. The business description should therefore follow the material reality of the operation: making macaroni, noodles, spaghetti, bihun, sohun, couscous or analog rice, not a looser food-brand narrative that drifts outside the recorded scope.

The investment picture is also straightforward. Nationally, the record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In editorial terms, that is a full foreign-ownership opening at the national layer. Bali does not add a separate percentage, and this record does not mark the activity as blocked there: l4_bali_blocked is false and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is precise: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium." The relevant Bali moratorium rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, but this record says that block does not apply here. For a foreign-owned Bali setup, the honest conclusion is therefore clean: this code is nationally open up to 100%, and the Bali record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium note provided.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign-owned Bali setup, the honest conclusion is therefore clean: this code is nationally open up to 100%, and the Bali record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium note provided.

editorial.headline: Prepared Meals Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10750 covers packaged, preserved cooked meals for resale, with full foreign ownership available nationally and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10750 is the industrial code for making prepared meals: food that has been processed, seasoned, cooked, preserved, packaged, and labelled for resale. The record points to meals kept in durable form, such as canned or frozen products, rather than food made for immediate consumption at a restaurant or by a caterer. The core idea is manufacturing, not service. A product in this activity is a cooked meal product entering the market as a packaged good.

The scope is broad but not loose. It includes prepared dishes made from meat or poultry; fish-based dishes such as pepes, presto, fish jerky, fried baby fish, battered shrimp, battered fish, and fish and chips; meals containing pasta and rice; vegetable dishes; frozen pizza; and croque-monsieur. The record also sets an important boundary: to qualify as a meal, the processed food must contain at least two different main ingredients, excluding seasoning. That distinction keeps the activity focused on composite cooked meals rather than simple fresh foods or single-ingredient preparations.

The registration picture is unusually clean. The activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the record does not reserve it for only one size of operator. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing recorded as 100. In plain English, the national investment position allows full foreign ownership for this activity, subject only to the facts actually stated in the record. The source named for that national PMA position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali does not change that conclusion in this slim record. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, l4_bali_blocked is false, and the stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this activity is not marked as blocked by that rule. The honest reading, therefore, is direct: a foreign investor can treat KBLI 10750 as nationally open, with no Bali PMA moratorium block shown in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is direct: KBLI 10750 is nationally open, and the Bali record does not mark it as blocked.

editorial.headline: Coffee Processing With a Clear National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10761 covers the industrial transformation of coffee into roasted, ground, instant, decaffeinated, extracted, and related products.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10761 is the processing side of coffee: the work that turns coffee into a finished or semi-finished product rather than simply selling it as a bean or drink. The slim record defines the activity through drying, roasting, grinding, and extraction, with the output ranging from roasted coffee and ground coffee to instant coffee, decaffeinated coffee, coffee extracts, coffee essences, other coffee products, and coffee substitutes. Its boundary is also clear: it does not include grinding coffee powder at the premises of a coffee trader.

That makes this a manufacturing-style classification for founders who are building the production layer of a coffee business. It is not just a cafe identity, a retail counter, or a branding exercise. The activity belongs where coffee is materially processed: dried, roasted, milled, extracted, or turned into a product that can be packaged, supplied, or distributed. The record opens the code across the full scale ladder: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practical editorial terms, that means the classification is not reserved only for large plants; it can also describe smaller operators, provided the registered activity is truly coffee processing as defined in the scope.

Nationally, the investment picture is straightforward. For national investment purposes, the record lists the PMA status as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. There is no lower cap in the slim record, and no extra condition should be read into it. For a foreign-owned company choosing the right activity code at national level, KBLI 10761 therefore reads as an open coffee-processing classification, supported in the record by Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

The Bali layer is also unusually clear. In Bali, the record shows no block on this activity: l4_bali_blocked is false, and its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. It gives a specific rationale: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". That matters because the Bali moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province. For this code, however, the recorded Bali result is not a prohibition. The honest conclusion is that KBLI 10761 is nationally open to full foreign ownership and, on the Bali record supplied here, not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers turning tea leaves into dried tea packaged in bags, pads, capsules, or other formats, including blending with natural ingredients like mate, spices, herbs, and dried flowers. It also includes producing tea extracts—both liquid concentrates and powders—but excludes ready-to-drink beverages.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this business line is fully open to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: matched with aggregation.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Pengolahan Teh (10762)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs who want to produce value-added tea products, herbal blends, or tea extracts for export or premium local markets—but who are comfortable starting outside Bali for now.

editorial.headline: Tea Processing as a Foreign-Open Manufacturing Activity
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10762 covers dried, blended, and extracted tea products, and the record treats it as nationally open to full foreign ownership with no Bali PMA block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10762 is about the work that turns tea leaves into a finished dry product. The record describes processing tea leaves into dried tea, then packaging that tea in bags, pads, capsules, or other forms of packaging. It also includes derivative tea products, provided they are not ready-to-drink tea beverages. In practical terms, this is the production side of tea: the handling, transformation, blending, extraction, and packaging that create shelf-ready tea formats before they become a beverage served to the consumer.

The scope is broader than plain dried tea. The record also includes mixing tea with natural ingredients such as mate, spices, herbs, and dried flowers. That makes the activity relevant not only to conventional black, green, or other dried teas, but also to blended products where tea remains the base and natural ingredients shape the final profile. It also covers extraction from tea leaves, including liquid tea extract concentrate and powdered tea extract. The common thread is processing: this code is not framed around a cafe, a drink counter, or ready-to-drink bottled tea, but around manufacturing and packaging tea-based products from the leaf onward.

The scale picture is unusually straightforward. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That means the classification is not reserved only for large manufacturing operations in the record; it can describe a small producer as well as a larger processing facility, so long as the actual activity remains inside the stated scope. The useful editorial distinction is not size alone, but the activity boundary: dried tea, packaged tea, natural-ingredient blends, and tea extracts sit inside this record, while ready-to-drink tea beverages are expressly outside it.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clean. The record marks PMA status as TERBUKA and gives pma_max_asing as 100, so the foreign-ownership ceiling should be read as 100%. The source given is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali does not add a separate ownership percentage in this record, and none should be inferred. On the Bali side, the status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and l4_bali_blocked is false. The reason given is precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this record’s Bali conclusion is that KBLI 10762 is not blocked by that moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: This code is not about serving tea; it is about processing tea leaves into packaged, blended, or extracted products.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Soy-Sauce Manufacturing With a Clear PMA Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10771 covers soy-based kecap and taoco production, open across business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10771 is a manufacturing activity for kecap: the production of soy sauce made from soybeans or other legumes. Its scope also reaches taoco, whether made from fresh soybeans or other legumes, or from residual material left over from kecap production. In plain English, this is the industrial classification for businesses turning legumes into fermented or processed soy-condiment products, with the record drawing the boundary around kecap and taoco rather than the broader universe of sauces.

The registration picture is unusually straightforward. The activity is open to every scale listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the classification is not reserved only for a large factory or only for a household-scale producer. It can describe a small production operation, a growing mid-sized processor, or a larger industrial setup, provided the registered business activity is genuinely the making of kecap or taoco from the materials described in the scope.

Nationally, the foreign-investment status is also clear. In the record, the activity is labelled TERBUKA, its pma_max_asing is 100, and the source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Rendered practically, that is a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling at the national level. There is no lower foreign-share cap in this slim record, and no additional national threshold, licence, capital floor, or timing rule is supplied here. The honest reading is therefore limited and precise: as a national PMA classification, this activity is open up to full foreign ownership according to the fields provided.

Bali does not change that conclusion into a block in this record. For Bali, the status reads OK_or_HIGHER_RISK while l4_bali_blocked remains false. Its stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule itself says Bali blocks all Low plus Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently, but this record does not place KBLI 10771 inside that blocked result. The key point is that this activity is nationally open and not blocked in Bali, but only within the limits of the record itself.
editorial.pullQuote: The key point is that this activity is nationally open and not blocked in Bali, but only within the limits of the record itself.

editorial.headline: Iodised Salt Processing, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers processing salt into iodised consumer salt, open across all business scales nationally but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under the recorded moratorium.
editorial.body:
This KBLI activity is narrow and practical: it covers the processing of salt into iodised salt for consumption. The record’s Indonesian scope points to transformation rather than trade or extraction: the business activity is the handling of salt so that it becomes iodised consumer salt. That makes the classification useful for founders who need the registration to match the productive step itself, not a broader food, retail, or distribution activity.

Nationally, the code is marked **TERBUKA** for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. The record also opens the activity across **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** scales, so the national picture is unusually straightforward: the activity is not confined to a single business size, and the stated PMA ceiling is full foreign ownership. The cited national source is **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**, and there is no additional national cap, threshold, licence, tax, timeline, or capital figure in the slim record.

Bali changes the answer completely. The record marks the Bali status as **Blocked (risk class)**, with `l4_bali_blocked` set to true. The stated reason is: **OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026**. In plain English, the national PMA openness does not translate into a usable Bali PMA registration path today. A foreign founder reading only the national ceiling would see 100%; the Bali-side record says the registration is blocked because the activity falls under the province’s moratorium treatment for low and medium-low risk KBLI.

That distinction is the core planning point. For Indonesia as a whole, this is a foreign-open iodised consumer salt processing activity. For Bali, the same activity is blocked for PMA registration under the recorded rule: **Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent)**, with the moratorium source identified as **Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP**. The clean reading is therefore not that Bali has a lower percentage ceiling, or a special foreign-share formula, or a local partnership condition. The record gives none of those. It says nationally open at 100%, but Bali-blocked under the risk-class moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign founder reading only the national ceiling would see 100%; the Bali-side record says the registration is blocked.

intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally this activity is open to foreign ownership. It is conditionally available — only by declaring the qualifying higher-risk scope. Confirm that scope genuinely fits your operation before planning a Bali setup.

editorial.headline: Food-Standard Industrial Salt, Open Nationally and Nuanced in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the processing of salt into food-standard industrial input for food and beverage manufacturing, open nationally to PMA but requiring precise Bali-side OSS verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10773 is a manufacturing activity with a narrow, practical purpose: it covers processing salt into food-standard industrial salt used in the production of assorted food and beverages. The record frames it as an input industry, not a retail or consumer-facing category. Its centre of gravity is the transformation of salt into a standardised industrial ingredient for downstream food and drink production.

The registration profile is broad. The record opens this activity across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, which means the classification is not reserved only for large industrial players. A smaller producer and a larger factory can both sit inside the same activity description, provided the declared business activity remains within the recorded scope. For founders, the important point is that scale affects how the activity is assessed in OSS and in Bali; it does not change what the activity is.

Nationally, the investment picture is clear. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA for PMA and gives the foreign-ownership ceiling as 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national record treats this as foreign-open up to full foreign ownership. The same slim record also carries a technical scope note: basic inorganic chlor and alkali chemical industry using a mercury process is prohibited for new investment, business expansion, and development. That note should be read as a scope boundary inside the record, not as a general licence condition invented outside it.

Bali is more delicate than the national headline. The record does not mark this activity as fully blocked in Bali, but it does flag it as Blocked (scope-dependent) and explains the reason directly: “OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity”. The underlying Bali rule is also explicit: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. So the honest reading is not that Bali has a separate foreign-ownership cap. It does not, in this record. The honest reading is that national PMA openness is real, while Bali registration depends on the exact declared scope and live OSS risk posture.
editorial.pullQuote: National PMA openness is real here, but in Bali the decisive issue is the exact declared scope and live OSS risk posture.

data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan pembuatan bumbu masakan, baik dalam keadaan sudah diramu maupun belum, baik berbentuk bubuk maupun lainnya, seperti bumbu gulai, bumbu kari, bubuk merica, bubuk jahe, bubuk jinten, bubuk pala, bubuk cabai, dan bubuk kayu manis. Kelompok ini juga mencakup kegiatan pembuatan penyedap masakan, baik yang asli maupun sintetis kimia, seperti monosodium glutamat (MSG), serbuk vanili, serta pembuatan saus dan rempah-rempah, seperti mayones, tepung moster, moster olahan, saus tomat, saus tiram, dan saus selada; dan pengganti garam yang digunakan sebagai bumbu pada produk pangan. Kelompok ini juga mencakup kegiatan pembuatan petis dan cuka makan. Kelompok ini tidak mencakup kegiatan pembuatan terasi udang, lihat kelompok 10295.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers manufacturing cooking spices and seasonings, whether pre-mixed (like gulai or curry blends) or single-ingredient powders (pepper, ginger, chili, cinnamon, nutmeg). It also includes producing flavor enhancers (MSG, vanilla powder), condiments and sauces (mayonnaise, mustard, ketchup, oyster sauce, salad dressing), and salt substitutes used as seasoning.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.

editorial.headline: Seasoning Manufacture With a Clean National and Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10779 covers the industrial making of cooking seasonings, sauces, flavour enhancers, vinegar, and related food-seasoning products across all business scales.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10779 is the manufacturing home for cooking seasonings in the broad, practical sense of the word. The scope reaches beyond a single culinary format: it covers seasonings that are already blended or still unblended, powders and other forms, and named examples such as gulai seasoning, curry seasoning, powdered pepper, ginger, cumin, nutmeg, chilli, and cinnamon. In plain English, this is the code for businesses turning spice, flavour, and seasoning inputs into packaged ingredients for kitchens and food production.

The record also places flavour enhancers, sauces, spice preparations, salt substitutes for food seasoning, petis, and edible vinegar inside the same activity. That matters because the code is not limited to dry spice powder. It includes original and chemically synthetic cooking enhancers such as monosodium glutamate and vanilla powder, as well as products such as mayonnaise, mustard flour, processed mustard, tomato sauce, oyster sauce, and salad sauce. The common thread is manufacturing: the activity is about making these seasoning and condiment products, not merely trading them.

On scale, the record is unusually straightforward. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the same KBLI can describe a small producer formalising a narrow seasoning line or a larger manufacturer operating at industrial scale. Nothing in the slim record adds a minimum capital threshold, a special timing rule, or a separate technical permit detail, so those should not be read into the code. The usable fact is narrower and stronger: all four listed business scales are open in the record.

The national-versus-Bali picture is also clear. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing recorded at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Rendered as ownership language, that is a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling at the national level. Bali does not add a separate percentage in this record. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and l4_bali_blocked is false. The record gives a precise reason: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule still matters as context because the record states that Bali province blocks all Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. But for this activity, the record’s conclusion is not a Bali block; it is a nationally open activity whose Bali-side entry is marked as not blocked by that moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Baby and Special-Purpose Foods, Open Nationally and Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10791 covers the making of baby foods, dietary foods, and medical-purpose foods, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 10791 is a manufacturing code for foods made for specific early-life, dietary, and medical needs.** Its scope covers the making of baby food, food for dietary purposes, and food for medical purposes. The record names infant formula, follow-up milk, other follow-up foods, baby foods and homogenised-ingredient foods, growth formula, complementary foods for breastfeeding, children’s snack foods, drinks for pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, and foods for people with certain diseases. The common thread is not a broad food category but a production activity focused on foods whose intended users are clearly defined by age, nutrition stage, pregnancy or breastfeeding, diet, or health condition.

The scale picture is unusually straightforward. The record opens the activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** operators, so the classification is not framed as only a large-factory lane. A small producer and a larger manufacturer may both find the code relevant, provided the real activity is the making of the covered products. That scale breadth does not add extra obligations in the record; it only tells us who can register under the code. For editorial purposes, the important point is that the code follows the product and production scope, not the ambition level of the applicant.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clean. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. In plain terms, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to the full stated ceiling. There is no lower percentage in the slim record, no special national threshold, and no minimum-capital figure to infer. The honest national reading is therefore direct: for this KBLI activity, the record supports full foreign ownership at the national level.

The Bali-side picture is also clear, but it has to be stated precisely. The record marks **l4_bali_blocked** as false and gives the Bali status as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**. Its reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” That matters because the stated Bali moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. This record does not create a separate Bali ownership percentage, quota, or partnership condition. The honest reading is national openness without a Bali moratorium block, not a separate Bali ownership cap.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is national openness without a Bali moratorium block, not a separate Bali ownership cap.

editorial.headline: Wet Cakes, Nationally Open but Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10792 covers short-life Indonesian wet cakes and related traditional foods, open nationally to all business scales but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10792 is the activity code for making *kue basah*: moist, relatively short-life Indonesian cakes and snacks such as wajik, lemper, kue lapis, lumpia, and martabak. The record also places tape and lempok inside this activity. In practical terms, this is not a general bakery code or a broad packaged-food category; it is a focused manufacturing classification for traditional wet cakes and closely related foods whose character is freshness, local preparation, and limited shelf life.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The slim record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. That means the code can describe a small producer, a growing workshop, a mid-sized food business, or a large-scale manufacturing setup, depending on the actual business footprint. The editorial point is simple: the activity itself is not confined to one commercial size. It can sit behind a modest local food operation or a larger formal production business, as long as the registered activity is the making of the wet cakes and related products described in the scope.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clear. The record marks the PMA status as TERBUKA and gives a pma_max_asing value of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Rendered plainly, that is a 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity. On the national reading alone, a foreign-owned company would see this as an open manufacturing activity, not one capped below full foreign ownership. There is no basis in the slim record to add a special licence, a capital threshold, a timing rule, or any additional operating condition; the record only gives the ownership status, source, eligible scales, scope, and Bali restriction.

Bali changes the answer. The record says l4_bali_blocked is true, with the status Blocked (risk class). The stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026. The moratorium rule is broader than this one activity: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, with the cited source being Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. So the honest conclusion for KBLI 10792 is deliberately split. Nationally, it is open to PMA up to 100%. In Bali, a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA today because the Bali-side record blocks it under the province’s risk-class moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, KBLI 10792 is open to PMA up to 100%; in Bali, the record blocks it for foreign-owned registration today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers manufacturing food products where coconut is the key ingredient, such as coconut milk (liquid, concentrated, or powder), coconut cream, desiccated coconut, nata de coco, coconut flour, and even coconut-based soy sauce. Essentially, it’s turning raw coconut into packaged, value-added food items for sale.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is 100% open to foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Produk Makanan dari Kelapa (10793)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Entrepreneurs who want to process coconut raw materials into manufactured food products, often targeting export markets or the growing health-food segment.

editorial.headline: Coconut Food Manufacturing With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10793 covers coconut-based food products and is open nationally and in Bali for PMA registration under the record supplied.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 10793 is the manufacturing lane for coconut as food, not coconut as a vague plantation story.** The record defines it through the making of food products from coconut: thick and liquid coconut milk, powdered coconut milk, coconut sauce, sari kelapa in the form of nata de coco, dried grated coconut, coconut cream, and coconut flour. In plain English, this is where the coconut becomes a processed food ingredient or finished food product. The emphasis is on transformation: coconut is not merely handled, traded, or described as a raw commodity, but made into specific edible products that can sit inside a formal manufacturing activity.

That scope matters because it gives founders a clean commercial picture without needing to stretch the activity beyond the record. A business registering this activity could be built around one product line, such as coconut flour, or around a broader coconut-food processing operation that includes several of the named outputs. The record also makes the scale position unusually straightforward: the activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the classification is not written only for industrial-scale operators. It can describe small, middle, and large manufacturing setups, as long as the actual activity remains within the coconut food products named in the scope.

The national foreign-ownership picture is equally direct. The record lists the PMA status as TERBUKA, setting the foreign-ownership ceiling at 100%. There is no partial cap to explain and no reduced percentage to soften. On the national reading supplied here, foreign investors may use this activity up to the full stated ceiling, with the source identified as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That is the clean national answer: this coconut food manufacturing activity is open for PMA, and the record’s maximum foreign ownership is 100%.

Bali does not change that answer in this record. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says it is not blocked. The stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low plus Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this activity is not caught by that block on the supplied facts. So the honest national-vs-Bali reading is not a warning that Bali shuts the door. It is the opposite: nationally open, open at every listed business scale, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the moratorium rule described in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is simple: KBLI 10793 is nationally open to full foreign ownership and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the supplied record.

editorial.headline: The Everyday Snack Industry With a Clear Bali PMA Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10794 covers the making of krupuk, chips, peyek, and similar foods, with national foreign ownership open up to 100% and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10794 is the industrial home for one of Indonesia’s most familiar food categories: krupuk, keripik, peyek, and the wider family of crisp, dry, snack-like products that sit close to them. The record describes a broad manufacturing activity, not a narrow single-product trade. It includes chips and peyek made from different kinds of nuts, shrimp crackers, fish crackers, starch crackers, and similar foods such as emping, kecimpring, karak, gendar, and opak. It also reaches into more specific snack products named in the scope, including lung chips, snail chips, skin chips, anchovy peyek, and shrimp peyek.

That scope matters because the code is built around making the product, not merely selling it. A founder using this activity is positioning the business as a producer in the snack-food manufacturing chain: transforming ingredients into packaged or ready-to-distribute crisp foods of the kind listed in the Indonesian scope. The code is open across all recorded business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In plain terms, the record does not confine this activity to either cottage production or large factories. It can describe a small producer, a growing mid-sized operation, or a larger industrial setup, provided the actual activity remains within the manufacturing scope captured here.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is straightforward. The PMA status is marked TERBUKA, and the listed foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That is the clean national reading: the record allows full foreign ownership for this activity, with the source given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower national cap in the slim record, so there is no basis to invent one. For a foreign-owned structure, the important point is therefore not a national ownership restriction, but whether the intended place of registration creates a separate Bali-side problem.

On Bali, the record does not mark this activity as blocked. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason is explicit: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this code is not caught by that block on the record provided. The honest conclusion is therefore unusually clean: KBLI 10794 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record supplied here does not block PMA registration under the stated moratorium logic.

editorial.headline: Plant-Based Milks, Creamers, and the Quiet Industrial Core
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10795 covers plant-derived beverage bases, non-dairy creamers, vegetable-fat emulsions, and substitute cheese, open nationally and not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10795 sits inside food manufacturing, but its real subject is the engineered middle of the modern plant-based aisle. The record covers the making of plant extracts from multiple crops: soy milk, oat or wheat-based drinks, almond, cashew, and other nut-based preparations. It also covers plant-based creamer, vegetable-fat emulsions derived from coconut or palm oil for use in food or beverages, and the production of substitute cheese. In practical terms, this is not a cafe, a trading label, or a small blending counter by default; it is the activity code for manufacturing the plant-derived bases and fat systems that later appear in drinks, mixes, creamers, and dairy alternatives.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, which means the same KBLI can describe a very small producer as well as a larger industrial manufacturer, provided the registered activity is still the making of the covered products. That matters because the business identity here is defined by production, not by branding language. A founder using this code should be able to point back to the manufacturing scope: plant-based extract, vegetable creamer, vegetable-fat emulsion, or substitute cheese. If the proposed business is only retailing packaged products, serving drinks, or marketing a finished brand without manufacturing, that distinction is not supplied by this record and should not be smuggled into the code.

Nationally, the record is clear: PMA status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership figure is 100%. That is the national ownership position given here, and it should be read plainly. A foreign-owned company can treat this activity as open at the national level, with no lower foreign-share ceiling stated in the slim record. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, and the ownership number comes directly from the record rather than from any inferred food-sector rule.

The Bali reading is also clean, but it needs precision. For Bali, the record shows no block on this activity: l4_bali_blocked is false, while the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The same record also states the moratorium rule: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. For this code, however, the supplied Bali field says the moratorium does not block it. The honest conclusion is therefore not a hidden Bali cap or a special local percentage; it is that this nationally open manufacturing code is not recorded here as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is not a hidden Bali cap; it is that this nationally open manufacturing code is not recorded here as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Dodol Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making of dodol from rice flour or glutinous rice flour, coconut milk, and sugar, with Bali not blocking PMA registration under the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10796 is a manufacturing activity with a narrow, food-specific centre of gravity: the making of dodol from rice flour or glutinous rice flour, coconut milk, and sugar. The record allows for additional ingredients, but the defining act is still the cooking process, carried through until the product reaches the intended texture. This is not a general sweets category in the way founders sometimes use the word informally. It is about producing dodol as an industrial activity, with its identity anchored in ingredients, heat, and texture.

That clarity matters because registration follows the activity, not the brand story. A founder using this code is registering a production business, whether the operation is modest or scaled. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, which means the code is not reserved only for a narrow enterprise size. A small maker, a growing food producer, and a larger industrial setup can all sit within the registered scale options, provided the registered activity remains the making of dodol as described in the scope.

Across Indonesia, the foreign-investment position is clear. The activity carries a TERBUKA PMA status, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In plain English, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to full foreign participation. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower ceiling in the slim record, and there is no separate condition here that would justify inventing one. For a foreign founder reading the table, the national signal is therefore clean: this activity is open, and the cap shown is 100%.

The Bali reading is also clean, but it has to be read on its own terms. The record does not mark this activity as blocked in Bali. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason given is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; here, however, the record’s own Bali conclusion is that this activity is not blocked by that moratorium. So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is not a contradiction. Nationally it is open to PMA up to 100%; in Bali, this record does not block PMA registration under the stated moratorium logic.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally it is open to PMA up to 100%; in Bali, this record does not block PMA registration under the stated moratorium logic.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Herbal Infusion Manufacturing Without a Bali PMA Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10797 covers non-tea herbal brews and refreshing drinks, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10797 is a manufacturing classification for herbal infusions: the processing of plant-based brews such as mint, vervain, and chamomile, including herbal steeped drinks that are not tea and refreshing beverages. Its center of gravity is production, not retail presentation or wellness language. The activity is about turning specified herbal ingredients into drinkable infusions and related refreshment products.

The record opens this activity across the full business-scale ladder: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the code is not framed as a narrow cottage activity or as a category reserved only for large industrial operators. A small producer and a larger manufacturing setup can both sit inside the same activity description, provided the registered activity is genuinely the processing of herbal infusions as described in the scope.

Nationally, the PMA picture is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives the foreign-ownership ceiling as 100%. In plain English, the national classification is open to foreign ownership up to the full stated ceiling. There is no additional capital number, licence condition, production threshold, or operating timeline in the slim record, so none should be read into the code. The national source attached to the record is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, but the operational takeaway here is simply that the activity is nationally foreign-open.

Bali does not change that into a hidden percentage cap. The Bali-side status in the record is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the Bali block flag is false. Its basis is precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The provincial moratorium rule in the record blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this activity is not caught by that block on the facts supplied. The honest reading is therefore straightforward: for this code, a foreign-owned registration is nationally open and, on the Bali moratorium fields provided, not blocked in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: For this code, the honest reading is straightforward: nationally foreign-open, and not blocked by the Bali moratorium fields provided.

Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Seaweed Food Processing Meets Bali’s PMA Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10798 covers food products made from seaweed, nationally open to foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record’s risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10798 is a manufacturing activity for food ingredients and prepared food products made from seaweed. The record’s Indonesian scope is precise: it covers the making of seaweed-based food preparations such as agar-agar, carrageenan, and nori sheets, as well as other forms of processing seaweed into food preparations. In plain English, this is not seaweed farming, trading, restaurant service, or general packaged-food retail. It is the industrial conversion of seaweed into recognizable food materials and processed edible products.

The scale profile is broad. The slim record opens this activity to Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so it is not confined to only one business size. A founder reading the code should see it as a production category that can sit across small, medium, or large operations, depending on the actual business structure and registration path. The common thread is the activity itself: processing seaweed into food products such as agar, carrageenan, and sheet nori. The code is therefore useful for businesses whose core registered activity is the making of these seaweed-derived foods, rather than merely handling seaweed as a raw commodity or selling finished goods made elsewhere.

Nationally, the investment signal is clear. Drawing on Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, the record classifies the activity as TERBUKA and sets pma_max_asing at 100. That means the national layer treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to 100%. On the national reading alone, a foreign-owned company would not be facing a foreign-shareholding cap inside this record. That national openness matters, but it is not the whole answer for a founder planning to register the activity in Bali.

The Bali position is the decisive constraint. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and gives the reason as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” It also states the moratorium rule directly: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest reading is simple: although KBLI 10798 is nationally foreign-open up to 100%, a foreigner cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today under the record’s Bali-side rule. The difference is not a Bali ownership percentage or a separate local cap; it is a registration block tied to the Bali moratorium and the risk class described in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: Although KBLI 10798 is nationally foreign-open up to 100%, a foreigner cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today.
