editorial.headline: The Wide, Practical World of Other Prepared Food Manufacturing
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10799 covers finished food products that sit outside narrower categories, and the record treats it as nationally foreign-open and not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10799 is a broad manufacturing home for prepared food products that are real, finished, and industrially identifiable, but not classified elsewhere in the record. Its scope stretches from soups and broths to imitation honey and caramel, from short-life foods such as sandwiches and raw pizza to collagen, cellulose, animal-intestine, and other sausage casings. It also includes probiotics, yeast, meat and seafood extracts and juices, egg products such as salted eggs and egg albumin, artificial concentrates such as essences, plant-protein food products, food additives derived from plants, animals, or microorganisms such as pectin, artificial sweeteners such as stevia, and other food products not already covered, including cincau.

The editorial importance of this code is its breadth. It is not describing a restaurant, a farm, or a trading activity; it is describing manufacturing: the making of food products. A founder would look here when the product is a prepared food item or ingredient-like food output that does not fit a narrower classification in the supplied scope. The record opens the activity across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the code is not presented as only a large-factory category or only a small-producer category; the slim record places the activity across the full scale ladder it provides.

Nationally, the investment picture is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives pma_max_asing as 100, so the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain English, the national line in the record is that PMA participation is open up to full foreign ownership. The supporting source named in the record is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no separate percentage, threshold, capital rule, timeline, licence, or tax position in the slim record, so none should be read into the classification.

Bali does not add a hidden ownership cap in this record. The Bali field is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and l4_bali_blocked is false. The reason is stated directly: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". That is the honest national-vs-Bali reading: this is nationally foreign-open, and the supplied Bali moratorium rule does not block PMA registration for this activity. The record’s Bali moratorium rule blocks all Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this activity is recorded as not blocked by that rule.
editorial.pullQuote: That is the honest national-vs-Bali reading: this is nationally foreign-open, and the supplied Bali moratorium rule does not block PMA registration for this activity.

editorial.headline: Animal Feed Rations With National PMA Access and No Bali Moratorium Block
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making of animal feed rations for pets and livestock, open across business scales and nationally available to foreign investment.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10801 is a manufacturing activity: the making of various animal feed rations, covering both pet animals and livestock. The record is deliberately broad, and that breadth matters. It does not narrow the activity to one species, one channel, or one production format; its defining feature is the preparation of rations used as animal feed. In plain English, this is the code for businesses whose core activity is producing formulated feed for animals, whether the market is companion animals or farm animals.

The registration picture is unusually wide on scale. The record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the activity is not framed only as a large industrial category in the slim record; it is available across the full listed scale ladder. For founders, this is the practical starting point: the same activity description can sit behind a small feed operation or a larger manufacturing business, as long as the registered business is genuinely engaged in making animal feed rations within the scope stated here.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position could not be clearer. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling shown in the record is 100%. The cited source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national reading supplied here, this is not a partially closed activity and the record does not impose a lower foreign-share cap. A foreign-owned company can therefore read the national layer as open, with the ownership ceiling expressed at the full percentage recorded.

Bali adds the important local test, but here it does not overturn the national opening. The province-wide moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, under the cited governor letter. This activity, however, is not marked as blocked in Bali. In Bali, it carries the status OK_or_HIGHER_RISK; the stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: nationally open to PMA, and not blocked by the Bali moratorium on the facts supplied in this record.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is therefore clean: nationally open to PMA, and not blocked by the Bali moratorium on the facts supplied in this record.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the manufacture of concentrated animal feed — both for pets and livestock. It includes processing that transforms raw agricultural materials into nutrient-dense feed mixes, typically done as a standalone industrial activity rather than on the farm itself.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, the government permits 100% foreign ownership for this business. In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Konsentrat Pakan Hewan (10802)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur aiming to produce specialized animal feed concentrates (for pets or farm animals) — provided they can set up in a region other than Bali where PMA is still allowed.

editorial.headline: Animal Feed Concentrate Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Viable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10802 covers the making of concentrated animal feed for pets and livestock, with access across all business scales and no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10802 is a manufacturing activity, not a trading label or a broad agricultural catch-all. Its subject is the making of animal feed concentrate: a formulated, concentrated input used for animals, whether the end market is companion animals or livestock. The record draws the activity around that act of production. It also marks an important boundary inside the scope itself: feed-concentrate processing that cannot be separated from animal husbandry is treated outside this activity. In practical terms, this code is for a business whose registered activity is the manufacture of the concentrate itself.

That manufacturing character matters because the record opens the activity to the full scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. The code is therefore not reserved in the record for one size of operator. A small producer, a medium industrial plant, or a larger manufacturing setup can all sit within the stated scale opening, provided the activity being registered remains the production of animal feed concentrate described in the scope. The editorial point is simple but useful: this code is about a specific product-making activity, and the record does not narrow it to a single business scale.

Nationally, the PMA picture is straightforward. Under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, the record classifies the activity as TERBUKA and sets pma_max_asing at 100. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national foreign-ownership ceiling shown in this record is 100%. There is no lower national cap stated here, and there is no additional condition in the slim record that should be invented around it. The national reading is therefore clean: foreign ownership is open up to the stated ceiling.

The Bali reading is also materially important, because Bali applies a province-side moratorium rule to certain PMA registrations. Here, however, the record does not mark KBLI 10802 as blocked. The l4_bali_blocked field is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason is given plainly: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. That means this record does not present the Bali moratorium as a barrier for this activity. The honest national-vs-Bali picture is therefore aligned: nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and not blocked for Bali PMA registration under the moratorium status recorded here.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the production of distilled alcoholic beverages (whiskey, brandy, gin, vodka, arak, soju, liqueurs, etc.), including blending and mixing to achieve specific ethanol levels, as well as the manufacture of neutral spirit.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Although Bali's local moratorium does not block this activity outright, the national investment regulation classifies it as completely closed to foreign ownership (TERTUTUP 0%). Therefore, a foreign-owned PMA company cannot register this KBLI in Bali—only a 100% Indonesian-owned entity is permitted.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Penyulingan, Pemurnian, dan Pencampuran Minuman Beralkohol (11010)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Closed. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.

editorial.headline: Distilled Spirits Production Is Closed to Foreign Ownership
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 11010 covers the making, purifying, and blending of distilled alcoholic drinks, but the record closes it to PMA ownership nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 11010 is a manufacturing code for distilled alcoholic beverages that are ready to drink.** Its scope covers the making of spirits through distillation or purification, whether the process is modern or traditional. The record’s examples are direct and specific: whisky, brandy, gin, vodka, tequila, arak, genever, soju, liqueurs, and mixed alcoholic drinks. It also covers the blending of distilled alcoholic beverages, or the mixing of raw beverage materials, to reach a desired ethanol level. Neutral alcoholic beverages without flavour are inside the same frame.

The code is therefore not a general drinks-trading label, and it is not a catch-all for every alcohol-related activity. The record draws the line around distillation, purification, blending, and neutral alcoholic-beverage production. It expressly leaves out alcohol made without distillation, synthetic ethyl alcohol, ethyl alcohol from fermented materials, and bottling or labelling when that activity belongs to wholesale trade or is done for a fee or contract. For a founder, the practical reading is simple: this code is about the industrial act of producing or blending distilled alcoholic beverages, not merely packaging, distributing, or handling them as a downstream service.

On scale, the record is broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all listed as open scales for this activity. That means the code is not framed only for a large factory profile; the official scale field spans the full ladder from micro through large enterprise. But scale openness is not the same thing as foreign-investment openness. Nationally, the PMA status is TERTUTUP, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 0%. The cited source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national record does not treat this as a foreign-owned business line. A foreign investor looking at this activity should read the zero ceiling as the central fact, not as a technical footnote.

Bali does not soften that picture. The Bali status is also TERTUTUP, and the record marks the activity as blocked for Bali PMA registration today. The Bali reason must be read carefully: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” That sentence says the Bali moratorium is not the operative reason at large scale, because the moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province. Even so, the result recorded here remains closed. The honest conclusion is therefore quiet but firm: KBLI 11010 describes a real distilled-spirits manufacturing activity across all business scales, yet it is not available as a foreign-owned registration route nationally or in Bali under this record.
editorial.pullQuote: The record does not treat distilled-spirits manufacturing as a foreign-owned business line; the zero ceiling is the central fact.

intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Minuman Beralkohol Hasil Fermentasi Anggur dan Hasil Pertanian Lainnya (11020)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Closed. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.

editorial.headline: Fermented Alcohol Manufacturing Is Closed to PMA Investors
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 11020 covers wine and other non-distilled fermented alcoholic drinks, but the record closes it to foreign ownership nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 11020 is the manufacturing home for alcoholic beverages made through fermentation rather than distillation. In plain English, the activity covers the making of wine from grapes and from other fruits, including still wine, sparkling wine, mead, fruit wine, rice wine, sticky-rice wine, brem Bali wine, vegetable wine, tuak, tonic wine, and sake. It also includes sparkling wine production, wine made from concentrated grape juice, non-distilled fermented drinks such as cider, perry, mead, other fruit wines, and alcoholic mixed beverages, as well as vermouth-like drinks, wine blending, and low-alcohol or non-alcoholic wine.

That scope matters because this is not merely a retail or hospitality label. The record is describing industrial production: the making, blending, and formulation of fermented beverage products. A founder using this code would be registering the manufacturing activity itself, across the four business scales listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. The scale range is broad, but the investment signal is not: broad scale availability does not make the activity open to foreign ownership.

Nationally, the record marks the PMA status as TERTUTUP, with `pma_max_asing` at 0. The practical reading is direct: this activity is closed to foreign ownership under the record supplied here. There is no percentage to optimize around, no partial foreign ceiling to structure up to, and no workaround implied by the listed business scales. The source field points to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, but the operative facts available in this slim record are the closed PMA status and the 0 foreign-ownership maximum.

Bali does not soften that conclusion. The Bali-side status is also TERTUTUP, and `l4_bali_blocked` is true, so a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today on the basis of this record. The record’s Bali reason states: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” Its moratorium field separately says that Bali province blocks all low and medium-low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently. Taken together, the honest editorial point is narrow and important: for KBLI 11020, the barrier is not a hidden Bali percentage or a local quota. The record simply closes the activity to PMA nationally and marks it closed in Bali as well.
editorial.pullQuote: For KBLI 11020, broad scale availability does not make the activity open to foreign ownership.

editorial.headline: Malt-Based Alcohol Production With a Clean National Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 11030 covers malt-based alcoholic beverages, from beer to stout, and the record marks it nationally open to foreign investment across every listed business scale.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 11030 is the manufacturing lane for alcoholic drinks made from malt.** The Indonesian scope names beer, ale, porter, and stout, and it also includes the making of beer with low alcohol or without alcohol. In plain English, this is not a bar, a distributor, or a hospitality activity; it is the activity of producing malt-based beverages themselves. The scope is narrow enough to be useful: it turns on the material and process described in the record, namely beverages made from malt, including the familiar beer-family styles named there.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** operators, so the classification is not reserved only for large producers. A founder reading the record should still keep the distinction clear: the scale field says who the activity is open to in the classification data, while the record does not add any separate operating licence, tax threshold, production limit, facility rule, or timeline. Those details cannot be assumed from this slim record. What can be said is that the activity is available across the full scale range listed in the record.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clean. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the maximum foreign ownership figure is **100%**, sourced in the record to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. That means the national field does not describe a partial cap for this activity; it records a full foreign-ownership ceiling. For a foreign-owned setup, that is the central national fact: the activity is marked open, and the ceiling shown in the record reaches one hundred percent.

The Bali reading is also important, but it should not be inflated beyond the record. Bali’s moratorium rule in the data says the province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, with the source listed as **Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP**. This record, however, marks **l4_bali_blocked** as false and gives the Bali status as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**. Its stated reason is: **OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium**. So the honest national-versus-Bali picture is not a contradiction. Nationally, the activity is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, this record does not mark it as blocked by the moratorium because of the risk-status reasoning stated above.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, the activity is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, this record does not mark it as blocked by the moratorium because of the risk-status reasoning stated above.

editorial.headline: Malt Production With a Clear PMA Path in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 11040 covers the industrial making of malt from barley, rye, or other cereals, and the record treats it as nationally open to foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
KBLI 11040 is about malt as an industrial ingredient, not the finished products that may later be made from it. The record defines the activity as the making of malt from barley, rye, or other cereals. In plain English, this is the processing step that turns cereal grain into malt: a specialised upstream activity for food, beverage, and ingredient supply chains. The scope is deliberately centred on malt production itself, while the record keeps downstream alcoholic drinks and malt extract or syrup products outside this activity.

For business registration, the scale position is unusually broad. The slim record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so the code is not framed only as a large industrial category. A small producer, a mid-sized processor, or a larger plant can all sit within the same activity description, provided the registered business is genuinely making malt from the cereals named in the scope. That matters because the code is defined by the production activity, not by a brand story, retail channel, or final consumer market.

The national investment picture is clean. The record marks the PMA status as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That means the national line, on this record, is not a partial foreign cap. A foreign-owned company can read the national entry as open up to full foreign ownership, without inventing an extra percentage, minimum capital rule, or licensing condition beyond what the record actually says.

The Bali picture is also not a hidden closure. The province-level moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. But this activity is marked `l4_bali_blocked: false`, with the reason stated as: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". So the honest reading is that KBLI 11040 is nationally open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the moratorium record provided here. The caveat is procedural discipline: do not turn that into a made-up Bali percentage, quota, partnership rule, or licence timeline. The Bali field says not blocked; it does not create a separate Bali ownership ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is that KBLI 11040 is nationally open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the moratorium record provided here.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers turning raw water into packaged drinking water that is ready to consume directly — still or sparkling, with or without added minerals, and possibly infused with oxygen or carbon dioxide. Essentially, it’s the industrial production of bottled water, mineral water, or enhanced water in sealed containers.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, a PMA can own 100% of this business. In Bali, it is not blocked by the moratorium, but it is flagged as medium-high to high risk. That means you can register a foreign company here, but approval is not automatic — the license will be location‑specific and subject to extra scrutiny on permits (like environmental impact and zoning) at the chosen address. It’s open but requires a higher‑compliance site.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Air Kemasan (11051)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur aiming to manufacture branded bottled still or sparkling water at scale in Bali, typically to supply hotels, restaurants, or retail channels directly from a local production facility.

editorial.headline: Packaged Drinking Water, Fully Open Nationally and Clear for Bali PMA
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 11051 covers the processing of raw water into packaged drinking water, with national PMA ownership open up to 100% and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 11051 is the industrial code for packaged drinking water. Its scope is the processing of raw water into drinking water that is packaged and ready for direct consumption. The record is broad on formulation: the finished product may contain minerals or not, may include added gas such as oxygen or carbon dioxide, and may also be produced with or without added minerals. The common thread is not the flavour profile or the marketing claim, but the activity itself: taking raw water through an industrial process so it becomes packaged drinking water ready to consume.

That makes this a practical manufacturing classification rather than a narrow product label. A business registering under this code is anchoring itself in the production of bottled or otherwise packaged drinking water, including mineral and non-mineral variants, still or gas-added versions, and mineral-added forms when those are part of the same processing activity. The available scale range is unusually straightforward in the slim record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all open. In plain English, the code is not confined to a single business size; the record allows it across the full stated scale ladder.

The national PMA position is equally clear. The record marks KBLI 11051 as TERBUKA and gives a pma_max_asing of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national foreign-ownership ceiling in this record is 100%. There is no lower national cap stated here, and no additional threshold, licence, capital rule, or timeline appears in the slim record, so none should be read into the classification. The national picture is open, and the ownership number is explicit.

The Bali-side reading does not reverse that conclusion. For Bali, l4_bali_blocked is recorded as false, while the status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. Its reason is specific: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this code is not marked as blocked. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: nationally, KBLI 11051 is open to PMA up to 100%; in Bali, the record does not show a moratorium block for PMA registration.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Refill Drinking Water, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 11052 covers refill drinking-water production through filtration, from manual depots to automatic tap water machines, and the record keeps both national PMA access and Bali treatment open.
editorial.body:
KBLI 11052 is a practical water-industry activity: the making of drinking water that can be consumed directly through refill depots, whether the depot is operated manually by people or through an automatic tap water machine. The record defines the work as processing raw water into drinking water using filtration equipment. That is the center of the activity, and it is also the limit of what can be said from the record: this code is about producing refill drinking water, not a broader packaged-beverage or distribution narrative.

The registration base is unusually broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the code is not confined to one business size. A small refill-water depot and a larger operation can both sit inside the same registered activity, provided the activity remains the one described in the scope: turning raw water into ready-to-drink refill water through filtration, with either manual or automatic filling. That breadth matters because the code reads less like a niche exception and more like an activity designed to cover the ordinary range of refill-drinking-water operations.

Nationally, the PMA picture is clean. Sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, the record classifies the activity as TERBUKA and sets pma_max_asing at 100. In plain English, the national record treats this KBLI as open to foreign ownership up to 100%. There is no lower foreign-equity ceiling in the slim record, and no additional national threshold, capital figure, permit condition, or timing rule is stated here. The honest national reading is therefore simple: for this activity, the record shows a fully open PMA position at national level.

Bali does not add a hidden percentage in this record. On the Bali fields, l4_bali_blocked is false, while the status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason given is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” That sits against the stated Bali moratorium rule, under which Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently. For this code, however, the record does not mark a Bali block. The accurate reading is that KBLI 11052 is nationally open to PMA and, on the Bali fields provided here, not blocked by the Bali moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Soft Drinks, Without the Bali Moratorium Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 11053 covers non-alcoholic soft-drink manufacturing, open across business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record provided.
editorial.body:
KBLI 11053 is the manufacturing category for soft drinks: beverages without alcohol, excluding non-alcoholic beer and non-alcoholic wine. In practical terms, the record places here the production of flavored and/or sweetened non-alcoholic drinks such as lemonade, orangeade, cola, fruit-flavored drinks, milk-flavored drinks, coffee-flavored drinks, tea-flavored drinks, and tonic water. It also includes other non-alcoholic beverages such as soy-based drinks, drinks made from fruit nectar, and powdered soft drinks.

That scope matters because this is not merely a retail label or a bottling activity. The activity is the making of the drink itself: formulating, producing, and bringing a non-alcoholic beverage product into industrial form. The record also draws the outer edge of the category by excluding several adjacent activities, including fruit and vegetable juice production, milk-based beverage manufacturing, tea, coffee and mate products, alcoholic beverages, non-alcoholic wine, non-alcoholic beer, edible ice for consumption, and standalone bottling or labelling when that work is part of wholesale trade or performed on a fee or contract basis.

On registration scale, the record is unusually broad. KBLI 11053 is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, which means the activity is not reserved in the slim record for only a narrow size of operator. A small producer of powdered soft drinks and a larger manufacturer of carbonated or flavored beverages sit inside the same activity description, provided the real business activity remains the manufacture of the covered non-alcoholic drink products.

The national foreign-investment picture is clean. The activity is recorded as TERBUKA, and pma_max_asing is set at 100, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the source. In plain English, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to 100%. The Bali picture is also not a moratorium block on this record: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the stated reason is “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The Bali moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, but this activity is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than blocked. So the honest reading is straightforward: a foreign-owned setup is nationally open, and the slim record does not mark it as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is straightforward: a foreign-owned setup is nationally open, and the slim record does not mark it as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This KBLI covers the production of non-factory-packaged beverages that don't fall under other drink manufacturing codes—think fresh coconut water, sugarcane juice, palm sap water, or traditional powdered drinks like sekoteng. It typically involves small-scale or artisanal preparation rather than mass bottling or canning.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this activity is fully open to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.

editorial.headline: Other Beverage Manufacturing, Without the Bali Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 11059 covers small-to-large production of other drinks, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 11059 is the catch-all space for beverage manufacturing that sits outside the more specifically named drink categories. In practical terms, the record points to the making of other drinks that are typically not packaged through factory-style production: palm sap water, sugarcane juice, coconut water, and sekoteng powder. The common thread is not a single ingredient, but a production activity: turning these drink products into a business line that needs to be registered under an industrial beverage classification.

The scale position is unusually broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so this is not written only for a large plant or only for a household-style producer. It can describe a small producer formalising a local drink operation, a growing medium enterprise, or a larger manufacturer, provided the registered activity remains within the scope of these other beverage products. That breadth matters because the code is not merely about what is sold; it is about the production activity that the business is declaring to OSS.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The PMA status is marked TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In plain English, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to full foreign control. There is no separate capital threshold, licence condition, operating timeline, or special tax rule in the slim record, so none should be read into it. The useful conclusion is narrower and stronger: for this activity code, the national investment field says open, and the ownership ceiling field says 100%.

The Bali reading is also clear, but it needs precision. Bali province has a moratorium rule that blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently. This record, however, does not mark KBLI 11059 as blocked in Bali. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with the reason stated as: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is not a hidden Bali percentage or a local partnership condition. It is simpler: nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, and, on this record, not blocked by the Bali moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the manual production of kretek cigarettes—a blend of chopped tobacco, cloves, and flavorings—hand-rolled using ambri, paper, or tipping wrappers. It includes both standard hand-rolled kretek (SKT) and those with a filter tip. The activity is strictly about the craftsmanship-intensive rolling process, not machine-made varieties.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this business line is fully open to 100% foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: matched with aggregation.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Sigaret Kretek Tangan (12001)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur with deep tobacco-industry experience looking to produce artisanal, hand-rolled kretek at scale—but who must set up outside Bali or explore domestic partnership structures.

editorial.headline: Hand-Rolled Kretek Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 12001 covers manual kretek cigarette production, nationally open to foreign ownership and not marked as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 12001 is a tightly defined manufacturing activity: the making of **hand-rolled kretek cigarettes**. The record describes a product built from chopped tobacco, chopped kerosok, chopped cloves, and added flavouring materials, producing the distinctive aromatic kretek mixture. Its defining feature is not only the blend, but the method: the cigarettes are rolled manually by hand, using wrapping materials such as ambri, papir, or tipping.

The scope also reaches both ordinary hand-rolled kretek cigarettes and filtered hand-rolled kretek cigarettes. That matters because the code is not framed as tobacco trading, retailing, or general cigarette activity. It is about the production process itself: preparing the kretek mixture and turning it into manually rolled cigarettes within the boundaries stated in the record. A founder using this code should therefore read it as a manufacturing classification for the specific hand-rolled kretek line described, not as a wider commercial umbrella.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It is open to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** operators. In practical classification terms, that means the activity is not reserved in the record for only one business size. A small producer and a larger industrial operator are both within the scale range, provided the registered activity is still the hand-rolled kretek manufacturing activity described here. The code’s editorial centre is therefore clear: a manual kretek manufacturing business, available across the full scale ladder listed in the slim record.

The national-vs-Bali picture is also clean. Nationally, the PMA status is **TERBUKA**, with `pma_max_asing` at **100%**, based on **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. Bali does not add a separate foreign-ownership percentage in this record, and the record does **not** mark the activity as blocked for PMA registration in Bali. Its Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, with the reason given as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The Bali moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently; here, the recorded Bali reason places this activity outside that block.
editorial.pullQuote: This code is nationally open to full foreign ownership, and the Bali record does not mark it as blocked for PMA registration.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the industrial production of machine-rolled kretek cigarettes, using a mix of shredded tobacco, cloves, and flavoring, wrapped automatically in paper or tipping. It includes both regular and filter machine-made kretek cigarettes.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: A foreign-owned PMA can legally pursue this cigarette manufacturing in Bali—it is not blocked by the local moratorium. Because the activity is classified as medium-high to high risk, you will need a verified commercial address and must pass stricter regulatory checks, but registration is permitted.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: code renumbered.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Sigaret Kretek Mesin (12002)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: This fits a foreign entrepreneur with deep tobacco-industry experience who wants to set up a large-scale, mechanized kretek factory in Bali for export or the domestic market.

editorial.headline: Machine-Made Kretek Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers automated kretek cigarette production, including filtered variants, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
Machine-made kretek manufacturing is a precise industrial activity: the making of kretek cigarettes from chopped tobacco, chopped kerosok, chopped cloves, and additional flavouring ingredients that produce the characteristic aromatic blend. The defining feature is not just the product, but the method. The cigarettes are rolled automatically by machine, using wrapping materials named in the record as ambri, papir, or tipping. The scope also expressly includes both machine-made kretek cigarettes and machine-made filtered kretek cigarettes.

That makes this a manufacturing registration rather than a retail, trading, or hospitality category. The record points to production: ingredients are combined, the blend is formed, and the cigarette is machine-rolled into its finished format. A founder choosing this activity should be describing an operation built around making the product itself. The scale picture is unusually broad: the record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In plain terms, the activity is not framed only for large factories; the registration field is available across the scale ladder named in the record.

The national investment picture is also clear. The activity is marked TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling in the record is 100%. That means the national field, as captured here, is fully open to foreign ownership rather than capped below full foreign participation. The legal source cited for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no basis in this record to add a special minimum capital figure, a licence timeline, a tobacco-specific filing sequence, or a separate operating threshold; those details are simply not present in the slim record and should not be inferred.

For Bali, the important point is that the record does not mark this activity as blocked. Bali’s moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, but this activity is recorded with the status OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason given is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” So the honest reading is not a contradiction between national openness and a Bali prohibition. It is nationally open, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, and the Bali-side record says it is not blocked by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is simple: this activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, and the Bali record does not block it under the moratorium.

editorial.headline: White-Cigarette Manufacturing Without the Bali Barrier
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 12003 covers non-clove cigarette manufacturing, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 12003 is a manufacturing category with a narrow, concrete center of gravity: the making of cigarettes or sigarettes that do not contain clove components.** The record’s Indonesian scope is brief, but it is enough to separate this activity from broader tobacco language: this is not a general trading label, not a retail label, and not a catch-all for every tobacco-related business. It is an industrial activity, concerned with producing a specific type of cigarette product, defined by the absence of clove content.

That manufacturing character matters because the record opens the activity across the full registered business-size range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practical classification terms, this means the code is not reserved only for a large industrial operator in the way many founders might instinctively assume from the word “industry.” The record allows it to sit at every listed scale. The editorial point is not that every scale will look operationally identical, but that the slim record itself does not close the category to smaller registered scales. Anyone reading this code should therefore begin with the activity definition and the registered scale, rather than importing assumptions from the product’s commercial sensitivity.

Nationally, the ownership picture is unusually clean in the record. The PMA status is marked TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership value is 100%. That means the national line, as stated here, is full foreign openness for this activity code. There is no lower foreign-share cap in the slim record, and no invented threshold should be added to it. The cited PMA source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, but the operative editorial conclusion from the record is simpler: for KBLI 12003, the national classification does not itself impose a foreign-ownership ceiling below full ownership.

Bali is also clear, but for a different reason. The province’s moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently. This code, however, is not marked as blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is precise and should be kept precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” So the honest national-versus-Bali picture is not a hidden contradiction. Nationally, it is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, the record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium logic because the recorded large-scale OSS risk sits above the blocked Low and Medium-Low band.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest picture is simple: nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, and not blocked in Bali under the moratorium logic recorded here.

editorial.standfirst: KBLI 12004 covers the drying and cutting of tobacco leaves, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.

The record’s Indonesian scope is practical rather than decorative. The registered scale still has to match the real business being declared, but the slim record itself does not exclude any of the listed scales.

Nationally, the PMA picture is clear. The record marks the activity as **TERBUKA**, with `pma_max_asing` at **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. editorial.headline: The Quiet Industrial Craft Behind Cigarette Seasoning
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 12005 covers the making of cigarette flavoring materials, with national PMA access open across every business scale and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
KBLI 12005 sits inside a narrow but technically important corner of tobacco manufacturing: the making of **bumbu rokok**, the flavoring and seasoning inputs used in cigarettes. The slim record names cigarette or tobacco sauce and cigarette capsules as examples, which is enough to define the activity without overstating it. This is not the retailing of cigarettes, not plantation work, and not a broader tobacco category. Its center of gravity is production: the preparation of the flavoring materials that shape the finished cigarette experience before the product reaches any consumer-facing channel.

For founders, the practical classification point is that this code is open across the full scale ladder recorded in the data: **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**. That matters because the same activity can appear in very different forms, from a smaller production setup to a larger industrial operation. The record does not attach extra thresholds, licence names, capital figures, or technical conditions to those scales, so none should be assumed. The clean reading is simply that the activity is registerable across all four stated business scales, with the commercial substance remaining the manufacture of cigarette seasoning inputs such as tobacco sauces and capsules.

The national PMA picture is also unusually direct. The record marks the activity as **TERBUKA**, with `pma_max_asing` at **100**. In plain English, the national foreign-ownership ceiling is **100%**. The source line given for that national position is **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. There is no capped minority position in the slim record, and no special national percentage below full ownership. For a foreign-owned company assessing this activity at the national level, the core fact is therefore openness: the classification is not nationally closed to PMA, and the recorded ceiling allows full foreign ownership.

editorial.headline: Other Tobacco Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 12009 covers defined tobacco-product manufacturing, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 12009 is the manufacturing home for tobacco products that sit outside the main named categories while still being precisely defined. The Indonesian scope is not vague: it covers the making of other tobacco products, including cigars, kretek cigars, kelembak kemenyan cigarettes, kelobot cigarettes, and kawung cigarettes. It also includes prepared tobacco formats such as fine-cut tobacco, pipe tobacco, snuff, homogenised or reconstituted tobacco, molasses tobacco, chewing tobacco, and nicotine pouches. The word "other" therefore needs careful reading. It does not turn the code into a general tobacco business label; it points to a specific production activity around the product forms listed in the record.

The scale position is unusually broad. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar registrations, so the record does not reserve it only for large industrial operators. A small maker and a larger manufacturer both sit within the scale language, as long as the registered activity remains the making of these covered tobacco products. That distinction matters editorially because the scope is about production. It is not framed here as retailing, distribution, marketing, or a broad commercial identity around tobacco; the centre of gravity is the manufacture of the listed products themselves.

Nationally, the foreign investment position is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership figure supplied in the record is 100%. In plain English, the national data does not place a foreign equity cap below full ownership for this activity. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, and there is no second national number to balance against it. For a founder reading this classification, the important point is that the national foreign-ownership ceiling is complete, not partial, according to the slim record.

Bali does not introduce a separate percentage in this record, and it should not be described as if it does. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the code is not marked as blocked. The reason given is: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium." The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this activity is recorded outside that block. The result is an aligned national-versus-Bali reading: open nationally up to 100% foreign ownership, and not blocked by Bali's PMA moratorium on the record supplied.

editorial.headline: Textile Fibre Preparation Before the Fabric Begins
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 13111 covers the industrial preparation of textile fibres, open nationally to foreign ownership and not blocked for Bali PMA registration under the record’s risk reading.
editorial.body:
KBLI 13111 sits at the beginning of the textile chain: before fabric is woven, knitted, finished, or sold, the fibre itself has to be made workable. The record defines this activity as the preparation of textile fibres across several material families. It includes scutching ramie fibre, twisting or winding and washing silk fibre, removing grease from wool, carbonising wool, dyeing sheep wool, and the separation, carding, and combing of fibres from animal hair, plant sources, and synthetic or artificial materials.

That makes this a technical processing category, not a retail or design label. Its centre of gravity is the conversion of raw or semi-raw fibre into a cleaner, more aligned, more usable input for later textile production. The scope is broad in material terms: animal-derived fibre, plant fibre, and man-made fibre all appear inside the record. But the activity remains specific in function. It is about preparation: cleaning, separating, aligning, winding, washing, dyeing where stated, and making fibre ready for the next industrial step.

On registration scale, the record is unusually clear. KBLI 13111 is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In plain English, the activity is not reserved in the record for only a small workshop profile or only an industrial-scale operator. A micro or small fibre-preparation business can sit under it, as can a medium or large enterprise, provided the registered activity is genuinely the preparation of textile fibre described in the scope. The scale openness matters because this is the kind of activity that can range from specialised fibre handling to more substantial industrial preparation, while still remaining within the same recorded activity frame.

The national foreign-investment picture is also clear. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with `pma_max_asing` at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. So nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling shown in the record is 100%. Bali does not add a separate percentage here. The Bali-side record marks the status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with `l4_bali_blocked` set to false. The reason given is precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this activity is not blocked under the record’s Bali reading because of that higher-risk classification at large scale. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: KBLI 13111 is nationally foreign-open at the recorded ceiling, open across all listed business scales, and not blocked for Bali PMA registration by the moratorium as recorded.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is therefore clean: KBLI 13111 is nationally foreign-open at the recorded ceiling, open across all listed business scales, and not blocked for Bali PMA registration by the moratorium as recorded.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Industrial Yarn Spinning With a Clear Bali Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 13112 covers the spinning and processing of non-sewing yarn, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 13112 is the industrial activity of turning fibre into yarn, with one important boundary: it excludes sewing thread. The record describes a broad textile-manufacturing scope, beginning with the spinning of fibres into yarn from many kinds of raw material, whether new or recycled. It also includes the technical finishing steps that make yarn commercially usable in different textile contexts: texturizing, twisting, folding, cabling, and the covering or dipping of synthetic and artificial yarn. Even paper yarn sits inside the same activity field.

That breadth matters because this is not framed as a narrow craft category. It is the upstream production of yarn itself: the material that later becomes fabric, components, or other textile goods. The activity is open across the full business-scale ladder recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practical classification terms, that means the code is not reserved only for one size of operator. The same KBLI can describe a small spinning operation or a larger industrial facility, provided the declared activity remains within the recorded scope of non-sewing yarn and the listed processing steps.

Nationally, the investment position is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives a pma_max_asing of 100, which means the foreign-ownership ceiling should be read as 100%. There is no partial foreign cap in the slim record, and no extra capital threshold, licence condition, or operational timetable is stated here. The national source named for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned company, the important conclusion is simple: at the national level, this activity is open rather than closed or capped below full foreign ownership.

Bali is equally clear-cut, although the basis for that conclusion is different. Bali’s moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. This code, however, is not marked as blocked in Bali. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason given is precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. So the honest reading is not that Bali creates a separate percentage, quota, or partnership condition. It does not, in this record. The record says the Bali moratorium does not block this PMA registration because the relevant large-scale OSS risk sits in the medium-high or high-risk band rather than the blocked low-risk bands.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is not that Bali creates a separate percentage, quota, or partnership condition; it is that the moratorium does not block this PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Thread Sewing Yarn With a Full National Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 13113 covers the making and finishing of sewing thread, open across business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record provided.
editorial.body:
KBLI 13113 is a narrow but important textile-manufacturing activity: the making of sewing thread. The record describes production from either fibre or yarn as raw material, then includes the finishing and engineering steps that turn that input into usable sewing thread: texturizing, twisting, folding, cabling, and covering or dipping. In plain English, this is not general garment work or fabric retail. It is the industrial preparation of the thread itself, including the treatments that give sewing thread its strength, texture, ply, finish, and practical performance.

The activity is open across the full scale spectrum shown in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because it frames the code as usable not only for a large spinning or finishing operation, but also for smaller manufacturing setups whose declared activity is genuinely the production or processing of sewing thread. The key editorial point is precision. A founder should read this as a manufacturing classification for thread-making and thread-finishing work, not as a broad textile label that can casually absorb adjacent activities.

Nationally, the record is straightforward: the PMA status is TERBUKA, and the listed foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That means the national field supplied here marks the activity as open to foreign investment up to full foreign ownership. The source named in the record is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the slim record adds a separate licence, threshold, timeline, tax treatment, or capital rule, so none should be inferred from this classification note.

The Bali picture is also clean, but it needs to be stated carefully. The record does not mark the activity as blocked in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason given is: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently; this record’s Bali-side reason says this activity is not caught by that block. So the honest reading is that KBLI 13113 is nationally foreign-open and, on the supplied Bali fields, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers machine weaving of textiles using various materials—from natural fibers like cotton, silk, or wool to synthetic, recycled textile waste, paper, or glass fiber—to produce woven fabrics on powered looms.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: matched with aggregation.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Pertenunan Tekstil dengan Mesin (13121)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur looking to set up a textile weaving factory using machine looms and diverse raw materials.

editorial.headline: Machine Weaving for Textiles Is Open, Including in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 13121 covers machine-based textile weaving across new, recovered, and specialty fibres, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 13121 is the industrial activity of weaving textiles with machine looms.** The Indonesian scope describes *pertenunan tekstil dengan alat tenun mesin*, meaning textile weaving carried out using mechanical weaving equipment rather than a handloom-only or purely artisanal framing. Its material range is broad: new materials, recovered materials, silk, cotton, wool, plant fibres, artificial fibres, paper fibre, glass fibre, recovered textile waste, and new textile fibre all sit within the record’s stated scope.

That breadth matters because the code is not written around a single fabric, fashion niche, or end product. It is about the weaving activity itself: transforming permitted textile inputs into woven textile output by machine. A founder registering under this activity should therefore read the code through the production process first, then through the materials used. The record supports a textile-weaving business that may work with conventional fibres as well as recovered or specialised fibres, provided the activity remains machine-based textile weaving.

On business scale, the record is unusually straightforward. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practical registration terms, that means the activity is not reserved only for a narrow enterprise band in the slim record: micro, small, medium, and large operators all appear in the permitted scale list. That does not create extra obligations or approvals by itself; it simply tells us that the classification is available across the listed business scales.

The national-versus-Bali picture is also clean. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, sourced in the record to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali does not add a separate percentage in this record. Instead, the Bali field marks the code as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with the stated reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently, but this code is not marked as blocked. The honest conclusion is therefore simple: on the record provided, a foreign-owned setup can register this activity nationally and is not blocked by the Bali moratorium.
