editorial.headline: A Quietly Broad Category for Unusual Footwear Manufacturing
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 15209 covers footwear made beyond the standard categories, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the slim record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 15209 sits in the manufacturing world, but its centre of gravity is not ordinary footwear. The slim record defines it as the making of other footwear not already captured by the standard footwear manufacturing categories, with examples such as shoes made from banana-stem sheaths and water hyacinth. It also includes gaiters and similar goods. In practical English, this is a category for footwear production that is still industrial, still product-based, and still clearly about making wearable foot-related goods, but which does not fall into the more conventional footwear lanes.

That makes the code particularly relevant for founders working with alternative materials, craft-linked production, or niche footwear formats that need a formal industrial classification. The record is explicit that the activity is open across all business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because it means the classification is not written only for large factories or only for small workshops. A modest producer and a larger manufacturing operation can both sit within the scale language of the record, provided the actual activity remains inside this specific scope.

Nationally, the PMA position is clean. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 is cited for the record’s TERBUKA status and its pma_max_asing of 100. In plain terms, the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no basis in the slim record to add a hidden sectoral cap, special licence, minimum capital figure, or extra ownership condition. The responsible reading is therefore narrow but clear: as a national investment classification, this activity is foreign-open up to the stated ceiling.

The Bali picture is also unusually direct. The record does not mark the activity as blocked in Bali. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this entry is not captured as blocked by that rule. So the honest conclusion is not that Bali adds a separate foreign-ownership percentage, quota, or partnership condition. The record simply says this code is not blocked by the Bali moratorium, while preserving the national 100% ceiling as the only ownership percentage given.
editorial.pullQuote: The responsible reading is narrow but clear: nationally foreign-open, and not marked as blocked by Bali’s moratorium in the slim record.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Sawn Timber Is Nationally Open, but Bali Blocks PMA Registration
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16101 covers the primary conversion of logs into worked timber, with all business scales listed nationally, yet Bali blocks PMA registration under its risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16101 is the industrial first step between a felled log and usable timber. The record describes sawmilling, slicing, debarking, cutting, and planing logs into beams, rafters, battens, and boards. It also reaches more finished forms of prepared board, including surfaced-four-sides timber and boards with eased edges on two or four corners. The scope is still timber preparation rather than assembled furniture or a downstream installation trade: it is about turning raw logs into standardized wooden material that other industries can use.

The activity is broad enough to include several practical outputs beyond ordinary planks. The record names timber for railway sleepers, unassembled wooden flooring, and pencil-slat raw material. That matters because the code is not just a small workshop category for rough sawing. It can describe a timber-processing operation whose commercial product is already shaped, smoothed, or specified for later industrial use, provided the activity remains within the recorded conversion and preparation of logs into wood components.

Nationally, the picture is straightforward. The PMA status is recorded as open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, and the source given is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The scales open to the activity are Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so the record does not confine the code to a single size of enterprise. On the national reading alone, a foreign-owned company can treat this as an open timber-processing activity, subject only to the facts stated in the record and without any extra threshold or licensing condition invented around it.

Bali changes the answer. The record marks the Bali status as Blocked (risk class) and says the code is blocked there for PMA registration. Its stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule is also explicit: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. So the honest advice is not that the national 100% ceiling disappears, or that Bali applies a separate percentage. It is simpler and stricter: nationally open does not mean registrable by a foreign-owned company in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open does not mean registrable by a foreign-owned company in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Wood Preservation Is Nationally Open, but Bali Blocks PMA
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16102 covers wood preservation by drying, chemical treatment, or soaking; nationally it is open to 100% foreign ownership, while Bali blocks PMA registration under its risk moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16102 is the activity of preserving wood. The Indonesian scope describes preservation through drying, chemical treatment, and soaking wood with preservatives or other materials. That definition is the center of the code. It points to a treatment activity rather than a vague label around wood. For a founder, the useful reading is narrow: if the business is built around extending the usable life of wood through the methods named in the record, this is the activity the record is describing. The scope keeps the editorial lens on process: drying, chemical treatment, and soaking are not examples added for color; they are the actual boundaries supplied by the slim record.

The scale picture is broad without being vague. The record opens 16102 to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar undertakings, so it is not confined in the record to a narrow operator size. Those scale names are the only scale facts available here; there is no threshold, timeline, or capital figure in the record. At the national PMA layer, the record is also direct: pma_status is TERBUKA and pma_max_asing is 100. In plain English, the national record treats wood preservation under this code as open to foreign ownership up to 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 given as the source.

The Bali reading is the point that changes the conclusion. The national door is open, but Bali has closed the registration route for PMA. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and gives the reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, which is blocked by the Bali moratorium of May 2026. The moratorium rule supplied with the record is blunt: Bali province blocks Low and Medium-Low risk PMA registration island-wide and permanently. This is exactly the national-vs-Bali split founders miss when they stop reading after the national PMA line.

That is a Bali-side block, not a separate Bali foreign-ownership percentage, and the record gives no Bali cap to quote. A founder looking only at the national investment line would see an open PMA category with a 100% ceiling. The same founder looking at Bali must stop at the provincial layer: for PMA registration on the island, the record says blocked because of the risk-class moratorium. This distinction matters because the record does not convert a 100% national ceiling into a smaller Bali ceiling. It creates a different answer at the provincial registration layer: open nationally, blocked for PMA in Bali. In Bali, under this record, a foreign-owned company cannot register this activity as PMA.
editorial.pullQuote: The national door is open, but Bali has closed the registration route for PMA.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Rattan and Bamboo Preservation Meets Bali’s PMA Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16103 is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but the record blocks PMA registration for this activity in Bali.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 16103 covers a narrow but important industrial activity: preserving rattan, bamboo, and similar materials.** The record’s scope is deliberately concise. It does not describe furniture making, trading, harvesting, construction, or downstream craft production. It points to the preservation activity itself: treating or maintaining rattan, bamboo, and similar materials so they can remain usable within the wider material and manufacturing chain.

That clarity matters because this is not a code reserved for only one business scale. The slim record marks it open to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**. In practical registry terms, the activity can be held by operators from micro businesses through large-scale enterprises, provided the registration follows the scale and structure reflected in the record. Nothing in the record adds a special threshold, licence, capital minimum, or operational condition beyond those scale categories, so none should be read into it.

Nationally, the investment picture is straightforward. The record marks the activity as **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. On the national reading, then, a PMA structure is not capped below full foreign ownership. This is the clean national signal: for KBLI 16103, the record allows full foreign participation at the national level.

Bali changes the outcome. The record marks the Bali status as **Blocked (risk class)** and sets **l4_bali_blocked** to true. Its recorded reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule is broader and sharper: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. So the honest conclusion is not that this activity is nationally closed. It is nationally open, even to 100% foreign ownership, but a foreigner cannot register this KBLI for a PMA setup in Bali under the Bali-side block recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 16103 is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but the Bali record turns that openness into a practical PMA block on the island.

editorial.headline: Rattan Processing With a National Green Light and a Bali Stop Sign
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16104 covers the processing of rattan into semi-finished materials, open nationally to all business scales but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16104 is a production code for the processing of rattan into semi-finished material. The record names polished rattan, rattan core, and rattan skin as examples, which places the activity in the middle of the value chain rather than at the retail or finished-goods end. Its commercial logic is practical: taking raw rattan and preparing it into usable inputs for the next stage of manufacture.

That scope matters because this is not presented as a narrow boutique activity. The record opens it across every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In registration terms, the code can sit with a small local operator as well as a larger industrial setup, so long as the activity remains within the stated processing field: turning rattan into semi-finished materials such as polished rattan, core, and skin.

Nationally, the PMA picture is straightforward. The code is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national reading alone, that is a clean foreign-investment signal: the record does not show a reduced equity cap, a special threshold, or a partial foreign limit. A foreign-owned company looking only at the national PMA status would see an activity that is open.

Bali changes the answer completely. The Bali-side status is Blocked (risk class), and the record states that the activity is blocked for PMA because the OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, bringing it under the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026. The moratorium rule is broader than this single activity: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. The honest reading is therefore split but not ambiguous: KBLI 16104 is nationally open to foreign ownership up to 100%, yet a foreigner cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali under the record provided.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is split but not ambiguous: nationally open, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Wood Particle Manufacturing Is Nationally Open, but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16105 covers wood particles, wood flour, wood wool, and woodchips, with all business scales listed nationally but PMA registration blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16105 is a manufacturing code for making wood particles and similar wood-derived materials. The record describes a scope that includes wood wool, wood flour, and sliced or chipped wood, including woodchips. In plain English, this is not a furniture, retail, or forestry-harvesting description; it is the industrial activity of turning wood into particle-form inputs and related materials. The emphasis is on production: taking wood and processing it into forms that can be used as industrial feedstock, components, or intermediate material.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The slim record lists this activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses. That means the code is not reserved in the record for only one size of operator. A small production setup and a larger industrial facility both sit within the scale language supplied here, provided the registered activity remains inside the stated scope: particle wood and comparable products such as wood wool, wood flour, and woodchips. The editorial point is that scale does not narrow the code; the activity definition does.

Nationally, the PMA picture looks open. According to the record, PMA is marked TERBUKA, with a pma_max_asing of 100 and Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as its source. Rendered plainly, the national foreign-ownership ceiling in this record is 100%. On the national reading alone, a foreign-owned company is not capped below full ownership by the field supplied here. There is no extra threshold, minimum capital, licensing condition, or timeline in the slim record, so none should be added to the interpretation.

Bali changes the practical answer. The same record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and gives the Bali status as Blocked (risk class). Its reason is specific: OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, which places the activity inside the Bali moratorium. The moratorium rule supplied in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest national-vs-Bali conclusion is sharp: KBLI 16105 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, but a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today under the Bali-side record provided.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 16105 is nationally open to foreign ownership, but the Bali record turns that openness into a registration block for PMA on the island.

editorial.headline: Plywood Manufacturing: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16211 covers the industrial making of plywood, from ordinary panels to laminated and construction-grade sheets, but Bali blocks PMA registration for it today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16211 is the plywood-manufacturing category: the industrial making of ordinary plywood such as tripleks, multiplex, interior plywood, and exterior plywood. Its scope also reaches construction plywood, including concrete-form plywood and waterproof plywood, which places the activity in the practical world of panels made for building, finishing, and repeated physical use. The record is broad but still specific: it is about making plywood, not trading it, designing interiors with it, or handling forestry upstream.

The category also includes laminated plywood, including laminated teak plywood, laminated rosewood plywood, polyester plywood, and decorative plywood. That matters because the code is not limited to basic sheet production. It can cover higher-finish panels where the surface treatment is part of the manufactured product. The scope extends further to plywood, including laminated plywood, made from bamboo, rattan, and similar materials. In plain English, this is a manufacturing code for turning wood or comparable plant-based material into layered panel products, from utilitarian construction sheets to decorative laminated boards.

The national picture is clear. Nationally, the record designates the activity as TERBUKA and lists a pma_max_asing of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national classification shown here allows full foreign ownership, and the activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. Those scale labels are important because the record does not reserve the activity only for large manufacturers; it shows the category open across the full listed scale range.

Bali is the hard stop. The record says l4_bali_blocked is true and gives the reason: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule is also explicit: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” So the honest conclusion is not that this plywood category is nationally closed; it is nationally open. The problem is local registration in Bali. A foreigner cannot register this KBLI for PMA in Bali today under the Bali-side rule recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: This plywood category is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s moratorium turns that national openness into a local PMA block.

l4_bali.reason: Not among the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026. The low/medium-low risk tier was named only in the Governor's January 2026 request letter (B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP); check the risk tier and zoning on OSS before filing.

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)

editorial.headline: Veneer Manufacturing Is Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Veneer manufacturing is nationally foreign-open up to 100%, but this record blocks PMA registration in Bali under the province's risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16212 is a narrow industrial activity: it covers the making of veneer, the thin facing layer described in the record as serutan pelapis, produced by rotary peeling, slicing, or similar methods. The Indonesian scope is compact, but its meaning is exact. This is the manufacturing step itself, not a broader promise about trading, downstream products, or related industries that are not named in the slim record. For a founder, the important discipline is to keep the registration aligned with the recorded act of production: veneer made through peeling, slicing, and comparable processes.

The scale position is broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so the code is not presented here as belonging only to one size of operator. That does not create any extra capital figure, threshold, permit, or timeline; the slim record gives scale categories and nothing more. It says this activity can sit across the listed scale ladder, while leaving every other business condition outside the text. The editorial reading should therefore stay clean: the activity is veneer manufacturing, and the record recognises it across all four stated scales.

Nationally, the PMA line is straightforward. The activity is marked TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with the source given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national record treats this veneer-manufacturing activity as foreign-open up to full foreign ownership. That is the national picture only. It should not be diluted into a maybe-open reading, and it should not be inflated into wider claims about licences, taxes, operational permissions, or processing timeframes that the record does not contain.

Bali changes the answer. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and the Bali status as Blocked (risk class). The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, placing the activity inside Bali's PMA moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, with the source named as Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. A foreign-owned company may see national openness for KBLI 16212, but it cannot register this activity in Bali under the Bali-side rule recorded here.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16213 covers laminated wood production such as barecore, blockboard, and lamin board, with a clear national opening but a Bali registration block for PMA.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16213 is the industrial activity for making laminated wood. The record defines its scope as the manufacture of laminated wood products such as barecore, blockboard, and lamin board. In plain English, this is not general timber trading or a broad furniture category; it is a manufacturing classification for engineered wood panels and related laminated wood formats. The activity sits in the productive middle of the wood-processing chain, where raw or semi-processed wood is turned into layered, bonded material for further use.

The registration picture is broad at the scale level. The record opens the activity to Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so the code is not framed as a single-size industrial activity. Small, medium, and large businesses can all appear in the scale field for this KBLI. That matters because the business description should match the real operation: a company making laminated wood products under this classification is registering a manufacturing activity, not merely describing a downstream sales channel or a vague wood-products business.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national record alone, this reads as an activity open to foreign ownership up to the full stated ceiling. There is no lower national cap in the slim record, and no additional national threshold, licence, timeline, or capital condition is provided here. The honest national summary is therefore simple: KBLI 16213 is nationally open for PMA, with the record showing a 100% maximum foreign-ownership figure.

Bali changes the practical answer. The record marks this activity as l4_bali_blocked: true, with the Bali status Blocked (risk class). The stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently, with the source listed as Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. So the correct investor-facing reading is not that Bali has a separate percentage cap. It is sharper than that: despite the national PMA opening, a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali under the Bali-side block recorded here.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

l4_bali.reason: Not among the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026. The low/medium-low risk tier was named only in the Governor's January 2026 request letter (B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP); check the risk tier and zoning on OSS before filing.

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)

editorial.headline: Other Wood Panels: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16219 covers engineered wood-panel manufacturing, open nationally to foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the recorded moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16219 is the manufacturing category for other wood panels: engineered sheets made from wood fibre, particles, strands, chips, or honeycomb structures. The record names fibreboard explicitly, including low density fibreboard, medium density fibreboard, and high density fibreboard, alongside particle board, oriented strand board, chip board, and honeycomb board. In plain English, this is not furniture making or timber trading; it is the industrial production of panel materials that other builders, fabricators, or manufacturers may later use.

The activity is open across the scales listed in the record: Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the code is not framed as a narrow large-factory category only; the record presents it as available to small, medium, and large operators. For founders, the practical reading is that the code can describe a range of wood-panel production setups, from smaller manufacturing operations to larger industrial facilities, as long as the registered activity is genuinely the making of these panel products.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership figure in the record is 100%, with the cited national basis being Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national layer alone, that means the code is recorded as foreign-open, with no lower ownership ceiling shown in the slim record. There is no basis here to invent a special licence, capital threshold, tax condition, or extra timing rule; the record gives the national opening, the ownership ceiling, the source, and the permitted scales.

Bali is the decisive complication. The record marks this activity as blocked for PMA registration in Bali, with the status Blocked (risk class). The stated reason is precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule is also stated directly: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest reading is this: KBLI 16219 may be nationally foreign-open, but a foreigner cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali today under the record provided.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 16219 may be nationally foreign-open, but a foreigner cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali today under the record provided.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Wood Building Components: Reserved to Domestic Capital, and Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers wooden construction components across all business scales — foreign shareholding is 0%, and Bali's risk-class moratorium blocks PMA registration on top of that.
editorial.body:
This is a manufacturing activity built around wood as a construction material. The scope covers wooden building materials used mainly for construction: beams, rafters, roof frames finished on all four sides, and supporting posts made from finger-jointed wood with adhesive or connected with metal. It also reaches the more visible architectural elements of a building: doors, windows, shutters, frames, stairs, stair rails, wooden mouldings, wooden shingles, parquet blocks and strips assembled into panels from solid wood or engineering wood, decorative wall boards, and name boards.

The registration picture is broad at the national level. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale businesses, so the code is not confined to one enterprise size. For foreign investment the position is the opposite of broad: Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — lists this activity at entry #3 as open to domestic capital only. Foreign shareholding is 0%, so a PT PMA cannot hold this code anywhere in Indonesia.

Bali changes the practical answer. The record marks the Bali status as Blocked (risk class) and sets l4_bali_blocked to true. The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, placing it inside the Bali moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA, island-wide and permanently. The immediate planning consequence is simple: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali under the record as written.

Two separate obstacles sit on this activity, and they do not have the same reach. The national one is the reservation to domestic capital, and it applies wherever the company is registered. The Bali one is the moratorium, which stops PMA registration for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk — this one is, at every scope at the large scale. Registering somewhere other than Bali removes the second obstacle and leaves the first standing, which is the opposite of what a reader of the Bali half alone would conclude.
editorial.pullQuote: The immediate planning consequence is simple: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali under the record as written.

editorial.headline: Wooden Prefabricated Buildings, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16222 covers wood-dominant prefabricated buildings and elements, nationally open to foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16222 is a manufacturing activity, not a general construction label. Its centre of gravity is the processing of wood into prefabricated buildings and building elements whose material is dominated by wood. The record names mobile homes and caravans as examples, and it also includes wooden partitions that belong to the same manufacturing logic. In practical terms, this is the industrial making of repeatable wooden structures and components before they reach their final site.

The code is broad in scale. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so it can describe a small producer of wooden prefabricated elements as well as a larger factory-scale manufacturer. That scale range matters because the activity is defined by what is being made, not by a single business size. A founder using this code should therefore read it as a production category for wood-dominant prefabrication, with room for different operating footprints inside the same activity description.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clean: the record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, with Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 as the cited source. On the national layer alone, that means the activity is open to PMA participation up to full foreign ownership. There is no separate condition in the slim record about minimum capital, additional licensing, local partnership, tax treatment, or a phased timeline, so none should be read into the classification.

Bali is the hard limit. The same record marks the Bali status as Blocked (risk class) and sets l4_bali_blocked to true. The stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026. So the honest reading is this: KBLI 16222 may be nationally foreign-open, but a foreign-owned company cannot register it in Bali today under the Bali-side rule recorded here.

editorial.headline: Wood Packaging Manufacturing Is Nationally Open, but Bali Blocks PMA Entry
editorial.standfirst: This code covers the making of wooden packaging and load-handling products, open across all business scales nationally but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Wood packaging manufacturing is a practical, industrial activity: the making of wooden boxes, packing cases, crates, wooden drums and similar wood-based containers. The record also brings in wooden pallets, pallet boxes and other wooden load boards, along with barrels, tubs, buckets, other wood products, and wooden cable reels. In plain English, this is the business of turning timber into containers and handling units for goods that need to be stored, shipped, stacked, rolled, or moved with some physical protection. The scope is not decorative furniture or retail display; it is the useful, logistics-facing side of wood manufacturing.

The activity is open to every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because it makes the code structurally broad. A small workshop making crates for local distribution and a larger plant producing pallets or cable reels for industrial supply both sit within the same activity description, provided the work stays inside the recorded scope. The record also marks the national PMA position as TERBUKA, with a pma_max_asing of 100. For a foreign-owned company, the national reading is therefore clear: the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, based on Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali changes the practical answer. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and gives the reason: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule in the record is broader and sharper: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” So although the code is nationally open to foreign ownership, a foreign investor cannot treat Bali as available for PMA registration today. The obstacle is not a separate Bali percentage cap; the record gives no Bali-side percentage. It is a Bali registration block tied to the risk classification and the moratorium rule.

The honest conclusion is simple but important. Nationally, this is a foreign-open manufacturing code for wooden packaging, pallets, barrels, buckets, cable reels and related wood containers, available across micro through large scale. In Bali, however, the same activity is blocked for PMA registration under the recorded provincial moratorium. A founder reading the code should separate the two layers: the national investment list says open, but the Bali operating reality says not registerable for PMA on this record.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Rattan and Bamboo Weaving Is Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM — Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16291 covers woven goods made from rattan or bamboo; Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II allocates the activity to Indonesian cooperatives and MSMEs, so a foreign-owned company cannot register it anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
This KBLI activity is for making woven goods whose main material is rattan or bamboo. The record’s scope is practical and material-led: mats, webbing, lampit, hand fans, woven wall panels, and woven bags, including women’s bags and laptop bags. Its centre of gravity is not general craft trading or a broad lifestyle label; it is manufacturing, where the defining feature is the woven article and the principal input is rattan or bamboo.

That makes the registration question more specific than it first appears. The code is available across the full range of business scales listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. A small workshop producing hand fans and woven panels, a growing bag producer, and a larger woven-goods manufacturer can all sit inside the same activity description if the actual production remains within the stated scope. The record also draws a boundary away from footwear and woven headwear, so the clean reading is to keep this code for rattan-and-bamboo woven goods themselves, not every product that happens to use a woven element.

The ownership position is set by Perpres 10/2021, as amended by Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran II: rattan and bamboo weaving is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM (p.4, entry 14 "Industri barang anyaman", sub-row "Rotan dan bambu", KBLI 16291). A foreign investor can be neither a cooperative nor a UMKM, so the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for rattan and bamboo weaving is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this code anywhere in Indonesia. editorial.headline: Woven Plant Goods With a Bali Registration Wall
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16292 covers woven goods made from plant materials other than rattan and bamboo, nationally open to PMA but blocked for foreign registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16292 is the industrial home for woven goods made from plant materials other than rattan and bamboo. The record describes a broad, tactile field: pandan, mendong, banana stem sheath, corn leaves, purun, ketak, water hyacinth, abaca fibre, other natural fibres, coconut leaves, grass, and similar materials. Its examples are everyday and craft-facing at once: mats, doormats, bags, and handicrafts. In plain English, this is not trading in finished craft goods; it is the making of woven products whose primary input is non-rattan, non-bamboo plant material.

That scope matters because it gives the activity a particular character. It can sit close to village-scale handwork, but the classification itself is not reserved only for micro producers. The slim record opens the activity to every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. A founder reading the code should therefore see a manufacturing category that can accommodate small workshops as well as larger production setups, so long as the activity remains within the stated material and product scope. The record does not add quality marks, export requirements, product thresholds, or special permits, so none should be inferred.

The national investment picture is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the recorded maximum foreign ownership is 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nationally, then, this is a foreign-open activity with no recorded foreign-equity cap below full ownership. For a foreign-owned structure outside the Bali-specific constraint described in the record, the national line is clean: the code is open, the ceiling is 100%, and all four stated scales appear in the record.

Bali is the hard stop. The same record marks `l4_bali_blocked` as true and gives the Bali status as `Blocked (risk class)`. Its reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Low or Medium-Low on every scope, which places the activity inside Bali’s moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record is categorical: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest reading is this: KBLI 16292 may be nationally open to foreign ownership, but a foreigner cannot register this PMA activity in Bali today under the Bali-side rule recorded here.

editorial.headline: Wood Carving Is Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM — Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 16293 covers non-furniture wooden craft and carving production; Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II allocates it to Indonesian cooperatives and MSMEs, so a foreign-owned company cannot register it anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16293 is a manufacturing activity for wooden craft and carved objects that are not furniture. The record describes the activity through its products: reliefs, masks, statues, wayang, flower vases, frames, lampshades, souvenirs, ashtrays, tissue boxes, jewelry boxes, wall-decoration products, and name boards. In practical terms, this is the code for makers whose output is decorative, cultural, gift-oriented, or object-based rather than furniture-based. The centre of gravity is the making of crafted and carved wooden goods, not a retail shop, not a gallery, and not a furniture line.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so it can describe anything from a very small producer to a large manufacturing operation, provided the activity remains within this non-furniture wooden craft and carving scope. That matters because this code is not limited to one size of enterprise in the national classification record. A founder reading the scope should therefore focus less on the aesthetic style of the goods and more on whether the business is actually producing the listed kinds of wooden craft or carving products.

The ownership position is set by Perpres 10/2021, as amended by Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran II: non-furniture wood carving is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM (p.4, entry 15 "Industri kerajinan ukiran dari kayu bukan mebeller: ukiran kayu, relief, topeng, patung, wayang", KBLI 16293). A foreign investor can be neither a cooperative nor a UMKM, so the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for wood carving is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this code anywhere in Indonesia. editorial.headline: Wood, Rattan, and Bamboo Tableware Meets Bali’s PMA Stop Line
editorial.standfirst: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this craft-manufacturing activity is still blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record’s risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the making of kitchenware and tableware whose main materials are wood, bamboo, and rattan. The record’s scope is practical and domestic: graters, spatulas, ladles, rice scoops, pestles and mortars, chopping boards, spoons, forks, chopsticks, glasses, plates, bowls, trays, lunch boxes, steamers, baskets, mats, toothpicks, and similar items. It is a manufacturing code for objects that sit close to everyday food culture, not a general furniture, craft-retail, or hospitality activity. Its centre of gravity is production: turning those natural materials into utensils and serving pieces intended for cooking, eating, carrying, or presenting food.

The registration picture is broad at the business-scale level. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, which means the code is not framed only for household workshops or only for industrial operators. A small bamboo utensil maker and a larger tableware producer can both sit within the same defined activity, provided the business being registered is genuinely the manufacture of the listed kitchen and dining goods. That breadth matters because the scope itself is material-specific and product-specific: the unifying point is not brand style or sales channel, but the making of kitchen and eating implements from wood, rattan, and bamboo.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clean. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 identifies the PMA status as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing set at 100. In plain English, the national layer treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to 100%. There is no ownership cap below full foreign ownership in the slim record, and there is no additional national qualification stated here. For a founder reading only the national investment layer, this looks straightforward: the activity is open, the ceiling is full foreign ownership, and the source is explicitly named.

Bali changes the answer. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and gives the Bali status as Blocked (risk class). The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, which is blocked by the Bali moratorium dated May 13, 2026. The moratorium rule in the record is broader still: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, with the source identified as Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. So the honest conclusion is narrow but decisive: this activity may be nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, yet a foreign-owned company cannot register it in Bali today under the Bali-side block recorded here.

editorial.headline: Wood Pellets and Biomass Fuel, Nationally Open but Scope-Sensitive in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers pressed firewood, wood pellets, and solid biomass fuels, with PMA registration nationally open but Bali requiring exact OSS scope verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 16295 sits in the practical, material end of Indonesia’s biomass economy. The record defines it as the manufacture of firewood and wood pellets made from sawdust or pressed substitute materials, including coffee grounds or soybean seeds. It also covers the making of solid fuel from biomass and pellets from coconut husk. In plain English, this is not a broad renewable-energy licence or a trading classification; it is a production activity for compressed wood and biomass-based fuel products.

The scale picture is unusually straightforward at the national level. The record opens this activity to **Micro, Small, Medium, and Large** business scales, so it is not reserved only for industrial-scale operators. A small producer working with coconut husk pellets and a larger factory processing sawdust into wood pellets both sit within the activity described, provided the declared business activity matches the actual production scope. For founders, the key discipline is precision: the scope is about making the fuel product, not stretching the classification into unrelated energy, logistics, or sales activity.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The record marks the activity as **TERBUKA**, with **pma_max_asing** at **100**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. That means the national record does not place a foreign-ownership ceiling below full foreign ownership. On the national reading alone, this is an open PMA activity, and the headline is not a hidden cap or a partial-ownership structure.

Bali is the more careful reading. The record does **not** mark the activity as outright Bali-blocked, but it does mark the Bali status as **Blocked (scope-dependent)**. The reason is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity.” That must be read alongside the moratorium rule in the record: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” So the honest conclusion is narrow: nationally this activity is foreign-open, but in Bali a PMA registration depends on the exact OSS activity and risk profile declared. A founder should not treat the national 100% foreign-ownership position as automatic Bali clearance; the decisive question is whether the exact declared scope is registrable under Bali’s moratorium filter.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is not the same thing as automatic Bali clearance; the exact OSS scope is the decisive point.

editorial.headline: Wood, Cork, Rattan, and Bamboo Goods That Bali Blocks for PMA
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to foreign ownership, but the record marks it as blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the province’s risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
For KBLI 16299, the activity is a broad manufacturing lane for wood, cork, rattan, bamboo, straw, and similar goods that sit outside the more specifically named categories. The record’s Indonesian scope is intentionally practical rather than poetic: it covers the making of miscellaneous wooden items, including weaving tools, shoe lasts and shoe trees, clothes hangers, toothpicks, slate pencils, dowels, abacuses, rulers, blackboards, and wooden work tools such as plastering tools, hammers, wooden plane bodies, tool handles, pallets, washboards, and similar goods. It also covers cork articles such as sheets, stoppers, discs, rings, liners, and floats.

The commercial shape of the code is unusually wide. The slim record says it is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale businesses, so it can describe anything from a small maker operation to a larger manufacturing setup, provided the activity remains within the stated scope. That breadth matters because the code is not about one signature product. It is about a class of making: small functional goods, workshop implements, household or industrial accessories, and cork-based components, all tied together by material and by the fact that they are not covered elsewhere in the record.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The record marks the PMA status as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. In plain English, the national line is that foreign ownership can reach 100% for this activity. That is the part a founder might notice first, and it is real. But it is not the whole operational answer for Bali, because the Bali-side status in the same record is blocked.

The honest Bali reading is therefore direct: a foreigner cannot register this as a PMA activity in Bali today. The reason given is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026”. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, with the listed source as Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. So the practical conclusion is not that the code is nationally closed. It is nationally open, but Bali blocks the PMA registration pathway because of the province’s moratorium logic.
editorial.pullQuote: The practical conclusion is not that the code is nationally closed; it is nationally open, but Bali blocks the PMA registration pathway.

l4_bali.reason: Not among the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026. The low/medium-low risk tier was named only in the Governor's January 2026 request letter (B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP); check the risk tier and zoning on OSS before filing.

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Manufacturing paper pulp from wood, other fibers, or recycled paper — bleached, semi-bleached, or unbleached pulp. This includes mechanical, chemical, and semichemical processes to produce pulp.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Small scale**: Medium-High risk. NIB + Standard Certificate — issued within 7 working days.

**Medium scale**: Medium-High risk. NIB + Standard Certificate — issued within 7 working days.

**Large scale**: High risk. NIB + Business License (Izin) — full review required.

**PMA:** Fully open to PMA — 100% foreign ownership allowed.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Unchanged from KBLI 2020 — direct match.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Starting a paper pulp mill in Bali? Let me help you understand the licensing and regulations for processing wood and other fibers into pulp.

editorial.headline: Pulp Manufacturing With a Clear National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 17011 covers the industrial making of paper pulp from wood, other fibres, cotton linters, de-inking, and recycled paper streams.
editorial.body:
KBLI 17011 is the industrial activity behind paper pulp: the making of pulp from wood, other fibres, and used paper. The record’s scope is broad but specific. It includes bleached, semi-bleached, and unbleached pulp, whether produced through mechanical, chemical, dissolving or non-dissolving, or semi-chemical processes. It also covers cotton-linters pulp, de-inking, and pulp made from recycled paper. In plain English, this code is not about paper retail, printing, packaging design, or general waste collection. It is the manufacturing process that turns fibre inputs into pulp as an industrial material.

The scale picture is unusually open in the record. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so the registration frame is not confined to a single enterprise size. That does not make every project identical in practice, but it does mean the slim record does not reserve the code only for large operators or exclude smaller scales. A founder choosing this code should therefore read the scale field as part of the core classification: the activity is defined by the pulp-making process, not by a single business-size profile.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. The record marks the code as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, with the source listed as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That is the only ownership percentage available in the record, and it is a national figure. On the face of this slim record, a foreign-owned company is not nationally capped below full ownership for this activity.

The Bali picture is also clear, but it needs careful wording. The record does not mark KBLI 17011 as blocked in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason is stated as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. For this code, the recorded Bali logic is therefore not a separate Bali ownership cap, quota, or local-partnership condition. It is simply that, because the recorded OSS risk at large scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, the Bali moratorium does not block PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: For this code, the Bali record is not a separate ownership cap; it is a moratorium screen that the activity is recorded as passing.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)

editorial.headline: Printing and Writing Paper, Open Nationally and Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the manufacture of newspaper paper and other printing or writing paper, open nationally to foreign ownership and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 17012 is a manufacturing classification for paper made to carry words.** The slim record describes its scope as the making of newspaper paper and other printing paper or writing paper. In practical terms, this is not a retail or publishing activity; its centre of gravity is the industrial production of paper itself. The Indonesian title, *Industri Kertas Budaya*, points to paper used for communication, reading, printing, and writing, while the operative scope keeps the definition narrow: paper for newspapers, other print uses, and written use.

The registration picture is broad. The record opens the activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** scale operators, so it is not reserved in the data for one size of enterprise. A small producer and a larger industrial setup sit under the same activity code when the underlying activity remains the manufacture of the covered paper types. That scale openness matters because it frames the code as a production category rather than a niche carve-out. The record does not add any threshold, capacity test, capital figure, licence detail, or timeline, so none should be read into it.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clean. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the foreign-ownership ceiling in the record is **100%**. That means the national classification is open to foreign ownership up to the stated ceiling, with the source given as **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. The honest national reading is therefore straightforward: for this activity, the record does not show a foreign-ownership cap below full ownership. It also does not describe any special condition attached to that national openness, so the editorial conclusion has to stay with what is actually present: open PMA status, a 100% ceiling, and coverage across all listed business scales.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion in this record. The Bali-side status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and `l4_bali_blocked` is false. The reason is explicit: **OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium**. The province’s moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this activity is not marked as blocked here. So the national-vs-Bali picture is unusually aligned: nationally open to PMA, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the slim record supplied. The right caveat is not an invented Bali percentage or partnership condition; it is simply the record’s own risk-based note explaining why the moratorium does not block it.

editorial.headline: Security Paper Is a Nationally Open Industrial KBLI
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 17013 covers the manufacturing of high-trust paper products, from banknote and cheque paper to stamps, and the record leaves it nationally open to foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
KBLI 17013 is not ordinary paper manufacturing. The activity described in the record is the making of paper whose value depends on trust: banknote paper, cheque paper, security paper, watermark paper, duty-stamp paper, postage stamps, revenue stamps, and similar products. In plain English, this is an industrial classification for paper products designed to carry financial, fiscal, postal, or verification significance. The emphasis is not on generic packaging, stationery, or pulp output, but on paper made for controlled, recognisable, and official use.

That scope matters because the registered business is defined by what it manufactures, not by the eventual institution that uses the paper. A company under this KBLI is positioned as a producer of secure or high-value paper articles: items such as bank notes, cheque paper, watermarked paper, meterai, prangko, and comparable products. The slim record opens the activity across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the classification itself is not confined to one registered business size. The scale line should be read exactly as written: every listed scale is open in the record.

The national foreign-investment position is clean. The record marks the PMA status as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national ceiling stated in this record is 100% foreign ownership. There is no smaller cap in the slim record, and no additional ownership condition is stated here. The editorial point is therefore simple but important: nationally, this KBLI is open, and the record gives the foreign-ownership ceiling as the full 100%.

Bali does not change that into a separate percentage. The Bali-side status in the record is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and l4_bali_blocked is false. The reason is given as: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this activity is not marked as blocked by that rule. So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is unusually direct: KBLI 17013 is nationally open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership, and the Bali record does not block PMA registration under the stated moratorium logic.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Specialty Paper Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 17014 covers specialty papers and paper finishing, open across all business scales with a 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling.
editorial.body:
KBLI 17014 is the activity code for manufacturing specialty paper. The record describes a focused industrial field: papers made for specific technical or functional uses, including cardiopan, litmus paper, metallic paper, acid-proof paper, pattern paper, coated paper, and celopan paper. It also covers paper-working processes that add a surface or functional layer by coating, glazing, gumming, or laminating. In plain English, this is not general paper trading or a broad stationery category; it is the making and finishing of specialised paper products.

The registration profile is unusually broad on scale. The record opens this activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** businesses, so the code is not framed only for large industrial players. A small producer working on a narrow specialty line and a larger manufacturer operating at industrial scale both sit inside the same activity description, provided the work remains within the described specialty-paper and finishing scope.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The record marks the PMA status as **TERBUKA** and gives a **100%** maximum foreign-ownership figure, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. That means the national record does not impose a foreign-share ceiling below full ownership for this activity. The important editorial point is not to overcomplicate that: for the national PMA reading, the code is open, and the ownership figure in the record is full foreign ownership.

Bali does not change that into a blocked case on the record provided. The Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and `l4_bali_blocked` is false. The stated reason is: **OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium**. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this activity is expressly marked as not blocked by that rule. So the honest national-versus-Bali conclusion is straightforward: KBLI 17014 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record does not block it under the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is straightforward: KBLI 17014 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record does not block it under the moratorium.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)
