data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Manufacturing various types of paper including magnetic paper, creped paper, laminated or foiled paper if combined with cardboard, cellulose wadding, handmade papers, and carbon/stencil sheets in rolls or large sheets.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Small scale**: Medium-Low risk. NIB + Standard Certificate — issued automatically.

**Medium scale**: Medium-Low risk. NIB + Standard Certificate — issued automatically.

**Large scale**: High risk. NIB + Business License (Izin) — full review required.

**PMA:** Fully open to PMA — 100% foreign ownership allowed.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Unchanged from KBLI 2020 — direct match.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Planning to produce specialized paper products like magnetic or creped paper in Bali? I can assist you with the licensing and production methods.

editorial.headline: The Paper Code for Specialist, Smaller-Batch Manufacturing
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 17019 covers non-standard paper production, from magnetic and crepe paper to cellulose wadding, and is nationally open to foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 17019 is not the broad story of ordinary paper.** The record defines it as a home for more specialised paper manufacturing: magnetic paper, crepe or crinkled paper, laminated and foil products when the lamination is with paper or paperboard, cellulose wadding and cellulose webs made from cellulose fibre, handmade paper, and carbon or stencil paper in rolls or large sheets. In plain English, this is the activity code for producers working at the edges of paper as a material: technical paper, converted paper, craft paper, and paper-based inputs that are not described here as packaging, publishing, or stationery retail.

The scale picture is unusually straightforward. The record opens this activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** operators, so the same classification can frame a small handmade-paper workshop, a mid-sized cellulose-web producer, or a larger industrial operation making more technical paper products. That range matters because the activity is defined by what is made, not by a single factory profile. A founder should therefore read the scope carefully: the anchor is manufacturing, and the listed products are the boundary of the code’s logic.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clean. The record marks the PMA status as **TERBUKA** and gives a maximum foreign ownership figure of **100%**. That means the national line in this slim record is not a minority cap, not a partial ceiling, and not a special-condition narrative. The source field is limited to the stated presidential regulations, so the editorial point should remain disciplined: for this activity, the national record says foreign investment is open up to the recorded ceiling.

The Bali reading is also direct, but for a different reason. The Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the record says it is **not blocked** by the province’s PMA moratorium because OSS risk at scale Besar is **Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi**. The moratorium text in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this activity is not captured by that block on the facts provided here. The practical conclusion is therefore simple: KBLI 17019 is nationally foreign-open, and the Bali-side record does not block it under the stated moratorium rule.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 17019 is nationally foreign-open, and the Bali-side record does not block it under the stated moratorium rule.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity

editorial.headline: Corrugated Paperboard Is an Industrial Code With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making of construction paper, packaging paper, and board products, and the record treats it as nationally open and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 17021 is not a retail paper trade or a general printing category. The slim record defines it as manufacturing: the making of construction papers such as insulating paper, condenser paper, roofing board, and building board; wrapping and packaging papers such as kraftliner, corrugating medium, ribbed kraft paper, kraft paper, machine-glazed paper, and machine-finished paper; and a wide board family including postcard card stock, londen paper, plywood-style board, multiplex board, bristol, straw board, chip board, duplex, ivory or boxboard, art board, and art paper. In plain English, this is the industrial layer behind packaging stock, board material, and paperboard inputs used before they become finished boxes, panels, or printed goods.

The record opens the activity across the full scale ladder: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the code is not framed only for large mills or capital-heavy manufacturers, even though the product family naturally points toward production facilities, machinery, material handling, and supply-chain customers. A small or medium operator may sit closer to specialised board or paper processing; a larger operator may be closer to integrated industrial output. The record does not add operational thresholds, licence timing, production capacity, or capital figures, so those should not be read into the classification. What it does say is simpler: this activity is open to all listed business scales.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership value in the record is 100%. That means the national entry shown here is fully open on the foreign-ownership field provided by the record, with its source given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no smaller foreign cap in the slim record and no conditional percentage attached to Bali. A founder reading this code should separate the national ownership field from every other operational question: the record supplies a national PMA ceiling, not a complete factory-readiness checklist.

The Bali picture is also clean, but for a different reason. The record does include Bali's island-wide moratorium rule: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. For this specific activity, however, `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. So the honest reading is not that Bali creates a special percentage cap, partnership quota, or local carve-out. It is that the record marks this code as not blocked in Bali under the stated moratorium logic, while nationally preserving a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is not that Bali creates a special percentage cap, but that this code is not blocked under the moratorium logic shown in the record.

intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Planning a paper packaging factory in Bali? Let me help you with the licensing requirements and how to set up your operations efficiently.

editorial.headline: Paper and Carton Packaging Manufacturing Is Open, Including in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 17022 covers the making of paper and carton packaging, from corrugated boxes to paper sacks, and the record treats it as foreign-open nationally and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 17022 is the industrial code for making packaging and boxes from paper or carton. Its scope is broad but still specific: the activity is manufacturing, not trading, designing, or distributing packaging. The record covers all kinds of paper and paperboard packaging used for wrapping and packing goods, including boxes for cigarettes and other products, corrugated paper and paperboard boxes, folding paperboard boxes, solid-board boxes, other paper and paperboard containers, paper sacks and bags, and office file boxes or similar goods. In plain English, this is the code for a factory-side business that turns paper or carton materials into containers and packing formats.

The scale picture is unusually straightforward. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so it is not framed as a niche reserved only for one size of operator. A small producer making paper sacks and a larger manufacturer producing carton boxes sit within the same described field, provided the activity remains the making of those paper or carton packaging products. That breadth matters because the scope is written around the product family rather than a single end market: consumer goods, office storage, cigarette boxes, folding cartons, and corrugated packaging are all named as examples inside the same manufacturing envelope.

Nationally, the investment signal is clean. The national record lists PMA status as TERBUKA and sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 100%. That means the national record does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. The source field ties that national position to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, but the practical editorial point is simpler: on the national reading supplied here, KBLI 17022 is open to foreign investment at the full stated ceiling. There is no basis in this slim record to add a minimum capital figure, a special licence, a tax treatment, or an operational threshold.

The Bali reading is also explicit, and it should not be made more dramatic than the record allows. Bali’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, but this record marks KBLI 17022 as not blocked. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The honest national-vs-Bali picture, therefore, is that this paper and carton packaging manufacturing activity is foreign-open nationally and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the moratorium described in the record. The decisive point is that Bali does not add a separate ownership percentage here; it simply does not block this activity under the stated moratorium logic.
editorial.pullQuote: The decisive point is that Bali does not add a separate ownership percentage here; it simply does not block this activity under the stated moratorium logic.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices

editorial.headline: Tissue Paper Manufacturing With a Clear National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 17091 covers the manufacturing base behind household tissue, sanitary paper goods, cotton paper products, and related absorbent paper articles.
editorial.body:
KBLI 17091 is a manufacturing classification for tissue paper and closely related absorbent paper products. Its scope is broad, but still clearly bounded: the making of paper for household supplies, cotton paper goods, and products made from cellulose wadding. In plain English, this is the industrial activity behind cleaning tissue, facial tissue, kitchen tissue, lens tissue, paper handkerchiefs, paper towels, paper napkins, toilet tissue, baby diapers, adult diapers, animal diapers, underpads, sanitary napkins, pantyliners, tampons, breast pads, insert pads, and napkins for cups, plates, and trays. The record also includes cotton paper and cotton paper goods, including towels or wipes, cigarette paper, plugwrap paper, and tipping paper.

The registerable business profile is not confined to one enterprise size. The slim record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, which means the classification can describe anything from a small paper-goods producer to a large industrial manufacturer, as long as the activity remains within the stated tissue, sanitary, cotton paper, or cellulose-wadding scope. The useful editorial point is that the code is not about retailing these goods, branding them, or distributing them; it is about making the paper and paper-based articles themselves.

For Indonesia as a whole, the foreign-investment position is straightforward. The record marks PMA status as TERBUKA and gives pma_max_asing as 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Rendered plainly, the national ceiling is 100% foreign ownership. There is no lower cap in the record, and there is no additional threshold or capital figure to infer. For a foreign-owned setup, the national reading is therefore clean: this activity is open, and the recorded foreign-ownership ceiling reaches 100%.

Bali does not introduce a separate foreign-ownership percentage in this record. In Bali, the record shows OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with l4_bali_blocked set to false. The reason is also explicit: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". That matters because the moratorium rule states that Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. This record does not place KBLI 17091 inside that blocked result. The honest conclusion is that KBLI 17091 is nationally open for PMA and, on the Bali fields supplied here, not blocked by the Bali moratorium.

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices

editorial.headline: A Broad Home for Unprinted Paper Goods and Paperboard Products
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 17099 covers ready-to-use paper and paperboard goods, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 17099 is the wide residual home for paper and paperboard goods that are not captured elsewhere in the classification. In practical terms, it covers the making of ready-to-use writing paper, printing paper, computer printout paper, copy paper, adhesive paper, registers, accounting books, binders, albums, notebooks, and education or commercial stationery of a similar character. It also reaches further into paper-based containers and components: boxes, bags, wallets, absorbent pads, cellulose cigarette filters, labels, filter paper, filter paperboard, paper rolls, paperboard rolls, bobbins, egg trays, moulded pulp goods, wallpaper, vinyl- or textile-coated wall coverings, and newly created paper products.

The record also makes clear that this is not only a finishing category for familiar stationery. It includes paper and paperboard made or prepared through processes such as coating, glazing, gumming, and laminating, as well as carbon paper and stencil sheets cut into consumer-ready form. It covers EKG paper, unprinted office stationery such as envelopes and letter paper, and paper-based tableware including plates, cups, straws, and similar goods. The boundary matters: printed office stationery and cards are outside the activity, so the editorial center of gravity here remains unprinted, manufactured, ready-to-use paper and paperboard products.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. Registration is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the activity can describe a small local paper-goods producer as well as a larger manufacturing operation, provided the actual business remains inside the scope above. The code is therefore not defined by one product alone, but by a manufacturing logic: paper or paperboard is converted, prepared, shaped, coated, assembled, or finished into usable commercial, office, educational, packaging, wall-covering, tableware, filtration, moulded-pulp, or novelty goods.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is unambiguous. It is listed as TERBUKA, with a pma_max_asing of 100, and the cited sources are Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Put simply, the national cap on foreign ownership is 100%. The Bali side does not introduce a separate ownership percentage. It records l4_bali_blocked as false and gives the Bali status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with the reason: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this record, however, does not mark the activity as blocked. The honest reading is therefore clean: nationally foreign-open, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the supplied Bali record.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup pencetakan koran, majalah dan terbitan berkala lainnya seperti tabloid, majalah, jurnal, pamflet, buku dan brosur, naskah musik, peta, atlas, poster, katalog periklanan, prospektus dan iklan cetak lainnya, buku harian, kalender, surat-surat bisnis dan barang-barang cetakan komersial lainnya, kertas surat atau alat tulis pribadi dan barang-barang cetakan lainnya hasil mesin cetak, ofset, klise foto (fotogravur), fleksografi dan mesin cetak sejenisnya, mesin pengganda, mesin cetak komputer, dan mesin cetak huruf timbul termasuk mesin cetak cepat; pencetakan pada label atau tanda pengenal (litografi, pencetakan cetak gulung, pencetakan fleksografi dan sebagainya); pencetakan, dengan atau tanpa adanya media perantara ke bahan tekstil, plastik, kaca, logam, kayu dan keramik; pengukiran menggunakan laser pada bahan tekstil; mencetak ulang melalui komputer, mesin stensil dan sejenisnya; jasa fotokopi dokumen bukan bagian dari penawaran jasa pendukung kantor. Barang cetakan ini biasanya merupakan barang yang dilindungi hak cipta. Kelompok ini juga mencakup pencetakan tanda, tatakan gelas bir, dan foto; dan kegiatan pencetakan periklanan. Pembuatan label dari kertas atau karton termasuk kelompok 17099.

**Small scale**: Low risk. NIB only — issued automatically.

**Medium scale**: Low risk. NIB only — issued automatically.

**Large scale**: High risk. NIB + Business License (Izin) — full review required.

intel_2026.whatChanged: Unchanged from KBLI 2020 — direct match.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Planning a general printing facility in Bali? I can help you navigate the licensing process and ensure your operations meet all regulatory standards.

editorial.headline: General Printing, Open Nationally but Scope-Sensitive in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 18111 covers broad commercial and editorial printing, with full national foreign ownership but a Bali registration picture that depends on the declared scope.
editorial.body:
KBLI 18111 is the broad house of general printing: the production of newspapers, magazines, periodicals, books, brochures, music manuscripts, maps, atlases, posters, advertising catalogues, prospectuses, diaries, calendars, business correspondence, stationery and other commercial printed matter. Its scope is not limited to one technique. The record includes printing by press, offset, photogravure, flexography, duplicating machines, computer printers, letterpress and fast-printing machines, as well as printing on labels or identification marks. It also reaches printing on textile, plastic, glass, metal, wood and ceramic surfaces, laser engraving on textiles, reprinting through computers or stencil machines, stand-alone document photocopying, signs, beer coasters, photos and advertising printing.

This is therefore the KBLI a business would look at when the activity is the act of printing itself: turning editorial, commercial, promotional or documentary content into physical output through printing machinery or related processes. It can sit behind a neighbourhood print shop, a specialist commercial printer, an advertising print operation, a document-copying counter, or a larger industrial facility producing printed goods at scale. The record expressly opens the activity to **Mikro**, **Kecil**, **Menengah** and **Besar** scales, so the classification is not reserved for one size of operator.

Nationally, the investment signal is straightforward. The record marks the activity as **TERBUKA**, with `pma_max_asing` at **100**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. In plain English, the national record treats this as open to foreign ownership up to 100%. That does not mean every Bali registration is automatic, because the Bali-side field is deliberately more cautious: `Blocked (scope-dependent)`, with `l4_bali_blocked` set to false.

The honest Bali reading is scope-dependent, not a separate ownership cap. The record says: “OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity.” It also records the provincial moratorium rule: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” So the practical conclusion is narrow but important: KBLI 18111 is nationally foreign-open, yet in Bali the declared activity and live OSS risk treatment matter. A foreign-owned setup should not treat the national 100% ceiling as the whole answer; it should verify the exact printing scope before relying on Bali registration.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 18111 is nationally foreign-open, but in Bali the exact declared printing scope is the part that decides the registration risk.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)

editorial.headline: Special Printing for Indonesia’s Most Sensitive Paper Trails
editorial.standfirst: A precise KBLI for printing stamps, secure documents, financial papers, passports and airline tickets, nationally open to PMA and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
Special printing is not ordinary commercial printing dressed in formal language. The record defines this activity around items that carry public trust, financial value, official identity, or controlled circulation: postal stamps, tax stamps, documents, cheques and other confidential papers, revenue stamps, banknotes, cheque forms, giro forms, shares, bonds, stock certificates, passports, and airline tickets. In plain English, this is the printing of sensitive instruments where the object being printed is part of an administrative, fiscal, financial, travel, or securities system.

That scope gives the code its character. A business registering this activity is not simply producing brochures, packaging, or general stationery. It is positioning itself in the specialised production of controlled paper-based instruments and official-format documents. The slim record opens the activity across every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the code is not confined to a single business size in the record; it can describe a small specialised operator as well as a larger printing facility, provided the activity remains within the defined special-printing scope.

The national investment picture is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, while the recorded foreign-ownership ceiling remains 100%. There is no partial cap to soften or interpret here: nationally, the record treats this activity as open to foreign investment up to full foreign ownership, with the stated source being Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That is the national baseline, and it should be read exactly as such, without adding extra licensing assumptions, capital figures, or operational thresholds that the record does not provide.

Bali adds a separate but, in this case, non-blocking filter. The province’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently. This record, however, marks Bali as not blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason given is “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: this activity is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record does not block it under the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: This is not ordinary commercial printing; it is the production of sensitive instruments where the printed object carries administrative, fiscal, financial, travel, or securities value.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: 3D Printing as a Broad Manufacturing Activity
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 18113 covers three-dimensional printing across materials, scales, and ownership models, with Bali marked as usable rather than moratorium-blocked.
editorial.body:
KBLI 18113 is the activity code for three-dimensional printing: the production of objects through 3D printing for various purposes, using materials such as polymers, plastics, clay, metal ore, and other materials. Its scope is deliberately material-led rather than narrowly product-led. The record does not tie the activity to one finished article, one industry, or one customer type; it describes a printing capability that can be applied across different use cases, as long as the core activity is 3D printing itself.

That breadth matters for founders because this is not written as a micro-only craft activity or as a large-industry-only classification. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. In plain terms, the same activity code can describe a small 3D-printing setup, a growing production studio, or a larger operation, provided the registered business is genuinely carrying out the covered 3D-printing activity. The scale choice is therefore not a decorative field: it is part of how the business presents its operating size inside the OSS framework.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. Under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, the record lists the activity as TERBUKA and sets pma_max_asing at 100. That means the national record does not place a lower foreign-ownership ceiling on this activity. A PMA founder reading the code nationally should see it as open up to 100% foreign ownership, without inventing additional capital thresholds, sector licences, or side conditions that are not present in the slim record.

The Bali reading is equally important, because national openness is not always the end of the analysis. Here, however, the record does not mark the code as Bali-blocked. Its l4_bali_status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason is explicit: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. For this code, the recorded Bali reason says the Besar-scale OSS risk sits at Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so the moratorium does not block it. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: KBLI 18113 is nationally foreign-open and, on the supplied Bali record, not blocked by the Bali moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: The Hidden Craft Behind Finished Print
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 18120 covers the prepress, binding, plate-making and finishing work that turns print materials into usable objects.
editorial.body:
KBLI 18120 is not the act of printing itself, but the specialised support work that makes printing possible and presentable. The record describes prepress and premedia services, binding, and related finishing services. In practical terms, this is the craft and technical layer between a design file, a printing process, and the finished printed object: books, brochures, magazines, catalogues and other printed materials that need to be folded, assembled, stitched, glued, trimmed, bound or finished with details such as gold stamping.

The scope is deliberately broad because printing support is both physical and digital. It includes composing, typesetting, photographic typesetting, and entering prepress data into forms usable across printing processes and other visual media. It also includes scanning, optical character recognition, and electronic assembly. The same activity can prepare data files for multimedia applications across paper printing, CD-ROM and internet use. On the production side, it reaches into plate-making, image and plate arrangement for press and offset processes, cylinder preparation for gravure through engraving or etching, computer-to-plate processing including photopolymer plates, and preparation of plates or forms for relief printing and stamping.

That breadth explains who may register it. The slim record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so it is not reserved only for large industrial operators. A small bindery, a prepress studio, a plate-preparation service, or a larger post-print finishing operation can all sit within the same activity when the work matches the recorded scope. The common thread is that the business supports printing through preparation, technical artwork, proof-making, binding, finishing, sample mounting or related post-print services, rather than being defined by a single product category.

The national investment picture is clean. The record marks the PMA status as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, with the cited source listed as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali does not change that into a local closure in this record. Bali is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK while l4_bali_blocked is false. The reason stated is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium still matters as context because the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. But for this activity, the record’s own Bali conclusion is that it is not blocked by that moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is that KBLI 18120 is nationally foreign-open and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Recorded Media Reproduction, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 18201 covers the reproduction of master copies of sound media, software, and data, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 18201 is about replication, not authorship. Its core activity is the reproduction of master copies into recorded media: vinyl records, compact discs, tapes carrying music or other audio recordings, and copies of software or data onto disks and magnetic tape. The emphasis is on taking an existing master and producing copies from it. That makes this an industrial and media-distribution activity, sitting between content ownership, software distribution, and physical recording formats.

The scope is also careful about what it is not. The record does not place blank-recording media manufacturing inside this activity, and it does not treat the original making of sound recordings on records, cassettes, or similar formats as part of this code. For a founder, that boundary matters because the registration should describe a reproduction business: copying from masters into recorded sound, software, or data media, rather than manufacturing empty media or creating the original sound recording itself.

On scale, the record is broad. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the activity is not framed only for large industrial operators. A small duplication outfit, a mid-sized media reproduction service, or a larger software-and-data media replication business can all sit within the scale range shown in the record, provided the actual activity remains within the reproduction scope described above.

The national PMA position is clean: the record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100. In plain terms, the national foreign-ownership ceiling shown here is 100%, under the cited source Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali does not add a separate percentage in this record. Instead, the Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason is stated as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this activity is not marked as blocked here. So the honest reading is that KBLI 18201 is nationally open to PMA and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Film and Video Duplication, Without the Bali Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 18202 covers the reproduction of film and video recordings from master copies, with full national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 18202 is a production-backroom activity, not a creative commissioning category. Its centre of gravity is the reproduction of recorded film and video media: making copies from master recordings, compact discs, tapes, and other carriers that contain moving images, films, or video recordings. In plain English, this is the business of duplicating recorded visual media from an existing source, rather than originating the film or video itself.

That distinction matters because the scope is operationally specific. A founder using this code is positioning the company around reproduction work: taking an existing master copy and turning it into recorded media copies. The slim record marks the scope as covering the whole activity described, and it opens the code across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That makes the category broad in company-size access while still narrow in what the activity actually does.

Nationally, the record lists the PMA status as TERBUKA and a pma_max_asing of 100, citing Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In practical editorial terms, the national ceiling shown here is 100% foreign ownership. There is no lesser national percentage in the record, and there is no minimum-capital figure, special timeline, tax rule, or additional obligation stated in the slim record.

The Bali reading is also clear, but for a different reason. Bali’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, according to the listed governor-letter source. This record, however, marks l4_bali_blocked as false and gives the Bali status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” So the honest conclusion is not that Bali imposes a separate foreign-ownership percentage, because no such Bali percentage appears here. The conclusion is simpler: on this record, KBLI 18202 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and it is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: On this record, the Bali story is not a hidden ownership cap, but the absence of a moratorium block.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

This does not include making briquettes or distilling gas through pipelines.

**Small / Medium scale**: Medium-High risk. NIB + Standard Certificate — issued within 7 working days.

**Large scale**: Medium-High risk. NIB + Standard Certificate — issued within 7 working days.

**Small / Medium scale**: Medium-Low risk. NIB + Standard Certificate — issued automatically.

**PMA:** Fully open to PMA — 100% foreign ownership allowed.

editorial.headline: Coke-Oven Products as a Fully Open Industrial Classification
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 19100 covers coke-oven operations and related coal-derived products, open nationally to PMA ownership and not blocked in Bali under the record’s moratorium test.
editorial.body:
KBLI 19100 is an industrial classification for the coke-oven side of coal processing. The record places within its scope the operation of coke ovens, the production of coke and semi-coke, pitch and pitch coke, coke-oven gas, raw coal tar and lignite tar, and the agglomeration of coke. In plain English, this is not a general trading label or a light manufacturing wrapper. It is a production classification for facilities that transform coal-linked inputs into coke-oven and tar-derived industrial products.

The scale position is broad. The record says the classification is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar business scales. That matters because the activity is not reserved in the slim record for only one size of operator. A founder reading this should understand the classification first as an industrial scope, then as a registration lane that the record marks open across every listed scale. The words do real work here: if the registered business is actually operating coke ovens or producing the listed coke, pitch, gas, tar, or agglomerated coke products, this is the activity described by the record.

Nationally, the PMA picture is unusually direct. With PMA status marked TERBUKA, the foreign-ownership ceiling stands at 100%. On the record alone, that means the activity is open to foreign investment nationally up to full foreign ownership, with the source stated as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no basis in this record for adding a minimum-capital figure, a separate permit condition, a processing threshold, or a special ownership formula. The national rule presented here is simply that the activity is open, and the percentage ceiling is complete.

The Bali side is also clear, but for a different reason. The record does not mark this classification as blocked in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. Its reason is stated as: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this classification is not caught by that block on the record provided. So the honest national-versus-Bali reading is clean: KBLI 19100 is foreign-open nationally, and the Bali moratorium field does not block it for PMA registration.

data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan pemurnian dan pengilangan minyak bumi yang menghasilkan bahan bakar seperti avigas, avtur, gasolin, minyak tanah atau kerosin, minyak solar, minyak diesel, minyak bakar atau bensin, pelarut/solvent, termasuk gas minyak cair/liquid petroleum gas (LPG) dari hasil pengilangan minyak bumi.

persyaratan: Persyaratan Administratif a. Surat Permohonan b. Daftar Penerima Manfaat (Beneficial Ownership) c. Identitas dan Surat Kuasa Narahubung d. Surat Pernyataan tertulis diatas materai mengenai: 1) Kesanggupan Badan Usaha memenuhi aspek keselamatan, kesehatan kerja dan pengelolaan lingkungan hidup 2) Kesanggupan memenuhi kewajiban Badan Usaha 3) Kesanggupan Badan Usaha memenuhi ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan 4) Kesediaan dilakukan audit kepatuhan terhadap ketentuan peraturan perundang- undangan 5) Kesanggupan Badan Usaha menjamin dan bertanggung jawab bahwa sarana dan fasilitas yang dimiliki/ dikuasai layak beroperasi dan mampu dijalankan sesuai dengan kaidah keteknikan yang baik selama masa operasi 6) Badan Usaha bebas dari konflik atau permasalahan hukum lainnya dengan pihak lain 7) Dokumen persyaratan dan keterang-an/ pernyataan yang diberikan adalah benar adanya dan apabila dikemudian hari terbukti tidak benar akan dicabut Izin Usahanya sesuai dengan peraturan perundang undangan 8) Kesanggupan Badan Usaha menerima penunjukan dan penugasan dari Menteri untuk menghasilkan dan/ atau mengusahakan jenis BBM untuk pemenuhan cadangan BBM Nasional

Persyaratan Teknis (Izin Usaha Sementara) a. Studi Kelayakan b. Kesepakatan awal (MoU/HoA/Perjanjian Jual Beli) dengan calon pemasok bahan baku Minyak Bumi dan/atau dokumen lain yang mengindikasikan tersedianya pasokan dengan calon pemasok yang difasilitasi oleh SKK Migas c. Persetujuan Kesesuaian Kegiatan Pemanfaatan Ruang atau Persetujuan Pemerintah/ instansi yang berwenang sesuai ketentuan yang berlaku atau pengelola kawasan yang berwenang mengenai lokasi untuk pembangunan fasilitas dan sarana d. SK Izin Usaha Sementara/ Perpanjangan (apabila ada) e. Jaminan kecukupan pendanaan, yang dibuktikan dengan: 1) Laporan keuangan 3 (tiga) tahun terakhir yang sudah diaudit 2) Dokumen kesepakatan dengan pihak lain untuk pendanaan (men-cantum-kan nominal tertentu) atau 3) Surat keterangan dari bank umum yang berkedudukan di Indone-sia, yang menerangkan bahwa Badan Usaha memiliki kemampuan pendanaan dengan nominal tertentu

Persyaratan Teknis (Izin Usaha/ Perpanjangan/ Penyesuaian) a. Studi Kelayakan b. Persetujuan Lingkungan c. Berita Acara Pemeriksaan Keselamatan Instalasi dan Peralatan terkait Fasilitas dan/atau Sarana yang ditandatangani oleh Petugas Direktorat Teknik dan Lingkungan Migas/PLO yang masih berlaku/ sesuai ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan d. Kontrak Perjanjian Pasokan Bahan Baku Minyak Bumi paling sedikit memuat sumber, volume, jangka waktu kesepakatan, dan waktu dimulainya pasokan e. Memiliki laboratorium uji terakreditasi untuk melakukan pengujian terhadap mutu produk yang dihasilkan sesuai standar dan mutu yang ditetapkan Menteri f. SK Izin Usaha Sementara dan/atau Izin Usaha/ Penyesuaian/ Perpanjangan (apabila ada) g. Dokumen hasil uji laboratorium atas seluruh parameter sesuai standar dan mutu (spesifikasi) yang ditetapkan Pemerintah

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the industrial refining and processing of crude oil into finished fuel products like gasoline, diesel, kerosene, jet fuel, and LPG. It’s large-scale downstream oil processing, turning raw petroleum into usable energy sources.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible. The block is due to a local policy pausing low and medium-low risk business approvals for foreign investors, making it effectively closed in Bali for now.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Code for Petroleum-Fuel Refining
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 19201 covers large-scale petroleum refining into fuels and LPG, nationally open to PMA ownership and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium logic.
editorial.body:
KBLI 19201 is a heavy industrial code for the refining and purification of petroleum into usable fuels. The record defines its scope through the output of that process: avigas, avtur, gasoline, kerosene, solar fuel, diesel fuel, fuel oil or petrol, solvents, and LPG produced from petroleum refining. In plain English, this is not a trading, storage, or retail fuel activity. It is the industrial conversion of crude petroleum into refined fuel products.

The registration signal is correspondingly narrow. The record opens this activity only at **Besar** scale, which fits the nature of the work described: petroleum refining is capital-intensive, infrastructure-heavy, and industrial rather than small-format commerce. A founder reading this code should therefore treat it as a large-scale industrial classification, not as a general umbrella for every fuel-related business. The scale field is doing real work here: it tells you who this code is built for in the registration system.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership picture is straightforward. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the recorded maximum foreign ownership is **100%**. That means the national rule in this slim record treats the activity as open to foreign ownership up to the full recorded ceiling. The source attached to that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower cap, quota, local-shareholder condition, or special ownership threshold in the record, so none should be read into it.

The Bali picture is also clear, but for a different reason. The province’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, permanently, according to the record. KBLI 19201 is not marked as blocked: `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the Bali reason says, “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The honest conclusion is therefore not that Bali creates a separate percentage, partnership requirement, or local cap. It is simply that this nationally open, large-scale refining activity is recorded as **not blocked by the Bali moratorium**, because the risk level at Besar scale sits above the Low and Medium-Low band targeted by that rule.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest Bali reading is not a hidden local cap, but a moratorium test that this large-scale refining code does not fail.

intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Planning to produce lubricating oils in Bali? Let me help you understand the licensing requirements and environmental regulations for your facility.

editorial.headline: Lubricant Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Clear for Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 19202 covers oil-based lubricating oils, oils and greases, with all recorded scales open and no Bali PMA block in the slim record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 19202 is the manufacturing category for lubricants: the making of lubricating oil, oil and grease that are oil-based. The scope is product-led and industrial in character. It does not describe trading, repair, distribution or advisory work; the activity in the record is the making of the lubricant materials themselves. That gives the code a fairly clean editorial centre: this is about producing oil-based lubricant goods, not merely handling them after manufacture.

The scale field is broad in the record. KBLI 19202 is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar, so the activity is not confined to one recorded business scale. A founder reading the code should treat those scale names as the operative scale language, because they are the only scale categories supplied. The record does not add extra operating conditions, thresholds or technical qualifications, so the careful reading is limited to what is stated: all four listed scales are open for this activity.

Nationally, the PMA status remains TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain English, the national record presents this activity as open to foreign ownership up to the full recorded ceiling. The cited source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, but the practical editorial point is the combination of status and ceiling: open nationally, with no reduced foreign percentage stated in the slim record.

Bali is often the harder reading because the province applies a separate moratorium rule to PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, island-wide and permanent. Here, however, the Bali field does not block PMA registration: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the reason is exactly, "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi -> not blocked by moratorium". The important point is that the Bali filter does not turn a nationally open activity into a closed one here. On this record, KBLI 19202 remains nationally open and is not marked as blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The important point is that the Bali filter does not turn a nationally open activity into a closed one here.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)

editorial.headline: Turning Used Lubricating Oil Back Into Productive Use
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 19203 covers the manufacture of usable products from waste petroleum material, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 19203 is a focused industrial classification for making usable products from waste petroleum material. In plain English, the activity is about taking used lubricating oil and processing it back into something that can be used again, including fuel or lubricating oil. The record frames the scope as manufacturing, not trading, collection, consulting, or general waste management. Its centre of gravity is the conversion of used lubricating oil into a product with renewed utility.

The scale profile is unusually broad: the activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the classification is not reserved in this record for one operating size only. A smaller manufacturing setup and a large industrial operation can both sit inside the same activity description, provided the actual business remains within the stated scope: making products from waste petroleum material, with the example given of used lubricating oil becoming fuel or lubricating oil.

Nationally, the investment picture is straightforward. The record marks PMA status as TERBUKA and gives a pma_max_asing of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Put plainly, the national foreign-ownership ceiling shown here is 100%. There is no lower cap, minimum-capital rule, licence timeline, tax treatment, or additional national condition in the slim record, so none should be read into the classification. For a foreign-owned setup, the usable national signal is therefore simple: this activity is nationally open to PMA at the stated ceiling.

The Bali reading is also clear, but for a different reason. Bali’s moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. This activity, however, is not marked as blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason is given as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The honest conclusion is that, on this record, KBLI 19203 is nationally open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the stated moratorium logic.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Base Lubricating Oil, Before the Additives Enter the Story
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 19204 covers petroleum processing into base lubricating oil, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 19204 is a narrow industrial classification with a clear point in the lubricant chain. It covers the processing of petroleum into base lubricating oil, the raw lubricant material that will later be processed into lubricating oil before certain additives are introduced. That distinction matters. The activity described here is not the final branded lubricant as a market object; it is the base oil stage, where petroleum is converted into the foundational material from which lubricant products can subsequently be made.

The record opens this activity across the full range of business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practical registration language, that means the classification is not confined in the record to only one scale tier. A founder reading the code should understand it as available from the smallest listed scale through large-scale industrial registration, subject only to what the record itself says. The scope is industrial and specific, but the scale access in the record is broad.

The national PMA picture is straightforward. The activity is marked TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Put plainly, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign investment without a foreign-share cap below full ownership. The cited PMA source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no basis in the slim record to add a minimum capital figure, a special licence, a tax treatment, a timeline, or a separate compliance threshold. The only national ownership number in the record is 100%, and that is the number to use.

Bali does not change that into a block on this record. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with l4_bali_blocked marked false. The reason is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently, but this classification is not blocked here because the record’s Bali-side reasoning places the large-scale OSS risk at Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: nationally, KBLI 19204 is open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership, and under the Bali fields supplied here it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium.

editorial.headline: Briquette Manufacturing With a Scope-Dependent Bali Read
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 19205 covers briquette production from petroleum, coal, peat, or lignite, with national PMA openness but a Bali registration note that depends on the exact declared scope.
editorial.body:
KBLI 19205 is a manufacturing code for briquettes made from petroleum, coal, peat, or lignite. The slim record is deliberately broad: it includes production carried out at the mining site and production done away from it, and it also includes briquettes made from petroleum, coal, peat, or lignite purchased from another party. In plain English, the activity is about turning those fossil or peat-based materials into briquette form, not about a retail channel, an energy-service model, or a neighbouring industrial activity.

The registration scale is equally broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the code is not framed only for heavy industrial operators. It can sit on the books of a smaller manufacturing setup as well as a larger one, provided the registered activity remains exactly within the scope described: making briquettes from petroleum, coal, peat, or lignite, whether the input material is tied to a mining location or bought from outside. That exactness matters because this record’s Bali treatment is not a simple yes-or-no editorial footnote.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean: the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with the source listed as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national reading alone, this is a foreign-open activity with no lower percentage cap shown in the record. The Bali field, however, is more conditional. It does not mark the code as outright blocked, because l4_bali_blocked is false, but its status is Blocked (scope-dependent). The stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity.

That means the honest Bali reading is not to invent a local percentage cap, a partnership condition, or a separate Bali quota. The record gives none. What it does give is a province-level moratorium rule: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent), with the source listed as Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. For this code, the practical editorial conclusion is therefore cautious and narrow: nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership, but in Bali the PMA registration outcome depends on the exact OSS risk/scope declared, and the record itself says to verify live OSS per exact activity.

editorial.headline: Biofuel Blending Has a Clear PMA Route in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 19206 covers the industrial blending of petroleum-refinery products with biofuel, and the record treats it as nationally open and registrable in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 19206 sits in a technical but commercially important corner of energy manufacturing: the blending of products from petroleum refining with biofuel. The record describes activities such as mixing alcohol with petroleum products, including gasohol, and blending diesel with FAME to produce biodiesel. In plain English, this is not fuel retailing or general trading; it is the industrial act of combining refinery outputs with biofuel inputs into blended fuel products.

The registration picture is broad on scale. The slim record opens the activity to Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, which means the classification is not reserved only for large industrial operators. A founder reading this code should understand it first as a manufacturing activity defined by the blending process itself: the business identity comes from what is being mixed, and from the fact that petroleum-refinery products and biofuel are being combined into fuel blends.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position could scarcely be clearer. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling shown in the record is 100%. That is the only ownership percentage in the record, and it is a national figure. The cited source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national reading, therefore, this is not a capped activity for foreign ownership under the data supplied here; a PT PMA can look at the national line as open up to full foreign ownership.

The Bali side does not reverse that conclusion in this record. The Bali status is Open in Bali (high-risk track), and l4_bali_blocked is false. The reason given is explicit: “Nationally TERBUKA and the Besar scale is 'Tinggi' -> survives the Bali moratorium (which blocks only Rendah/Menengah Rendah). Registrable by a PT PMA in Bali. [NB-3 28 June 2026]” The moratorium rule still matters, because Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, but this record says KBLI 19206 survives that filter. The honest reading is therefore clean: nationally open, 100% foreign ownership shown, and registrable by a PT PMA in Bali according to the supplied Bali assessment.

The served per_skala was lifted verbatim from the generic pre-split 19291 row (PP28 Lampiran I.F row No.187, image-verified on the 300-dpi render of PDF 394937 p.525): that page carries ONLY the Kecil/Menengah block (Menengah Rendah, 'NIB dan Sertifikat Standar', Otomatis, three location-keyed kewenangan tiers) — the served Besar row (Tinggi, 'NIB dan Izin') is not retrievable from the pinned sources as hunted, and the canonical's status_mapping 'CODICE_RINUMERATO' is contradicted by the image-verified three-way split. Detached under the plan's preregistered divergence rule: two independent cross-family seats (Codex refuter dissent; blind GLM extractor, needs_quarantine=true) flagged the cross-vintage generic payload against the conductor's initial clean, and the conductor could not affirmatively certify the pre-split basket payload for this blending-specific 2025 code. per_skala detached; no replacement authored. OSS RBA 2025 ruang-lingkup (fetched 2026-09-22) confirms 19206's own Besar-only blending scope; the pre-split 19291 PP28 row stays as the disputed audit trail.

data.judul: Industri Produk Lainnya dari Hasil Kilang Minyak Bumi
data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan pembuatan produk lainnya dari hasil kilang minyak bumi, seperti aspal/ter, aspal modifikasi karet, bitumen dan lilin (dapat digunakan untuk lapisan jalan, atap, kayu, kertas dan sebagainya), serta kokas petroleum/petroleum coke, termasuk pembuatan produk untuk industri petrokimia dan bermacam-macam produk, seperti white spirit, vaselin, lilin parafin, dan jeli minyak bumi/petroleum jelly. Kelompok ini juga mencakup pembuatan produk dari bahan limbah minyak bumi selain minyak pelumas, seperti sludge oil.

editorial.headline: Beyond Fuel: The Industrial By-Products of Refining
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the manufacture of non-fuel refinery-derived products, from bitumen and petroleum coke to waxes, white spirit, and petroleum jelly.
editorial.body:
This activity is not about selling fuel. It is the manufacturing category for the other material outputs of petroleum refining: asphalt or tar, rubber-modified asphalt, bitumen, and waxes used for surfaces and coatings such as roads, roofs, wood, and paper. It also reaches into heavier and more specialised refinery derivatives, including petroleum coke, products for the petrochemical industry, white spirit, vaseline, paraffin wax, and petroleum jelly. The record also includes products made from petroleum-waste materials other than lubricating oil, such as sludge oil.

That range gives the code a deliberately industrial character. It is for operators turning refinery outputs into usable intermediate or finished materials, not for a narrow retail or distribution activity. A company registering under it should be able to recognise itself in the act of making these products: processing, formulating, or producing refinery-derived goods for construction, industrial, petrochemical, or material-use contexts. The scope is broad, but it is still anchored in one clear idea: manufacture of other products from petroleum refinery results.

The scale position is unusually open. The slim record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In plain English, the registration window is not limited to large industrial players only; the scale field recognises the full span of business sizes listed in the record. That does not create extra licences, capital figures, or operational permissions by itself. It simply means that, for this activity, the record’s scale field does not exclude micro, small, medium, or large registration categories.

The foreign-ownership picture is also clear. Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a PMA reading the record, that means the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. The Bali-side result does not contradict that national ceiling. The record says l4_bali_blocked is false and gives the reason as: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record remains strict — Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent) — but this activity is not marked as blocked in Bali. The honest conclusion is therefore direct: nationally open to foreign ownership up to 100%, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the Bali status recorded here.
