editorial.headline: Porcelain Technicalware With A Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 23933 covers porcelain laboratory, electrical, and industrial ceramic equipment, open nationally to PMA and not blocked for Bali registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23933 is a manufacturing classification for a precise corner of the ceramics industry: porcelain and ceramic equipment made for laboratory, electrical, technical, chemical, and industrial use. Its scope is not general tableware or decorative ceramics. The record points instead to functional technicalware: mortars and pestles, filter plates, chemical tubes, bottles and jars, crucibles, fuse housings, low-voltage and high-voltage insulators, ferrite and ceramic magnets, and ceramic products used in laboratory, chemical, and industrial settings.

That makes the activity relevant to founders who are setting up a production business around engineered porcelain or industrial ceramics, where the object being made matters as much as the material. A company registering this code should be able to recognise itself in the manufacturing act described by the scope: making the laboratory apparatus, electrical components, technical porcelain pieces, or ceramic industrial products themselves. The open scale range is broad. The record lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so the classification is not confined to a single enterprise size band.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. The code is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical editorial terms, that means the national record does not impose a foreign-shareholding cap below full foreign ownership for this activity. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the slim record adds a special capital number, operating threshold, licence timeline, or sector-specific condition, so those should not be read into the code from outside assumptions.

Bali is also clear, but for a different reason. The province’s moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island, yet this activity is not blocked in the Bali field. The Bali reason says the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it falls outside that moratorium block. The status is therefore not a hidden prohibition: it is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with l4_bali_blocked set to false. For a foreign investor reading the code today, the honest conclusion is that KBLI 23933 is nationally open to full foreign ownership and, on the record provided, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Porcelain Sanitaryware Is Fully Open, Including in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 23934 covers the manufacture of porcelain sanitary fixtures, open across all business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23934 is a manufacturing category for porcelain sanitary equipment. Its scope is practical and material-specific: the making of sanitary fixtures from porcelain, including toilets, bidets, washbasins, urinals, sinks, and bathtubs. This is not a catch-all for bathroom trading, installation, or services; the record points to industrial production of the porcelain fixtures themselves.

The code is open to every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the activity can be registered by very small operators as well as larger manufacturers, provided the registration matches the actual activity being carried out. For a founder, the key editorial point is to treat the product scope carefully. The code is anchored in porcelain sanitary equipment, so the commercial story should begin with what is made, not merely where the products are sold or used.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, a PMA structure is nationally open for this activity, and the record does not impose a lower foreign-share cap. There is no basis here to invent a special threshold, minimum capital figure, extra licence, tax treatment, or timeline. The national reading is simply that foreign ownership may reach 100% under the cited investment-list source.

The Bali picture is also unusually direct. Bali’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis, but this record says KBLI 23934 is not blocked by that moratorium. The reason given is that at Besar scale the OSS risk sits in the Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi band, which keeps it outside the blocked Low and Medium-Low category. So the honest conclusion is not a warning that foreigners are barred in Bali; it is the reverse. Based on this slim record, porcelain sanitaryware manufacturing is nationally open to PMA and not moratorium-blocked in Bali.

editorial.headline: Sanitary Ceramics With a Clear Bali Opening
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the manufacture of ceramic and clay sanitary ware, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
For code 23935, the activity is tightly drawn: it is the industrial manufacture of sanitary equipment made from clay or ceramic. The record names toilets, bidets, washbasins, urinals, sinks, and bathtubs as the relevant examples, which gives the category its practical shape. This is not a general building-materials label and not a retail trade activity; its centre of gravity is production. The business being registered is the maker of the sanitary ware itself, turning clay or ceramic into fixtures used in bathrooms, washrooms, and built environments.

The registration profile is broad. The slim record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so it can describe a small producer as well as a larger manufacturing operation, provided the registered activity remains within the stated manufacturing scope. That breadth matters because sanitary ceramics can sit across very different operating footprints: a modest workshop producing selected fixtures, or a larger plant producing multiple lines of toilets, basins, urinals, sinks, and baths. The code does not, by itself, add a minimum size, a capital threshold, or a special licensing promise; it simply identifies the manufacturing activity and the scales at which it is open.

Nationally, the PMA picture is clean. The status is TERBUKA, with a pma_max_asing of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Put simply, the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no partial foreign cap in the record to soften or complicate that conclusion. For founders reading this as an investment classification, the national message is therefore direct: this sanitary-ceramics manufacturing activity is open to foreign investment up to full foreign ownership under the cited source.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion on the record provided. The province’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis, but this activity is not blocked because the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. On the Bali assessment, the status remains OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, while l4_bali_blocked is false. That means the honest Bali reading is not a hidden prohibition: a foreign-owned company can register this activity in Bali today, subject to the activity staying within this manufacturing scope and without inventing extra conditions beyond the record. The key distinction is that Bali’s moratorium is real, but on these facts it does not catch this code.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers manufacturing non‑building products from clay, ceramic, or porcelain that don’t fit under the more specific stoneware or building‑material codes — think ceramic furniture, decorative art pieces, tableware, and similar finished goods made from fired clay.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Produk Bukan Bahan Bangunan Lainnya dari Tanah Liat atau Keramik dan Porselen (23939)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs planning to produce ceramic furniture, art porcelain, or specialty clay‑based goods — and Bali is not off the table: this KBLI's large-scale risk class sits above the moratorium's Low/Medium-Low band, so a PMA can still register it here.

editorial.headline: Clay, Ceramic and Porcelain Products Beyond Building Materials
editorial.standfirst: A precise KBLI for makers of non-building clay, ceramic and porcelain goods, nationally open to foreign investment and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is for manufacturers working with clay, ceramic and porcelain outside the building-materials lane. Its scope is deliberately residual but still quite concrete: it catches products made from those materials that are not otherwise classified in the record, including ceramic furniture and other ceramic goods. In plain terms, this is not about tiles, bricks or construction inputs. It is for the workshop, factory or production house making other finished objects from clay, ceramics or porcelain, where the material defines the industrial activity.

That breadth matters because the code is open across every business scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. A small ceramic studio and a larger industrial producer can both sit within the same activity description if the actual work is manufacturing these non-building products. The editorial point is not that every business will look alike, but that the classification is built around the production activity itself: making the goods, not simply trading them, displaying them or using them as part of another service.

Nationally, the investment picture is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership recorded is 100%. There is no foreign-share haircut in the slim record, so the national reading is clean: a foreign-owned company can use this activity code up to full foreign ownership, with the cited basis given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the record adds a minimum capital figure, special licence, production threshold or timetable, so none should be inferred. The reliable fact is the national openness, the 100% ceiling, and the availability across the listed scales.

Bali is often where the sharper question appears, because the province applies an island-wide, permanent moratorium blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA. Here, however, the Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which means it is not blocked by that moratorium. The honest conclusion is therefore not a hidden restriction but a usable distinction: nationally open, 100% foreign-owned, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the moratorium described in the record. For a founder, the discipline is to keep the classification tied to real manufacturing of non-building clay, ceramic or porcelain products, then read Bali through the recorded risk reason rather than assuming the moratorium catches everything.

editorial.headline: Cement Manufacturing With a Clear Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 23941 covers the making of cement products, nationally open to PMA, with Bali treating it outside the moratorium block at large scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23941 is the industrial home for cement manufacturing: the making of multiple forms of cement, including hydraulic cement and cement associated with charcoal or iron slag. Its scope reaches across the familiar and technical categories named in the record: portland cement, natural cement, aluminium-containing cement, slag cement, superphosphate cement, and other cement types. In plain English, this is not a trading or contracting label; it is for the activity of producing cement itself.

The registration picture is unusually broad by scale. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so the classification is not reserved only for large industrial players. That matters editorially because the code describes the activity, while the scale tells us who may sit inside it. A small producer and a large industrial operator may both be within the same activity description if what they do is the manufacturing of cement covered by the scope.

Nationally, the PMA position is clean: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That means the record does not impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership. The source cited for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, and there is no basis in the slim record to add side conditions, minimum capital figures, special licences, or timelines. The honest national reading is therefore simple: for foreign investment classification, this cement-manufacturing activity is open up to 100% foreign ownership.

Bali is where the reading must become more precise, but not more dramatic than the record allows. The provincial moratorium blocks all low and medium-low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali on a permanent, island-wide basis. This activity, however, is not marked as blocked in Bali. The reason given is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, placing it outside the moratorium block. So the honest Bali conclusion is not that cement manufacturing is casually frictionless; it is that, on the record provided, PMA registration is not blocked by the Bali moratorium because the relevant large-scale risk level is medium-high or high.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest Bali conclusion is not that cement manufacturing is casually frictionless; it is that PMA registration is not blocked by the Bali moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Lime Manufacturing That Remains Open in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers industrial lime production from limestone, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
Activity code 23942 is about the making of lime from limestone: quicklime, wall lime, plastering lime, slaked lime, and hydraulic lime. The scope is industrial rather than decorative. It points to the transformation of limestone into different lime products used in construction and related material supply, with the record describing the activity through the products made rather than through a specific plant size, technology, or customer market.

That matters because registration follows the activity as defined, not a founder’s branding of the business. A company making these forms of lime would sit here when its substance is the production of lime from limestone. The record opens the activity across **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** scales, so it is not framed as a category reserved only for large industrial operators. A small producer and a larger manufacturer can both fall within the same activity description if the registered business is genuinely making the lime products named in the scope.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is clear. The activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with **pma_max_asing** at **100%**. In plain English, the record permits foreign ownership up to the full national ceiling for this activity. There is no lower foreign-share cap in the slim record, and there is no additional national condition stated here beyond the open PMA status and the cited source. For founders, that makes the national reading unusually clean: the activity is foreign-open, and the ownership ceiling shown in the record is complete foreign ownership.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion in this record. The province’s moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide, but this activity is not marked as blocked. Its Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the stated reason is that OSS risk at the **Besar** scale is **Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi**, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. The honest Bali-side reading, therefore, is not that foreign investors are barred from registering this activity in Bali, but that the moratorium block does not apply on the facts given. The decisive point is narrow and important: this is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record does not add a PMA block.
editorial.pullQuote: This is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record does not add a PMA block.

editorial.headline: Gypsum Manufacturing With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers gypsum made from calcined gypsum or calcium sulfate, and remains nationally open to foreign ownership while not being blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the industrial making of gypsum: material formed from calcined gypsum, also described in the record as calcium sulfate, with calcined dolomite included in the scope. That is the useful editorial boundary. The activity is not a general construction-material label, and it is not a catch-all for every mineral product. It is centered on the manufacturing process that turns those stated inputs into gypsum within the registered business activity.

For founders, the registration story is unusually broad on business scale. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. In plain English, that means the code is not reserved only for large factories or excluded from smaller registered businesses by scale. A founder should still read the scope narrowly: the strength of the registration comes from matching the actual operation to the making of gypsum from the materials named in the record, rather than stretching the label to cover adjacent lines of business that are not stated here.

The national foreign-investment position is clean. Classified as TERBUKA, the activity permits foreign ownership of up to 100%. For a PMA structure, the important consequence is that the national rule does not impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, and the record gives no additional national condition, threshold, timeline, licence, tax treatment, or minimum-capital figure for this editorial to add.

Bali is also clear, but for a different reason. The province’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, under the cited governor letter. This activity is not blocked in Bali because the Bali reason states that at Besar scale the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not caught by that moratorium. The honest reading is therefore not a warning that foreign investors are shut out of Bali today. It is the opposite: nationally open at 100% foreign ownership, and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium on the record provided. The practical discipline is to keep the registration faithful to the gypsum-manufacturing scope and the stated scale-risk basis, because the Bali conclusion rests on those fields exactly.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This KBLI covers the manufacture of items whose main component is cement, often mixed with other minerals or plant fibers. It includes decorative products (statues, pots, reliefs, furniture, sinks) and construction materials (tiles, bricks, autoclaved aerated concrete, paving blocks, corrugated fiber‑cement sheets).
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, the activity is fully open for 100% foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Barang dari Semen (23951)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur wanting to produce decorative or building‑material cement goods, but who must currently look outside Bali for PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Cement Goods Manufacturing With Room to Scale in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A broad manufacturing category for cement-based decorative, building, and construction goods, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the manufacture of goods in which cement is the main constituent. The scope is broad: it reaches from decorative objects such as statues, flower pots, jars, furniture, raised relief work, reservoirs, troughs, tubs, ponds, sinks, and window frames, through to cement-based building materials such as tiles, bricks, blocks, autoclaved aerated concrete, paving blocks, sheets, panels, ventilation products, and non-asbestos fibre-cement boards, pipes, and layered sheets. It also includes construction components, structural and non-structural, for roads, bridges, housing, buildings, and water structures.

That breadth matters because this is not a narrow craft category dressed up as industry. It can describe small cement goods workshops, building-material production, and heavier component manufacturing: concrete utility poles, spun piles, square piles, prestressed concrete sheet piles, girders, box culverts and covers, concrete pipes, and beam, column, or wall components all sit inside the recorded scope. The common thread is not the final market but the material logic: cement as the principal base, sometimes mixed with other mineral or fibrous materials, and shaped into finished goods for decoration, construction supply, or infrastructure use.

The registration scale is equally broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so the code can serve both smaller producers and larger industrial setups. Nationally, it is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national investment line allows a fully foreign-owned PMA structure for this activity, subject only to the facts actually stated in the record: the open status, the 100% ceiling, the cited presidential-regulation basis, and the listed operating scales.

Bali does not change that into a closure. The province’s moratorium rule blocks PMA registration for low and medium-low risk activities, but this record says the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi and therefore not blocked by the moratorium. The Bali status is still written cautiously as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, which is the honest reading: this is not a Bali-blocked activity for PMA, but its Bali clearance rests on the record’s higher-risk classification at large scale. For founders, the practical takeaway is clean and narrow: cement goods manufacturing under this activity is nationally foreign-open, available across all listed scales, and not barred from PMA registration in Bali by the stated moratorium logic.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers manufacturing goods where limestone or chalk is the primary raw material. Think of classic blackboard chalk, artist's pastels/drawing chalk, and filler compounds like wall putty or wood dempul.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, a foreign-owned PMA can hold 100% of this business. In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Barang dari Kapur (23952)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs who want to produce chalk-based stationery items or industrial putty/filler products.

editorial.headline: Lime Goods Manufacturing With a Clear Bali Opening
editorial.standfirst: A focused manufacturing code for lime-based goods, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the moratorium record.
editorial.body:
This activity is a narrow but practical corner of manufacturing: making goods whose main constituent is lime. The slim record points to products such as writing chalk, drawing chalk, and putty, which places the code in the world of simple mineral-based articles rather than quarrying, construction contracting, or broad chemical production. The editorial point is its specificity. A founder registering here should be able to recognise the activity in the finished article: lime is the principal material, and the business is making goods from it.

The registration window is broad by business scale. The record opens the activity to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** operators, so the code is not framed only for industrial-scale factories. A small producer of chalk or putty can sit within the same activity description as a larger manufacturing operation, provided the core activity remains the production of lime-based goods. That matters because the scale field does not narrow the activity to one end of the market; it confirms that the code can be used across the full scale range listed in the record.

At the national level, the position on foreign investment is straightforward. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the maximum foreign ownership is **100%**. In plain English, the national record treats this as open to foreign investment up to full foreign ownership. There is no foreign-share cap below full ownership in the slim record, and there is no extra national threshold, licence, capital number, or timing requirement stated here. The only defensible reading is that, on the national PMA field, this activity is open at the stated ceiling and sourced to the presidential regulation references recorded for it.

Bali is where many KBLI readings become less honest if the moratorium is ignored, but this record does not show a Bali block. The Bali-side status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and `l4_bali_blocked` is false. The reason is important: at **Besar** scale, OSS risk is recorded as **Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi**, so the activity is not blocked by Bali’s province-wide moratorium, which applies to Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. That does not turn the code into a promise of approval, and it does not add facts outside the record. It simply means the honest Bali conclusion today is that PMA registration is not shown as blocked by the moratorium for this activity.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers manufacturing various gypsum products like boards, sheets, and panels for construction purposes. It also includes making building materials from plant substances such as wood wool, reeds, and straw that are bonded together with gypsum plaster.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally this activity is open to foreign ownership, and in Bali it is NOT blocked by the 13 May 2026 moratorium — its OSS risk class at the large-enterprise (Besar) scale is medium-high or high, which the moratorium leaves open. A PT PMA can pursue this code in Bali, subject to the standard licensing for its risk class.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Barang dari Gips (23953)? Here is the honest national-vs-Bali picture before you plan a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur who can meet the higher-risk licensing requirements — one of the doors that stays open in Bali.

editorial.headline: Gypsum Building Products, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 23953 covers construction-facing gypsum goods, with registration open from micro to large scale and full foreign ownership available nationally.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23953 is a manufacturing code for making goods from gypsum for construction use. Its centre of gravity is practical building material: gypsum boards, sheets, panels, and other formed products that enter the construction supply chain. The scope also reaches a more specific class of building goods made from plant-based substances, including wood wool, reeds, and straw, where those materials are bound together with gypsum plaster. In plain English, this is not a general construction service code; it is for producing gypsum-based construction materials.

The registration profile is broad. The activity is open to micro, small, medium, and large business scales, so it can describe anything from a small production operation to an industrial manufacturer, as long as the registered activity stays within the stated gypsum-goods scope. That breadth matters because the code is not limited to a single commercial size or a single format of product. What defines it is the material and output: gypsum goods for construction, including panels and other building-material forms.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The activity is marked open for PMA, with a maximum foreign shareholding of 100%, under the cited national investment framework. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national record does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. The important discipline is not to read extra conditions into that openness: the slim record gives the ownership ceiling, the open status, the source, and the eligible scales, but no separate threshold, licence, tax, or capital figure.

Bali does not reverse that national position here. The Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and it is not blocked by the province’s PMA moratorium. The reason is specific: at large scale, the OSS risk level is medium-high or high, which keeps it outside the Bali rule that blocks all low and medium-low risk KBLI for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. The honest reading is therefore straightforward: KBLI 23953 is nationally open to full foreign ownership and, on the Bali-side record provided, is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers the manufacture of various building and industrial materials that contain asbestos, such as corrugated or flat asbestos fiber boards, pressurized asbestos pipes, and coated asbestos products.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: matched with aggregation.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Barang dari Asbes (23954)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign manufacturer of construction materials who wants to produce asbestos-based building products, but must look outside Bali for PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Asbestos Goods Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Not Moratorium-Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers asbestos-containing building and industrial goods, with national PMA access up to full foreign ownership and Bali registration not blocked by the moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23954 covers the manufacturing of goods that contain asbestos, with the record centering the activity on building-material and industrial uses. In practical English, this means production of items such as corrugated asbestos fibre board, flat asbestos fibre board, pressurised asbestos pipe, layered asbestos products, and other asbestos-containing goods for the uses named in the scope. The important editorial point is that this is not a general construction, trading, or installation category; the activity described is manufacturing.

The scale position is broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises, so the code is not framed as belonging only to large industrial operators. A founder reading the classification should still treat the scale as a registration fact rather than a business-model shortcut: the listed scales say who may register the activity, while the scope says what the registered activity must actually do. Here, the common thread is the making of asbestos-containing goods, not the downstream sale or use of every material that might appear in a construction supply chain.

Nationally, the PMA signal is clear. The status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership field is 100%. That means the national record does not impose a foreign-shareholding cap below full ownership for this activity. The source attached to that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no basis in the slim record to add a minimum capital rule, sector licence, tax treatment, timing expectation, or extra threshold; those facts are simply not present here.

Bali is also unusually clean in this record. The province's moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA registration across Bali on a permanent basis, but this activity is not marked as blocked. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason given is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. The honest reading is therefore not a warning that Bali is closed, but a precise distinction: nationally open, full foreign ownership allowed, and not caught by Bali's Low or Medium-Low PMA moratorium on the facts supplied.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is nationally open, full foreign ownership allowed, and not caught by Bali's Low or Medium-Low PMA moratorium on the facts supplied.

intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this activity is fully open to 100% foreign ownership. editorial.headline: Ready-Mix Concrete and Mortar, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers non-fire-resistant mortar and ready-mix concrete manufacturing, open to all business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
For KBLI 23955, the activity is industrial production of nonrefractory mortar and ready-mix concrete. In plain terms, this is the making of mortar that is not fire-resistant, together with ready-to-use concrete formats and related surface-finishing materials. The record names dry mixed mortar, ready mixed concrete, dry mixed concrete, plaster skim coat, white skim coat, and grey skim coat as examples of what sits inside the scope. That gives the code a practical, materials-focused identity: it is about manufacturing prepared cementitious products, not about contracting, installation, distribution, or project delivery.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The slim record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the code is not reserved only for large industrial operators. A small producer of finishing plaster and a larger ready-mix concrete operation are both within the scale universe described by the record, provided the registered activity remains the manufacture of the covered products. The editorial distinction matters because the scope is defined by what is made: non-fire-resistant mortar, ready-mix or dry-mix concrete, and the listed plaster or skim-coat materials.

Nationally, the PMA position is clean: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national record does not impose a reduced foreign-equity cap for this code. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the slim record adds a special national threshold, minimum capital number, extra timeline, or sector-specific licence condition, so the honest reading should not invent one. The national story is simply that this manufacturing activity is open to PMA up to full foreign ownership.

Bali is also workable on the record provided, but for a specific reason. The province’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, yet this code is not blocked because the Bali reason says OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. In English: at large scale, the recorded OSS risk level is medium-high or high, so the Bali moratorium does not stop PMA registration for this activity. The Bali status is therefore not a contradiction of the national openness; it is the local risk-filter result that allows the national PMA openness to remain usable in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The national story is full PMA openness, and the Bali story is that the moratorium does not block it because the recorded large-scale risk sits above the Low and Medium-Low band.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers manufacturing marble products for household decorations (table tops, ornaments, statues), building materials (tiles, bathtubs), and marble furniture like tables and chairs.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible. A direct PMA setup in Bali is therefore not feasible at this time; existing local companies or non-PMA structures may be alternatives.

editorial.headline: Marble Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making of marble goods for interiors, buildings, display, and furniture, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23961 is about manufacturing finished goods from marble, not merely trading stone or installing surfaces after the fact. The record describes a workshop or industrial operation turning marble into household and display pieces such as tabletops, ornaments, and statues; building-related goods such as tiles and marble bathtubs; and furniture such as marble tables and chairs. Its centre of gravity is fabrication: taking marble as material and producing durable objects for homes, projects, interiors, and furnishing uses.

That breadth matters because the activity can sit at very different business sizes. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale businesses, so it is not reserved only for a large factory profile. A small atelier producing decorative objects, a growing workshop supplying marble furniture, and a larger manufacturer making construction-facing marble products all sit within the described scope, provided the actual activity remains the making of marble goods covered by the record. The editorial point is simple: this is a production code for marble articles across domestic, display, building-material, and furniture uses.

At the national level, the position on foreign investment is uncomplicated. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership recorded is 100%. There is no lower foreign-share ceiling in the slim record to soften or qualify that national position. For a foreign-owned setup, the national reading is therefore fully open on ownership, with the cited source being Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali does not change that answer into a prohibition on the facts supplied here. The province’s moratorium rule blocks low and medium-low risk activities for PMA, but this record says the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and explains that, at Besar scale, OSS risk is medium-high or high, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. In practical editorial terms, the honest lede is not a warning that foreigners cannot register it in Bali; it is that marble-goods manufacturing is nationally open to full foreign ownership and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali. The real discipline is to keep the activity tightly matched to making marble goods, because that is the scope that carries the ownership and Bali reading here.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest lede is that marble-goods manufacturing is nationally open to full foreign ownership and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers turning granite stone into finished goods — from tabletops, ornaments, and statues for households, to tiles and bathtubs for construction, and even full furniture like granite tables and chairs. It’s essentially a granite workshop manufacturing custom or stock products for interiors and building supply.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Barang dari Batu Granit (23962)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur who wants to craft and export high-end granite decor, building materials, or furniture, but under current rules they would need to look outside Bali for setup.

editorial.headline: Granite Goods Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making of granite household pieces, building materials, and furniture, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23962 is for manufacturers turning granite into finished goods, not merely trading stone or installing it on site. Its scope is practical and product-led: granite tabletops, ornaments, and statues for household or display use; granite tiles and bathtubs for building purposes; and granite tables and chairs for furniture. The common thread is the making of objects from granite, with the finished item determining the activity’s commercial identity.

The record is unusually broad on scale. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so the same activity can describe anything from a compact workshop making decorative granite pieces to a larger industrial operation producing building materials or furniture. That breadth matters because the category is not limited to one buyer type. A registrant may be serving homes, interiors, construction inputs, or furniture demand, as long as the underlying activity remains the manufacture of goods from granite.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clean: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a pma_max_asing of 100. In plain English, a PMA structure is nationally open up to full foreign ownership. The record cites Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the source for that position. There is no partial foreign-equity cap in the national field, so the important national message is not one of restriction but of eligibility.

Bali adds a separate filter, and here the result is also workable. The provincial moratorium rule recorded here blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA across Bali, but this activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The reason given is that, at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which places it outside the blocked Low and Medium-Low band. The Bali status is therefore not a contradiction of the national opening: on this slim record, granite goods manufacturing is nationally open to PMA and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Manufacturing of stone products other than marble or granite — stone statues, reliefs, decorative items for household, garden, and display. If you're carving, shaping, or finishing stone (especially soft limestone) into decorative or artistic products, this is the code.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Risk: Rendah (Low)** for Small/Medium scales — only NIB required. **Menengah Tinggi (Medium-High)** for Large scale — NIB + Sertifikat Standar required with detailed facility documentation, production plans, QC equipment calibration, and 7-day issuance at Governor level.

**PMA:** Fully open (TERBUKA), 100% foreign ownership allowed. IDR 10B minimum investment. Large-scale operations require ISO 9001 certification.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct match from KBLI 2020. No changes.
intel_2026.baliContext: Batubulan village is THE stone carving center of Bali. Paras stone (soft Balinese limestone) carvings are iconic — temple guardians, garden statues, wall reliefs, water features. The export market is strong for garden and temple decorations shipped to Australia, Europe, and the US. Production is labor-intensive and deeply tied to local artisan communities. PMA entities typically handle design, quality control, and export logistics while local carvers do the actual work.
intel_2026.youllAlsoNeed:
- 23961 — If you work with marble or granite specifically
- 16293 — If you also produce wood carvings
- 47781 — If you retail souvenirs and crafts
- 46734 — If you wholesale cement, lime, sand, or stone as construction material
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Starting a stone carving business in Bali? 23969 is open to PMA — Batubulan village is the center of this centuries-old craft industry.

editorial.headline: Stonework Beyond Marble and Granite, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A focused manufacturing category for non-marble, non-granite stone goods, open across business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23969 is a practical manufacturing code for stone products that sit outside the marble and granite lane. Its scope is broad but still clearly bounded: it covers the making of goods from other kinds of stone for furniture, household use, display, and construction materials. In plain terms, this is where a workshop or factory making stone tables, mortars, cobek, grinding stones, whetstones, stone slabs, crushed stone, stone ash, mosaic cubes, monuments, or ornamental stone belongs, provided the material is not marble or granite.

That distinction matters editorially because this is not a catch-all for every premium stone surface or quarry-adjacent activity. The record frames the code around fabrication: turning stone into useful, decorative, or building-related goods. A founder looking at this category should read it as a manufacturing identity, not merely a trading label. The examples range from highly domestic objects such as kitchen grinding tools to architectural and memorial products, which gives the code a wide commercial field while keeping the core activity anchored in making physical stone goods.

The scale picture is unusually straightforward. The code is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so it can fit anything from a small producer with a tight product line to a larger industrial operation. Nationally, the PMA position is also clean: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. There is no partial foreign cap in the slim record, so the correct reading is that a foreign-owned company may hold the full national allowance for this activity.

Bali is where many otherwise simple readings become less obvious, but this record is explicit. The province’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island, permanently. This activity is not blocked in Bali: the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason given is that at Besar scale the OSS risk sits at Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so the moratorium does not stop PMA registration. The honest conclusion is therefore not a warning dressed up as an opportunity, but a narrow and precise one: nationally this code is foreign-open up to 100%, and in Bali it is not caught by the moratorium on lower-risk PMA activity.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This group includes manufacturing natural or artificial abrasive powder or granules on a backing of cloth, paper, or other material, which may be cut, joined, frameless, or produced by other methods. It covers the production of abrasive products such as coated abrasives (like sandpaper), bonded abrasives (like grinding wheels), and natural or artificial abrasive stones used for scraping, sharpening, cutting, grinding, and/or polishing.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally this activity is open to foreign ownership, and in Bali it is NOT blocked by the 13 May 2026 moratorium — its OSS risk class at the large-enterprise (Besar) scale is medium-high or high, which the moratorium leaves open. A PT PMA can pursue this code in Bali, subject to the standard licensing for its risk class.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: code renumbered.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Produk Abrasif (23991)? Here is the honest national-vs-Bali picture before you plan a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur who can meet the higher-risk licensing requirements — one of the doors that stays open in Bali.

editorial.headline: Abrasive Product Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers the industrial making of abrasive grains, coated abrasives, grinding products, and abrasive stones for cutting, sharpening, polishing, and finishing work.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23991 is a manufacturing code for abrasive products: the quiet, technical materials that make cutting, grinding, sharpening, scraping, smoothing, and polishing possible. Its scope reaches from natural or artificial abrasive powders and grains to abrasive materials mounted on cloth, paper, or other bases. It also covers products that are cut, joined, made without a frame, or otherwise formed into usable abrasive goods.

In plain English, this is the industrial home for sandpaper-style coated abrasives, bonded grinding products, and natural or artificial abrasive stones used as working surfaces or tools. The activity is not framed as retail, repair, contracting, or equipment operation; the record points to production. A founder using this classification should therefore be describing a business that makes abrasive products themselves, not merely one that uses abrasives in another workshop process.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so the code can fit anything from a small producer to a larger industrial operation, provided the registered activity remains within the described manufacturing scope. That breadth matters because abrasives sit inside many supply chains: construction, metalworking, woodworking, fabrication, maintenance, and finishing all depend on them, but the classification is anchored in the making of the abrasive material or product, not the downstream trade that consumes it.

For foreign-owned registration, the national position is clean: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100%. That means the slim record does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership at the national level. The Bali picture is also open on the facts given here. Bali’s moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI island-wide, permanently, but this activity is not blocked because the record places the OSS risk at Besar scale in the Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi range. The honest reading is therefore straightforward: a foreign investor can treat this as nationally open, and the Bali moratorium does not itself close the door for PMA registration under this record.

editorial.headline: Where Natural Asphalt Becomes an Industrial Product
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 23992 covers the processing and refining of asphalt rock and comparable asphalt-based materials, with national PMA access open across all recorded scales.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 23992 is an industrial code for turning asphalt-bearing stone into usable asphalt-derived products.** The record frames the activity as the processing and/or refining of natural asphalt rock, including Buton asphalt, and goods derived from asphalt rock or similar materials. In plain English, this is not general construction work and not road contracting; it is the manufacturing and treatment layer where a mined or natural asphalt material is processed into an industrial product.

The scope also draws a clean boundary around what this activity is not. The record excludes petroleum-refinery outputs such as asphalt, tar, bitumen, and wax. That distinction matters because the commercial identity of this code rests on the material source: asphalt rock and comparable materials, not downstream products from oil refining. For a founder, the practical question is therefore whether the planned operation is built around processing or refining asphalt stone and its derivatives. If the business model is instead centred on refinery-derived asphalt products, this record does not give that activity a home.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It marks the activity as open to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** operators, which means the code is not confined to a single enterprise size in the data provided. A small processor, a mid-sized manufacturer, and a large industrial operation can all sit within the recorded scale band, provided the real activity stays inside the defined scope. The scale breadth should not be confused with a licence, timeline, or facility requirement; the record gives scale eligibility, not a separate compliance checklist.

The national-versus-Bali picture is straightforward. Nationally, the PMA status is **TERBUKA**, with a recorded foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. Bali does not add a separate percentage in this record. Its status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the record says the activity is not blocked: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The Bali moratorium rule itself blocks all low and medium-low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently, but this record’s Bali reason places the relevant large-scale risk level outside that block. The honest reading is therefore that KBLI 23992 is nationally foreign-open and, on the data supplied here, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is that KBLI 23992 is nationally foreign-open and, on the data supplied here, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Refined Non-Metal Minerals With a Clear National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 23993 covers industrial refining of non-metal minerals into new physical and chemical forms, open nationally to PMA and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23993 is an industrial manufacturing classification for non-metal minerals that have moved beyond extraction or simple handling. The scope is the making of products through refining, smelting, direct reduction or metallurgical processes, and other chemical processes applied to non-metal minerals or their derivatives. The defining point is transformation: the output has different physical and chemical properties from the input material. The record gives a wide range of possible forms, including lumps, powder, granules, ingots, pellets, rods, wire, discs, and other forms.

In plain English, this is where a non-metal mineral becomes an engineered industrial product. The examples in the record are specific and technical: metallurgical-grade silicon, polysilicon, and silicon ingots. That gives the activity a heavy manufacturing character rather than a retail, trading, or small workshop profile. The business is about controlled processing, material conversion, and industrial output, not merely collecting or selling raw mineral material.

The registration scale is broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the classification is not reserved only for large operators in the national taxonomy. At the same time, the substance of the activity naturally points to operators who can describe a real production process: refining, smelting, reduction, metallurgy, or chemical transformation. A founder choosing this code should be able to show that the planned activity matches that manufacturing scope, because the classification is anchored in process and output, not in a general connection to minerals.

The national foreign-investment position is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with a PMA foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali does not change that into a separate percentage or local cap in this record. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record states: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” That matters because the Bali moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, island-wide and permanent. Here, however, the record does not mark the activity as blocked. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: nationally this is fully open to PMA, and the Bali record does not block PMA registration for this activity under the stated moratorium logic.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is straightforward: nationally this is fully open to PMA, and the Bali record does not block PMA registration for this activity.

data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan pembuatan berbagai macam produk mineral nonlogam lainnya yang tidak diklasifikasikan di tempat lain, seperti tepung kaolin, kalsinasi kaolin, tepung gips, dan tepung talk serta pengeringan dan penggilingan tanah liat menjadi bubuk tanah liat, termasuk juga kegiatan pembuatan batu korek api (lighter flint); bahan friksi dan barang tak berbingkai dengan bahan pokok substansi mineral atau selulosa; bahan penyekat dari mineral, seperti wol terak, wol batu dan jenis wol lainnya; vermikulit tereksfoliasi (exfoliated vermiculate), tanah liat yang dikembangkan dan sejenis penyekat dengan panas, bahan penyerap suara; barang dari berbagai substansi mineral, seperti mika dan barang dari mika, barang dari tanah gambut (peat) sebagai bahan pembakar; korundum buatan; karbon dan serat karbon (kecuali kain dari serat karbon), grafit dan produk dari grafit, seperti bahan baku anoda dalam bentuk pasta atau bubuk; serta serat grafit dan produk turunannya (kecuali elektroda dan peralatan elektrik).
Kelompok ini tidak mencakup kegiatan pemurnian produk mineral nonlogam, lihat kelompok 23993.

editorial.headline: A Broad Industrial Home for Non-Metal Mineral Products
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 23999 covers specialised non-metal mineral manufacturing, open nationally to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23999 is a broad industrial category for non-metal mineral products that sit outside more specific classifications. Its scope covers the making of kaolin flour and calcined kaolin, gypsum flour, talc flour, and the drying and milling of clay into clay powder. It also reaches into more specialised materials: lighter flint, friction materials, unframed goods based on mineral substances or cellulose, mineral insulation such as slag wool and rock wool, expanded clay, exfoliated vermiculite, heat-insulating materials, and sound-absorbing materials.

The record also places mica goods, peat goods used as fuel, artificial corundum, carbon and carbon fibre products, graphite products, graphite fibre and related derivatives within the same activity, while excluding carbon-fibre fabric, electrodes, electrical equipment, and the refining of non-metal mineral products. In practical terms, this is not a retail or trading code. It is for manufacturers dealing with processed mineral inputs, industrial insulation, friction or refractory-type materials, graphite-based inputs, and other mineral-substance products that the classification does not place elsewhere.

On scale, the code is unusually broad: it is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses. That matters because the activity can describe both smaller mineral-processing operations and larger industrial manufacturing facilities. The record does not add a separate capital threshold, licence list, operating timeline, or tax treatment, so none should be assumed. What it does say is enough for a clean registration reading: the activity is nationally marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

For Bali, the record is also clear. It marks l4_bali_blocked as false and gives the Bali status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” That is the key distinction. Bali’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently, but this record does not place KBLI 23999 inside that blocked outcome. The result is a genuinely open reading: nationally open to foreign ownership up to 100%, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the Bali-side record provided.

editorial.headline: Basic Iron and Steel at Industrial Scale
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24101 covers the foundational making of iron and crude steel, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA in Bali under the record supplied.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24101 is not a decorative manufacturing code. It is the industrial base of iron and steel: the making of iron and steel in basic form, beginning with materials such as iron ore pellets, sponge iron, pig iron, and moving into crude steel forms such as steel ingots, billets, blooms, and slabs. The record also places alloy iron and alloy steel inside the same field, together with furnace activity, steel converters, rolling mills, and finishing. In plain English, this is the code for turning mined products, scrap, and other sources into the basic iron and semi-finished steel forms that sit upstream of many later manufacturing chains.

The scope is broad because the activity is broad. It includes pig iron in basic block form, ferro-alloys, directly reduced iron products made from iron ore, hollow iron products, iron produced through electrolysis or other chemical refining processes, iron granules and iron powder, steel ingots and other basic steel forms, the remelting of iron or steel scrap ingots, and semi-finished steel from mining products and other sources. The important editorial point is that the code is about primary transformation, not retailing, trading, installation, or downstream fabricated goods. It is a heavy manufacturing category for the basic production stage itself.

The record opens this activity across the full business-scale ladder: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the classification is not reserved in the record to one scale only, even though the commercial reality of iron and steel production will usually be shaped by plant, process, energy, raw material, and finishing capacity. For registration analysis, however, the slim record says the scale availability is complete. A founder reading this should therefore separate the legal classification question from the practical industrial question: the code describes the activity; the record states which scales are open to it.

Nationally, the PMA picture is clean. For this activity, the record lists TERBUKA and sets pma_max_asing at 100, citing Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In Bali, the same record does not mark it as blocked. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record is still important: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. But this activity, on the supplied record, is not caught by that block. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: KBLI 24101 is nationally open to foreign ownership up to 100%, and the Bali record supplied does not block PMA registration for it.

editorial.headline: Steel Rolling With a Clear National and Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24102 covers the rolling of steel into bars, beams, sheets, rails, wire and related formed products, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24102 is the industrial activity of rolling steel, both hot and cold. In plain English, the record places this code around the transformation of steel into rolled products: steel wire rod, round bar, flat bar, reinforcing bar, structural profiles such as H-beams and I-beams, strip, rail, plate, hot-rolled sheet and cold-rolled sheet. The scope also reaches coated and uncoated steel sheets, the rolling of steel scrap, and the making of hot-rolled billets or pieces where the activity remains inside this steel-rolling family.

The texture of the scope matters because this is not a narrow trading label or a generic metalworking description. It includes open sections made by hot rolling, solid sections produced through cold drawing, grinding and turning, and open sections formed progressively through rolling machines, press folding, or flat-steel rolling. It also includes steel wire, whether single wire or strand, when produced through cold drawing, tempering and stressing. The record extends to steel sheet piles or welded open steel sections, and steel railway material in the form of rails that are not yet installed. The centre of gravity is therefore clear: this is manufacturing capacity for rolled steel forms, from bar and profile to sheet, wire and rail material.

On scale, the code is broadly available in the record. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar business scales, so the registration frame is not confined to one size of operator. A smaller workshop, a medium industrial operation, or a large-scale mill may all sit within the scale vocabulary given here, provided the registered activity is genuinely the rolling and forming described in the scope. The editorial point is that the code should be read by activity, not by ambition: what matters is whether the business is making these rolled steel products, including the specified hot-rolled, cold-rolled, drawn, formed, coated or uncoated outputs.

The national PMA picture is straightforward. Under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, the record lists the activity as TERBUKA and gives pma_max_asing as 100. Rendered commercially, that means the national foreign-ownership ceiling shown by the record is 100%. The Bali layer is also unusually clean compared with activities that are caught by the province’s Low and Medium-Low risk moratorium. Here, l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated basis is specific: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule still matters as background because the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, but this activity is not marked as blocked by that rule in the supplied record. The honest reading is therefore: nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and not blocked for Bali PMA registration by the Bali moratorium field in this record.

editorial.headline: Iron and Steel Pipe Manufacturing, Open Nationally and in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24103 covers industrial pipe, tube, hollow profile, and fitting production from iron and steel, with full foreign ownership open nationally.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24103 is an industrial manufacturing classification for making iron and steel tubes, pipes, pipe joints, and related hollow steel profiles. Its scope is not retail, trading, or installation; it is the production side of the pipe economy. The record describes activity that includes seamless steel tubes, pipes, and hollow profiles formed through hot rolling, hot drawing, hot extruding, cold rolling, or cold drawing. It also includes welded steel tubes and pipes produced through welding and hot or cold forming, as a continuation of cold rolling or cold drawing processes.

The classification also reaches the fabrication of steel pipe fittings. The examples in the record are technical and specific: flat flanges, flanges with forged collars, butt-welded fittings, threaded fittings, and socket-welded fittings. In plain English, this is a code for factories that shape iron and steel into pipe systems and the connecting parts that allow those systems to be assembled. The centre of gravity is heavy manufacturing: metal input, industrial forming, welding or drawing processes, and finished pipe or fitting products.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. KBLI 24103 is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses. That means the classification is not reserved only for large factories in the record itself; the available scale bands run from micro through large. For founders, the important editorial point is to separate the business scale question from the foreign-ownership question. The scale field says who may register the activity by size category. The PMA field says whether foreign investment is nationally open, and here the national status is TERBUKA with a pma_max_asing of 100.

The Bali picture is also clear from the record. Nationally, foreign ownership is open up to 100%, under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali does have a province-level moratorium rule in this dataset: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” But this specific record is not marked as blocked in Bali. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” So the honest reading is direct: KBLI 24103 is foreign-open nationally, and the Bali record does not block PMA registration for it today.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 24103 sits in heavy manufacturing: iron and steel are formed into pipes, tubes, hollow profiles, and the fittings that make pipe systems usable.
