data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Precious Metals at the Basic-Materials Stage
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24201 covers the industrial making of precious metals in basic forms, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for Bali PMA on this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24201 sits at the industrial beginning of the precious-metals chain. The record describes the activity as the making, refining, smelting, alloying, and casting of precious metals into basic forms: ingots, billets, slabs, bars, pellets, blocks, sheets, pigs, alloys, and powders. Its examples are deliberately material and unfinished: silver ingots, gold ingots, and platinum pellets. This is not a retail-facing description and not a jewellery description. It is about producing the base metal forms from which further industrial, commercial, or manufacturing activity can proceed.

That matters because the code is framed around process and form, not around a single commodity story. A founder registering this activity is telling OSS that the business handles precious metals at the primary industrial stage: purification, melting, blending into alloys, and casting into standardized shapes or powders. The scope is broad enough to cover different precious metals and several basic output formats, but it is still bounded by the record's own wording. The activity is the industrial creation of those base forms; anything beyond that would need its own source before it could be claimed.

On scale, the record is unusually clear. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. In practical editorial terms, this means the classification is not reserved in the record for only large industrial operators; it can be registered across the full scale ladder stated in the slim record. That does not create extra rights, licences, or operational permissions by itself. It simply tells us which business scales the record marks as open for this KBLI activity.

The national-vs-Bali picture is also straightforward. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For Bali, the record does not mark this activity as blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is precise: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium that blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The honest reading is therefore clean: on this record, a foreign-owned company can treat KBLI 24201 as nationally open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali, while still respecting the record's limits and not inventing any Bali-specific percentage, quota, or side condition.
editorial.pullQuote: On this record, KBLI 24201 is nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: The Basic Metals Code for Non-Ferrous Smelting and Casting
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24202 covers the industrial base where non-ferrous metals are refined, melted, alloyed, and cast into primary forms.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24202 is not a retail or workshop category. It is an industrial code for making non-ferrous metals in their basic forms: ingots, billets, slabs, rods, pellets, blocks, sheets, pig metal, powders, granules, alloys, cathodes, bearing metal, and related primary outputs. The record places brass, aluminium, zinc, copper, tin, rare-earth metals, and rare-earth alloys inside its scope, including the group of 15 lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium. In plain English, this is the upstream metal-making activity before those materials become components, consumer products, or construction inputs.

The operative verbs are refining, smelting, alloying, and casting. That matters because the code is anchored in transformation at the basic-metal stage, not merely trading, storing, or using finished metal. A business using this code is positioning itself as a producer of primary non-ferrous metal forms: the plant that turns material into ingots, billets, slabs, rods, pellets, cathodes, powder, granules, or alloys. The Indonesian scope is broad, but it is also specific: it repeatedly returns to non-ferrous metals in basic form, including rare-earth metals and their alloys.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. That does not make every project operationally simple, and the record does not give any capital, licensing, tax, land, or timeline detail. What it does say is that the KBLI scale door is not confined to a single business size. A founder reading this should separate that scale eligibility from the physical reality of the activity itself: this is still an industrial metals code whose scope is defined by smelting, refining, alloying, and casting primary non-ferrous outputs.

The national-vs-Bali picture is clean. Nationally, the code is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. For a PMA reading of the record, that means the national field does not show a foreign-equity cap below full foreign ownership. Bali is also not marked as blocked: the Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason is stated as “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium text in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this record does not place KBLI 24202 inside that blocked result. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: on the fields provided, KBLI 24202 is nationally foreign-open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the stated moratorium rule.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is straightforward: KBLI 24202 is nationally foreign-open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the stated moratorium rule.

editorial.headline: Non-Ferrous Metal Rolling With a Clear Bali Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24203 covers hot and cold rolling of non-ferrous metals, and the record marks it as nationally foreign-open and not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24203 is the activity code for rolling non-ferrous metals: not the broad romance of “metal industry,” but the more exact work of turning copper, aluminium, silver, zinc, magnesium, tin, and platinum into plates, sheets, strips, foils, and related forms. The record covers both hot rolling and cold rolling. It also reaches into the finishing and forming steps that produce metal wire, including drawing, tempering, and stressing, whether the wire is single or stranded, and whether or not it functions as an electrical conductor.

That makes the code most relevant to businesses whose actual registered activity is the milling and rolling of non-ferrous metal inputs into these intermediate metal products. The examples in the record are practical and industrial: copper plate, aluminium plate, copper sheet, aluminium sheet, silver strip, zinc strip, aluminium strip, magnesium sheet, tin foil, and platinum strip. The emphasis is on the process and output form. If the business is built around this rolling, forming, and wire-making scope, this is the activity being described.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar as open to the activity, so the code is not presented as belonging only to large industrial operators. A registrant may sit at any of those listed business scales, provided the activity itself matches the scope. That matters because this is a process-led classification: the decisive question is not how glossy the business looks from outside, but whether the registered activity is the rolling of non-ferrous metals and the related wire-forming processes described in the record.

The national foreign-ownership picture is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership recorded is 100%. In plain English, the slim record treats this code as nationally open to foreign investment up to full foreign ownership, with the source given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The Bali picture is also clear, but for a different reason: the record marks Bali as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and says, verbatim, “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this code is not flagged as blocked. So the honest reading is direct: for KBLI 24203, the record shows a nationally foreign-open activity and no Bali moratorium block today.
editorial.pullQuote: For KBLI 24203, the record shows a nationally foreign-open activity and no Bali moratorium block today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers the extrusion of non-ferrous metals (like aluminum and copper) into bars, rods, and custom profiles—including those used as electrical conductors. It does not cover pipe or pipe fitting production, which falls under a separate code.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is fully open to 100% foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Ekstrusi Logam Bukan Besi (24204)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign manufacturers or electrical infrastructure suppliers seeking to produce aluminum, copper, or other non-ferrous metal profiles in Indonesia—but who must currently look outside Bali.

editorial.headline: Non-Ferrous Metal Extrusion, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24204 is a manufacturing code for aluminium, copper, and other non-ferrous extrusions, open across business scales and not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24204 covers the extrusion of non-ferrous metals: aluminium bars, copper bars, aluminium rods, copper rods, and other non-ferrous extruded products formed in circular, square, or other cross-sections. The record also brings electrical-conductor extrusions into the scope, so the practical centre of the code is shaped non-ferrous metal output rather than general metal trading or broad fabrication. It is an industrial activity with a clear physical process: metal is pressed through a profile to produce consistent bars, rods, and related extruded forms.

That makes the code relevant to operators whose business is built around repeatable metal-production capacity. The available scales are broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all open in the record. In plain English, the activity is not reserved only for a large industrial company. It can sit at different operating sizes, provided the registered business scale matches the actual setup. The editorial point is important: the code is defined by the extrusion activity and the non-ferrous material, not by a brand position, customer type, or downstream sales channel.

Nationally, the PMA position is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with `pma_max_asing` at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-invested company, that means the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no lower national cap in the slim record, and there is no stated sector-specific ownership dilution to invent. The foreign-investment reading is therefore straightforward: this activity is open at the national level, including for full foreign ownership.

The Bali picture is also relatively clear, but for a different reason. The record does not mark KBLI 24204 as blocked in Bali: `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`. The reason given is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this activity is not caught by that block on the stated risk reading. So the honest conclusion is not a hidden Bali ownership cap or a local-partner condition. It is simpler: nationally open, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the slim record.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers manufacturing tubes, pipes, and pipe fittings made from non-ferrous metals (like aluminum, copper) and steel, not from iron alone.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, 100% foreign ownership is allowed. In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.

editorial.headline: Metal Pipe Manufacturing Is Nationally Open and Bali-Cleared
editorial.standfirst: For tubes, pipes, and fittings made from non-ferrous metal and steel, the record gives a clean PMA answer: open nationally and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is about making physical pipe products: tubes, pipes, and pipe fittings made from non-ferrous metal and steel. The scope is industrial and material-specific. It is not a trading entry, an installation service, or a general metalworking label. The record points to manufacturing itself: the production of tabung, pipa, and sambungan pipa, with a clear material boundary around non-ferrous metal and steel.

The scope also keeps one important edge in view. Seamless copper tube/pipe is mentioned as outside this activity’s coverage, so the clean reading is that this entry should be used where the business is producing the covered pipe and fitting products, not where the activity is specifically the seamless copper tube/pipe carve-out. That distinction matters because the registration should follow the product actually manufactured, not the broader idea of “metal pipes” in ordinary language.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so the activity is not framed only for heavy industrial operators. A small producer and a large manufacturing company can both sit inside the scale range if the registered activity matches the stated scope. Nationally, the PMA position is equally direct: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a pma_max_asing of 100. In plain English, the national record allows foreign ownership up to 100%, under the cited national source Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

The Bali reading does not undercut that national openness. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and the record says l4_bali_blocked is false. The record identifies the precise reason: “At scale Besar, OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. That means the Bali moratorium rule still matters as background, because the province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. But for this activity, the record’s own Bali result is not a block. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: nationally foreign-open, capped at no less than the recorded 100%, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the data provided.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is clean: nationally foreign-open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the data provided.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Nuclear Fuel Manufacturing, With Bali Still Open on the Record
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24206 covers uranium and thorium fuel-cycle manufacturing at large scale, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24206 is not a generic metalworking activity. The record defines it around the industrial production of nuclear fuel materials: making uranium metal and related compounds from pitchblende or other ores, producing uranium alloys and dispersions including cermet, forming ceramic products and mixtures containing natural uranium or its compounds, and smelting or refining uranium metal from uranium-bearing ores. It also includes uranium and thorium enrichment as one integrated chain of activity for producing nuclear fuel.

The scope then extends beyond material processing into the small final-cycle side of non-reactor nuclear installations. The record includes both operation and construction of small non-reactor final-cycle nuclear installations. In plain English, this is a highly specialised nuclear-fuel and nuclear-installation activity, not a broad manufacturing bucket. A founder reading the code should treat the uranium, thorium, enrichment, smelting, refining, and non-reactor installation language as the centre of the classification.

On scale, the record is narrow. The only scale open to this activity is **Besar**. That matters because the code is not presented as a micro, small, or medium activity in the slim record; it is framed as a large-scale business activity. Nationally, the PMA status is **TERBUKA**, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. On the national layer alone, the record therefore describes a foreign-open activity with no reduced foreign-share cap.

The Bali picture is also explicit, and it should not be made more dramatic than the record allows. Bali’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, but this record marks KBLI 24206 as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, with **l4_bali_blocked** set to false. Its stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The honest reading is that, on this record, a foreign investor is not blocked from PMA registration in Bali by the provincial moratorium. The limitation visible here is not a Bali ownership cap; it is simply the record’s own combination of large scale, national openness, and Bali non-blocked status.

editorial.headline: Iron and Steel Casting With a Clear Bali Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24310 covers the foundry work of melting, blending, and casting iron and steel into rough cast products, with all business scales open in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24310 is a foundry activity: the melting, mixing, casting, or pouring of iron and steel into rough cast products. The record frames the output as cast iron, cast steel, and alloy cast steel, not finished retail goods or downstream installation services. Its scope also reaches semi-finished iron and steel castings, grey cast iron, spheroidal graphite cast iron, malleable cast iron, cast-steel products, cast-iron tubes, pipes, hollow profiles, tube and pipe fittings, seamless steel tubes and pipes made through centrifugal casting, and fittings made from cast steel.

That makes this a production code for operators whose business is the casting process itself. The scale picture is broad: the record lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar as open to this activity. In plain terms, the classification is not written only for heavy industrial players; it can sit across the whole scale range in the slim record. The commercial substance, however, remains specific: iron and steel are melted or cast into rough or semi-finished forms, including tube, pipe, profile, and fitting outputs when those outputs arise from the casting activity described.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clean. The record marks the PMA status as TERBUKA and gives pma_max_asing as 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. A foreign investor reading only the national field would see a fully open national ceiling. There is no lower percentage cap in the record, and no extra threshold, capital rule, or licensing condition appears in the slim data, so none should be implied.

The Bali side is also clear, but it should be read for what it actually says. The province-wide moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, but this activity is not marked as blocked in Bali. Its l4_bali_status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” For this code, the honest national-vs-Bali reading is therefore aligned: it is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium field provided.

editorial.headline: Non-Ferrous Metal Casting, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 24320 covers the melting, alloying, and casting of non-ferrous metals, with national PMA access at 100% and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 24320 is the industrial language for foundry work outside iron and steel: the melting, alloying, casting, and pouring of non-ferrous metals into basic forms. In practical terms, the record points to cast copper and its alloys, cast aluminium and its alloys, and cast nickel and its alloys. It also reaches into semi-finished casting from aluminium, magnesium, titanium, zinc, and similar metals, along with light-metal casting, heavy-metal casting, precious-metal casting, and die-casting for non-ferrous metals.

That scope matters because this is not written as a narrow retail or trading activity. It is production: taking metal through heat, composition, moulding, and casting into forms that can sit early in a manufacturing chain. The Indonesian description is broad enough to catch both basic cast forms and semi-finished non-ferrous outputs, while remaining anchored to one clear boundary: these are not iron-and-steel casting activities. For a founder, the clean reading is that the business identity sits around the foundry process itself, not merely the downstream sale of finished goods.

The registration picture is also unusually straightforward in the slim record. The activity is open to Micro, Small, Medium, and Large scales, so the scale field does not reserve the code only for a large industrial operator. Nationally, the PMA status is marked TERBUKA, with `pma_max_asing` at 100 under the stated source, Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That means the record does not show a national foreign-shareholding cap below full ownership for this activity. It is a nationally open code for foreign investment, subject only to the facts actually recorded here.

Bali does not change that conclusion in this record. The province’s moratorium rule is stated as blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but KBLI 24320 is not marked as blocked. Its Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`, and the reason given is that OSS risk at Large scale is Medium-High/High, therefore not blocked by the moratorium. The honest national-versus-Bali picture is therefore clean: nationally open at 100% foreign ownership, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the moratorium data supplied in the record.

data.judul: Industri Produk Logam Struktural Bukan Aluminium untuk Konstruksi Ringan
data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan pembuatan produk logam struktural bukan aluminium, seperti pagar besi, teralis, pintu, jendela, lubang angin, tangga, dan produk-produk konstruksi ringan lainnya.
Kelompok ini tidak mencakup pembuatan produk logam struktural baja untuk konstruksi berat, seperti untuk jembatan, menara listrik tegangan tinggi, pintu air, dan sejenisnya, yang termasuk dalam kelompok 25113, sedangkan pembuatan ketel uap, bejana tekan, dan sejenisnya, termasuk dalam kelompok 25130.

editorial.headline: Light Construction Metalwork, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 25111 covers non-aluminium structural metal products for light construction, open across all business scales and nationally available to full foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25111 is the manufacturing lane for non-aluminium structural metal products used in light construction. In plain English, it covers the making of iron fences, grilles, doors, windows, vents, stairs, and similar light-construction metal goods. The emphasis is on fabricated structural products that belong to ordinary building work, not heavy structural steel or specialised pressure equipment.

That makes the code practical for operators whose business is fabrication rather than installation advice, retail trading, or general contracting. A workshop producing metal doors, stair elements, window frames, ventilation pieces, or security grilles would read naturally within the scope described in the record. The activity is also not confined to one business size: the record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the same classification can describe a small fabrication shop or a larger manufacturing operation, provided the activity remains within the stated light-construction product scope.

The national investment position is straightforward. According to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, the record classifies the activity as TERBUKA and sets pma_max_asing at 100. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national ceiling should be read as 100% foreign ownership. There is no partial cap in the slim record, and no additional national threshold, licence, tax, timeline, or minimum-capital condition is stated here, so none should be added to the interpretation.

The Bali picture is also unusually clean. The record does not block this activity for PMA registration in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium. The moratorium itself is still important context: the record says Bali blocks all Low plus Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. But this activity, on the record provided, sits outside that block. The honest conclusion is therefore simple: nationally, KBLI 25111 is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, the record does not mark it as blocked.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is therefore simple: nationally, KBLI 25111 is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, the record does not mark it as blocked.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. editorial.headline: Aluminium Structure Work for Light Construction
editorial.standfirst: For KBLI 25112, the record describes a manufacturing activity that is nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25112 is a manufacturing code for aluminium structural products used in light construction. The record describes the activity as the making of aluminium window frames, door frames, aluminium trellis, aluminium roofing or awnings, rolling doors, aluminium blinds, and other light-construction products. Its centre of gravity is fabrication: turning aluminium into building-facing elements that define openings, shading, access, screening, and other lightweight structural uses.

That makes this a practical industrial code, not a general trading label or a loose construction-service category. A founder using it should be able to point back to the making of the products themselves: the frame, the door, the awning, the rolling door, the blind, or a comparable aluminium product for light construction. The record is also broad on business size. It is open across **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**, so the activity is not reserved in the record for only one scale of enterprise. It can describe a smaller fabrication setup as well as a larger aluminium-products manufacturer, provided the activity remains within the recorded scope.

The national PMA picture is straightforward. The record marks the activity as **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. In plain English, the national field says this activity is open to foreign investment up to full foreign ownership. The cited PMA source in the record is **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. Nothing in the slim record adds a special national licence, capital threshold, tax treatment, or timeline, so none should be read into the code from this editorial alone.

Bali is where this record needs careful reading, but not a manufactured warning. The Bali-side status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and `l4_bali_blocked` is false. The record’s reason is explicit: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule itself says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this record does not mark 25112 as blocked. So the honest national-vs-Bali conclusion is aligned rather than contradictory: nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and not blocked by the Bali moratorium according to the provided Bali risk reasoning.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is aligned: nationally open to full foreign ownership, and not marked as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity involves manufacturing structural steel components for heavy construction—like bridge frameworks, high-voltage transmission towers, aircraft hangars, and lock gates. It’s large-scale, engineered metal fabrication, not light-gauge steel framing for houses.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is fully open to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, it is not blocked by the current moratorium on PMA, but it is classified as medium-high risk (at every business scale, from micro to large), so you must get location-specific approval and may face extra permits or zoning restrictions before registration.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Produk Logam Struktural Baja untuk Konstruksi Berat (25113)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign manufacturers or contractors wanting a heavy steel fabrication facility in Bali—ideally to serve major infrastructure projects or marine engineering needs that justify the industrial setup.

editorial.headline: Structural Steel for Heavy Construction, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 25113 covers the fabrication of major steel structural products, from bridges and hangars to power towers and water gates.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25113 is a manufacturing activity for structural steel products used in heavy construction. Its scope is not ordinary metalwork in a loose sense; the record points to steel structures made for demanding built assets: bridges, hangar buildings, high-voltage electricity towers, and water gates. The common thread is scale, structural function, and the production of steel components that become part of large infrastructure or heavy building works.

That makes this code most naturally relevant to businesses whose main activity is fabrication rather than design, contracting, trading, or installation. A founder registering it should be comfortable describing the business as an industrial producer of steel structural products. The scale field is broad: the record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses. In plain terms, the classification is not reserved only for large industrial groups, even though the examples in the scope clearly sit in the world of heavy construction.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with `pma_max_asing` at 100. That means the national foreign-ownership ceiling shown in the record is 100%. There is no lower foreign-stake cap in the supplied data, and no separate licence, capital threshold, tax condition, or timeline is stated here. The source field is also explicit: Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned setup, the national picture is therefore clean: this is recorded as open, and the ceiling is full foreign ownership.

The Bali reading is also unusually clear. The record does not mark this activity as blocked in Bali. Its Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`, and the stated reason is: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". That matters because the Bali moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. Here, the record says the activity is not blocked by that moratorium. So the honest national-vs-Bali conclusion is not a contradiction: nationally this is foreign-open, and on the Bali side the supplied record does not block PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest national-vs-Bali conclusion is not a contradiction: nationally this is foreign-open, and on the Bali side the supplied record does not block PMA registration for this activity.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Other Structural Metal Products, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 25119 covers specialised structural metal products for construction, open to every business scale and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25119 sits in a practical corner of construction manufacturing: the making of other structural metal products used in building and infrastructure work. The record describes it as structural metal product manufacturing for construction, including non-steel structural metal products for heavy construction. In plain English, this is not a trading code and not a design consultancy. It is a manufacturing activity tied to the physical production of structural metal components for construction purposes, with the emphasis on products that fall outside the narrower structural metal categories named elsewhere in the classification system.

The scale profile is unusually broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, which means the classification is not reserved only for large industrial operators. A small workshop and a larger manufacturing plant may both sit inside the scale map, provided the registered activity remains within the scope: making structural metal products for construction. That breadth matters because the same KBLI can describe very different operational realities, from modest fabrication capacity to heavier construction-oriented production. The editorial point is not that all scales face the same operational pathway, but that the record itself does not close the activity to any of the listed scales.

Nationally, the PMA picture is clear. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives a pma_max_asing of 100, which means the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no reduced national cap in the data, and no additional ownership condition is stated in the slim record. For a foreign-owned setup, the honest national reading is therefore straightforward: this activity is open, and the record supports full foreign ownership at the national level under the cited PMA source.

The Bali reading is also relatively clean, but for a different reason. For Bali, the record shows l4_bali_blocked as false, with the Bali status recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than blocked. The reason given is: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". That matters because the Bali moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province. Here, the record’s Bali-side conclusion is not a separate Bali ownership percentage, and it is not a partnership quota. It is simply that, on this record, the activity is not blocked by the moratorium because the relevant risk reading at large scale is above the blocked risk band.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is that KBLI 25119 is nationally open to full foreign ownership and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Metal Tanks and Pressure Vessels, Open Nationally and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 25120 covers metal storage tanks, insulated vessels, LPG cylinders, autoclaves, and silo tanks, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25120 is a manufacturing classification for metal tanks, water reservoirs, vats, and similar containers made for equipment, storage, or industrial use. The record makes clear that the scope is not limited to simple storage. It includes vessels that may be lined or thermally insulated, and it extends into pressure-related products for compressed or liquefied gas, including autoclaves, LPG cylinders, and silo tanks. In practical terms, this is the code for fabrication businesses whose product is a metal vessel with an equipment, storage, or industrial function, rather than a disposable or transport-focused package.

That boundary matters because the record also separates this activity from ordinary metal packaging and from transport-container manufacturing. The emphasis here is on tanks, reservoirs, vats, pressure cylinders, and comparable industrial vessels. A founder using this code would need the commercial reality of the business to match that manufacturing profile: the making of metal storage or pressure containers, not merely trading them, filling them, or producing general-purpose packaging. The Indonesian scope is unusually concrete, and its examples help keep the classification anchored in the physical product being made.

On scale, the record is broad. It marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the classification is not framed in the slim record as a scale-exclusive activity; small workshops and larger industrial manufacturers can both sit inside the same KBLI identity if the actual activity remains the manufacture of these metal vessels. For a founder, the useful reading is that scale is not the deciding filter here. The deciding filter is the product: metal tanks, water reservoirs, vats, gas cylinders, autoclaves, LPG cylinders, silo tanks, and similar industrial containers.

The national foreign-investment position is also direct. The record marks PMA status as TERBUKA and gives pma_max_asing as 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Put plainly, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to 100%. The Bali-side result is not a contradiction of that national openness. In Bali, its status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, while l4_bali_blocked remains false. The reason given is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA in Bali, but this record says KBLI 25120 is not blocked by that rule. For this activity, the honest picture is therefore unusually clean: nationally open to PMA, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the moratorium record supplied.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, the honest picture is unusually clean: nationally open to PMA, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the moratorium record supplied.

Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This group covers the manufacture of steam generators and other vapour generators, including their parts and accessories; radiators for central heating systems that are not electrically powered; condensers for steam power units; marine or power boilers; and nuclear reactors with their components and accessories, except isotope separators. It also includes auxiliary equipment used with steam generators, such as condensers, superheaters, steam collectors, and accumulators. Not covered are electric ovens and electric water heaters, turbine boiler sets, household heating appliances, and isotope separators.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally this activity is open to foreign ownership. In Bali its registrability depends on scope: the OSS risk class is low on some sub-scopes but higher on others, and only the higher-risk scope is registrable for a PT PMA under the moratorium. It is conditionally available — only by declaring the qualifying higher-risk scope. Confirm that scope genuinely fits your operation before planning a Bali setup.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Generator Uap Bukan Ketel Pemanas (25130)? Here is the honest national-vs-Bali picture before you plan a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur whose operation genuinely matches the higher-risk scope — otherwise treat it as blocked in Bali.

editorial.headline: Steam-Generation Manufacturing With a Scope-Dependent Bali Check
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 25130 covers industrial steam-generation equipment and is nationally open to foreign ownership, but Bali registration depends on the exact risk profile declared in OSS.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25130 sits in a heavy-industrial corner of manufacturing: the making of steam generators and other steam-generation systems, together with their components and supporting equipment. The record’s scope is broad but still specific. It covers steam generators, central-heating radiators that do not use electricity, condensers for steam-power units, and auxiliary installations used with steam generators, including condensers, superheaters, steam collectors, and accumulators. It also reaches marine boilers, power boilers, and nuclear reactors with their components and equipment, while excluding isotope separators.

That makes this code a registration home for businesses whose real activity is manufacturing serious steam or power-generation hardware, not merely trading equipment or installing generic heating appliances. The activity can be registered across the full business-scale ladder shown in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practice, the commercial profile will often depend on the declared industrial scope, because the covered outputs range from components and accessories to complete generators, condensers, boilers, and reactor-related equipment.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The record marks the code as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national rule in this slim record allows a PMA company to hold the activity up to full foreign ownership. There is no lower national cap in the data, and there is no separate minimum-capital, licence, tax, timeline, or technical-permit detail provided here to add.

Bali is more conditional. The record does not mark this activity as outright blocked in Bali, but it does mark the Bali status as Blocked (scope-dependent). The reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is low on some scopes and higher on others, and the record says registration as PMA in Bali must be verified live in OSS against the exact declared activity. This matters because the Bali moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. So the honest reading is not that KBLI 25130 is simply closed in Bali, nor that it is automatically safe there. It is nationally open, but Bali registration turns on the precise scope and OSS risk classification declared at the time of filing.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 25130 is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but in Bali the decisive question is the exact activity and risk profile declared in OSS.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the manufacture of military and law enforcement weapons (artillery, machine guns, rocket launchers) as well as civilian firearms, ammunition, and explosives—including pistols, shotguns, air rifles, grenades, and torpedoes.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Foreign shareholding in this sector is capped at 49%: without the Minister of Defence's approval, foreign shareholders can hold up to 49% of a PT PMA and the rest must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The cap is set by Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III, entry #7, and the record notes a route above it — the approval of the Minister of Defence. Bali's moratorium does not block the activity: it reaches only low and medium-low risk lines, and this one sits above that band.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Senjata dan Amunisi (25200)? Nationally this carries PMA status: TERBATAS — capped at 49% foreign ownership, may exceed 49% with Menteri Pertahanan approval. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign defense contractors, specialized weapons manufacturers, or ammunition producers ready to navigate a high-scrutiny setup in Bali.

editorial.headline: Weapons and Ammunition Manufacturing: Foreign Ownership Capped at 49%
editorial.standfirst: This code covers the industrial manufacture of military, police, civilian, sporting, and protective firearms, ammunition, explosives, and ballistic missile systems.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25200 is the manufacturing category for weapons and ammunition. Its centre of gravity is not retail, training, security services, or equipment brokerage, but production: military artillery, cannons, rocket launchers, flamethrowers, grenade launchers, torpedo tubes, machine guns, heavy projectile weapons, light firearms such as pistols, revolvers, rifles, and shotguns, and the ammunition that serves them. The record also includes gas rifles, spring rifles, air rifles, war ammunition, shotgun, revolver, and pistol bullets, and military explosive devices such as bombs, grenades, torpedoes, mines, rockets, and missiles.

The scope is broader than a narrow defence-factory label. It also covers the manufacture of firearms and ammunition for hunting, sport, or protection, and it expressly reaches intercontinental ballistic missiles. That makes the code industrially precise but commercially wide: the activity is defined by making the weapon, ammunition, explosive, or missile system, not by the eventual user alone. A founder reading this should see a production classification for arms and munitions, spanning military-grade systems through certain civilian-use firearms and ammunition, all inside one activity record.

On business scale, the record is unusually broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all listed as open. Foreign shareholding in this activity is capped at 49%. Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — lists it at entry #7, and the record notes a route above that ceiling: the approval of the Minister of Defence. Without that approval the 49% ceiling is the national position, and the remaining shares cannot be in foreign hands.

Bali's moratorium does not block it. That moratorium suspends new PMA registration for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk, and this one is recorded above that band. What the record does limit is the foreign side of the shareholding — 49%, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia — with the defence-ministry approval as the recorded route above it.
editorial.pullQuote: The reading is not a hidden Bali prohibition and not a national opening either: foreign shareholding stops at 49%, and Bali's moratorium is not what stops it.

data.judul: Penempaan, Pengepresan, Pencetakan, dan Pembentukan Logam; Metalurgi Bubuk
data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan
- penempaan, pengepresan pencetakan, dan pembuatan logam, baik baja, besi, maupun logam bukan besi, menjadi logam dalam bentuk logam tempaan, logam pres, atau logam gulungan;
- pembuatan benda logam secara langsung dari bubuk logam dengan proses pemanasan atau pengepresan, seperti metalurgi bubuk.
Kelompok ini juga mencakup kegiatan
- pemotongan atau pembersihan kerak pada logam setelah proses pembentukan, tanpa ada proses lanjutan lain.
Kelompok ini tidak mencakup
- pembuatan bubuk logam, lihat subgolongan 2410 dan 2420.

editorial.headline: Where Metal Takes Its Finished Shape
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 25910 covers forging, pressing, shaping, rolling and powder-metallurgy metal work, open across every business scale and nationally open to foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25910 is the industrial code for the point at which metal is physically formed into usable shape. Its scope covers forging, pressing, moulding and making metal from steel, iron and non-ferrous metals into forged, pressed or rolled forms. It also includes making metal objects directly from metal powder through heating or pressing: the powder-metallurgy process named in the record. This is not the extraction of metal, nor the making of metal powder itself; it is the shaping and formation stage, including cutting or descaling after the forming process when there is no further processing.

That makes the activity broad, but not vague. A founder registering under this code is describing a business whose core work is metal transformation by force, pressure, heat or forming technology. The registered scale can be Mikro, Kecil, Menengah or Besar, so the record does not reserve this activity for only large industrial operators. It can describe a small metal-forming workshop as well as a larger production business, provided the activity remains within the stated scope: forging, pressing, moulding, rolling, powder metallurgy, and the limited post-forming cleaning or cutting allowed by the classification text.

The national foreign-investment picture is straightforward. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100. In plain English, the national framework treats this code as open to foreign ownership up to 100%, using the source stated in the record. There is no lower cap in the slim record, and no special threshold, licence, capital figure or timeline is stated here; those should not be inferred from the classification alone.

Bali does not change that into a closure on this record. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and l4_bali_blocked is false. The reason given is precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. Because this record’s Bali reason places the large-scale OSS risk at Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, the activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The honest reading is therefore clean: nationally open, 100% foreign ownership in the record, and not marked as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is clean: nationally open, 100% foreign ownership in the record, and not marked as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Metal Finishing With a Clean National and Bali Signal
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 25920 covers specialist metal working and coating services, open across all business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25920 is the industrial code for metal working and metal coating: the practical, often invisible layer of production that turns metal parts into finished, treated, cleaned, strengthened, polished, joined, or marked components. The record describes a broad workshop and service field: plating, anodizing, heat treatment, deburring, sandblasting, tumbling, cleaning, colouring, engraving, non-metal coatings such as plastic, enamel, porcelain, lacquer, and varnish, hardening, polishing, welding, joining, sawing, grinding, drilling, shaping, sharpening, and laser cutting or writing on metal. In plain English, this is not the making of every metal object from scratch; it is the specialist processing, finishing, preparation, repair, and treatment of metal and metal products.

The commercial profile is deliberately wide. The slim record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale businesses, so it can describe a small finishing shop, a mid-sized industrial service provider, or a larger operation serving manufacturing clients. That breadth matters because the activity is defined by the process applied to metal rather than by one narrow end product. A founder registering under this code should therefore read the scope around the actual services performed: coating, cleaning, polishing, engraving, welding, cutting, heat treatment, and other specific metal-working services are the centre of gravity.

Nationally, the signal is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the record gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, with Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 as the PMA source. That means the national record does not show a foreign-share cap below full ownership. There is no licence, capital threshold, timeline, tax rule, or operating permit stated in the slim record, so none should be inferred from the classification itself. The safe reading is narrower and cleaner: as a national investment classification, this activity is open to PMA up to the percentage stated in the record.

The Bali picture is also clean, but for a different reason. The record marks Bali status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and says it is not blocked. Its reason is precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium text in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this activity is not treated here as blocked by that rule. So the honest lede is not a warning that Bali shuts it down. For this record, KBLI 25920 is nationally open to foreign ownership and, on the Bali-specific fields provided, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: For this record, KBLI 25920 is nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity is about manufacturing a broad range of hand tools: construction tools like pliers and screwdrivers, agricultural tools like hoes, shovels, sickles and axes, plus tool accessories (drill bits, hammers, milling blades). It also covers pressing tools, moulds, swaging tools, and blacksmith equipment such as forges and anvils — basically, making the durable metal implements used in workshops, farms, and forges.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is fully open for 100% foreign ownership (PMA). However, in Bali it is currently blocked for new PMA registrations due to a moratorium on low and medium-low risk business activities. That means you cannot establish a foreign-owned company in Bali for this hand-tool manufacturing activity right now, even though the national rules would allow it.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Perkakas Tangan (25931)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs with experience in tool and die making, hand-tool production, or agricultural equipment manufacturing who want a 100% foreign-owned factory in Indonesia (but must choose a location outside Bali under current restrictions).

editorial.headline: Hand Tool Manufacturing, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 25931 covers the making of hand tools and related tool equipment, with national PMA access at 100% but a Bali PMA block under the recorded moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25931 is the industrial code for making hand tools: the practical, durable implements used in workshops, farms, building sites, repair benches, and small production floors. The record names carpentry hand tools such as pliers and screwdrivers; agricultural hand tools such as hoes, shovels, sickles, egrek, dodos, and axes; and equipment for hand tools whether powered or not, including drill bits, hammers, and grinding knives. It also reaches into the making of press tools, mould boxes and moulds, crimping tools, and blacksmith tools such as forging tools and anvils.

That scope makes this a manufacturing activity rather than a trading, retail, or repair category. The centre of gravity is fabrication: turning metal, tool components, and workshop processes into finished or supporting tools. It is broad enough to cover both familiar manual implements and more specialised tool-making equipment, but it remains anchored in what the slim record actually lists. For a founder, the useful reading is simple: this code is for producing the tools themselves, not merely selling them or using them as part of another service.

On scale, the record is unusually clean. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That means the classification is not presented as a narrow large-industry lane only, nor as a protected micro activity only. A small workshop making agricultural hand tools and a larger manufacturer producing press tools or drill-bit equipment both sit within the same recorded scale range, provided the activity being registered matches the manufacturing scope above. The code therefore has a wide operational envelope, but that should not be confused with automatic permission in every location or ownership structure.

The national-versus-Bali picture is the real decision point. Nationally, the record marks KBLI 25931 as TERBUKA for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain terms, the national record does not impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership. Bali is different. The record says the activity is blocked for PMA registration in Bali: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” It also records the moratorium rule as: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” So the honest reading is this: KBLI 25931 is nationally foreign-open, but a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today under the Bali-side record supplied here.

editorial.headline: Metal Cutting Tools, Open Nationally, Conditional in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A metal cutting-tool manufacturing code that is nationally open to 100% PMA, while Bali turns on declared scope and live OSS risk reading.
editorial.body:
KBLI 25932 is a manufacturing code for metal cutting tools, not for a broad metals business or a retail label. The scope centres on making cutting articles from metal: machetes, serrated knives, razors, razor blades, scissors, hair clippers, short knives or daggers, swords, bayonets, and traditional weapons. It also includes machine-facing output - knives and blades for machines or mechanical equipment, plus saws and saw blades. The common line is the made cutting edge itself. The scope is item-specific enough to hold handheld blade products, grooming blades, traditional weapons, and mechanical blades in the same manufacturing class. Whether the article is handheld, grooming-related, weapon-related, or fitted to equipment, the record keeps the activity inside manufacturing.

The registration story starts broad. The slim record marks national PMA status as TERBUKA and gives the foreign-ownership ceiling as 100%. It opens the code across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so the activity is not presented as belonging only to one size of operator. On the national line, then, this is a clean foreign-open manufacturing activity: the record does not cap foreign ownership below full control, and it does not narrow the available scale set.

Bali is where the title has to be read with more discipline. The record does not mark the code as categorically blocked in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false. But the Bali status is Blocked (scope-dependent), and the reason makes the condition explicit. OSS risk at scale Besar is low on some scopes and higher on others; PMA registration in Bali is described as available only by declaring the higher-risk scope, with live OSS verification per exact activity. The national door is open, but in Bali the practical question is which exact cutting-tool activity OSS sees when the business is declared.

The backdrop is the Bali moratorium rule recorded in the slim record: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. The Bali fields give a status and a reason rather than another ownership number. For a founder, the practical reading is narrow but important. A large-scale declaration that OSS treats as higher risk has a route to verify. A low or medium-low risk reading runs into the provincial moratorium. The honest editorial answer is therefore neither panic nor simplification: nationally open to 100% PMA, open across all recorded scales, and usable in Bali only where the exact declared scope clears the recorded Bali condition.
editorial.pullQuote: The national door is open, but in Bali the practical question is which exact cutting-tool activity OSS sees when the business is declared.
