data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Precious-Metal Goods With a Bali Registration Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32119 covers specialised precious-metal goods, nationally open to foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the record’s moratorium rule.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32119 is not a broad jewellery category. The record frames it as the manufacture of other valuable goods from precious metals: precious-metal coins, whether or not they are legal tender; engraving services on personal items, including items that are not themselves made of precious metal; and specialised precious-metal articles for technical and laboratory use. Its scope also reaches comparable precious-metal goods for other uses, such as watch straps, watch bands, cuff links, and cigarette cases.

That mix gives the code a particular character. It sits where craft, personalisation, and small high-value metal objects meet more technical applications. The laboratory examples in the record are concrete: spatulas, crucibles, cupels, platinum grills for catalysts, and anodes for electroplating. In plain English, this is a manufacturing activity for precious-metal goods that are valuable, specialised, or functional, without turning the code into a catch-all for every precious-metal product.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so it can describe anything from a small engraving or precious-metal workshop to a larger manufacturing setup, provided the activity stays within the stated scope. Nationally, the PMA position is also clear: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national reading alone, this is therefore foreign-open up to full foreign ownership.

Bali changes the practical answer. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and gives the reason as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026”. The linked moratorium rule is broader still: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent)”. For a foreign founder, that is the honest conclusion. Nationally, KBLI 32119 is open. In Bali, the record says PMA registration is blocked today, not because the national foreign-ownership ceiling is low, but because Bali’s recorded moratorium blocks this risk class for PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, KBLI 32119 is open; in Bali, the record says PMA registration is blocked today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Imitation Jewellery Manufacturing, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32120 covers imitation jewellery and similar metal accessories, nationally open to PMA, but not registrable by foreign investors in Bali under the record’s moratorium rule.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32120 is the manufacturing activity for imitation jewellery and closely related personal adornments. In practical terms, the record points to rings, bracelets, brooches, earrings, necklaces and similar small items made outside the category of precious jewellery. The line is important: this activity does not cover jewellery made from precious metals, base metals mixed with precious metals, genuine gemstones, pearls, or precious-metal watch straps. Its centre is costume-style jewellery: pieces made from base materials, sometimes plated with precious metal, sometimes using imitation stones such as imitation gems or imitation diamonds.

The same scope also includes the manufacture of metal watch straps, provided those straps are not made from precious metal. That makes the code broader than decorative jewellery alone, but still tightly framed around non-precious personal accessories. A founder using this code should read it as a production classification, not retail, not trading, and not high-jewellery craftsmanship. The record describes making the items themselves: imitation jewellery, small personal adornments, and non-precious metal watch straps.

On the national investment side, the record is straightforward. Nationally, the PMA status is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The activity is also open across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In national terms, therefore, KBLI 32120 is not presented as a closed category for foreign investors. A foreign-owned company can look at the national line and see an open manufacturing activity with no foreign-share cap below full ownership in the slim record.

Bali changes the answer. The record marks `l4_bali_blocked` as true and gives the reason: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” It also states the provincial rule directly: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” The honest reading is that a foreign investor cannot register this KBLI for PMA in Bali today, even though the national PMA status is open and the national ownership ceiling is 100%. This is not a separate Bali percentage, quota, or partnership condition; the record gives none. It is a Bali-side block based on the moratorium rule and the recorded risk classification.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is that a foreign investor cannot register this KBLI for PMA in Bali today, even though the national PMA status is open.

editorial.headline: Traditional Instruments Are Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM — Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32201 covers the making of Indonesian traditional musical instruments; Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II allocates it to Indonesian cooperatives and MSMEs, so a foreign-owned company cannot register it anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32201 is about craft, sound, and cultural manufacture rather than performance or retail. The record defines it as the making of traditional musical instruments with roots in Indonesian cultural history or customary practice. These are instruments played by plucking, bowing, blowing, or striking: angklung, calung, kecapi, bamboo flute, kolintang, gong, traditional trumpet, gambang, rebab, and tifa are all within the recorded scope. The same record also brings in whistles, call horns, and other blown sound-signalling instruments, so the code is not limited to ceremonial instruments alone. Its centre of gravity, however, is clear: physical production of traditional sound-making objects.

The registration picture is broad at the national scale. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, meaning the record does not reserve this manufacturing activity for only one size of operator. A small workshop making bamboo flutes and a larger facility producing gongs or other traditional instruments would both sit inside the scale range named in the record, as long as the activity remains the making of the instruments covered by the scope.

The ownership position is set by Perpres 10/2021, as amended by Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran II: the making of traditional musical instruments is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM (p.6, entry 23 "Industri alat musik tradisional antara lain: Angklung, Gordang Sembilan, Dambus, Kolintang, Gendang Beleq, Sasando, Tifa", KBLI 32201 — the list is by example, not a restriction). A foreign investor can be neither a cooperative nor a UMKM, so the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for instrument making is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this code anywhere in Indonesia. No separate Bali percentage applies and none should be read into it. Bali's provincial overlay does not change that answer: the record lists 32201 outside the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026, but the national reservation already decides the PMA question.
editorial.pullQuote: Traditional instrument making is a Koperasi-and-UMKM activity under Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II: the PT PMA route is closed nationwide, not just in Bali.

editorial.headline: Nontraditional Musical Instruments, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32202 covers the making of modern acoustic and electronic instruments, with full national PMA openness but a Bali registration block for foreign investors.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 32202 is the manufacturing lane for nontraditional musical instruments.** Its scope is broad but still specific: instruments played by plucking, bowing, blowing, or striking, including guitars, basses, trumpets, saxophones, clarinets, harmonicas, violins, cellos, double basses, drums, xylophones, metallophones, pianos, organs, pianicas, accordions, and tuning forks. It also reaches into electronic sound, covering instruments whose sound is produced or amplified electronically, such as digital pianos and synthesizers.

That makes the activity a manufacturing classification, not a retail, performance, recording, or audio-equipment category. The record also draws a boundary around what is outside the activity: microphones, loudspeakers, headphones, similar components, and toy musical instruments are not part of this scope. In practical terms, the code is for a business that makes the instrument itself, whether the object is an acoustic string instrument, a brass or woodwind instrument, a percussion instrument, or an electronic keyboard-based product.

Nationally, the investment picture is clean. The record marks the activity as **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**, under **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. It is also open across all listed business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. On the national register, then, this is not a partially capped activity. A PMA structure is not being squeezed by a foreign-share limit inside the slim record; the ceiling is the full figure shown there.

Bali changes the answer completely. The record says `l4_bali_blocked` is true, and gives the reason plainly: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule is equally direct: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” So the honest reading is this: KBLI 32202 is nationally foreign-open, but a foreign investor cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali today under the Bali-side block recorded here. The contradiction is not in the activity itself; it is between the national openness and the province-level moratorium applied to the recorded OSS risk profile.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 32202 is nationally foreign-open, but a foreign investor cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali today under the Bali-side block recorded here.

editorial.headline: Sports Equipment Manufacturing, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32300 covers the making of sports equipment and gear, nationally open to foreign ownership but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under the record’s moratorium rule.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 32300 is a manufacturing code for the equipment behind competitive and recreational sport.** Its scope is broad: balls, rackets, clubs, bats, nets, table-tennis tables, ski gear, surfboards, fishing equipment, hunting and shooting equipment, mountaineering gear, sport-specific leather gloves and headgear, swimming tubs and children’s pools, skates, bows and arrows, gymnastics equipment, fitness-centre equipment, and athletics equipment. The common thread is not apparel or ordinary footwear; it is the production of physical sporting goods and sporting apparatus, made from various materials, for professional and amateur use.

That makes the code relevant to founders who are actually producing sports goods rather than merely trading, coaching, renting space, or running a sports venue. A factory producing inflated balls, a workshop making rackets or bats, a manufacturer of fitness-centre equipment, or a producer of climbing and mountaineering gear all sit naturally inside the record’s stated scope. The activity can serve both indoor and outdoor sport, and both competitive and leisure markets, so the editorial centre of gravity is manufacturing capability: materials, product design, production standards, and the ability to turn sporting equipment into finished goods.

On scale, the record is unusually straightforward. KBLI 32300 is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar registrations. In practical terms, the code is not presented as a narrow large-industry-only classification; it can describe anything from a small specialist maker to a large manufacturer, as long as the declared business activity remains inside the record’s manufacturing scope. Nationally, it is also marked **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. On the national reading alone, a foreign-owned PMA structure is therefore possible up to full foreign ownership.

The Bali answer is different, and it is the point a founder should not miss. The record marks Bali as blocked for this code: **Blocked (risk class)**. The reason given is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, and the Bali moratorium blocks that risk class for PMA registration. The moratorium rule in the record is explicit: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest reading is this: KBLI 32300 is nationally foreign-open, even up to 100%, but a foreigner cannot register this PMA activity in Bali today under the Bali-side rule recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 32300 is nationally foreign-open up to 100%, but the record’s Bali moratorium makes the PMA registration answer in Bali a clear no.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Game Equipment Manufacturing: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making of rule-based games and related equipment, with full national PMA openness but a Bali-side block for foreign registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32401 is the manufacturing home for games that are built around rules, play equipment, and table-based or social play. The slim record describes a broad production activity: playing cards such as dominoes and similar cards, marbles, bekel, board games including electronic board games, chess equipment, arcade or coin-operated games, and the specialised tables and equipment used for billiards, casino games, bowling, table games, parlour games, fun-fair games, puzzles, and educational toys. In plain English, this is not the operation of a game venue. It is the industrial making of the objects and equipment used in those games.

The scale profile is unusually straightforward. Across the record, the activity is available to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the classification is not framed only for a large manufacturer; it can also describe smaller production businesses, provided the actual activity remains the making of the game tools, tables, puzzles, or equipment covered by the scope. The breadth matters because the same code can sit behind very different physical products: a small educational-toy maker, a board-game producer, or a larger manufacturer of arcade and table-game equipment can all belong here if their activity is still the manufacturing described in the record.

Nationally, the PMA picture is also clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives `pma_max_asing` as 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned company, that is the national headline: the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no lower national cap in the slim record, and there is no separate national caveat to add. The correct reading is full national openness for PMA ownership, across the activity as described.

Bali is where the legal reading changes sharply. The record says `l4_bali_blocked` is true, with the reason: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026". The moratorium rule is equally direct: "Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent)". So the honest founder-facing conclusion is not that Bali has a smaller foreign-ownership percentage, a local-partner formula, or a special quota. None of those appears in the record. The conclusion is simpler and more severe: although this activity is open nationally to 100% foreign ownership, a foreigner cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali under the Bali moratorium recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: This is a nationally open manufacturing activity, but the Bali record turns that openness into a PMA registration block on the island.

editorial.headline: Toy and Recreational Drone Manufacturing: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32402 covers a broad toy-making industry, but the Bali record turns a nationally open PMA activity into a local registration dead end.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32402 is the manufacturing code for toys, interpreted broadly. The record covers the making of dolls from wood, fabric, rubber and similar materials, together with doll clothing and accessories. It also reaches toy weapons, toy sets, character figures, action figures, toy animals, toy musical instruments, scale models, recreational models, electric toy trains, construction games, ride-on wheeled toys made for play, plastic two-wheelers and tricycles, and recreational drones. In plain English, this is not a narrow craft category. It is the industrial production of play objects, miniature worlds, character merchandise, toy vehicles, and leisure drones.

That breadth matters because the record opens the activity across every business scale listed: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. A small domestic maker of dolls sits in the same activity family as a larger producer of construction toys, action figures, or recreational drone products, so long as the activity remains within the manufacturing scope described. The code is therefore structurally flexible. It can accommodate modest production as well as larger factory-style operations, provided the registered activity is genuinely toy manufacturing rather than an adjacent product line outside the record.

Nationally, the investment signal is clear. For PMA, the record assigns TERBUKA status and sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national reading alone, a foreign-owned company can hold the full equity position for this activity. There is no lesser foreign stake, special threshold, additional licence, or capital figure in the record, so none should be inferred. The national framework says open; the recorded ownership ceiling says 100%; the eligible scales run from Mikro through Besar.

Bali is the decisive exception. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and gives the reason verbatim: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule is broader still: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest answer for a foreign investor is not that this activity is partly open in Bali, or open with a Bali percentage, or available through an implied workaround. It is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but a foreigner cannot register this KBLI for PMA in Bali today under the Bali-side record.
editorial.pullQuote: It is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but a foreigner cannot register this KBLI for PMA in Bali today under the Bali-side record.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This KBLI covers the manufacturing of furniture used in medical, dental, and veterinary procedures—items like operating tables, hospital beds, IV stands, professional massage chairs, and dental examination chairs. It includes both mechanically and electrically driven equipment, essentially specialized healthcare furniture production.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this activity is 100% open to foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, it is not blocked by the current moratorium, but it falls under a higher-risk classification (medium-high/high). This means that while a PMA can be registered here, the business location will face stricter verification—zoning and address suitability will be checked, so you must secure a compliant commercial address and expect additional due diligence.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.

editorial.headline: Medical Furniture With a Clear PMA Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32501 covers the making of clinical, surgical, dental, veterinary, and care furniture, with the record showing national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32501 is a manufacturing code for furniture built for clinical work rather than ordinary interiors. The record describes the making of furniture for surgery, care, dentistry, and veterinary medicine, whether mechanically or electrically operated. Its examples are practical and equipment-like: operating tables, infusion stands, hospital beds, professional massage chairs, and chairs used for dental examination and treatment. In plain English, this is the industrial production of medical and care-use furniture, where the object being made is designed for treatment, examination, support, or procedure settings.

That scope matters because the activity is not just about furniture as a broad consumer category. The record points to furniture used inside medical, dental, veterinary, and care environments, including items that may move mechanically or electrically. A company registering this activity should therefore be looking at production, not retail, service provision, clinic operation, or general furnishing work. The scales open to this code are broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all named in the record. That makes the registration frame accessible across the full recorded scale range, from small industrial activity through larger manufacturing operations.

The national foreign-investment picture is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling recorded here is 100%. That means the slim record treats the activity as nationally open to foreign ownership up to the full ceiling stated in the data. The cited source for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no basis in the record to add another capital rule, licence condition, timing requirement, or sector-specific threshold, so the editorial reading should stay disciplined: the national data says open, and the stated ceiling is 100%.

The Bali side is also important, because this is where many KBLI readings can become misleading if national openness is treated as the whole answer. Here, however, the Bali record does not block the code. The status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and l4_bali_blocked is false. The reason given is specific: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this code is not marked as blocked by that rule. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: for this record, KBLI 32501 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and Bali is not shown as blocking PMA registration under the recorded moratorium logic.

data.judul: Industri Peralatan Kedokteran dan Kedokteran Gigi, serta Perlengkapan Ortopedi dan Prostetik
data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup pembuatan peralatan dan perlengkapan untuk pemeriksaan kesehatan, operasi, kedokteran gigi dan kedokteran hewan, seperti alat-alat bor gigi, peralatan tes mata, jarum suntik, peralatan sterilisasi, peralatan pijat, peralatan pernapasan buatan, perlengkapan ortopedis dan prostetik (crutches, surgical belts dan trussers, serta korset dan sepatu ortopedis), termometer kedokteran, tungku pembakar laboratorium kedokteran gigi, mesin pembersihan ultrasonik laboratorium, peralatan sentrifus tipe laboratorium, pelat yang tetap berada di dalam tubuh secara permanen, misalnya untuk mengganti sebagian atau seluruh tulang, alat suntik, jarum suntik, kateter, cannulae dan sebagaiya, peralatan kedokteran gigi, gigi buatan dan sebagainya yang dibuat di laboratorium kedokteran gigi, mata buatan dari kaca dan peralatan tubuh palsu lainnya, seperti mata palsu, tengkorak palsu dan bagian-bagian dalam tubuh palsu, sepatu ortopedis yang dibuat sesuai ukuran alas kaki ortopedis dan sol khusus untuk mengoreksi kondisi ortopedis, dan peralatan elektromekanis untuk perawatan kulit. Kelompok ini juga mencakup pembuatan berbagai peralatan dan perlengkapan dalam bentuk instrumen bedah, seperti gunting, pinset, dan tang.

editorial.headline: Medical Device Manufacturing With a Clear National and Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32502 covers the factory side of medical, dental, veterinary, orthopaedic and prosthetic equipment, with national PMA access open up to full foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32502 is a manufacturing code, not a clinic, distributor, or professional health-service category. Its centre of gravity is the making of physical equipment used in examination, surgery, dentistry, veterinary medicine, orthopaedics and prosthetics. The record reaches from dental drills, eye-test equipment, syringes, sterilisation equipment, artificial respiration equipment and laboratory centrifuges to prosthetic body parts, orthopaedic footwear, permanent internal plates, dental-laboratory products, artificial eyes and surgical instruments such as scissors, tweezers and forceps.

That breadth matters because the activity is defined by production. A company registering here is positioning itself as a maker of medical, dental, veterinary, orthopaedic or prosthetic equipment and related instruments. The slim record also opens the scale picture widely: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all listed as open. In practical editorial terms, this is not framed as a narrow industrial slot reserved only for the largest factories; the record recognises the activity across the full scale range it names.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clean. Nationally, PMA remains TERBUKA, with maximum recorded foreign ownership at 100%. That means the national record does not impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. The stated source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, and nothing in the slim record adds a separate capital threshold, licence condition, operational timeline, or tax treatment. The safe reading is therefore simple: the national classification is open to PMA, including full foreign ownership, for the activity as scoped in the record.

The Bali picture is also clear, but it needs to be stated with precision. The record marks `l4_bali_blocked` as false and gives the reason: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The moratorium rule in the record says that Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this activity is not marked as blocked here. So the honest national-vs-Bali conclusion is not a hidden warning or a manufactured caveat: KBLI 32502 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali-side record does not block PMA registration under the stated moratorium logic.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is not a hidden warning: KBLI 32502 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali-side record does not block it under the stated moratorium logic.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers the manufacturing of various ophthalmic products and eyewear, including prescription glasses, sunglasses, safety goggles (for dust, swimming, diving, welding), radiation-protection glasses, and lenses including contact lenses.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this activity is fully open for 100% foreign ownership (PMA). However, in Bali it is currently blocked for PMA companies because of a moratorium targeting low and medium-low risk activities. That means a foreign-owned company cannot obtain the necessary license in Bali for this activity under the present restrictions.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Industri Kacamata (32503)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs in eyewear manufacturing—from frames and lenses to safety and protective goggles—who intend to set up a production facility in Indonesia, though they must be aware that Bali is not an option for PMA registration at this time.

editorial.headline: Eyewear Manufacturing Is Open Nationally, but Not for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32503 covers the making of ophthalmic goods, eyewear, frames, lenses and contact lenses, with national PMA openness but a Bali registration block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32503 is the manufacturing classification for eyewear and ophthalmic goods. Its scope is practical and broad: it covers the making of vision-assistance glasses, sunglasses, protective and safety goggles, radiation-protection eyewear, eyewear frames, spectacle lenses and contact lenses. In plain terms, this is the code for producing the object itself, not merely selling it, fitting it, prescribing it or distributing it. The record points to the industrial activity: turning optical and protective eyewear products into manufactured goods.

That breadth matters because the classification is not reserved for one business size. The slim record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. A very small producer and a larger factory are therefore both within the scale language of the code, provided the actual registered activity remains the manufacture of the listed ophthalmic and eyewear products. The operative boundary is the scope itself: glasses for vision assistance, sunglasses, safety goggles for dust, swimming, diving or welding, radiation-protection glasses, frames, spectacle lenses and contact lenses.

Nationally, the investment picture is clear. The code is marked TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling in the record is 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. That is the national position: a PMA company can, on this record, be fully foreign-owned for this activity. There is no lesser national percentage to infer, no additional capital threshold to add, and no licence condition stated in the slim record. The clean reading is that, at the national level, KBLI 32503 is foreign-open up to 100%.

Bali is the hard stop. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and gives the reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, so it is blocked by the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently. That does not create a Bali foreign-ownership percentage; it creates a registration block. So the honest conclusion is simple: eyewear manufacturing may be fully foreign-open nationally, but a foreigner cannot register this PMA activity in Bali under the Bali status recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: Eyewear manufacturing may be fully foreign-open nationally, but the Bali record turns that openness into a registration block for PMA.

editorial.headline: Sterile Medical Supplies and Dental Materials Manufacturing
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32509 covers the making of specialised medical, dental, and surgical-use supplies, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32509 sits in the practical, material side of health care: the manufacturing of medical and dental equipment, plus other supporting supplies used in clinical and surgical settings. The scope is concrete rather than abstract. It includes sterile surgical cloth and thread, tissue paper, personal protective masks such as FFP2, FFP3, and surgical masks, surgical drapes, surgical gowns, head covers, and wound dressings for health services. It also reaches into dental and orthopaedic materials: dental cement and fillings, dental wax, other dental plaster preparations, and bone reconstruction cement.

That makes this a manufacturing activity for businesses producing physical inputs used by clinics, hospitals, surgery rooms, dental practices, and health-service providers. The common thread is not retail, distribution, or professional medical service; it is the making of these goods. A company registering this code should be able to describe its activity as production of the listed medical, surgical, dental, or related health-care supplies, not merely trading them or using them as part of another service.

The scale picture is unusually broad in the slim record. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale businesses. That matters because the code is not framed only for large industrial operators; the record recognises every listed business scale. At the same time, the nature of the goods is specialised. Sterility, protective use, surgical use, dental preparation, and reconstruction materials all point to a sector where the registered activity should be stated with care and matched closely to what the company actually manufactures.

Nationally, the investment signal is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The Bali picture is also not blocked in this record. Bali’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently, but this record marks the Bali status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and says: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. So the honest reading is straightforward: this activity is nationally open to foreign ownership up to 100%, and the slim record does not mark it as blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Stationery Manufacturing Is Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32901 covers the making of writing and drawing instruments, open at every business scale nationally but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32901 is the industrial home for the manufacture of writing and drawing tools and their accessories. Its scope is practical and product-led: black pencils, coloured pencils, pens, ballpoint pens, pen holders, screen-printing pens, compasses, drawing brushes, slates, drafting tables, rapidographs, screen-printing equipment, letraset, and crayons. editorial.headline: Typewriter and Printer Ribbon Manufacturing, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32902 covers the manufacture of typing, drawing, and computer-printer ribbons, with national foreign ownership open but Bali PMA registration blocked.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32902 is a narrow manufacturing code for the production of ribbons used in writing, drawing, and printing machines. The record describes it as covering the making of various kinds of typewriter or drawing-machine ribbons, including typewriter ribbons, computer-printer ribbons, and other writing-machine ribbons. In plain English, this is not a general stationery code and not a broad printing-service activity. Its center of gravity is the industrial making of the ribbon component itself: the consumable strip that carries ink or print material for machines designed to type, draw, or print.

The scale picture is unusually simple. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so it is not framed as an activity reserved only for a large factory or only for a small workshop. A founder could read the scope as covering anything from a compact ribbon-making operation to a larger industrial setup, provided the registered business activity remains inside the manufacture of those machine ribbons. The key discipline is scope: the code follows the product being made, not the wider commercial ecosystem around office supplies, printing services, or equipment trading.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is also clear. The PMA status is marked TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership figure in the record is 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national layer alone, that means the activity is open to foreign ownership up to the full percentage stated in the slim record. There is no lower foreign-share cap in the record, and there is no stated minimum-capital figure, special licence, tax condition, or timeline here to add. For a national read, the honest conclusion is straightforward: KBLI 32902 is a foreign-open manufacturing activity at the recorded ceiling.

Bali changes the practical answer. The record marks `l4_bali_blocked` as true and gives the Bali status as `Blocked (risk class)`. Its reason is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, with source `Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP`. So the editorial bottom line is not that the activity is nationally closed. It is not. The bottom line is that a foreigner cannot register this KBLI as a PMA in Bali today, even though the same record shows the national PMA layer as open.
editorial.pullQuote: The national layer says open, but the Bali layer is decisive for anyone trying to register this as a PMA on the island.

editorial.headline: Craft Goods That Are Nationally Open, But Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32903 covers plant, animal, floral and shell-based craft manufacturing, open nationally to all business scales but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 32903 is a manufacturing code for craft goods that sit outside a narrower named category.** The record describes the making of handicraft items from plant and animal materials: coconut tree products, shells, coconut fibre, roots, leather, ivory, horn, bone, feathers and hair. It also includes preserved animals and taxidermy, wreaths, circular flower arrangements and flower baskets, as well as artificial flowers, fruits and leaves. The scope extends to painted craft goods and to craft items made from fish skin and shells, including pearl oyster shell such as *Pinctada maxima*, mabe shell and other shells.

That breadth matters because this is not only a souvenir label or a retail-facing craft identity. It is an industrial activity code for making the objects themselves. A registrant using this code is identifying the production of craft goods from the materials named in the record, including natural plant materials, animal-derived materials, preserved forms, floral arrangements, artificial botanical objects and shell-based work. The scale field is unusually broad: the activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. In plain English, the record allows the code to be used across the full business-scale range, from micro operators to large-scale businesses, provided the registered activity stays inside this described manufacturing scope.

Nationally, the investment picture looks open. PMA status is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 is named as the source for that national position. On the national reading alone, a foreign-owned company is not capped below full ownership for this activity. That is the clean national rule in the slim record: open status, 100% maximum foreign ownership, and availability across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales.

Bali is the decisive exception. The record marks this code as blocked for Bali PMA registration: l4_bali_blocked is true and the Bali status is Blocked (risk class). The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, blocked by the Bali moratorium in May 2026. The moratorium rule in the record is broader still: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest national-vs-Bali conclusion is direct. KBLI 32903 is nationally foreign-open up to 100%, but a foreigner cannot register it in Bali today under the Bali-side block recorded here.

editorial.headline: Safety Protection Equipment Manufacturing, Fully Open Nationally
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32904 covers the making of personal safety and protective equipment, with PMA ownership open nationally up to 100% and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32904 is a manufacturing activity for equipment whose purpose is bodily protection: the things used when work, sport, emergency response, or hazardous environments require a physical layer of safety. The record’s scope is broad but concrete. It includes protective clothing and fire-resistant clothing, safety belts for wire workers and other job-use belts, life jackets, hard plastic head protection such as construction helmets, and other plastic safety equipment including sports helmets and similar helmets. It also reaches firefighting protective wear, bulletproof vests, radiation-protection equipment such as aprons and gloves, metal safety headgear and other metal personal protective equipment, ear and nose plugs, gas masks, and PPE including face shields.

The important editorial point is that this is not a trading description and not a service wrapper. The activity is the making of safety-protection equipment itself. A founder using this code is registering an industrial activity centred on producing protective goods, from wearable protection to specialised equipment named in the scope. The record also makes the scale picture unusually straightforward: it is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the classification is not reserved only for large factories in the slim record; the same activity label can sit across the full scale ladder recorded here.

Nationally, the PMA position is clean. The activity is marked TERBUKA in the record, and pma_max_asing is 100, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as its source. In plain English, the national foreign-ownership ceiling shown in the record is 100%. There is no lower foreign-stake cap in the data, and no additional national threshold or licensing condition is stated in the slim record. For an international founder reading this classification, that matters: the record does not merely say foreign investment is possible; it says the national ceiling reaches full foreign ownership.

Bali is also not blocked in this record, but the reason is specific and should be kept precise. With l4_bali_blocked set to false, the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The record gives the reason as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” That must be read alongside the moratorium rule supplied in the record: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. Here, however, the record does not place this activity inside the blocked side of that rule. So the honest national-versus-Bali picture is aligned: nationally open up to 100% PMA, and not blocked by the Bali moratorium in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: The record does not merely say foreign investment is possible; it says the national ceiling reaches full foreign ownership.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Coconut Coir Fiber, Nationally Open but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32905 covers industrial processing of coconut husk into coir materials, with all business scales open nationally but PMA registration blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32905 is a narrow but important industrial activity: the processing of coconut husk into raw materials. The record identifies three outputs at the center of the scope: coconut coir fiber, or cocofiber; coconut coir powder, or cocopeat; and rubberized curl coir, known in the Indonesian text as serat sabut kelapa berkaret or sebutret. This is not the retailing of coconut products or the cultivation of coconuts. It is the conversion of husk into industrial material.

The business-scale picture is unusually broad. The slim record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. In practical registration terms, that means the classification is not reserved only for large factories or only for small household-level activity. It can describe a small processor as well as a larger industrial setup, as long as the registered activity remains within the stated processing scope: coconut husk transformed into cocofiber, cocopeat, or rubberized coir.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling in the record is 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. On the national layer, then, this is a foreign-open activity with no lower percentage cap appearing in the slim record. That matters, because it means any restriction in this draft cannot be invented from the nature of the product, the location, or an assumed local-partner rule. The only national ownership number here is the 100% figure.

Bali changes the outcome. The record marks this activity as blocked for Bali PMA registration, with the Bali status Blocked (risk class). The stated reason is that the OSS risk at Besar scale is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, bringing it under the Bali moratorium that blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island. So the honest conclusion is simple: nationally, KBLI 32905 is open to foreign ownership; in Bali, a foreigner cannot register it today because the Bali-side block applies. There is no Bali percentage cap in the record, and no separate Bali quota or partnership condition to describe. The restriction is a registration block, not a reduced foreign-ownership ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, KBLI 32905 is open to foreign ownership; in Bali, a foreigner cannot register it today because the Bali-side block applies.

editorial.headline: False Hair, Real Manufacturing Rules
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32906 covers the making of wigs, false beards, false eyelashes and similar products, nationally open to PMA but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32906 is a manufacturing code for the production of false-hair and similar appearance products. The slim record defines the activity as the making of wigs, false beards, false eyelashes, and other similar products. That makes the code about production, not retailing, salon services, beauty consulting, or distribution. Its centre of gravity is the factory or workshop activity: turning materials into finished false-hair products that can enter the market under this industrial classification.

The code is open across the full business-scale ladder recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practical registration language, that means the activity is not confined to one size of Indonesian business in the record. A micro workshop, a small maker, a mid-sized manufacturer, or a large-scale producer can all sit inside the scale range shown for this activity, provided the registration itself follows the applicable OSS pathway for the chosen scale and location. The editorial point is simple: the activity scope is narrow, but the eligible business scales are broad.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture looks open. The record marks PMA status as TERBUKA and gives the maximum foreign ownership as 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the source. On the national data alone, a foreign-owned company can read this as a fully open manufacturing activity, not a capped one. There is no lower foreign-share ceiling in the slim record, so the national number should be stated plainly and not diluted with invented caveats.

Bali changes the conclusion. The record marks Bali as Blocked (risk class) and sets l4_bali_blocked to true. The reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026”. Read together with the moratorium rule in the record, Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, under Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. So the honest operational lede is this: KBLI 32906 may be nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but a foreigner cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali today under the Bali-side rule recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 32906 may be nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but a foreigner cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Buttons, Zippers, and the Bali PMA Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32907 covers the manufacture of buttons, zippers, and supporting components; nationally it is open to foreign ownership, but Bali blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32907 is a small industrial category with a practical role in garment, accessory, and product supply chains. The record defines it as the manufacture of various kinds of buttons, including hook buttons and press buttons, together with the manufacture of zippers and other supporting components. In plain English, this is not retail, tailoring, or fashion branding. It is the production side: the activity of making the fasteners and related parts that other businesses may later use in finished goods.

The scale position is broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so it can describe anything from a very small production setup to a larger industrial business, provided the activity remains within the stated manufacturing scope. That matters because the code is not framed around one narrow company size. It is an industrial activity that can be registered across every listed scale in the record.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the stated maximum foreign ownership is 100%, with the source given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national reading alone, this is therefore a foreign-open activity with no lower ceiling shown in the record. A foreign investor looking only at the national PMA field would see a clean answer: the activity is open, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%.

Bali changes the practical answer completely. The record marks this code as blocked in Bali, with the reason stated as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule is also explicit: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest editorial conclusion is not that the code is partly open in Bali, or that Bali applies a separate percentage cap. It is that a foreigner cannot register this KBLI as a PMA in Bali today, even though the same activity is nationally marked TERBUKA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor looking only at the national PMA field would see a clean answer, but Bali changes the practical answer completely.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Lighter Manufacturing Is Nationally Open, But Bali Blocks PMA Registration
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32908 covers the manufacture of metal and plastic lighters; nationally it is open to foreign ownership, but Bali blocks PMA registration under its risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32908 is a narrow manufacturing code: it covers the making of various kinds of lighters, using metal or plastic as the base material. The record does not limit the activity to one operating technology. It includes lighters operated mechanically, electrically, or through another mechanism. In plain English, this is the industrial production of lighter products, not retail, distribution, import, repair, or a broader household-goods category.

The activity is open across the full scale range listed in the record: **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**. That matters because the code is not reserved in the slim record for only one class of operator. A small producer and a large manufacturer sit under the same activity description if what they are doing is the manufacture of lighter products from metal or plastic. The record gives no separate process threshold, output volume, factory-size test, licence condition, or capital number, so none should be read into it.

Nationally, the investment picture is clean. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, with **pma_max_asing** recorded as **100** under **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national record presents this activity as open up to a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. There is no partial national cap in the slim record, and there is no additional national qualification stated here beyond the code, the activity scope, the scale availability, and the cited PMA source.

Bali is the decisive complication. The same record marks the Bali side as **Blocked (risk class)**, with **l4_bali_blocked** set to true. The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale **Besar** is **Rendah/Menengah-Rendah** on every scope, so the activity is blocked by the Bali moratorium dated May 13, 2026. The moratorium rule in the record is broader and sharper: Bali province blocks **all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA**, island-wide and permanently, with the source given as **Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP**. So the honest reading is not that the code is unclear, or that Bali has a separate foreign-share percentage. The honest reading is that KBLI 32908 is nationally open to PMA, but a foreigner cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali today under the Bali rule recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 32908 is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali blocks PMA registration for it under the risk-class moratorium recorded in the file.

editorial.headline: A Broad Manufacturing Code That Stops at Bali’s PMA Gate
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32909 captures miscellaneous manufactured goods, nationally open to PMA, but the record marks it blocked for foreign registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32909 is the residual home for manufacturing that does not sit neatly elsewhere. The Indonesian scope describes the making of goods not otherwise classified: signs, many kinds of umbrellas, smoking pipes and electronic cigarettes, badges, trophies, medals, stamps, walking sticks, lampshades, candles, brooms, palm-fibre brushes, cigar and betel containers, combs, perfume sprayers, vacuum bottles and vacuum vessels for personal or household use, natural non-animal leather such as plant-based leather from certain fungi, tailor’s mannequins used to dress garments, coffins, and other products not yet covered in another group. In plain English, this is not one product line but a catch-all manufacturing activity for varied finished articles.

That breadth matters for founders. The record opens this activity across the full scale ladder: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. A small workshop, a mid-sized producer, or a larger manufacturer may all appear within the registered scale universe, provided the activity being registered is genuinely the making of these miscellaneous products. The code’s value is its breadth; its risk is the same breadth. It should not be used as a vague label for trading, distribution, services, or a product whose manufacturing scope is not actually described by the record.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. The slim record marks the code as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national record treats the activity as open and allows the foreign ownership ceiling to be stated cleanly as 100%. There is no lower foreign-share cap in the record, and no invented qualification should be added to it.

Bali is the decisive exception. The same record sets l4_bali_blocked to true and gives the reason: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” It also states the moratorium rule as: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” So the honest reading is not that this activity is impossible nationally; it is that a foreigner cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today under the Bali-side record. For Bali planning, the national openness is real, but it does not override the local block recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the activity is open to 100% foreign ownership, but in Bali the record’s practical answer is blocked for PMA registration.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Industrial Metal Repair Is Open Nationally, But Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33111 covers repair and maintenance for structural metal products, tanks, reservoirs, steam generators, and related fabricated-metal equipment.
editorial.body:
For a foreign-owned company looking at Bali, the decisive point is simple: this activity is nationally open, but the record blocks PMA registration in Bali today. KBLI 33111 sits in the repair-and-maintenance side of fabricated metal products, covering work on structural metal products, tanks, water reservoirs, metal containers, steel shipping drums, steam generators, and related steam-generator auxiliary machinery such as condensers, heaters, collectors, and steam accumulators. It also reaches specialised equipment named in the record, including nuclear reactors except isotope separators, marine engine parts, power-boiler parts, radiator work equipment, and central-heating equipment of a similar kind.

This is not a retail, advisory, or general maintenance label. Its scope is industrial and equipment-heavy: keeping fabricated-metal structures and pressure, storage, steam, and heating-related assets in working condition. The practical identity of the code is therefore repair and upkeep of metal infrastructure and machinery that already exists, rather than manufacturing new products or supplying a broad facilities-management service. The Indonesian scope is broad, but it is still bounded by the listed objects: structural metal goods, tanks and reservoirs, containers and drums, steam-generation equipment, and the specified associated machinery and parts.

On business scale, the record is unusually open. It names Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, which means the activity is available across the full scale ladder recorded here. Nationally, the PMA status is also clear: TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national reading is that foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership for this activity in the record. A foreign investor analysing Indonesia at national level would therefore see a clean foreign-open classification, not a partially capped one.

Bali changes the conclusion. The Bali-side status is Blocked (risk class), and the record marks l4_bali_blocked as true. The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, and that this is blocked by the Bali moratorium of May 2026. The moratorium rule in the record is island-wide and permanent: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. So the honest national-versus-Bali picture is not a subtle caveat. Nationally, KBLI 33111 is open to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, a foreign-owned registration is blocked because the provincial moratorium catches this risk class.
