data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Where Weapon Repair Stands Open, Including Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33112 covers repair and maintenance of weapon and ammunition products, with full national foreign ownership and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33112 is a repair-and-maintenance activity, not a manufacturing description or a trading category. Its stated scope is the repair and maintenance of weapon and ammunition products, including firearms and cannon or artillery. The record also makes room for weapons used in sporting or recreational activity, so the practical centre of the code is the technical servicing of these products rather than a broad retail or defence-services story.

The registration surface is unusually broad in scale terms. The slim record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. That means the code is not framed only for large establishments in the classification record; it can be used across the full scale ladder listed in the source. The activity remains specific, however: it is about reparasi dan pemeliharaan, repair and maintenance, of the weapon and ammunition products named in the scope.

Nationally, the PMA position is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives pma_max_asing as 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national foreign-ownership ceiling in this record is 100%. There is no lower percentage to explain, no special ownership split to infer, and no extra capital or licensing condition supplied here. The only ownership number available is the national PMA ceiling, and it points to full foreign openness at the national level.

The Bali picture is also direct, but it needs to be stated carefully. Bali's moratorium rule in the record says the province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. For this code, however, l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The record's reason is explicit: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". So the honest reading is not that Bali creates a separate ownership cap, quota, or partnership requirement. It is that this activity is nationally open to PMA at 100%, and the Bali-side record does not block it under the stated moratorium reason.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is that this activity is nationally open to PMA at 100%, and the Bali-side record does not block it under the stated moratorium reason.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers repairing and maintaining a wide range of factory-made metal products—things like cutting tools, hand tools, agricultural and household metal gear, non-structural containers, wire goods, safes, filing cabinets, and even mobile welding services.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this business is 100% open to foreign ownership. However, in Bali, a local moratorium on low and medium-low risk activities (in effect since 13 May 2026) currently blocks foreign-owned companies from registering this activity, so a PMA setup for these services is not possible right now.

editorial.headline: Mobile Metalwork Repair Meets a Bali Registration Wall
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33119 covers repair and maintenance for fabricated metal goods, nationally open to foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33119 is a practical repair-and-maintenance activity for fabricated metal products: the work of keeping metal tools, containers, wire goods, safes, filing cabinets, and other non-structural metal items usable after they leave the factory. Its scope reaches familiar equipment used in agriculture, carpentry, workshops, and households, and it explicitly includes mobile welding that moves from site to site. This is not manufacturing a new metal product; it is the service layer that repairs and maintains fabricated metal goods already in use.

The registration base is broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale operators, which means the category can describe anything from a small repair outfit to a larger maintenance business, provided the activity remains inside the stated scope. The wording points to general-purpose metal goods rather than structural metal works, so the editorial center of gravity is everyday fabricated-metal utility: cutting tools, hand tools, common equipment, metal containers, wire goods, safes, cabinets, and similar items that need technical maintenance rather than replacement.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. The activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with `pma_max_asing` at **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. On the national record alone, a foreign-owned PMA structure is not capped below full foreign ownership. That matters because the activity may look modest, but the national investment signal is clear: the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, not a partial stake, and the open status applies across the scales listed in the slim record.

Bali is the decisive exception. The record marks this activity as blocked in Bali: `l4_bali_blocked` is true, with the reason that **OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, blocked by the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026**. The moratorium rule is also explicit: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, with the source given as **Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP**. So the honest reading is narrow but important: KBLI 33119 is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet a foreigner cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali today under the Bali-side block recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 33119 is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet a foreigner cannot register it as a PMA activity in Bali today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

data.judul: Reparasi dan Pemeliharaan Mesin untuk Keperluan Umum
data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup reparasi dan pemeliharaan mesin untuk keperluan umum yang tercakup dalam golongan 281, seperti reparasi dan pemeliharaan mesin kapal laut atau kereta api, pompa, kompresor dan peralatan yang terkait, mesin tenaga uap atau zat cair, katup atau klep, roda gigi (persneling) dan peralatan kemudi, tungku pembakar pada proses industri, alat pengangkat dan pemindah, mesin dan peralatan kantor kecuali komputer dan perlengkapannya (cash register, mesin fotokopi, kalkulator, mesin ketik), perkakas tangan yang digerakkan tenaga, peralatan pendingin dan pembersih udara, timbangan, serta mesin penjual otomatis.

editorial.headline: The Essential Work of General Machinery Repair
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33121 covers the repair and maintenance of general-purpose machinery, from pumps and compressors to office machines, industrial burners, lifting equipment, and vending machines.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33121 is the practical code for keeping general-purpose machinery in working order. Its scope is repair and maintenance, not the manufacture or sale of machinery. The record places within it a broad industrial and commercial field: marine or railway machinery, pumps, compressors and related equipment, steam or liquid power machinery, valves, gears and steering equipment, industrial process burners, lifting and handling equipment, powered hand tools, cooling and air-cleaning equipment, scales, vending machines, and office machines except computers and their peripherals. In plain English, this is the activity code for businesses whose core service is maintaining the machinery that lets factories, offices, transport systems, and service operations keep running.

The breadth of the record matters because this is not a niche workshop category. It can cover a repair business serving industrial equipment, a maintenance provider for pumps and compressors, a service operation for lifting and handling machinery, or a specialist maintaining cash registers, photocopiers, calculators, typewriters, scales, and vending machines. The unifying test is functional rather than decorative: the business repairs and maintains general-purpose machinery within the stated scope. If the activity is centered on computers and their peripherals, the record expressly leaves that outside this code. If the work is the repair and maintenance of the machines named in the scope, this code is the natural editorial home.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so it can fit anything from a small maintenance outfit to a larger service company. That does not mean the operating reality is identical at every scale; it means the slim record marks all four scales as open for registration. A founder reading this code should therefore focus less on forcing the business into a particular size label and more on whether the declared activity truly matches the machinery-repair scope described above.

The national-vs-Bali picture is clean. Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% under the cited PMA source. Bali does not add a separate percentage in this record. Its Bali-side status is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule recorded here says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; for this code, however, the record does not mark it as blocked. The honest reading is therefore straightforward: KBLI 33121 is nationally foreign-open, and the Bali record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is therefore straightforward: KBLI 33121 is nationally foreign-open, and the Bali record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Special-Purpose Machinery Repair Without a Bali Moratorium Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33122 covers the repair and maintenance of specialised industrial, agricultural, construction, processing, and extraction machinery.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33122 is a practical, equipment-facing activity: the repair and maintenance of machinery built for special purposes. The record frames it around machinery used in production, extraction, construction, agriculture, forestry, metalworking, transport infrastructure, and industrial processing. In plain English, this is not general workshop work. It is the upkeep of the machines that keep specialised sectors operating: agricultural tractors and farm machinery, forestry and logging equipment, metal-cutting and metal-forming machine tools and their accessories, metallurgical machinery, mining and excavation machinery, oil and gas field machinery, construction machinery, and machinery used for food, beverage, tobacco, textile, garment, leather-garment, and paper manufacturing.

That breadth matters because the activity is defined by the machine’s function, not by a single customer type. A founder registering under this code would be positioning the business around technical repair and maintenance for specialised machinery across those listed fields. The slim record marks the activity as open across all stated business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the code is not presented here as reserved only for a large industrial operator; it can describe a smaller maintenance provider as well as a larger service operation, provided the registered activity remains within the repair and maintenance scope described in the record.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The record marks PMA status as TERBUKA and gives a pma_max_asing of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In editorial terms, the national rule shown here is that foreign ownership may reach 100% for this activity. There is no lower foreign-stake cap in the slim record, and there is no extra threshold, licence, capital figure, or timeline stated here to add. For a foreign-owned setup, the honest national reading is therefore straightforward: the activity is foreign-open at the national level, with the recorded ceiling at 100%.

The Bali reading is also important, because Bali applies a moratorium rule that blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province. This record, however, does not mark KBLI 33122 as blocked in Bali. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” So the honest conclusion is not a hidden Bali prohibition. On this record, KBLI 33122 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium because the recorded Bali reason places the relevant Besar-scale OSS risk above the moratorium’s Low and Medium-Low block.
editorial.pullQuote: On this record, KBLI 33122 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium.

editorial.headline: Repairing the Instruments That Keep Technical Systems Measured
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33131 covers repair and maintenance for measuring, testing, navigation, and control equipment, nationally open to foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33131 is a technical maintenance activity, not a general repair bucket. The record places it around the repair and upkeep of equipment made in the measuring, testing, navigation, and control field: aircraft engine equipment, vehicle-emission testing equipment, meteorological instruments, physical, electrical, and chemical testing or inspection equipment, research or survey equipment, detection equipment, radiation monitoring equipment, and similar devices. In plain English, this is the workshop and service activity behind instruments that need to stay reliable because other decisions depend on their readings.

That scope matters because the activity is defined by the kind of equipment being maintained. It is concerned with apparatus used to measure, test, inspect, detect, navigate, control, survey, or monitor. A business registering this code should therefore be anchored in repair and maintenance work for those instruments, rather than in manufacturing, trading, consulting, or operating the measured systems themselves. The slim record also shows that the activity is open across the full Indonesian business-scale spectrum: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In other words, the classification can sit behind a small specialist service operation or a larger technical-maintenance business, provided the activity remains within the stated repair-and-maintenance scope.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clear. The PMA status is marked TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership value is 100. That makes this a nationally foreign-open activity under the cited source, with no lower foreign-ownership ceiling appearing in the record. The honest national reading is therefore straightforward: for Indonesia as a whole, the record presents KBLI 33131 as open to PMA ownership up to 100%, across the listed business scales.

Bali changes the practical conclusion. The Bali-side status is marked Blocked (risk class), and the record says the code is blocked in Bali because “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026”. The moratorium rule is broader still: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent)”. So the useful editorial lede is not that this code is nationally closed. It is not. The point is sharper: a foreign investor may see a 100% national PMA ceiling, but cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today under the Bali moratorium logic recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor may see a 100% national PMA ceiling, but cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Maintaining Indonesia’s Advanced Medical Equipment
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33132 covers the technical repair and upkeep of irradiation, electromedical, and electrotherapy equipment, with national openness but a scope-sensitive Bali pathway.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33132 is the maintenance trade behind some of the most sensitive equipment in a modern health system. The record defines it as repair and maintenance of irradiation, electromedical, and electrotherapy equipment: MRI machinery, medical ultrasound equipment, pacemakers, hearing aids, electrocardiography equipment, electromedical endoscopy equipment, irradiation equipment, and similar devices. In plain English, this is not general workshop repair. It is the activity of keeping specialist clinical technology functional, serviced, and available for use.

The scope is written broadly enough to cover the equipment category rather than a single device type. That matters for founders because the commercial identity of the business should match the declared activity with care: a company presenting itself around MRI servicing, ultrasound equipment upkeep, pacemaker-related maintenance, hearing-aid repair, ECG equipment, electromedical endoscopy support, or irradiation equipment maintenance is still operating inside the same recorded field when the work is repair and maintenance of those devices. The slim record also places the activity across all business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In other words, the record does not reserve this KBLI only for large operators; it is open across the listed scale range.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership stated in the record is 100%. The cited source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national table treats this activity as open to full foreign ownership. There is no foreign-share reduction to explain here, and no lower ownership ceiling appears in the record.

Bali is more nuanced. The record does not mark the activity as simply blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false. But it does mark the Bali status as Blocked (scope-dependent), and the reason is explicit: “OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity”. That sits beside the Bali moratorium rule in the record: Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. The honest reading is therefore not “Bali is open in the same way as the national table.” It is this: nationally, KBLI 33132 is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, PMA registration depends on the exact declared scope and its OSS risk treatment, so the activity must be checked against the precise activity formulation before it is treated as registrable.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, KBLI 33132 is foreign-open up to 100%; in Bali, PMA registration depends on the exact declared scope and its OSS risk treatment.

editorial.headline: Optical and Photography Equipment Repair, Open Nationally but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33133 covers commercial repair and maintenance of photography and optical equipment, with a clean national PMA opening but a hard Bali registration block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33133 is a specialised repair-and-maintenance activity for photography and optical equipment when that equipment is mainly used commercially. In plain English, this is the workshop layer behind professional lenses, cameras, microscopes outside the excluded electron and proton types, telescopes, binoculars, prisms, and similar optical instruments. The scope is technical rather than retail: the code is about keeping the equipment working, serviced, and repaired, not about selling the equipment or using it as part of a studio, laboratory, or observatory business.

The record opens the activity across every business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the code is not confined to one size of operator in the national classification. A small repair counter and a larger commercial maintenance operation can both sit inside the same activity definition if the work matches the recorded scope. The common thread is the object of the service: photographic and optical equipment, used commercially, repaired or maintained as equipment.

Nationally, the PMA picture is simple. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100 under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national record does not impose a foreign-shareholding cap below full ownership for this activity. There is no separate condition in the slim record to add, qualify, or soften that point. The national classification is open; the national ceiling is 100%.

Bali is the decisive exception. The record marks l4_bali_blocked as true and gives the status as Blocked (risk class). The reason is not a sectoral judgement about photography or optics; it is the Bali-side risk-class rule recorded here: OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, which puts the activity inside the Bali moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest reading is precise: KBLI 33133 is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but a foreigner cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Electric Power Equipment Repair: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the repair and maintenance backbone of electric power equipment, with national PMA openness but a Bali-side block under the record's risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33141 is a service activity for keeping electrical power equipment in working order. The Indonesian scope points to repair and maintenance, not manufacture or retail: power machinery, distribution machinery, transformers, electric motors, generators, motor-generator devices, switchgear and switchboards, relay equipment, and industrial controllers. In plain English, the code sits where electrical infrastructure becomes an ongoing technical responsibility. It is for the workshop or service operator whose registered activity is to maintain and repair the machines that move, transform, switch, relay, or control electrical power.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The slim record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so the classification is not reserved only for a large industrial plant or a single scale of operator. A smaller repair business and a larger maintenance operation can both be within the record's scale language, provided the actual registered activity remains the repair and maintenance scope described above. That breadth matters because the code's commercial reality can range from focused electric-motor service to heavier transformer or industrial-control maintenance, but the legal reading in this record is still anchored to one activity: repair and maintenance.

Nationally, the PMA signal is open. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives a pma_max_asing of 100, which means the foreign-ownership ceiling should be rendered as 100% for this national view. There is no lower percentage, special local share, capital threshold, operating condition, or licensing detail in the slim record, so none should be read into it. On the national layer alone, a foreign investor looking at this activity sees an open PMA classification supported by the cited presidential-regulation source.

The Bali reading is the decisive one. Nationally, this is an open industrial-service activity; in Bali, the same record blocks it for PMA registration. The stated Bali reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, and the record connects that result to the Bali moratorium in May 2026. The moratorium rule supplied in the record is island-wide and permanent for Low and Medium-Low risk PMA activity. So the honest conclusion is direct: a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today, even though the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, this is an open industrial-service activity; in Bali, the same record blocks it for PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Repairing the Power Behind Electric Mobility
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33142 is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s risk-class moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33142 is the repair-and-maintenance home for the hardware that keeps electric mobility and electrical storage working after installation. Its Indonesian scope covers the repair and upkeep of electric-car charging stations, batteries, and electric accumulators, including those used for electric motors and related equipment within the battery and accumulator manufacturing family. In plain English, this is not the business of selling vehicles or producing batteries from scratch; it is the technical aftercare layer that keeps charging and storage assets usable, serviced, and maintained.

That makes the activity practical and infrastructure-facing. A company registering under this code is positioning itself around maintenance capability: diagnosing, repairing, servicing, and preserving charging points, batteries, and accumulators once they are already in circulation. The scale aperture is broad. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so the code is not framed only for a large industrial platform. It can describe a smaller specialist repair operation as well as a larger maintenance business, provided the registered activity remains inside the stated repair-and-maintenance scope.

Nationally, the PMA picture is straightforward. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a `pma_max_asing` of 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For founders reading the national investment list, that means foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership in the record supplied here. A foreign-owned company can treat the national ceiling as 100%, without inventing an additional ownership limit, capital figure, licence condition, or staging requirement that the record does not contain.

Bali is the decisive exception. The same record marks the Bali layer as `Blocked (risk class)`, with `l4_bali_blocked` set to true. The reason is not an ownership cap or a sector-specific local partnership condition; it is the provincial moratorium: at Besar scale, OSS classifies every scope here as Low or Medium-Low risk, and Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide on a permanent basis. The honest lede, therefore, is simple: a foreign investor may see KBLI 33142 as nationally open, even to 100% foreign ownership, but cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today because the Bali moratorium blocks it.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor may see KBLI 33142 as nationally open, even to 100% foreign ownership, but cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Electrical Repair That Is Nationally Open but Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A practical repair-and-maintenance code for other electrical equipment, open nationally to every business scale but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali today.
editorial.body:
This activity is the repair and maintenance of other electrical equipment: the kind of work that keeps lighting equipment, current-carrying and non-current-carrying wiring equipment, cable-circuit components, and similar electrical equipment in working order. The record’s Indonesian scope is broad but not vague: it points to equipment in the electrical categories referenced by the record, and it frames the activity as repair and maintenance, not manufacturing, retail, or installation. In business terms, this is a workshop or service-operation code for maintaining the electrical apparatus around lighting and wiring systems.

Nationally, the code is marked **TERBUKA** for foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%** under **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. That national status matters because it says the activity is not closed at the Indonesian level. The scale picture is also unusually wide: the record opens it to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**. A very small repair operator, a growing maintenance shop, and a large service company can all sit inside the national scale envelope described by the record. Nothing in the slim record adds a special licence, capital threshold, tax rule, or timing requirement, so none should be read into the classification itself.

The Bali reading is the controlling practical point for a foreign-owned setup on the island. Although the national table is open up to 100% foreign ownership, the record says **l4_bali_blocked** is true. The stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” In plain English, a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today as a PMA activity. That is not because the national PMA table closes the activity; it is because Bali’s moratorium blocks it locally on the risk-class basis recorded here.

The moratorium text in the record is blunt: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” The source is listed as **Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP**. So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is split: this is a legitimate, nationally open electrical repair-and-maintenance activity with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, available across all listed business scales, but it is blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the province-level moratorium recorded in the slim record.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally this electrical repair activity is open to 100% foreign ownership, but in Bali the record makes the practical answer no.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Ship and Floating-Structure Repair With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers repair, maintenance, and modification work for vessels and floating offshore structures, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33151 is the repair-and-maintenance home for marine transport assets: ships, boats, yachts, recreational or sports craft, and comparable vessels. Its scope also reaches the repair, maintenance, and modification of offshore floating structures, which gives the activity a practical breadth beyond ordinary dockside fixes. The common thread is not trading vessels or operating voyages; it is keeping vessels and floating structures serviceable, maintained, repaired, or modified.

That makes the code relevant to operators whose business is technical service rather than transport itself. A workshop repairing boats, a maintenance provider handling yachts, or a specialist working on floating offshore structures would read this scope as a repair-and-care activity. The record opens registration across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the classification is not limited to one business size. It can describe a small repair operation as well as a large-scale marine maintenance business, provided the actual activity remains within the stated repair, maintenance, and modification scope.

The national foreign-investment position is clean: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain English, the national record treats this as fully open to PMA ownership, rather than imposing a lower foreign-share cap. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For founders, the key editorial point is that the foreign-ownership question should not be blurred with the operational description: the code covers repair and maintenance work, and nationally the investment status is open up to the full stated ceiling.

editorial.headline: Rail Rolling Stock Maintenance, Open Nationally and Usable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33152 covers the repair and maintenance of locomotives, railway carriages, and other rail-track vehicles, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33152 is a narrowly industrial activity: the repair and maintenance of locomotives, railway carriages, and other vehicles that run on rail tracks. Its scope is not the rebuilding or alteration industry, which the record expressly excludes, but the service work that keeps rail vehicles in operating condition. In plain English, this is the maintenance side of rail rolling stock: technical, asset-heavy, and tied to vehicles whose function is defined by the railway system itself.

The registration picture is unusually broad by scale. The slim record marks this activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, which means it is not confined to one size of business in the classification record. A smaller workshop-style registration and a larger industrial maintenance operation sit under the same activity description, provided the registered business is still doing what the scope says: repair and maintenance of locomotives, railway carriages, or other rail-road vehicles, not manufacturing-style reconstruction or conversion.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clean. The record lists the PMA status as TERBUKA and sets its maximum foreign ownership figure at 100%. That is the only ownership ceiling stated here, and it is a national figure sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The practical editorial point is simple: this KBLI is nationally open to foreign ownership in the data provided. For a foreign-owned company, the national classification signal is open rather than capped below full ownership.

Bali does not add a separate ownership percentage in this record, and none should be inferred. The Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with l4_bali_blocked marked false. The stated reason is: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, permanently, but this activity is not blocked under the given Bali reason. So the honest national-vs-Bali reading is not a contradiction: KBLI 33152 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record does not mark it as blocked by the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest national-vs-Bali reading is not a contradiction: KBLI 33152 is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record does not mark it as blocked by the island-wide moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Aircraft Maintenance, Including Drones, Is Foreign-Open in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33153 covers approved aircraft maintenance work, with national PMA access up to 100% and no Bali moratorium block in the slim record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33153 is a maintenance code for aviation work. Its centre of gravity is the repair and upkeep of aircraft, including drones, aircraft engines, and aircraft equipment. That makes it a technical service category rather than a manufacturing or rebuilding category: the slim record expressly excludes alteration, inspection, and rebuilding of aircraft and aircraft engines. In plain English, this is where an approved maintenance organisation would sit when its business is keeping aircraft or aviation equipment serviceable, not remaking them.

The record is unusually broad on business scale. It is open to micro, small, medium, and large operators, which matters because aircraft maintenance is not always a single kind of company. Some registrants may be highly specialised maintenance outfits; others may be larger approved maintenance organisations with broader capability across aircraft, drones, engines, and associated equipment. The common thread is the activity itself: repair and maintenance within the stated scope, carried out as an aircraft maintenance organisation.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The PMA status is open, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That national position is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no partial foreign cap in the slim record, so the editorial conclusion should not soften that point: at the national level, this activity is open to full foreign ownership according to the data provided.

Bali does not reverse that outcome in this record. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the Bali block flag is false. The reason is specific: at large scale, the OSS risk sits at medium-high/high, so it is not caught by Bali’s moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record blocks all low and medium-low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, permanently, but this activity is not blocked on the facts supplied here. The honest Bali reading is therefore straightforward: a foreign-owned setup can look at this activity as nationally open and not moratorium-blocked in Bali, while keeping the registration aligned to the precise maintenance scope described above.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest Bali reading is straightforward: this activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and is not moratorium-blocked in the record.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: KBLI 33159: Repair Work for Transport Outside the Motor-Vehicle Lane
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali depends on the exact declared scope because low and medium-low risk PMA activity is blocked island-wide.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33159 sits in a narrow but important repair-and-maintenance lane: transport equipment that is outside the usual motor-vehicle, motorcycle, and bicycle categories. The scope named in the record covers the repair and upkeep of other transport tools, including war vehicles, horse-drawn carriages, animal-drawn carts, and similar forms of transport. In plain English, this is not a general garage classification. It is a maintenance home for transport equipment that falls outside the everyday road-vehicle frame, with the record explicitly separating repair of other non-motor transport equipment from repair of war vehicles.

That distinction matters because the activity is broader than a picturesque carriage workshop, but still tightly defined by the equipment being repaired. A founder reading this code should treat the declared activity as the centre of the analysis: the business is about repair and maintenance, not the sale, rental, manufacture, or operation of the transport equipment itself. The record does not add extra licence language, capital thresholds, or operating conditions, so none should be implied. Its practical meaning is simply the maintenance activity described: keeping these specified kinds of transport equipment serviceable.

Nationally, the posture is straightforward. The record marks the activity as open for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is also open across all listed business scales: micro, small, medium, and large. On the national view, then, this is not a restricted foreign-equity activity in the supplied record. A foreign-owned company can read the national line as fully open, subject only to the exact activity it is registering and the scale it selects. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, which is the source field supplied for the PMA position.

Bali is more exacting. The record does not say this code is flatly blocked for PMA in Bali today; `l4_bali_blocked` is false. But the Bali status is scope-dependent, and the reason is operationally important: Bali registration as PMA is available only where the exact declared scope falls into the higher-risk side of the activity, while some scopes at large scale are low risk. That matters because the Bali province rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. For this code, the honest reading is therefore conditional rather than universally open: nationally it is open up to 100% foreign ownership, but in Bali a PMA filing depends on declaring the exact registrable, higher-risk activity and verifying that position live in OSS before relying on it.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally this activity is fully foreign-open, but in Bali the decisive question is the exact scope declared in OSS.

editorial.headline: KBLI 33190: The Repair Work That Bali Will Not Register for PMA
editorial.standfirst: A broad repair-and-maintenance activity is nationally open to foreign ownership, but Bali’s risk-class moratorium blocks PMA registration for it today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33190 is a practical, catch-all home for repair and maintenance work on equipment that does not sit elsewhere in the main division. Its scope is not glamorous, but it is commercially real: repairing fishing nets, including patching; repairing snares, ropes, canvas, and tarpaulins; repairing storage bags for fertiliser and chemicals; renewing wooden pallets, shipping drums, and similar containers; repairing amusement equipment and gambling machines; repairing historic organs and other musical equipment; and repairing hospital beds. The common thread is not the customer sector, but the work itself: keeping specialised, often work-critical equipment usable.

That breadth matters for founders because this activity can serve very different markets. A workshop repairing nets and tarps for field use, a service team maintaining hospital beds, or a repair operator handling pallets and shipping drums could all sit within the same activity description when the work matches the stated scope. The record opens the activity across every business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In other words, the classification is not reserved only for large industrial operators; it can also fit smaller repair businesses, provided the registered activity remains inside the defined repair-and-maintenance scope.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position looks straightforward. The activity is marked TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with the cited basis given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Taken only at the national level, that means a PMA structure is not capped below full foreign ownership in this record. There is no basis here to add a special capital threshold, licence condition, tax treatment, or timeline, so those should not be assumed from the classification alone.

Bali is the decisive complication. The Bali field says the activity is blocked for PMA registration, because OSS risk at Besar scale is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, and Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. The practical conclusion is blunt: although KBLI 33190 is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today under the stated moratorium. For a Bali setup, that local block is not a footnote; it is the controlling fact.
editorial.pullQuote: Although KBLI 33190 is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Industrial Installation Is Nationally Open, but Bali Says No
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33201 covers specialist installation and integration of industrial machinery, equipment, and systems; nationally it is foreign-open, but Bali blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
For a foreign-owned company looking at Bali, the practical answer comes first: KBLI 33201 cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. Nationally, the activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%** under the cited presidential regulations. Bali’s position is different. The province blocks this activity for PMA because, at **Besar** scale, its OSS risk classification is **Rendah** or **Menengah-Rendah** across every scope, bringing it inside Bali’s island-wide moratorium on Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA.

The activity itself is a serious industrial-services category. It covers specialist installation or mounting of industrial machinery and equipment, plus the assembly and integration of industrial equipment and systems. The integration side is broad: hardware and software can be brought together, in whole or in part, for large-scale or small-scale industrial systems. The record places the work in factories, warehouses, processing facilities, power-generation support systems, and other industrial environments where machinery, controls, equipment, and production infrastructure need to be installed or made to work as a functioning system.

In practical terms, the scope includes installing industrial machines in factories, installing process-control equipment and assemblies, and installing other industrial equipment such as communications equipment, mainframes or similar computers, irradiation equipment, and medical gas or electromedical equipment. It also includes millwright work, machine rigging, bowling-alley equipment installation, warehouse machinery and equipment installation, large-scale warehouse racking that is not part of the building, self-service charging stations, and industrial facilities such as loading and discharging stations, winding shafts, chemical plants, iron foundries, blast furnaces, coke ovens, and desalination or purification systems for power plants. The record also draws a boundary: building-related installations such as escalators, electrical wiring, burglar alarms, and air-conditioning systems are treated as construction activity, not this industrial installation category.

The registration audience is wide on paper. The activity is open across **Mikro**, **Kecil**, **Menengah**, and **Besar** scales, so the code can describe anything from a smaller specialist installer to a larger industrial systems integrator. The national PMA picture is unusually clean: it is open, and the recorded ceiling is 100% foreign ownership. But Bali changes the decision. The provincial moratorium, sourced to the governor’s letter, blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently. Since this activity is blocked on that risk basis in Bali, the commercially honest reading is simple: nationally available does not mean Bali-registerable for a foreign-owned setup.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally available does not mean Bali-registerable for a foreign-owned setup.

editorial.headline: Industrial Dismantling Is Nationally Open, but Bali Blocks PMA
editorial.standfirst: This code covers the dismantling of industrial machinery, equipment, and systems, with national PMA access but a Bali registration block for foreign-owned companies.
editorial.body:
This activity is about taking industrial machinery, equipment, and systems apart. Its scope is broad enough to cover both hardware and software, and it can apply to a whole system or only part of one. The scale of the work is not what defines the code: the record expressly includes dismantling on both large and small scales. In plain terms, this is the business of dismantling industrial assets, not installing them, integrating them, or demolishing civil buildings.

That distinction matters because the code sits around a very practical operational moment in an industrial asset's life. A factory line, production system, control setup, or other industrial equipment package may need to be removed, separated, decommissioned, or partially broken down. The activity here is the dismantling itself. It is not the original assembly of the system, and it is not the construction-sector demolition of the building that may surround it. Founders should read the scope as a technical industrial service, not as a general construction or installation category.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. The record marks the activity as open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. The code is also open across the full scale range listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. On the national face of the classification, then, this is not a restricted activity for PMA ownership, and the record does not state any foreign-share cap below full ownership.

Bali changes the answer. The Bali status is blocked by risk class, and the reason is specific: at Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, which places it inside Bali's PMA moratorium from May 2026. The moratorium rule in the record is province-wide and permanent for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. So the honest operating conclusion is sharp: while this activity is nationally open to foreign ownership, a foreign-owned company cannot register it in Bali today under the Bali rule recorded here.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally this industrial dismantling activity is open to full foreign ownership, but Bali's risk-class moratorium blocks PMA registration today.

editorial.headline: Installing Indonesia’s Weather, Climate, and Geophysical Eyes
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 33203 covers the installation of meteorological, climatological, and geophysical equipment, nationally open to PMA and not blocked in Bali under the recorded risk position.
editorial.body:
KBLI 33203 is for the practical installation layer behind weather, climate, and geophysical observation. Its scope is not research, forecasting, or data interpretation as such; the record defines it around putting equipment in place. That includes small, medium, or large installations such as automatic weather stations, humidity measuring devices, and volcanic-activity monitors. The slim record also identifies the relevant installation subclassification as IN014 for meteorological, climatological, and geophysical installation, which helps frame this as a technical installation activity rather than a broad environmental consultancy.

The commercial profile is unusually broad on scale. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so it can fit a small specialist installer as well as a larger engineering contractor handling more substantial deployments. That matters because the equipment named in the scope can sit in very different operating contexts: a compact humidity measurement setup, an automated weather station, or a monitoring system tied to volcanic activity. The common thread is installation competence, not the ownership of the data network or the public authority that may ultimately use the information.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is clean. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 is the cited basis for the record’s TERBUKA status and pma_max_asing of 100. In plain English, a PMA structure can hold up to 100% foreign ownership at the national level for this activity. The same record does not add a reduced foreign-share ceiling, a mandatory local partner, a minimum capital figure, or a sector-specific licence condition, so none should be read into it. For founders, the important editorial point is that this is a nationally foreign-open technical installation code across all listed business scales.

Bali requires a separate reading because the island’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, according to the recorded gubernatorial source. KBLI 33203 is not blocked in Bali on the slim record, because the Bali reason states that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, and therefore it is not caught by that moratorium. That is the honest national-versus-Bali picture: this activity is nationally open up to full foreign ownership, and the Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than blocked. The Bali entry does not give a separate local foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition, so the Bali conclusion should stay disciplined: not blocked by the stated moratorium, with the recorded higher-risk position doing the work.
editorial.pullQuote: That is the honest national-versus-Bali picture: this activity is nationally open up to full foreign ownership, and the Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than blocked.

editorial.headline: Fossil Power Generation, Open Nationally and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers fossil-fuel electricity generation, including carbon-credit sales by the power producer, with full national PMA access and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
This activity is about the operation of electricity-generating facilities that produce power from non-renewable fossil sources. The record names natural gas, coal, petroleum, petroleum products, peat, and other fossil fuels as the energy base. In plain terms, it is the KBLI home for an enterprise whose business is running the generating plant itself, not merely trading equipment, advising on energy, or handling downstream distribution. The scope also includes the sale of carbon units, or carbon credits, when that activity is carried out by the electricity generation company.

That carbon-credit inclusion matters editorially because it keeps the code centred on the producer. The commercial identity here is still a power-generation business: a company operating facilities that create electricity from fossil inputs and, where relevant, monetising carbon units as part of that same generating-company activity. Nothing in the record adds a special threshold, timetable, licence, tax treatment, or technical permit, so the clean reading is deliberately narrow: register this when the described operating activity is the business you are actually conducting.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It is open to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar** enterprises, so the registration frame is not limited to a single business size. A founder should read that as a scale-access statement, not as a promise that every project will be simple in practice. Power generation is infrastructure-heavy by nature, but the slim record only authorises one conclusion on KBLI access: all four listed Indonesian enterprise scales are available for this activity.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The code is marked **TERBUKA**, and the national foreign-ownership ceiling is **100%**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. Bali does not overturn that access for this record. The province’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA registration across the island, but this activity is not blocked because, at **Besar** scale, its OSS risk is **Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi**. The honest reading is therefore not a warning that foreign investors are shut out of Bali; it is the opposite. For this activity, a PMA can look at Bali without a moratorium block in the slim record, while still respecting the exact risk and scale framing stated there.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, a PMA can look at Bali without a moratorium block in the slim record, while still respecting the exact risk and scale framing stated there.

editorial.headline: Non-Emitting Power Generation Stands Open Nationally and in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This KBLI covers non-renewable power generation without emissions, open to every business scale and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is for the operation of power-generation facilities that produce electricity from non-renewable sources which do not generate emissions. The record gives nuclear, hydrogen, and ammonia as the defining examples, so the centre of gravity is not ordinary fuel switching or a broad clean-energy label; it is electricity production from a specified class of non-renewable, non-emitting sources. The scope also reaches the sale of carbon-credit units when that activity is carried out by the power-generation company itself, tying the credit activity to the generator rather than treating it as a free-standing trading business.

The practical registrant is therefore a company operating the generating facility, or a generating company whose own carbon-credit sales sit alongside that power activity. The record opens the code across all listed business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth matters because the classification is not reserved in the record for a single size of operator. A founder should still read the scale language as a registration fact, not as a promise about project economics, grid access, financing, land, technology readiness, or operational approvals; none of those details appears in the slim record, so they should not be inferred from the KBLI text.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national classification is open to foreign ownership up to the full stated ceiling. Because the ceiling is not below 100%, the record does not create a foreign-share cap lower than full ownership. The editorial point is simple but important: for this activity, the national investment field does not show a restriction inside the data provided here.

Bali tells the same direction, with a specific local reason. The island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, but this activity is not blocked in Bali because the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and l4_bali_blocked is false. That means the honest Bali reading is not that the activity is off-limits to foreign investors today; it is that this non-emitting, non-renewable power-generation code sits outside the Bali moratorium block described in the record. The useful conclusion for founders is disciplined: nationally open to PMA up to 100%, open across the listed scales, and not moratorium-blocked for PMA registration in Bali on the reason stated.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers operating power plants that generate electricity from renewable sources—like solar, wind (onshore/offshore), hydro, geothermal, tidal, wave, ocean, and biofuel gas. It also includes selling carbon credits generated by these facilities. It excludes non-renewable generation and electricity from waste incineration.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is open to 100% foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: matched with aggregation.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Pembangkitan Tenaga Listrik dari Sumber Energi Terbarukan (35120)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign renewable energy developers and independent power producers who want to build and operate green generation assets and monetize carbon credits.

editorial.headline: Renewable Power Generation Is Open, Including in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers renewable electricity generation, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block recorded for large-scale registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 35120 is the activity code for operating power-generation facilities that produce electricity from renewable energy sources. In practical terms, the record points to renewable-source electricity generation across a broad energy mix: biofuel gas, hydropower, onshore and offshore wind, photovoltaic solar, thermal energy, geothermal energy, tidal power, wave power, and marine energy. It also includes carbon-credit sales when those sales are carried out by the electricity-generation company itself.

The scope is deliberately tied to generation from renewable sources, not to electricity production in general. The record excludes production from non-renewable energy sources and also excludes electricity production through waste combustion. That boundary matters for founders because the code is not a flexible label for every power project; it is a renewable-generation classification, with carbon-credit activity only where it belongs to the generating company.

On scale, this is unusually broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar business scales. That means the code can sit behind very different operating profiles, from smaller renewable-generation businesses through larger infrastructure-scale projects, as long as the registered activity remains inside the stated renewable-generation scope. The editorial point is simple: the classification is broad in technology and broad in scale, but still narrow in source. The electricity must come from the renewable sources described in the record.

The national foreign-investment position is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the recorded maximum foreign ownership is 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. Bali does not add a moratorium block on this record: the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the Bali reason says that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the province’s moratorium. That matters because the Bali rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide on a permanent basis. Here, the record’s Bali-side conclusion is that the moratorium does not block PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: The national position is clean: this renewable power-generation activity is open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali record does not impose a moratorium block.
