editorial.headline: Turning Non-Hazardous Waste Into Power and Bioenergy
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 38211 covers non-hazardous waste processing that produces energy outputs, with full national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the slim record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 38211 is an energy-and-waste activity, not a general recycling label. The slim record describes the disposal or processing of non-hazardous waste through incineration or other methods where the output is energy: electricity, steam, renewable fuel oil, bioenergy, ash, or other energy products. Its centre of gravity is therefore conversion. The business activity begins with waste or non-hazardous residual material and ends with a usable energy product, including bioenergy, renewable fuel oil, or electricity.

That scope matters because it gives the code a specific industrial profile. A founder registering this activity is not simply collecting waste, sorting materials, or providing a civic cleaning service. The record frames the activity around treatment that produces something energetically useful. It also expressly includes non-hazardous waste processing for bioenergy and/or renewable fuel oil, and non-hazardous waste and refuse processing that produces electricity. In plain English, this is the KBLI for a waste-to-energy activity when the material is non-hazardous and the commercial point is the energy output.

The record opens the activity across every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth is important, because the same KBLI can describe a small-scale operator as well as a large project, provided the registered activity remains inside the stated scope. The foreign-investment position is also clean at the national level. The record classifies PMA as TERBUKA and sets maximum foreign ownership at 100%. On the national reading, this is therefore not a closed activity for foreign ownership under the data supplied here.

The Bali picture is also unusually direct. The record does include Bali's island-wide moratorium rule: Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. But this specific record is not marked as blocked. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason given is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The honest conclusion is narrow but useful: based only on this slim record, KBLI 38211 is nationally foreign-open up to 100%, and it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium recorded here. That does not create any extra Bali percentage, quota, partnership condition, or operational promise; it simply means the Bali-side blocker in this record is not triggered.
editorial.pullQuote: Based only on this slim record, KBLI 38211 is nationally foreign-open up to 100%, and it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium recorded here.

editorial.headline: Organic Compost, Open Nationally, Stopped in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers compost made from organic waste and plant ash; nationally it is TERBUKA for PMA, but Bali blocks PMA registration under its moratorium.
editorial.body:
Code 38212 describes a modest but exact production activity: making compost from organic waste and plant ash, framed in the record as natural organic fertilizer. The scope is not expansive prose; it gives a material input and a resulting product. That restraint matters. A serious reading should not add adjacent waste work, retail work, environmental services, or any licence condition that is not written here. The activity is simply the production of organic compost from the organic-waste and plant-ash inputs named in the slim record.

The scale picture is unusually clean. For Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, the record indicates the activity is open. That does not create a separate story for each scale; it says the listed scale range is open. It also does not give capital thresholds, turnover tests, employee counts, or special scale-based conditions. For registration analysis, the only defensible sentence is the narrow one: this activity is available across the four scales named in the record.

Nationally, the PMA line is also clean. The status is TERBUKA, and the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with the source given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Read plainly, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to that ceiling. That 100% figure is a national figure. It is not a Bali-specific allowance, and it should not be converted into a Bali cap, quota, or partnership condition. There is no second Bali percentage in the record.

editorial.headline: Non-Hazardous Waste Treatment With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 38219 is for operators handling non-hazardous waste disposal and treatment, nationally open to PMA and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 38219 sits in the practical infrastructure of waste management:** the operation of land used for disposing of non-hazardous waste and rubbish, and the treatment of non-hazardous waste through heat, burning, incineration, or other methods. The record also includes organic waste treatment for disposal, and thermal treatment of non-hazardous waste that does not produce electricity. In plain English, this is not a general recycling label and not an energy-generation category. It is the business activity for handling non-hazardous waste and bringing it to disposal or treatment, with the possible output of industrial raw materials or other by-products, but expressly outside electricity production.

That distinction matters because the code is grounded in process and operating responsibility. A company registering this activity is presenting itself as an operator of disposal land, thermal handling, incineration, or comparable treatment methods for waste that the record defines as non-hazardous. The scope is not limited to one business size: the record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. In registration terms, that means the activity can sit across the full range of business scales recorded here, from micro operations through large-scale operators, without the slim record excluding any scale category.

The national foreign-investment picture is unusually clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing recorded at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Said plainly, the national record treats this activity as open to foreign ownership up to 100%. There is no foreign-share cap below full ownership in the data supplied, and there is no extra threshold, licence, capital figure, tax condition, or timeline stated in the record. For a foreign-owned setup, the reliable national reading is therefore direct: this code is open, and the recorded foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%.

Bali does not change that into a hidden local cap. With l4_bali_blocked remaining false, the Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The record’s reason is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule itself blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently, but this record does not mark KBLI 38219 as blocked in Bali. The honest national-versus-Bali conclusion is therefore aligned rather than contradictory: nationally foreign-open, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the Bali moratorium data provided.

editorial.headline: Hazardous Waste Treatment Beyond the Radioactive Line
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 38221 covers nonradioactive hazardous waste treatment and disposal, nationally open to PMA and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 38221 is a serious environmental-services category: the treatment and disposal of hazardous waste, and of specific dangerous nonradioactive waste, before final disposal. The record places both government-managed and privately managed activity inside the scope. Its material range is broad but sharply defined: explosive substances, oxidising materials, flammables, toxic and irritant materials, carcinogenic and corrosive substances, infectious materials, and other preparations dangerous to human health and the environment.

In practical terms, this is not ordinary rubbish handling. The activity includes operating facilities for hazardous-waste treatment and specific nonradioactive waste treatment; treating and disposing of poisonous live or dead animals and other contaminated waste; burning hazardous waste; and disposing of used goods such as refrigerators in order to remove hazardous waste. The slim record also names B3 waste treatment for tank-cleaning activities that are not integrated with B3 collection, treatment, and utilisation, as well as B3 waste landfill activity. The common thread is controlled handling of dangerous material before, during, or at the point of disposal.

The registration picture is unusually wide. The record marks the code as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so it is not framed only as a large-company activity. Nationally, PMA status is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Put plainly: on the national investment record supplied here, a foreign-owned company may register this activity up to full foreign ownership.

Bali does not add a separate ownership percentage in this record, and none should be inferred. The Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says it is not blocked: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. That matters because the same record also states Bali’s moratorium rule: the province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. For this code, however, the supplied Bali assessment does not block PMA registration. The honest national-versus-Bali reading is therefore clean: this hazardous-waste treatment and disposal activity is nationally open to PMA at 100%, and the Bali moratorium record supplied here does not close it.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest national-versus-Bali reading is clean: this activity is nationally open to PMA at 100%, and the Bali moratorium record supplied here does not close it.

editorial.headline: Radioactive Waste Treatment With a Clear National Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 38222 covers the handling, storage, treatment, and disposal of radioactive waste, with national PMA access open and Bali not blocked by its moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 38222 is a narrowly defined activity: the treatment, disposal, and storage of radioactive waste. The record describes a field concerned with radioactive material after use, including waste in a transitional phase, decay during transport from hospitals, encapsulation, preparation, and other treatment of radioactive waste. In plain English, this is not a broad environmental-services category; it is the controlled handling of waste whose radioactive character is the defining feature of the business activity.

The scale profile is unusually broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the classification is not reserved in the data for only one size of operator. A founder reading the code should therefore separate two questions. First, whether the intended activity truly matches the scope: treatment, disposal, storage, transitional decay from hospital waste, encapsulation, preparation, or other radioactive-waste processing. Second, whether the business scale being registered fits one of the listed scale bands. On this record, all four scale bands are present.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is direct. The PMA status is marked TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership field is 100. That means the national record treats the activity as open to foreign ownership up to a 100% ceiling. The cited source for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower foreign-share number in the record, and there is no separate Bali percentage to add beside it. The honest national reading is therefore simple: as a national PMA matter, this activity is open at the full stated ceiling.

Bali needs its own, more careful reading, but not because the record blocks it. For Bali, the status remains OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with l4_bali_blocked set to false. The reason given is: “medium-high/high risk → not blocked by moratorium (verify per address)”. That matters because the moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, island-wide and permanent; this activity is not marked as caught by that block. The clean conclusion is that KBLI 38222 is nationally open to PMA and, on this slim record, not blocked by the Bali moratorium, while the address-level verification caveat remains part of the record itself.
editorial.pullQuote: The clean conclusion is that KBLI 38222 is nationally open to PMA and, on this slim record, not blocked by the Bali moratorium.

The served per_skala (from pp28_sources=['38220']) carries a GENERIC B3 (hazardous-substances) regime — 'Persetujuan Teknis dari Dirjen PSLB3', environmental-remediation funds, kewajiban on 'identifikasi Limbah B3 yang ditimbun' — conductor-verified on the canonical payload 2026-07-18 after a cross-family refuter flagged it. A PSLB3/B3 regime cannot be presumed to govern RADIOACTIVE-waste processing/disposal, which the 2025 revision deliberately carved out as its own class; the radioactive-specific licensing regime is not retrievable from the pinned sources. The dossier's D2 self-confirmation was also protocol-incomplete (neighboring_codes empty). per_skala detached. BPS Vol.2 sha 29f17b3b.

data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup pengolahan barang bekas dari logam dan sisa-sisa barang logam menjadi bahan baku sekunder. Hasil dari daur ulang/pemulihan material barang logam adalah bahan baku sekunder berbagai bentuk, seperti potongan-potongan atau serpihan logam. Kegiatan pada kelompok ini mencakup pemisahan dan pemilahan sampah logam, penghancuran secara mekanis sampah logam, reduksi mekanis sampah logam, pembongkaran, pemotongan dan pengirisan sampah logam, pembongkaran kapal dan alat apung lainnya (ship breaking) dan lainnya. Pembuatan barang logam baru yang menggunakan bahan baku sekunder, barang logam bekas dan sisa-sisa barang logam dimasukkan dalam kelompok yang sesuai pada kategori C.

editorial.headline: Metal Recovery as an Industrial Raw-Material Business
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 38301 covers the recovery of used metal goods and metal waste into secondary raw materials, with full scale access and foreign ownership nationally open.
editorial.body:
KBLI 38301 is not about making new metal products. Its centre of gravity is the recovery stage: taking used metal goods and remnants of metal goods, then processing them into secondary raw materials. The record describes the output in practical terms as recycled or recovered metal feedstock in various forms, including pieces and metal shavings. That makes this code part of the upstream material-recovery economy, where value is created before any later manufacturing step begins.

The operational scope is broad, but it stays within the logic of recovery. It covers separating and sorting metal waste, mechanically crushing it, reducing it by mechanical means, dismantling it, cutting it, and slicing it. The same scope also includes ship breaking and the dismantling of other floating equipment. What matters is the transformation of metal waste and used metal goods into secondary raw material. Once a business starts manufacturing new metal goods from that material, the record says that activity belongs in the appropriate manufacturing category, not here.

On scale, the record is unusually inclusive. KBLI 38301 is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. In plain English, the code can describe anything from a smaller recovery operation to a large-scale material-processing business, as long as the registered activity remains within the recovery of metal goods and metal remnants into secondary raw materials. The scale range is important because the same business description can sit across very different operating footprints, but the defining activity remains the recovery and processing of metal waste, not downstream metal-product manufacturing.

The national foreign-investment picture is clean. The record marks the PMA status as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The Bali picture is also clear, but for a different reason than many founders expect: the record does not mark this code as blocked in Bali. It lists the Bali status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and explains that the OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this record’s Bali reason places KBLI 38301 outside that block. The honest reading is therefore simple: nationally, foreign ownership is open up to 100%, and in Bali the record does not mark the activity as blocked by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is simple: nationally, foreign ownership is open up to 100%, and in Bali the record does not mark the activity as blocked by the moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Plastic Material Recovery With a Clear Bali Registration Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 38302 covers the recovery of used plastic into secondary raw material, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 38302 is the activity of recovering material from used plastic goods. In plain English, it is not general trading, product retail, or a broad waste-management label; the record defines a narrower industrial activity: processing used plastic items into secondary raw material. Its practical centre is the sorting of plastic and the processing of plastic waste into granules, the intermediary material that can return discarded plastic into a production chain.

That scope matters because this code is about transformation, not merely collection. The activity described in the record begins with plastic as waste or used goods and ends with a secondary raw material. For founders, the clean reading is therefore a plastic recovery operation whose core work is sorting and granulation. The Indonesian title, *Pemulihan Material Barang Plastik*, carries the same sense: plastic material recovery, with the emphasis on recovering usable material from goods that have already left their first life.

The code is open across the full scale range shown in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the activity is not framed only for large industrial operators; it can be registered at every listed business scale, from micro through large. Nationally, the PMA position is also straightforward. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives the foreign-ownership ceiling as 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the cited source. In ordinary investor language, the national rule in this record allows a fully foreign-owned PMA structure for this activity.

The Bali picture is unusually clean as well. The province’s moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, but this activity is not marked as blocked. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The honest reading is therefore not a hidden Bali cap or a local-percentage condition; the slim record contains none. For this code, the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling stands, and the Bali field says the activity is not blocked by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: For this code, the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling stands, and the Bali field says the activity is not blocked by the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Material Recovery Beyond the Usual Waste Stream
editorial.standfirst: This activity turns used rubber, textiles, glass, oils and other non-metal waste into secondary raw material, with national PMA access and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
38309 covers a practical, industrial corner of the circular economy: recovering other materials from used goods and waste so they can return as secondary raw material. The record describes work that may produce pieces, fragments or other secondary forms. Its scope is deliberately broad, including used rubber such as tyres, rubber waste processed into granules, used textiles and clothing recovered through mechanical or chemical processing, glass that is crushed, cleaned and sorted, used oil and cooking fat converted into secondary inputs, and food, beverage, tobacco, agricultural, fisheries and other non-metal waste processed for recovery.

That breadth matters because this is not a retail recycling story; it is a processing activity. The registered business is doing the work of sorting, cleaning, breaking down, recovering or transforming waste streams into usable inputs. The code can fit operators handling rubber, textile, glass, oil or other non-metal recovery, provided the activity stays within the record’s central idea: used material becomes secondary raw material rather than remaining waste. The scales open to it are also broad. The record lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar, so the activity is not framed only for large industrial players; it can also sit with smaller recovery operators if their actual business activity matches the scope.

Nationally, the PMA picture is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national record treats this activity as open to a fully foreign-owned PMA structure. There is no basis in the slim record to add a special licence condition, capital threshold, operating timeline or additional ownership qualification. The important point is narrower and stronger: for this specific activity, the national PMA field is open, and the ownership ceiling shown in the record is full foreign ownership.

The Bali reading is also specific. The record does not mark this activity as blocked for PMA registration in Bali. For Bali, it carries the status OK_or_HIGHER_RISK; the stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this activity is not caught by that block in the supplied data. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: nationally open, 100% foreign-owned in the record, and not Bali-blocked by the moratorium field provided here.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is straightforward: nationally open, 100% foreign-owned in the record, and not Bali-blocked by the moratorium field provided here.

editorial.headline: Carbon Capture as an Industrial Service Code
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 39001 covers carbon-capture services for industrial emissions, direct air capture, and temporary carbon handling before transport.
editorial.body:
KBLI 39001 is a service code for the technical act of capturing carbon emissions before they are released into the atmosphere. Its centre of gravity is industrial and engineered: power plants, manufacturing facilities, pre-combustion capture, post-combustion capture, oxy-fuel combustion capture, and direct capture from the surrounding air. The record also places within scope the separation, compression, and temporary storage of captured carbon before it is transported. In plain English, this is not a general environmental consultancy label. It is the operating lane for businesses whose work is to intercept carbon as a handled material in an engineered process.

That distinction matters because the scope is active, technical, and infrastructure-adjacent. The activity is not framed as natural absorption or natural carbon storage, which the record expressly excludes. Nor does the record add downstream claims about permanent storage, credits, certification, trading, or wider climate-finance obligations. The only safe reading is narrower and more precise: the business captures emissions from identified sources or directly from air, then prepares the captured carbon through separation, compression, and temporary storage before onward movement.

On scale, the record is equally direct. This code is open to the Besar scale. That fits the character of the work described: carbon capture is not presented here as a light retail or advisory activity, but as a substantial service category built around industrial sources and capture technologies. A founder registering under this code should therefore think of it as a large-scale operational activity, not as a broad umbrella for every business with a carbon or sustainability angle. The registration story begins with the activity itself: capture, technical processing, and temporary holding before transport.

The national foreign-investment position is clean. The record marks the code as TERBUKA and gives a pma_max_asing of 100, under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In practical editorial terms, that means the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. Bali does not reverse that position in this slim record: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the stated Bali reason is “medium-high/high risk → not blocked by moratorium (verify per address)”. The honest reading is therefore not a hidden prohibition, but an open national code that is not blocked by Bali’s listed moratorium rule, with the address-level verification caveat carried exactly by the record.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is an open national code that is not blocked by Bali’s listed moratorium rule, with address-level verification still carried by the record.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers the injection and permanent safe storage of carbon emissions into geological formations like old oil/gas reservoirs, saline aquifers, coal seams, basalt rock, both onshore and subsea. It also includes related support services performed on a fee or contract basis, but excludes carbon injection for enhanced oil recovery.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, it is 100% open to foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, this falls under a medium-high to high risk classification and is not blocked by the general moratorium on foreign investment, but requires careful address verification by authorities. You may need to demonstrate compliance with environmental and safety standards, and location approvals are a key checkpoint.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: code renumbered.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Aktivitas Penyimpanan Karbon (39002)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: This activity suits foreign carbon capture and storage specialists, climate-tech investors, or energy transition companies aiming to offer emission storage solutions in Indonesia.

editorial.headline: Carbon Storage With a Clean Bali Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 39002 covers geological carbon storage services, open nationally to full PMA ownership and not blocked for Bali at the large-business scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 39002 is a narrow but substantial activity: carbon storage in geological formations. The record defines it as services for exploring, injecting, and storing carbon emissions safely and permanently in subsurface formations. Its terrain is technical rather than generic environmental consulting: former oil and gas fields, saline aquifers, coal seams, basalt formations, onshore sites, and subsea formations all sit within the stated scope. The activity also includes support services for carbon storage when provided on a fee or contract basis.

The commercial shape is therefore closer to specialised infrastructure and field operations than to advisory work. The record names both carbon storage operation activities in geological formations and exploration of target injection zones in geological formations, each tied to a carbon storage licence area. It also draws a boundary around the activity by excluding the use of carbon for oil extraction aimed at improving oil recovery. In plain terms, this is the KBLI for storing carbon, not for using carbon as part of petroleum extraction.

On scale, the record is clear and spare: this activity is open to `Besar` only. That matters because the Bali-side assessment turns on the OSS risk character at that scale. Nationally, the PMA status is `TERBUKA`, with `pma_max_asing` set at 100. For a foreign-owned setup, the national picture is therefore straightforward: the record allows full foreign ownership, with the cited source given as `Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021`. There is no smaller-scale opening in the record, and there is no separate condition to infer beyond the single large-scale entry.

The Bali picture is unusually clean. The province’s moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, but KBLI 39002 is not blocked in Bali. Its Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`, and the reason is stated directly: `OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium`. That means the honest reading is not a hidden Bali cap, a local quota, or a special Bali ownership ceiling. The national foreign-ownership ceiling remains the only percentage in the record, and Bali’s note is simply that this large-scale, higher-risk profile is outside the moratorium block.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is not a hidden Bali cap, a local quota, or a special Bali ownership ceiling.

persyaratan: Persetujuan usaha penanggulangan pencemaran : a. Aspek adminis-tratif: 1) Akta pendirian perusahaan dan pengesahan dari Kementerian Hukum dan HAM, yang salah satu bidang usahanya bergerak di bidang penanggulangan pencemaran 2) Surat keterangan domisili perusahaan 3) Nomor Pokok Wajib Pajak (NPWP) dan 4) Fotokopi Kartu Tanda Penduduk (KTP) penanggung jawab perusahaan b. Aspek teknis: 1) Tenaga ahli meliputi: i. 6 (enam) orang personil operator ii. 1 (satu) orang penyelia (supervisor] dan iii. 1 (satu) orang teknisi pemeliharaanperalatan penanggulangan pencemaran

Memiliki peralatan dan bahan penanggulangan pencemaran paling sedikit terdiri atas: a. Alat pelokalisir (oil boom) sepanjang 200 m (dua raius meter) b. 1 (satu) set alat penghisap (skimmer] dengan kapasitas 10 (sepuluh) m3jjam c. 1 (satu) buah alat penampung sementara (temporary storage) dengan kapasitas 25 (dua puluh lima) m3 d. 1 (satu) pack bahan penyerap (sorbent) dan e. 100 (seratus) liter bahan penguran (dispersant)

editorial.headline: Remediation Work at the Hard Edge of Waste Management
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers specialised cleanup of polluted land, water, industrial sites, oil spills, toxic materials and related decontamination services.
editorial.body:
**39009 is not ordinary cleaning.** It is the classification for remediation and the management of other waste or garbage services, carried out by government or private operators, where the work is tied to pollution, contamination, hazardous materials, or specialised environmental response. The record describes soil and groundwater decontamination at polluted sites, whether handled in place or removed for treatment, using mechanical, chemical, or biological methods. It also covers the decontamination of industrial locations and factories, including nuclear sites and installations, and the cleaning of polluted surface water where pollutants or other chemicals have accumulated.

The scope is broad, but its centre is clear: this is the business of making contaminated places usable, safer, or controlled again. It includes oil-spill cleanup and other pollution response on land, surface water, oceans, seas, and coastal areas. It also includes asbestos reduction, toxic paint and other hazardous-material reduction, other special pollution-control activities, disinfectant spraying, and similar cleaning services. The slim record also names pollution-response companies for waters and ports, which places the activity firmly in the operational world of environmental incident management rather than routine janitorial work.

On registration scale, the record is unusually wide. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the classification can describe anything from a small specialised service provider to a large remediation operator. That matters because the activity itself can range from targeted decontamination work to complex pollution response across industrial, coastal, maritime, or port environments. The available scale field does not create any extra licence, threshold, capital rule, or operating condition; it simply says that all four business scales are open for this classification in the record.

The national foreign-investment picture is clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with the source stated as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali does not add a separate percentage in the record. Instead, the Bali entry says OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The stated reason is: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". So the honest reading is that this activity is nationally open to foreign ownership, and the Bali moratorium does not block PMA registration for it on the record provided.

editorial.headline: Residential Construction, Open at the PT PMA / Besar Tier
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41011 covers conventional residential construction from homes to apartments; 100% foreign ownership is open at the PT PMA / Usaha Besar tier, an IUJK licence is required, and the sederhana/madya segment is reserved to Koperasi/UMKM.
editorial.body:
KBLI 41011 is the construction activity for conventional residential buildings: building them, maintaining them, rebuilding them, and undertaking alterations or renovations. Its practical territory runs from individual homes and temporary residences to apartment blocks, flats and condominiums. The defining feature is the conventional construction method, with the activity framed around the residential building itself rather than a particular development format.

The registration base is broad. The activity is open across the full business-scale range stated in the record: micro, small, medium and large enterprises. That matters because the code is not presented as an activity reserved for one end of the market. A residential builder working on a modest home and an operator engaged in larger housing or apartment construction can sit within the same stated scope, provided the work is conventional residential construction or its maintenance, reconstruction, alteration or renovation.

The foreign-investment position at the PT PMA / Usaha Besar tier is open: 100% foreign ownership, no cap, no local-partner requirement. Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II p.6 (dialokasikan column) reserves a narrower slice — the sederhana/madya residential-building segment, including toko, ruko and warung buildings — to Koperasi/UMKM. That is a segment reservation inside the code, not a closure of the whole activity, and it does not reach the Besar-scale, fully foreign-owned structure. An IUJK (construction-services business licence) is required regardless of ownership tier.

Bali also has a permanent, island-wide moratorium blocking PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. This record does not identify KBLI 41011 as blocked under that rule. The honest reading is therefore neither a blanket prohibition nor an unqualified opening: full foreign ownership is available at the PT PMA / Besar tier, the smaller-scale residential segment is reserved to Koperasi/UMKM, and an IUJK applies throughout.
editorial.pullQuote: Residential construction is open to 100% foreign ownership at the PT PMA / Besar tier; the sederhana/madya segment is reserved to Koperasi/UMKM.

editorial.headline: Conventional Office-Building Construction, Open Nationally and Workable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41012 covers conventional construction, upkeep, rebuilding, alteration, and renovation of office buildings, including offices and rukan.
editorial.body:
KBLI 41012 is a construction activity for office buildings built by conventional methods. The slim record defines the scope around the building, maintenance, and rebuilding of office premises, with the same line also covering alteration and renovation. In practical terms, this is not a general property or office-use category; it is the activity of constructing and working on office buildings themselves, including ordinary offices and rumah kantor, or rukan.

The record also anchors this activity in the construction subclassification language: GT002 and BG002 are both named for office-building construction. That matters because the activity is framed as a construction line, not simply as real-estate ownership, office management, or commercial tenancy. A company using this activity should therefore be describing the work of putting up, maintaining, rebuilding, changing, or renovating office-building assets through conventional construction methods.

On scale, the record is broad. It is open to Besar, Menengah, Kecil, and Mikro. That means the activity is not presented here as only a large-contractor field, even though the foreign-investment reading naturally pays close attention to the Besar scale. The editorial point is simple: the activity can be registered across the full scale range shown in the record, but the investor profile still has to be read through the national PMA status and the Bali-side screening note.

Nationally, the record marks KBLI 41012 as TERBUKA, with a pma_max_asing of 100. The clean reading is that the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Bali does not add a separate percentage in this record. Instead, Bali is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason given is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, but this activity is not blocked on the Bali field supplied here. So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is not a hidden Bali cap; it is a nationally open activity that the record does not mark as moratorium-blocked in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is not a hidden Bali cap, but a nationally open construction activity that the record does not mark as moratorium-blocked.

editorial.headline: Industrial Building Construction With a Clear Bali Opening
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41013 covers conventional industrial building work, nationally open to PMA and not blocked for Bali registration under the record supplied.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 41013 is about the physical making and remaking of industrial buildings.** The record defines it as conventional construction for facilities used by industry: factory and manufacturing buildings, workshops, and industrial plant buildings used for the management and processing of nuclear materials. It also reaches beyond new construction into maintenance, rebuilding, alteration, and renovation of industrial buildings. editorial.headline: A Clear Path for Conventional Shopping-Building Construction
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41014 covers the conventional construction, upkeep, rebuilding, alteration, and renovation of shopping buildings, with national PMA access and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 41014 is about the physical making and remaking of places where commerce happens. The record defines it as conventional construction for shopping buildings: trade buildings, markets, malls, department stores, shops, shophouses, and warung. It is not limited to new construction. The same activity also covers maintenance, rebuilding, alteration, and renovation, so the scope reaches across the practical life of a retail property, from the first structure to later changes that keep it commercially usable.

That breadth matters because the activity is framed around the building method and the commercial use of the premises, not around the particular retail business that may later operate inside. A founder using this code is registering construction work for shopping-oriented buildings by conventional method. The slim record also identifies the construction subclassifications for this activity as GT004 and BG004, which keeps the editorial focus on the construction category itself rather than on the eventual tenant mix or trading activity inside the building.

The scale picture is unusually straightforward. The record marks this activity as open to Besar, Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah. In plain English, it is not written here as an activity reserved only for large contractors, nor only for smaller domestic operators. The registration window in the record spans all listed business scales, which is an important point for reading the code accurately: the same activity description can sit behind very different business sizes, from smaller works to large shopping-building construction.

The national-versus-Bali position is also clear. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling in the record is 100%, with the cited national source stated as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali then needs a separate reading because the record includes a provincial moratorium rule: Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. For this code, however, the Bali block is false. The record gives the reason directly: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. So the honest reading is not that Bali adds a hidden cap or a separate percentage. It does not, in this record. The honest reading is that KBLI 41014 is nationally foreign-open up to 100%, and the Bali moratorium does not block PMA registration for it on the facts provided.

editorial.headline: Healthcare Building Construction, Open Nationally and Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41015 covers conventional construction and renovation of healthcare buildings, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 41015 is the construction code for healthcare buildings built through conventional methods. The record defines it broadly: the activity includes building, maintaining, rebuilding, changing, and renovating facilities used for health services. In practical English, this is the code for constructing places such as hospitals, polyclinics, puskesmas, treatment halls, healthcare service buildings, and laboratory buildings. It is not a medical-service code; its centre of gravity is the physical building work for health infrastructure.

The scope is also precise about sub-classification signals. The record names the health-building construction sub-classification as GT005 and BG005, which keeps the activity anchored in construction rather than in the operation of the facilities themselves. That distinction matters editorially because the activity being registered is the conventional construction of the healthcare premises, including later changes and renovation, not the clinical business that may occupy the finished building.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. KBLI 41015 is open to Besar, Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah. That means the record does not frame this activity as belonging only to a large contractor or only to a small operator; it recognises the activity across the listed business scales. The important constraint for this article is that no extra threshold, project value, capital number, licence, or timeline appears in the slim record, so none should be inferred. The safe reading is simply that the activity is available across those stated scales.

The national-vs-Bali picture is clean. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with the source listed as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the Bali side, the record does not mark this activity as blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason given is explicit: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent; this activity is not caught by that block in the record. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: KBLI 41015 is foreign-open nationally and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Indonesian-owned contractors building educational facilities. editorial.headline: Educational Building Construction Is Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41016 covers conventional construction work for education buildings, from schools and course facilities to laboratories, renovations, and rebuilding.
editorial.body:
KBLI 41016 is the construction code for conventional educational buildings. The record describes a practical, physical scope: building, maintaining, and rebuilding structures used for education, including school buildings, course venues, and laboratories. It also includes changes and renovations to educational buildings. In plain English, this is not an education-service code; it is the construction activity behind the facilities where education happens.

The construction method matters because the record is specific: this code is for conventional building construction. It carries the education-building construction subclassification references GT006 and BG006, and its scope stays inside the built environment of education facilities. A company using this code should be registering for the work of constructing, maintaining, reconstructing, altering, or renovating those buildings, not for operating a school, running a course, or providing laboratory services.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The slim record marks this activity as open to Besar, Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah, so the activity is not framed only for large contractors. It can describe education-building construction activity across the listed business scales, provided the registered activity remains faithful to the scope. That breadth should not be confused with a free pass to add adjacent education or service activities; the record only supports the construction work named here.

Nationally, the position is closed to foreign ownership. The record allocates this bidang usaha to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 10/2021 as amended by 49/2021 (Lampiran II, the *dialokasikan* column), which sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 0%. A PT PMA cannot hold this activity anywhere in Indonesia, at any business scale.

Bali does not add a second restriction here, and that is worth stating plainly because it is easy to misread as good news. The record does not mark this activity as blocked in Bali, and the reason it gives is precise: OSS risk at the large-business scale is medium-high or high — so the province's moratorium on Low and Medium-Low risk activities does not catch it. That is true, and it changes nothing for a foreign investor: the national allocation already closes the activity to a PT PMA everywhere, so there is no Bali route left to unblock.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign-owned setup the honest reading is short: the bidang usaha is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM, so the ceiling is 0% and Bali never becomes the question.

editorial.headline: Conventional Hotel-Building Construction, Without a Bali Moratorium Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41017 covers conventional construction, maintenance, rebuilding, alteration, and renovation of accommodation buildings, with full national PMA openness and no Bali block recorded.
editorial.body:
KBLI 41017 is about the physical work behind accommodation buildings. Its scope covers the conventional construction, maintenance, and rebuilding of structures used for lodging, including hotel buildings, hostels, and losmen. It also reaches alterations and renovations of accommodation buildings, so the code is not limited to new-build projects. The defining point is the method and the asset: conventional building construction applied to places where guests stay.

This is the kind of activity a company would register when its business is the construction-side delivery of lodging buildings, not the operation of the accommodation itself. The record places it across the full scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth matters because the activity is not framed as only a large-contractor field, even though the Bali-side risk note specifically refers to the Besar scale. The record also lists construction sub-classification references GT007 and BG007, anchoring the scope in accommodation-building construction rather than a generic building category.

Nationally, the PMA picture is clean. The activity is marked TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain English, the slim record gives no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That conclusion should stay narrow: it comes from the recorded PMA status and maximum foreign-ownership field, sourced to the listed presidential regulations. Nothing in the record adds a special capital figure, licensing threshold, tax treatment, or timetable, so those should not be implied.

The Bali reading is also direct, but more nuanced than a generic “open” label. Under the record's Bali moratorium rule, every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA is permanently blocked throughout the province. This activity, however, is not marked as blocked: `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the reason given is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” So the honest editorial conclusion is that KBLI 41017 is nationally open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership, and the Bali record does not block it under the stated moratorium rule. The key is not to invent a Bali percentage or a separate local condition; the Bali-side fact is simply that the record marks it as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and not blocked for the reason stated.
editorial.pullQuote: KBLI 41017 is nationally open to full foreign ownership, and the Bali record does not block it under the stated moratorium rule.

editorial.headline: Entertainment and Sports Buildings, Built the Conventional Way
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41018 covers conventional construction, upkeep, rebuilding, alteration, and renovation of entertainment and sports buildings in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
KBLI 41018 is a construction activity code for buildings made by conventional methods and used for entertainment, culture, tourism, recreation, or sport. In practical terms, the record points to the physical work behind cinemas, cultural or arts buildings, tourism and recreation buildings, and sports buildings. The scope is not limited to new construction. It also includes maintenance, rebuilding, changes, and renovation of these entertainment and sports premises.

That breadth matters because this code is defined by the nature of the building and the construction method, not by the business that will later operate inside it. A developer, contractor, or project company using this classification is registering the activity of building or renewing the venue itself. The record also identifies the construction subclassification references for this activity as GT008 and BG008, which keeps the code anchored to the construction of entertainment and sports buildings rather than to event operation, cinema management, or hospitality activity.

On scale, the code is open across the full range listed in the record: Besar, Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah. That means the activity is not presented here as a scale-exclusive classification. A small contractor doing renovation work and a larger company taking on conventional construction of a sports or recreation building both sit within the same stated activity boundary, provided the work remains the construction, maintenance, rebuilding, alteration, or renovation of the relevant building type.

Nationally, the position is closed to foreign ownership. The record allocates this bidang usaha to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 10/2021 as amended by 49/2021 (Lampiran II, the *dialokasikan* column), which sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 0%. A PT PMA cannot hold this activity anywhere in Indonesia, at any business scale.

Bali does not add a second restriction here, and that is worth stating plainly because it is easy to misread as good news. The record does not mark this activity as blocked in Bali, and the reason it gives is precise: OSS risk at the large-business scale is medium-high or high — so the province's moratorium on Low and Medium-Low risk activities does not catch it. That is true, and it changes nothing for a foreign investor: the national allocation already closes the activity to a PT PMA everywhere, so there is no Bali route left to unblock.

editorial.headline: Conventional Construction for Indonesia’s Special-Use Buildings
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41019 covers conventional building work for civic, infrastructure, storage, religious, technical, and monumental facilities, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 41019 is a broad construction classification for buildings that do not sit in the ordinary residential or standard commercial frame. Its centre of gravity is conventional building work: development, maintenance, rebuilding, alteration, and renovation carried out by conventional construction methods. The scope is practical and physical rather than decorative. It reaches buildings used for religion, transport, government, storage, utilities, aviation support, public assembly, detention, data infrastructure, power infrastructure, signaling, towers, depots, pump houses, generator facilities, and even storage buildings for explosive materials. The sub-classification attached to the record is BG009, placing the activity squarely in “Konstruksi Gedung Lainnya” as recorded.

The defining feature is not one particular client type, but the kind of building being delivered. A company registering this activity is positioning itself for construction work on specialized buildings: a terminal or station building, a government building, an aircraft hangar, a data center, a meeting hall, a warehouse, a historic building, a power house, or another building of comparable use described in the scope. The record also explicitly includes changes and renovations to these buildings, so the activity is not limited to new-build projects. Maintenance, rebuilding, alteration, and renovation all remain inside the frame when they relate to the covered building types and the conventional method described by the classification.

On scale, the record is unusually clean. It is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the activity is not framed here as only a large-contractor category; the classification is available at every listed business scale. At the national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. The source field given for that national position is “Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.” There is no lower foreign cap in this record, and no separate condition is supplied that would justify narrowing the national reading beyond the fields provided.

The Bali picture is also clear, but it must be stated carefully. The record does include Bali’s moratorium rule: “Bali province blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA (island-wide, permanent).” For this activity, however, `l4_bali_blocked` is false and the Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`. The reason is given exactly as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” In plain English, the record does not mark this KBLI as blocked for PMA registration in Bali under that moratorium logic. The honest reading is therefore not a hidden Bali prohibition, nor a special Bali ownership cap, but a nationally open activity whose Bali-side record is not blocked by the stated moratorium.

intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Indonesian-owned prefabricated-building contractors. editorial.headline: Prefabricated Building Construction, Licensed at Every Business Scale
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 41020 covers on-site assembly of factory-made building components. It is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM, so foreign ownership is 0% nationwide; the absence of a Bali moratorium block does not create a route.
editorial.body:
KBLI 41020 is not about manufacturing the components themselves. The record defines it as construction activity at the building site, using prefabricated building materials produced by another unit. In practical terms, this is the site-side work of putting factory-made building elements into a finished building structure: precast concrete, steel, plastic, rubber, wood, aluminium, sandwich panels, and other factory-produced materials installed through fabrication, erection, or assembly methods. The construction-work subclassification noted in the record is KP001.

That scope matters because this code sits in the execution phase of a building project. A company registering it is presenting itself as the party that installs and assembles prefabricated building systems on-site, rather than as the producer of the panels, frames, or other materials. The scale profile is unusually broad: the record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the activity is not reserved only for large contractors in the classification record, even though actual project size and operational capacity may differ from one business to another.

Nationally, the position is closed to foreign ownership. The record allocates this bidang usaha to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 10/2021 as amended by 49/2021 (Lampiran II, the *dialokasikan* column), which sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 0%. A PT PMA cannot hold this activity anywhere in Indonesia, at any business scale.

Bali does not add a second restriction here, and that is worth stating plainly because it is easy to misread as good news. The record does not mark this activity as blocked in Bali, and the reason it gives is precise: OSS risk at the large-business scale is medium-high or high — so the province's moratorium on Low and Medium-Low risk activities does not catch it. That is true, and it changes nothing for a foreign investor: the national allocation already closes the activity to a PT PMA everywhere, so there is no Bali route left to unblock.
editorial.pullQuote: The national and Bali readings agree, but not in the direction this page used to suggest: the allocation to Koperasi and UMKM closes the activity to a PT PMA, and Bali has nothing left to block.

editorial.headline: Ground-Level Road Construction With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the building, upkeep, and rebuilding of roads and related ground-level civil works, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
This activity is the practical business of constructing road infrastructure on the surface of the land. The scope is not limited to one kind of road: it includes highways, medium roads, small roads, runway roads, taxiways, aircraft parking areas, and container-yard surfaces. The record also allows the work to include the construction, improvement, and maintenance of road fences or retaining walls, which places the activity firmly inside civil road works rather than a narrow paving-only trade.

For founders, the important point is that this is a construction activity with a broad scale profile. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so it can describe anything from a small registered contractor to a large civil-construction business. That does not add extra licensing facts by itself; it simply means the activity is not reserved, in the record, for one business scale only. The commercial identity is therefore defined by the work performed: building, maintaining, or rebuilding road structures on land.

Nationally, the PMA position is clear. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain English, the national record treats this as open to foreign investment up to full foreign ownership. That is the clean national reading, and it should not be softened into uncertainty or expanded into conditions that are not present in the data.

Bali is also clear, but for a different reason. The record does not mark this activity as blocked in Bali: `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`. The stated reason is that OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium that blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: on this record, the activity is nationally open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked by the Bali moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is straightforward: this activity is nationally open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked by the Bali moratorium.

editorial.headline: Bridge and Flyover Construction With a Clear Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 42102 covers the civil construction work behind bridges, elevated roads, flyovers, and underpasses, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42102 is a civil-infrastructure activity code, not a generic building-construction bucket. Its centre of gravity is the construction, maintenance, and rebuilding of bridge structures, including railway bridges, together with elevated roads, underpasses, and flyovers. The scope also reaches the practical works that make those structures usable and legible: retaining fences or walls, road drainage, markings, and traffic signs when they accompany the bridge or elevated-road work.

That makes this code relevant to operators whose registered activity is the physical delivery and upkeep of these transport structures. The slim record also identifies subclassification references for this activity as ST001 and BS002, both tied to civil buildings for bridges, elevated roads, flyovers, and underpasses. In plain English, the code is for the contractor-side activity of making these crossings, grade separations, and supporting road elements exist, function, and continue functioning.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this KBLI to Besar, Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah scales, so it is not framed here as a code reserved only for one business size. That does not mean every operator will face the same project profile or operational reality; it simply means the record lists all four scales as open. The editorial point is narrower and more important: registration scale should be read from the record, not inferred from the infrastructure-heavy nature of the work.

Nationally, the PMA position is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives the foreign-ownership ceiling as 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the source. Bali does not add a separate ownership percentage in this record. Instead, the Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The province’s moratorium rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, but this record does not mark KBLI 42102 as blocked in Bali. The honest reading is therefore straightforward: this is nationally open to PMA up to the stated ceiling, and the Bali moratorium does not block it on the facts provided here.

editorial.headline: Railway Track Construction With a Clear PMA Path
editorial.standfirst: Railway-line construction, maintenance, and rebuilding are nationally open to full foreign ownership, and the Bali record does not mark this activity as moratorium-blocked.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42103 is for the physical rail corridor itself: building, maintaining, and rebuilding railway lines. The slim record names railway track, underground rail, and conductor rail for trains, and it also allows the work to include rail installation, sleeper installation, and gravel fill for the railway bed. That makes the code less about a transport service than about the civil-construction activity that creates or renews the trackway. The boundary is equally important: the record excludes railway bridge construction, so the editorial center of this code is the rail line and its supporting track bed, not the bridge structure that may carry it.

On scale, the record is unusually broad. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so it is not framed only as a large-company activity in the classification data. A registrant should read that breadth carefully: the scope still describes rail construction, maintenance, and reconstruction, which means the business activity being registered must genuinely sit inside that track-construction envelope. The construction subclassification attached to the record is BS003, giving the activity a specific construction identity inside the record rather than a generic infrastructure label.

The national PMA picture is clean. The activity is marked TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling given in the record is 100%. In plain English, the national record presents this rail-construction activity as open to foreign investment up to full ownership. There is no lower ceiling in the slim record, no additional percentage tier, and no capital or licensing condition stated here, so none should be read into the classification summary.

For Bali, the important point is that the record does not show a moratorium block. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with the reason stated as: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. That matters because the moratorium rule in the same record blocks ALL Low + Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanent. This code is therefore not presented as one of the blocked Low or Medium-Low risk cases for Bali; the national openness and the Bali-side status point in the same practical direction.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Tunnel Construction With a Clear National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 42104 covers tunnel building, maintenance, and repair, with full national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42104 is for **konstruksi terowongan**: the construction of tunnels using boring machines and/or explosives, along with the practical structural work that makes a tunnel real, including formwork, reinforcement, and concrete casting. The scope is not limited to new build activity. It also includes the maintenance and repair of tunnel structures under the water surface, in hills or mountains, and below ground level.

That makes this a construction code for companies whose actual business is tunnel work itself, not a loose umbrella for adjacent infrastructure activity. The record gives one construction subclassification reference, **KK014**, which anchors the activity as tunnel construction. Within the slim record, the scale picture is broad: the activity is open to **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar**. In plain English, the code is not reserved only for large-scale operators in the classification data supplied here, even though the activity itself can involve heavy methods and serious engineering execution.

Nationally, the PMA position is clean. The record marks the code **TERBUKA**, with **pma_max_asing** at **100**, sourced to **Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021**. So the national reading is that foreign ownership can reach 100% for this activity. There is no lower foreign-share ceiling in the record, and no separate capital, timeline, licence, tax, or permit condition is stated here. The editorial conclusion has to stay inside that evidence: nationally, this is foreign-open, and the ceiling recorded is full foreign ownership.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Irrigation and Drainage Network Construction, Read Without Decoration
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the building, maintenance, and reconstruction of irrigation channels and drainage networks, nationally open to PMA and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42201 is a public-infrastructure kind of activity, but the record keeps its scope narrow and practical: it covers the construction, maintenance, and reconstruction of water-channel networks for irrigation and drainage networks. In plain English, this is not a general water business and not a broad civil-engineering umbrella. It is the work of making, keeping, or rebuilding the physical channel systems that move irrigation water and manage drainage. The slim record also anchors the construction sub-classification as BS004, which matters because it frames the activity as a construction-network category rather than a service advisory or trading activity.

The registration picture is unusually broad on business scale. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar, so the category is not reserved only for large contractors in the data provided here. A small operator and a larger construction company can both sit inside the same activity code, provided the activity itself remains the construction, maintenance, or rebuilding of irrigation and drainage networks. That scale range is important editorially because it prevents a false reading of the code as only a heavy-infrastructure lane. The scope is technical, but the record’s scale access is wide.

Nationally, the PMA position is clean: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Rendered in business language, that means the national record allows foreign ownership up to 100% for this activity. There is no foreign-share cap below full ownership in the slim record, and there is no separate national qualification invented here beyond what the record states. For a foreign-owned setup, the national signal is therefore not ambiguous: this is a foreign-open activity under the stated source.

The Bali picture is also clear, but it needs to be read carefully. The Bali moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. This activity, however, is not marked as blocked in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason given is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. That does not create a separate Bali ownership percentage, and it does not add a local quota or partnership condition. It simply means that, on this record, the activity is nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked by the Bali moratorium logic stated here.
editorial.pullQuote: On this record, the activity is nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked by the Bali moratorium logic stated here.
