editorial.headline: Water Infrastructure Construction With a Clean PMA Path in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 42202 covers the civil works behind clean-water capture, treatment, storage and distribution, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42202 is the construction activity behind clean-water infrastructure: the physical civil works that take raw water from intake to treatment, storage and distribution. The scope covers building, maintaining and rebuilding raw-water intake and conveyance structures, raw-water treatment buildings, drinking-water treatment buildings, drinking-water towers, drinking-water reservoirs, clean-water distribution pipe networks, drinking-water tanks and other supporting drinking-water facilities. In plain English, this is not bottled-water retail or general plumbing; it is the civil-construction category for the built systems that make clean-water supply possible.

The record opens this activity across the full scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the code is not framed as a narrow large-project category only. It can be registered by operators at different business scales, provided the registration follows the activity as described in the scope: construction, maintenance or reconstruction of clean-water civil infrastructure and its supporting facilities. The record also notes two construction sub-classification references, BS005 and ST002, both tied to this same clean-water civil-building activity.

Nationally, the PMA picture is direct. The record marks the code as TERBUKA, with `pma_max_asing` at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national foreign-ownership ceiling in this record is 100%. There is no lower foreign-stake cap stated here, and no extra ownership condition appears in the slim record, so none should be added by interpretation.

Bali is also clean in this record, but for a specific reason. The province-wide moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. KBLI 42202 is not marked as blocked: `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the Bali reason states, "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium." The honest reading is therefore neither alarmist nor casual: nationally this activity is foreign-open, and in Bali the record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium because the large-scale OSS risk sits above the blocked risk bands.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally this activity is foreign-open, and in Bali the record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Waste Infrastructure Construction With a Clear Bali Opening
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the civil works behind solid, liquid, and gas waste systems, and the record treats it as nationally foreign-open and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42203 is the construction activity behind waste-management infrastructure: the building, maintenance, and reconstruction of facilities and supporting structures for solid, liquid, and gas waste treatment. Its scope is not limited to one visible asset. The record names waste reservoirs, waste-pipeline networks, urban wastewater networks for domestic and industrial wastewater, disposal and incinerator buildings, final waste-disposal sites and their supporting buildings, septic-system installation services, and waste-treatment units connected to thermal, hydro, geothermal, and other renewable-energy generation. In plain English, this is the civil-construction lane for the physical systems that collect, move, contain, treat, burn, or dispose of waste.

The registration picture is unusually broad by scale. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so it is not framed only as a large-contractor category. Smaller operators may sit within the same activity when the work matches the scope, while larger contractors may use it for bigger waste-infrastructure projects. The construction subclassification attached to the record is BS006, for civil construction of solid, liquid, and gas waste-treatment infrastructure and facilities. That subclassification matters editorially because it reinforces the core identity of the activity: this is construction of waste-system infrastructure, not general environmental consulting, cleaning, transport, or operational management unless the work is actually the construction, maintenance, rebuilding, or installation described in the scope.

Nationally, the record is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership shown is 100%. That means the national record does not impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 is the source cited for that national position. For a founder or investor reading the category, the practical editorial point is simple: the national side does not present this as a closed activity, and the foreign-ownership ceiling in the record is the full 100%.

The Bali side is also clear, but it must be read precisely. For Bali, the status reads OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, while l4_bali_blocked is false. The record’s reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. The moratorium rule in the same record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently, but this activity is not marked as blocked under that rule. So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is not a contradiction: nationally it is foreign-open up to 100%, and in Bali the record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium because the listed Bali reason places the relevant large-scale OSS risk at Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest national-vs-Bali picture is not a contradiction: nationally it is foreign-open up to 100%, and in Bali the record does not block PMA registration under the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Civil Electrical Construction for Indonesia’s Power Infrastructure
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the civil works behind electricity generation, transmission, distribution, utilisation installations, and renewable-energy fields.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42204 is a construction activity for civil electrical infrastructure. In plain English, it covers the building, maintenance, and rebuilding of the physical works that allow electricity to be generated, transmitted, distributed, and used. The record names civil structures for power generation, transmission, distribution, and utilisation installations, including electric-vehicle charging stations. It also reaches solar and wind energy fields, local and long-distance electrical pipeline networks, substations, electricity poles, and towers. This is not a retail energy activity or a general advisory activity; its centre of gravity is the civil construction work that makes electrical infrastructure stand in the real world.

The scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, so the registration lane is not limited to large contractors on the face of the code. That matters because the same activity can appear in very different commercial forms: a smaller operator maintaining local electrical works, a medium contractor working on distribution infrastructure, or a larger business involved in power-related civil construction. The code’s scope is wide enough to follow the infrastructure, but the record keeps the classification tied to construction, maintenance, and rebuilding of civil electrical buildings and networks.

Nationally, the foreign-investment signal is clean. The record classifies the PMA status as TERBUKA, lists a pma_max_asing of 100, and cites Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the source. For a foreign-owned setup, that means the national foreign-ownership ceiling should be read as 100%. There is no partial cap in the record, and there is no separate national caveat stated beyond the source and status provided. The honest national reading is therefore straightforward: this activity is foreign-open at the national level, with the ownership ceiling stated at the full percentage shown in the record.

The Bali reading is also important, but for a different reason. For Bali, the record shows that this activity is not blocked: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The stated reason is precise: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” That means the Bali moratorium rule is relevant background, but it does not block this registration on the record provided. The province’s rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently; here, the record’s own Bali reason says the Besar-scale OSS risk position keeps it outside that block. The result is a code that reads as nationally open and, on this slim record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is that this activity is nationally foreign-open and, on this record, not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Telecommunications Infrastructure for Transport Navigation
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 42205 covers the civil construction backbone behind maritime, aviation, and railway telecommunication facilities, with full national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42205 is a construction classification for the physical telecommunications infrastructure that supports transport systems. Its scope is not general telecom service, content delivery, or network operation; the record frames it as the development, maintenance, and rebuilding of civil facilities used for maritime navigation aids, air-navigation telecommunications, and railway signalling and telecommunications. The examples are concrete: towers, poles, pipes, antennas, earth stations, and similar structures. In other words, this code sits where civil construction meets the communications layer that helps transport infrastructure function.

That makes the activity highly specific. A company using this code is registering a construction activity tied to transport-related telecommunications facilities, including the supporting buildings and structures named in the record. The subclassification attached to the scope is BS008, which reinforces the construction character of the activity. The scale field is broad: the record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the code is not reserved only for a large national contractor in the slim record; the classification itself is available across the listed business scales.

The national foreign-investment picture is clear. The record lists PMA status as TERBUKA and sets maximum foreign ownership at 100%. On the national reading, a foreign-owned company can use this activity code without a foreign-equity cap below full ownership. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the slim record adds a minimum capital number, special licence threshold, implementation timeline, tax treatment, or separate technical permit, so those points should not be inferred from this classification note.

The Bali-side reading is also important, but it is not a separate percentage story. Bali’s moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. For this code, however, `l4_bali_blocked` is false and the Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`. The stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. So the honest conclusion is measured but positive: nationally the code is fully foreign-open, and in Bali this record does not mark it as blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium. The Bali point should be described exactly that way, without inventing a local ownership ceiling or a partnership condition that the record does not contain.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the code is fully foreign-open, and in Bali this record does not mark it as blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Building the Physical Backbone of Telecommunications
editorial.standfirst: A construction activity for telecom exchanges, towers, stations, pipelines, and cable networks, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for Bali PMA registration in this record.
editorial.body:
This activity is about the hard infrastructure behind telecommunications: the construction, maintenance, and repair of central telecommunications buildings and their equipment. In practical terms, the record describes work on telephone and telegraph exchange buildings, transmitter tower buildings, microwave radar receiving structures, small earth-station buildings, and satellite stations. It also reaches into the physical networks that carry communication: local and long-distance communication pipelines, transmission networks, and telecommunication or telephone cable distribution networks built above ground, underground, or underwater.

That makes this a construction classification with a specifically telecommunications character. It is not merely general building work, and it is not only a cable-laying label. The scope ties together the structures that house telecom systems and the network routes that connect them. The listed construction subclassification is BS009, which anchors the activity in the construction taxonomy for central telecommunications construction.

The scale picture is broad. The record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so the classification is not reserved only for large enterprises. A small contractor maintaining local communication cable distribution, a medium business working on telecom transmission structures, and a large operator building or repairing central telecom facilities all sit within the same stated scale universe, provided the activity being registered matches the scope described in the record.

The national-vs-Bali picture is unusually clean. Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the Bali side, the record does not mark it as blocked: `l4_bali_blocked` is false, and the Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`. The stated reason is precise: "OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium". The moratorium rule still matters as background because Bali province blocks all low and medium-low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently, but this record’s Bali conclusion is that the activity is not blocked by that rule. The honest reading is therefore direct: for this code, the record describes a nationally foreign-open activity and does not block PMA registration in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest reading is direct: this record describes a nationally foreign-open activity and does not block PMA registration in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Groundwater Well Construction With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: A construction service code for drilling, excavating, and building groundwater wells, nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is a construction service for groundwater access: drilling or excavating, then building the physical structure of a drilled or dug groundwater well. The Indonesian scope is narrow but practical. It covers the construction work around groundwater wells, including both *sumur bor* and *sumur gali air tanah*. The record also identifies the relevant groundwater-well making or drilling sub-classification references as PL009 and PL005, which keeps the activity anchored in construction rather than water trading, hydrology consulting, or a broader utilities business.

The scale picture is unusually clean. The activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the record does not reserve the activity for one business size only; it recognises the same core activity from small operators through larger construction businesses. In plain terms, this is the kind of code that can be used by a contractor whose business model is the making, drilling, excavation, or construction of groundwater wells, provided the registered business activity stays inside that scope.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. For PMA, the record lists the status as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling set at 100%. That is the national picture: a foreign-owned company can, on this record, hold the full foreign stake for the activity. The source recorded for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the slim record adds a separate threshold, capital test, licensing condition, or timeline, so those should not be read into the code. The solid conclusion is simply that the national foreign-ownership gate is open up to 100%.

Bali adds the important local reading, and here the answer remains positive. The province’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis, but this record is not blocked. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with the stated reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. In practical editorial terms, the honest Bali picture is that this code is not caught by the Bali PMA moratorium on the data provided. So the national and Bali readings align: the activity is nationally open to foreign ownership, and the Bali-side record does not block PMA registration for this groundwater-well construction activity.

editorial.headline: The Utility Works Code for Unclassified Civil Infrastructure
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 42209 covers other utility-related construction work, nationally open to PMA ownership and not marked as blocked for Bali registration in this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42209 is a residual but important construction category: it captures utility-related civil works that sit outside the more narrowly named utility construction groups. In plain English, the record points to the building, maintenance, and rebuilding of other construction works for utility environments, including site and environmental arrangement, residential-area infrastructure, industrial estates, hospital-area infrastructure, and similar settings. It also carries construction sub-classification references for other irrigation, communication, and waste networks, as well as prefabricated civil-building construction work.

That makes this a practical code for contractors whose work is not defined by a single visible asset, but by the infrastructure layer around a place: the network, the prepared environment, the supporting civil works. The record opens it across all listed business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. So the scale question is not whether the code is reserved for large contractors only; the slim record says it can be registered from micro through large scale, depending on the business setup and the way the activity is presented in OSS.

The national PMA position is clean. The record marks KBLI 42209 as TERBUKA, with pma_max_asing at 100, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In founder language, that means the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. There is no partial foreign ceiling in the slim record, and no separate national caveat is stated here. For a foreign-owned company assessing whether the activity can sit inside a PMA structure, the national answer is therefore straightforward: this code is foreign-open up to 100%.

The Bali picture is also more precise than a blanket warning. The record does include the provincial moratorium rule: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. But KBLI 42209 is not marked as blocked in this slim record. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium”. So the honest conclusion is not that Bali imposes a special percentage, partnership, quota, or local cap. The record says Bali is not blocking this code under the moratorium logic described here, while the operative Bali-side reason is tied to the higher OSS risk treatment at large scale.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is not that Bali adds a separate ownership cap, but that this record does not mark KBLI 42209 as blocked by the Bali moratorium.

editorial.headline: Water-Resource Infrastructure Construction: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the construction and upkeep of water-resource infrastructure, open at every stated scale, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Water-resource infrastructure construction is the category for creating, maintaining, or rebuilding the physical systems that capture, direct, store, regulate, or defend against water. Its remit reaches dams and weirs, small reservoirs, water gates and regulators, water-carrying viaducts and siphons, check dams, dikes and flood-control channels, free-intake works, reservoirs, and pumping stations. This is therefore a category defined by built water works rather than by one asset type: it covers both initial construction and the continuing work of maintenance or reconstruction on that infrastructure.

The activity is open across the scales stated in the record: Besar, Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah. That breadth matters because the category follows the nature of the construction work, not one company size. Its definition places the operational focus squarely on construction, maintenance, and/or rebuilding of the named water-resource infrastructure. It is a precise physical remit, spanning flow-control structures, water-storage works, intake structures, flood-control works, and pumping stations.

At national level, the record marks this activity TERBUKA and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. In plain terms, foreign participation is open nationally with full foreign ownership permitted under the stated national source. Bali’s result is not a concealed reversal of that national position. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says that, at Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; it is therefore not blocked by the provincial moratorium. That moratorium blocks PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide and permanently. This activity does not fall into that blocked category on the Bali reading provided.

The distinction should remain crisp. National openness supplies the 100% foreign-ownership ceiling; Bali’s result says the province-wide PMA moratorium does not prohibit this activity. No Bali-specific ownership percentage or partnership condition is stated in the record. The responsible reading is straightforward: this is the category for actual water-resource infrastructure construction, maintenance, or rebuilding, and Bali’s moratorium is not the obstacle here.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali’s result is not a concealed reversal of that national position.

editorial.headline: Building the Framework of Indonesia’s Non-Fishing Ports
editorial.standfirst: This is the construction category for the hard infrastructure of non-fishing ports—open nationally to foreign investment, while Bali’s risk treatment keeps it outside the island-wide PMA bar.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the construction activity for the built fabric of a non-fishing port. It covers new construction, maintenance and reconstruction of jetty and trestle structures, as well as port infrastructure at sea, river and lake locations. The boundary also reaches into the water: coastal or in-water fill undertaken for port-building construction is expressly included. In plain terms, it covers the works that create, restore and maintain the physical framework of a port.

The recorded scope is deliberately wide within that framework. It includes waterways and canals, ports and river-route facilities, marinas, docks and locks; it embraces dredging, normalisation and maintenance of rivers, ports, swamps, lakes, shipping lanes, basins and canals. Such work may be light, medium or heavy. Supporting port buildings, including dedicated terminals, sit within the same activity. The connecting idea is infrastructure linked to a non-fishing port and its waterborne setting.

Registration access is listed for Large, Micro, Small and Medium scales. The activity is not reserved for one business scale, even though its scope reaches from maintenance work to substantial port infrastructure. Nationally, it is marked open to PMA, with a foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. The national PMA source recorded is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021: the activity is open at the national level without a foreign-equity cap below full ownership.

Bali requires a closer reading rather than a blanket conclusion drawn from national openness. The province’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity is not blocked under that moratorium. The Bali record says that at the Large scale its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, placing it outside the moratorium’s stated Low and Medium-Low reach. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The practical position is plain: a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today; the local record treats it as available while identifying its higher-risk position at the Large scale.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, because its stated risk position keeps it outside the island-wide PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Fishing-Port Construction, Open Nationally and Available in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making, upkeep and rebuilding of the physical infrastructure that allows a fishing port to work.
editorial.body:
This activity is the construction brief behind a fishing port’s working edge: building, maintaining and rebuilding jetties, trestles and port facilities, along with related infrastructure of the same kind. Its scope also reaches waterways or canals, ports and river-route facilities, docks and locks. In practical terms, it concerns the built systems that make maritime access, berthing and port operations possible—not a narrow single-structure job, but the construction and renewal of the wider port environment described in the classification.

Registration is open across every listed business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That matters because the activity is framed as a construction category broad enough to accommodate work at different organisational sizes, while remaining specific about its setting in fishing-port infrastructure. The national position is equally direct. Foreign investment is permitted, and the ceiling on foreign ownership stands at 100%. There is no partial-cap wording in the record to soften or qualify that national opening: a foreign investor may hold the full permitted stake.

Bali does not reverse that result. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk, island-wide. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. At the Large scale, its OSS risk classification is Medium-High or High, placing it outside the risk bands caught by the provincial restriction. The Bali position is therefore not a workaround or a conditional reading of a national rule; on the record supplied, the activity remains available for PMA registration in Bali today.

That distinction is worth holding clearly. National openness is not, by itself, a promise that every activity can be registered by PMA in Bali. Here, however, both layers align: the national framework permits up to full foreign ownership, and Bali’s moratorium does not bar this activity because of its stated risk position at the Large scale. For founders considering work on fishing-port buildings and related maritime facilities, the classification offers a clean regulatory starting point: an activity defined by substantial port infrastructure, open across the listed scales, and not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: Here, both layers align: national rules permit full foreign ownership, and Bali’s moratorium does not bar the activity.

editorial.headline: The Civil Works Behind Hydropower’s Water System
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the constructed water-control infrastructure of a hydropower plant, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
A hydropower facility depends on a set of works that guide and control water before and after it passes through the plant. This activity covers construction of the reservoir, intake, control gate, penstock and outflow. Read as a whole, it concerns the built water-management infrastructure of a hydropower project: the reservoir and the structures that receive water, control its movement, carry it onward through the penstock and take it out again. Rather than describing hydropower in general, the scope identifies those precise construction elements. Its place is therefore within the project’s physical waterworks.

Registration is open at every stated enterprise scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The national PMA position is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. Its cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The record presents scale access and foreign ownership together: a business at any of the four named sizes can undertake this activity when its work is the construction scope described here.

Bali’s position is equally clear, though it turns on the province’s risk-based moratorium. That rule permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI across the island. This activity is not marked as blocked. The Bali assessment records it as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and explains that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi — medium-high or high — and is therefore not blocked by the moratorium.

For a foreign-owned business undertaking these hydropower waterworks, the national and Bali readings align. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, the recorded risk position means the cited island-wide moratorium does not block it. There is no Bali-specific ownership cap or partnership condition stated in the record; the local conclusion rests on the activity’s recorded risk status and the moratorium’s stated reach.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership, this activity is not blocked by Bali’s cited moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Coastal Protection Construction: Open Nationally, Viable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making and upkeep of coastal defences, with full foreign ownership open nationally and no Bali moratorium block at higher-risk large scale.
editorial.body:
Coastal protection construction is the practical work of defending shorelines against the forces that reshape them. It covers the construction, maintenance and rebuilding of coastal-protection structures: groynes, breakwaters, seawalls, artificial headlands, beach nourishment, artificial reefs and comparable works. The code therefore addresses a specialised civil-construction activity whose purpose is not simply to build beside the sea, but to shape, reinforce or restore the edge between land and water.

Its scope is deliberately broad enough to follow a protection asset through its working life. A project may begin with a new structure, return later for maintenance, or require reconstruction where an existing defence must be renewed. The listed works also show the range of methods involved. Some structures interrupt or redirect coastal movement; others dissipate wave energy, reinforce a shoreline, replenish a beach or create a protective reef-like barrier. What unites them is their role as coastal-protection infrastructure.

Registration is open across every scale stated in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the activity is not framed as an undertaking reserved only for the largest contractors. The scale categories in the record leave room for businesses of different sizes to register the activity, while the work itself remains defined by its coastal-protection purpose and by the types of construction, maintenance and rebuilding it includes.

With a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, the PMA position is open nationally. In Bali, the picture remains open for this activity today: it is not blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium. The record places the relevant large-scale OSS risk at Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, whereas the moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI island-wide on a permanent basis. That distinction is the essential local reading. A foreign investor considering coastal-protection construction in Bali is not facing a moratorium block under the stated rule; the activity sits outside the blocked Low and Medium-Low risk band because its large-scale risk is classified higher.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor considering coastal-protection construction in Bali is not facing a moratorium block under the stated rule.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Water Infrastructure Works: Open Nationally, Available for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the construction, maintenance and repair of civil water infrastructure and related works, open to foreign investment nationally and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity covers civil water-infrastructure works and comparable civil works not otherwise captured within the classification. Its scope extends across the full working life of that infrastructure: construction, maintenance and repair. That framing is broad, but it is not vague. The activity is defined by its relationship to civil water infrastructure and related works, rather than by a single phase of delivery. New construction and later care for the same class of civil asset can therefore sit within one stated field of work.

The registration is relevant to an enterprise whose stated work includes building, maintaining or repairing civil water infrastructure and the related civil works described by the scope. It is open at every listed scale: micro, small, medium and large. That breadth matters because the defined activity is available to smaller and growing operators as well as larger enterprises; the record does not confine it to one business size. Editorially, it is a construction activity with a complete operational arc: create the infrastructure, maintain it, and repair it when needed.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is open. The record sets maximum foreign ownership at 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the cited source. For a foreign-owned company, the central point is straightforward: the national ceiling does not require the foreign stake to stop below full ownership. This is the national reference point for the activity, and it aligns directly with the stated open status.

Bali does not turn that national opening into a prohibition. This activity is not blocked for PMA registration there, and its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The reason is specific: at the large scale, its OSS risk is medium-high/high, placing it outside Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium for PMA on all low and medium-low risk KBLI. The honest Bali conclusion is therefore clean: the activity remains available for PMA registration in Bali, while the national maximum foreign ownership remains 100%.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest Bali conclusion is clean: the activity remains available for PMA registration in Bali, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%.

editorial.headline: Building Indonesia’s Oil and Gas Civil Infrastructure
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the construction and upkeep of the civil works that carry Indonesia’s oil and gas industry across land, underground routes and offshore waters.
editorial.body:
This activity is the civil-infrastructure end of the oil and gas business: building, maintaining and, where needed, rebuilding the physical structures used by both upstream and downstream operations. Its scope reaches above ground, below ground and into the water. Long-distance oil and gas pipelines and offshore platforms sit squarely within that terrain. The defining work is not the extraction or trade of petroleum itself, but the specialised civil construction that makes those activities physically possible.

The registration is open at every stated business scale: micro, small, medium and large. That breadth matters because the activity describes a class of construction work rather than a single project format. A business may be engaged in the development, maintenance or reconstruction of the relevant civil structures, provided its work remains within this oil-and-gas infrastructure scope. The record also identifies the construction sub-classifications ST006 and BS013, anchoring the activity in a clearly defined technical construction category.

Foreign investment is permitted nationwide, allowing foreign ownership of up to 100%. In Bali, the picture is also open for PMA registration rather than blocked by the province-wide moratorium. The reason is specific: at the large-business scale, OSS risk is classified as medium-high or high, so the activity is not caught by Bali’s permanent restriction on PMA registrations for low- and medium-low-risk activities. That is a meaningful distinction, not a cosmetic one. A business should still read its actual scale and risk position carefully, but the record’s conclusion is plain: this activity is not barred from PMA registration in Bali under that moratorium.

For founders, the practical reading is straightforward. This is a construction activity for the substantial civil systems behind oil and gas operations, available across the stated scale spectrum and fully open to foreign ownership nationally. Bali does not close the door to PMA registration for it; its large-scale risk position places it outside the moratorium’s blocked categories. The opportunity is therefore defined by technical scope and project capability, not by a Bali-specific PMA prohibition.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not close the door to PMA registration for it; its large-scale risk position places it outside the moratorium’s blocked categories.

editorial.headline: Mining Civil Works: Open Nationally, Clear of Bali’s PMA Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: Mining exploration and production infrastructure can be registered at every listed scale, with 100% foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block at the Large-scale risk classification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42992 concerns the civil works that support mining exploration and production: the construction, maintenance or reconstruction of their facilities, with environmental-impact control included in the activity’s scope. This is not confined to a single moment of construction. The record follows the facilities through being built, maintained and rebuilt, while expressly keeping environmental impacts within view. The work is identified through construction sub-classifications ST007 and BS014.

For registration, the activity is open at Large, Micro, Small and Medium scale. That is the full scale picture supplied for this code: not merely a Large-scale construction activity, but one whose stated availability reaches each of the four listed business scales. The scale distinction matters in reading Bali’s treatment, because the Bali reason specifically identifies the OSS risk result at the Large scale. It explains why this activity is not caught by the provincial moratorium described in the record.

Nationally, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain terms, the record sets no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. A foreign investor can therefore register it nationally with ownership up to that 100% ceiling. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is the national PMA position recorded for the activity; it should not be blurred with Bali’s separate local position.

In Bali, the picture remains open rather than blocked. Bali’s PMA moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide and permanently, yet this code’s Bali status is OK or Higher Risk. At the Large scale, its OSS risk classification is Medium-High/High, which is why the record says it is not blocked by the moratorium. For a foreign investor considering Bali, the honest reading is simple: registration is not barred by that moratorium. The national ceiling remains 100%; the Bali record adds no separate ownership percentage or partnership condition. Its Bali position is grounded in risk status, not an invented exception.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, registration is not barred by the PMA moratorium because the Large-scale OSS risk classification is Medium-High/High.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Geothermal Civil Works, Without a Bali Moratorium Barrier
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the construction and upkeep of geothermal facilities, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the province’s moratorium.
editorial.body:
What this activity captures is the built environment around a geothermal project, not a broad label for anything connected to energy. It is specifically construction services for the development, maintenance, and/or reconstruction of upstream and downstream geothermal facilities. The record names the working components: wells, steam-field facilities, and delivery pipelines. Taken together, these are the elements through which geothermal facilities are built, maintained, or rebuilt when required. The activity’s centre of gravity is durable civil works directed at named geothermal infrastructure.

The code is available to Besar, Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah businesses. It does not set out a scale-only version of the activity: those categories may register the same defined construction field, provided the work remains within its stated scope. Development, maintenance, and reconstruction are all included, but only when they concern upstream or downstream geothermal facilities such as the wells, steam-field facilities, and pipelines identified in the record. The classification is precise about the infrastructure it embraces, even as it accommodates businesses at every listed scale.

Nationally, the investment position is clear. The record classifies the activity as TERBUKA and gives a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. That is a full foreign-ownership ceiling, not a capped minority or majority share. For an investor assessing the activity on its national terms, there is no foreign-equity restriction below complete ownership stated in this record. The availability of Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales sits beside that national position, presenting a single activity open across the listed business scales.

Bali needs a separate reading because the province’s rule blocks PMA registration for every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, island-wide and permanently. This activity is not blocked under that moratorium. At the Besar scale, the record gives its OSS risk as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—placing it outside the risk bands named in the Bali rule. Its Bali status, OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, captures the distinction: it is not a low- or medium-low-risk route into the province, yet it is not prohibited for PMA registration by the stated moratorium. The straightforward conclusion is that a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today; nationally the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, and Bali’s moratorium is not the barrier.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Building the Places Where Sport Happens
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 42994 covers the construction, upkeep and rebuilding of sports facilities, from stadiums and pools to golf courses and athletic tracks.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42994 is the construction activity behind the physical settings of sport. Its scope reaches beyond a stadium build: it includes constructing, maintaining and rebuilding facilities such as football, baseball and rugby grounds; motor-racing tracks; basketball, hockey and tennis courts; golf courses; swimming pools; athletics tracks; archery ranges and indoor sporting arenas. The code therefore speaks to the built infrastructure that allows competition, training and public sport to take place.

The activity is open to businesses at large, micro, small and medium scales. That breadth matters because the scope can accommodate both major facility works and the continuing maintenance or redevelopment of existing sporting assets. The classification also records the relevant civil-construction subclassifications as ST009 and BS016, placing the work firmly in the specialist world of sports-facility construction rather than in the operation of sport itself.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward: the activity is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Put differently, the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. The governing reference listed for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the record adds a separate national ownership condition, so the editorial fact is simply the stated ceiling.

Bali calls for a more precise reading, without any cause for pessimism. This activity is not blocked by the provincial moratorium recorded here. Bali’s rule blocks PMA for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities across the province on a permanent basis; however, for this activity the OSS risk at the large scale is medium-high or high. That is why the record gives Bali the status `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK` and states that it is not blocked by the moratorium. For a foreign-owned construction business considering sports-facility work in Bali, the material distinction is clear: the activity remains open nationally at up to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali’s stated moratorium does not bar it on the recorded risk basis.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity remains open nationally at up to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali’s stated moratorium does not bar it on the recorded risk basis.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan pembangunan, pemeliharaan, dan/atau pembangunan kembali fasilitas bangunan sipil pengolahan, seperti pabrik pengolahan bahan kimia dasar; pengolahan pupuk; pabrik plastik dan pabrik pengolahan karet; pengolahan hasil agrokimia; pabrik pengolahan kimia lainnya, termasuk pabrik pengolahan produk farmasi dan petrokimia; pabrik mikroelektronika, produksi mikroprosesor, chip silikon dan wafer, mikrosirkuit, dan semikonduktor; pabrik pengolahan tekstil dan pakaian; pengolahan besi dan baja; pabrik pengolahan lainnya.
Kelompok ini tidak mencakup konstruksi bangunan sipil fasilitas pengolahan dengan sumber radiasi pengion, lihat kelompok 42997

Untuk Kantor Perwakilan BUJKA: a. Merupakan badan usaha jasa konstruksi berbadan hukum di negara asal b. Membayar biaya administrasi perizinan berusaha per jenis usaha sesuai peraturan perundang undangan yang berlaku

Untuk BUJK PMA: a. Penanam modal asing/ pemegang saham asing merupakan badan usaha jasa konstruksi berbadan hukum di negara asal yang dibuktikan dengan: 1) Akta pendirian yang dilegalisasi 2) Sertifikat perizinan bidang usaha jasa konstruksi berkualifikasi Besar di negara asal atau yang sejenis yang dilegalisasi b. Penanam modal dalam negeri/ pemegang saham dalam negeri merupakan badan usaha jasa konstruksi nasional berkualifikasi Besar yang dibuktikan dengan: 1) Perizinan berusaha sub sektor jasa konstruksi 2) Sertifikat Badan Usaha sub sektor jasa konstruksi

Untuk Kantor Perwakilan BUJKA: a. Melakukan perpanjangan Sertifikat Standar sesuai subklasifikasi setiap 3 tahun b. Melakukan Kerjasama Operasi (KSO) dengan BUJKN berkualifikasi Besar dan memiliki klasifikasi/ subklasifikasi sejenis yang tercatat di lembaga pengembangan jasa konstruksi sebelum mengikuti proses pemilihan c. KSO untuk pelaksanaan Pekerjaan Konstruksi atau Pekerjaan Konstruksi Terintegrasi dilaksanakan dengan ketentuan kriteria teknis KSO sebagai berikut: 1) Paling rendah 50% (lima puluh persen) dari nilai biaya pekerjaan konstruksi dikerjakan di dalam negeri 2) Paling rendah 30% (tiga puluh persen) dari nilai biaya pekerjaan pelaksanaan konstruksi dikerjakan oleh BUJKN mitra KSO

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the construction, maintenance, or reconstruction of civil structures for industrial processing facilities. Think large-scale plants for chemicals, pharmaceuticals, petrochemicals, microelectronics, textiles, steel, rubber, plastics, and agrochemicals. Essentially, it’s heavy industrial facility construction.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: At the national level, this KBLI is 100% open to foreign ownership. In Bali, it is not blocked by the moratorium, but it falls under a medium-high to high-risk classification. This means registration is possible but subject to location-specific permits and stricter checks—you must verify the exact address with local authorities before committing.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: code renumbered.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Konstruksi Bangunan Sipil Fasilitas Pengolahan (42995)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs or industrial contractors looking to build or refurbish a major processing plant in Bali, such as a pharmaceutical, electronics, or textile factory.

editorial.headline: Building Indonesia’s Processing Facilities: KBLI 42995
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 42995 covers the construction, upkeep and rebuilding of processing-facility civil works, open nationally to foreign investment and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42995 is the civil-construction activity behind processing facilities: the work of building, maintaining or rebuilding the physical infrastructure in which industrial processing takes place. Its scope reaches facilities for basic chemicals and fertiliser, plastics and rubber, agrochemicals, pharmaceuticals and petrochemicals, as well as microelectronics, silicon chips and wafers, textiles and clothing, iron and steel, and other processing plants. Construction of processing facilities using ionising-radiation sources sits outside this activity’s stated scope.

This is a code for the construction side of an industrial facility, rather than for the manufacture of the products made within it. The emphasis is on the civil works that allow a processing plant to be established, maintained or reconstructed across a broad industrial field. The record makes the activity available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the code is framed around the nature of the construction work, not a single processing industry or a single size of operator.

At the national level, the position is straightforward: the activity is marked TERBUKA for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the record permits full foreign ownership nationally for this activity. That national position is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, and it should be read as the ownership setting for this specific construction activity.

Bali’s position is also clear, but for a different reason. Bali permanently blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI across the province. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The record identifies the OSS risk at the Besar scale as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, placing it beyond the moratorium’s stated Low and Medium-Low trigger. A foreign investor can therefore register this activity in Bali today according to the record; the relevant Bali reading is not an exception to the national 100% ceiling, but a confirmation that the provincial moratorium does not block it.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today because the provincial moratorium does not block it.

editorial.headline: Building Military and Spaceport Civil Facilities
editorial.standfirst: A construction activity open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42996 covers the construction, maintenance and/or reconstruction of civil-works buildings for military facilities and spaceport facilities. Its stated examples include forts, protective shelters and military test centres. The category is concerned with the physical construction of those facilities: creating the built infrastructure, maintaining it, or rebuilding it when required. Maintenance and reconstruction are therefore part of the activity’s stated scope, alongside new construction. The record also identifies the construction subclassifications BS019 and ST011.

Registration is open to businesses at every scale listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That range gives the code a broad business-scale setting while keeping its subject matter tightly defined. What matters is that the work falls within the construction, maintenance or rebuilding of the named military and spaceport facilities. The activity is not framed as a general description of operations within such sites; it is a construction classification for their buildings and related civil-works structures.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100% under the stated source. In plain terms, the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership for this activity. That national position is important, but Bali carries its own recorded screening context, which should be read alongside it rather than assumed to follow automatically from the national status.

In Bali, this code is not marked as blocked by the moratorium. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and at Besar scale the OSS risk assessment is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; the record expressly says that it is not blocked by the moratorium. Bali’s island-wide, permanent rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity’s recorded large-scale risk placement is why the Bali result is not a prohibition. The honest reading is straightforward: it is nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership and is not moratorium-blocked in Bali on the record provided.
editorial.pullQuote: It is nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership and is not moratorium-blocked in Bali on the record provided.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Building Indonesia’s Ionising-Radiation Facilities
editorial.standfirst: This construction and consultancy activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, with Bali not marked as blocked by its PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the civil construction of facilities that use ionising-radiation sources: radiotherapy centres, nuclear-medicine facilities, diagnostic and interventional radiology sites, non-destructive testing facilities, particle-accelerator, radioisotope and radiopharmaceutical facilities, irradiation installations, calibration facilities, and radioactive-substance storage. It also includes construction work and/or construction consultancy for such facilities. The subject is therefore not radiation practice itself, but the built environment and construction expertise required for these highly specialised premises.

It is an activity for businesses delivering the civil works or construction-consultancy element of an ionising-radiation facility. The record makes the activity available at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth matters because the code is defined by the kind of facility being built or advised on, rather than by a single project size. A company’s work may sit in the design, advisory, or construction dimension of a radiotherapy, irradiation, calibration, or radioactive-storage facility, provided it remains within that stated scope.

Nationally, the position is direct: the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical editorial terms, the national framework does not reserve a portion of ownership for an Indonesian shareholder under this record. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national openness should be read alongside, rather than confused with, Bali’s separate PMA screening context.

For Bali, the record does not mark this activity as blocked. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, but this record notes that at the Besar scale the OSS risk classification is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. On the information supplied, that places the activity outside the moratorium block: a foreign investor may register it in Bali, rather than being turned away simply because the business is PMA. The important distinction is a narrow one—national ownership openness remains 100%, while Bali’s stated outcome is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK because the relevant Besar-scale risk classification is not within the moratorium’s barred categories.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor may register this activity in Bali because the record does not place it within the moratorium’s barred risk categories.

persyaratan: Standar Penetapan Kemampuan Badan Usaha Jasa Konstruksi /Sertifikat Badan Usaha (SBU) Subklasifikasi: BS007

Untuk Kantor Perwakilan BUJKA: a. Merupakan badan usaha jasa konstruksi berbadan hukum di negara asal b. Membayar biaya administrasi perizinan berusaha per jenis usaha sesuai peraturan perundang-undangan yang berlaku

Untuk BUJK PMA: a. Penanam modal asing/ pemegang saham asing merupakan badan usaha jasa konstruksi berbadan hukum di negara asal yang dibuktikan dengan: 1) Akta pendirian yang dilegalisasi 2) Sertifikat perizinan bidang usaha jasa konstruksi berkualifikasi Besar di negara asal atau yang sejenis yang dilegalisasi b. Penanam modal dalam negeri/ pemegang saham dalam negeri merupakan badan usaha jasa konstruksi nasional berkualifikasi Besar yang dibuktikan dengan: 1) Perizinan berusaha subsektor jasa konstruksi 2) Sertifikat Badan Usaha subsektor jasa konstruksi
kewajiban: Menyampaikan Laporan Kegiatan Usaha Tahunan
Melaksanakan ketentuan dalam peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang jasa konstruksi

Untuk Kantor Perwakilan BUJKA: a. Melakukan perpanjangan Sertifikat Standar sesuai subklasifikasi setiap 3 tahun b. Melakukan Kerja Sama Operasi (KSO) dengan BUJKN berkualifikasi Besar dan memiliki klasifikasi/ subklasifikasi sejenis yang tercatat di lembaga pengembangan jasa konstruksi sebelum mengikuti proses pemilihan c. KSO untuk pelaksanaan Pekerjaan Konstruksi atau Pekerjaan Konstruksi Terintegrasi dilaksanakan dengan ketentuan kriteria teknis KSO sebagai berikut: 1) Paling rendah 50% (lima puluh persen) dari nilai biaya pekerjaan konstruksi dikerjakan di dalam negeri 2) Paling rendah 30% (tiga puluh persen) dari nilai biaya pekerjaan pelaksanaan konstruksi dikerjakan oleh BUJKN mitra KSO d. KSO untuk pelaksanaan Jasa Konsultansi Konstruksi dilaksanakan dengan ketentuan kriteria teknis KSO sebagai berikut: 1) Seluruh pekerjaan jasa Konsultansi Konstruksi dilakukan di dalam negeri 2) Paling sedikit 50% (lima puluh persen) dari nilai pekerjaan jasa Konsultansi Konstruksi dikerjakan oleh BUJKN mitra KSO

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers building civil structures for nuclear reactors, whether for power generation, scientific research, or the production of radioisotopes and radiopharmaceuticals. It includes all construction work directly tied to the reactor facility itself, not just general site development.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is 100% open to foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, it is not blocked by the current moratorium, but it is classified as higher risk, meaning registration is possible yet subjected to elevated scrutiny. You will likely need site-specific approvals, and the process will intensively verify the physical address and compliance with zoning, safety, and environmental requirements before the license is issued.

editorial.headline: Building Indonesia’s Nuclear Reactor Civil Works
editorial.standfirst: This large-scale construction activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the civil construction of nuclear reactor facilities: reactors for energy, for research and testing, and for the production of radioisotopes and radiopharmaceuticals. It also encompasses micro power-reactor operations up to 30 MWt (up to 10 MWe), and small power-reactor operations above 30 MWt up to 1,000 MWt (above 10 MWe up to 300 MWe). The subject is therefore a highly specific construction field, defined by the physical reactor infrastructure and the purposes those reactors serve.

The registration route is open at the Large scale. That matters because the record does not present this as a small or medium-scale activity: its stated scale is Besar, or Large. For a founder or investor assessing the activity, that is the relevant commercial frame supplied by the classification record—civil construction in the nuclear-reactor context, undertaken at Large scale.

Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA, or open, to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. For the country as a whole, the record authorises complete foreign ownership at the national level. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national position should be read directly, rather than softened into a generic assumption that a specialised infrastructure activity must be closed or partially restricted: the record says it is open, and it gives the foreign-ownership ceiling as 100%.

Bali does not change that conclusion into a prohibition for this activity. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities island-wide, but this Large-scale activity is assessed in OSS as Medium-High/High risk. It is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. Bali’s recorded status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: the relevant point is not an additional Bali ownership cap or partnership condition, but that the activity sits outside the moratorium’s Low and Medium-Low risk bar. For this code, the national openness and the Bali position align: full foreign ownership is nationally available, and Bali does not block PMA registration on the stated moratorium ground.
editorial.pullQuote: For this code, full foreign ownership is nationally available, and Bali does not block PMA registration on the stated moratorium ground.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.
