editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering wholesale trade in agricultural products from oil-bearing fruit crops, the Bali position is unusually direct: this activity cannot be registered for PMA on the island today. That local outcome does not undo the national setting. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali reaches a different result because its permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities; at the Besar scale, every scope in this entry is recorded as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. The Bali result is therefore a block based on risk class.

The activity itself is tightly defined as wholesale trade in agricultural results from fruit crops that contain oil. Coconuts, oil palm and seedlings of oil-bearing fruit crops are the examples named in the scope. This is the commercial centre of the entry: wholesale dealing in agricultural output tied to those oil-bearing fruit crops. The examples give the category a clear factual boundary without changing its essential character as wholesale trade.

Nationally, the recorded availability spans Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. The entry’s PMA status is TERBUKA, and its national maximum foreign ownership is 100%. Those facts should be read at the national level, where the legal source cited is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. They do not amount to a Bali registration pathway. The record keeps the national ownership setting and the provincial PMA outcome distinct, and that distinction is decisive for a founder assessing an island-based setup.

Bali’s restriction is not a lower foreign-ownership percentage for this activity. It is a prohibition on PMA registration under the province’s stated permanent moratorium for low- and medium-low-risk activities. The record identifies the moratorium in May 2026 and marks the Bali status as blocked by risk class. The honest reading is therefore narrow but important: this wholesale activity is nationally open to foreign investment up to the recorded 100% ceiling, while a foreigner cannot register it for PMA in Bali today.

Its territory is therefore distinct in purpose: the activity concerns living stock moving through trade channels rather than food products. The stated examples give the category its practical shape—fish seed, ornamental fish, pearl shell and sponges—all handled as live aquatic goods in a wholesale setting.

The activity is open to businesses operating at **Menengah** and **Besar** scale. That matters because the code is not framed as a general catch-all for every form of aquatic commerce; it is a defined wholesale activity with a clear non-consumption focus. A business registering it should be able to see its commercial role in that description: trading live aquatic organisms and related stock at the scales expressly listed in the record.

At the national level, the position for foreign investment is straightforward. The code is marked **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%** under the cited Presidential Regulations. In plain terms, national policy allows full foreign ownership for this activity. There is no lower ownership cap recorded here, so the national ceiling is not an abstract signal of openness but the full percentage stated for foreign participation.

Bali requires a separate reading, and in this case it does not reverse the national position. Across the island, the province permanently blocks PMA registration for every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activity. This code, however, is not blocked by that moratorium: at the **Besar** scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Medium-High/High. Its Bali status is therefore **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, meaning a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today rather than being stopped by the provincial moratorium. The important qualification is not a hidden ownership restriction, but the risk position recorded at the large-business scale that places it outside the moratorium’s blocked categories.

It also includes the procurement and distribution of seeds and seedlings, including their sale or purchase across Indonesia’s borders. The common thread is commercial circulation: bringing these goods and inputs into trade at wholesale level.

The record makes the activity available at every listed business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. A business registering this activity should therefore read the scope as a whole, rather than reducing it to timber alone; bamboo, sandalwood, resin, forestry seedlings, wildlife breeding and other forest products are expressly within its stated reach.

Nationally, the position is clear. Foreign investment is permitted for the activity, with foreign ownership allowed to reach 100%. Put simply, the national record allows full foreign ownership of this activity. That openness is not qualified in the record by a lower national share cap, a business-scale exclusion or an additional national condition. For a founder assessing the Indonesian position in isolation, this is an activity open across the listed scales and open to foreign investment up to full ownership.

Bali is the decisive exception. Bali does not allow a foreign investor to register this activity today. At the Large scale, OSS risk is classified as Low or Medium-Low across every stated scope, placing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI activities. The record identifies the moratorium as the reason for the block and ties that block to May 2026. National openness therefore remains real, but it does not create a PMA registration route for this activity in Bali.

editorial.headline: Leather Wholesale: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in leather and imitation leather is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration today.
editorial.body:
At its plainest, this is the wholesale trade in leather and imitation leather. That compact definition is the discipline of the activity: it concerns wholesale commerce in those materials, without a need to stretch the category into a wider story. For a founder, that clarity matters. The activity is identified through the goods themselves—leather and imitation leather—and through its wholesale character. A sound registration narrative should stay anchored there. It is a category with a crisp boundary, and the useful question is whether the intended business truly falls within wholesale trade in leather or imitation leather.

The scale position is equally clear. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That range gives this single activity a broad formal landing place across the listed business scales. It does not change what is being registered: whether the enterprise is Micro or Large, the subject remains wholesale trade in leather and imitation leather. In practical terms, the scale list describes the available registration range, while scope keeps the business description honest. The two should be read together, rather than allowing size alone to define the venture.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is unambiguous: the activity is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is the national position recorded under the cited Presidential Regulations. Bali, however, is a decisive exception for PMA registration. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali record marks it blocked on risk-class grounds, explaining that at the Besar scale the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. Under Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium, all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI are blocked for PMA. The record dates that moratorium to May 2026. This is not a marginal local qualification to a national opening; for a PMA applicant choosing Bali, it governs the result.

The result calls for a clean separation of national and local facts. A 100% national ceiling confirms that foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership at the national level. It does not undo the Bali block. For a Bali-based PMA plan, the relevant conclusion is straightforward: the activity remains unavailable for registration under the province’s permanent moratorium, despite its nationally open status. That distinction keeps the discussion focused on the actual activity, its wholesale scope, the business scales named in the record, and the location-specific restriction that determines Bali’s present PMA outcome.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Agricultural Trade Activity That PMA Cannot Register in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in residual agricultural outputs and live animals is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is a wholesale-trade activity for agricultural outputs and live animals that have not been classified elsewhere. Its territory is deliberately residual: it takes in agricultural leftovers and waste, agricultural by-products used as animal feed, and other plants and plant seedlings not already named. Those examples matter because they explain why the category cannot be reduced to a single crop, feed product or animal. The common thread is wholesale dealing in these remaining agricultural outputs and live animals, within the scope described. It is a commercial classification with breadth, but that breadth is bounded by the examples and by the instruction that the goods are not otherwise classified.

Who can register it? The stated range is the full business-scale spectrum: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. This is not a large-company-only designation in the record; each of those four scales is open to the activity. Nationally, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The consequence is direct: the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity, rather than a reduced foreign share. This national PMA position is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The scale range and national ownership treatment should be read together, but neither removes the separate Bali condition.

Bali demands a separate conclusion, and it is decisive for a PMA applicant. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class), and the activity is blocked for PMA registration there. The reason given is specific: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low on every scope. That places the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium, which blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. This is the point at which the national and local pictures diverge. Nationally, the code is open and the maximum foreign holding is 100%; in Bali, the moratorium prevents a PMA registration for this activity.

That contrast should not be softened into a generic warning. A foreign investor can rely on the national openness as a statement about foreign ownership, yet cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. Nor is the Bali position a lower foreign-equity cap: the record describes a block, tied to risk classification and the moratorium. For a founder considering the activity in Bali, the decisive fact is therefore registration access, not the 100% national ceiling. The clean reading of the record is exact: wholesale trade in the specified residual agricultural outputs and live animals is nationally open to PMA, across all listed scales, but is blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the permanent moratorium.

editorial.headline: Rice Wholesale: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale rice trading is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the central fact is direct: wholesale rice trading cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. That Bali outcome does not change the national classification of the activity, but it does determine the practical position on the island. The activity itself is narrow and clear in scope: it covers the wholesale trade of rice. It is not an editorial shorthand for a wider food business; it is a classification for conducting rice trade at the wholesale level.

Nationally, the activity is marked **TERBUKA** and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. In other words, the national foreign-investment setting allows a fully foreign-owned PMA company for this activity. Registration is open across the listed business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth matters because the classification is not confined in the record to one company size; the national entry makes it available from micro through large scale.

Bali introduces a separate and decisive constraint. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, placing the activity within Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The Bali status is therefore **Blocked (risk class)**: blocked on the basis of its risk class. The moratorium is identified as taking effect in May 2026, under the cited Governor’s letter. For a founder assessing a Bali-based PMA structure, the national permission is real, but it is not an override of that island-wide restriction.

The useful reading is not that the national framework and Bali record disagree; they answer different parts of the same question. Nationally, wholesale rice trading is open to foreign capital, including full foreign ownership. In Bali, the activity is blocked for PMA registration because the recorded risk treatment brings it within the permanent moratorium. Any plan for this activity should begin with that distinction, rather than treating national openness as a guarantee of registrability in Bali.

editorial.headline: Fruit Wholesale: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Fruit wholesale can be fully foreign-owned nationally and operates at every listed scale, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
This activity is the wholesale trade in fruit, expressly including oranges, apples, pears and mangoes. Its scope is deliberately commodity-led: the record defines a commercial fruit category through wholesale trade and names those fruits as examples within it. For a business using the registration, the central proposition is clear—its stated line of activity is the wholesale market for fruit, with a scope broad enough to embrace several familiar varieties. The record places the named fruits together in the same wholesale activity.

The activity is available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That is significant because the record puts the same activity in reach across the complete range of scales it lists, rather than reserving it for a single size of enterprise. The national PMA position is just as direct: the status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In practical ownership terms, the national record permits full foreign ownership. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

That national answer is not the Bali answer. For a foreign investor, this activity cannot be registered in Bali today. The local status is Blocked (risk class), and its stated reason is precise: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk outcome is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. That brings the activity within Bali’s moratorium, recorded here in May 2026. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration, island-wide and permanently. The governing local fact is an outright PMA registration block for Bali.

The distinction is simple, but it should decide the reading of the entry. Nationally, fruit wholesale is fully open to foreign ownership up to the stated 100% ceiling and is available at every listed scale. In Bali, the proposed PMA registration stops at the moratorium because of the activity’s recorded risk-classification position. Both statements are true at once: the national ceiling is real, and it does not displace the Bali block. For a Bali-focused proposal, the local registration status is the decisive fact in this record.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign investor, this activity cannot be registered in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Vegetable Trading: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers wholesale trading in vegetables, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks foreign registration there despite full national foreign-ownership openness.
editorial.body:
This activity is the wholesale trading of vegetables, including spinach, water spinach and cabbage. It is a trading activity defined by the vegetable goods being wholesaled: the record is specific about the examples it includes, and that specificity matters when founders are matching a proposed business to the activity they intend to register. The national position is straightforward. Its PMA status is open, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, meaning a foreign investor may hold the entire business nationally.

The activity is open at every recorded business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth gives the code a clear commercial range, from micro and small enterprises through medium and large operations. For a founder, the useful reading is not that the activity changes character across those scales, but that the same wholesale-vegetable scope is recorded as available across all four of them.

Bali is where the national answer stops being the practical answer for PMA. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali record marks it as blocked by risk class: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk assessment is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across the scope. Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. The block is therefore not a reduction of the national 100% ownership ceiling; it prevents PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium.

That distinction should remain crisp in any planning discussion. Nationally, this is an open PMA activity with full foreign ownership permitted. In Bali, the current PMA route is blocked because of the recorded risk classification and the provincial moratorium effective from May 2026. The apparent contradiction is not one: the national foreign-ownership position and Bali’s PMA registration block operate as separate parts of the record, and both must be read together before treating this activity as available in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, this is an open PMA activity with full foreign ownership permitted; in Bali, the current PMA route is blocked.

editorial.headline: Coffee, Tea and Cocoa Wholesale: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks its registration on the island.
editorial.body:
For the wholesale trade of coffee, tea and cocoa, the decisive fact begins in Bali rather than with the national setting: a foreign investor cannot register this activity there today. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, however, its status is blocked by risk class, creating a clear difference between national openness and the position for PMA registration on the island.

The activity’s scope is direct and specific: wholesale trade in coffee, tea and cocoa. It is a trade classification, not a statement about processing, cultivation, retailing or any other commercial function beyond the wholesale activity identified in the record. That clarity matters. The registered activity should be read through the goods named in its scope and through its wholesale character, without extending it into activities the record does not include.

Registration is available at each stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. At the national level, that broad scale availability sits alongside a fully open PMA position. The 100% ceiling is not a partial foreign stake: it is the national maximum recorded for foreign ownership. The national position is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, and it presents this activity as open rather than subject to a lower foreign-ownership cap.

Bali is the operative exception, and it is not a minor qualification. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is recorded as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. The record identifies the moratorium as effective from May 2026 and attributes it to Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. For a foreign investor considering this wholesale activity in Bali, the honest conclusion is therefore simple: national 100% foreign ownership does not translate into a currently registrable PMA activity on the island.

The stated scope expressly includes margarine and products made from vegetable fats, with non-dairy creamer named as an example. It should therefore be read as a wholesale category that takes in the oils and fats themselves as well as the specifically named vegetable-fat-based products. The wording does not treat margarine or non-dairy creamer as outside additions: both sit within the activity’s stated scope. The commercial subject is the trade in that defined range of goods.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Trade in Agricultural Foods, Drinks, Spices and Seasonings
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium means it cannot be registered there today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46319 concerns the wholesale trade in other food and beverage products of agricultural origin. Its stated scope expressly includes seasoning plants and spices, placing these products at the centre of the activity’s commercial description. The operative language is wholesale trade: the record defines a business activity built around wholesale dealing in that category of agricultural food and drink. It does not provide a broader catalogue, so the stated examples are the clearest guide to what belongs within the classification. Seasoning plants and spices are the concrete examples supplied to make the category legible.

The code is open to registrations at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. On the national investment position, it is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 are the sources listed for that position. The result is unambiguous at national level: foreign investment may hold the activity up to the stated full ceiling. That national conclusion is an ownership setting, not a Bali registration guarantee; it answers the national ceiling for foreign participation, while a regional rule can still decide PMA registrability in Bali.

Bali is where a founder must draw a hard line between national openness and local registrability. The Bali status marks the activity blocked on risk-class grounds: a PMA applicant cannot register it in Bali today. The reason is given in operational terms. At Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah — Low or Medium-Low risk — and Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium blocks registrations in those risk bands. The record ties that block to May 13, 2026.

Someone reading only the national status could correctly see an activity open to 100% foreign ownership and still reach the wrong conclusion for Bali. The accurate reading holds both facts together: nationally the activity is open to PMA, while in Bali the moratorium blocks a PMA registration because of the specified risk treatment at the stated scale. For any Bali plan, that local block is the controlling fact.

editorial.headline: Beef Wholesale: Nationally Open, but Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale beef and processed beef, including preserved beef, is nationally open to full foreign ownership—but Bali’s risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity covers wholesale trade in beef and processed beef, including preserved beef. The scope does not treat processed beef as an afterthought; it names it directly, alongside beef that has been preserved. The practical reading is narrow but complete: this is a product-focused wholesale activity centred on the listed beef forms. No broader statement is necessary; the listed products establish the description.

The scale position is unusually clear. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises, so the formal scale field does not confine the activity to a single size of operation. That matters in reading the foreign-investment position: nationally, the activity is open to PMA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national record permits full foreign ownership for the activity. The national source cited for that treatment is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. These points answer different questions—what is in scope, which scales are open, and how much foreign ownership is permitted—but together they describe a nationally open registration picture.

Bali changes the result decisively. Today, a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali. The Bali entry is blocked by risk class, not by a lower Bali ownership ceiling. Its stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s rule, as supplied in the record, is island-wide and permanent: it blocks PMA for activities captured by those Low and Medium-Low classifications. This activity is therefore caught by the Bali moratorium. The record identifies that moratorium with May 13, 2026, and cites Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.

Someone assessing this activity needs to hold both facts at once. Nationally, its PMA status is open and full foreign ownership is permitted. In Bali, the same activity has no current PMA registration path because of the moratorium and the risk classification stated in the record. The scale list should not be mistaken for a Bali exemption: even though the activity is listed for Mikro through Besar nationally, the Bali reason expressly points to the Besar-scale classification across every scope. The result is direct. Bali presents a registration block for PMA, not a Bali-specific percentage or partnership route.

editorial.headline: Chicken Wholesale Has a National Opening—and a Bali Stop
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale chicken and processed chicken meat is nationally open to PMA, but foreign investors cannot register it in Bali under the province’s permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering Bali, the answer is direct: this activity cannot be registered there for PMA today. That finding sits beside—not against—a nationally open position. At national level, the record marks the activity TERBUKA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. The point is therefore not that wholesale chicken trade is off-limits to foreign capital in Indonesia. It is that the national opening does not override the Bali registration outcome set out for this activity.

The activity itself is specific and commercial: wholesale trade in chicken meat and processed chicken meat, including preserved chicken meat. It concerns the wholesale movement of those products, keeping both processed and preserved chicken meat within the stated scope. That inclusion gives the classification a clear commercial perimeter: it is not limited to fresh chicken meat alone, but expressly encompasses the processed and preserved forms named in the record. The description is concise, yet it establishes a coherent wholesale activity rather than a loose collection of food-related business lines.

Businesses may register this activity at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, or Besar scale. That breadth is worth reading plainly: the record does not confine the activity to one size of enterprise. It makes the classification available across the four named scales, from Mikro through Besar, for businesses whose activity falls within the stated wholesale scope. The scale entry answers the basic registration-position question without adding conditions that the record does not provide.

In Bali, however, the result changes decisively for PMA. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk to every scope in the record. Bali’s stated rule permanently blocks PMA registration, island-wide, for all KBLI assessed at Low or Medium-Low risk. On 13 May 2026, this activity was therefore blocked by that Bali moratorium, with the status Blocked (risk class). Nationally, the record permits a 100% foreign stake, but a foreign investor cannot register this PMA activity in Bali today. The Bali limitation is a location-specific registration barrier, not a different national foreign-ownership ceiling.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Meat Trade Is Open Nationally, but Not for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in meat and processed meat is nationally open across all listed scales, yet PMA registration for the activity is blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
For foreign investors, the defining fact is immediate: this activity cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. That Bali result does not erase the national classification. Nationally, it is open to PMA and carries a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The activity itself is wholesale trade in meat and other processed meat, including other preserved meat. The record defines the activity through that wholesale trade in those goods.

A business registering this classification is one undertaking that wholesale trade. The record makes the classification available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. The same activity is therefore stated across the full listed scale range, rather than being confined in the record to a single category. This gives the national picture its proper breadth: the classification reaches from Mikro through Besar, while remaining tied to the stated trade in meat, processed meat, and other preserved meat.

At national level, TERBUKA should be taken at face value: PMA is open and the recorded foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That is a national ownership position, not a guarantee of a Bali registration outcome. The distinction is the heart of this entry. National openness, expressed through the 100% ceiling, is real; yet it sits alongside a separate Bali status that must be read on the local record. The national PMA source cited for this position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali is not an ordinary footnote. Its status is blocked by risk class. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Low/Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s stated rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently; the record ties this block to the Bali moratorium recorded in May 2026. National openness is real, but it does not override Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium for the risk class recorded here. For an investor considering Bali, the local answer is unequivocal: PMA registration for this activity is blocked today.

editorial.headline: A Clear PMA Route for Wholesale Fishery Trade in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in fishery products and processed outputs is open to foreign investment nationally and remains available for PMA registration in Bali at the stated medium and large scales.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors can register this activity in Bali today. Its Bali position is not an exception made by ignoring the province’s PMA moratorium, but a result of the risk classification recorded for a large operation. Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment up to a 100 per cent ceiling. In Bali, it is not blocked by the moratorium because the stated OSS risk at Besar scale is Medium-High/High, rather than one of the risk bands the moratorium catches. That makes this an open route with a higher-risk operating context clearly signalled in the record.

At its centre is wholesale trade in fishery products and related processing outputs, not a narrow single-commodity line. The scope takes in food fish, shrimp, crabs, oysters, pearls, shellfish, seaweed, sponges and frogs, as well as processed fishery products. It therefore accommodates a notably varied merchandise mix, from aquatic foods to particular marine and related goods, while holding to one commercial function: wholesale dealing. The inclusion of processed products is important: the category reaches beyond unprocessed items to fishery-derived preparations as they enter commercial trade.

Who may use it is defined by scale as well as scope. The record opens registration to Menengah and Besar businesses, placing this activity in the medium- and large-scale business context. For founders, the practical discipline is straightforward: frame the undertaking around the products actually named and the wholesale role actually stated. Its broad product vocabulary should not be treated as an invitation to blur the business description; the code’s coherence comes from dealing wholesale in these products, including their processed forms, at one of its specified scales. The two stated scales also prevent an overly casual reading of national openness: openness permits foreign ownership, but does not erase the scale labels alongside it.

At the national level, the “TERBUKA” status and 100 per cent maximum foreign ownership establish the baseline. Bali leaves that national ownership position intact for this activity. The province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium applies to all Low and Medium-Low risk activities; this activity is recorded differently at the Besar scale, as Medium-High/High OSS risk. Accordingly, it is not blocked and carries the Bali status “OK_or_HIGHER_RISK”. That wording matters. It does not make the higher-risk classification disappear; it says that classification is precisely why the activity falls outside the stated moratorium. PMA registration is available in Bali because the stated large-scale risk band falls outside the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Egg Wholesale, With Bali’s PMA Door Closed
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to PMA, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks its PMA registration today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the defining fact about KBLI 46325 in Bali is straightforward: it cannot be registered for PMA there today. That conclusion does not change the national classification. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA and carries a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. But Bali applies a separate island-wide, permanent moratorium to PMA registration for every Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI. For this activity, the recorded OSS risk at the Besar scale is Low/Medium-Low across every scope, bringing it inside that Bali restriction. The result is a genuine split between national openness and Bali registration reality.

The commercial subject is wholesale trade in eggs and processed egg products. It is an activity defined by the circulation of these goods through wholesale channels, with eggs and egg products belonging together in the stated scope. That simple description matters: the code’s centre of gravity is the wholesale market for a specific food category. A clear internal description should keep that focus intact—eggs and their processed products, traded at wholesale—rather than allowing the activity to become a vague label for the wider food economy. In regulatory terms, scope is the boundary of what the code says it includes.

The national opening is not reserved for only one end of the business spectrum. The recorded scales open to this activity are Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That gives the code a broad formal scale range for businesses registering it. For PMA planning, the point is equally clear at the national level: the 100% ceiling means foreign ownership may reach the full shareholding position permitted by the record. The national basis cited is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. None of that national position removes Bali’s local PMA constraint.

Bali’s status is Blocked (risk class): blocked on the activity’s risk class. The stated reason is specific: at the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk, and the Bali moratorium consequently blocks PMA registration. The moratorium is recorded as applying from May 13, 2026, across the province on a permanent basis. This nationally open activity is blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: This nationally open activity is blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: Milk Wholesale: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale milk and dairy trade is nationally open to PMA with a 100% ceiling, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for the activity.
editorial.body:
At its centre, this activity is the wholesale trade of milk and dairy products. Its subject is direct and specific: milk and dairy products moving through a wholesale business. For a company description, the useful discipline is to keep the activity anchored to that trade. The record describes a defined commercial field, not an invitation to expand the description with functions, conditions or commitments it does not state. That precision keeps the registration narrative aligned with the activity as recorded.

The field is available to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises. That is a broad scale range: the same wholesale activity is recorded as open from Mikro through Besar, rather than being confined to one size of operator. The labels should be carried through exactly in the registration assessment. They signal the scales named by the record, while leaving no basis here for assumptions about turnover, capital, facilities, staffing or any other thresholds. The activity definition and its scale availability are distinct facts, and both deserve to be stated clearly. Nor does availability across those scales remove the need to assess Bali on its separately recorded terms.

At national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA, or open. The recorded foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 cited as the source. In practical ownership terms, this record states no national foreign-equity ceiling below 100% for the activity. The source line matters: openness and the 100% ceiling are recorded national settings, not conclusions inferred from the subject matter of wholesale trade. It is an important national conclusion, but it is not the whole location analysis.

In Bali, the conclusion is sharper: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA today. The record marks it Blocked (risk class). At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope; Bali’s moratorium, recorded in May 2026, blocks it on that basis. The provincial rule is island-wide and permanent, applying to all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. National openness remains true; it simply does not override the Bali restriction recorded for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not override Bali’s recorded PMA restriction.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Animal Oils and Fats: Nationally Open, Blocked for Bali PMA
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in animal oils and fats is nationally open to PMA at every recorded scale, yet Bali blocks its PMA registration under the island-wide risk moratorium.
editorial.body:
National openness does not decide the Bali outcome. A foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today, even though it is nationally **TERBUKA** for PMA and carries a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is the fact to hold in view from the outset: national access remains real, but it does not override Bali’s recorded island-wide restriction.

KBLI 46327 is the wholesale trade of animal oils and fats. Its scope is restrained and clear, defining both the goods at issue—animal oils and fats—and the commercial level at which they are traded: wholesale. The slim record offers no broader operational catalogue, and it need not. A precise reading stays with what is stated: this classification concerns the wholesale trade in those specified goods. The scope tells us exactly what is named, and nothing in this record supports a broader account.

Nationally, the activity is available at each scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. In other words, the scale field does not limit the activity to one size of enterprise. For founders, this identifies the range of businesses that may register the activity at the national level, from Mikro through Besar. It does not, however, answer the separate question of whether a PMA registration may be made in Bali. The record answers those questions in different fields, and they lead to different conclusions.

In Bali, the local answer is decisive for PMA: the status is **Blocked (risk class)**. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium of 13 May 2026. Under the provincial rule recorded here, Bali blocks PMA for all KBLI with Low or Medium-Low risk; the restriction is island-wide and permanent. There is no Bali-side foreign-ownership percentage stated for this activity, so the Bali result is a block, not a separate stake calculation. The honest conclusion is simple: a 100% national PMA ceiling does not make this activity registrable to a foreign investor in Bali.

editorial.headline: The Wholesale Honey Trade Open Nationally but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This broad wholesale category is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks it because its Large-scale scopes are Low or Medium-Low risk.
editorial.body:
This is a wholesale activity with a sharp geographic divide. At the national level, it is open to foreign investment and carries a 100% maximum foreign-ownership ceiling. In Bali, however, a foreign investor cannot register the activity under PMA today. The decisive fact is Bali’s permanent, island-wide bar on PMA registration for activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. The Bali rationale for this activity cites that moratorium in May 2026.

The activity itself concerns wholesale food and beverage products derived from animal husbandry and fisheries. It is a broad category, intended to take in qualifying trade that has not been set out elsewhere within its classification. The record gives two useful anchors: wholesale honey from beekeeping, and honey collected from forests. These examples keep the centre of gravity clear. The subject is wholesale commerce in animal- and fishery-derived foods and drinks, with honey specifically named as an illustration.

That breadth does not confine the activity to a particular company size. Registration is open across every scale in the record—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. For a nationally registered PMA company, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the stated ceiling is 100%. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In other words, the national entry permits foreign ownership up to its full stated limit; it does not place a lower foreign-share cap on this activity.

Bali reverses the practical answer for PMA registration. The local status is Blocked (risk class), and the reason is unusually direct: at the Besar scale, every scope is rated Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. Under the Bali rule cited in the record, all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI are blocked for PMA, across the island and permanently. So the national 100% ceiling is real, but it is not a route to PMA registration in Bali. It tells you the ownership position nationally; the Bali moratorium determines whether a PMA filing can be made there, and for this activity the answer is no.

editorial.headline: The National Opening—and Bali Stop Sign—for Bakery Wholesalers
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trading in bread, cakes and other bakery products is nationally open to foreign investment, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
This activity is the wholesale trade of bread, cakes and other bakery products: the commercial distribution layer that moves bakery goods through the market rather than their production. Nationally, it is classified as open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That is the starting point, and it is an important one: the national position is not a partial opening or a foreign-share cap, but a fully open ceiling under the cited presidential regulations.

The activity is open across the stated business scales—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. In practical terms, the classification accommodates wholesale bakery-product businesses at each of those registered scales. The scope remains specific, however: bread, cakes and other bakery products are the goods at its centre. A sound registration narrative should keep that commercial focus clear, because the code’s definition is framed around wholesale trade in those products.

For a foreign-owned company considering Bali, the national opening does not settle the question. Bali blocks PMA registration for this activity today. At the Besar scale, every listed scope is assessed in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, placing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The block is therefore not a reduction of the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a Bali-specific restriction on PMA registration.

That distinction deserves to be made without softening it. A foreign investor may see an activity that is nationally TERBUKA and assume Bali follows the same result. Here it does not. The Bali classification is Blocked (risk class), and the recorded basis is the low or medium-low OSS risk profile at the Besar scale together with the moratorium cited as taking effect in May 2026. For founders, the reliable reading is straightforward: national foreign-investment openness exists, yet Bali is not available for PMA registration of this activity under the stated provincial rule.

editorial.headline: Alcohol-Beverage Wholesale: The National Rule and Bali’s Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: This medium- and large-scale wholesale activity is open to 100% foreign ownership nationally; in Bali, its large-scale OSS risk places it outside the permanent PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46333 is the wholesale trade of alcoholic beverages: spirits, wine, malt drinks and beer. The scope identifies the goods, then identifies the business roles attached to them: alcoholic-beverage sub-distributor and distributor. In clear commercial terms, the activity is a wholesale undertaking dealing with those specified beverages through the distributor or sub-distributor roles expressly named in the record. It is not a broad label for alcohol generally; the scope anchors it in wholesale trade and in the beverage categories it lists.

The eligibility is equally specific. The record makes the code available at Menengah and Besar scale, so its stated audience is medium- and large-scale businesses carrying on that wholesale activity. That framing brings the activity, the market role and the scale together: a business is within the record’s description when it wholesales the listed alcoholic beverages as a distributor or sub-distributor, at one of those open scales. No smaller scale is stated in the record, and there is no need to infer one.

Nationally, the PMA setting is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. That is a complete foreign-ownership ceiling: a foreign investor may hold all of the equity under the national PMA setting shown for this code. The source recorded for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The record presents no separate national condition alongside that percentage, so the point should be read plainly: nationally, this wholesale activity is open to PMA at up to full foreign ownership.

Bali is a different jurisdictional check, but the answer here is not a blanket prohibition. That distinction matters because national openness and a provincial moratorium address different parts of the same registration decision. The Bali rule in the record permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities across the island. This code, however, is not marked blocked. The stated reason is specific: at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Medium-High/High, which places the activity outside the moratorium’s Low and Medium-Low range. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says it is not blocked by the moratorium. The stated Bali reason concerns risk and the moratorium, not a separate Bali ownership ceiling. The practical reading is clean: a foreign investor is not prevented by that Bali moratorium from registering this activity in Bali; the relevant national ceiling remains 100%.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, Bali’s PMA moratorium does not close what the national rule opens to 100% foreign ownership.

editorial.headline: The Wholesale Trade Behind Indonesia’s Non-Dairy Drinks
editorial.standfirst: Nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this wholesale activity is nevertheless blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
Wholesale trade in non-dairy beverages is a precisely defined commercial lane. Its scope is the wholesale trade of non-alcoholic drinks other than milk, expressly including fruit nectars, juices, soft drinks, mineral water and packaged water. The category is broad enough to encompass familiar everyday beverages, yet its centre of gravity remains clear: wholesale trade in the listed non-alcoholic products. For an enterprise, the relevance lies in the nature of the products handled and in the wholesale character of the activity.

The activity is open at every scale named in the record—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—rather than being confined to a single enterprise size. In registration terms, it is available to enterprises at each of those listed scales, from micro through large business. The scale picture is therefore broad, but not vague: the activity remains anchored to the specified beverages and to wholesale trade. The range tells a prospective registrant where it may sit by business size; the scope tells them what activity is being registered.

Nationally, the PMA position is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain terms, foreign ownership may reach the full stated ceiling under the national setting recorded for this activity. The distinction between an open status and its stated 100% ceiling is useful: the percentage supplies the precise national extent of foreign ownership rather than leaving it implicit. This national picture matters, but it does not settle the question for a business seeking PMA registration in Bali.

In Bali, the conclusion changes sharply. The activity is blocked because, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low/Medium-Low across every scope and the Bali moratorium blocks PMA registration on that basis. The moratorium is island-wide and permanent, and the recorded reason identifies it as the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026. Accordingly, a foreign investor cannot register this activity for PMA in Bali today. This is not a Bali-specific foreign-ownership cap alongside the national 100% ceiling; it is a registration block. National openness does not override Bali’s registration block. For a Bali PMA plan, that local block is the decisive fact.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not override Bali’s registration block.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Tobacco Wholesale: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Across tobacco products, vapes and smoking accessories, this wholesale activity is open to PMA nationally yet blocked from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46335 covers wholesale trade in processed tobacco products and cigarette flavourings, as well as smoking products and accessories. Its stated catalogue is concrete: kretek and white cigarettes; electronic cigarettes or vapes; lighters, pipes, cigarette-rolling equipment and e-liquid. In plain terms, it is the wholesale classification for a defined mix of tobacco-derived goods and the products used with them. The scope does not reduce the activity to a single kind of cigarette or a single smoking device; it carries both established tobacco products and the listed electronic format and consumables.

The code is open across Micro, Small, Medium and Large business scales. That breadth fits the way the activity is framed: a wholesale undertaking may be organised around processed tobacco, cigarette flavourings, smoking products or the listed accessories, provided it stays within that stated mix. The record is useful precisely because it names what sits inside the activity rather than leaving the description at the general word “tobacco”. A business using this code should therefore read its commercial identity through the items actually named in the scope—cigarettes, vapes, lighters, pipes, rolling tools and e-liquid—rather than treating the title as a loose umbrella.

At the national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is a national ownership result, not a promise about every provincial registration context: it says the code is nationally open to PMA and records a full foreign-ownership ceiling. For a founder, the distinction is important. The national field answers the ownership question for this activity at that level; it does not erase a separate Bali restriction recorded for the very same activity.

In Bali, the answer for PMA registration today is clear: a foreigner cannot register this activity there. The Bali classification is Blocked (risk class) because, at the Large scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, bringing the activity within the Bali moratorium dated May 13, 2026. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. It is a location-specific block on PMA registration in Bali, even though the national PMA position remains open.
editorial.pullQuote: It is a location-specific block on PMA registration in Bali, even though the national PMA position remains open.

editorial.headline: Other Food and Beverage Wholesale: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A broad wholesale category open to full foreign ownership nationally, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46339 covers the wholesale trade of food and beverage products that sit outside the most narrowly defined grocery categories. Its scope is deliberately broad: rice flour, tapioca flour, bakery premixes, caramel, processed honey and shrimp crackers all appear here, alongside snacks, cereals and cereal-based products, whether processed or unprocessed. It also includes soy-based drinks, ready-to-eat food and pet food. The category reaches further into specialised supply, covering nutritional food for babies, children and adults, as well as food additives and processing aids.

That breadth matters because the activity is defined by its wholesale role across a varied food system, from production inputs to prepared consumer goods. A business operating under this classification may therefore be dealing in products intended for baking, specialised nutrition, packaged consumption or animal care, provided they fall within the stated scope. The registration is open at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In practical terms, the national record permits full foreign ownership for this wholesale activity; it does not impose a foreign-share ceiling below full ownership. That openness is grounded in Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021, and it applies to an activity whose commercial range is considerably wider than its short title might suggest.

Bali is the decisive exception. Despite national openness, a foreign investor cannot register this activity for PMA in Bali today. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is classified as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, placing the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide block on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The record identifies the Bali moratorium of May 2026 as the immediate basis for the block. National foreign-ownership permission remains real, but it does not create a PMA registration route in Bali for this activity.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Textiles: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in textiles, batik cloth and household linen is nationally open to full foreign ownership—but Bali blocks PMA registration under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity cannot be registered in Bali by a foreign investor today. That is the decisive local fact about this wholesale textile activity, even though the national record marks it TERBUKA and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. The scope is focused on wholesale trade in products of the textile industry: assorted textiles and fabrics, batik cloth, and household linen—fabrics intended for domestic use. Those examples keep the activity grounded in the merchandise itself. It is wholesale trade in the textile goods expressly named in the record, from general fabric to batik and linen for household needs. National openness matters, but it is only one part of the practical reading.

The classification is available at every scale listed in the record: Micro, Small, Medium, and Large. That broad availability makes it relevant to businesses of different sizes, while leaving the activity’s subject unchanged: textiles, fabrics, batik cloth, and household linen in wholesale trade. At national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA and its maximum foreign ownership is 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 identified as the source. In practical terms, the national ceiling permits a fully foreign-owned PMA for this activity. The key question is therefore not whether national policy admits foreign ownership, but whether the province where registration is sought changes the result.

Bali does change it. Its local status is blocked on risk-class grounds. The stated reason is precise: at the Large scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low on every scope, and Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. For this activity, the cited moratorium dates to May 2026. The result should be stated without euphemism: for a foreign investor, this activity cannot be registered in Bali today. That does not reduce or rewrite the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling; it prevents Bali registration for PMA under the province’s stated risk-based rule.

The national and Bali positions answer different parts of the registration question. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA and can be fully foreign owned. In Bali, it is unavailable to PMA registration because its applicable risk classification falls within the permanent moratorium. That local block is the operative conclusion for a PMA considering this activity in Bali.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Clothing: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale clothing and apparel accessories are nationally open to PMA at every listed scale, but Bali blocks PMA registration under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the wholesale trade in clothing: garments moving through trade channels, including sportswear. The stated scope also includes clothing accessories—gloves, ties, clips and socks. That detail matters. The activity is not confined to garments alone; it embraces the named accessories alongside them. Sportswear sits within the garment coverage, while the accessories are expressly itemised rather than left to implication. Its practical centre is therefore clear and specific: the wholesale distribution of clothing and those accessories.

The registration picture is broad on scale. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses, so the record places it across every listed size category rather than reserving it for a single tier. All four labels are stated in the record, providing the complete scale view it supplies. At national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA and its foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In straightforward terms, the national record permits foreign ownership up to 100% for this activity. That national position is significant, but it is only one part of the location question.

In Bali, the outcome changes. The provincial status is Blocked (risk class), and PMA registration is blocked. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, every scope has a Rendah or Menengah-Rendah—Low or Medium-Low—OSS risk classification; that brings the activity within Bali’s moratorium of May 13, 2026. The moratorium applies island-wide and on a permanent basis, according to the rule supplied with this record. Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, but a foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today. The apparent contradiction is resolved by reading the national ownership setting and the Bali registration rule as separate facts.

Bali’s rule is not a lower local foreign-ownership percentage for this activity. It is a bar on PMA registration under the relevant risk treatment recorded here. The national ceiling remains 100%; it does not override the Bali outcome. A national ownership permission speaks to the permissible stake, while the Bali bar answers whether PMA registration can proceed in that location. For a founder deciding where to establish this activity, the honest conclusion is exact rather than conditional: the activity is nationally open to PMA across the listed scales, yet Bali does not allow its PMA registration under this moratorium.

That does not alter its national standing; it clarifies the practical divide between a nationally open activity and Bali’s separate, island-wide restriction on PMA registrations in Low and Medium-Low risk classes. The activity itself is wholesale trade in footwear: shoes, sandals and slippers. It sits in the commercial layer that moves finished footwear through the market in volume, rather than defining the making of the product or its sale in a retail setting. The scope is therefore direct and recognisable: businesses dealing in footwear at wholesale, with the category expressly encompassing those principal forms of footwear.

Registration is open across the full range of listed business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. At national level, this activity carries TERBUKA PMA status and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. In plain terms, the national framework permits full foreign ownership for this activity. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That position matters because it confirms that the foreign-investment question is not closed at the national level; the constraint arises from the Bali-specific treatment of the activity.

In Bali, the record classifies the activity as Blocked (risk class). At the Besar scale, its OSS risk classification is Low or Medium-Low across every stated scope, bringing it within Bali’s permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The stated reason records that block as applying under the Bali moratorium in May 2026. The result is unequivocal: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a route for PMA registration in Bali for this activity. A founder may read the national position as permissive, but must treat the Bali restriction as controlling for a Bali-based PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Textile Finished-Goods Wholesale: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale of finished textile goods is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration.
editorial.body:
**For a foreign investor considering Bali, the decisive fact comes first: this activity cannot be registered for PMA there today.** The barrier does not come from a national foreign-ownership limit. At national level, it is open to PMA, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. Bali reaches a different outcome because the activity is blocked under the province’s moratorium. This is not a secondary caveat added to an otherwise straightforward national position: it determines whether a PMA registration can be made in Bali. National openness does not create a Bali registration route.

The activity is wholesale trade in finished products of the textile industry. Its stated scope gives that phrase real edges: rope and cordage; textile carpets and rugs; sacks; varied knitted goods; fur goods; umbrellas and parasols; tarpaulins; ship sails; and parachutes. These are the kinds of textile-industry output traded at wholesale, already in finished form. The listed articles show the reach of the activity from ropes and carpeting to tarpaulins, ship sails and parachutes. Each example is named in the scope itself, making the perimeter of the activity concrete.

Who can register nationally? The record opens the activity to Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. That all-scale availability belongs to the national position and should not be read as an exception to Bali’s rule. In Bali, the decisive condition is risk: at the Large scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk. The province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA in those risk classes, and the record connects this activity’s block to that moratorium in May 2026. That is why the Large-scale risk assessment has a broader consequence for the Bali registration result stated here. Hence the clear, two-layer conclusion: a 100% foreign stake is permitted nationally, but PMA registration in Bali is blocked today.

The national PMA position is recorded under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The Bali restriction is separately tied to the provincial rule described in the record, not to a lower national ownership percentage. Neither layer cancels the other: they answer different parts of the same registration question.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Sewing Supplies: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale sewing supplies carry a fully open national foreign-investment position, but Bali’s risk-class moratorium makes PMA registration unavailable on the island.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46415 covers the wholesale trade in sewing supplies: needles, sewing thread and zippers. The category’s scope is deliberately concrete. Its examples identify the things being traded, preventing the activity from becoming a catch-all description for every commercial undertaking connected with textiles or clothing. The relevant business is wholesale dealing in the stated sewing supplies. For registration purposes, its identity begins with that exact, practical inventory: needles, thread and zippers.

Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA. It is open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. The record also admits every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That pairing gives the national position its full shape. The activity is not confined in the record to a single scale, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is not a partial stake. At the national level, founders can read the category as open across those stated scales with full foreign ownership permitted up to the recorded maximum.

Bali produces the decisive qualification. Foreign investors cannot currently register this activity as PMA in Bali. The Bali classification is blocked by risk class. Its recorded reason is precise: at the Besar scale, OSS assigns every scope a Low or Medium-Low risk outcome. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration. The record places this moratorium in May 2026. This is a direct registration block, not a Bali-side adjustment to the national 100% ceiling.

The national and Bali readings should be kept in their proper jurisdictions. Nationally, the record says TERBUKA and permits a foreign stake of up to 100%; in Bali, the moratorium supplies the present PMA outcome. Neither statement cancels the other. editorial.headline: Wholesale Furnishings: Nationally Open, PMA-Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale category spans carpets to medical-facility furniture, open nationally to full foreign ownership yet closed to PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
**A broad wholesale remit.** This activity covers wholesale trade in furniture, lighting equipment, carpets, mattresses and spring mattresses. Its scope runs from furnishings for households, offices and shops to outdoor furniture, as well as furniture for warehouses, churches and medical facilities. It is therefore a single wholesale classification with a notably wide furnishing brief: light fittings and soft furnishings sit alongside larger pieces intended for domestic, commercial and institutional settings.

**Available across the recorded business-scale range.** The relevant registrant is a business undertaking that wholesale trade, and the record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. In plain English, it is available to micro, small, medium and large businesses. The category remains anchored in the same wholesale furnishings scope at each of those recorded scales, giving the classification a coherent reach across the varied product lines named in the record.

**Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct.** PMA status is TERBUKA and the stated maximum foreign ownership is 100%. A PMA business may therefore register this wholesale activity nationally with foreign ownership up to that ceiling. That figure is the national position: it establishes the foreign-ownership ceiling for the activity, but it does not settle whether a particular province permits PMA registration in practice.

**Bali gives a different answer, and it should be stated plainly:** a foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali through PMA today. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every stated scope of the activity. Bali's island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA; the record links this block to that moratorium, issued in May 2026. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not displace Bali's local block. For this activity, nationwide foreign openness and Bali PMA registrability are distinct facts—and in Bali, the decisive fact is the block.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not displace Bali's local block.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Optical Trade That Bali Bars from PMA
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 46430 covers wholesale photographic and optical goods; national PMA openness is real, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks its PMA registration.
editorial.body:
For a foreign-owned company, KBLI 46430 cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. That is the practical starting point, even though the activity is open to foreign investment nationally. The code covers the wholesale trade of photographic equipment and optical goods: the commercial supply of items such as spectacles, binoculars and magnifying glasses. It gives wholesale distributors a defined place when their business is trading these goods in volume.

The scale invitation is broad. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises—Micro, Small, Medium and Large in plain English. This is not a category limited to one size of operator; its reach spans the listed business scales. The important distinction is the character of the work itself: wholesale trade in the specified photographic and optical goods. That specificity matters because the code describes a particular commercial activity, not a loose retail or services label.

At national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. Put plainly, the national setting allows full foreign ownership for this activity. The record traces that position to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It is a clear national answer, and it is commercially meaningful—but it is not the final answer for a company seeking to register its PMA presence in Bali.

In Bali, the status is Blocked (risk class). At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope of this activity. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for activities in those risk bands; for this code, the record identifies the May 13, 2026 moratorium as the blocker. The divergence is structural rather than numerical: Bali does not set a lower foreign-equity ceiling or add a local condition. It blocks PMA registration. A founder can therefore hold both truths at once: nationally the activity is open to 100% foreign ownership, while in Bali it is unavailable for PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity can be nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and still be unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.

intel_2026.baliContext: Pharmaceutical wholesale in Bali requires a PBF (Pedagang Besar Farmasi) license from BPOM — this is separate from and in addition to the standard OSS licensing. A licensed apoteker (pharmacist) must be appointed as responsible technical person. Bali's medical tourism sector (hospitals in Denpasar, Nusa Dua International Hospital) creates demand for specialized pharmaceutical supplies including imported drugs on compassionate use.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Pharmaceutical Supply for Human Use: Open Nationally, Viable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 46441 covers the wholesale distribution of pharmaceutical preparations for human use, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block at large scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46441 is the wholesale trade of pharmaceutical preparations intended for human use. Its scope is broad but specific: drug ingredients, natural-medicine ingredients, cosmetics, quasi-drugs, health supplements, medicines, and medicines made from natural ingredients all sit within the activity when their intended use is human. This is a distribution code, concerned with moving these preparations through wholesale trade rather than describing a retail or consumer-facing activity.

The record identifies two forms within the activity: a Pharmaceutical Wholesaler Branch and a Pharmaceutical Wholesaler. It is open across every listed business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar—so the code does not confine the activity to a single size of enterprise. That breadth matters because the scope combines conventional pharmaceutical products with health supplements, cosmetics, and natural-medicine preparations, while retaining one unifying boundary: each is intended for human use.

Nationally, the activity has TERBUKA status, allowing foreign ownership up to a ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the record places no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this code. The stated source for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national openness should be read as the ownership position for this particular wholesale activity, not as a claim about any other activity or category.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, island-wide, but this activity is not blocked by that moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which is why the record gives Bali the status OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than a moratorium block. For a foreign-owned wholesale pharmaceutical business considering Bali, the honest reading is therefore clear: full foreign ownership is available nationally, and Bali is not closed to PMA registration for this code under the stated moratorium rule; the relevant Bali context is its higher OSS risk at the Besar scale.
editorial.pullQuote: Full foreign ownership is available nationally, and Bali is not closed to PMA registration for this code under the stated moratorium rule.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)
