data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

data.judul: Perdagangan Besar Sediaan Farmasi untuk Hewan
data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup perdagangan besar, termasuk pemasukan/impor, pengeluaran/ekspor, dan peredaran, berbagai bentuk sediaan farmasi yang ditujukan untuk penggunaan hewan, seperti bahan baku obat hewan, kosmetik hewan, dan obat hewan.

per_skala.scope_uraian: Perdagangan Besar Obat Farmasi Untuk Hewan  (eksportir, importir, distributor)
persyaratan: Surat pernyataan memiliki Penanggung Jawab Teknis Obat Hewan (PJTOH) yang dilengkapi dengan pernyataan dari PJTOH, ijazah PJTOH, dan sertifikat pelatihan PJTOH
Surat pernyataan memiliki/menguasai sarana/ peralatan dan tempat penyimpanan obat hewan yang dapat menjamin terjaganya mutu
Dokumen struktur organisasi
Dokumen program pelatihan personel yang mencakup identifikasi kebutuhan pelatihan dan rencana pelaksanaannya
Surat pernyataan memiliki layanan pengaduan konsumen

Dokumentasi sarana: a. Kebersihan b. Pest control c. Area karantina, penolakan (rejected) dan pelulusan (released) d. Area penolakan (rejected) yang berada di lokasi yang terkunci e. Ventilasi dan penerangan yang memadai f. Tempat penyimpanan yang memadai sesuai dengan kriteria penyimpanan obat g. Ruang penyimpanan obat hewan terpisah dengan komoditi lain h. Pallet/rak untuk penyimpanan obat hewani. Alat pemadam kebakaran j. Alat pemantau suhu yang dikalibrasi k. Alat pelindung diri sesuai kebutuhan

Dokumen standar operasional prosedur berupa prosedur: a. Kebersihan ruangan b. Pengadaan/pembelian obat hewan c. Pengarsipan dokumen d. Penerimaan obat hewan e. Penyimpanan obat hewan f. pengeluaran obat hewan g. Penanganan produk kembalian dan kadaluwarsa h. Sistem K3 (Kesehatan dan Keselamatan Kerja) i. Pemantauan suhu j. Pemilihan jasa pest control k. Pengembalian dan penarikan kembali obat hewan (recall) l. Pengembalian obat hewan kepada pemasok m. Pemusnahan obat hewan n. Pengiriman obat dari produsen, pelabuhan/bandara ke customer tanpa melalui sarana penyimpanan perusahaan importir
kewajiban: Menyampaikan laporan ekspor/impor/ distribusi dan kegiatan usaha secara periodik kepada pimpinan instansi sesuai dengan kewenangannya.
Menjalankan kegiatan usaha sesuai dengan persyaratan dan standar yang telah ditetapkan.
Menyampaikan laporan permohonan persetujuan perubahan apabila terjadi perubahan data terhadap izin usaha yang telah terbit.

editorial.headline: Animal Pharmaceutical Wholesale: Open Nationally, Viable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the wholesale movement of animal medicines, ingredients and cosmetics, with a clear national opening and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Animal pharmaceutical wholesale is the commercial circulation of pharmaceutical preparations intended for animals. Its scope includes wholesale trade, import, export and distribution of veterinary medicinal products, animal-medicine raw materials and animal cosmetics. In practical terms, it is the activity for businesses operating as exporters, importers or distributors of animal pharmaceutical products and animal cosmetics—not a retail description, but a wholesale and circulation-facing one.

The activity is open across every recorded business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the record does not confine the activity to one end of the market. A business may be positioned around bringing veterinary preparations into Indonesia, moving them out of the country, or distributing them through the wholesale channel; the same scope also expressly includes raw materials for animal medicines and cosmetics intended for animals. The unifying thread is the trade and movement of pharmaceutical preparations for animal use.

Nationally, the position on foreign investment is unambiguous. The activity is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In other words, the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. Bali does not reverse that position. The province’s standing is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the activity is not blocked for PMA registration by the island-wide moratorium. The decisive Bali detail is scale-specific: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi or Tinggi, placing it outside the moratorium’s stated reach over Low and Medium-Low risk activities.

That makes this an unusually clean national-versus-Bali reading. Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium remains material because it blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI across the province. Yet this activity is expressly recorded as not blocked by that rule. For a foreign-owned wholesale business dealing in animal pharmaceutical preparations, the result is not a theoretical national opening that disappears on the island: the record supports a 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling and confirms that Bali’s moratorium does not bar PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: The national opening does not disappear in Bali: the activity is recorded as outside the island-wide PMA moratorium block.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Stationery: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale stationery and drawing supplies are nationally open to PMA, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering Bali, the decisive fact comes first: this activity cannot be registered there for PMA today. That is not a judgment on the market for stationery; it is the consequence of the Bali moratorium as applied to this activity’s risk classification at the Besar scale. Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA to PMA with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. Bali’s result is different: its status is Blocked (risk class), because the applicable OSS risk assessment is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope at the Besar scale.

The activity itself is wholesale trade in stationery and drawing equipment. In practical terms, it embraces the supply side of notebooks, sketchbooks, stationery and drawing tools: the movement of such goods through wholesale channels. The definition is deliberately product-led rather than a promise about a particular sales format, customer or operating model. That distinction matters in a registration context. The code speaks to an enterprise dealing wholesale in these goods, and its stated scope should remain the anchor when describing the business, rather than broadening it into adjacent kinds of commerce or adding services the record does not specify.

Registration is open at the Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. The record therefore identifies a wide range of business scales for the activity nationally, while keeping the activity itself tightly defined. For an investor, those two statements must be held together: scale eligibility does not erase the local PMA result. A foreign-owned applicant may see a nationally open classification and a 100% national ceiling, but neither converts the activity into a registrable PMA activity in Bali while the Bali restriction applies. editorial.headline: KBLI 46452: Wholesale Trade in Printed and Published Goods
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to PMA, but a Bali-wide risk moratorium means foreign investors cannot register it in Bali today.
editorial.body:
Wholesale trade is the commercial route through which printed and published goods move through the market. KBLI 46452 covers wholesale trade in printing and publishing goods in various forms, with books, magazines and newspapers expressly included as examples. Its subject is therefore the wholesale activity surrounding those goods: a business dealing in published and printed material across the forms named in the record. The definition is focused, but broad enough to encompass more than one kind of print publication within the same wholesale activity.

The activity is open across the full range of business scales listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That gives the code a wide operating frame, from micro and small businesses through medium and large enterprises. For a founder, the practical starting point is to match the registered activity to the wholesale trade in the relevant printed or published goods, rather than treating the code as a general label for the wider publishing economy.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In other words, the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. The reference given for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is the national ceiling for the activity and should be read as such: it establishes the foreign-ownership position at the national level, not a separate local registration outcome.

Bali is where the picture changes decisively. At present, a foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class) because, at the Besar scale, every scope is recorded in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk; the record says this is blocked by the Bali moratorium of 13 May 2026. That moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the national position, but it does not displace Bali’s registration block for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this activity is nevertheless unavailable for PMA registration in Bali today.

editorial.headline: The Kitchenware Wholesale Code That Stops at Bali’s PMA Gate
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 46491 embraces a broad household-goods wholesale trade nationally, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks its PMA registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46491 is a wholesale-trade classification for the practical objects that shape a kitchen and everyday household use. Its stated scope includes cookware such as pots and pans, as well as kitchen equipment. It also reaches consumer electronics—electric toothbrushes, radios, televisions, CD and DVD recorders and players, and stereo equipment. The range continues through porcelain and glass tableware, cutlery including spoons, knives and forks, wooden articles, woven goods and cork goods. What binds these varied products together is wholesale trade: the code gives a distributor a single classification for a deliberately broad basket of domestic and household-facing goods.

The activity is open at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That makes the classification relevant to wholesalers whose product range may run from kitchen and dining goods to consumer electronics and natural-material household articles. The breadth of the merchandise should not obscure the central point of the record, however. This is one defined wholesale activity, and its foreign-investment position has to be read in both the national and Bali settings.

Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In plain terms, the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. That is the national ceiling, but it is not the final word for a company considering Bali. National openness does not override Bali’s block on PMA registration.

For a foreigner seeking PMA registration, the operative Bali answer is direct: this activity cannot be registered in Bali today. The Bali record identifies the issue as class-risk blocking. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The recorded trigger dates to May 2026. This is not a lower Bali foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a registration block for PMA in Bali, despite the national 100% position.

editorial.headline: Sports Equipment Wholesale: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 46492 spans wholesale sports, fitness, outdoor-play and bicycle equipment—open nationally to full foreign ownership, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
For a foreign-owned business, the defining fact about KBLI 46492 is geographical: it cannot be registered in Bali today. This is not because the activity is nationally shut to foreign investment. Nationally, the code is open to PMA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium instead blocks PMA registration where a KBLI is Low or Medium-Low risk. At the Besar scale, every scope within this activity is assessed in one of those bands, so the moratorium closes the Bali route.

The activity itself is a wide wholesale category for the equipment that supports sport, exercise and outdoor recreation. It includes physical-training, gymnastics and athletics equipment such as treadmills, dumbbells and resistance bands. It also reaches outdoor sporting goods—balls, racquets and surfboards—as well as outdoor play equipment including trampolines, basketball hoops and swings. Wholesale bicycles, their parts and their accessories sit within the same frame. The practical picture is therefore not a narrow product niche, but the distribution layer for a varied range of sports and recreation equipment.

The record opens this activity to businesses at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters: the code accommodates the activity across the full scale range stated in the classification, while retaining one coherent wholesale identity. For a national PMA structure, the foreign-ownership position is equally clear. The activity is TERBUKA, and the stated national ceiling is 100%; there is no partial foreign-ownership limit in the record to read into that position.

Bali is the decisive exception, and it should be read as an operating constraint rather than softened into a footnote. Its result follows the risk assessment at the Besar scale, where every scope is Low or Medium-Low risk, bringing the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium from May 13, 2026. National openness and Bali’s block can both be true at once: the first describes the national foreign-investment position, while the second determines that PMA registration for this activity is unavailable in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Musical Instruments, and Bali’s Closed PMA Door
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale musical-instrument trade is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium makes PMA registration unavailable on the island.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46493 concerns wholesale trade in a broad range of musical instruments. Its stated scope includes traditional instruments such as kecapi, bamboo flutes, calung, angklung, kolintang, gamelan, rebab, rebana, tifa and sasando. It also reaches modern instruments including flutes, saxophones, harmonicas, trombones, guitars, mandolins, ukuleles, harps, basses, violins, cellos, pianos, organs, drums and tuning forks. The range is explicit: traditional and modern instruments sit together within one wholesale activity.

The recorded scale access is equally direct. Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all open to this activity. That gives the classification a place for businesses at each of the four recorded scales, without changing the thing being registered: wholesale trade in the instruments within its stated scope. The activity description answers what is traded; the scale listing establishes that it is open across the recorded micro, small, medium and large categories.

At national level, the PMA picture is unambiguous. The activity is marked TERBUKA and its maximum foreign ownership is 100 per cent. In other words, the national foreign-ownership ceiling permits full foreign ownership for this activity, with the record citing Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as its PMA source. This is a national position for this one wholesale activity, and its significance lies in the clarity of that ceiling rather than in any assumed provincial outcome.

That provincial outcome is decisive in Bali. A PMA company cannot register this activity in Bali today. Its Bali status is Blocked (risk class): at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, and the record identifies the Bali moratorium as the reason for the block. That moratorium is island-wide and permanent, blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities from PMA registration; the stated Bali reason identifies it in May 2026. The national 100 per cent ceiling remains the national fact, but it does not remove the Bali block.
editorial.pullQuote: A PMA company cannot register this activity in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Jewellery and Watch Wholesale: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in jewellery, watches and their parts is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
**The trade has a wider remit than finished goods alone.** This activity covers wholesale trade in a range of jewellery and watches, as well as the related parts that make a watch complete. The scope expressly reaches watch casings, straps, frames and timekeeping movements. In practical terms, its subject is the wholesale circulation of those named goods and components: finished jewellery and watches, but also associated watch parts. That is the useful boundary to keep in view. The record defines a wholesale activity with a product range that extends from the visible article to the specific components named within its scope. It does not confine the activity to completed goods alone.

**Nationally, the activity is broadly available.** It may be registered at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scale. It is also designated open to foreign investment, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Put plainly, the national setting allows foreign ownership up to 100% for this activity. The scale availability and the foreign-investment position are separate pieces of the national picture, but together establish an open starting point: it may be registered at every scale named in the record, and its foreign-ownership ceiling is not below full ownership. That is the national position relevant to a foreign investor before Bali is considered.

**That national openness is not the Bali outcome.** A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today through PMA. At the Large scale, every scope is rated Low or Medium-Low risk in OSS. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for activities within those Low and Medium-Low risk classifications. The record attributes this result to Bali’s May 2026 moratorium. The restriction therefore follows the risk result attached to this activity at the Large scale across every scope. It is a firm local registration barrier, rather than a reduction of the national foreign-ownership ceiling. The national figure remains 100%, but it does not override Bali’s PMA block.

**The point for a proposed Bali registration is clarity, not interpretation.** The code’s national status is open; Bali’s status is blocked by risk class. Both statements are true, and neither should be used to blur the other. A reading that stops at the national ceiling misses the provincial moratorium. A reading that begins and ends with Bali does not change the national description of the activity or its 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. For this particular wholesale trade, the honest picture is a national opening alongside a permanent Bali block on PMA registration, rooted in the Low and Medium-Low risk outcome recorded at the Large scale.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Toy Wholesale Activity That Bali Blocks for PMA
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in toys and play equipment is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s moratorium blocks PMA registration today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering this activity, a foreigner cannot register it through PMA in Bali today. At the national level, the activity is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Bali applies a different, island-wide rule to the risk class recorded at Large scale. The OSS assessment for every scope is Low or Medium-Low risk; the province’s moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. That contrast should be read exactly as the record states it: a 100% national ceiling alongside a Bali-side PMA block.

This is the wholesale trade in play equipment and toys: traditional and modern formats, from board games and dolls to card games, model kits, electronic games and video-game consoles. The defining commercial position is wholesale, rather than the particular kind of play product; the category gathers these ranges under one trading activity. That breadth gives the description a clear centre of gravity: supplying the toy and game trade across formats, not merely handling a single product type. The record names both traditional and contemporary forms, placing familiar physical playthings and electronic gaming hardware within the stated wholesale scope.

Registration is open across the full scale range listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. This is not a category reserved for one company size. A small distributor and a large-scale wholesaler fall within the same stated range of eligible scales, so the commercial description does not turn on an invented revenue threshold, headcount test or capital figure. Scale remains important to the Bali result, however: the record identifies the OSS risk assessment at Besar scale as Low or Medium-Low across every scope, which is the stated basis of the block there.

The two positions should be read together, without allowing one to erase the other. National openness is real: the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. But it does not override the Bali position. The stated Bali block is tied to its moratorium of May 13, 2026; this permanent, island-wide rule prevents PMA registration of activities classified Low or Medium-Low risk, and this activity is marked blocked under it. Anyone choosing Bali as the proposed place of registration therefore has a straightforward present-tense answer: foreign PMA registration is not available there, even though the national setting is fully open.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Bags and Luggage: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans the wholesale trade of bags, wallets, luggage, backpacks and related carrying goods, nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46496 is the wholesale trade category for bags, wallets, luggage, backpacks and comparable carrying goods. Its scope is broad in material as well as use: leather, imitation leather, textiles, plastic, rubber and other materials are all included. The products range from handbags, shopping bags, school bags and sports bags to wallets, cosmetic cases, knife or sword sheaths, and camera cases. The commercial focus is wholesale trade—the supply and distribution layer behind these goods—rather than a narrow product identity.

The category is open across every stated business scale: micro, small, medium and large. That matters because the activity is not framed as exclusive to a particular size of operator. A business working in this wholesale field can sit anywhere along that scale spectrum, provided its actual operations remain within the defined range of bags, luggage, wallets and related items. The scope is practical rather than decorative: it follows the goods being traded and the wholesale character of the activity.

At the national level, the PMA position is clear. The activity is **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In other words, a foreign-owned business may hold the full ownership permitted nationally for this activity. That national position is sourced to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021, and it should be read as the baseline for the code—not as a shortcut around provincial conditions.

Bali is precisely where the picture changes. A foreigner cannot register this activity as a PMA business in Bali today. Its Bali status is blocked by risk class: at the large scale, every scope is assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The stated basis is the Bali moratorium of May 2026. National openness therefore remains real, but it does not make PMA registration available for this activity in Bali under the recorded provincial rule.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, but it does not make PMA registration available for this activity in Bali.

editorial.headline: The Household-Goods Trade That Is Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity spans practical household goods and specialist supplies, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium changes the answer for foreign investors.
editorial.body:
This activity is a broad wholesale home for household goods and equipment that do not sit more neatly elsewhere. Its scope runs from cleaning tools and non-electric toothbrushes to electric bicycles, monowheels, hoverboards and scooters; recorded media on cassette, CD and DVD; and a substantial range of baby equipment, including prams, strollers, walkers, carriers and car seats. It also includes sports medals and trophies, tents and sleeping bags, promotional goods, imitation jewellery, household chemicals such as detergents and floor cleaners, and educational teaching aids.

That breadth is its defining feature. The activity is not organised around one product category or one retail setting, but around the wholesale distribution of varied household-related goods. A business using it may therefore deal in everyday domestic necessities alongside recreational, promotional, educational and specialist-use items, provided they fall within the stated scope. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so its commercial reach is not confined to one size of enterprise.

At the national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national record permits this activity to have 100% foreign ownership. That is an important baseline, but it is not the complete answer for a business intending to register in Bali. National openness does not override the Bali-specific position recorded for this activity.

In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity for PMA today. At the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, bringing it within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): the constraint is not a reduced foreign-share allowance, but a registration block under that moratorium, recorded as taking effect in May 2026. For a founder, the practical conclusion is crisp: the activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the stated risk-based rule.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness to 100% foreign ownership does not override Bali’s risk-based PMA registration block.

editorial.headline: Computer Wholesale Is Nationally Open—but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Code 46511 covers wholesale computers and connected peripherals; it is nationally open to foreign investment, but Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering Code 46511, the central fact is immediate: this activity cannot be registered as a PMA business in Bali today. Nationally, the code is open to foreign investment with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In Bali, however, the applicable provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration. The contrast is not a technicality; it is the practical boundary around this activity on the island.

The activity is wholesale trade in computers and computer peripheral equipment. Its stated scope includes printers, multifunction printers that print, scan, copy and send faxes, and which can generally connect to computers and networks. It also includes interactive whiteboards and video-conferencing equipment. Read as a commercial category, this is the wholesale side of supplying the hardware and connected equipment that sits around computer use, communication and collaboration.

The code is open across the full stated business-scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters nationally because the activity is not confined in the record to one size of operator. Yet the Bali result turns on the risk position recorded for the Besar scale: across every scope, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis, and this code is therefore marked Blocked (risk class) under the moratorium introduced in May 2026.

This leaves a clean but demanding reading of the record. The national rule permits full foreign ownership for this wholesale activity; the Bali rule prevents PMA registration for it. Neither fact cancels the other. A founder looking at Indonesia at large can rely on the national openness stated for the code, while a founder planning a Bali PMA must treat the provincial block as decisive. The relevant question is not whether computer wholesale is nationally foreign-open, but whether the intended registration sits in Bali—and for PMA, the record’s answer is no.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not override Bali’s decisive block on PMA registration for this activity.

The registration field is broad in business scale, not in the activity’s object. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises. A business registering under it may operate at any of those stated scales, provided its activity remains within the wholesale trade described by the code. The practical question is therefore not whether the category can accommodate a smaller or larger enterprise, but whether the proposed operation genuinely concerns the listed electronic components and equipment.

The national foreign-investment position is straightforward. The code is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. It is not framed as a retail activity, a content business, or a manufacturing operation; its commercial centre of gravity is the wholesale trade in these blank and removable media products.

The activity is open across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. For this wholesale activity, the national framework says foreign investment is open, while Bali’s risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration on the island. editorial.headline: Agricultural Machinery Wholesale: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but a permanent Bali moratorium prevents PMA registration there today.
editorial.body:
A foreign-investment company cannot register this agricultural and forestry machinery wholesale activity in Bali today. That is the practical starting point, despite a nationally open foreign-investment position with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In Bali, the activity is blocked by the province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every stated scope of this activity, bringing it within that restriction.

The commercial substance is wholesale trade in the working equipment behind farming and forestry. It includes ploughing equipment, fertiliser spreaders and seed planters; harvesting and threshing equipment; milking machinery; machinery for poultry and beekeeping operations; tractors used in agriculture and forestry; and lawn-mowing machinery. This is therefore an equipment-trading activity rather than a farming operation itself: its centre of gravity is the wholesale supply of machines and tools used across cultivation, livestock-related work, harvesting, and forestry. Its stated boundary is also clear: wholesale trade in fertilisers and agrochemical products, and wholesale trade in animal feed, sit outside the scope.

The activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. Nationally, it is marked TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100% under the cited presidential regulations. That national openness is real, but it is not a route around Bali’s local PMA restriction. For a founder considering Bali as the registration location, the decisive fact is not the national ownership ceiling but the Bali classification outcome: the relevant risk treatment triggers the permanent moratorium. The result is straightforward—this activity may be nationally available to a fully foreign-owned company, yet it cannot be registered as PMA in Bali under the current provincial rule.

That distinction matters because the activity’s commercial identity remains broad and recognisable: it serves the wholesale movement of agricultural and forestry machinery across the full chain of field preparation, planting, harvesting, livestock systems, and grounds maintenance. But location changes the registration answer. National openness does not overcome the island-wide Bali moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not overcome the island-wide Bali moratorium.

editorial.headline: Industrial and Office Machinery Wholesale: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A foreign investor can pursue this wholesale activity nationally, but cannot register it in Bali today: its Large-scale risk classification triggers the island-wide PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is the wholesale trade of industrial machinery and office machines—excluding computers and computer peripherals—together with their parts and equipment. Its industrial side includes machinery for wood and metal processing, production robots, additive-manufacturing machinery such as three-dimensional printers, and computer-controlled industrial equipment for textile production, sewing and knitting. Its office-equipment side includes cash registers, calculators, photocopiers not connected to a computer or network, paper shredders and automated teller machines. The scope is therefore deliberately practical: machinery used to make, process, administer or equip, rather than the computer hardware expressly left outside it.

The registration is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That matters because the activity is not framed as belonging only to a large industrial operator. It can serve businesses trading specialist processing machinery, office equipment or their associated parts and equipment at any of those recognised scales. The code’s centre of gravity remains wholesale trade, however. The record describes the machinery, equipment and parts that may be traded; it does not extend the activity beyond that stated commercial scope.

The position on foreign investment is unambiguous at the national level. The activity is marked open, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In national terms, then, foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership for this activity. The relevant source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national openness should be read plainly, but not treated as a shortcut around Bali’s separate PMA position.

In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity today. At the Large scale, every scope within the record is classified as Low or Medium-Low risk, and that classification places it inside Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. This is not a contradiction of the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling: the national figure states the ownership ceiling, while Bali’s rule blocks PMA registration for this activity because of its risk classification. For a foreign-owned business considering this wholesale activity in Bali, that local restriction is the decisive fact.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not override Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium for this activity.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Sea Transport Equipment: Nationally Open, Bali PMA Blocked
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
This activity covers wholesale trade in a range of sea transport equipment, whether motorised or non-motorised. Its scope also expressly includes the wholesale trade of spare parts and equipment for that transport. The definition therefore holds the principal equipment and its supporting commercial inventory together: sea-transport equipment on one side, and the parts and accessories used with it on the other. It is a wholesale activity with a deliberately broad product frame, rather than a narrow description of one vessel type or one particular component.

The record makes the activity available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That is an important part of the classification’s practical shape. A business operating at any of those stated scales can fall within the activity’s scope when its work is the wholesale trade described here. The scale listing is broad, while the commercial subject remains specific: the wholesale supply of varied marine transport equipment, including both motorised and non-motorised forms, plus related spare parts and equipment.

For foreign investment at the national level, the position is open. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain English, the record permits full foreign ownership nationally for this activity. That national position should be read as a national ownership setting, supported by the cited Perpres sources, rather than as an assurance that every Indonesian location applies the same PMA registration outcome.

Bali is the decisive local exception. Today, this activity cannot be registered as PMA in Bali by a foreign investor. The record states that, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope; Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. National openness is not a substitute for Bali eligibility: in Bali, the moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity. The distinction is sharp but straightforward—100% foreign ownership is the national ceiling, while Bali’s current risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration there.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is not a substitute for Bali eligibility: in Bali, the moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity.

editorial.headline: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trading in non-car, non-motorcycle land transport equipment is nationally open to foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the Bali conclusion comes first: this activity cannot be registered for PMA in Bali at present. The restriction does not overturn its national foreign-investment position; it reflects Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for KBLI activities classified as Low or Medium-Low risk. For this activity, every scope at the Large scale falls into that Low or Medium-Low OSS risk range, bringing it within the moratorium.

The commercial territory is wholesale trade in a broad range of land transport equipment, whether powered or unpowered, excluding cars, motorcycles, and similar vehicles. It expressly includes items such as locomotives and railcars, alongside wholesale trading in their various spare parts and accessories. In practical terms, the registered enterprise is positioned as a wholesale trader of those transport assets and their supporting components—not merely of one named item, but across the category described by the activity’s scope.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. The activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100% under the cited presidential regulations. It is also open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. Those two facts matter together: the national framework permits full foreign ownership and does not limit the activity to a single enterprise-size category. A founder assessing an Indonesian business structure can therefore read the national position as fully open on ownership.

Bali requires a separate reading. The obstacle is not a reduced foreign-ownership ceiling in Bali; it is the prohibition on PMA registration created by the permanent moratorium. Because the record identifies Low or Medium-Low OSS risk across every scope at the Besar scale, a nationally open, 100%-foreign-owned company still cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali. The distinction is essential: national openness describes the ownership ceiling, while the Bali rule determines whether PMA registration is available on the island at all.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness may permit 100% foreign ownership, but it does not create a PMA registration route in Bali for this activity.

editorial.headline: Air-Transport Equipment Wholesale: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale air-transport equipment, parts and accessories are nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-class moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 46594** covers wholesale trade in a range of air-transport equipment and, alongside the equipment itself, wholesale trade in its parts and accessories. Both elements are part of the stated scope: the equipment, and the components and fittings associated with it. It is a classification for the wholesale side of that commercial activity. The inclusion of parts and accessories is explicit rather than incidental. The scope therefore places equipment and its associated components in the same wholesale undertaking. For a founder reading the boundary, the essential point is simple: this is trade in air-transport equipment and the parts and accessories that belong to that trade, at wholesale level.

It can be registered at every scale named in the record—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That availability matters because it does not confine the activity to a single band of business scale. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA and foreign ownership may reach 100%. The national reference listed for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Taken on its national terms, therefore, the activity is fully open to foreign ownership, not merely open with a partial foreign stake.

Bali produces a different answer. In Bali today, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA. The Bali classification is Blocked (risk class): at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for all KBLI activities in the Low and Medium-Low risk bands. The stated Bali source is Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. The obstruction is not a reduction of the national foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a block on PMA registration in Bali for an activity in those risk classes.

The distinction has to be held plainly rather than smoothed over. The national record says 100% foreign ownership is permitted, and the activity is available from Mikro to Besar. The Bali record says the PMA route is blocked under the provincial risk-class moratorium. For a business considering this precise activity, those statements are both true at once: national foreign ownership is fully open, while Bali does not presently admit a PMA registration for it.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali today, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA.

editorial.headline: KBLI 46599: Machinery Wholesale, Nationally Open but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This broad machinery-wholesale activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet PMA registration in Bali is blocked under the province’s permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46599 covers wholesale trade in machinery, equipment and associated supplies that fall outside more specifically grouped machinery activities. Its practical territory is wide: prime movers, turbines and power-generation machines; production robots other than processing robots; trade, navigation and service machinery; cables, switches and installation equipment; machine tools; measuring equipment; and mining, construction and civil-engineering equipment such as excavators. It also includes traffic barriers, bollards, street and traffic lights, road signs, and bus- and tram-stop equipment. The scope extends to wholesale of weapons, weapons systems and ammunition, including tanks and armoured combat vehicles.

That breadth matters because this is not a single-product activity. It is a wholesale classification for businesses supplying industrial, infrastructure, technical and public-realm equipment across a varied set of use cases. The record opens it to operators at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, allowing the activity to serve businesses from micro through large scale. What unifies the category is the wholesale function and the equipment-led nature of the trade, rather than one customer sector or one type of machinery.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. A foreign investor may therefore hold the entire national ownership allowance for this activity. In Bali, however, the answer changes decisively. Today, a foreigner cannot secure PMA registration for this activity in Bali. At the Besar scale, every scope within the record is assessed by OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah, placing it within Bali’s moratorium.

That is an island-wide, permanent provincial rule: Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA. The block is recorded under the Bali risk-class status Blocked (risk class) and is tied to the moratorium of 13 May 2026. The distinction is essential for founders: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remain real features of the activity, but they do not make PMA registration available in Bali where the provincial risk-based restriction applies.
editorial.pullQuote: Today, a foreigner cannot secure PMA registration for this activity in Bali.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the wholesale distribution of brand-new motor vehicles — from passenger cars and specialty vehicles (like ambulances, fire trucks, minibuses, and caravans) to lorries, trailers, semi-trailers, and other cargo or transport motorised units. It is strictly about bulk, business-to-business trade, not direct retail to end consumers.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this business is 100% open to foreign ownership (PMA). However, in Bali, a regional moratorium on new PMA registrations for certain risk classes currently blocks this activity, despite its low/medium-low risk rating — meaning a foreign-owned company cannot obtain this KBLI locally until the moratorium lifts.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: code renumbered.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Perdagangan Besar Mobil Baru (46611)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs looking to import and wholesale new cars, trucks, or specialised vehicles on a large scale, typically targeting fleet buyers, dealers, or government contracts.

editorial.headline: Nationally Open New-Vehicle Wholesale, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity spans new cars and commercial vehicles, open nationally at every business scale but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity through PMA in Bali today, even though it is nationally open to foreign investment. The activity is wholesale trade in new cars, with a scope extending beyond passenger vehicles to special cars such as ambulances, caravans, minibuses and fire engines. It also includes trucks, trailers, semi-trailers, goods vehicles and other motorised transport vehicles. In practical terms, it is a single wholesale activity spanning the new passenger, specialist and freight-carrying vehicles expressly named in its scope.

The registration field is broad in business-scale terms. Enterprises at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales can all undertake this activity. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA and its foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, under the stated Perpres basis. A national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% does not create a PMA registration path in Bali. It establishes the national position for the activity; the Bali outcome is governed by a separate, explicitly recorded restriction.

In Bali, the result is unambiguous: the activity is marked Blocked (risk class) for PMA registration. The record attributes this to OSS risk at the Besar scale, where every scope is classified as Low or Medium-Low risk, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium from May 2026. That provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA, island-wide and permanently. There is no Bali-specific foreign-ownership percentage or partnership condition recorded here; the barrier is the moratorium triggered by the stated risk classification.

The honest reading is therefore two-level. At the national level, this is an open PMA activity with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling and access across all four stated enterprise scales. In Bali, however, it is not an available PMA registration route. The national openness remains real, but it cannot be treated as permission to establish the activity through PMA on the island while the permanent, island-wide moratorium applies.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Used Vehicle Wholesale Is Nationally Open—But Not for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans wholesale used vehicles from passenger cars to specialist transport, open nationally across every business scale but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Used-vehicle wholesale is broader than a forecourt of pre-owned passenger cars. It covers the wholesale trade of used cars, including specialist vehicles such as ambulances, caravans, minibuses and fire engines, as well as trucks, trailers, semi-trailers, goods vehicles and other motorised transport vehicles. The defining idea is wholesale trade: moving used vehicles through the commercial supply chain rather than presenting a retail-facing activity.

The activity is open to Micro, Small, Medium and Large businesses. That breadth matters because the record does not confine the trade to a particular operating scale or vehicle category. A business may therefore organise itself around used passenger cars, commercial fleets, specialist vehicles, or a mixed vehicle portfolio, provided its activity remains within the stated wholesale scope.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear: the activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The record cites Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 for that national position. In other words, the national framework permits full foreign ownership for a company registered to carry out this wholesale activity. That national openness, however, is not the end of the practical analysis for an investor whose intended place of registration is Bali.

In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity through PMA today. The Bali assessment marks it as blocked because, at the Large scale, the OSS risk classification across every included scope is Low or Medium-Low. Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities from PMA registration across the island, on a permanent basis; the recorded trigger is the moratorium of May 2026. The result is a direct geographical constraint: national permission for up to 100% foreign ownership does not create a PMA registration route for this activity in Bali. For founders, the useful reading is straightforward—understand the wholesale scope first, then treat the Bali restriction as decisive when the proposed PMA registration is on the island.
editorial.pullQuote: National permission for up to 100% foreign ownership does not create a PMA registration route for this activity in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Automotive Parts: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, yet a Bali-wide PMA moratorium blocks registration there today.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this wholesale automotive-parts activity in Bali today. That is the practical starting point, even though the national position is open. The activity itself is the wholesale trade of new and used motor-car spare parts, components, equipment and accessories, including tyres, as well as automotive batteries and accumulators. It is a supply-chain classification: the business is concerned with wholesale distribution of the parts and accessories that keep cars supplied and maintained.

The record opens the activity to every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the classification is defined by what is traded—automotive parts, components, equipment, accessories, batteries and accumulators—rather than by a narrow company-size profile. A business operating at any of those listed scales can fall within the activity where its commercial function is wholesale trade in those goods.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Read on its own terms, that is a fully open national foreign-investment position: the foreign stake is not capped below full ownership. But the national reading is not the final answer for a Bali registration. The location-specific restriction in the record changes the result decisively.

Bali records the activity as Blocked (risk class). At the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk, and Bali’s May 2026 moratorium blocks PMA registration on that basis. The stated provincial rule is island-wide and permanent: it blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. So the honest picture is not a qualified version of national openness. Nationally, this activity is open to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, PMA registration is blocked under the provincial moratorium. That conclusion concerns the PMA registration position specified in the record, and it is the condition an investor must take seriously before treating the national ceiling as an available Bali entry route.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, this activity is open to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, PMA registration is blocked under the provincial moratorium.

editorial.headline: New Motorcycle Wholesale: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in new motorcycles and mopeds is open to PMA nationally, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration there today.
editorial.body:
Wholesale is the key word here. This activity covers the wholesale trade of new motorcycles, expressly including motor bicycles or mopeds. The scope gives a concise commercial picture: new two-wheeled vehicles, sold at wholesale. It is not a vague label for the wider motorcycle economy; its stated centre is the wholesale trade itself and the fact that the vehicles are new. For a founder choosing the description, that provides a disciplined boundary. The undertaking being put forward should be understood through the recorded activity—wholesale trading in new motorcycles, with mopeds included—rather than through a broader story about the sector.

The national scale picture is broad and simple. The record lists every scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—as open to this activity. Those labels tell the reader who may place the activity at their declared business scale: an enterprise in any of the four recorded categories. They do not alter the substance of the code. Whether a business is Mikro or Besar, the stated activity remains the same wholesale trade in new motorcycles, including mopeds. That distinction matters because the record's scale access and its activity description are both explicit, and they should be read together without stretching either one.

At the national level, PMA status is TERBUKA, with maximum foreign ownership set at 100%. In other words, the national record presents the activity as open to PMA with no foreign-share ceiling below full ownership. Bali supplies a different answer, and it is the answer that controls a Bali registration today. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk outcome is Low or Medium-Low on every scope. Bali’s stated moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. This activity is consequently recorded in Bali as Blocked (risk class).

This is therefore not a minor local footnote to the national position. A foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today, notwithstanding the 100% national ceiling. The Bali restriction is island-wide and permanent under the moratorium rule supplied with the record; it is not described as a district-specific measure. The stated reason connects the block to the Low or Medium-Low OSS risk result at the Besar scale, and to the Bali moratorium on May 13, 2026. Read as a whole, the position is exact: national foreign ownership is open to 100%, while PMA registration in Bali is blocked.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today, notwithstanding the 100% national ceiling.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the wholesale trade of used motorcycles, including motor bikes and mopeds. It focuses on buying and selling pre-owned two-wheeled vehicles in bulk, typically supplying retailers or other businesses rather than selling directly to end consumers.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is 100% open for foreign ownership (PMA). However, in Bali, the local moratorium (dated 13 May 2026) blocks it because its OSS risk classification for 'Besar' scale falls into the Low or Medium-Low category on every scope. As a result, a foreign-owned company cannot currently register this activity in Bali.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Renumbered/adjusted from KBLI 2020. Under KBLI 2020, trade in used motorcycles was often folded into the 45xxx retail codes with no wholesale/retail distinction; KBLI 2025 isolates the wholesale trade under 46632.
intel_2026.baliContext: Used motorcycle trading is active throughout Bali — rental fleets refresh their stock regularly, creating volume supply. SAMSAT (vehicle registration authority) compliance for title transfer (balik nama) is mandatory for each vehicle. Export of used motorcycles to other islands or overseas requires transport documentation and customs clearance. The market is large but fragmented — formal PMA wholesale operations compete with informal traders.

editorial.headline: Used Motorcycle Wholesale: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Used-motorcycle wholesale is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s risk-class moratorium blocks PMA registration for it.
editorial.body:
Wholesale trade in used motorcycles, including motorised bicycles and mopeds, is the commercial terrain of this activity. Its language is deliberately wholesale: it is concerned with the trade in previously owned two-wheelers at that level of commerce. That category extends beyond motorcycles alone, since motorised bicycles and mopeds are expressly included. The record places the activity within a practical set of business sizes—Micro, Small, Medium and Large—so its definition is not confined to one scale. For a founder, that gives the activity a clear frame before the investment question begins: used two-wheelers, traded wholesale, across the named scale categories.

Nationally, that investment question has an unambiguous answer. The PMA status is open, and foreign ownership may reach 100%. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The 100% figure is the stated foreign-ownership ceiling; it is not a number that needs to be inferred. National openness, however, should not be mistaken for a blanket geographical assurance. The Bali entry carries a separate result, drawn from the activity’s OSS risk classification and the province’s rule.

Bali is where the answer changes sharply. The Bali status is blocked by risk class. At the Large scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope in the record. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. On the facts supplied here, that prohibition applies to this activity. A foreign investor therefore cannot register it in Bali through a PMA business today, even though the national PMA position is open and permits up to 100% foreign ownership.

The useful reading is not to dilute either side of the record. There is a national pathway characterised by an open PMA status and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In Bali, there is a different present result: blocked PMA registration, because the activity falls within the risk bands captured by the provincial moratorium. This distinction is the centre of the entry, not a footnote to it. Anyone evaluating wholesale trade in used motorcycles, motorised bicycles and mopeds should hold both statements together: the national investment setting is open; Bali does not allow a PMA registration for the activity.

editorial.headline: Motorcycle Parts Wholesale: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale motorcycle parts and accessories are nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks this activity there.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46633 covers the wholesale trade of motorcycle spare parts and accessories. Its scope is direct: it concerns commercial trading at the wholesale level, with motorcycle parts and their accessories forming the subject of the activity. For founders, the operative distinction is equally direct—the code concerns wholesale trade in these goods. The record presents this as a defined trading activity, not a broad description of the motorcycle sector.

The activity is open across the full set of listed scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That gives the code a wide scale profile in the national classification, from Mikro through Besar. The scale question and the foreign-ownership question should nevertheless be read separately. The former identifies the business scales open to the activity; the latter determines how foreign ownership is treated nationally and, in Bali, whether PMA registration remains available at all.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign capital may hold the full stake in this activity at the national level. The record cites Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 for that treatment. This is a genuine national opening, and it should be stated without dilution. Yet it is not the final answer for a business intended to register in Bali, where the record supplies a separate and decisive local position.

Bali changes the answer completely. Its status is Blocked (risk class), and the activity is marked as blocked. A foreign investor cannot register this activity through PMA in Bali today. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. That places it within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium, which blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA. The record locates that moratorium in May 2026. National openness is real, but it does not override Bali’s island-wide permanent PMA block.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, but it does not override Bali’s island-wide permanent PMA block.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

Analisis kelayakan usaha paling sedikit memuat rencana sumber pasokan, calon konsumen, spesifikasi komoditas, lokasi, sarana dan fasilitas, skema usaha, Penggunan Tenaga Kerja Asing dan Tenaga Kerja Lokal, komitmen TKDN dan dokumen analisis keuangan meliputi rencana biaya investasi, harga beli, Komponen dan besaran LPG, LNG, BBG, dan/atau CNG, serta perhitungan keekonomian b.
