Badan Usaha Niaga dapat melaksanakan penunjukan penyalur dengan ketentuan sebagai berikut: a. Penyalur wajib berbentuk Koperasi, usaha kecil dan/atau Badan Usaha Swasta Nasional b. Penyalur bukan untuk usaha per-seorangan, ditujukan untuk badan usaha yang berbadan hukum, dan hanya untuk usaha PMDN c. Penyalur hanya dapat menerima penunjukan dari 1 (satu) Badan Usaha Niaga Migas untuk masing- masing jenis komoditas BBM, BBG, LPG, dan/ atau LNG d. Penyalur wajib menggunakan logo dan merek dagang BU Niaga Migas e. Penyalur menyampaikan laporan kegiatan penyalurannya kepada Badan Usaha Niaga Migas f. Memenuhi kewajiban lainnya sesuai dengan peraturan perundangan g. Memiliki kontrak perjanjian kerjasama penunjukan penyalur h. Penyalur memiliki dokumen NIB, Persetujuan lingkungan hidup, persetujuan kegiatan pemanfaatan ruang, dan keselamatan sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan i. Penyalur memiliki/menguasai sarana fasilitas dengan ketentuan sebagai berikut: 1) Penyalur BBM, LPG, BBG, dan LNG yang menyalurkan Bahan Bakar di Stasiun Pengisian Bahan Bakar untuk transportasi Darat, transportasi Laut, dan transportasi udara (SPBU, SPBN, SPBG, dsb) wajib memiliki Sarana dan Fasilitas pengisian Bahan Bakar 2) Penyalur BBM, BBG/ LPG/ LNG yang menyalurkan selain di Stasiun Pengisian Bahan Bakar untuk transportasi Darat, transportasi Laut, dan transportasi udara (agen BBM, agen LPG, agen LNG dsb) wajib memiliki Sarana dan fasilitas pengangkutan untuk kegiatan penyaluran dengan transportasi darat 3) Untuk kegiatan penyaluran dengan transportasi laut/ sungai, Penyalur dapat menguasai sarana dan Fasilitas pengangkutan j. Penyalur selain penyalur LPG PSO dan Minyak Tanah hanya dapat menyalurkan bahan bakar kepada konsumen pengguna langsung untuk kepentingan sendiri dan tidak diperjualbelikan kembali k. Penyalur dilarang menjual/ menyalurkan kepada Badan Usaha Niaga Migas l. Penyalur LPG Bersubsidi (PSO) dan Minyak Tanah PSO wajib menunjuk Sub Penyalur dalam melaksanakan kegiatan penyaluran m. Penyalur wajib menjual jenis BBM Umum, Jenis LPG Umum, dan LNG sesuai dengan harga yang ditentukan oleh Badan Usaha Niaga n. Stok (cadangan) bahan bakar yang ada di fasilitas penyalur merupakan milik/ dicatat sebagai stok Badan Usaha Niaga
Badan Usaha Niaga wajib melaporkan penunjukan penyalurnya kepada Ditjen Migas

Persyaratan Administratif a. Surat Permohonan b. Daftar Penerima Manfaat (Beneficial Ownership) c. Identitas dan Surat Kuasa Narahubung d. Surat pernyataan tertulis di atas materai mengenai: 1) Kesang gupan Badan Usaha memenuhi ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan 2) Kesanggupan memenuhi aspek keselamatan, kesehatan kerja dan pengelolaan lingkungan hidup 3) Kesanggupan memenuhi kewajiban badan usaha 4) Kesediaan dilakukan audit kepatuhan terhadap ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan 5) Kesanggupan badan usaha menjamin dan betanggung jawab bahwa sarana dan fasilitas yang dimiliki/ dikuasai layak beroperasi dan mampu dijalankan sesuai dengan kaidah ketekni kan yang baik selama masa operasi 6) Badan usaha bebas dari konflik atau permasalahan hukum lainnya dengan pihak lain 7) Dokumen persyaratan dan keterangan/ pernyataan yang diberikan adalah benar adanya dan apabila dikemudian hari terbukti tidak benar akan dicabut izin usahanya sesuai dengan peraturan perundang-undangan 8) )Kesanggupan menerima penunjukan dan penugasan dari Menteri untuk melaksanakan penyimpanan dalam rangka penyediaan cadangan penyangga energi atau cadangan operasi dan pemenuhan kebutuhan minyak bumi di dalam negeri pada fasilitas dan sarana penyimpanan miliknya (untuk kegiatan usaha niaga minyak bumi).

Persyaratan Teknis (Izin Usaha Sementara) a. Studi Kelayakan paling sedikit memuat lokasi, sarana dan fasilitas, komoditas (untuk 1 komoditas wajib memiliki/ menguasai 1 fasilitas penyimpanan), skema usaha, rencana pasokan, Penggunaan Tenaga Kerja Asing dan Tenaga Kerja Lokal, realisasi kegiatan usaha Niaga Migas yang pernah dijalani sebelumnya (apabila ada) dan analisis keekonomian (rencana biaya investasi, harga jual, dan indikator kelayakan usaha) serta rencana merek dagang dan rencana spesifikasi produk yang akan diniagakan untuk kegiatan niaga umum Bahan Bakar Minyak dan/atau Hasil Olahan b. Persetujuan Kesesuaian Kegiatan Pemanfaatan Ruang atau Persetujuan Pemerintah /instansi yang berwenang sesuai ketentuan yang berlaku atau pengelola kawasan yang berwenang mengenai lokasi untuk pembangunan fasilitas dan sarana c. Kesepakatan awal (HoA atau MoU) jual beli dengan pemasok dan/atau dokumen yang mengindikasikan tersedianya pasokan dengan calon pemasok Minyak Bumi yang difasilitasi oleh SKK Migas untuk kegiatan Niaga Minyak Bumi dan/atau Niaga umum Hasil Olahan d. Rencana pembangunan sarana dan fasilitas Niaga Minyak Bumi dan/atau Niaga Umum Hasil Olahan yang dimiliki dan/atau dikuasai berupa fasilitas penyimpan an Minyak Bumi dan/atau Hasil Olahan beserta data titik koordinat berupa Data Georeference Standard Datum WGS84 dan e. Rencana penggunaan sarana dan fasilitas Niaga Umum Bahan Bakar Minyak berupa kepemilikan sarana dan fasilitas penyimpan an dengan jumlah keseluruhan paling sedikit 1500 KL (seribu lima ratus kiloliter) dan kebutuhan fasilitas penyimpanan selanjutnya dapat menguasai / sewa Sarana Fasilitas Penyimpanan BBM dimaksud dapat berupa tangki darat, floating storage, tangki penyimpanan BBM di Fasilitas Sarana Pengisian Bahan Bakar untuk Transportasi Darat, Laut, dan Udara dan fasilitas penyimpanan lain sesuai ketentuan peraturan lainnya Beserta data titik koordinat berupa Data Georeference Standard Datum WGS84 baik yang: 1) Dimiliki dengan jangka waktu pembangunan sarana dan fasilitas penyim panan dan/ atau 2) Dikuasai, dengan sewa eksklusif kepada pihak lain f. Badan Usaha Niaga yang melakukan kegiatan pencampuran (blending) untuk menghasilkan Bahan Bakar Minyak dan/atau Hasil Olahan wajib memiliki/ menguasai fasilitas pencampuran (blending) Badan Usaha Niaga hanya dapat melakukan blending dengan komoditas hasil blending yang tercantum dalam Izin Usaha g. Surat Persetujuan Penggunaan Permukaan Perairan untuk Lokasi Penyimpanan (penetapan Titik Koordinat) dari instansi yang berwenang, untuk fasilitas penyimpanan di perairan h. SK Izin Usaha Sementara dan/atau Izin Usaha/Penyesuaian / Perpanjangan (apabila ada) i. Jaminan kecukupan pendanaan, yang dibuktikan dengan : 1) Laporan keuangan 3 (tiga) tahun terakhir yang sudah diaudit 2) Dokumen kesepakatan dengan pihak lain untuk pendanaan (mencantum kan nominal tertentu) atau 3) Surat keterangan dari bank umum yang berkedudukan di Indonesia, yang menerangkan bahwa Badan Usaha memiliki kemampu an pendanaan dengan nominal tertentu

Persyaratan Teknis (Izin Usaha/ Perpanjangan Izin Usaha) a. editorial.headline: Fuel Wholesale Is Nationally Open, but Bali Turns on Risk Scope
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity spans conventional, renewable and low-carbon fuels, with full national foreign ownership but a scope-sensitive PMA route in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the wholesale trade of fuels and closely related products: fossil fuels alongside lower-carbon or carbon-free alternatives, as well as grease, lubricants and oils. Its commercial range is unusually broad, taking in crude petroleum, diesel, gasoline, fuel oil, kerosene and solar; biofuels, recycled-carbon fuels and synthetic fuels; charcoal, coal, coke, firewood, wood pellets, biomass and naphtha. It also includes LPG, LNG, butane, propane and their related bio or renewable forms, whether blended or pure, plus nuclear fuel. Hydrogen sits outside the group’s stated boundary.

The code is open to businesses at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. In practical terms, it is for an enterprise whose activity is wholesale distribution across that fuel-and-related-products universe, rather than a narrow label for one commodity alone. The breadth matters because the record describes distinct fuel forms, product families and energy sources within a single wholesale activity. A founder should therefore match the registered activity to the precise business scope being undertaken, especially where the product mix reaches beyond conventional petroleum fuels.

At the national level, the PMA position is straightforward: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a full national foreign-ownership position, supported in the record by Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali, however, is not a simple extension of that national reading. The province permanently blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island. For this activity, the Bali result is scope-dependent rather than categorically blocked: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is low for some scopes and higher for others.

That distinction is the operative one for a foreign-owned business considering Bali. The record says PMA registration in Bali is available only by declaring the higher-risk scope, and it directs verification in live OSS for the exact activity. National openness therefore remains real, but it does not itself settle the Bali registration outcome. The relevant question is not whether fuel wholesale is nationally open—it is—but whether the particular activity scope declared in Bali falls on the registrable side of the province’s risk-based rule.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not by itself settle the Bali registration outcome.

editorial.headline: The Trade Behind Indonesia’s Metal Supply Chain
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 46721 covers wholesale trade in metal ores and concentrates, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Wholesale trading in metal ores and concentrates is the commercial activity at the upstream edge of the metals economy: moving raw mineral materials and concentrated metal-bearing products through trade channels rather than describing their extraction or processing. KBLI 46721 covers both ferrous and non-ferrous ores and concentrates, including nickel, copper, aluminium, iron and gold, as well as other precious metals such as silver and platinum. Its subject is therefore a defined wholesale market in mineral inputs and concentrates.

The activity is open across the full business-scale range recorded for it: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the code is not framed around a single company size or a narrow market position. It describes the wholesale trade itself, whether conducted at a micro, small, medium or large scale. The practical distinction is the nature of the goods being traded—metal ores and concentrates—rather than an implied restriction to one class of enterprise.

For foreign investment, the national position is direct. TERBUKA status applies to the activity, and its foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain terms, foreign investment is nationally open up to full ownership for this activity. That is the relevant national position for a foreign-owned company considering registration under this code; the record supplies no additional national threshold, licence condition or capital requirement, so none should be inferred.

Bali’s position is also clear, but it rests on the province’s risk-based moratorium rather than on a separate ownership cap. Bali permanently blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the island. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is classified as Menengah-Tinggi or Tinggi. For a foreign-owned business registering this activity in Bali today, the honest conclusion is that the provincial moratorium does not prevent PMA registration under this code. Nationally, full foreign ownership remains available; in Bali, the activity is not among those stopped by the Low and Medium-Low risk restriction.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this metal-trading activity is also not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Semi-Finished Metal Wholesale: Open Nationally, Barred for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity spans ingots to rolled steel and steel sheet, open nationally to full foreign ownership but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register PMA for this activity in Bali today. That is the decisive local fact, even though the national record marks the activity TERBUKA and sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 100%. The Bali block follows the risk treatment applied to the listed scopes: at the Besar scale, every scope is classified in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration; this activity falls within that bar, recorded against the moratorium in May 2026.

The activity is wholesale trading in semi-finished metal products. It covers products of metal-ore smelting and casting, including ingots, bars, rods, billets, slabs and matte. It extends to rolled steel, tubes and pipes, profiles and hollow profiles, as well as metal powders, metal flakes and metal wire without insulation or enamel coating. The scope also expressly includes steel-sheet wholesale on one’s own account, with the cutting work ordinarily connected to that trade. Gold bullion wholesale does not form part of this activity.

Registration is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. For the national foreign-investment reading, the record gives both clarity and source: TERBUKA, a maximum foreign ownership of 100%, and Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The 100% figure is the national ceiling; it is not a Bali-specific permission. The stated scale range and national ownership position describe the activity nationally, without altering the Bali result.

That division should be read without smoothing it away. The same wholesale activity is nationally open to PMA at up to 100% foreign ownership and nevertheless unavailable for PMA registration in Bali. In the Bali record, the reason is risk-based: all of its scopes at the Besar scale sit in the Low or Medium-Low OSS categories captured by the permanent provincial moratorium. National openness is real, but it does not make a Bali PMA registration possible today.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, but it does not make a Bali PMA registration possible today.

editorial.headline: Metal Construction Wholesale: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale metal construction materials are open to full foreign ownership nationally, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
Wholesale metal construction materials are the practical subject of this activity. It covers wholesale trade in metal building materials, from wire rope and insect-screen wire to nails, nuts, bolts, hinges, latches, locks and keys. Water tanks, water towers, rolling doors and awnings are equally within the recorded scope. These examples give the category its commercial texture: a wholesale activity concerned with the metal components and installations used in construction, access, storage and cover. Its identity is broad enough to hold those varied goods together, yet specific in its focus on wholesale trade in metal construction materials.

The record makes the activity available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. This is not a category held back for only the largest wholesale houses, nor is it framed as an activity confined to the smallest operators. The same stated scope is open at each of the four scales. That matters because the register speaks in terms of one coherent wholesale activity, even as the catalogued goods range from fasteners and hardware to tanks, towers, rolling doors and awnings. Scale availability therefore does not alter the activity’s essential description; the core remains wholesale trade in the listed metal construction materials.

Nationally, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In national terms, foreign capital is therefore not capped below full ownership for this activity. But the national setting is not the Bali answer. Bali marks the activity Blocked (risk class) and records it as blocked: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. That is the central distinction. editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity spans porcelain toilets, basins, baths and wall tiles—open to full foreign ownership nationally, but unavailable to PMA registration in Bali.

For a foreign investor considering this activity in Bali, the decisive fact is straightforward: it cannot be registered there as a PMA business today. That is not because the national position is closed. Across Indonesia, the activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali applies an island-wide, permanent bar on PMA for KBLI activities assessed at Low or Medium-Low risk. For this activity, OSS places every scope at Low or Medium-Low risk at the Large scale, so the Bali moratorium blocks the registration.

The activity itself is wholesale trade in porcelain construction materials. Its practical subject matter is clearly defined: porcelain toilets, bidets, washbasins, urinals, sinks, bathtubs and wall tiles. The code is therefore about the wholesale dealing of these construction-related porcelain products, not a broad catch-all for construction activity. That specificity matters when reading the national openness alongside Bali’s restriction: the assessment attaches to this stated activity and its scopes.

Registration is open across the full business-size range listed for the activity: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. The Bali issue arises at the Large scale, where every scope is assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. Under the provincial moratorium, that risk outcome is enough to prevent PMA registration. The restriction is not described as a partial local cap on foreign ownership; it is a block on PMA registration for this activity in Bali.

That produces a clean but important distinction. At the national level, foreign investment is permitted up to 100%, so there is no national foreign-ownership cap below full ownership for this activity. In Bali, however, the applicable risk classification brings it within the permanent provincial moratorium. A founder should therefore read the national investment position and the Bali registration position as separate facts: nationally open does not make this activity registrable as PMA in Bali.

editorial.headline: Wooden Construction Materials: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale wooden construction materials are nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
Wooden construction materials, in this activity, are defined as a wholesale subject with a deliberately broad product boundary. The scope includes boards, scantling, roof battens, trim boards, telephone and electricity poles, sleeper beams, door and window frames, and door and window leaves. It also names wood tiles, wooden shingles, plywood—including tripleks, interior plywood and plywood for concrete formwork—together with teak wood, particle board, chip board and wood veneers. The organising idea is not wood in the abstract, but wholesale trade in the specifically listed materials and components for construction. Sheet goods, joinery pieces, finishing stock and heavier construction elements are all expressly present in that definition.

The registration frame is equally broad across business scale. The record admits Micro, Small, Medium and Large businesses (Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar), so an operator registering this activity can fall at any of those listed scales. That detail deserves a careful reading: the activity’s listed scale eligibility is national information, while Bali’s outcome turns on the recorded risk treatment of the Besar scale. The two points sit in the same record but answer different questions—who may register nationally at the stated scale, and whether a PMA registration can be made in Bali.

Nationally, the position is open. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, citing Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. In practical terms, the record allows a fully foreign-owned PMA registration for this activity at national level. It is not presented as a minority-cap category or as closed in the national field: the ceiling stated for this code is 100%. That is the national baseline. It does not, however, decide Bali’s distinct registration outcome.

In Bali, the answer is unambiguous: a PMA business cannot register this activity today. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class). Its recorded reason is that OSS places the Besar-scale risk at Low or Medium-Low across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium. The block is recorded as applying from May 2026. The contrast is therefore not a reduced foreign-ownership percentage in Bali; it is a block on PMA registration. A national ceiling of 100% remains the national position, but it does not displace Bali’s block for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: A national ceiling of 100% remains the national position, but it does not displace Bali’s block for this activity.

editorial.standfirst: This paint-trading activity is open to full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for it today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering Bali, the answer is blunt: this paint-trading activity cannot be registered as PMA there today. That conclusion should not obscure the commercial activity itself. The recorded scope is wholesale trade in a range of paints used for construction—primers, paints for metal, wood paints and wall paints. It also includes retail trade in enamel, putty and plamir. Taken together, those details describe a trade-facing activity built around construction paint and related finishing or preparation materials. The named categories matter: primer, metal, wood and wall paints make the scope practical rather than abstract, while enamel, putty and plamir extend the listed trade to related retail goods.

The registration horizon is broad on enterprise scale. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses, expressly covering micro, small, medium and large scales in its own terms. That breadth matters because the activity’s stated availability is not confined to a narrow company size. Yet a scale listing answers only one part of the decision. It should be read beside the national foreign-investment position and the Bali-specific restriction, which affects how the same activity can be registered for PMA. The commercial scope, the available scales and the location of registration each carry their own weight.

Across Indonesia, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. For the national position recorded here, that is a fully foreign-owned ceiling—not a partial one. Bali changes the operative picture. At the Besar scale, every scope is classified Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration in those Low and Medium-Low risk classes, and the reason recorded for this activity identifies that moratorium in May 2026. Its Bali status is Blocked (risk class): the block follows the risk classification.

The practical reading is correspondingly exact. National openness and a 100% ceiling are real, but neither creates a Bali PMA registration route for this activity while the recorded Bali block applies. A founder can therefore understand the commercial scope and the available business scales without mistaking national openness for local availability. For foreign investors, the decisive distinction is not what the activity sells but where PMA registration is being sought. In Bali, the record’s answer is a current block; nationally, it remains open at the stated 100% ceiling.

editorial.headline: Building-Material Wholesale: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Foreign ownership is open nationally, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium bars registration of this building-material wholesale activity.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity as a PMA business in Bali today. That is the practical starting point, even though it is nationally open to foreign investment. The activity is wholesale trade in a varied basket of building materials: cement, sand, nails and paint are expressly within its scope. It is the trade function behind supplying construction materials through wholesale channels, rather than a description of a single product line.

The registration is available across the full business-scale range listed in the record—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth is useful context for founders: the classification is framed around the wholesale activity, and the record opens it from the smallest named scale through the largest. The stated examples give the activity its practical shape. A wholesale offer spanning cement, sand, nails and paint sits squarely within the description; the material mix is deliberately broad rather than confined to one of those items.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the national maximum foreign ownership is 100%. Foreign capital can therefore hold the entire national ownership ceiling for this activity. The source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The national signal is full foreign openness, which makes the Bali restriction especially important to read as a location-specific registration outcome rather than as a national ownership limit.

Bali changes the answer completely. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is recorded as Low or Medium-Low across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium recorded in May 2026. Under the stated provincial rule, that moratorium blocks PMA registration on an island-wide, permanent basis. Accordingly, a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. This is not a reduced Bali foreign-ownership percentage alongside the national 100% ceiling; it is a block on PMA registration in the province. For a founder weighing locations, the decisive distinction is simple: nationally the activity is open, while Bali does not admit PMA registration for it under the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the activity is open, while Bali does not admit PMA registration for it under the stated moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Building Materials and Tools: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration because every scope is Low or Medium-Low risk at the Large scale.
editorial.body:
This activity is wholesale trade in a broad practical range of construction materials and associated equipment. Its defined scope includes wallpaper; plastic pipes and hoses; Formica; corrugated plastic sheet; flat and layered asbestos cement; asbestos-cement drainage pipes; manual hand tools; electric-powered hand tools; water heaters; and boilers. It is an activity of distribution, bringing those goods into the wholesale market rather than defining a construction service or a retail format. The scope is deliberately concrete: it reaches from wall finishes and piping components to tool lines and heating equipment. The grouping holds together surfaces, sheets and pipe-related goods with manual, electrically powered and heating equipment.

Registration is open at Micro, Small, Medium, and Large scales. The record makes no separate national scale-specific foreign-ownership ceiling among those stated scales. Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA—open to foreign investment—with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. The national position is therefore clear: foreign participation is permitted up to full ownership under the cited Presidential Regulations. This establishes national availability for the wholesale activity precisely as defined by the scope. It should be read alongside the local registration conditions the record expressly identifies for Bali, because they govern whether a PMA registration can proceed there.

In Bali, the answer changes decisively. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. At the Large scale, OSS assesses every scope within the activity as Low or Medium-Low risk, and Bali consequently blocks it under the moratorium applying across the island. The rule is permanent: the province blocks PMA registration for all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI activities. The governing issue is not a reduced national ceiling: nationally, the ceiling remains 100%. In Bali, the record instead identifies a risk-classification block and the moratorium as the reason PMA registration cannot proceed. That is the local position that matters at filing.

The practical reading is deliberately two-level. National rules leave full foreign ownership available for the wholesale distribution of the materials, tools, water heaters and boilers listed in the scope. Yet a founder considering Bali must treat the provincial PMA outcome as controlling at the point of registration. National openness does not overcome a permanent, island-wide block where this activity’s scopes carry Low or Medium-Low risk classifications. That separation demands precision: the national PMA setting says what ownership is permitted in the country, while the Bali classification says whether registration is allowed on the island. Both statements can be true at once, and this record requires them to be read together.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not overcome a permanent, island-wide block where this activity’s scopes carry Low or Medium-Low risk classifications.

editorial.headline: The Wholesale Trade Behind Indonesia’s Non-Metallic Minerals
editorial.standfirst: A broad wholesale activity spanning industrial minerals, stones, clays and chemical inputs, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not barred by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is the wholesale trade in non-metallic minerals: the commercial movement of materials ranging from diamonds, corundum and graphite to quartz sand, fluorite, iodine, sulfur and phosphates. Its scope also reaches salt, asbestos, talc, mica, magnesite, kaolin, feldspar, bentonite, gypsum, dolomite, calcite, zircon, quartz stone, perlite, clay and limestone for cement. The common thread is not a single end market, but a wholesale role across a wide mineral catalogue used in industrial, construction and processing supply chains.

The registration is open at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the activity is framed as a trading category rather than as a narrowly defined product line. A business operating under it is positioned around wholesale commerce in the listed non-metallic mineral materials, whether the relevant commercial operation sits at a micro, small, medium or large scale.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In practical terms, a foreign investor may hold the full ownership stake nationally for this activity. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021; there is no lower foreign-ownership ceiling in the record to qualify that national position.

Bali requires a more exact reading, but not a more pessimistic one. The province permanently blocks PMA registrations for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities island-wide. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, placing it outside the risk categories caught by the Bali restriction. The Bali status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: a signal that the activity is not moratorium-blocked, while the large-scale OSS risk classification remains material to how it is understood locally. For a foreign-owned business considering Bali, the honest conclusion is that this activity is not barred from PMA registration there under the stated moratorium rule.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium, because its large-scale OSS risk sits outside the Low and Medium-Low categories the province blocks.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Trade in Radioactive Minerals: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the wholesale movement of radioactive minerals and specified uranium and thorium materials, with foreign ownership open nationally up to 100%.
editorial.body:
Wholesale trade in radioactive minerals is a narrowly defined activity with serious material at its centre. It covers the wholesale trade of radioactive minerals including radium, thorium, uranium, monazite and other radioactive mineral substances. Its stated scope also extends to the transfer, export and/or import of uranium ore, thorium ore, concentrated uranium and concentrated thorium. In practical terms, this is the commercial wholesale layer around these named materials: their trade, movement and the specified cross-border transactions set out in the activity description.

Every listed business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—is open to this activity. That breadth matters because the code is not framed as a category reserved for one business size. A registrant may sit at any of those listed scales, while still remaining within the defined wholesale scope. The operative boundary is therefore the material and transaction description itself: radioactive minerals and the specifically identified ores and concentrates, rather than a generalised minerals-trading label.

At national level, the PMA position is unambiguous. The activity is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. For a foreign-owned enterprise, that means the national ceiling does not require an Indonesian ownership share under this record. The basis cited for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It is a clear national opening, but it should be read alongside Bali’s distinct provincial screening position rather than treated as a substitute for it.

In Bali, this activity is not blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium described in the record. Bali permanently blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA across the island; this activity sits outside that blocked outcome. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The honest conclusion is straightforward: a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, subject to the higher-risk position recorded for the Large scale—not because Bali ignores its moratorium, but because this activity is not within the Low or Medium-Low risk group that moratorium blocks.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is straightforward: a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, subject to the higher-risk position recorded for the Large scale.

editorial.headline: Radioactive Materials and Ionising Generators, Clearly Defined
editorial.standfirst: An open PMA activity for wholesale trade and specified imports of radioactive materials and ionising-radiation generators, available at every listed business scale.
editorial.body:
Wholesale trade in radioactive materials and ionising radiation generators is a tightly stated commercial activity. It covers the wholesale trade of radioactive substances and ionising-radiation generators, while its scope expressly includes the import of ionising-radiation generators and the import of radioactive substances. Those import lines are part of the record itself, not an extrapolation from the word “wholesale”. The result is a registration category with a defined commercial focus: the stated trading and import activity in those named materials and generators.

The business that registers here is the undertaking carrying on that stated wholesale trade, including the specified import lines. It is open at every scale named in the record—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—so the category is available across the full listed range of enterprise sizes. There is no scale singled out as the only route into the activity. For founders, that means the scale selection is broad while the commercial activity remains specific: wholesale trade in radioactive substances and ionising-radiation generators, with both import activities expressly included.

At national level, the foreign-investment reading is direct. The PMA status is TERBUKA and foreign ownership may reach 100%. In practical ownership terms, the record places no national ceiling below full foreign ownership for this activity. The 100% ceiling matters because it is expressly stated for this particular registration category and its stated scope. Foreign capital can therefore enter under the national position presented here, at any of the listed scales.

Bali does not overturn that national position. The provincial assessment is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and the activity is not blocked by Bali's moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High. The moratorium described in the record permanently blocks PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the island; this activity lies outside that blocked band. The honest Bali conclusion is clean: a foreigner can register this activity in Bali today. The record’s reasoning is risk-based, with no separate Bali ownership ceiling or partnership condition stated.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Chemical Wholesale Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for it.
editorial.body:
In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA today. That conclusion sits beside a very different national position: the activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The distinction matters because national openness does not override Bali’s stated, island-wide rule for PMA registration. For this activity, the Bali result is recorded as **Blocked (risk class)**.

The activity itself is wholesale trade in a broad range of non-hazardous basic or industrial chemical materials and goods. Its stated scope includes printer ink, essential oils, industrial gases—including hydrogen—chemical adhesives, dyes, synthetic resins, methanol, paraffin, flavourings and fragrances, soda, industrial salt, acids and sulphur. It is, in other words, a wholesale commercial category for supplying chemical inputs and related goods, while expressly excluding hazardous materials. The breadth of that list should not be mistaken for a licence to extend beyond the stated boundary: the record defines the category through non-hazardous chemical materials and goods.

The national record opens the activity to businesses operating at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. It also identifies the national PMA position through Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For an investor assessing the national framework alone, the message is straightforward: there is no foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. The scale listing is equally broad, covering the full range from micro to large enterprises.

Bali changes the practical answer for PMA registration. The record states that, at the Besar scale, every scope is classified as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration on an island-wide, permanent basis. That is the decisive local fact: this is not a case of a reduced Bali foreign-ownership percentage or a conditional local partnership. It is a registration block for PMA in Bali, despite the 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling. Anyone considering this activity in Bali should therefore read the national openness and the provincial restriction together, with the Bali PMA block determining the local position.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Fertiliser and Agrochemicals: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale fertiliser and agrochemical trade is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium prevents PMA registration of the activity there.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is a wholesale-trade activity: fertilisers and agrochemical—agricultural chemical—products are the goods named in its scope. The definition matters because it identifies the commercial activity through both its mode of trade and its product set. A business registering here is identifying its work as wholesale trade in those products. That is the fixed centre of the activity, and the reference point for reading its available scales and investment position.

The record opens the activity to every stated business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. In other words, the wholesale trade described here is available across all four classifications listed in the record. The essential question remains straightforward: whether the enterprise’s activity is the wholesale trade of fertilisers and agrochemical products. The scale field then confirms that each of the four named classifications is open for that activity.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is just as unambiguous. The status is open, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. A foreign investor may therefore hold the full stake in a nationally registered business carrying on this wholesale activity. That national position is grounded in the cited Presidential Regulations 10/2021 and 49/2021. It is an important answer, but only to the national ownership question; it does not by itself settle whether a PMA registration can proceed in a particular province.

Bali produces the decisive qualification. This activity is marked as blocked for PMA registration there because, at the Large scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registrations in those risk categories. The result is plain: nationally open at 100% does not translate into the ability to register this PMA activity in Bali today. The provincial restriction does not change the activity’s wholesale scope or its national foreign-ownership ceiling; it determines the local registration outcome in Bali, where the activity is blocked under the recorded risk classification and moratorium of May 2026.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open at 100% does not translate into the ability to register this PMA activity in Bali today.

l4_bali.reason: Not among the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026. The low/medium-low risk tier was named only in the Governor's January 2026 request letter (B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP); check the risk tier and zoning on OSS before filing.

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers wholesale trading of hazardous materials (known as 'B2')—substances that are toxic, carcinogenic, teratogenic, mutagenic, corrosive, or irritant, and therefore pose significant health and environmental risks.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this business is 100% open to foreign ownership, but Bali classifies it as medium-to-high risk. It isn’t blocked by the current moratorium, yet every address must pass strict zoning, safety, and environmental checks before a license is issued—so location approval is critical.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: code renumbered.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Perdagangan Besar Bahan Berbahaya (B2) (46753)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: This suits a foreign chemical supplier or industrial wholesaler needing a regulated distribution presence in Bali.

editorial.headline: Hazardous-Materials Wholesale: Foreign-Open, Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in hazardous materials is open to PMA at every listed business scale; in Bali, its Medium-High/High risk at the Besar scale keeps it outside the permanent moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46753 is the wholesale-trade classification for materials described as hazardous because they are toxic, carcinogenic, teratogenic, mutagenic, corrosive or irritating. That is the core of the activity: commerce at wholesale in substances whose stated properties give them their hazardous character. Its scope also covers the full field of foreign trade—imports and exports—for B3 materials that can be used and materials subject to restricted use. The classification therefore draws its boundary from the hazardous properties named in the scope, while placing those materials in a wholesale-trade setting rather than around one named product line.

The record places the activity within reach of businesses at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. This is a broad scale profile. The activity is not confined in the record to one enterprise size; a business at any of the four named scales may register it. The shared activity remains the wholesale trade described in the scope. Scale identifies the stated range of operators, while the scope identifies what is being traded.

Bali requires a separate reading, since the province’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities island-wide. For this activity, the record does not mark PMA registration in Bali as blocked. Its stated reason is risk at the Besar scale: OSS assigns it Medium-High/High risk at that scale, placing it outside the moratorium’s stated low- and medium-low-risk reach. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. This matters because national openness alone would not settle Bali’s position; the provincial rule has its own risk-screening logic.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Wholesale trading of medical devices and laboratory equipment — diagnostic equipment, surgical instruments, hospital furniture, lab instruments, and medical consumables sold to hospitals, clinics, laboratories, and healthcare distributors.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Micro / Small / Medium / Large scale**: Medium-high to high risk. NIB + Izin (full license) required, not automatic.


**PMA:** Fully open to PMA — 100% foreign ownership allowed.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Renumbered/adjusted from KBLI 2020. This is the KBLI 2025 code for the old 46444 (alat kesehatan — medical devices). Do not confuse it with 46430 (consumer optics): corrective lenses and diagnostic devices belong here, not there.
intel_2026.baliContext: Bali's healthcare infrastructure is expanding — BIMC Hospital, Siloam Hospitals, and RSUP Sanglah upgrades are creating procurement demand. Medical device wholesale requires a PAK (Penyalur Alat Kesehatan) license from the Ministry of Health — separate from and in addition to OSS licensing. Imported medical devices must have an AKL/AKD number from BPOM (medical device registry). Medical tourism growth in Bali and Nusa Dua is driving demand for higher-spec equipment.
intel_2026.youllAlsoNeed:
- Ministry of Health PAK license — mandatory separate from OSS
- BPOM AKL/AKD registration for each medical device product
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Medical device wholesale in Bali? Let me explain the PAK license from the Ministry of Health and BPOM device registration requirements.

editorial.headline: Supplying the Tools Behind Human Care
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity covers laboratory and medical equipment for human use, remains open to full foreign ownership nationally, and is not blocked for PMA registration by Bali’s moratorium.
editorial.body:
Wholesale here means supplying the equipment behind human diagnosis, treatment and care: laboratory instruments, medical devices, surgical equipment, orthopaedic equipment and similar goods intended for people. The scope expressly includes both Medical Device Distributors and branches of those distributors. Its centre of gravity is therefore clear. This is a trading activity for specialised human-health and laboratory equipment, bringing several equipment families together under one wholesale function.

The activity is open to businesses at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scale. That range gives the category a broad commercial footing without changing what is being registered: the wholesale trade of laboratory, medical, surgical, orthopaedic and related equipment for human use. A distributor and a distributor branch are both named within the scope, while the scale options recognise that this form of trade may be undertaken by businesses at markedly different stages of development. The commercial identity, however, remains precise rather than expansive: supplying these specified goods at wholesale.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. The activity is open to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In ownership terms, that means the record allows full foreign ownership at the national level. This is a meaningful distinction for founders assessing a distribution business in the health-equipment field: the national position does not leave the foreign stake capped below full ownership. At the same time, that openness belongs to this defined wholesale activity and its stated equipment categories; the clarity of the scope is part of the category’s value.

Bali needs to be read through its own moratorium rule. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low- and Medium-Low-risk activities across the island. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The stated reason is its OSS risk position at the Large scale—Medium-High/High—which places it outside the moratorium’s blocked Low and Medium-Low classes. For a foreign investor considering Bali, the conclusion is therefore straightforward: the activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not barred from PMA registration in Bali by the province’s moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not barred from PMA registration in Bali by the province’s moratorium.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)

editorial.headline: Veterinary Medical Equipment, at Wholesale Scale
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 46792 covers the wholesale movement of animal-health equipment, open nationally to foreign investment and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46792 is the wholesale activity behind the professional equipment used in animal health: laboratory, diagnostic and surgical equipment, alongside comparable tools for animals. Its scope is practical rather than clinical. It covers bringing those goods into Indonesia, sending them out, and distributing them through the market—the commercial infrastructure that places specialist equipment in the hands of animal-health operators.

The registration audience is correspondingly broad but clearly defined: exporters, importers and distributors. The activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, making it relevant both to an established distribution operation and to a business entering the supply chain at a smaller scale. The code describes the wholesale movement of equipment, not the delivery of animal-health treatment itself; that distinction keeps the commercial role of the business in focus.

At the national level, PMA is classified as TERBUKA and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. In plain terms, the record permits full foreign ownership for this activity at the national level. That openness is supported by the cited PMA source, Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For founders assessing a foreign-owned vehicle, this is a meaningful point of clarity: the wholesale trade in these specialised animal-health goods is not framed here as a partially reserved activity.

Bali’s position is also more straightforward than many founders may expect. This activity is not blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium, which applies to all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so the moratorium does not block PMA registration for this code. The Bali status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK—not a claim that the activity is risk-free, but a clear indication that the permanent moratorium is not the barrier here. The national openness and Bali position align: this is an activity a foreign-owned wholesale business can register in Bali today, subject to the record’s stated higher-risk classification at the Besar scale.

editorial.headline: Rubber and Plastics Wholesale: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in basic-form rubber and plastics is fully foreign-open nationally, but Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
This activity is wholesale trade in rubber and plastic materials in their basic forms. The formulation matters because it identifies the commercial activity by the form of the materials and by wholesale trade, not by an added claim about a particular finished product, client, or production step. The record therefore supplies a clean perimeter: rubber and plastic in basic form, sold at wholesale. For a registration decision, that restraint is useful. It keeps attention on the activity actually described and avoids turning a broad materials-trading description into promises the reference does not make. The defining phrase should be treated as the whole stated scope.

The national position is equally direct. Its status is TERBUKA, and foreign ownership can reach 100%. In practical ownership terms, the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership. The activity is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so the scale field does not reserve the listed wholesale activity for a single business size. For someone mapping a proposed business against the reference, this provides two clear national markers: the activity is open to PMA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. These are national attributes, grounded in the listed Perpres source.

Bali changes the outcome completely. The local status is Blocked (risk class) and the record explicitly marks it blocked. A foreigner is unable to register this activity as PMA in Bali today. The given reason is risk classification: at the Besar scale, OSS places every scope at Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s rule blocks PMA for activities in those risk classes across the island, on a permanent basis. The condition applies to the risk classification recorded for every scope at that scale, rather than to an ownership percentage. This is not a partial ownership adjustment; it is a registration block.

The two geographic readings must be held at once. Nationally, this is an open wholesale-trade activity with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling and scope across all named scales. In Bali, the class-risk moratorium governs the present PMA result, so national openness cannot produce a Bali PMA registration. A national 100% ceiling does not overcome Bali’s island-wide PMA moratorium. That distinction is why a national answer alone would be incomplete: the Bali result is recorded directly as a block, with its reason stated in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% ceiling does not overcome Bali’s island-wide PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Wholesale Paper and Cardboard: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A foreign investor cannot register wholesale paper and cardboard in Bali today: although the activity is nationally open to PMA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks it.
editorial.body:
Paper and cardboard are the paired materials at the centre of this wholesale activity. The scope is direct: it covers wholesale trade in paper and cardboard. That clarity matters. The registration describes the commercial act of supplying those materials on a wholesale basis; it does not invite a broader reading than the stated group. Paper and cardboard are named together, so the activity should keep that paired material focus. For founders, the practical starting point is therefore a business whose activity is wholesale paper and cardboard, defined by the scope itself rather than by an assumed downstream use.

At national level, the activity is marked TERBUKA for PMA and has a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Every scale named in the record sits within that national opening, from Mikro through Besar. Taken on its own national terms, that is a fully foreign-owned registration position rather than a partial foreign-stake allowance. The underlying national reference recorded here is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. None of this expands the activity’s scope: it remains wholesale trade in paper and cardboard.

Bali changes the answer decisively. This record marks the Bali status Blocked (risk class) and confirms that PMA registration is blocked. The reason is specific: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. The moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, permanently. In plain English, a foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today—even though the national setting is TERBUKA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The block concerns PMA registration; it does not alter the stated definition of wholesale paper and cardboard.

This is not a national-versus-local preference that can be softened by the activity’s general openness. It is a geographical constraint on PMA registration in Bali, triggered by the stated risk classification at the Besar scale and applied island-wide under the Bali rule. A founder can accurately hold both facts at once: national policy sets a 100% foreign ceiling, while Bali blocks PMA registration for the activity. That distinction is the decision-making fact, and it should be read before treating national openness as a Bali registration outcome. For an investor, the national ceiling does not overturn the island-wide block.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness sets the ceiling, but Bali’s permanent PMA block determines the registration outcome on the island.

editorial.headline: Paper Goods Wholesale: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale paper and cardboard goods—from bags and tissue to disposable diapers and sanitary pads—are nationally open to full foreign ownership, but PMA registration is blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
Wholesale paper and cardboard goods are the subject of this activity, best understood through its everyday inventory. It covers wholesale trade in paper bags, toilet tissue, disposable diapers and disposable sanitary pads: goods spanning packaging, hygiene and routine supply. Rather than treating those examples as exhaustive, the scope places them within a wider wholesale grouping of paper and cardboard goods. The classification therefore provides one commercial description for a varied but recognisably related set of products.

editorial.headline: The Scrap Trade Open Nationally but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in used goods, scrap and recyclable material is fully foreign-open nationally, yet a permanent Bali moratorium prevents PMA registration there today.
editorial.body:
**The immediate point for a foreign investor is stark:** this activity cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. That is a Bali-specific outcome, not a description of the national position. Nationally, it is TERBUKA for PMA, and its maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In Bali, however, the permanent, island-wide moratorium closes the PMA registration route. The contrast is categorical: the national ceiling establishes that full foreign ownership is allowed, while the Bali rule prevents the PMA registration needed to use that national setting in the province. Both statements are true at once.

At its core, this is wholesale trade in used goods and scrap: metal and non-metal cuttings and materials for recycling. The record defines a substantial handling role around those goods. It includes collecting them, sorting and separating them, and dismantling goods that still yield useful parts—cars are the example given—before packing or repacking, storage and delivery. The commercial object is the purchase and sale of residual goods that still retain value. The boundary is equally important: these steps can prepare, organise and move goods, but the scope expressly excludes any real transformation of them.

The activity is open at every listed enterprise scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. No one scale is presented as the sole route into the category; each is included in the record. For a PMA registration assessed nationally, the position is direct: TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. Full foreign ownership is therefore available in the national setting. Yet that national figure is a ceiling, not a promise that PMA registration will be accepted in every provincial setting. Bali supplies a separate and decisive local result.

Bali’s barrier arises from the risk classification recorded for this activity, rather than from a different commercial definition. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah on every scope in the record. Bali blocks PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk classifications under an island-wide, permanent moratorium; the stated moratorium date is May 2026. National openness therefore does not translate into a PMA registration route in Bali for this activity. The honest reading is to hold both facts together: the national 100% ceiling is real, and so is Bali’s current block.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness therefore does not translate into a PMA registration route in Bali for this activity.

editorial.headline: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A foreign investor cannot register this wholesale activity in Bali today, even though it is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership across every business scale.
editorial.body:
At its centre, this is a broad wholesale category for products not otherwise included in the preceding wholesale groupings. Its expressly stated examples move from textile fibre and precious stones—diamonds, gems, sapphires and others—to e-liquid for electronic cigarettes. They also include wooden packaging in the form of boxes, crates, drums and similar forms, as well as wooden cable reels, pallets and other wooden transport boards. What joins these lines is not a single material or customer market, but their placement within this residual wholesale field. The scope should therefore be read for the products it expressly names, rather than as a shortcut for a narrower specialty trade.

The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses. That is the complete scale range given in the record, which does not narrow the category to a particular enterprise size. At the national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical ownership terms, the national record permits a foreign investor to hold the entire stake. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The point is straightforward: the national setting is not a partial-ownership exception; the listed ceiling is full foreign ownership.

That clarity is undone in Bali. A foreigner cannot obtain PMA registration for this activity in Bali today. It is marked Blocked (risk class): the OSS assessment at the Besar scale is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every stated scope, and the record says this triggers Bali’s moratorium. The island-wide, permanent provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The stated block is tied to the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026, and cites Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.

This creates a precise, not paradoxical, reading. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA with a 100% ceiling and across all four named business scales. In Bali, however, that national position does not produce a PMA registration path, because its large-scale OSS risk classification falls inside the province’s permanent moratorium. Anyone evaluating the activity for a Bali establishment needs to treat those statements as simultaneous: full national foreign-ownership openness on one hand, and a current Bali PMA block on the other.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, the activity is open to PMA with a 100% ceiling; in Bali, it has no PMA registration path.

editorial.headline: Self-Service Wholesale Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This broad, self-service wholesale activity permits 100% foreign ownership nationally, yet PMA registration is blocked in Bali under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
For a foreign founder considering Bali, the immediate answer is blunt: this activity cannot be registered there as a PMA business today. The code covers self-service wholesale or cash-and-carry trading in a wide variety of goods without a particular product specialism. Prices are set in advance; buyers select and take their own goods, then pay at a cashier. Its defining feature is therefore the wholesale format itself: a broad, non-specialist assortment handled through self-service, rather than simply any enterprise selling many types of goods.

Nationally, the position is open. The activity is listed as TERBUKA for PMA and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. It is also open at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. The record therefore does not confine the activity to one category of operator or reserve it for a narrower scale. For an investor reading the national framework, the starting point is clear: PMA participation is permitted, and the national foreign-ownership ceiling is full. The cited basis for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali does not simply inherit that national result. Its local status is Blocked (risk class), and the stated reason is specific: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. That brings the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, recorded as applying from May 2026. The practical result is categorical for a foreign-owned registration on the island: despite being nationally open, this activity is blocked for PMA in Bali.

This is a distinction that needs to remain sharp in any setup decision. The national 100% ceiling describes the level of foreign ownership the national framework permits; it does not override Bali’s local, risk-based PMA restriction. Nor does national availability across Mikro through Besar alter the Bali outcome, because the Bali finding is tied to the stated OSS risk position at Besar scale across every scope. Taken together, the record supports one precise conclusion: this is a nationally PMA-open self-service wholesale activity, available across the listed scales with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, but it cannot be registered as PMA in Bali under the island-wide permanent moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, but it does not override Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA block for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.
