editorial.headline: Traditional Wholesale Is Open Nationally but Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A traditional, negotiation-led general wholesale activity open nationally to PMA at 100%, yet blocked for PMA registration across Bali under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46902 is the general, non-specialist wholesale activity for a broad assortment of goods when the business does not use a self-service system. The operative picture is traditional wholesale, where prices are generally settled through negotiation. That is the centre of gravity of the activity: wholesale trade in varied goods, rather than a format defined by a particular specialism or by self-service. The scope expressly points to traditional wholesalers and traditional wholesale warehouses, grounding the activity in a conventional bargaining-led wholesale setting.

Eligibility is broad by business scale. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so its formal scale coverage runs from micro through large business. Its goods description remains equally broad: various goods may be traded wholesale without a specified specialisation, provided the system is not self-service. Taken together, those points make the activity legible: it is defined by the general character of its wholesale trade and its traditional transaction format, while remaining available at every listed scale.

Nationally, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national position should be read exactly as recorded: foreign investment is open at the national level. Bali produces a different practical conclusion. A foreigner cannot register this activity through PMA in Bali today. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class), and the stated reason is that, at Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. The Bali moratorium dated 13 May 2026 blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA, island-wide and permanently.

The result is a clean jurisdictional split, not a partial Bali ownership cap. The only foreign-ownership figure in the record is the national ceiling of 100%; Bali’s conclusion is instead a block on PMA registration based on the stated moratorium. The national ceiling therefore does not create a Bali registration route for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% ceiling is not a Bali permission: for this code, the Bali PMA route is blocked by the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Self-Service Food Retail: National Limits and Bali’s Closed Door
editorial.standfirst: This code covers self-service retail led by food, beverages or tobacco, yet its national foreign-ownership ceiling is 0% and Bali expressly closes it to PMA.
editorial.body:
This activity is the self-service retailing of a broad mix of everyday goods in which food ingredients, prepared food, beverages or tobacco remain the dominant offer. Prices are set in advance; customers select items themselves and pay at a cashier. The format may also sell selected non-food items—household furnishings, children’s toys, medicines, medical devices and clothing—but these do not alter the central character of the business: food, beverages or tobacco lead the assortment. Hypermarkets and supermarkets are expressly within its scope.

The code is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because scale does not dilute the operating identity. Whether the enterprise is small or large, it remains a self-service retailer whose principal merchandise is food, beverages or tobacco, with any permitted non-food range remaining secondary to that retail core.

Nationally, the PMA position is limited, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 0%. In practical terms, the record does not present this as a route for foreign equity participation. The applicable national reference is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. A registration decision should therefore begin with the actual retail model—self-service checkout, predetermined prices and a food-, beverage- or tobacco-led range—rather than with the presence of ancillary household or consumer goods on the shelves.

Bali is more direct still. The provincial status is closed, and the stated reason is that minimarkets and supermarkets are reserved for Indonesian citizens and closed to PMA. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today through PMA. Bali also maintains an island-wide, permanent block on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities; the record identifies that provincial rule separately. The essential conclusion is not a matter of branding or store size: this self-service retail activity is nationally limited to a 0% foreign-ownership ceiling and expressly closed to PMA in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today through PMA.

editorial.headline: The Neighbourhood Shop, Nationally Open but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This is the everyday mixed-goods shop centred on food, drinks or tobacco—open nationally to full foreign ownership, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the defining fact is straightforward: this activity cannot be registered through PMA in Bali today. Nationally, it is open to foreign investment with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali, however, marks the activity as closed to PMA. The provincial position sits alongside a permanent, island-wide rule blocking all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities for PMA, while the stated Bali rationale reserves minimarkets and supermarkets for Indonesian citizens.

The activity itself belongs to the texture of daily provisioning. It covers retailing a varied mix of necessities principally made up of foodstuffs or prepared food, beverages, and tobacco, conducted outside the self-service model of a minimarket, supermarket, or hypermarket. A shop may also sell selected non-food items—clothing, household furniture, or children’s toys—without changing the essential character of the business. The familiar reference point is a *warung* or a shop for basic household needs: practical, mixed in its stock, and oriented around everyday purchases rather than a self-service retail format.

The national classification does not confine the activity to one business size. It is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the category describes the nature of the retail operation rather than imposing a single commercial profile. What holds it together is the principal emphasis on food, drinks, or tobacco within a varied-needs retail offer, and the fact that it is not run as a self-service convenience store or larger self-service outlet.

The geographic distinction should therefore be read without smoothing over its consequence. A national PMA opening and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a Bali registration route where the Bali status is TERTUTUP. For an investor considering Bali, the present answer is not a qualified yes: PMA registration for this activity is closed. For activity planning elsewhere in Indonesia, the national record remains fully foreign-open; in Bali, the provincial restriction is the operative reality.
editorial.pullQuote: A national PMA opening does not create a Bali registration route where Bali marks the activity as closed.

editorial.headline: A Self-Service Retail Format Open Nationally, but Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This self-service, non-food retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
This activity covers self-service retailing of a wide mix of goods that are principally not food, beverages or tobacco. Its natural setting is the department-store format: a customer moves through a broad assortment rather than a single specialised line. Clothing, furniture, jewellery, children’s toys, sporting equipment and cosmetics are among the goods identified in the scope. The defining feature is both the breadth of the merchandise and the self-service system through which it is sold.

The category is available across the stated business scales, from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah and Besar. In practical terms, it is the activity classification for a retailer operating that broad, self-service general-merchandise model. The scope does not narrow the business to one product family; it describes a retail operation whose main offer is a varied non-food assortment, with the department store offered as its clearest example.

At the national level, PMA is open, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That is a clear national setting for foreign investment in the activity. Bali is the decisive exception. data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Nationally Open Retail, but Off-Limits to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A mixed non-food retail activity open to all scales and 100% foreign ownership nationally—but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is retail of a varied assortment of goods that are principally neither food, beverages nor tobacco, conducted other than through a self-service system. The stated scope names clothing, household furnishings, jewellery, children’s toys and cosmetics among the merchandise that may be brought together. These goods sit under a single management, which gives the activity its character: a mixed, integrated non-food retail offer rather than a shop defined by one narrow product line. The record also evokes a general-goods shop as an example, but the operative idea is the managed assortment of varied merchandise.

Who can use the activity? The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises. That is a complete scale range, from micro through large. It does not convert the classification into a different activity at each size: the subject remains the same integrated retail of varied, primarily non-food goods. The scale field establishes where registration is open; the scope sets the practical boundary, centred on the mixture of goods and the single management that brings it together.

At national level, the foreign-investment position is unusually straightforward. The activity is marked TERBUKA for PMA, and its maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In plain terms, national treatment allows a fully foreign-owned PMA registration for this activity. The record assigns that position to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower national foreign-ownership cap to interpret: the stated national ceiling is 100%.

Bali is the decisive qualification—and it is not a softer local ownership limit. Today, a foreign investor cannot obtain PMA registration for this activity in Bali. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, and the record says that this triggers Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities from PMA island-wide and permanently; the activity is therefore marked Blocked (risk class). The reason records the block in May 2026. The honest reading is that the national 100% ceiling remains the national position, while Bali’s PMA registration block governs the Bali outcome.

editorial.headline: Paddy and Palawija Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Specialised retail of paddy and palawija is open to 100% foreign ownership nationally, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
**A foreign investor cannot register this activity as a PMA business in Bali today.** That is the point that should lead any reading of the code, because its national status and its Bali outcome are materially different. Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA—open to PMA—and its foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In Bali, the record classifies it as blocked for PMA registration. It is not a contradiction: the fields describe different regulatory levels. The distinction is not a reduced national ownership allowance; it comes from Bali’s risk-based moratorium, which applies island-wide and permanently to PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities.

KBLI 47211 is specialised retail trade in paddy and palawija, a crop group illustrated in the record by unhulled rice, corn, sweet potatoes, cassava, taro, soybeans, peanuts, black beans and peas. Its scope is deliberately particular. It describes retailing of that named agricultural basket, bringing grain and maize together with tubers and legumes under one focused commercial activity. The examples do more than decorate the title: they set the working boundaries of what the activity is about, keeping the editorial focus on paddy and the palawija crops expressly identified in the record.

The registration field is broad. The activity is open at every stated scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—Micro, Small, Medium and Large. This is a full scale range, rather than a narrow size classification, and it gives the activity a national place from the smallest listed band through to the largest. But that breadth does not alter the ownership reading. The 100% ceiling is national; it must not be recast as Bali permission. Both readings have to be retained at once. National foreign-ownership capacity and an ability to register a PMA business in Bali are separate questions in this record.

Why Bali differs is stated with some precision. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk level is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, and the record identifies the moratorium in May 2026 as the reason for this code’s Bali block. intel_2026.whatItMeans: Retail sale of alcoholic beverages not consumed on premises. Liquor stores, wine shops, bottle shops. Covers all alcohol classes: Class A (under 5%), Class B (5-20%), and Class C (over 20%). If customers buy bottles and take them home, this is the code — not 56301 (bars).
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Medium/Large scale ONLY** (no Micro/Small). HIGH risk (Tinggi). NIB + full License (Izin) — specifically SKP-A, SKP-B, and SKP-C (Surat Keterangan Pengecer Minuman Beralkohol) for each alcohol class. Requires SIUP-MB from the Ministry of Trade, plus approval from local Dinas Perdagangan. You must obtain a Letter of Appointment from a licensed alcohol distributor before you can legally stock and sell.

**PMA:** TERBATAS with special conditions — the Perpres 10/2021 lampiran admits foreign investment in alcoholic-beverage retail only through special distribution networks and designated locations (no fixed equity percentage is published), with partnership with UMKM/Koperasi as the registered condition. This is NOT fully open — structure and location determine whether OSS accepts the registration.

OSS will auto-reject if your geotagged location falls within the prohibited radius. The bootleg alcohol crackdown (arak oplosan deaths make headlines regularly) means authorities scrutinize supply chain documentation heavily. Every bottle needs a paper trail. editorial.headline: Alcohol Retail, Where the Sale Ends Before the Drink Begins
editorial.standfirst: Specialist retail of alcoholic drinks spans every listed business scale, but foreign-investment access in Bali turns on the exact declared scope and its OSS risk.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is specialist retail of alcoholic beverages for consumption elsewhere, rather than drinks served to be consumed where they are bought. Its territory is broad in format while remaining precise in purpose: spirits such as whisky, brandy, gin, arak, rum and sake; wine; and malt-based drinks including beer, ale and stout all sit within the stated scope. The retail sale may take place indoors, at roadside stalls, from shop-front verandas, in movable market spaces, through other media, or online. The record also expressly includes alcohol retailers in duty-free shops and retailers of Group B and C alcoholic beverages.

The activity is available to micro, small, medium and large businesses. That breadth of scale should not be mistaken for a simple national foreign-investment invitation. Nationally, the PMA position is recorded as restricted, with the foreign-ownership setting described as “special” rather than expressed as a general percentage ceiling. The supplied reference is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In practical editorial terms, this is a retail activity with a clearly defined commercial subject, but a national PMA status that requires it to be read as restricted rather than assumed to be fully foreign-open.

Bali introduces a narrower, scope-sensitive distinction. The record does not say that PMA registration is blocked outright for this activity in Bali. Instead, it says the outcome depends on the scope declared. At the large-business scale, OSS risk is low for some scopes and higher for others. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities; for this record, PMA registration in Bali is available only when the higher-risk scope is declared. The conclusion is therefore neither a blanket refusal nor an automatic approval. For a founder seeking PMA registration, the decisive issue is the exact scope declared and its live OSS risk classification.
editorial.pullQuote: For a founder seeking PMA registration, the decisive issue is the exact scope declared and its live OSS risk classification.

editorial.headline: Retailing Non-Alcoholic Drinks: Broad in Format, Closed to PMA
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans specialist retail of take-away non-alcoholic drinks at every business scale, but it is closed to foreign investment nationally and cannot be registered as PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the specialist retail sale of non-alcoholic drinks intended for consumption away from the point of sale. Its scope includes soft drinks such as lemonade, soda water, passion-fruit drinks, bottled tea, mineral water and *beras kencur*, alongside coffee drinks and other non-alcoholic beverages. The defining distinction is straightforward: these are drinks not consumed directly on the premises.

The retail format is deliberately broad. Trade may take place inside a building, at a roadside stall, from a shopfront, at a flexible and movable market stall, through other media, or online. That gives the activity a wide commercial footprint while retaining a clear focus on retailing drinks for off-premises consumption. It is open to businesses operating at the Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales.

The ownership position, however, is unequivocal. Nationally, this activity is closed to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 0%. A foreign investor therefore cannot register this activity as a PMA business in Indonesia. The availability of several business scales does not alter that ownership status; scale describes the sizes at which the activity may be conducted, while the PMA classification determines the foreign-investment route.

Bali offers no separate opening. The activity is also closed for PMA registration in the province, and a foreigner cannot register it in Bali today. The stated reason is that, at the Large scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The moratorium is identified as taking effect on May 13, 2026. For founders, the conclusion is not a question of choosing a different retail location or format within Bali: the national foreign-ownership closure already governs the activity, and Bali’s moratorium reinforces the same result at the provincial level.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor therefore cannot register this activity as a PMA business in Indonesia.

l4_bali.reason: Not a Bali-specific rule: nationally TERBATAS (0% max foreign ownership), per Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

editorial.headline: Tobacco Retail Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans tobacco, smoking accessories, e-cigarettes and e-liquids—open nationally to full foreign ownership, yet blocked for PMA registration across Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this retail activity in Bali today. That is the practical starting point, even though the activity is nationally open to foreign investment with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali’s island-wide permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities, and this activity falls within that restriction: at the Besar scale, every scope is classified as Low or Medium-Low risk. The block is tied to the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026.

The commercial scope is wider than a cigarette counter. It covers retail sales of tobacco in forms including kretek cigarettes, white cigarettes, cigars, clove tobacco cigarettes, loose tobacco, nasal tobacco, and tobacco for pipes or rolling papers. It also includes the retail sale of smoking products and accessories such as lighters, pipes and cigarette-rolling equipment. Electronic cigarettes and e-liquid sit within the same activity, placing conventional tobacco retail and vaping products inside one defined retail scope.

This is an activity for a retailer dealing directly in those products and accessories, rather than a description of a single product format or outlet style. It is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar business scales. Nationally, the investment setting is clear: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign ownership ceiling of 100%, under the cited presidential regulations. That national openness, however, does not override the provincial PMA registration block in Bali.

For founders, the important distinction is not semantic but operational. A nationally open activity may still be unavailable for PMA registration in Bali when the provincial moratorium applies. Here, the relevant Bali status is Blocked (risk class) because the recorded Besar-scale risk classification is Low or Medium-Low throughout the activity’s scopes. The national position remains full foreign ownership; the Bali position is that PMA registration is blocked island-wide under the permanent moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not override Bali’s island-wide block on PMA registration for this activity.

editorial.headline: Rice Retail Is Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM — Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: This activity — retail of rice (beras) as a specialised store — is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 49/2021's Lampiran II, which sets foreign ownership at 0% and puts it out of reach of a PT PMA anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
Retail rice is a more precise activity than its plain title suggests. It covers the specialised retail sale of a range of rice varieties, including Cianjur, Cisadane, Saigon and glutinous rice. The focus is not merely rice as a commodity, but its sale through a retail activity dedicated to the category and its distinct varieties. That specificity gives the activity a clear commercial identity: a business built around retailing rice in its many recognised forms.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity is 0%. Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II p.13-14, entry 46, sub-row "Beras" (ex-KBLI 2020 47241) allocates retail of rice (beras) as a specialised store to Koperasi and UMKM (the *dialokasikan* column), so a PT PMA cannot register it anywhere in Indonesia — not only in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The Perpres 49/2021 annex allocates retail of rice (beras) as a specialised store to Koperasi and UMKM, so the national ceiling is 0% — not a local Bali restriction on an otherwise-open activity.

editorial.headline: Coffee and Sugar Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A specialised retail activity for coffee, sugars and tea is nationally open to foreign investment, but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
**A foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today.** That is the decisive local fact, even though the activity is nationally classified as open to PMA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. The gap is not a minor local preference: Bali’s stated status is a risk-class block. At the Besar scale, OSS places every scope under Low or Medium-Low risk; Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for all KBLI in those risk bands. The record identifies the moratorium as effective from May 13, 2026.

On its commercial terms, this is specialised retailing of coffee, white sugar, brown or palm sugar, and tea. It concerns a retailer focused on those named products, rather than an undefined general-trade proposition. The activity should be read at that level of specificity: retail trade in coffee, the stated sugars, and tea. The scope does not supply a product hierarchy, operating format, or wider-service claim, so none should be assumed. Its clarity lies in the product set itself and in the fact that it is retail trade.

The registration profile spans Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 cited as the PMA source. Those national facts remain meaningful, but they do not erase the separate Bali result. The same record that says the activity is TERBUKA nationally says it is Blocked (risk class) in Bali.

For a founder, the conclusion must preserve both truths without softening either. A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling describes the national position; it does not create a route to PMA registration in Bali where the moratorium applies. Nor is the Bali constraint presented as a percentage cap or partnership requirement. It is a block linked to the stated OSS risk classification at the Besar scale and the Bali-wide rule for Low and Medium-Low risk classifications. That is the current practical boundary for this activity in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling describes the national position; it does not create a route to PMA registration in Bali where the moratorium applies.

editorial.standfirst: This activity — retail of processed meat (daging olahan) as a specialised store — is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 49/2021's Lampiran II, which sets foreign ownership at 0% and puts it out of reach of a PT PMA anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
**This is a retail activity defined by processed meat.** The scope is specialised retail sale of varied processed-meat products, not a broad food-trade label. Its examples—sausages, bakso meatballs, and abon, a shredded-meat preparation—make the commercial centre of gravity clear: the sale of meat that has already been prepared or processed. The scope spans products made from beef, pork, poultry, lamb, rabbit, goat and camel, as well as other fresh meats named in the record. The record presents a retail activity whose identity comes from the processed nature of its merchandise. That specificity keeps the registration anchored to a particular retail offer rather than to meat in general.

**The scale range is broad.** The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That is the whole stated scale spectrum, so it is not presented as a narrow category available only to one business size. The scope remains specialised retail of processed-meat products of the kinds described in the record. For operators, this produces a clear description: a specialty retail business centred on processed-meat goods. The four scale labels set out the stated business-size range; they do not broaden the activity into meat commerce generally. Its boundaries remain merchandise-led and retail-specific.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity is 0%. Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II p.13-14, entry 46, sub-row "Daging dan ikan olahan" (ex-KBLI 2020 47245 — split heir, together with 47246, of the one row naming both meat and fish) allocates retail of processed meat (daging olahan) as a specialised store to Koperasi and UMKM (the *dialokasikan* column), so a PT PMA cannot register it anywhere in Indonesia — not only in Bali.

editorial.standfirst: This retail activity spans salted, dried and other processed seafood products, but foreign-investment registration in Bali is blocked by the province-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is the retail sale of processed fish, shrimp and shellfish products. Its scope includes salted or dried seafood, alongside products such as fish sausage, fish balls and shredded fish. The examples range across anchovy, shark, scad, grouper and other fish, as well as shrimp, tiny shrimp, squid, clams, mussels and shellfish. The classification is deliberately broad in its retail setting: it covers sales conducted inside a building as well as relevant trade from roadside stalls, shop-front verandas, and movable or pushable market stalls.

That breadth matters because the activity describes the point of sale, not a single product format or a single retail environment. A business may register it for the retail trade of varied processed seafood products, whether the offering is anchored in dried and salted goods or in processed forms such as sausage, fish balls and shredded fish. It is open across the full listed scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The record therefore gives the activity room to serve small retail operations and larger businesses within the same classification.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity is 0%. Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II p.13-14, entry 46, sub-row "Daging dan ikan olahan" (ex-KBLI 2020 47245 — split heir, together with 47245, of the one row naming both meat and fish) allocates retail of processed fish (ikan olahan) as a specialised store to Koperasi and UMKM (the *dialokasikan* column), so a PT PMA cannot register it anywhere in Indonesia — not only in Bali.

editorial.headline: Fuel Retail at Indonesia’s Filling Stations: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the sale of transport fuel at filling facilities, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
This activity is the retail sale of fuel through filling facilities serving land, sea and air transport. Its reach is broader than the familiar roadside station: it includes petroleum fuel, gaseous fuel, LPG, LNG and other fuel types, including hydrogen, supplied for motor vehicles, speed boats and generators. The setting is the fuel-filling facility itself, whether serving cars and motorcycles or transport beyond the road. In practice, the activity may also sit alongside sales of lubricants, cooling products, cleaning materials and other goods used for cars and motorcycles.

It is an activity open across every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the description is framed around operating infrastructure and the direct retail supply of fuel, rather than a narrow product category. The business is defined by the point of sale and the transport use it serves: a facility where fuel is made available to vehicles, vessels or generators, with the familiar adjacent range of vehicle-care goods permitted within the same commercial setting.

For foreign investment, the national position is direct. The activity is classified as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Accordingly, the national record allows this activity to have full foreign ownership. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower foreign-ownership cap in the record to qualify that national position.

Bali does not reverse that result. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA activities classified as Low or Medium-Low risk across the island. This activity is not marked as blocked: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not caught by that moratorium. Bali’s recorded status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For an investor considering a fuel-filling operation in Bali, the honest reading is therefore straightforward: the activity remains open for PMA registration, while the relevant record identifies the Besar-scale activity as carrying a medium-high or high OSS risk classification rather than a moratorium block.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not reverse the national position: this activity remains open for PMA registration.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Fuel Retail Beyond Filling Stations: The National and Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers retail fuel distribution beyond filling-station premises, from fuel agents to specified LPG agents, with national foreign ownership open up to 100%.
editorial.body:
This activity is for retail trade in petroleum fuel, gaseous fuels and other fuels conducted outside fuel-filling facilities. Its scope includes fuel oil, LPG, LNG, CNG and other fuel types supplied for land, sea and air transport, whether or not lubricant sales accompany the trade. In practical terms, it speaks to the agent model: fuel agents and specified LPG agents, including agents for 3 kg LPG.

It is an activity available across the full business-scale range recorded here: micro, small, medium and large. That breadth matters because the classification is not confined to a single size of operator. The common thread is the retail supply of fuel outside filling-station premises, rather than a particular corporate form, sales channel or commercial ambition beyond the scope stated in the record.

Nationally, the position is open to foreign investment. The foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, under the cited presidential regulations. That is a clear national setting, but Bali requires its own reading rather than an automatic assumption. The Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the activity is not marked as blocked for PMA registration. For large-scale operations, the OSS risk assessment is medium-high or high; the record therefore states that it is not blocked by Bali’s moratorium.

The distinction is material because Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. This activity is not placed in that blocked position in the record. A foreign investor considering fuel-agent or specified-LPG-agent retail activity in Bali can therefore read the result plainly: national ownership is open up to 100%, and Bali does not block this activity under the stated moratorium basis. The operative caution is not a hidden prohibition, but the need to keep the business within the actual fuel-retail scope described here and to recognise the recorded higher-risk position at large scale.
editorial.pullQuote: National ownership is open up to 100%, and Bali does not block this activity under the stated moratorium basis.

editorial.headline: Lubricants Retail Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers retail sales of vehicle lubricants and cooling products—open nationally to all business scales, yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign-owned business cannot register this retail activity in Bali today. That is the decisive local fact for a code that, at national level, is otherwise open to foreign investment. The activity itself is focused and practical: retail trade in lubricating oils and cooling products for motor vehicles. It belongs to the everyday maintenance economy, serving the fluids and products that keep vehicles operating within their intended temperature and lubrication requirements.

The national position is unambiguous. The activity is listed as open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is also open across the full range of stated business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In other words, the national framework does not reserve the activity for a particular size of enterprise, nor does it impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership in the record provided. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali changes the practical result for PMA registration. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): blocked on risk-class grounds. At the Besar scale, every scope is classified in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. That moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA across the province, and is described in the record as island-wide and permanent. The block is therefore not a national restriction on the retail sale of lubricants and cooling products; it is Bali’s local PMA-registration position.

For founders, the distinction deserves to be read plainly rather than softened. A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not create a route to PMA registration in Bali where the provincial moratorium applies. The activity remains nationally open across Mikro through Besar scales, but Bali’s risk-based block governs the local PMA outcome. The relevant Bali moratorium is identified as taking effect on May 13, 2026, with the stated source being the Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not create a route to PMA registration in Bali where the provincial moratorium applies.

editorial.headline: Computer Retail Is Open Nationally, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers specialist retail sales of computers and related equipment—nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the specialist retail trade of computers and their equipment. Its scope includes personal computers, laptops, printers, photocopying machines, interactive whiteboards and video-conferencing equipment. The common thread is a retail offer centred on computing hardware and its associated tools: the kind of business that places these products before end customers through a dedicated sales operation. The definition is broad enough to encompass a varied technology assortment, but specific in its commercial focus on computers and the equipment that supports their use.

At national level, the foreign-investment position is clear. The activity is listed as **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership allowance of **100%**. In practical terms, a foreign investor may hold the full ownership stake nationally under this activity. The record also makes the activity open across the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the code is not presented as the preserve of one business size: it is available from micro through large-scale enterprise, while retaining the same specialist retail character.

Bali is where the national permission stops being the whole answer. Today, a foreign investor has no route to register this activity as PMA in Bali. The Bali record marks it as blocked on risk-class grounds: at the Besar scale, OSS classifies every scope within the activity as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. That classification brings the activity within Bali’s permanent, province-wide moratorium, recorded here from May 13, 2026. The restriction is therefore not a reduced foreign-ownership percentage or a local ownership condition. It is a bar on PMA registration in Bali for this activity.

The distinction should be read exactly as it stands. Nationally, this is a fully foreign-open specialist computer-retail activity, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling and access across all stated business scales. In Bali, however, the relevant question is no longer how much foreign ownership is permitted. The moratorium prevents PMA registration altogether. For founders considering this activity, that is the decisive geographic fact: the national opening remains real, but it does not create a PMA registration path in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, this is fully open to foreign ownership; in Bali, the moratorium prevents PMA registration altogether.

editorial.headline: The Business of Selling Physical Video Games in Indonesia
editorial.standfirst: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this physical-games retail activity is nevertheless unavailable for PMA registration anywhere in Bali.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering KBLI 47402, the essential conclusion is geographical: it cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. That is despite a national classification of TERBUKA and a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The Bali result is not a reduced ownership allowance. It is a registration block, applied under the province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium for PMA activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. The record states that, at the Besar scale, every scope of this activity carries a Low or Medium-Low OSS risk assessment; Bali therefore marks it Blocked (risk class).

At its centre, this is a retail trade activity for video-game console equipment and for video-game products sold in physical form. The record is specific about the tangible formats: cartridges, CDs, DVDs, and other physical forms. That focus gives the classification its practical shape: the retail sale of equipment and physical game products. Direct sales are also noted in the recorded scope.

The classification is available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The record therefore opens the activity across the full stated range of scales. Yet it also provides the decisive Bali-specific detail for a foreign-owned registration: the risk finding cited for the Besar scale connects this activity to the province-wide PMA moratorium. National scale availability should be read alongside, rather than in place of, the Bali registration position.

Nationally, the position is straightforward: PMA is open, with ownership permitted up to 100%, under the cited Perpres sources. In Bali, the conclusion is equally straightforward but different: a PMA investor cannot register this activity on the island today, because the relevant Low and Medium-Low risk categories are blocked permanently. These are two distinct layers of the same record—national access on one hand, and a Bali-specific registration prohibition on the other—without turning the national 100% ceiling into a Bali permission.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, a PMA investor cannot register this activity on the island today, because the relevant Low and Medium-Low risk categories are blocked permanently.

editorial.headline: Software Retail Is Nationally Open, but Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailing physical, perpetual-use software is open to foreign ownership nationwide, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for the activity.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this software-retail activity in Bali today through PMA. The record attributes the block to Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium, dated 13 May 2026, for PMA activities classified Low or Medium-Low risk. That local restriction creates a sharp boundary around an activity the national record otherwise marks as open to PMA. The national and provincial readings need to be kept distinct from the start.

At its core, the activity is specialised retail sale of software supplied in physical form with perpetual rights of use. The category is defined by those two details: a physical format and a continuing right of use. The scope also expressly refers to direct sales, without further qualification. Its practical centre is a retail transaction in a tangible software product for which the customer receives a non-expiring right to use it.

The activity is available to businesses at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That broad formal range is important context, but it does not erase the Bali outcome. The record identifies the OSS risk at Besar scale as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. In Bali, that classification falls within the stated moratorium, which blocks PMA registration for all activities carrying Low or Medium-Low risk. The block follows the risk class rather than an implied commercial distinction.

Across Indonesia, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with maximum foreign ownership set at 100%. In plain terms, a foreign investor may hold the full ownership stake nationally for this activity. Bali does not present a lower ownership percentage here; it presents a block on PMA registration. The result is therefore two-level: national openness establishes the foreign-ownership ceiling, while the Bali moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity on the island. The national setting is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021; Bali’s rule is attributed to Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness establishes the ownership ceiling, while Bali’s moratorium stops the PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retail sales of phones and their accessories are nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register this retail-phone activity as PMA in Bali today. The national entry position is open, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100 per cent, but the island-level conclusion runs in the other direction. The record states that, at large scale, every scope is Low or Medium-Low risk. That classification puts the activity under Bali’s province-wide, permanent PMA moratorium from 13 May 2026. The result is a block on PMA registration in Bali, notwithstanding the nationally open status.

At its core, this is the retail sale of telephones and the items sold around them. It embraces mobile phones, smartphones and telephone sets, alongside accessories including screen protectors, cases or protective covers, chargers and hands-free devices. Its scope is commercially specific: a consumer retail activity defined by the phone itself and the accessories that protect, charge or support it. The record names both the principal products and their immediate supporting goods, giving the activity a clear retail centre of gravity.

The scale is deliberately broad. Micro, small, medium and large businesses are all open scales for the activity, so the record does not confine participation to a single size of enterprise. That breadth, however, should not blur the two separate questions a founder must answer. One is national ownership eligibility: the activity is open to PMA, with full foreign ownership allowed at the national ceiling. The other is whether that PMA registration can be made in Bali. On the facts recorded, it cannot. The large-scale risk classification is the point at which the Bali restriction becomes decisive.

This is therefore a case where a national permission is real yet cannot be treated as a Bali registration path. The Bali position is a block tied to the applicable risk class, rather than a reduced foreign-ownership ceiling. Nothing in the record reduces the national 100 per cent ceiling; equally, nothing in it creates a Bali exception to the moratorium. The clean reading is simply this: the activity remains nationally open to PMA across its stated scales, while Bali presently bars PMA registration because the activity falls within the moratorium’s Low or Medium-Low risk reach.
editorial.pullQuote: The clean reading is simply this: the activity remains nationally open to PMA across its stated scales, while Bali presently bars PMA registration because the activity falls within the moratorium’s Low or Medium-Low risk reach.

editorial.headline: Office-Machinery Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailing typewriters, calculating machines and cash registers is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
This activity is specialist retail in office machinery other than computers. Its stated examples—typewriters, calculating machines and cash registers—make the commercial focus unusually concrete: it concerns retail trade in office equipment within that defined category. The phrase “specialist retail” matters because the record gives the activity a focused subject rather than a generic office-business label. Computers are expressly outside the stated scope, so the activity remains centred on the office machines named in the definition.

At the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, registration remains open. Each of those four classifications is explicitly listed as open, so the national record does not confine this retail activity to one business scale. That provides an important national baseline for founders assessing the activity’s formal scope. It is not, however, a universal permission: the scale field says which classifications are open nationally, not whether PMA registration remains available in a particular location.

At the national level, this activity is TERBUKA to PMA and has a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical English, the national position permits full foreign ownership for this defined retail activity. The source named for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Read on its own, the national entry is direct: no lower national foreign-ownership cap is stated. But that answer belongs to the national layer. The record also supplies a separate Bali layer, whose effect is not softened by the 100% national ceiling.

Bali produces the decisive present-day qualification. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is described as Low/Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, and this activity is consequently marked as blocked for PMA registration. The moratorium is recorded as applying in May 2026. Nationally open to full foreign ownership does not make the activity registrable for PMA in Bali today. That outcome is not a reduction of the national percentage; it is a Bali registration block arising from the risk-based moratorium. A founder should hold both conclusions together: the national framework admits a 100% foreign stake, while Bali currently closes the PMA registration route for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to full foreign ownership does not make the activity registrable for PMA in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Audio and Video Retail Is Nationally Open—But Not for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This specialised retail activity spans audio, video and recording equipment, open nationally across every business scale but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, this activity cannot be registered as PMA in Bali today. That is the decisive local fact for a business centred on the island, even though the national position is open and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. The contrast is not a technical footnote: nationally open retail scope does not override Bali’s permanent, island-wide block on PMA registrations for activities classified as Low or Medium-Low risk.

The activity is specialised retail trade in audio and video equipment. Its scope includes radios, televisions, video equipment, tape recorders, audio amplifiers and cassette recorders, alongside stereo equipment, recordable media, and equipment for recording and playing CDs and DVDs. In practical terms, it describes a retail business built around the sale of dedicated sound, image and playback equipment rather than a general retail category. The record’s breadth matters: it reaches both the equipment itself and the media and devices used to record or play it.

At the national level, the activity is open to businesses at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. It is also nationally open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. For an investor considering the national framework alone, that is a clear position: this activity may be structured with full foreign ownership. The applicable source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali changes the result for PMA registration. At the Large scale, the OSS risk assessment is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, placing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. So the national 100% ceiling remains the national ceiling, but it does not make a PMA registration available in Bali. For founders, the responsible reading is straightforward: the business activity is nationally foreign-open across all listed scales, while Bali currently blocks its PMA registration because of the recorded risk classification and moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Textile Retail: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Textile retail is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
At national level, this is an activity open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. On Bali, the answer changes: a foreign-owned business cannot register this activity for PMA today. The Bali record marks it as blocked under the province’s island-wide, permanent moratorium. The stated trigger is its OSS risk treatment at the Besar scale—Low or Medium-Low across every scope—rather than the national foreign-ownership setting.

Retail textile trade here means selling a defined range of fabrics and related materials. The covered stock begins with textiles made from natural, synthetic, and blended fibres, then sets out woven fabrics such as cotton and polyester sarongs and silk or mixed-fibre suiting. It also embraces printed fabrics in cotton, polyamide, and waterproof cloth; batik made by hand, stamp, or a combination of both; and knitted fabrics in wool, rayon, and wool/cotton. The activity extends to retailing base materials used to make carpets, decorative wall hangings, embroidery, and needlework. Taken together, the scope is materially specific: the commercial subject is the textile itself and the stated craft-related inputs.

The registration is open across the full listed scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. It captures a business operating at any of those listed scales while retaining a specific commercial subject: retailing the stated textiles and related base materials. The scale list identifies the available registration range; it does not broaden the merchandise described by the scope.

The practical reading requires the national and Bali positions to stay separate. The national position is clear: PMA is TERBUKA, and the national ceiling is 100%. Bali does not erase that national classification, but it does block PMA registration for this activity under its own permanent, island-wide moratorium. The record ties that outcome to the Low or Medium-Low OSS risk result at Besar across every scope and identifies the moratorium in May 2026. For a foreign founder, Bali is therefore not an available PMA-registration location for this activity today, even though the national setting allows full foreign ownership.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign founder, Bali is therefore not an available PMA-registration location for this activity today, even though the national setting allows full foreign ownership.

editorial.headline: Textile Household Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Specialist retail in household textiles is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s risk-based PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register a PMA business under this activity in Bali today. That is the decisive local fact, even though the national setting is open and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA where the risk classification is Low or Medium-Low. Here, every stated scope at the Large scale is assessed Low/Medium-Low, bringing the activity within that moratorium. Its Bali status is recorded as blocked by risk class, with the cited moratorium from May 2026.

The activity itself is specialist retail in textile household supplies. Its scope runs from tablecloths and bed sheets to tarpaulins, pillowcases, mosquito nets, mattress fabrics and pillow fabrics. Mop cloths and household linen sit within the same retail scope, alongside pillows and bolsters. What connects these goods is their place in equipping and maintaining the home: practical textiles for everyday use, as well as the soft goods used across household spaces.

Scale does not narrow the national coverage. The record opens the activity to Micro, Small, Medium and Large businesses, giving the same national classification to retailers operating at very different sizes. It also makes clear that foreign participation is not subject to a national ownership ceiling below full ownership: the ceiling is 100%. The listed national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. National openness is therefore real, but it is not a substitute for the Bali position where the local moratorium applies.

The accurate reading keeps those two levels separate. Nationally, this is an open activity across all four stated scales, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In Bali, the result is not a lower percentage or a conditional route; it is a PMA registration block because the Large-scale risk outcome across the stated scopes is Low/Medium-Low. For anyone considering this retail activity in Bali, that local restriction is the controlling position.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, but in Bali the Low/Medium-Low risk outcome produces a direct PMA registration block.

editorial.headline: Sewing Supplies Retail: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retail trade in sewing supplies is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration there today.
editorial.body:
Retailing sewing supplies is the full terrain of this activity. It covers the retail trade in sewing equipment and supplies, with sewing thread and needles given as the record’s concrete examples. That framing is more useful than a generic retail label: the activity is defined by the sewing supplies it offers at retail. For a founder shaping the registered activity, the point is straightforward but consequential: thread and needles are the named centre of gravity, within retail trade in sewing supplies.

Nationally, the position is unambiguous. The PMA status is **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In plain terms, the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership. The activity is open across every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. Those categories establish a notably broad national frame for registration, rather than confining the activity to one particular business scale. The stated PMA sources are Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021.

Bali changes the conclusion completely for PMA registration. The Bali status is **Blocked (risk class)**, and the record expressly marks the activity as blocked. Foreign investors cannot register this activity in Bali at present. The stated reason is that its OSS risk at the Besar scale is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing it within Bali’s moratorium from May 2026. That provincial rule blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk categories across the island, permanently.

The important reading is therefore layered, not contradictory. National openness and a 100% ceiling do not create a PMA registration route in Bali while the permanent moratorium applies. The national foreign-ownership position remains clear, but Bali’s block is decisive for a PMA registration on the island. For anyone considering this retail activity in Bali, the honest conclusion is not a qualification to be navigated around: the current Bali position is blocked.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and a 100% ceiling do not create a PMA registration route in Bali while the permanent moratorium applies.

editorial.headline: Retailing the Materials That Make a Building
editorial.standfirst: A broad construction-material retail activity, nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked from PMA registration across Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign-owned company cannot register this activity in Bali today. Nationally, the position is markedly different: the activity is open to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That contrast matters because the classification is not a narrow retail niche; it covers the sale of construction materials across the practical vocabulary of building, repair and fit-out.

Its scope reaches from metal supplies—wire rope, insect screen, nails, bolts, hinges, locks, water tanks, rolling doors, awnings and sheet metal—to porcelain sanitary and wall products such as toilets, bidets, basins, baths and tiles. It also includes a substantial timber range: boards, beams, mouldings, poles, frames, doors, windows, wooden tiles and roofing, plywood, interior plywood, teak wood, particle board, chip board, veneers and plywood for concrete formwork. Clay, lime, cement and glass materials are included too, alongside roof tiles, bricks, refractory brick, floor and wall tiles, irrigation pipes, concrete rings, cement, sand, stone, plastic pipes and hoses, corrugated plastic sheet, asbestos-cement products and sanitary equipment. Direct sales are expressly outside the stated scope.

The registration pathway is available across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Yet the Bali position is decisive for a PMA applicant. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every part of the activity’s scope. Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The result is a block on PMA registration in Bali, notwithstanding the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling.

This is therefore a classification where national openness should not be mistaken for local availability. The national rule permits complete foreign ownership; Bali’s operative restriction prevents the PMA registration itself. For a founder assessing this activity, the useful reading is not that the activity is partially open or commercially conditional in Bali, but that its national PMA status and Bali registration outcome point in opposite directions.
editorial.pullQuote: The national rule permits complete foreign ownership; Bali’s operative restriction prevents the PMA registration itself.

editorial.headline: Sheet Glass Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This construction sheet-glass retail activity is open to 100% foreign ownership nationally, but PMA registration in Bali is blocked by the province’s permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
Sheet glass retail is set out through the practical variations used in construction supply: clear sheet glass, opaque sheet glass, coloured clear sheet glass, and engraved sheet glass. KBLI 47522 covers their retail trade as construction materials, and the stated scope also notes direct sales. The classification stays closely tied to these specified sheet-glass products while recognising a tangible range of finishes and treatments within that construction-material setting.

The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises. This places the same retail activity across every scale named in the record: micro and small enterprises sit within its stated range, as do medium and large enterprises. The record does not assign different glass types to different business scales; it presents the full construction-glass retail scope alongside the complete four-tier range. For a founder, the practical reading is clear: eligibility runs from Mikro through Besar, with the stated subject remaining sheet glass for construction.

At the national level, the PMA position is direct. The status is TERBUKA, and the recorded maximum foreign ownership is 100%. A foreign-owned enterprise can therefore look to a national ownership ceiling of 100% for this activity. The cited national PMA basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national openness is a meaningful fact, but it is not the whole operational answer for a business proposing to register the activity in Bali.

In Bali, the answer changes completely. A foreigner cannot register this activity for PMA there today. Its Bali status is Blocked (risk class), and the stated reason is specific: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low/Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. This is not a lower Bali-specific foreign-ownership percentage; it is a block on PMA registration. National openness is real, but it does not override Bali’s registration block.

editorial.headline: Retailing Tools, and Bali’s PMA Line
editorial.standfirst: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this tools retailer nevertheless cannot be registered as PMA in Bali under the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
Retailing tools is a deceptively precise trade. KBLI 47523 covers the retail sale of tools and equipment for tradespeople, whether operated by hand or powered by electricity. The examples supplied—hammers, saws and screwdrivers—give the classification a practical centre of gravity: it concerns the equipment itself, sold at retail, rather than a vague notion of construction or workmanship. The scope makes clear that both hand-operated and electrically powered equipment belong inside the activity. The result is a retail classification with a defined merchandise focus: tools and equipment for the trade.

Who can register it? The record does not confine the activity to a single business size. It opens the classification to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth is material: the same defined retail activity is available across the stated scale range, while the description remains anchored in the sale of the specified tools and equipment. For founders, the scale field is a clear signal about eligibility by size, not a reason to stretch the underlying scope. A business should still be intelligible as a retailer of the tool and trade-equipment range described here.

At national level, the PMA position is equally direct. The status is TERBUKA, with maximum foreign ownership of 100%, and the cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national record allows this activity to be held by a PMA with full foreign ownership. There is no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership in the supplied data. That conclusion is important because it identifies the national position clearly—but it does not decide where such a PMA may be registered.

Bali changes the answer decisively. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. The stated reason is not a foreign-ownership percentage or a local-partnership term. It is risk classification at the Besar scale: every scope is recorded as Rendah/Menengah-Rendah, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. The rule in the record is island-wide and permanent, blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. So the honest reading holds both facts at once: nationally, 100% foreign ownership is open; in Bali, the PMA registration route is blocked.

The stated scope encompasses electric and electronic fire alarms, fire extinguishers, emergency blocks, smoke-extraction systems, safes and strongboxes. It is a retail category built around supplying equipment for urgent situations and protection, rather than delivering a technical service alongside the sale.

That boundary is explicit. The activity covers the sale of the equipment without installation or maintenance services. This is more than a drafting detail: the commercial identity is product-led retail, with the equipment itself at its centre. A business should therefore be described through the trade in alarm, fire-suppression, smoke-extraction and secure-storage equipment, not through promises to fit, maintain or service those systems. The scope also expressly refers to direct selling.

The registration field is broad in scale, with Micro, Small, Medium and Large all open. Nationally, the status is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. For a founder assessing the activity outside Bali, that is the clear investment baseline supplied by this record.

Bali’s provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA, island-wide and permanently; this activity is therefore caught by the moratorium of 13 May 2026. editorial.body:
This activity is the retail sale of paints, varnishes, lacquers and other construction coatings. Its practical territory runs from primers and metal, wood and wall paints to enamel, putty, filler, varnish and lacquer. It is a trade activity centred on the materials that finish, protect and prepare built surfaces—not merely on paint as a single product category. The stated scope also includes direct sales, giving the activity a clear retail character across the coating range.

Nationally, the position is open. Foreign ownership may reach 100%, under the national PMA position recorded for this activity. The activity is open at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because it describes a retail activity available across the full scale range, rather than one confined by the record to a particular size of enterprise. The national opening is recorded with Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 as its source.

Bali changes the result decisively for PMA registration. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The relevant Bali status is Blocked (risk class): the restriction arises from the activity’s risk classification at that scale, not from any reduction in the national foreign-ownership ceiling.

This is therefore a case where the national and Bali answers must be kept distinct. The national record permits up to full foreign ownership; Bali’s provincial moratorium nonetheless blocks PMA registration for the activity. The Bali restriction is recorded as taking effect in May 2026, with Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP identified as the source. For founders, the useful reading is exact rather than optimistic: the activity remains nationally open, but that national openness does not produce a PMA registration route in Bali while the stated moratorium applies.

editorial.headline: Renewable-Energy Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailing renewable-energy materials is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the decisive fact comes before the product category: this activity cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. Nationally, it is open to PMA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. In Bali, however, the status is blocked on risk-class grounds. The record attributes that result to the OSS classification at the Besar scale, which is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, and to Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registrations for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The moratorium is recorded as beginning on May 13, 2026.

The activity itself is carefully bounded. It is retail trade in renewable-energy materials: solar collectors that do not generate electricity, photovoltaic panels, and other materials of the same kind. The examples matter because they define a goods-focused activity. A non-electricity-generating solar collector and a photovoltaic panel are both expressly within the stated retail scope. Installation services, by contrast, are excluded. The code therefore concerns the supply of specified renewable-energy materials rather than the installation work that may follow their sale.

Nationally, access is stated across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That breadth says the activity can be registered at each of those scales under the national classification; it does not alter the provincial PMA outcome. Bali’s blocking reason specifically locates the issue at Besar: for every scope, the OSS risk is either Low or Medium-Low. With the moratorium applying island-wide and permanently to those risk classes for PMA, the national foreign-ownership ceiling does not become a Bali registration route.

This is a case where two true statements must be read together. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 is the cited national source for an activity that is PMA-open to 100% foreign ownership. Bali’s documented position is still a block, not a partial opening. The practical reading is exact and limited: a business retailing the specified renewable-energy materials without installation can fall within this national activity and is open across the listed scales nationally; a foreign-owned PMA registration for it in Bali cannot proceed under the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness to 100% foreign ownership does not become a Bali registration route.
