editorial.headline: The Fine Line in Selling Floors and Furnishings
editorial.standfirst: A retail activity open nationally to full foreign ownership, yet unavailable for PMA registration anywhere in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the retail trade in the finishing elements that give an interior its texture and atmosphere: carpets and rugs, curtains and drapes, and wall and floor coverings such as wallpaper, tiles, laminate and vinyl flooring. Its boundary matters. The activity expressly does not extend to retailing the building-material category of floor tiles, laminate and vinyl. In practice, the registration should reflect the retail offer as it is actually presented, with the distinction between interior coverings and the excluded building-material retail activity kept clear.

The activity is open to businesses at every stated scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth makes it relevant to a modest specialist shop as well as to a larger-format retail operation. The common thread is not the size of the premises or catalogue, but the retail sale of the named furnishing and covering products. A business built around carpets, window dressings, wallpaper, and eligible floor-covering lines belongs in this commercial frame when those goods are the substance of its retail activity.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. The activity is classified as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. A foreign investor can therefore hold the full permitted ownership interest at the national level. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national openness, however, is not the whole operating picture for an investor considering Bali.

In Bali, a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA today. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): at the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS at Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The block has applied under the Bali moratorium since May 2026. For this activity, national permission to reach 100% foreign ownership does not translate into a PMA registration route in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: National permission to reach 100% foreign ownership does not translate into a PMA registration route in Bali.

editorial.headline: Furniture Retail: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Furniture retail is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
Furniture retail, in this record, means the retail sale of furnishing items: tables, chairs, wardrobes, beds, bookcases, shoe racks, buffets, mattresses and mattress bed frames. The scope is product-led and concrete, covering the pieces through which rooms are furnished rather than reducing the trade to a single product line. Storage and display furniture sit beside sleeping furniture, so the activity holds together a broad but intelligible retail offer. Its centre of gravity is the sale of furniture itself, as the listed examples consistently make clear. Each item gives the category a recognisable commercial boundary.

The activity is available, under the record, to enterprises at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That full spread is not a throwaway classification detail: those are the business scales expressly available for the activity, from Mikro through Besar. It says nothing about a preference among them; each is named in the stated availability. The breadth of that eligibility situates furniture retail as an activity open across the recorded scale spectrum, while leaving the PMA question to the national and local rules given separately. For founders, that scale field answers the availability question—not foreign ownership or Bali’s local PMA decision.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA—open—and the recorded maximum foreign ownership is 100%. Put plainly, the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership of this activity. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, is cited as the source for that national position. This is a clear starting point for reading the code, yet it cannot be read as an automatic Bali outcome. The slim record presents national ownership and Bali PMA registration as distinct parts of the same compliance picture. The 100% figure is a ceiling, not a Bali registration approval.

In Bali, the conclusion changes decisively. The status is Blocked (risk class), and the record marks PMA registration blocked. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low on every scope. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium—recorded in May 2026—blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The result is direct and should not be softened: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today, even with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. editorial.headline: Household Electrical Retail: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retail in household electrical goods, lighting and fittings is open nationally to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47592 is the retail activity for household electrical equipment, lighting equipment, and their fittings. Its practical territory is broad but coherent: washing machines and refrigerators; fans, vacuum cleaners and floor polishers; mixers, irons and blenders; and the lighting and electrical fittings that complete a domestic installation. Incandescent and fluorescent lamps, starters, ballasts, reflectors, cables, switches, sockets, fittings and fuses all sit within the stated scope. It is a retail classification built around the electrical equipment of the home and the components that illuminate and connect it.

The activity is available to operators at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That range matters because the description does not confine this retail work to a single size of enterprise: the same stated activity can be registered across those four scales. For a foreign-owned company, the national position is direct. The PMA status is TERBUKA and the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Under the national record, full foreign ownership is permitted for this activity, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 cited as the source.

Bali changes the operative answer completely. PMA registration for this activity is not available to a foreign investor in Bali today. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class), and the record marks it as blocked. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope, placing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI island-wide, permanently. The moratorium identified in the record is dated the thirteenth of May 2026.

That creates a sharp but straightforward reading. National foreign investment openness does not translate into a PMA registration path in Bali for this retail activity. The 100% national ceiling remains the national figure; it is not a Bali entitlement. For founders considering this specific business, the relevant fact is the location-specific registration outcome: the national framework records it as open, while the Bali moratorium blocks it. The scope remains useful for understanding the business itself—appliances, lighting equipment and electrical fittings—but it does not override the Bali block.

editorial.headline: Kitchen & Tableware Retail: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity welcomes fully foreign ownership nationally, while Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium closes the registration route on the island.
editorial.body:
In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity today. That is the practical starting point for a retail business dealing in crockery, kitchen supplies and tableware: national investment policy calls it TERBUKA and allows full foreign ownership, but Bali’s PMA position is blocked. The distinction matters because the national permission is real, yet it does not create a Bali registration route. The record’s Bali status, Blocked (risk class), identifies a restriction tied to risk class rather than a softened local qualification.

The commercial subject is richly specific. It is retail trade in fragile household tableware and the tools surrounding cooking, serving and storing food: plates, basins, bowls, cups, teapots, spoons, forks and food carriers; jars and baby bottles; pots, trays, buckets, thermoses and jerry cans; as well as mortars and pestles, coconut graters, cutting boards, ladles, baskets, steaming vessels, food covers, satay skewers and meat grinders. Taken together, the scope describes the everyday material culture of the kitchen and dining table, from the vessel that holds a meal to the implement that prepares it.

Nationally, this activity is open to PMA. The maximum foreign share recorded is 100%, so the national position permits a business in this activity to be fully foreign-owned. The record also opens it across the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. At each of those stated scales, the activity remains the retail provision of this defined range of household goods. The scale labels establish the stated range of business scale; the slim record gives no further ranking or condition within them.

Bali changes the result without changing what the activity is. For the Besar scale, the record states that every scope is OSS Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA for activities carrying either of those risk levels, and the record dates this block to May 13, 2026. It is therefore not accurate to present the 100% national ceiling as a Bali opportunity: for a foreign investor seeking to register this activity in Bali, the answer is no today. The relevant local constraint is the moratorium documented under Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
editorial.pullQuote: National permission is real, yet it does not create a Bali registration route.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Trade With No Bali PMA Route
editorial.standfirst: Retail musical-instrument trade is open to full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali blocks PMA registration for the activity under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
Retail musical-instrument trade is a category with a pleasingly broad retail vocabulary. It covers the sale of instruments from Indonesia’s traditional repertoire—kecapi, bamboo flute, calung, angklung, kolintang, gamelan set, rebab, rebana, tifa and sasando—alongside modern instruments including saxophone, harmonica, trombone, guitar, mandolin, ukulele, harp, bass, violin, cello, piano, organ and drums. The inclusion of tuning forks makes the perimeter especially clear: the activity is about musical instruments and their retail presence, not a narrow genre or a single tradition. Its scope lets traditional and modern instruments sit under the same retail roof without asking the business to choose between them.

The registration scales are uncomplicated: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all open to this activity. That gives the category one consistent description across those listed scales. The important qualifier is geographical, not a difference in the kind of instrument being sold. A shop centred on bamboo flutes and angklung, or one offering guitars, pianos and drums, falls within the stated retail scope; its scale can be any of the four listed.

At the national level, the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. That is an unambiguous national ceiling: a foreign investor may hold the full ownership interest nationally. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. But national status alone does not settle the answer on the island. The Bali register marks the activity Blocked (risk class), so a foreigner cannot register it in Bali today as PMA.

The reason is specific. At Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, and Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities from PMA registration. Therefore, the national 100% ownership ceiling remains a national fact, while the Bali outcome is a block on PMA registration. It is a clear distinction worth preserving: full national foreign ownership does not create a Bali PMA route for this retail activity under the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: Full national foreign ownership does not create a Bali PMA route for this retail activity under the stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: Household Goods Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailing brooms, brushes, mats and mopping articles can be fully foreign-owned nationally, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
**Nationally, this is an entirely foreign-open retail activity. In Bali today, however, a foreigner cannot register it through PMA.** The national ceiling is 100%, but the Bali outcome is a block, not a reduced ownership allowance. Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium prevents PMA registration for activities carrying Low or Medium-Low risk. For this activity, OSS places the Large scale at Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope, bringing it within the block recorded from May 13, 2026. Nationally open to full foreign ownership does not make this activity registrable for PMA in Bali.

The activity itself is retail trade in other household equipment and supplies not classified elsewhere within its household-goods subdivision. The record gives a practical view of the merchandise: twig brooms, fibre brooms, brushes, mats, mops and mop cloths. These examples define a retail category centred on household cleaning and related supplies. Its scope is deliberately residual: it covers the household articles within the subdivision that are not otherwise classified there, rather than being confined to one named product.

The registration field is broad in scale. The record marks the activity open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses. Across those stated scales, the commercial activity remains the same described retail trade: household equipment and supplies of the kind represented by brooms, brushes, mats and mopping articles. The scale listing does not change the nature of the category; it identifies the business sizes to which the record opens it.

The national and Bali positions must therefore be read separately. At the national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA and maximum foreign ownership is 100%, making full foreign ownership available under the cited Presidential Regulations. In Bali, the decisive point is the recorded risk-class block at the Large scale. The moratorium is island-wide and permanent, and the record says it blocks PMA registration in Bali for this activity. For a foreign founder considering Bali, the conclusion is plain: this activity may be nationally open, yet it cannot be registered there through PMA today.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to full foreign ownership does not make this activity registrable for PMA in Bali.

editorial.headline: Stationery Retail Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans everyday writing and drawing supplies, open nationally to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration across Bali.
editorial.body:
Retail trade in writing and drawing supplies is broader than the quiet image of a neighbourhood stationery counter might suggest. It covers the retail sale of pencils, pens, markers, ballpoint pens, sign pens and mechanical pencils, alongside compasses, drawing brushes, technical pens, crayons and pastels. The scope also reaches into whiteboards, drawing tables, screen-printing equipment, typewriter ribbons, watercolours and oil paints, as well as erasers, correction fluid or tape, ink, sharpeners, rulers and chalk. It is, in other words, the retail activity for a business trading in the practical tools of writing, marking, drawing and presentation.

The classification is open across every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the activity is not confined in the record to one size of operator or one narrow retail format. A business may register this activity whether its commercial footing is micro, small, medium or large, provided its retail trade sits within the stated range of writing and drawing supplies. The scope is specific in its merchandise, but not slight: it includes both the everyday implements of school and office use and the materials and equipment associated with drawing, painting and screen printing.

At the national level, the position is unequivocal. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For an investor considering the activity on a national basis, that is the relevant opening: the code is open to PMA and permits foreign ownership up to the stated ceiling.

Bali is the decisive exception. In Bali today, a foreigner has no route to register this activity as PMA. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, and Bali's permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The Bali status is therefore Blocked (risk class). This is not a qualification of the national ownership ceiling; it is a separate Bali registration barrier. The activity remains nationally open, but that openness does not create a PMA registration route in Bali while the stated moratorium applies.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali offers no PMA registration route for it today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: The Printed Page’s Retail Code Has a Clear Bali Boundary
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 47612 covers retail trade in printed and published goods, nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47612 is the retail code for the physical output of printing and publishing: the practical paper trail of commerce and correspondence, alongside reading and reference material. Its scope includes invoices, receipts, business cards, labels, envelopes, diaries, address books, greeting cards, postcards, stamps, fiscal stamps, albums, notebooks, drawing books, ruled and graph paper, atlases, Braille letters, newspapers, magazines, bulletins, dictionaries, science books and picture books. The activity is not defined by one product category so much as by a retail shelf of printed and published materials, from everyday stationery to material intended to inform, record or circulate.

The code is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because its scope can accommodate a modest retail operation as well as a larger-format business, without changing the core activity: selling these printed and published goods at retail. Nationally, the PMA position is equally direct. The activity is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In national terms, therefore, foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership for this activity.

Bali is where the position changes decisively. In Bali today, a foreign investor has no PMA registration route for this activity. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, placing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The record identifies the moratorium as taking effect on the thirteenth of May, two thousand twenty-six.

That contrast should be read plainly rather than softened. National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a route for PMA registration in Bali when the provincial moratorium applies. The code remains a broad retail home for printed and published products, and it remains available across Mikro through Besar scales in the recorded national framework. But for a foreign-owned setup in Bali, the present answer is not conditional or speculative: PMA registration is blocked under the stated Bali rule.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not create a route for PMA registration in Bali when the provincial moratorium applies.

editorial.headline: Paper Retail Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity spans everyday paper, board and paper-based goods; it is nationally open to foreign investment but cannot be registered as PMA in Bali under the permanent moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47613 covers the retail sale of paper, cardboard and goods made from them. Its working catalogue is broad but coherent: HVS paper, tracing paper, kraft paper, thin and coloured papers, Manila and buffalo-skin board, fibreboard, wrapping paper, food and beverage packaging board, paper bags, coated paper and board, stationery paper, stencil sheets, carbon paper and duplicator paper. In plain terms, this is the retail trade of paper and board products used for writing, copying, wrapping, packaging and related everyday purposes.

Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all open scales for the activity. That matters because the classification is not confined to a single commercial footprint: the record accommodates operations from micro through large scale. The scope remains retail throughout. Its centre of gravity is the sale of paper, cardboard and paper-based merchandise, rather than a claim about manufacturing, distribution or any wider activity that the record does not state.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is marked TERBUKA and carries a maximum foreign ownership allowance of 100%. A foreign investor can therefore read the national position as fully open on the foreign-ownership ceiling recorded here. The legal source listed for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no smaller national foreign-share cap in this record to soften or qualify that conclusion.

Bali is the decisive exception for a PMA applicant. Foreign applicants cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. At the Besar scale, every scope is recorded in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, and that assessment places the activity within Bali’s moratorium introduced in May 2026. The provincial rule is island-wide and permanent for this purpose: the Bali status is blocked because of the risk class, not because the national foreign-ownership ceiling is anything less than 100%. The honest reading is therefore two-part: nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under the recorded moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this activity is nevertheless unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under the recorded moratorium.

editorial.headline: A National Opening, a Bali PMA Stop
editorial.standfirst: This activity embraces specialist sports-goods retail nationwide, yet foreign investors cannot register it for PMA in Bali under the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47620 is the retail activity for sports equipment and supplies, but its practical terrain is wider than a rack of balls or racquets. The stated scope includes fishing equipment; hunting weapons and ammunition; camping goods; boats; and bicycles, including electric bicycles, unicycles, hoverboards, scooters and Segways. It also takes in specialist sports footwear—football boots, ice skates and ski boots—and specialist sports apparel for skiing, martial arts and ballet. Parachutes, tents and sleeping bags sit within the same retail perimeter. Ordinary, non-specialised sports footwear, including tennis, basketball, gym and training shoes, is expressly outside it.

The relevant question for a founder is therefore whether the proposed assortment belongs to this specialised retail field, not whether it merely has a sporting association. The record admits the activity at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That range matters because the activity is framed as retail trade across a broad set of named goods and formats, from mobility equipment to outdoor and specialist-performance articles. The classification detail stays focused on those specified retail lines.

At the national level, the PMA position is clear. The status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership stated for this activity is 100%. In plain terms, the national record treats it as open to foreign investment up to a full foreign stake. That national opening is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It should be read as the national position for this activity rather than as an answer to where it may be registered within Indonesia.

That distinction decides the Bali outcome. Bali marks the activity as blocked by risk class, and the record says that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. Those ratings place the activity inside Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The result is direct: a foreigner cannot register this activity for PMA in Bali today. The national 100% ceiling remains the national ceiling; it does not override the Bali moratorium. For a plan centred on Bali, that is the operative fact—not a marginal qualification to an otherwise open national classification.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% ceiling remains the national ceiling; it does not override the Bali moratorium.

editorial.headline: Toy Retail Is Nationally Open but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailers of toys, party equipment and toy drones can register across all stated scales nationally, but Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
**A foreign investor cannot register this retail activity in Bali today.** Nationally, it is open to PMA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. Bali reaches a different result: it is blocked for PMA registration by the province’s island-wide, permanent moratorium. The recorded reason is specific. At the Besar scale, every scope is classed by OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk, placing this activity within the restriction applied in May 2026.

At heart, this is a focused retail activity for games, toys and party equipment. The catalogue is intentionally broad: dolls, marbles, bekel, congklak, scrabble, carrom, musical-instrument toys, toy cars, toy weapons, toy cooking implements and toy household furniture all sit within it. The same is true of party costumes, masks, party souvenirs—including make-up and joke articles—and magic equipment. Retail sale of toy drones is expressly included, giving the activity a contemporary edge alongside its more familiar play and celebration merchandise. The list moves from small playthings to more elaborate themed purchases, but its organising principle remains the sale of play and party goods.

Registration is open at every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth is significant, but it does not turn the classification into a catch-all retail label. The activity remains anchored to retail merchandise listed above: playthings, party articles and toy drones. For a founder preparing the business, the useful discipline is to make the retail offer intelligible in those terms, matching the registered activity to what will actually be sold. Those scale labels identify who may enter the activity nationally, while its merchandise identifies what the retail business is.

The contrast is therefore binary, not marginal. At national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with the stated maximum foreign ownership of 100% and the cited basis of Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In Bali, the stated status is Blocked (risk class). The island-wide permanent rule blocks PMA where the recorded risk treatment is Low or Medium-Low; for this activity, the Besar-scale OSS assessment triggers that outcome. Full foreign ownership is a national possibility, but it does not provide a PMA registration path in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: Full foreign ownership is a national possibility, but it does not provide a PMA registration path in Bali today.

editorial.headline: The Retail Business Where Art, Music and Collecting Meet
editorial.standfirst: This activity brings together specialist retail in art, music, recorded media and collecting—open nationally to full foreign ownership, but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is a specialist retail home for the cultural and recreational objects that invite attention rather than impulse. It covers the sale of recorded media; musical instruments, sheet music and related accessories such as strings, music stands and metronomes; and collectible material including stamps and coins. It also includes commercial art galleries, alongside the retail of art supplies—from beads and clay to canvas, oil paints and watercolours. The common thread is not one product category but a retail practice built around making, listening, collecting and exhibiting.

That breadth gives the activity a recognisable commercial shape. A business may trade in the practical tools of artistic work, the equipment and scores that support musical practice, or objects whose value lies in rarity, cultural interest or collection. A commercial gallery belongs within the same activity, placing the sale and presentation of art alongside more conventional specialist retail. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so the classification is not reserved for one size of operator.

Nationally, the position is direct: the activity is TERBUKA to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That national opening is grounded in Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. But Bali requires a separate reading. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. At the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk; Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. The Bali status is therefore Blocked (risk class), reflecting a provincial barrier that sits alongside—not beneath—the national openness.

For founders, the important distinction is between the activity’s national investment position and its current registrability in Bali. Full foreign ownership is available nationally, yet that does not create a route for PMA registration on the island where the permanent moratorium applies. The business itself remains clearly defined: specialist retail for recorded media, music, collecting, art materials and commercial gallery activity. The constraint is geographical and regulatory, not a narrowing of that underlying scope.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Retail Clothing, Nationally Open but Off-Limits for Foreign Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers broad retail clothing sales across every business scale, with full national foreign ownership available but PMA registration blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
Retail clothing is the business of selling garments made from textiles, leather or artificial leather. Its scope runs from shirts, trousers, suits, coats and jackets to pyjamas, kebaya, blouses, skirts, house dresses, underwear, bras, gowns, baby clothes, dancewear, traditional dress, mukena and robes. It also includes general sportswear that has not been designed for one particular sport. This is deliberately a broad apparel-retail activity: the defining question is the retail sale of clothing within that stated range.

The activity is open to businesses at the Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. Nationally, its PMA status is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That makes the national position unusually direct: foreign investment can hold the full permitted stake in a business registered for this activity. The record attributes that national position to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021.

Bali is where the picture changes decisively. In Bali today, a foreigner cannot register this activity as a PMA. The Bali classification is blocked on risk-class grounds, because at the Large scale its OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities from PMA registration. The result is not a reduced foreign-ownership percentage or a conditional local partnership route; it is a registration block for PMA on the island.

For a founder, the important discipline is to keep the two positions separate. National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remain the national framework for this retail-clothing activity. They do not override the Bali moratorium. A business may fit the activity’s broad clothing scope and be eligible across all four listed scales, yet still be unable to make a PMA registration for it in Bali under the current risk-based provincial restriction. The practical reading is therefore clear: the activity is nationally open to foreign investment, but presently unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Bali’s Bag-Retail Paradox
editorial.standfirst: This specialist retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium closes the registration route on the island.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this retail activity in Bali today, even though it is nationally open to foreign ownership. The island-wide Bali moratorium blocks PMA registration for activities assessed at Low or Medium-Low risk; at the Besar scale, every scope in this activity falls within those bands. That result is not a question of product mix or a discretionary local reading. It follows from the recorded risk classification and applies permanently across the province. For founders considering a Bali vehicle, the first practical fact is therefore the restriction itself: national openness does not create a Bali PMA registration route while this moratorium governs it.

Nationally, this is specialist retail for bags, wallets, suitcases, backpacks and related goods. Its material range is deliberately broad: leather, imitation leather, textiles, plastic, rubber and other materials all sit within the activity. The retail offer may encompass handbags, shopping bags, school bags, document bags and sports bags, alongside wallets, cosmetics cases, knife or sword sheaths, camera and eyewear cases, and pencil cases. Umbrella retail is included as well. The common thread is a dedicated retail activity for carrying, storing and protecting personal belongings, rather than a narrow retail format defined by one material or one product style.

The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the commercial concept can be framed across the full listed scale range, from a modest specialist shop to a larger operation. It does not, however, alter the Bali position for PMA: the recorded finding at the Besar scale is Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope, bringing the activity within the province-wide moratorium. Scale availability and PMA registrability in Bali are therefore separate questions in this record.

At national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, under the cited Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In Bali, the decisive condition is the permanent rule blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, supported here by Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. The clean reading is neither a hidden cap nor a conditional workaround: full foreign ownership is nationally permitted, while Bali PMA registration for this activity is blocked.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Retail sale of pharmaceutical preparations for humans at a pharmacy (Apotek). This is the most heavily regulated retail code in the 47xxx range. An Apotek can dispense prescription drugs (obat etis), over-the-counter medications, and galenical preparations. The key distinction: only an Apotek — not a drug store (Toko Obat) — can handle prescription medications.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Risk: Menengah Tinggi (Medium-High)** across all scales (Micro/Small/Medium/Large). NIB + Standard Certificate required — issued within **14 working days** (fiktif positif applies).

**Requirements:**
- Surat Izin Praktek Apoteker (SIPA) — Pharmacist Practice License
- Surat Tanda Registrasi Apoteker (STRA) — Pharmacist Registration Certificate
- Sertifikat Kompetensi Apoteker — Pharmacist Competency Certificate

**Post-issuance obligations:**
- Must have a licensed Pharmacist (Apoteker) responsible for operations at all times
- Comply with pharmacy operational standards (storage, hygiene, temperature control)
- Submit periodic activity reports

**PMA:** Fully open (TERBUKA), 100% foreign ownership allowed. However, technical regulations may impose specific capital structures and elevated infrastructure standards for PMA pharmacies.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct match from KBLI 2020. No changes to scope or classification.
intel_2026.baliContext: Despite being TERBUKA 100%, foreign pharmacy operations in Bali are almost exclusively large chains — Watson's, Guardian, Century Healthcare. The barrier is not the PMA status but the regulatory depth: physical inspections of premises verify storage conditions, hygiene standards, temperature-controlled storage for specific medications, and the mandatory on-site Pharmacist. A PMA pharmacy must meet elevated service and infrastructure standards — you cannot operate a simple drug kiosk under this code. The SIPA licensing process for the responsible Pharmacist involves verification through the local Dinas Kesehatan (Health Department), which in Bali can add 4-8 weeks to your timeline. If your concept is simpler — vitamins, supplements, OTC health products — consider 47722 (Toko Obat) instead.

editorial.headline: An Apotek Activity Open Nationally—and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers the pharmacy retail sale of human pharmaceutical preparations and specified health goods, with full national foreign-ownership availability and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
An apotek operating under this activity is a retail setting for human pharmaceutical preparations in their many practical forms: tablets, capsules, ointments, powders, solutions, parenteral solutions and suspensions. The stated range is broad within that pharmacy setting, spanning preparations for skin, eye, dental, ear, respiratory and digestive conditions, high blood pressure and hormone disorders, alongside vitamins and health supplements. The defining point is not simply the product catalogue, but its retail sale through an apotek.

The scope also includes specified health-related goods made of rubber. These include condoms, breast pumps, feeding teats, blood bags, surgical gloves, rubber pipettes, family-planning devices and rubber stoppers for small pharmaceutical vials. Taken together, the activity describes a pharmacy retail operation able to handle both medicinal preparations for human use and the named health necessities that sit alongside them. It is open to businesses at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is recorded as TERBUKA for PMA, with maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In other words, the national record allows foreign ownership to reach the full ceiling stated for this activity. Its stated availability across every listed business scale gives the code a consistent national footing, from Mikro through Besar, rather than reserving it to one end of the scale spectrum.

Bali requires its own reading, because the province permanently blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA registration across the island. This activity is not recorded as blocked by that moratorium. Bali marks it as OK or higher risk, and the record notes that, at Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. The practical conclusion from the record is therefore clear: a foreign-owned apotek retail business under this activity is nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership, and it is not barred from PMA registration in Bali by the stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: Non-Pharmacy Pharmaceutical Retail Is Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM — Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers retail sales of human pharmaceutical preparations beyond conventional pharmacies—but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium changes the practical answer for foreign founders.
editorial.body:
This activity is the retail trade of pharmaceutical preparations for human use outside a conventional pharmacy setting. Its scope is broad in form rather than in medical purpose: tablets, capsules, ointments, solutions, parenteral solutions and suspensions all sit within it. The record specifically includes products associated with skin, eye, dental, ear, respiratory, digestive, blood-pressure and hormonal conditions, alongside vitamins and health supplements. In practice, it reaches drug stores, Type B village pharmacies and pharmaceutical market stalls, as well as mobile and internet-based medicine sales.

The activity is open across the full stated scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the code is not framed as a niche format reserved for a single kind of outlet. It accommodates a fixed retail presence, market-based selling, circulation through mobile sales, and an online channel. The common thread is the retail sale of pharmaceutical preparations for people; the setting may change, but the activity remains defined by that retail function.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity is 0%. Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II p.13-14, entry 46, sub-row "Barang dan obat farmasi untuk manusia bukan di apotik" (ex-KBLI 2020 47722) allocates retail of non-prescription pharmaceutical goods outside a pharmacy (Toko Obat) as a specialised store to Koperasi and UMKM (the *dialokasikan* column), so a PT PMA cannot register it anywhere in Indonesia — not only in Bali.

editorial.headline: Natural-Medicine Retail: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity covers natural medicines for human use in shops, market stalls and street-vendor settings; it is nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This is a retail activity for natural medicines intended for people, with a scope wider than the word herbal alone suggests. It includes jamu, standardised herbal medicines (OHT), phytopharmaceuticals and other natural medicines for human use. The materials may originate from plants, animals or minerals, while the goods may take the form of pills, capsules, powders or liquids. Health supplements and quasi-medicines also sit within the stated scope. In practical terms, the activity encompasses a natural-medicine shop as well as street vendors and market-stall traders dealing in these goods.

The recorded business scales span Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That range reflects a scope not confined to one retail setting: the same activity expressly includes fixed shops alongside informal market and street-trading formats. What unifies those settings is the retail sale of natural-medicine products for people, including the named traditional, herbal and phytopharmaceutical categories, rather than the size or appearance of the selling venue.

At the national level, PMA is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. A fully foreign-owned PMA position is therefore available at the national level for this activity; the foreign stake is not capped below full ownership. The stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This distinction deserves careful reading: national openness establishes the ownership ceiling for the activity, but it does not by itself settle whether PMA registration is available in every location.

In Bali, the conclusion is direct: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA. The record marks it as blocked because, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. Bali’s moratorium, effective May 13, 2026, blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. The national 100% ceiling remains the national position, but it does not overcome this Bali-specific PMA block.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness establishes the ownership ceiling for the activity, but it does not by itself settle whether PMA registration is available in every location.

editorial.headline: The Cosmetics Shop Code That Stops at Bali’s PMA Gate
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet foreign investors cannot register it in Bali under the province’s permanent PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Retail cosmetics for human use sit at the centre of this activity: the sale of make-up, fragrance, hair products, nail products, skincare, personal-hygiene products and shaving preparations. Its scope also includes traditional cosmetics, alongside items such as body powder, beauty cotton and baby powder. In practical terms, this is the retail territory of a cosmetics shop, but the record also expressly reaches cosmetics street vendors and market-stall traders.

The code is built for retail rather than manufacture or service provision. Its examples make that distinction tangible: eye shadow, mascara, face cream, lipstick and lip liner; cologne, toilet water and perfume; shampoo, hair tonic and hair oil; nail polish, nail cream and cuticle remover. The same retail frame extends to baby oil, cleansing lotion, masks and foot cream, as well as spray and cream deodorants, traditional body treatments and shaving cream. The common thread is the sale of cosmetics intended for people.

Every stated business scale is open for registration: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. At the national level, the PMA position remains TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national setting for a foreign-owned cosmetics retail activity. It does not, however, settle the question for an investor seeking to register in Bali.

In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity today. The record marks it as blocked for PMA registration because, at the Besar scale, every scope carries a Rendah or Menengah-Rendah OSS risk classification. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA; for this activity, the relevant moratorium is identified as beginning in May 2026. The result is not a partial local caveat on the national 100% ceiling, but a direct barrier to PMA registration in Bali. A founder can read the national position as fully open while still needing to treat Bali as unavailable for a PMA registration under this code.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the activity is open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali is unavailable for PMA registration under this code.

editorial.headline: Health-Equipment Retail: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign founder, the practical headline is stark: this health-equipment retail activity cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. That conclusion sits beside—not beneath—the national position. Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. The distinction is central, not semantic. The national ceiling answers the ownership question; Bali’s rule answers whether the activity may be registered there for PMA at all. A plan that relies only on the national position therefore misses the operational boundary the Bali record sets.

The scope is retail trade in health equipment for people, expressed in the record as a health-equipment store. It includes instruments and aids such as thermometers, blood-pressure monitors, hearing aids, orthopaedic prostheses and neck braces. The named items are not incidental illustrations: they show the activity’s practical territory, spanning measurement, monitoring, hearing and physical support for human use. The expressly identified shop format keeps the classification grounded in retail trade of these products rather than an abstract commercial label.

Every listed business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—remains open for registration. The record thus presents a complete scale range, from Mikro through Besar, for this activity. In its national PMA position, it is TERBUKA and carries a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. That is an unequivocal national setting: a foreign investor can hold the full stated maximum. The applicable national reference identified for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali’s barrier is tied to risk classification, not a lower foreign-ownership figure. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns every scope within this activity a Low or Medium-Low risk classification. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration. For this activity, the effect is the recorded blocked status, Blocked (risk class), with the block tied to the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026. National openness does not change Bali’s current block on PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not change Bali’s current block on PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Animal-Medicine Retail, With Bali’s Risk Line in View
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 47726 covers the retail trade in veterinary medicines, open nationally to foreign investment, while Bali access turns on its risk category at scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47726 is the retail trade in pharmaceutical medicines for animals. Its scope is practical and wide-ranging: medicines sold as powders, tablets, capsules, ointments, granules, solutions, suspensions and aerosols, as well as medicines for fish. The activity belongs in the everyday commercial ecosystem of veterinary pharmacies, animal-medicine depots, pet shops, poultry shops and dedicated animal-medicine stores. It is not defined by a single product format or animal type; it is defined by the retail sale of pharmaceutical medicines for animals.

The code is open to registration at small, medium and large scale. Nationally, it is also open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is the straightforward national position: a foreign-owned business may register this activity, and the code is not confined to a particular business scale. For founders, the important discipline is to keep the activity description close to what the code actually covers—retail trade in animal pharmaceutical medicines, including fish medicines, through the stated types of retail outlets.

Bali adds a separate lens, but not a contradiction. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all low-risk and medium-low-risk KBLI activities across the island. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. At large scale, its OSS risk is medium-high or high, which places it outside the category caught by Bali’s permanent PMA restriction. The Bali status is therefore recorded as OK or higher risk: not an unrestricted abstraction, but a clear indication that the provincial moratorium does not stop PMA registration for this activity.

That distinction matters because national openness and Bali treatment must be read together, rather than treated as interchangeable. Here, the national ceiling is full foreign ownership, while Bali does not impose a recorded Bali-specific ownership cap or partnership condition. Its relevance lies in the risk-based moratorium—and, on the record, this code sits beyond the low and medium-low risk activities that Bali blocks for PMA. The result is a genuinely open national activity whose Bali position remains available because its large-scale OSS risk is medium-high or high.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium does not block this activity because its large-scale OSS risk is medium-high or high.

editorial.headline: Traditional Animal Medicines: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailing traditional or natural animal medicines is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
**In Bali today, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA.** That is the governing fact for a business devoted to retailing traditional or natural medicines for animals. The activity takes in a range of those products and the settings through which they are sold: veterinary pharmacies, animal-medicine depots, pet shops, poultry shops and animal-medicine stores. This is a retail definition with a specific subject matter: animal medicines described as traditional or natural.

The scope is useful precisely because it joins product and point of sale. It does not leave the reader with an abstract category; it places the work inside the outlets named in the record, from a veterinary pharmacy to a poultry shop. A business registering the activity is registering the retail operation described by that scope. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth gives founders one consistent retail activity across the four stated scales, while the underlying focus remains the sale of traditional or natural animal medicines.

At the national level, this activity carries TERBUKA PMA status, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In plain terms, the national record permits full foreign ownership for this activity; it does not state a lower foreign cap. The source recorded for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder considering the activity at national level, that is a clean opening and an important baseline. It should, however, be read as a national statement, not as a conclusion about every place in Indonesia.

Bali supplies the decisive qualification. Its status is Blocked (risk class), meaning it is blocked by risk class. The Bali record says that at the Besar scale, every scope is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah, and connects the block to the Bali moratorium beginning 13 May 2026. The provincial rule is stated broadly: Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. The restriction is location-specific in the record, not a revision of the national ceiling. Despite the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. National openness should not be mistaken for a Bali registration route.
editorial.pullQuote: Despite national openness to 100% foreign ownership, a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Pet Cosmetics Retail: Nationally Open, Bali PMA Blocked
editorial.standfirst: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling meets a permanent, island-wide Bali block on PMA registration, making location—not scale—the decisive fact.
editorial.body:
**What the activity covers.** This is a retail classification for cosmetics made for animals: perfume, shampoo, soap, powder, cream and lotion. The scope is concrete about the stock a business sells, rather than leaving animal cosmetics as an abstract category. It also expressly includes the retail settings named in the record—veterinary pharmacies, animal-drug depots, pet shops, poultry shops and animal-drug stores. Read together, those details give the activity a clear commercial shape: retail trade in animal-care goods, with cosmetics specifically identified among them.

**Who may register it.** The activity is open at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That is a complete scale range in the record, not a category reserved for one narrow size of enterprise. For a founder, the important distinction is therefore not whether the business is micro or large, but where PMA registration is being contemplated. The listed scales establish the breadth of the activity; foreign ownership and local registration conditions determine the practical route.

**Nationally, the position is straightforward.** The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain English, the national record permits full foreign ownership for this activity. Its stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower national foreign-stake cap in the record. Yet the national ceiling answers the ownership question; it does not by itself establish that PMA registration is available in every location.

**Bali is the decisive exception.** A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. Bali marks it Blocked (risk class): at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. That places it within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, recorded here as the Bali moratorium of May 2026. The cited basis is Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. National openness therefore remains real, but it does not create a PMA registration route in Bali for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness permits full foreign ownership, but it does not create a PMA registration route in Bali.

editorial.headline: Retailing Pharmaceutical Inputs and Medical Devices in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and remains available for PMA registration in Bali, including at larger operational scale.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the retail sale of pharmaceutical-preparation inputs, traditional-medicine raw materials known as *simplisia*, and other medical devices. Its scope extends across products for both people and animals, giving it a practical reach into specialist health-related retail rather than a single consumer category. It also encompasses veterinary pharmacies, animal-medicine depots, pet shops, poultry shops, and animal-medicine stores.

The code is open to businesses at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale. That breadth matters: the activity is not confined to a particular size of operator in the record. A founder considering this line of business should therefore understand the code as a retail framework for specified pharmaceutical and animal-health inputs, medical devices, and the listed veterinary and animal-retail formats, rather than as a general description of the wider health economy.

At the national level, PMA is classified as TERBUKA and its foreign-ownership ceiling stands at 100%. In plain terms, the record allows full foreign ownership at the national level. There is no lower foreign-share cap recorded for this activity, and the national reference cited is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record states that operations at Besar scale carry Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi OSS risk, placing them outside the province-wide permanent PMA block for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. The result is straightforward: this activity is not blocked by Bali’s moratorium for PMA registration. The distinction is important because Bali’s restriction is broad for the risk bands it names, while this record expressly places the larger-scale case beyond that block.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this activity is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Photography Retail: Nationally Open, Barred for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 47731 covers the retail sale of cameras, projection and sound equipment—open to full foreign ownership nationally, yet barred from PMA registration in Bali under its moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47731 is the retail activity for photographic equipment and its supporting apparatus. Its scope embraces still cameras and cinematographic cameras, cinematographic projectors, sound-recording and sound-reproduction equipment, image projectors and overhead projectors. It also reaches photographic flash apparatus, camera frames and bodies, image-projector equipment, and film-cassette transfer equipment. The through-line is clear: this is an activity defined by selling the equipment and accessories used to capture, record, reproduce or project images and sound. The formal title is broad enough to include both the core devices and the operational kit around them.

The registration audience is therefore a business undertaking this particular form of retail trade, rather than an abstract technology label. The record opens it to Micro, Small, Medium and Large enterprises, so the code is not confined to one company size. editorial.headline: Eyewear Retail: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans retail sales of eyewear and optical products, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium prevents foreign-investment registration there today.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this eyewear-retail activity as PMA in Bali today. That is the practical starting point, even though the national position is fully open to foreign investment. The distinction matters because the activity itself is straightforward and familiar: retailing a range of eyewear products, from vision-correction glasses and sunglasses or light-filtering glasses to contact lenses, soft lenses, and spectacle frames. It also includes optical specialists whose work includes selling glasses.

This is therefore a retail activity centred on the customer’s choice, fitting, and purchase of optical goods. Its scope is broad enough to accommodate both everyday eyewear and products connected with vision assistance, while expressly including the retail role of an optical expert. The record places the activity within direct sales, and opens it across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth describes who may register it by scale; it does not alter the separate foreign-investment treatment that applies in Bali.

Nationally, the code is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In other words, the national framework permits full foreign ownership for this activity. The governing PMA source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder assessing the national market, this is an open category rather than one subject to a stated foreign-equity cap below full ownership.

Bali reaches a different operational result. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope of this activity. Bali’s rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide and permanently, and the resulting Bali status is Blocked (risk class). The record ties that block to the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026. So the national permission remains real, but it does not create a route for PMA registration in Bali while that island-wide moratorium applies. For this activity, the honest reading is simple: nationally open to full foreign ownership; unavailable for PMA registration in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Timepiece Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s island-wide risk moratorium blocks it for PMA registration.
editorial.body:
In Bali, a foreigner cannot register this retail activity as PMA today, even though its national position is open. KBLI 47734 covers the retail sale of varied timepieces: wristwatches, pocket watches, wall clocks, alarm clocks and bells. It also covers retail sales of watch and clock parts. The scope places the activity outside direct sales, keeping the description anchored in the retailing of timekeeping goods and their components. Its stated range runs from personal watches to wall clocks, alarms, bells and their retail parts.

That business is open to registration at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. At the national level, the PMA status is Open and the permitted foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. A PMA company therefore has a national route to full foreign ownership of this activity; the record does not present a partial foreign-share limit. The cited national basis is Presidential Regulations 10/2021 and 49/2021. For founders assessing the activity outside the Bali restriction, the availability of all four listed scales and the 100% ceiling are the essential national facts.

Bali, however, answers a different question: whether the activity may be registered there as PMA. The answer is no. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class), and the reason identifies the OSS risk at the Large scale as Low/Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration. It is an island-wide, permanent rule. The result is a complete block on PMA registration in Bali, rather than a reduced foreign-ownership percentage.

This is why the national and Bali positions should not be blended. Nationally, the record permits up to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, the moratorium prevents PMA registration of the same activity. The difference is not a question of the product range: wristwatches, clocks, alarms, bells and parts remain the defined retail scope. It is a location-specific PMA outcome arising from the stated risk classification and Bali rule. For this code, a full national foreign-ownership ceiling does not produce a Bali PMA registration route.

editorial.headline: Jewellery Retail Is Nationally Open—But Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity permits full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks its PMA registration on the island.
editorial.body:
At the national level, this is an open foreign-investment retail activity, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Its territory is jewellery retail: the sale of goods made from precious stones, diamonds, diamond powder, gemstones, imitation gemstones, precious metals and non-precious metals. The description is broad in the articles it captures—rings, necklaces, bracelets, earrings, hairpins, brooches, belts and precious-metal buttons are all expressly included—while remaining precise about the commercial act: retail trade in jewellery goods.

The range of materials is equally deliberate. It embraces jewellery made with platinum, gold and silver, as well as pieces involving gemstones or their imitations, without reducing the activity to one material or one form of adornment. The registration is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That means the stated activity can be registered across all four listed business scales; the scope remains the retail sale of the jewellery goods described, rather than being confined to a single size of enterprise.

In Bali, however, the national rule is not the end of the inquiry. A PMA investor cannot register this activity in Bali today: its Bali position is blocked at the risk-class level. The record places the OSS risk assessment for the Besar scale at Low or Medium-Low across every scope. That brings the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activity. The Bali result is a registration block, not a different national ownership percentage.

The distinction is clean, but consequential. Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%, within the stated retail scope and across the four listed scales. In Bali, PMA registration is unavailable because the risk classification triggers the provincial moratorium. These are not competing readings to be averaged into a softer answer: they are two geographic layers of the same decision. The national ceiling remains national; for a PMA registration on the island, the Bali block is decisive.

editorial.headline: Used Household Retail: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Used household furnishings sit within a nationally open activity, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium closes the registration route for this trade.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register a PMA business for this activity in Bali today. That outcome is not a judgement on the trade itself; it follows Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. The contrast is decisive: national openness does not create a Bali registration path where the provincial rule blocks it.

The activity is retail trade in used household equipment. Its subject is recognisably domestic: used tables, chairs, wardrobes, beds and sideboards, together with used items for eating and drinking. The category is shaped by the character of the goods being offered at retail—their previous use and their household purpose. It gives a clear commercial home to a retail operation built around second-hand furnishings and household dining items, whether the stock centres on larger pieces of furniture or the practical objects that accompany life at home.

Registration is open across the full set of enterprise scales recorded here: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the activity is not presented as belonging only to a small trader or only to a larger operator. The record permits the same retail subject at each of those scales. For a founder, the useful discipline is to keep the activity description equally clear: the business is retailing used household equipment, not merely dealing in goods that happen to have been used.

Bali changes the practical conclusion for PMA registration. The OSS risk assessment at the Large scale is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, placing the activity within the class caught by the Bali moratorium dated May 2026. Bali’s status is therefore blocked on risk-class grounds, notwithstanding the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. A founder considering this activity should read those two facts together: it is fully open to foreign ownership at the national level, but a foreigner cannot register it as PMA in Bali under the stated provincial rule.

Second-hand fashion retail is a distinct retail activity: the sale of pre-owned clothing, footwear and clothing accessories. Its practical inventory is familiar—used shirts, trousers, coats, shoes, scarves and hats—but the classification is defined by the retail trade in those used goods, rather than by a particular style, resale channel or customer profile. It gives a clear home to an operator whose business is built around bringing used apparel and related items to market.

The activity is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the classification is not written only for a large-format retail proposition. It accommodates the activity at each of those recognised scales, while keeping the commercial focus precise: used garments, used footwear and used apparel complements sold at retail.

At the national level, the PMA position is straightforward. The activity is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In other words, national treatment permits full foreign ownership for this activity. That national openness is grounded in Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021, and should be read as the national ownership setting—not as a guarantee that every provincial registration environment reaches the same result.

Bali is the decisive exception. PMA registration for a foreigner is not available for this activity in Bali today. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns low or medium-low risk across every scope, placing the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. The recorded restriction took effect through the Bali moratorium on 13 May 2026. The contrast is therefore real rather than technical: a 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not overcome Bali’s local PMA block for this activity. For a founder assessing the opportunity, the honest conclusion is simple: nationally open, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under the stated risk-based moratorium.

editorial.headline: The Used-Electronics Trade Bali’s PMA Moratorium Stops
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but a Bali-wide PMA moratorium blocks registration in Bali today.
editorial.body:
A business under this activity trades in used electrical and electronic goods at retail: second-hand radios, tape recorders, televisions, washing machines, electric irons, and hair dryers or curlers. Nationally, it is open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In Bali, however, the practical answer is unequivocal: a foreign investor cannot register this activity for PMA today. The activity is blocked by Bali’s moratorium on PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities, applied island-wide on a permanent basis.

The character of the business matters. This is not a general description of electronics retail, but a defined trade in previously used electrical and electronic items. The examples give the category its useful commercial shape: household appliances sit alongside consumer audio and television equipment, while personal-care electrical goods are also expressly within scope. It is therefore an activity grounded in the resale of used equipment, rather than the manufacture, repair, or unspecified distribution of those goods.

The registration is open across the full stated range of business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That broad national availability does not soften the Bali result for PMA. The Bali classification records that, at the Besar scale, every scope carries a Low or Medium-Low risk assessment. That is the condition that brings the activity within the provincial moratorium. The national position and the Bali position are consequently not competing descriptions of the same outcome; they operate at different levels. Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%. In Bali, PMA registration is blocked.

For founders, the important discipline is to keep those two truths in view at once. The national foreign-investment setting signals that this used-electronics retail activity is open in principle. Bali’s province-wide rule then determines that the activity cannot be registered there as PMA because of its risk classification. That is not a marginal qualification to be discovered after choosing a scale or assembling a product range; it is the central local constraint. A business plan built around the retail resale of used electrical and electronic goods must treat Bali’s PMA block as decisive from the outset.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%; in Bali, PMA registration is blocked.
