editorial.headline: Second-Hand Building Materials: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity is nationally open to PMA ownership of up to 100%, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for it today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47745 covers the retail trade of used construction materials and used sanitary ware. Its practical territory is the resale of items such as second-hand sinks, toilets and water tanks: goods that have already had one life in a building and are being offered again through retail trade. The scope also expressly places direct sales alongside that activity. It is a focused commercial category, concerned with the retail circulation of used building and sanitation fixtures rather than a broad claim over the construction economy.

Nationally, the classification is marked **TERBUKA** for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The national reference recorded for it is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain terms, the national setting does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That is the national position founders should begin with—but it is not the final answer for a business intending to register in Bali.

The code is open across the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the activity may be structured at any of those stated business scales; the record does not reserve this resale trade for one particular size of operator. A founder should therefore define the business by what it actually sells—used construction materials and sanitary goods—and by the retail activity described here, rather than assuming that the national PMA setting alone settles the location question.

In Bali, the answer is decisive: a PMA business cannot register this activity there today. Bali classifies it as **Blocked (risk class)**. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent block on all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The recorded reason ties that result to the Bali moratorium of May 2026, with the cited source being Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. The national 100% ceiling remains the national ceiling; in Bali, however, the moratorium prevents PMA registration for this code.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% ceiling remains intact, but Bali’s moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity today.

editorial.headline: Antiques at Retail: Bali’s PMA Line
editorial.standfirst: Retail trade in antiques is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for the activity.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor intending to register this activity in Bali, the decisive answer is simple: it cannot be registered there as a PMA activity today. That local result sits alongside a markedly different national position. KBLI 47746 is nationally open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The two statements are not competing readings of the same rule; they describe the national opening and the Bali outcome for this activity. For a founder, the practical point is to keep both levels in view from the beginning: national openness does not become a PMA registration route in Bali.

The activity itself is retail trade in antiques. Its scope identifies the sort of goods meant by that label: used jars, used bokor bowls, used chandeliers, and used marble tables and chairs. These examples keep the description grounded in physical antique goods rather than an abstract retail category. The code concerns the retail sale of such antique articles; that stated activity description should anchor the registration conversation. In English, *Perdagangan Eceran Barang Antik* is most directly read as retail trade in antique goods.

The activity is open across every scale listed: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—micro, small, medium and large. That is a broad scale range. It means the stated availability does not begin only at a large-enterprise designation, nor is it confined to a micro or small business category. Scale and foreign ownership answer different questions: the first identifies the enterprise sizes open to the activity, while the national PMA position records the foreign-investment ceiling. Together, they give the national headline: retail antiques, all four listed scales, and 100% foreign ownership.

Bali’s block follows the recorded risk treatment and the province-wide moratorium. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope of the activity. Under Bali’s rule, PMA registration is blocked for activities carrying those risk classifications, island-wide and permanently; this outcome is tied to the Bali moratorium of May 2026. The result is categorical for a PMA registration in Bali: however fully foreign-owned the activity may be nationally, it is blocked there. The cited local policy source is Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not become a PMA registration route in Bali.

editorial.body:
PMA registration for this activity is not available to foreign investors in Bali today. The category covers the retail sale of other second-hand goods not otherwise included within its defined group: a residual but legitimate space for businesses whose trade is in used goods outside the more specifically described retail activities. Its breadth is precisely its character; the activity is defined by what it sells—other pre-owned goods at retail—rather than by a narrower product identity.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. The activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. editorial.headline: Pet-Animal Retail: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership across every stated scale, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this pet-animal retail activity as PMA in Bali under the position recorded here. That conclusion matters because the national setting is otherwise unequivocal: the activity is open to foreign investment, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The Bali restriction is therefore not a softened version of the national rule, nor a question of a reduced ownership share. It is a block on PMA registration in the province.

The activity itself is straightforward but broad in the animals it encompasses. It covers the retail sale of companion animals, including cats, dogs, snakes, rabbits and monitor lizards, alongside other pet animals. The scope also records direct sales. In practical editorial terms, this is the retail end of the pet-animal trade: a business whose defining activity is selling the animals themselves to customers, rather than merely operating around the wider pet economy.

The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth gives the classification a clear national operating range, from the smallest stated business scale through to the largest. For a founder assessing foreign participation, however, the national openness is only half the answer. The national ceiling permits full foreign ownership, but location changes the registration outcome. An activity can be fully open in the national investment setting and still be unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.

Bali’s reason is explicit. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is recorded as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, placing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis; the record identifies the moratorium as taking effect in May 2026. For this activity, the honest Bali position is therefore categorical: full foreign ownership remains the national ceiling, but PMA registration in Bali is blocked by the province’s risk-based rule.

For a founder, that distinction matters because the registered activity should reflect the actual retail business being established, not a wider ambition that the record does not define.

In other words, the national framework does not impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity.

Bali is the exception that cannot be treated as a footnote. The record states that, at the Large scale, the OSS risk classification is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. That classification brings the activity within Bali’s moratorium, which blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA on a permanent, island-wide basis. The result is not a reduced foreign-ownership percentage or a conditional local pathway in the record; it is a block on PMA registration in Bali. A national opening therefore does not translate into a Bali registration route for a foreign-owned company pursuing this activity today.

editorial.standfirst: Retailing ornamental fish, aquatic seed and other live, non-food aquatic life can be wholly foreign-owned nationally—but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium closes the PMA registration route.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47753 concerns the retail sale of live fish and other live aquatic organisms that are not intended for consumption. Its scope is precise about the stock: ornamental fish, pearl oysters, sponges, milkfish fry, shrimp fry, fish seed and clear lobster seed are all named examples. What binds them is their live, non-food character. The activity is defined less by a single species than by a particular kind of aquatic material, with seed forms sitting alongside more familiar ornamental and marine organisms.

Registration is open at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters. The record makes this one retail activity available from micro through large-scale operation, rather than limiting it to a narrow size band. At the national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA and its foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In direct terms, the national position permits a foreign investor to own the business fully. Bali changes the practical result decisively. A foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today: its Bali status is blocked by risk class. The supplied reason is specific. Bali’s stated moratorium prohibits PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the island, permanently. It took effect on May 13, 2026, according to the cited gubernatorial letter. The national record offers an open PMA status and a 100% ceiling; Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium nevertheless closes PMA registration for the activity. Neither fact cancels the other. For a founder assessing this retail trade in live, non-food aquatic life, the crucial distinction is geographic: national foreign ownership may be fully open, while the Bali registration route is unavailable. It is the distinction that prevents national openness from being mistaken for permission to register PMA in Bali.

editorial.headline: Feed Retail’s Split Decision: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailing feed for livestock, poultry, fish and companion animals is nationally open to PMA, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks its PMA registration.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity is the retail trade in feed for livestock, poultry and fish, alongside food for companion animals. The stated range is concrete: feed rations and concentrates for livestock, poultry and fish, plus bone meal, blood meal and shell meal. It also covers retailing various fish-feed products from public-roadside stalls, the front porch of a shop, or movable and pushable market premises. Those examples include fish feed, fish-feed concentrates and shell meal. The scope is expressly identified as other than direct selling.

The activity is open at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. This is a scale-wide statement of access to the specified retail activity, not an invitation to blur its boundaries. The record remains focused on defined feed and food products, and on retail settings that include fixed shops as well as the named roadside and market formats. For a founder, the classification begins with that practical distinction: this is a retail activity for animal-feed and companion-animal-food products within the stated scope.

Nationally, it carries open PMA status, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national record permits full foreign ownership of the activity. Its stated source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali gives a different result. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today, despite its national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The Bali record marks the activity as blocked. Its stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope; it is therefore caught by the Bali moratorium recorded on May 13, 2026.

That moratorium is described as island-wide and permanent, applying to all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The consequence is unambiguous: national openness does not provide a Bali registration path for this activity. A founder considering this retail scope should treat the national 100% ceiling and Bali’s PMA block as simultaneous facts, rather than competing descriptions of the same rule. The work may be clearly defined, and every scale may be listed as open, yet Bali remains a registration stop for PMA.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today, despite its national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Cut Flowers, Florists and Bali’s PMA Line
editorial.standfirst: This retail floristry activity is open nationally to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47761 covers the retail trade of cut flowers and florist activity, with direct sales also noted in its stated scope. It is a code for the point at which flowers are sold at retail: the commercial activity of offering cut flowers and floristry to customers. Its definition is concise, and that clarity matters. The code is concerned with retail trade in this field, rather than an implied wider chain of cultivation, processing or any other activity not stated in the record.

The activity is open across the full stated range of business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That makes it a category available from the smallest enterprise scale through to large business. For a founder, this is the practical starting point: the scale of the enterprise does not, at the national level, remove the activity from the listed range open to it. The scope remains retail trade in cut flowers and florist activity; the scale describes the business category through which that activity may be registered.

Nationally, the PMA position is unequivocally open. Foreign ownership may reach 100%, under the cited Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 basis. There is no national foreign-share cap below full ownership in this record. But that national opening is not the whole registration picture for a business intended for Bali. For PMA, the decisive distinction is simple: national openness does not create a registration route in Bali.

In Bali, this activity is blocked for PMA registration. At the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, placing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The record identifies the Bali position as `Blocked (risk class)`, and attributes the block to the moratorium of May 13, 2026. This is not a reduction in the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a Bali-specific registration barrier. A founder can therefore read the position cleanly: the activity is nationally open to PMA with up to 100% foreign ownership, while a foreigner cannot register it as PMA in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: For PMA, the decisive distinction is simple: national openness does not create a registration route in Bali.

editorial.headline: Plant Retail Is Nationally Open, but PMA Registration Is Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This plant-and-seedling retail activity permits 100% foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium prevents PMA registration there today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor seeking to register KBLI 47762 in Bali, the answer is no today. The activity is the retail sale of plants and seeds or seedlings for plants other than forestry plants. Its stated retail field includes medicinal plants and ornamental plants, with examples ranging from orchids, roses, jasmine and tuberose to aquatic ornamentals and seedlings for ornamental or medicinal plants. It is a defined plant-retail activity whose merchandise runs from mature plants to the material used to grow them.

The national position is explicit: its PMA status is TERBUKA, and foreign ownership can reach 100%. The activity is available at every listed scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth describes the national landscape for this activity. It does not, however, settle whether a PMA applicant can enter the register in a particular province.

In Bali, the local result is direct: PMA registration is blocked. The record identifies the reason as an OSS risk classification at the Besar scale, where every scope falls within Low or Medium-Low risk. This places the activity within Bali’s moratorium recorded on the thirteenth of May 2026. The provincial rule is island-wide and permanent. For a PMA applicant, the conclusion is not that Bali adds a softer local qualification; this activity cannot be registered there.

The distinction should be read without collapsing one jurisdiction into the other. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA and records a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In Bali, the permanent moratorium controls the registration outcome because the stated risk treatment is Low or Medium-Low at the large scale. The two facts coexist: national openness is real, while Bali is unavailable for PMA registration today. For founders, the point is concise but consequential: this activity may sit in an open national category, yet Bali is not a place where a foreign investor can register it.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, while Bali is unavailable for PMA registration today.

editorial.headline: Fertiliser and Pest-Control Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This specialist retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership across every listed business scale, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks PMA registration there.
editorial.body:
Bali is not currently a place where a foreign investor can register this activity. That is the controlling local fact, despite the national record classifying the activity as TERBUKA and setting a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The activity is specialist retail for fertilisers and pest-control products, not a broad label for agricultural commerce. Its subject is the retail sale of inputs used to nourish crops or deal with pest pressure. The scope also records direct sales, placing the activity in a sales setting as well as in a clearly defined product field.

The product range is specific enough to give the activity a distinct retail identity. It includes single manufactured fertilisers such as urea, ZA, TSP and DSP; compound and mixed fertilisers, including monoammonium phosphate, diammonium phosphate and nitrogen-phosphate-potassium products; and natural fertilisers such as compost, dolomite and lime. The pest-control side is equally broad within its speciality: insecticides, fungicides, rodenticides, herbicides, nematicides and acaricides are all named. This is a retail operation built around fertilisation and pest-management products, across manufactured, mixed and natural forms.

The national entry makes room for micro, small, medium and large businesses. That scale coverage is stated expressly, so the record does not confine the activity to a particular size of operation. Its PMA position is equally direct: TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Read nationally, those fields support one uncomplicated conclusion: foreign ownership may reach the full 100% ceiling for this retail activity.

Bali changes the operating conclusion, without changing the national ceiling. At the large scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope in the record. Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. The record links this result to the Bali moratorium noted in May 2026. A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not overcome Bali’s permanent PMA block for this activity. For a foreign founder, the conclusion is not a qualified Bali opening: registration in Bali is blocked.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not overcome Bali’s permanent PMA block for this activity.

editorial.headline: Ornamental Plant Retail: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retail sales of pots and growing media are nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
**For a foreign investor, this is not a Bali registration opportunity today.** The activity is nationally marked TERBUKA for PMA and carries a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. Yet the Bali entry is unequivocal: it is blocked for PMA registration. That is the central fact for a founder weighing location. National openness defines the position beyond the provincial restriction; it does not itself make a PMA registration available on the island. It is the primary planning distinction in this record, rather than a secondary qualification to be noted later.

The commercial focus is tightly drawn: retail trade in the supplies and media used for ornamental plants, including pots and growing media. The scope also explicitly includes direct sales. In plain English, this is a retail activity for the practical articles that accompany ornamental planting, with the sale of those articles—not a broad label for unrelated activity—at its core. The record names the examples rather than leaving the activity as an abstract category, giving pots and growing media particular weight in its account of the retail offer. The language points to a business whose offer centres on these supplies, served through retail and direct-sale channels.

The listed company scales are Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The record therefore admits the activity at every one of those named scales, from Mikro through Besar, without changing its stated retail subject. That scale coverage matters in reading the entry correctly: the same basic activity is described in one place, while the Bali outcome is assessed separately through its risk-based provincial rule. Direct sales remain expressly in scope alongside the retail description. The scale labels are stated plainly and do not alter the named subject of the activity.

Bali is the decisive constraint. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope. Bali’s rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration, island-wide and permanently; for this activity, the record specifically ties the block to the Bali moratorium of 13 May 2026. A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling is thus a national fact, not a Bali availability statement. It cannot be treated as permission to register a PMA for this activity in Bali while the provincial block stated in the record applies. This is why the national and Bali fields must be read together, without allowing one to erase the other.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling is a national fact, not a Bali availability statement.

editorial.headline: Forest Plant Retail: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity is open to full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium prevents registration there today.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. That is the decisive local fact, even though the national position is fully open to foreign ownership. The activity is the retail trade of forestry plants, forestry seeds and seedlings, and parts of forestry plants. Its scope also places it beyond direct sales: this is a defined retail activity for bringing forestry planting material and related plant parts to market.

The permitted business scales are broad: Micro, Small, Medium and Large enterprises may undertake the activity. That breadth matters because the code is not framed as a niche reserved for one size of operator. A business may be established across the full stated range of scales, provided its actual operations remain within retail trading of forestry plants, seeds, seedlings and plant parts. The record does not extend the activity into cultivation, production or any other commercial function; its centre of gravity is retail trade.

At the national level, the PMA status is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national framework allows full foreign ownership for this activity. The stated basis is Presidential Regulations 10/2021 and 49/2021. For a founder assessing Indonesia at national level, that is a clear opening: foreign capital is not capped below full ownership for this code.

Bali reaches a different operational outcome. For the Large-scale registration in this record, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities from PMA registration. The result is not a reduction in the national ownership ceiling; it is a local bar on PMA registration in Bali for this activity. The distinction is essential: nationally, full foreign ownership is open; in Bali, the applicable risk classification brings the activity within the moratorium. The local position is recorded as blocked by risk class, under the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, full foreign ownership is open; in Bali, the applicable risk classification brings the activity within the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Retail Kerosene: Nationally Open, Bali Registrability Not Yet Verified
editorial.standfirst: Retail kerosene trade is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s registration position for it has not yet been verified — pending case-by-case review, the activity is blocked.
editorial.body:
Retail kerosene trade is exactly what this activity describes: the retail sale of kerosene. It is a retail-facing activity, defined by the product and the act of selling it at retail rather than by a broader supply-chain claim. That narrow definition matters. A registration under this activity should accurately describe a business carrying out retail kerosene trade, keeping the declared operation aligned with the scope recorded for it. The point is neither to stretch the label into a general energy business nor to attach duties that the record does not state; it is to read the activity for what it is: retailing kerosene.

This page currently carries no verified licensing rows for this activity:. That gap is more consequential than a generic statement that an activity is open or closed, because until the licensing rows are re-verified we cannot say which operating scales this activity is registered under, or whether a large-enterprise (Usaha Besar) tier exists for it. Treat any scale reference on this page as provisional until confirmed at oss.go.id.

Nationally, the investment status is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In national terms, that is an unambiguous opening: the record allows the maximum foreign stake of 100% for this activity. But that national signal does not by itself establish a PMA registration route in Bali. The requirement we located is a commercial one and nationality-neutral — Perpres 191/2014 Pasal 3(1), 8(1) and 9 make subsidised-fuel distribution an assignment to a Badan Usaha that already holds an Izin Usaha Niaga Umum plus storage and distribution facilities. We hold no verified licensing rows for this code, so its Bali risk tier is unknown and we will not state a Bali position; it is treated as blocked until verified case by case.

Bali’s provincial setting reinforces the need to separate a national ownership ceiling from local registrability. Its permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI for PMA — but because this code currently carries no verified licensing rows, we cannot confirm which risk tier it falls under, or whether that moratorium applies to it. The practical reading is direct: a foreign investor may see a nationally open activity, yet the Bali registration position for it has not yet been established. For Bali, the decisive fact is not the national ceiling, but the unresolved licensing record: this activity is blocked pending case-by-case verification, not confirmed as closed.
editorial.pullQuote: A nationally open activity can still be blocked from PT PMA registration in Bali when its licensing record has not yet been verified.

editorial.headline: LPG Cylinder Retail: Nationally Open, Not Registrable for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers retail sales of cooking LPG cylinders, open nationally to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
At the national level, KBLI 47772 is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, however, a foreign investor cannot register this activity for PMA today. The difference is not a contradiction: Bali’s province-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. For this activity, the OSS risk at the Besar scale is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every listed scope, placing it inside that Bali block.

The activity is specific in purpose and product. It covers retail trade in liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplied in cylinders for cooking. The stated scope also includes Sub Pangkalan LPG Tertentu and Pangkalan LPG Tertentu, the particular LPG sub-base and base formats named in the record. This is a retail classification centred on bottled cooking gas: its language does not broaden into a general account of the gas sector, and its commercial focus remains the sale of LPG cylinders to the retail market.

The classification is open to enterprises at every recorded scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That scale range describes who may register the activity by business size. Its national investment position is a separate matter: the code is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%, under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The national opening is clear, but it does not displace Bali’s PMA restriction where the activity falls within the risk classes covered by the provincial moratorium.

For founders, the essential distinction is straightforward. Nationally, the record permits a PMA stake up to the full 100% ceiling. In Bali, the present result is a registration barrier rather than a reduced foreign-ownership limit: PMA registration is blocked because the activity’s Besar-scale OSS classification is Low or Medium-Low throughout the stated scope. The Bali reason identifies the moratorium in May 2026, while the governing rule describes it as island-wide and permanent. The resulting Bali status is therefore unambiguous: Blocked (risk class).
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this activity is nevertheless blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Chemical Retail: Nationally Open, but Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This specialist chemical-retail activity permits up to 100% foreign ownership nationally, yet PMA registration is blocked in Bali under the province’s risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
Chemical retail can sound broad, but this activity is explicitly specialist. It is the retail trade in chemical materials, with the scope naming caustic soda, soda ash, baking soda, ammonia, colourants and preservatives. Those examples identify the materials around which the retail offer is organised. Read as a business description, the code has a clear centre of gravity: selling chemical inputs and products at retail, with the named substances illustrating the kinds of stock within its scope.

A business registering this activity is therefore a specialist chemical retailer. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises, so its listed scale range runs from micro through large. That breadth is useful context, but it does not dilute the core activity. Across those scales, the defining subject remains specialised retail trade in the chemical materials specified in the scope.

Nationally, the PMA position is open. The maximum foreign ownership recorded for the activity is 100%, meaning the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership. The national reference attached to that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is a straightforward national reading: the activity is not closed to PMA, and the stated foreign-ownership ceiling permits a fully foreign-owned business. Yet national openness answers only the national question; it does not itself settle whether the activity can be registered under PMA in a specific province.

Bali is where the distinction becomes decisive. A foreign investor cannot register this activity under PMA in Bali today. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk assessment is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, putting it within Bali’s moratorium. That provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA island-wide and permanently; the activity’s recorded Bali reason ties the block to the moratorium from May 2026. This is not a smaller Bali foreign-ownership ceiling or a partnership condition. It is a registration block for PMA in Bali, even though the national record allows foreign ownership up to 100%.
editorial.pullQuote: A national ceiling of 100% does not overcome Bali’s PMA registration block.

editorial.headline: Essential-Oil Retail Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Specialist retail of aromatic and refreshing essential oils spans every listed business scale, but Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration despite a nationally open 100% ownership position.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today, despite its nationally open PMA position and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The activity is specialist retail in aromatic and refreshing essential oils: a focused trade in products such as ylang-ylang, citronella, eucalyptus, sandalwood, lawang, tengkawang, wintergreen, castor, cardamom, nutmeg, delas and vetiver oils. The emphasis is on retailing that defined family of oils, rather than on a broader description of the sector.

The record makes the activity open to businesses at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That range matters because the classification is not confined to one size of enterprise: the same specialist-retail activity is available across the full set of listed scales. For a founder or adviser reading the code closely, the practical starting point is therefore the nature of the trade itself—retail sales of the specified aromatic and refreshing essential oils—and the business scale at which it is being registered.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%, under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. But national openness is not the same thing as PMA registrability in Bali. In Bali, the status is blocked at the risk-class level. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope of this activity; that places it within the Bali moratorium dated May 13, 2026. The provincial rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities across the island, permanently.

This is not a reduced Bali ownership ceiling or a local condition that can be read as a qualification to the national 100% figure. It is a block on PMA registration in Bali for this activity. The national record remains clear about foreign ownership; the Bali position is equally clear about where that national openness cannot presently be used. For anyone assessing this retail activity, both statements must be held together.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is not the same thing as PMA registrability in Bali.

editorial.headline: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity may be wholly foreign-owned nationally, yet its risk classification closes it to PMA registration anywhere in Bali.
editorial.body:
Code 47779 is a retail classification for chemical materials, aromatic or freshening goods—including essential oils—and fuel other than motor-vehicle fuel. Its stated scope gives it a deliberately practical shelf: gelatin, thermal-insulation materials other than plastic and rubber, polishing materials, camphor and firewood are named examples. It also admits direct selling. That mixture matters. The activity is best understood through the retail transaction in those stated goods, rather than through a broad claim to every product that might be sold beside them. Its commercial identity comes from retailing the specified materials and articles, not from making, processing or transporting them.

At national level, the PMA position is unambiguous: it is open, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. All four scale bands—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—are open for registration. For a founder, this is not a minor formatting point; it sets the national starting position. A business organised around the stated retail scope can be treated as a foreign-investment activity nationally without an equity cap below full foreign ownership appearing in this record. The scale list is equally broad: none of the recorded scales is excluded from the national opening. The code is clear on its national face, even though that clarity does not answer the place-specific question of Bali.

Bali reverses the practical answer for PMA registration. A foreign national has no route to register this activity as PMA in Bali today. The record marks its Bali status as blocked by risk class and states why: at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA for all activities in those Low and Medium-Low risk bands; for this code, that rule is decisive. The moratorium is identified as a May 2026 measure. The distinction is essential: the national ceiling remains 100%, but it does not create a Bali route for PMA registration. The record gives a categorical Bali outcome—national openness, alongside a present Bali block for PMA.
editorial.pullQuote: The national ceiling remains 100%, but it does not create a Bali route for PMA registration.

editorial.headline: A Clear National Opening, a Closed Bali Door for Souvenir Retail
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity welcomes PMA nationally at full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium closes the registration route for foreign investors.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the retail sale of souvenirs, handicrafts and religious goods made from a wide range of materials. Its territory is deliberately practical rather than narrowly decorative: statues, masks, reliefs, carved names, puppets, frames, lamp shades, trays, bags, baskets, mats, hats, blinds, wall decorations, doormats and fans all sit within its commercial frame. So do smaller keepsake and display articles, from key rings and ashtrays to flower vases, candleholders, medals, trophies, plant pots and ornamental objects made from shells, bone, horn or other materials.

The point is retailing these goods, including an art gallery where the gallery sells the handicraft items concerned. That distinction gives the activity a recognisable commercial centre of gravity: it is for the sale of objects intended as mementos, crafted pieces, decorative articles and religious merchandise, rather than a general description of culture or artistic production. The scope is broad enough to accommodate both everyday souvenir retail and a more curated presentation of craft goods, provided the gallery is selling those goods.

Registration is open across the stated business scales: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. Nationally, the activity is classified as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a full national opening for PMA participation, supported by the cited Presidential Regulations. It is an important starting point, but it is not the whole operating picture for a founder considering Bali.

In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity through PMA today. At the Large scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for those risk classifications. The moratorium took effect in May 2026. The result is stark but clear: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a PMA registration path for this activity in Bali under the stated provincial rule.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a PMA registration path for this activity in Bali under the stated provincial rule.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: A Painting Trade That Cannot Be Registered as PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A foreigner cannot register this nationally open painting-retail activity as PMA in Bali today.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity is the retail trade in paintings: portraits, animal paintings and landscapes, together with art-gallery activity when the gallery sells paintings. The definition is deliberately commercial. It concerns the point at which paintings are presented to buyers and sold through a retail operation or a selling gallery, rather than the creation of the work itself. The named examples illustrate the category’s range without changing its centre of gravity: the business is the sale of paintings, and a gallery belongs within it when sales are part of that activity. Whether the paintings are portraits, animals or landscapes, the record treats them as objects of retail sale; the gallery reference is equally specific about sales.

The registration picture is broad at the national level. The record opens the activity to micro, small, medium and large businesses; it does not reserve the trade for one particular operating scale. Its PMA status is open, and its national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That is a full-ownership ceiling, stated on the national basis of Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That scale range captures both the smallest listed form and the largest without changing the national PMA conclusion recorded for the activity. A foreign investor assessing a retail painting business or an art gallery that sells paintings can therefore read the national position plainly: the activity is available across the listed scales and national rules permit foreign ownership up to 100%.

Bali supplies the decisive qualification. This activity is blocked for PMA registration there, with the record identifying the issue as a risk-class block. At the large scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. That result triggers Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA for the activity, dated 13 May 2026. That finding is not an optional caution or an administrative footnote; it determines the local PMA outcome even though the national record remains open. National openness does not create a Bali PMA registration route for this activity. The contrast is not a smaller Bali foreign-ownership ceiling: the Bali record states a block. A proposal that fits the national scope—retailing paintings, including a gallery’s sale of them—must therefore keep the two jurisdictions in view: full foreign ownership is nationally permitted to the stated ceiling, while Bali’s moratorium prevents PMA registration for the same activity.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not create a Bali PMA registration route for this activity.

editorial.headline: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali: Retail Machinery Under KBLI 47791
editorial.standfirst: This broad machinery-retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks its registration there today.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the retail sale of a wide field of machinery, its equipment, components and spare parts. Its agricultural range includes tractors and equipment for ploughing, fertilising, sowing, planting, mowing, spraying, peeling and threshing, as well as rice-milling units and milking machines. The same retail scope extends to hand- and foot-operated sewing machines, electric sewing machines, overlock, embroidery and oversum machines, alongside generators, welding machines, coffee and flour grinders, saws, lathes, turbines, waterwheels, looms, knitting machines and printing machines.

The appropriate registrant is therefore a business engaged in retailing these kinds of machines and their related equipment or parts, rather than a business defined by one narrow machine category. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth is commercially meaningful, but it also matters to the regulatory reading: the Bali finding in this record turns on the risk treatment at the Besar scale.

Nationally, the position is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA and the national maximum foreign ownership is 100%, meaning a foreign investor may hold the entire foreign-owned stake nationally. Bali, however, produces a different practical result. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk treatment is Low or Medium-Low across every scope recorded for this activity. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities from PMA registration. Components and accessories are not peripheral additions: they are expressly within the activity’s stated subject. The scope also says it goes beyond direct sales, giving the category a broader retail expression while keeping its focus on water-transport equipment and associated parts.

The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises. In other words, the code is stated as available across each of the four listed business scales, rather than being confined to a single tier. That breadth is a useful point of orientation for founders: the retail subject remains the same whether the registration sits at a micro, small, medium, or large scale. The record’s structure is equally plain: all four scale labels appear in the open-to list, with no scale exclusion within that set.

At the national level, the foreign-ownership position is direct. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership figure is 100. A foreign-owned business may therefore hold the full ownership stake nationally. Here, 100 is the stated ceiling: no lower foreign stake is stated at the national level. The source record attributes that national position to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. These are national terms, however; they do not settle whether the same registration is available in a particular province.

Bali changes the result decisively for PMA registration. The record marks its Bali status as Blocked (risk class) and says it is blocked. The stated reason is that the OSS risk at the Besar scale is Low/Medium-Low on every scope; that brings the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The moratorium is recorded in May 2026. A foreign-owned business cannot register this activity in Bali today, even though the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. The provincial block sets the operative boundary for Bali without altering the national ceiling.

editorial.headline: Farm-Tool Retail: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Agricultural-tool retail is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks its registration there.
editorial.body:
Retail trade in agricultural tools may sound narrow until the shop floor comes into view. This activity covers the retail sale of farm implements: hoes, ploughs, sickles, crowbars and non-mechanical rice threshers. The record also places it alongside direct selling. The category is defined by the sale of those practical agricultural tools, not by a broad label alone; its examples give the description its useful boundaries.

That specificity matters when the activity is stated in a company’s registration. The named goods range from digging and cutting implements to crowbars and a rice-threshing tool that is explicitly non-mechanical, giving the retail offer a distinctly agricultural-tool focus. It is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. The slim record supplies no further operating prescription, so the sound reading is a disciplined one: keep the description anchored to the listed retail goods and to direct selling, rather than adding conditions it does not state.

Nationally, the investment posture is clear. The activity is TERBUKA for PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. A foreign investor can therefore hold the full national foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity in a PMA registration. The national basis cited in the record is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That clarity is substantial, yet it is not the end of the analysis for a business intended to register in Bali.

Bali changes the conclusion decisively. For a foreign investor, registering this activity in Bali is not permitted today. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk assessment is Low/Medium-Low across every scope, and the record identifies this as the trigger for Bali’s moratorium in May 2026. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not turn into a Bali registration route when that moratorium applies. For founders, the honest answer is simple: national openness exists on the record, while Bali is blocked for PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Motor-Rider Gear Retail: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity covers essential rider equipment, from helmets and rainwear to gloves and masks—nationally open to full foreign ownership, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
PMA registration for this activity is not available to foreigners in Bali today. The activity is the retail sale of motor-vehicle rider equipment: helmets, jackets, raincoats, gloves and masks, offered through direct sales as well. It is a practical retail category built around the things riders wear for protection and comfort on the road—not the vehicles themselves, but the equipment that accompanies their use.

The registration scope is broad in business scale. It is open to micro, small, medium and large enterprises, allowing the activity to sit within anything from a modest specialist shop to a larger retail operation. That breadth matters because the commercial character remains the same across the scales: the business is retailing rider gear named within the activity’s scope. The record does not add separate operational requirements or carve-outs, so the useful reading is a disciplined one: register only for the retail activity described, at a scale the business genuinely occupies.

At the national level, the PMA position is clear. The activity is open, and foreign ownership may reach 100%. In ordinary terms, there is no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That national openness is grounded in the cited PMA source, but it should not be mistaken for a guarantee of registrability in every location.

Bali is the decisive exception. For PMA registration, the activity is blocked under Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. The record identifies the relevant risk position at large scale as low or medium-low across every scope, which places the activity within that moratorium. The result is straightforward: full foreign ownership is nationally permitted, yet a PMA company cannot register this activity in Bali under the stated provincial rule. Founders considering Bali should treat that as the controlling present-tense fact, rather than relying solely on the national ownership ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: Full foreign ownership is nationally permitted, yet a PMA company cannot register this activity in Bali under the stated provincial rule.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Plastic Wrapping Retail: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Plastic wrapping retail is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali currently blocks PMA registration under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
An overseas investor cannot register this activity through PMA in Bali today. KBLI 47796 covers the retail trade in plastic wrapping goods: plastic sold by weight, rubbish bags and plastic bags. It is a tightly defined retail activity focused on these everyday packaging items. The scope identifies the goods in question clearly, including plastic sold by weight, rubbish bags and plastic bags, and notes that it extends beyond direct sales.

Nationally, however, the position is open. The record classifies the activity as open to PMA and gives a maximum foreign ownership of 100%, meaning the national framework allows full foreign ownership. Registration is open across the stated business scales—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. For founders, that establishes the national baseline: this is a retail activity whose stated ownership ceiling is not below full foreign ownership, and whose listed scales run from Mikro through Besar.

Bali provides the decisive local qualification. The Bali record marks the activity as blocked for PMA registration because, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every stated scope. Bali's island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities from PMA registration. The record connects this particular block to the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026. For this activity, national openness does not translate into a PMA registration route in Bali.

This is therefore not a case for treating the national 100% ceiling as a proxy for present-day availability in Bali. The national classification remains relevant to the activity's general PMA position and stated scales, while the Bali restriction governs the island-wide PMA-registration reality described in the record. A founder considering plastic wrapping retail needs to hold both facts at once: the activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali presently blocks its PMA registration on the risk-class ground stated here.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, national openness does not translate into a PMA registration route in Bali.

editorial.headline: Where ‘Other New Goods’ Meets Bali’s PMA Barrier
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 47799 covers specialised retail of new goods not otherwise classified, nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47799 is a deliberately broad retail category: specialised sales of new goods that are not classified elsewhere. Its scope includes cleaning materials, bamboo, sandalwood, damar resin, weapons and ammunition. That range is the point. The activity is defined not by one product line or a single kind of shop, but by the retail sale of particular new goods that sit outside more specifically described activity categories. It is a classification for businesses whose merchandise may be highly varied, while remaining within specialised retail.

The registration picture is broad at the business-scale level. Businesses at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales may undertake this activity. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In practical terms, the national record does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That national openness is an important part of the classification’s commercial reading, but it is not the whole Indonesian picture for a founder choosing Bali as the place of PMA registration.

In Bali, a foreigner cannot register this activity through PMA today. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): at the Besar scale, every scope is assessed as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, placing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The record identifies this restriction as taking effect through the Bali moratorium of May 2026. The national ceiling of 100% therefore remains a national position, while Bali’s PMA registration outcome is blocked.

That distinction deserves to be read plainly. A founder can accurately see an activity that is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, across every listed business scale, and still face a complete Bali-specific PMA registration barrier. For this code, the decisive Bali issue is not the nature of bamboo, cleaning materials, sandalwood, resin, weapons or ammunition as individual products. It is the activity’s risk treatment at the Besar scale and the province’s stated moratorium rule. The classification is nationally open; Bali’s PMA door is closed.
editorial.pullQuote: The classification is nationally open; Bali’s PMA door is closed.

editorial.headline: New-Car Retail Is Open Nationally, but Not for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the retail sale of new passenger cars and recreational vehicles, with full foreign ownership nationally but a decisive Bali restriction for PMA registration.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the first fact is the decisive one: this activity is open nationally to PMA registration with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, however, a foreigner cannot register it for PMA today. The provincial position is not a subtle qualification to an otherwise open classification; it is a block on PMA registration under Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.

The activity itself is narrowly legible. It covers the retail sale of new cars, including passenger cars and vehicles intended for camping or recreational use, such as caravans and motor homes. That definition gives the code its commercial centre of gravity: the sale of new vehicles to the retail market. It is a useful distinction because the record speaks directly to what is being sold and names the vehicle types within scope, rather than adding wider activities that are not stated.

Registration is open across the full set of recorded business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. Yet scale is also where Bali’s restriction becomes explicit. At the Besar scale, every recorded scope is assessed as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk. Under Bali’s moratorium, those risk categories are blocked for PMA on an island-wide and permanent basis. The result is clear even though the national PMA setting is fully open: the provincial restriction governs the practical outcome for a PMA registration in Bali.

That contrast should be read plainly. Nationally, the activity permits up to 100% foreign ownership under the cited investment framework. In Bali, the same activity is blocked for PMA registration because of the stated risk classification and the provincial moratorium. The national foreign-ownership ceiling remains a real national fact, but it does not create a Bali registration route while the Bali restriction applies. For founders, the relevant question is therefore not whether the activity is nationally open, but whether the intended registration location is Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the activity is open to 100% foreign ownership, but in Bali a foreigner cannot register it for PMA today.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. editorial.headline: Used-Car Retail: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: The retail sale of pre-owned passenger cars and camping vehicles is open nationally to foreign investment, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the retail sale of used cars: passenger cars, along with camping vehicles such as caravans and motorhomes. The definition is useful precisely because it is concrete. It concerns a retail activity in pre-owned vehicles, and its examples give the proposed business a practical frame. For a founder, that means beginning with the activity itself: a used-vehicle retail operation whose stock includes the passenger and camping vehicles identified in the record. That scope matters because it tells the reader what is being sold at retail, while retaining the record’s concrete examples as the boundary for the description. The description does not need stretching to convey a recognisable commercial proposition—placing those used vehicles before retail buyers.

Registration is open to Micro, Small, Medium and Large businesses. That breadth makes scale an explicit part of the activity’s profile, not a footnote. They are all recorded as open for the activity. Scale is an eligibility field here, while the Bali risk reason specifically singles out the Large scale when explaining its PMA block. An investor or founder should therefore state the intended scale accurately at the outset and keep the national investment position distinct from the Bali outcome. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Put plainly, the recorded national position permits foreign ownership up to the full 100% ceiling. That reading is anchored to the cited source, Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

In Bali, however, the conclusion is different and immediate: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA there today. Bali classifies it as blocked under the risk rule. The stated reason is that, at the Large scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low on every scope. The provincial moratorium then blocks PMA registration island-wide and permanently for the Low and Medium-Low risk classifications it covers. This is not a second foreign-ownership percentage or an exception to the national ceiling. The national ceiling remains 100%; Bali’s effect is a registration block. The record dates the moratorium to May 2026.

That separation is the essential point for decision-making. The activity’s national openness, its 100% foreign-ownership ceiling and its availability to every listed business scale do not override Bali’s position for PMA. It is important not to substitute the national number for Bali’s result: those fields answer different questions in the same record. The appropriate conclusion is neither a softened national summary nor a Bali-specific ownership calculation. At national level, the activity stands open to PMA on the recorded terms. In Bali, a PMA registration for it is blocked by the permanent, island-wide moratorium. Keeping these two levels separate preserves the record’s real message: a plainly defined used-car retail activity can be open nationally to foreign investment while unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national ceiling does not override Bali’s permanent block on PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Car Parts Retail Is Nationally Open. Bali’s PMA Door Is Closed
editorial.standfirst: Retailing new and used car parts, components, equipment and accessories is nationally open to PMA, but cannot be registered for PMA in Bali under the province’s standing moratorium.
editorial.body:
**For a foreign investor, the first fact is decisive:** this activity cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. Nationally, it is open to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. Bali, however, blocks it at the large-business scale because every scope is assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. That assessment places the activity within the province’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This is a real divide between the national setting and the Bali registration position.

The activity itself is retail trade in car parts, components, equipment and accessories, whether new or used. It is a business centred on the aftermarket and replacement ecosystem: the commercial sale of the items that support, equip or renew a car, rather than the sale of the car itself. Its boundaries are also clear. It does not extend to retail fuel sales or to the repair and maintenance of cars and motorcycles. The registered activity is therefore the retail operation for parts and accessories, including pre-owned stock, not a broader vehicle-service undertaking.

Registration is open across micro, small, medium and large business scales. That range is important, but it does not erase the Bali-specific result. The relevant Bali finding is tied to the large scale, where every scope falls into the Low or Medium-Low risk classification. Under Bali’s rule, those risk categories are blocked from PMA registration across the island on a permanent basis. The issue is not a reduced Bali foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a direct block on PMA registration.

The accurate reading is therefore two-tiered. At national level, foreign investment may hold up to 100% of this retail activity, and the activity is open across all four business scales. In Bali, a PMA applicant encounters a hard stop under the provincial moratorium cited for May 13, 2026. National openness remains meaningful as the national position, but it cannot be presented as present-day PMA availability in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness cannot be presented as present-day PMA availability in Bali.

editorial.headline: New Motorcycle Retail: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: New-motorcycle retail is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-class moratorium blocks PMA registration for the activity.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47831 defines the retail sale of new motorcycles, expressly including motorised bicycles and mopeds. The point is not merely the word “motorcycle”: the record brings the moped within the same activity boundary. That gives the code a crisp commercial centre—retail trade in new two-wheeled vehicles—and the reading should stay within that stated scope. Its subject is the sale of new motorcycles and the expressly included forms of motorised bicycle and moped.

For registration purposes, this activity is open at every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That is a full spread across the listed business sizes, rather than an activity confined in the record to one end of the scale spectrum. A founder considering this activity should therefore distinguish scale availability from the separate question of foreign investment. The scale field identifies the business sizes open to the activity; it does not displace either the national PMA position or Bali’s own PMA result.

The national rulebook takes a plain view of foreign investment in this activity. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. Put plainly, the national record allows the foreign stake to reach full ownership for this activity. That national conclusion is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It is the proper national baseline for a foreign-owned business, but it is not the final answer for a registration proposed in Bali.

Bali supplies the hard boundary. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Low/Medium-Low across every scope. Under Bali’s stated permanent, island-wide moratorium, all Low and Medium-Low risk activities are blocked for PMA. The record identifies this activity as blocked by that Bali moratorium from May 13, 2026, with Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP as its source. Accordingly, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. The island result is not a lower Bali foreign-ownership percentage: it is a block on PMA registration under Bali’s risk-class rule. Nationally the ceiling remains 100%; in Bali the PMA route is unavailable.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the ceiling remains 100%; in Bali the PMA route is unavailable.
