editorial.body:
This activity covers the retail sale of used motorcycles, extending to motorised bicycles and mopeds. Its focus is firmly on the retail transaction: bringing pre-owned two-wheeled vehicles to market for buyers. The definition is concise, yet it establishes a clear operating centre for the enterprise. The relevant business is the one retailing a used machine, whether the vehicle is described as a motorcycle, a motorised bicycle or a moped. That precision gives the activity a distinct commercial identity.

Registration is available at each stated scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. This gives the classification a wide stated range of enterprise size, from Mikro through Besar, without changing the underlying activity. A small retail operation and a larger company can therefore look to the same activity description when their work is the retail trade described in the record. The scale list is an eligibility signal; the substance remains the retailing of used motorcycles, motorised bicycles and mopeds.

At the national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In ordinary terms, the national record permits this activity to be fully foreign owned. That is a significant starting point, but it is not a Bali registration permission. Bali records the activity as blocked for PMA registration. The reason given turns on its OSS risk position at the Besar scale: every scope is classified Low or Medium-Low risk. In Bali, that risk character is decisive because the province’s stated moratorium captures all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA.

The Bali measure is described as permanent and island-wide. Its result is direct: a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today, despite the national 100% ceiling. For a founder reading the code, the right conclusion is not that the national allowance is misleading, but that it operates at a different level from the provincial registration outcome. The national position is open; the Bali route is currently closed for PMA registration. The national ceiling therefore cannot be read as a Bali registration permission.

editorial.headline: Motorcycle Parts Retail: Open Nationally, Barred to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailing new or used motorcycle parts and accessories is nationally open to PMA, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47833 covers the retail trade in motorcycle parts and accessories, whether new or used. It concerns the retail point at which replacement components and add-ons meet the customer, with the record also placing the activity alongside direct sales. The definition is deliberately product-specific: motorcycle parts and accessories, rather than a broad description of every commercial activity connected with motorcycles. Its scope expressly extends to both new and used stock, keeping the activity anchored to the retail sale of those goods.

Registration is open at every scale named in the record: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth does not make the classification a catch-all business description; it means the stated retail activity may be undertaken across those business scales. For a founder, the practical starting point is to keep the operating description precise: retail sale of motorcycle parts and accessories, new or used. The national investment position is equally direct. The activity is open to PMA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% under the cited Presidential Regulations.

That national opening does not carry through to Bali. In Bali today, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA. The Bali record marks it as blocked by risk class: at the Large scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration. The stated moratorium date is May 2026, and the result for this activity is not a softer local preference or a reduced foreign-ownership allowance: it is a registration block for PMA in Bali.

The distinction calls for an exact reading. Nationally, the code is open to foreign investment up to 100%; in Bali, its relevant risk classification brings it within an island-wide PMA prohibition. Both propositions come from the same record and must be held together rather than collapsed into a single claim of openness. A business may fit the retail scope and be available across every listed scale at the national level, yet that does not change the Bali registration outcome for a PMA applicant. For decisions involving Bali, the blocked status is the decisive fact.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this activity is nevertheless blocked from PMA registration in Bali.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers running a digital platform—like a website or mobile app—that purely matches retail sellers with buyers to place orders, earning a fee or commission in the process, without ever stocking or taking ownership of the goods being sold.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines, and some scopes of this KBLI fall in that band — but at least one large-scale (Besar) scope carries a higher risk class, so the code remains registrable as a PMA in Bali on that scope.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: matched with aggregation.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Platform Digital Intermediasi Perdagangan Eceran (47901)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: This fits a foreign entrepreneur creating a commission-based online marketplace (e.g., an e-commerce platform, food delivery aggregator, or curated retail app) that never holds inventory.

editorial.headline: The Platform That Connects the Sale Without Owning the Goods
editorial.standfirst: A retail marketplace can be nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet its route through Bali depends on the precise scope declared in OSS.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the business of running the digital meeting place for a retail transaction. The platform—whether a website or mobile application—brings sellers and buyers together so a good can be ordered. Its economic role is intermediation: it earns compensation or a commission, paid by the seller or the buyer, without supplying the goods or taking ownership of those it intermediates. That distinction gives the activity its centre of gravity. The operator enables the sale; it is not the merchant of the goods moving through the platform.

The scope is broad, but it is not indiscriminate. Its text expressly sets out exceptions involving PPMSE and PSP operators, both for those based within Indonesia and those based outside Indonesia that conduct electronic-commerce business in the country. For the activity as recorded, the available business scales run from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah to Besar. That breadth matters: the classification is not framed as a large-platform category alone, nor as a category reserved for an early-stage operator. It follows the practical function of the platform—facilitating a retail order for a commission—rather than the scale at which that function begins.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. The activity carries TERBUKA status and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. In plain terms, the national record permits full foreign ownership. That is the national position for this activity, supported by the cited presidential-regulation source. It should be read alongside the defined role of the platform: foreign participation is open for an operator whose business is to connect retail sellers and buyers for orders, while remaining outside the supply and ownership of the goods themselves.

Bali requires a more exact reading. The record does not mark the activity as outright blocked for PMA registration, but classifies the outcome as dependent on scope. Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. At the Besar scale, however, the OSS risk can be low for some scopes and higher for others. The stated route for PMA registration in Bali is therefore to declare the higher-risk scope, with PPMSE given as the relevant platform-trade example. A national 100% ceiling remains meaningful, but it does not settle the Bali filing by itself: the exact activity declaration must be checked live in OSS.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling is an opening, not a substitute for the precise Bali scope that OSS accepts.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Retail intermediary services via other media — mail order, catalog sales, online retail through non-platform channels, TV shopping. If you sell products directly to consumers through channels that aren't a physical store or a digital marketplace platform, this is the code. Critical distinction: selling your own goods = retailer (this code); providing a platform for others to sell = digital platform (63xxx).
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Risk: Rendah (Low)** for most retail intermediary activities (all scales). Only NIB required. However, direct selling (MLM/network marketing) at Large scale is **Tinggi (High)** — requires NIB + Izin, PT structure, marketing plan, code of ethics, and Ministry-level approval within 5 days.

**PMA:** Fully open (TERBUKA), 100% foreign ownership allowed.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Aggregated from multiple 2020 codes — combines 47909 with 12 subsidiary PP28 codes covering various retail intermediary types including online retail, direct selling, and auction houses.
intel_2026.baliContext: Common code for D2C (direct-to-consumer) brands selling online from Bali — surfwear brands, organic skincare lines, artisan crafts. If you're running a Shopify store from Canggu shipping products directly to customers, this is your code. But if you're building a marketplace where other sellers list products, you need 63900 (web portal) or 47901 (digital retail intermediation platform) instead.
intel_2026.youllAlsoNeed:
- 47901 — If you sell through dedicated online retail platforms
- 63900 — If you operate a web portal or marketplace
- 62110 — If you also develop the software/platform yourself
- 53200 — If you handle your own courier/delivery logistics
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Selling products online from Bali? 47909 covers non-platform D2C retail — let me explain the distinction from marketplace codes.

editorial.headline: Retail Intermediation: Nationally Open, Bali Depends on Scope
editorial.standfirst: This category covers specified retail-brokerage services, with full national foreign ownership but a scope-sensitive PMA route in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47909 covers retail intermediation services that do not fall within another specified retail category. In practical terms, it includes brokerage for retail transactions conducted by mail or telephone; auction-house activity for third-party goods, whether new or used, including online auctions; and retail motor-vehicle trade agents. Its boundary matters: the scope expressly excludes the specified non-exempt electronic-commerce-system operators and intermediary-facility providers, whether established in Indonesia or operating e-commerce activity there from abroad.

The category is available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth suits an activity defined by its role in connecting transactions, rather than by a single channel or product type. The registration should therefore follow the precise service actually being performed—mail or telephone brokerage, third-party auctions, online auctions, or motor-vehicle retail agency work—because the scope is detailed and its exclusions are explicit.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. The activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. A foreign investor may therefore hold the business in full under the national classification. The governing source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The national openness is meaningful, but it is not the whole practical answer for a business intending to register in Bali.

Bali’s position is scope-dependent, reflected in the status Blocked (scope-dependent). The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities across the island. For this category, the OSS risk at the Besar scale is low for some scopes and higher for others. Registration as PMA in Bali is available only where the declared activity falls within the higher-risk scope; the record identifies PPMSE in platform-trade situations as an example. National openness is real, but Bali eligibility turns on the exact scope declared in OSS. The live OSS result must therefore be checked against the precise activity before treating a Bali PMA registration as available.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, but Bali eligibility turns on the exact scope declared in OSS.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity

Kondisi dan jaminan barang serta memberi penjelasan penggunaan, perbaikan dan pemeliharaannya d. Program pemasaran (marketing plan) e. Kode etik
Perusahaan yang telah melakukan perekrutan penjual langsung wajib:
Memberikan alat bantu penjualan (starter kit) kepada setiap penjual langsung yang paling sedikit berisikan keterangan mengenai barang, program pemasaran (marketing plan) dan kode etik

editorial.headline: Tourist Rail Across Regions, and Bali’s PMA Picture
editorial.standfirst: A dedicated long-distance sightseeing rail operation is open to full foreign ownership nationally and is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium at Besar scale.
editorial.body:
This activity is the operation of dedicated tourist trains for longer interregional journeys, where rail travel itself is part of the visit. Its defining setting is not routine point-to-point service but sightseeing by train over a comparatively substantial distance between regions. The wording matters: it frames a tourism operation whose special train is designed around the experience of moving through a landscape, rather than merely moving passengers from one urban stop to another.

For founders, that distinction gives the activity a clear commercial identity. The business being registered is the operation of the tourist train service, anchored in interregional travel and a purpose-built tourism proposition. It is not a general label for any rail-adjacent visitor attraction. The focus remains a special sightseeing train for longer journeys between regions, keeping the scope as deliberate as the experience it describes.

The registration scales available are Menengah and Besar. This is a concise but meaningful boundary: the record does not identify it as a small-scale activity. The available scales establish the stated operating range without adding financial, operational, or other thresholds that the record does not provide. For this activity, Menengah and Besar are the relevant scales.

At the national level, the PMA position is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In ordinary terms, the record does not impose a national foreign-share cap below full foreign ownership for this activity. Bali’s result is also favourable, but for a specific reason rather than a blanket assumption. Bali permanently blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province. This activity is not caught by that moratorium: at Besar scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, and the record marks it as not blocked. Put plainly, a foreign investor can find an open national PMA route and a Bali position that is not barred by the stated island-wide moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity is not caught by Bali’s moratorium: at Besar scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, and the record marks it as not blocked.

editorial.headline: Intercity Rail: The Integrated Passenger Service
editorial.standfirst: Operating long-distance intercity passenger trains, including integrated sleeping or dining cars, is nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the operation of intercity passenger rail services that connect regions over relatively long distances. Its centre of gravity is the rail provider’s passenger journey: transporting people between places through an intercity service, rather than merely supplying a train or an ancillary amenity. Sleeping cars and dining cars can sit within the activity where they are an integrated part of that same passenger service.

That distinction gives the code its practical shape. The registrant is the operator of the intercity passenger railway service itself—the business responsible for making the long-distance journey available to passengers. The record opens the activity to Menengah and Besar scales, framing it as an undertaking for operators working at those stated business sizes. Where additional onboard facilities are offered, they belong to the picture only insofar as they remain part of the provider’s integrated passenger-transport service.

Nationally, the foreign-investment setting is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the record allows foreign ownership up to full ownership at the national level. This is a useful clarity point for founders: the activity is not presented as a nationally restricted foreign-investment category. The commercial proposition, however, remains specific—an intercity rail passenger operation, with long-distance regional travel as its defining service and integrated sleeping or dining facilities as possible components of that operation.

Bali requires a separate reading, but the result here is straightforward. The province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. For this activity, the record states that OSS risk at the Besar scale is Medium-High/High and expressly says it is not blocked by the moratorium. In Bali, the activity is not screened out by the island-wide PMA moratorium because its stated large-scale risk sits above the blocked categories. There is no separate Bali-side ownership percentage or partnership condition stated in the record, so none should be inferred.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, the activity is not screened out by the island-wide PMA moratorium because its stated large-scale risk sits above the blocked categories.

editorial.headline: Freight Rail, Open Nationally and Clear of Bali’s PMA Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers rail freight from industrial goods to energy carriers, with national foreign ownership open to 100% and no Bali moratorium block at large scale.
editorial.body:
Freight rail transport is the business of moving goods by rail: over long-distance routes or short dedicated freight lines. Its remit spans agricultural output, mining and quarrying products, petroleum fuels and processed products, LPG, LNG and CNG, carbon-free energy carriers such as hydrogen and ammonia, dangerous goods, hazardous and toxic waste, and industrial products. The transport may concern gases, solids or liquids, according to the cargo’s storage needs and conditions. Freight carried by cable or suspended railway, as well as long-distance traction services, also sits within this activity.

The natural registrant is an operator whose commercial work is the rail carriage of those goods. The code is open at medium and large business scales, reflecting a transport activity that can serve varied cargo types and rail configurations rather than a single commodity niche. Its breadth matters: it can accommodate both conventional industrial freight and cargo that demands particular care because of its form, energy role or hazardous character.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. Foreign investment may hold up to 100% ownership in the activity. In Bali, the equally important point is that a PMA registration is not blocked by the province’s moratorium. Bali permanently blocks PMA registrations for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the island, but this activity’s OSS risk at the large scale is Medium-High or High, placing it outside that moratorium block.

That makes the Bali reading more precise than a generic statement that rail freight is foreign-open. The national position permits full foreign ownership, while the Bali record confirms that the province’s specific moratorium does not close the door for this activity at the large scale. For a founder, the practical significance is clear: this is a rail-freight operating activity available at medium and large scales, with no additional Bali moratorium block recorded for PMA.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and Bali’s position align here: full foreign ownership is permitted, and the provincial moratorium does not block the activity at the large scale.

editorial.headline: Urban Tourist Rail Transport: Open Nationally, Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This urban tourist rail activity is open to foreign investment nationally, with full foreign ownership permitted and no Bali moratorium block for PMA registration.
editorial.body:
This activity is the operation of tourist trains that run on dedicated tracks as part of urban transport. Its setting is a tourism area, and its transport logic remains urban: the service operates within a city transport context. The record’s own illustration is a cable car serving a tourism precinct. That example keeps the focus on the operational fact that matters here—the running of rail-based tourist transport on a special route within an urban network. The definition puts three elements side by side: an operator of the service, the dedicated route it uses, and the urban-tourism setting in which it moves people. Those elements should remain visible when a business describes what it intends to register.

Who may register it is equally defined by scale. The record opens this activity to medium and large enterprises, so the business profile should be built around one of those two stated scales rather than an assumed smaller category. At national level it is marked open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. This is not merely a broad invitation to tourism businesses: it is the ownership position attached to the described operating activity. A founder or investor therefore has a clear national reading: foreign capital can enter, and the stated ceiling allows full foreign ownership. The record cites Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as its national source. The important editorial discipline is to keep that national position attached to this activity’s particular scope and stated scales, not turn it into a claim about a wider transport or tourism market.

Bali changes the question from what foreign ownership is permitted nationally to whether provincial policy blocks PMA registration. Here the answer is clean: it does not. Bali’s result is recorded as OK or higher risk, and this activity is not blocked by the province-wide, permanent PMA moratorium. The accompanying reason is specific: at the Large scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, and it is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. That is a Bali-side risk classification, not a second foreign-ownership percentage or a local-partnership requirement; neither is supplied in the record. For an investor assessing this exact activity, the honest combined reading is straightforward. Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%; in Bali, PMA registration is not stopped by the stated moratorium. The large-scale risk label is still part of the Bali picture and should be read as such—present, explicit, and not a reason to invent further conditions.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%; in Bali, PMA registration is not stopped by the stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: The Urban Rail Systems That Keep a City Moving
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers urban and commuter rail passenger operations—from trams and monorails to metro, elevated and airport-link services—open nationally to foreign investment at every scale permitted.
editorial.body:
Urban rail passenger transport is the operating backbone behind the rail systems that make a city legible at speed. It covers the movement of passengers within an urban area through rail-based modes including trams, monorails, electric trains, underground railways and elevated railways. The scope is deliberately broad enough to follow the modern city: cable-hauled trams, funiculars, gondola railways, autonomous rail trains and comparable systems belong here when they form part of an urban or commuter route network.

That emphasis on the network matters. The activity is not defined by one vehicle or one piece of track, but by the operation of passenger transport as an urban system. It also includes rail connections running from a city to its airport or port, recognising that metropolitan mobility extends beyond the centre to the gateways through which people arrive and depart. In practice, this is an activity for the operator responsible for carrying passengers across a city’s rail corridors, stations and connected commuter routes.

Registration is open at the **Menengah** and **Besar** scales. That places the activity in the hands of businesses equipped to operate a transport system rather than a small, incidental rail service. The scale distinction is useful editorially as well as commercially: the subject here is public-facing urban mobility infrastructure, where the operator’s role is to deliver a functioning passenger service across a defined city or commuter network.

Foreign investment is **TERBUKA** nationwide, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. Bali does not alter that conclusion through its island-wide permanent restriction on PMA registration for low and medium-low risk activities. At the **Besar** scale, the OSS risk classification is medium-high or high, so the activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The Bali position is therefore not a hidden prohibition: it is recorded as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, meaning the activity remains available for PMA registration there rather than being caught by the province-wide low-risk and medium-low-risk restriction.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not turn this nationally open urban-rail activity into a hidden prohibition for PMA registration.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers scheduled urban passenger transport within a city or town area, moving people along fixed routes—think city buses, minibuses, or similar shuttle services that operate on designated paths inside an urban zone. It does not include rail-based urban transit or rural passenger transport.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: This activity (intra-city urban public transport) is open to foreign investment through a PMA company. The risk classification and licensing shown here earlier were carried over from a different KBLI-2020 code (inter-city transport) and do not apply to this activity, so they have been removed from this page; the correct risk tier and licensing are not yet reliably defined for this code. Before registering or investing, confirm the current requirements with the Bali Zero team.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: matched with aggregation.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Angkutan Perkotaan (49213)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign entrepreneur with solid transport-operations experience who wants to set up an urban public-transit service on fixed routes, typically in a busy Balinese city like Denpasar, and who is prepared to navigate local address verification and medium-high-risk compliance steps.

editorial.headline: Urban Transport on a Fixed Route
editorial.standfirst: A fixed-route urban transport activity open to foreign investment through a PMA company; whether Bali's PMA moratorium applies is not yet classifiable pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.
editorial.body:
Urban Transport covers the movement of people from one place to another within an urban area on established routes. In practical terms, it is the scheduled, route-bound side of city mobility: city buses and other bus services operating within a route framework. The defining feature is not simply that the service moves passengers in a city, but that its operations are tied to a trayek—an assigned route rather than an undefined transport activity.

The activity is open to Micro, Small, Medium and Large enterprises. That breadth matters because the classification does not reserve the activity for a single business size or operating model. A founder registering under this code is therefore placing the enterprise within a formal urban-route transport category, with the scale of the business stated directly in the record rather than inferred from the kind of vehicles or network it may operate.

Nationally, the PMA position is clear: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Foreign investment is therefore permitted up to full ownership at the national level. The relevant source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is a meaningful distinction in a sector where the formal route-based nature of the activity should be read carefully: the record supports foreign participation in the activity itself, not a broader claim about every operational question a transport business might encounter.

Whether Bali's PMA moratorium applies to this activity cannot be determined until its risk tier is established — the earlier reading was based on a risk classification carried over from a different activity (code-number collision) and has been removed. Confirm with the Bali Zero team before planning a Bali setup. The activity remains open to foreign investment through a PMA company nationally, a separate and unaffected fact.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity remains open to foreign investment through a PMA company nationally — whether Bali's moratorium applies is not yet classifiable pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.

data._data_note: KBLI 2025 code 49213 'Angkutan Perkotaan' (intra-city urban bus transport on a fixed trayek) had per_skala detached 2026-07-17 after a code-number collision was found: the old served per_skala carried KBLI-2020 code 49213 = 'Angkutan Bus Antarkota Dalam Provinsi (AKDP)' (inter-city, Gubernur authority), the wrong regulatory basis for an intra-city activity (preserved unchanged under per_skala_disputed_pp28_collision as a historical audit trail — never reused). Per-ancestor adjudication (research/operations/2026-07-18-kbli-batch-a-plan.md §A-6(b)-RESOLVED; conductor gate PR #2721/#2740) determined the correct regulatory basis for this intra-city scope is the MERGE of 3 PP 28/2025 Lampiran I.I rows whose regimes are substantially identical for the urban scope, each image-verified on the official BPK render (doc 394945): 49214 'Angkutan Bus Kota' (row 9, p.I.I.40-41), 49219 'Angkutan Bus Dalam Trayek Lainnya' (row 11, p.I.I.51 — ONLY its kabupaten/kota tier; the antar-provinsi/Menteri and dalam-provinsi/Gubernur tiers of 49219 do not apply to this intra-city scope and are excluded from the restore), and 49413 'Angkutan Perkotaan Bukan Bus, Dalam Trayek' (row 14, p.I.I.65-66). All 3 confirm the same regime for the urban scope: Ruang Lingkup Seluruh, Skala Usaha Mikro+Kecil+Menengah+Besar, Kategori Risiko Menengah Tinggi, Perizinan NIB dan Sertifikat Standar, Jangka Waktu 5 Hari, PB UMKU none, and municipal-level Kewenangan (Bupati/Wali Kota for 49214 and the used 49219 tier; Wali Kota for 49413). per_skala restored from these 3 per-ancestor rows (12 rows: 3 scopes x 4 skala tiers); persyaratan/kewajiban bullet text for these rows was not transcribed in this pass and is left empty pending a follow-up extraction, not fabricated here. The OLD per_skala_disputed_pp28_collision block is preserved verbatim and untouched by this restore.

editorial.headline: Rural Passenger Transport, With a Clear Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers passenger travel within one regency beyond urban-route overlap, open at every business scale and nationally to up to 100% foreign ownership.
editorial.body:
Rural passenger transport is defined here with useful precision: carrying passengers from one place to another within a single regency, on services that do not intersect with urban passenger-transport routes. That boundary is the centre of the activity. The point is not merely that journeys occur outside a city, but that they remain within one regency and sit apart from urban routes. For a founder, the practical reading is straightforward: the registered activity should describe a passenger-transport operation whose service pattern genuinely fits that geographical and route-based scope. It is a focused description, and its limits matter as much as its promise.

Indonesia’s scale treatment is notably broad: micro, small, medium and large businesses are each open to this activity. That makes the code relevant across different operating footprints without changing what the activity itself is. The scope remains passenger transport inside a single regency and outside intersecting urban routes; business size does not extend that scope. The record also marks the activity as open to foreign investment, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign ownership may reach 100% nationally for this activity.

Bali needs a separate reading, and this record supports a positive one rather than an automatic ban. Its Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and it is not blocked for foreign-investment registration under the provincial moratorium. The stated reason is specific: at the Large scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High. Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks foreign investment for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. Because the recorded risk position at the Large scale is Medium-High/High, this activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The record gives no separate Bali foreign-ownership ceiling; the national 100% ceiling is the figure stated for foreign ownership.

Taken together, the record offers a clean sequence of questions. Does the proposed service carry passengers between places within one regency while avoiding intersection with urban transport routes? At which of the four open scales will it operate? And does its investment structure fit the nationally open foreign-investment position and its 100% ceiling? In Bali, the answer supplied by this record is that there is no moratorium-driven foreign-investment block, resting on the Medium-High/High OSS risk recorded for Large-scale operation.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, this activity is not blocked for foreign-investment registration under the provincial moratorium.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This KBLI covers urban, commuter, and suburban land transport for passengers that isn’t classified elsewhere — think private shuttle services, corporate employee transfers, or chartered vans for door-to-door city travel. It specifically excludes railway, tourist trains, and standard city/rural bus networks already covered in other groups.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, 100% foreign ownership (PMA) is allowed, but in Bali this activity falls under medium-high risk. editorial.headline: The Urban Passenger Transport Category Beyond the Usual Routes
editorial.standfirst: A category for scheduled urban, rural, commuter and suburban passenger transport that remains fully foreign-open nationally and is not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity covers other passenger transport by land through urban or rural systems, including commuter and suburban services not otherwise classified. Its defining operating pattern is public-facing and structured: transport runs on regular routes, collecting and setting down passengers at designated places and times. In plain terms, it is for passenger movement within the wider daily geography of towns, cities and surrounding communities—where a normal route and a predictable stopping pattern are central to the service.

The activity is open across the full stated business-scale range: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the category describes a transport function rather than a narrow operating format. The record’s emphasis remains on the system of service—land-based passenger carriage through an urban or rural, commuter or suburban network—and on the discipline of regular routes, stops and timing.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is direct: the activity is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. There is no partial foreign-equity cap in the record to soften or qualify that position. For a foreign-owned business assessing the category nationally, the classification is therefore fully open under the cited investment framework.

In Bali, the position calls for closer reading without turning unduly negative. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for activities carrying Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity is not marked as blocked by that moratorium. The Bali record identifies its OSS risk at Large scale as Medium-High/High, placing it outside the stated moratorium trigger. Its Bali status is therefore “OK or Higher Risk”: not an assertion that every operating detail is frictionless, but a clear indication that the province-wide PMA block does not close this activity. The honest conclusion is straightforward: foreign participation is fully open nationally, and Bali does not block PMA registration for this category under the recorded moratorium assessment.
editorial.pullQuote: Foreign participation is fully open nationally, and Bali does not block PMA registration for this category under the recorded moratorium assessment.

editorial.headline: The Long Route: Interprovincial Passenger Transport
editorial.standfirst: A route-bound passenger-transport activity that may cross more than one province, foreign-open nationally and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is about passenger transport between cities, not merely travel that happens to be long. The journey moves from one city to another, crosses regency or municipal boundaries, and passes through more than one province. It is also tied to a route. Those elements give the definition its shape: a route-bound interprovincial service whose geography crosses both local and provincial lines. More exactly, the scope brings together city-to-city passenger transport, the listed boundary crossings, and a route attachment. It also reaches pioneering interprovincial services, typically for remote, outermost and disadvantaged areas that are not yet commercially profitable to serve.

The listed registration range runs from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah to Besar. That breadth does not alter the activity’s core description. At each of those scales, the record still concerns passenger movement between cities across the stated boundaries, on a route. It also retains the pioneering-service inclusion, rather than treating it as a separate activity. The scale field therefore answers who may register: businesses at every one of the four listed scales.

Nationally, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. Put plainly, this activity may be wholly foreign owned at national level. That national result is decisive on the ownership ceiling, but it is not a substitute for looking at the Bali status in its own terms. The record supplies both, and they need to be read together: the national foreign-ownership ceiling on one hand, and the provincial moratorium result on the other.

Bali does not block PMA registration for this activity under its island-wide, permanent moratorium. The rule blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk activities; this record says the OSS risk at the Besar scale is Medium-High/High. Its Bali status is therefore recorded as OK or higher risk, and the stated reason is that it is not blocked by the moratorium. There is no separate Bali foreign-ownership percentage or partnership condition given here. The careful conclusion is simple: 100% is the national ceiling, and Bali’s moratorium does not prevent PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity may be wholly foreign owned nationally, and Bali’s moratorium does not prevent its PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Intercity Passenger Transport Within a Province
editorial.standfirst: A route-bound passenger service that is nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity covers scheduled passenger transport between cities within a single Indonesian province, crossing regency or municipal boundaries while remaining tied to an established route. It also includes services linking directly adjoining regencies or municipalities that have not yet been served by intercity or urban routes. The scope reaches further still: pioneer intercity services within a province, typically serving remote, outermost and disadvantaged areas where commercial operation has not yet proved attractive. Border bus transport and provincial intercity bus transport sit within that same practical frame.

The code is open to businesses at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That breadth matters because the activity is defined by the character of the passenger service—intercity, within one province, and route-bound—rather than by a single business size. A prospective operator should therefore read the scope closely: the work is not simply moving people from place to place, but providing the specified form of passenger transport across local-government boundaries within the province.

At the national level, PMA may enter this activity on a TERBUKA basis, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In plain terms, the record places no foreign equity cap below full ownership at the national level. Its stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national position is the starting point, but Bali requires its own reading rather than a reflexive assumption that every foreign-open activity is treated identically on the island.

For Bali, this activity is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium. The moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province on a permanent, island-wide basis; this activity falls outside that blocked category. At Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—so the Bali assessment is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. **For Bali, this activity is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium.** The result is a straightforward one: foreign investors may treat the national 100% ceiling as applicable here, while keeping the stated Large-scale OSS risk classification clearly in view.
editorial.pullQuote: For Bali, this activity is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium.

intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is 100% open to foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.

editorial.headline: Cross-Border Routes, Open to Foreign Investment
editorial.standfirst: This route-based, city-to-city cross-border transport activity is open nationally to full foreign ownership and is not caught by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Angkutan Lintas Batas Negara is a route-bound form of transport: movement from one city to another that crosses a national border as part of an established route. The classification turns on that concrete pattern of movement. A city-to-city journey, the crossing of a frontier, and a route to which the service is tied are all present in its stated scope. Read together, those elements give the activity its operating identity: cross-border transport conducted along a route, rather than a loose reference to travel that happens to reach another country.

Its registration window is not confined to one end of the business-size range. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises. That is a deliberately practical point: the classification is not reserved for a single scale of operator. The activity must still match its stated route-based, cross-border scope, but the record places it across all four listed business categories. For a founder, scale is therefore an eligibility statement in the classification, not a reason to dilute the definition of the activity itself.

At the national level, PMA is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling stands at 100%. The implication is plain: full foreign ownership is permitted at the national level. A 100% ceiling is not a partial cap; the national entry allows foreign capital up to complete ownership. The record cites Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the source for that position. This is the national baseline from which the Bali question has to be assessed—without adding conditions that the record does not supply.

Bali deserves an equally direct reading. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity, however, is not marked as blocked. Its Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`, and the record states that at the Besar scale its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, meaning it is not blocked by that moratorium. The central fact is simple: full national foreign ownership is permitted, and Bali does not block PMA registration under its moratorium. For this activity, Bali is an available place to register rather than an exception to national PMA openness.
editorial.pullQuote: The central fact is simple: full national foreign ownership is permitted, and Bali does not block PMA registration under its moratorium.

editorial.headline: KBLI 49229: Intercity Passenger Transport, Nationally and in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A clear route for other long-distance passenger transport, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium at the large-business risk classification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 49229 covers other long-distance, intercity passenger transport not classified elsewhere. Its practical centre of gravity is passenger carriage by land: services operating through urban or rural transport systems, running on regular routes and picking up and setting down passengers at designated places and times. The definition is deliberately broad, but not vague; it describes a transport activity organised around a route, a service pattern and the movement of passengers between places.

The activity is open across the full business spectrum: micro, small, medium and large. That matters because the code is not framed solely for a large transport operator. It gives a registration home to the same defined passenger-transport activity at each of those scales, while retaining the essential character of regular-route land carriage. The scope should therefore be read as an operational description, not as an invitation to stretch the activity beyond what the route-based passenger service actually covers.

Nationally, the position on foreign investment is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, a foreign investor can hold the entire business nationally within this activity code. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower foreign-ownership cap in the record to obscure that position.

Bali requires a more exact reading, but the conclusion remains constructive. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, reflected in the Bali status OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali at that scale, the record’s point is clear: the provincial moratorium does not prevent it. National openness is therefore not merely theoretical here; the Bali-specific restriction described in the record does not close this activity at the stated large-business risk classification.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is therefore not merely theoretical here; the Bali-specific restriction described in the record does not close this activity at the stated large-business risk classification.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: General cargo road transport — operating trucks, pickups, and box vans to transport various types of goods on public roads. This is commercial freight transport that accepts different cargo types in a single vehicle, not specialized hazardous or refrigerated cargo.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Micro / Small / Medium / Large scale**: Medium-High risk. NIB + Standard Certificate — issued within 5 working days.


**PMA:** Fully open to PMA — 100% foreign ownership allowed.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Renumbered/adjusted from KBLI 2020. KBLI 2020: 49431 → KBLI 2025: 49231 (ANGKUTAN BERMOTOR UNTUK BARANG UMUM) + 49232 (BARANG KHUSUS).
intel_2026.baliContext: Road freight is essential to Bali's supply chain — goods from Java arrive via Gilimanuk ferry port and are redistributed by truck to all corners of the island. The Gilimanuk–Denpasar corridor is the main artery. Traffic congestion in South Bali (Kuta, Seminyak, Denpasar) significantly affects delivery times and operating costs. Large truck access is restricted in Kuta/Legian tourist areas during peak hours. Driver shortages and aging fleet are ongoing operational challenges.

- 52101 — Warehousing for staging cargo

editorial.headline: General Goods by Road: The Business Behind the Load
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers general goods transport by motor vehicle—open nationally to full foreign ownership, with no Bali moratorium block identified at the large-business risk level.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the operation of general goods transport by motor vehicle. It is the business of moving freight that may comprise more than one type of goods, using vehicles such as trucks, pick-ups, open-bed vehicles and enclosed box vehicles. The emphasis is operational: the enterprise is organised around carrying goods on the road. The record expressly accommodates more than one type of goods, giving the activity a general-goods character rather than limiting it to one cargo type.

Businesses may register across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That is a broad scale profile. The classification does not confine the activity to a small operator or reserve it for a large one. Its defining work remains goods transportation with motor vehicles, and its listed examples give the scope a practical physical shape: trucks, pick-ups, open beds and closed box bodies. The activity is therefore best understood as a road-freight operation whose business is the movement of general goods.

Across Indonesia, the foreign-investment position is unambiguous. PMA is classified as TERBUKA, with the recorded maximum foreign ownership at 100%. For a foreign-owned company, that means the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership for this activity. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Here, openness is not merely a broad description: it sits alongside a stated ownership ceiling, giving the national position a definite reading for a business considering PMA registration.

Bali requires a separate reading, but it does not reverse the national result. The Bali assessment is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and this activity is not flagged as blocked for PMA registration under the province’s moratorium. The record gives the reason: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is medium-high/high, so the moratorium does not block it. Bali’s stated rule is a permanent, island-wide PMA block for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. That province-wide rule is real, yet this activity falls outside the recorded block. The honest picture is therefore clear: full foreign ownership is nationally permitted, and the Bali moratorium is not the recorded barrier to PMA registration for this activity.

editorial.headline: Specialist Motor Freight, Built for a Single Cargo
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers motor-vehicle freight dedicated to one cargo type, spanning fuels, hazardous goods, containers, live cargo and heavy equipment.
editorial.body:
This activity is for operating motor vehicles that carry goods in a purpose-built, single-cargo role. Its terrain is specialist freight rather than general haulage: petroleum fuels and processed oil products; LPG, LNG and CNG; hazardous goods and hazardous and toxic waste; carbon dioxide; heavy equipment; containers; and motor vehicles all sit within its stated scope. So do the movement of live plants and animals, the distribution of fish and other aquatic life, and the distribution of carbon-free fuels such as hydrogen, ammonia and related compounds in gaseous, solid or liquid form.

The common thread is not a particular vehicle or commodity market, but the dedicated nature of the transport operation. The vehicle is deployed for goods that are specifically carried as one type of cargo. That makes the activity broad in its cargo list while remaining sharply defined in its operating character: it is specialist motor freight for cargoes whose transport profile calls for that focus. Water distribution by truck is expressly outside the stated scope.

Registration is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In practical terms, the national record does not place a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That openness belongs to the activity as recorded; it does not add unstated operational permissions or conditions for any particular cargo.

Bali’s position is also not a blanket closure here. The provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities across the island, but this activity is not blocked by that rule. The record identifies its OSS risk at the Besar scale as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, placing it outside the moratorium’s stated Low and Medium-Low reach. For a foreign investor considering Bali, that is the decisive distinction: the activity remains available for PMA registration rather than being caught by the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, this specialist freight activity remains available for PMA registration rather than being caught by the island-wide moratorium.

editorial.headline: Non-Motorised Freight: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Non-motorised freight is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet PMA registration for a Bali address is closed by the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
Freight does not always arrive under engine power. This activity covers the carriage of goods by non-motorised means, including carts, animal-drawn vehicles and pack animals. The examples make the operational boundary concrete: the activity is about cargo moved without a motor. Its boundary is equally clear. Passenger transport by non-motorised vehicle sits outside this remit, so the defining question is not merely how a vehicle moves, but whether it is carrying goods.

That scope is open across the full business-scale range named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. It is therefore an activity for enterprises from the smallest scale through to large business, provided their work remains within non-motorised goods transport. At the national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA. Foreign ownership may reach 100%, which means the record sets no national foreign-ownership cap below full ownership for this activity. The national result is direct: PMA is open, and the ceiling is 100%.

Bali produces a different registration answer. For a Bali address, PMA registration is blocked, notwithstanding the national 100% ceiling. The record's Bali status is Closed (Bali moratorium), and its reason turns on the Besar scale being classified as Rendah, or Low risk. Bali's PMA moratorium applies island-wide and permanently to activities classified Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity consequently falls within the moratorium's reach for PMA registration in Bali. The point is not a lower Bali foreign-ownership percentage. The record describes a closed registration position under the moratorium.

The resulting picture needs both levels held together. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA and can be fully foreign-owned within the stated ceiling. In Bali, that national openness does not create a PMA registration route for a Bali address. The code remains a precise category of non-motorised freight, with four named scales open to it; the Bali result arises from the moratorium and the recorded Low-risk classification at Besar scale. For founders, the distinction is the substance: scope and national ownership remain clear, while the Bali PMA outcome is closed.
editorial.pullQuote: For a Bali address, PMA registration is blocked, notwithstanding the national 100% ceiling.

editorial.headline: Railways Beyond the Usual Route
editorial.standfirst: A fully foreign-open rail activity that remains registrable in Bali because it sits outside the province’s PMA moratorium trigger.
editorial.body:
KBLI 49291 covers the operation of rail services that do not form part of long-distance intercity rail or short-distance urban rail transport. Its territory includes cable railways, gondolas and other rail operations when they are outside those transport systems. The stated scope also reaches the development and provision of special railways. It is therefore a defined operational category for rail infrastructure and services with a purpose distinct from everyday intercity or city transit.

The boundaries matter. Short-distance urban tourist rail transport is outside this activity, as are cable railways, gondolas, chairlifts and similar systems when they operate as part of an amusement or recreation venue. The code is for the railway activity itself within its stated terrain, rather than a catch-all label for every rail-linked attraction or local transport service. It is open at Menengah and Besar scales, giving the category a clear commercial range without extending it beyond the scales recorded.

Nationally, the position is direct: the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That means foreign participation is open up to full ownership at the national level. The policy source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For founders, the important discipline is to keep the proposed operation faithful to the defined scope: rail services outside intercity and urban short-distance transport, including the specified cable and special-railway operations.

Bali does not reverse that national opening. The province’s permanent rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, but this activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which is why it is not blocked by the moratorium. A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today. The result is unusually clean: a nationally open activity, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, that remains available for PMA registration in Bali because its recorded risk position falls outside the moratorium’s reach.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today because its recorded risk position falls outside the moratorium’s reach.

editorial.headline: Tourist Transport Has a Clear National Route—and a Distinct Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: For sightseeing journeys by road, the national position is fully open to foreign ownership; Bali’s specific moratorium does not block it.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity is the operation of land transport for tourism and sightseeing. It covers the practical journey itself: a visitor travelling alone or a group travelling together on a tour. In clear terms, it is road-based tourist transport, including tourist bus transport, for the purpose of seeing places. Its boundary matters. Transport operating within a tourist attraction as part of running a tourism destination or area sits outside the stated scope. This is the transport operation for the tour, rather than the operation of the destination where a visitor happens to travel.

The national investment position is direct. The activity is marked open for PMA, with maximum foreign ownership of 100%. There is therefore no national foreign-ownership cap below full ownership for this activity. Registration is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, giving the category a broad formal reach across business sizes. The underlying subject remains tightly defined, however: tourism-oriented land journeys for individual or group travel, not every transport service connected with a visitor experience.

Bali requires its own reading. The province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The recorded reason is specific: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. That is the basis for its Bali position as not blocked by the moratorium; it is not an invitation to blur the provincial rule or to treat the national setting as the only relevant one.

The result is clear: nationally the activity is open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership, while in Bali it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium. For a founder, the useful distinction is between the defined transport activity itself and the separate question of operating transport within a tourism destination or area. The former is the subject here, and the Bali record places it outside the moratorium’s stated Low and Medium-Low risk bar.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the activity is open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership, while in Bali it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium.

editorial.headline: Taxi Transport: Nationally Open, With a Clear Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers metered, door-to-door taxi passenger transport within a limited operating area, open nationally to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Taxi transport, in this classification, is a tightly defined passenger-service activity rather than a catch-all for moving people by car. It covers journeys in specially marked passenger vehicles fitted with taximeters, serving passengers door to door within a limited operating area. The definition matters because it places the commercial centre of gravity on a recognisable taxi operation: a marked vehicle, a metered fare mechanism, and a bounded territory of operation.

The activity is open across the full stated range of business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That makes it relevant to operators entering at a modest scale as well as to larger businesses building a more substantial transport presence. The record does not divide the activity into separate commercial models within those scales; its common thread is the same taxi service described above. A registration should therefore be read through that practical service: passenger transport by specially marked, taximeter-equipped cars, offered from door to door in a limited area.

Nationally, the position is direct. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain terms, foreign investment is fully open at the national level for this activity. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower foreign-ownership ceiling in the record to qualify that national position, so the ownership reading is not a partial-opening story: it is a fully open one.

Bali requires a separate reading, but it is not a contradiction. The provincial moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. This activity is not marked as blocked. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK because, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; the record expressly says it is therefore not blocked by the moratorium. For a foreign investor, that is the honest conclusion: taxi transport is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali does not block PMA registration for this activity under the stated moratorium. The Bali position rests on the recorded higher-risk treatment at the Besar scale, not on an invented exemption or a separate ownership cap.

- transportasi ambulans, lihat kelompok 86994.

intel_2026.whatYouNeed: While nationally open for 100% foreign ownership, this activity is classified as medium-high risk in Bali. It is not blocked by the current moratorium, but registration requires careful address verification and likely additional permits due to the risk level—making it possible but more complex than low-risk activities.

editorial.headline: Special Passenger Transport: Fixed-Route Mobility, Nationally Open
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers organised passenger services with fixed origins or destinations, from employee and school transport to shuttles serving stations, ports and airports.
editorial.body:
Special Passenger Transport is the category for organised passenger journeys that begin or end at a fixed point. Its practical territory is familiar: pick-up and drop-off services, employee transport, residential transport and services that connect passengers between transport modes. It also expressly includes operating school vehicles or buses, employee pick-up vehicles or buses, and shuttle buses serving stations, ports or airports. The defining feature is not simply that passengers are moved, but that the service is structured around a settled origin, destination or connection point.

That makes the activity relevant to operators building regular mobility around workplaces, neighbourhoods, schools and transport gateways. It can be registered at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. The scope is specific about the services it embraces, while drawing one clear boundary: ambulance transportation is outside it. For an operator, the category therefore describes recurring, purpose-built passenger movement rather than a catch-all label for every kind of road journey.

Across Indonesia, the foreign-investment position is clear. For this activity, TERBUKA status sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 100%. In other words, foreign ownership may reach the full national ceiling for this activity. The applicable PMA source recorded here is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national openness matters, but it should not be mistaken for a generic statement about every operating context; the Bali picture is recorded separately and deserves to be read on its own terms.

In Bali, this activity is not blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium. The stated rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. Here, the recorded Bali position is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so the activity is not caught by that moratorium. For a foreign investor considering Bali, that is the honest conclusion from this record: the activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and is not blocked there by the stated low-risk and medium-low-risk PMA restriction.

It also includes app-based or traditional rental of cars, bajaj, bentor, and similar vehicles with a driver.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Foreign-owned (PMA) companies are permitted for this activity nationally and Bali does not impose a moratorium block. However, this is classified as a medium-high to high-risk business, so you must secure a suitable commercial address and ensure compliance with higher risk licensing requirements before operating.

intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Angkutan Sewa (49295)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs aiming to run a chauffeured vehicle rental or ride-hailing service, particularly those targeting Bali's tourism or local transport market with a fleet of cars with drivers.

editorial.headline: A Clear Route for Driver-Provided Passenger Hire
editorial.standfirst: For charter, excursions and door-to-door driver-provided hire, this activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and remains available for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Rental Passenger Transport covers door-to-door passenger journeys in public passenger cars where the fare is agreed between the user and the transport provider. Its centre of gravity is the arranged trip: charter work, excursions and other seasonal charter transport are expressly within scope. The category also includes the hire of cars or other private vehicles with a driver, whether arranged through an app or not, as well as driver-provided hire using vehicles such as bajaj, kancil and bentor.

The agreed fare is part of the definition, as is the provision of a driver. This is therefore a category built around passenger movement on terms settled between provider and user, rather than around one particular booking channel or vehicle type. Registration is open at the Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. The stated scope carries the same central idea across those scales: passenger transportation with a driver, encompassing door-to-door journeys, charter and excursion work, and app-based or non-app-based vehicle hire.

Nationally, foreign investment is open, and the stated foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Put plainly, foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership at the national level for this activity. That position is recorded under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali’s position is also materially clear: the record marks the activity as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and does not block PMA registration. At the Large scale, the OSS risk is Medium-High/High, placing it outside Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA.

Accordingly, a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today. That conclusion is precise rather than expansive: Bali’s moratorium remains permanent and island-wide for PMA in the Low and Medium-Low risk categories, while this record identifies Medium-High/High OSS risk at the Large scale and expressly says it is not blocked by that moratorium. For founders, the essential reading is straightforward: this is an open national activity with a Bali position that remains available on the record presented.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Motorcycle Passenger Transport, Open Nationally and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers motorcycle-based passenger transport, including online ojek services and motorcycle hire with a driver or operator.
editorial.body:
Motorcycle passenger transport is a defined operating business, not simply the use of a motorcycle to get someone from one place to another. Its scope includes carrying passengers on two-wheeled motor vehicles through conventional motorcycle-taxi services and app-based ojek services. It also includes hiring out a motorcycle together with a driver or operator. The common thread is clear: the business is organised around passenger movement by motorcycle, whether the service is ordered directly, coordinated digitally, or supplied as a vehicle-and-driver arrangement.

The record opens this activity to medium and large enterprises. That framing matters because it places the code in a business context beyond an informal description of motorcycle work: the registered activity encompasses an enterprise providing and organising passenger transport by two-wheeled vehicle. The scope is broad enough to include both conventional and online modes, yet specific about the vehicle and service model. A business relying on this classification should therefore be able to describe its real operation in those terms: transporting passengers by motorcycle, or providing a motorcycle with its driver or operator.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the record does not impose a national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That is the national picture: an activity open to foreign investment at up to 100%, for the medium and large scales identified in the record.

Bali requires a separate reading, and it is more precise than a blanket assumption about foreign-owned businesses on the island. This activity is not blocked by Bali’s moratorium because it is recorded as medium-high or high risk, rather than within the low and medium-low risk categories covered by that province-wide, permanent restriction on PMA registration. Its Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The remaining instruction is practical rather than prohibitive: verify the position for the specific address. So the honest conclusion is not that Bali closes this activity to foreign investment today; it is that the moratorium does not block it, while the address still needs to be checked.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this activity is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium, though the specific address still requires verification.

editorial.headline: Nationally Open, Bali-Blocked: Non-Motorised Passenger Transport
editorial.standfirst: This passenger-transport activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but PMA registration in Bali is blocked by the province’s permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is about moving passengers without a motor. Its practical territory spans horse-drawn carriages—delman, bendi, andong and dokar—alongside becak, bicycle-taxi rides and the rental of non-motorised passenger vehicles. It is a specific passenger-transport category, not a catch-all for every vehicle without an engine: passenger transport within tourist areas and transport of goods are outside its stated scope. The distinction matters because the activity is defined by the journey offered to a passenger, whether the operator supplies a ride or hires out a non-motorised vehicle for that purpose. The names in the scope make clear that both passenger rides and non-motorised passenger rental belong here when they remain within that stated field.

The registration profile is broad on business scale. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises, so the classification is not confined to a small informal operation or a particular business size. Every one of the four listed scales is included. Nationally, it is TERBUKA to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain terms, the national setting permits full foreign ownership; no lower foreign-equity cap is stated in the record. Its national reference is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali changes the answer decisively. Today, a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali. The recorded Bali status is a block grounded in risk class: in OSS, the Besar-scale assessment across every scope is Low or Medium-Low risk. That places the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration where the recorded risk class is Low or Medium-Low. The moratorium is attributed to Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, and the recorded reason dates the block to May 2026.

This is not a qualification of the national 100% ceiling; it is a different local registration outcome. At the national level, full foreign ownership is allowed. In Bali, the same foreign-investment route is blocked by the provincial moratorium. That is why national eligibility cannot be treated as a Bali result, however straightforward the national ownership position may appear. For founders, the editorial point is simple but consequential: the activity’s transport scope and its national openness do not override the Bali PMA block. The registerable path therefore turns on location as well as the stated activity.
editorial.pullQuote: Today, a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali.

editorial.headline: The Space Beyond City and Intercity Passenger Transport
editorial.standfirst: This residual passenger-transport category is open nationally to foreign ownership and is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 49299 is the place for operating other passenger land transport that sits outside intercity and urban transport and is not classified elsewhere. Its scope is deliberately residual: it identifies a genuine operating activity by the space it occupies around more specifically defined forms of passenger transport. That makes precision in the business description especially important. The registered activity should reflect the operation of passenger transport by land, while remaining faithful to the boundary stated in the code’s own scope.

The activity is open to businesses at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That broad scale access matters because the code is not reserved for a single size of operator. A founder’s registration can therefore be framed around the actual scale of the proposed operation, without the record imposing a separate scale-based exclusion. The code’s practical character is operational rather than speculative: it concerns the running of passenger transport, not a general transport-services label.

At the national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain terms, the record allows the activity to be registered with up to full foreign ownership at the national level. That is the national starting point, supported in the record by Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It should not, however, be mistaken for an automatic answer to Bali, where the provincial PMA moratorium is assessed through risk status.

For Bali, the answer is favourable on the facts supplied: this activity is not blocked by the moratorium. Bali permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI across the island, but the record identifies the Besar-scale OSS risk here as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. The Bali status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and there is no Bali-specific foreign-ownership figure or partnership condition stated in the record. For a foreign founder, the honest conclusion is straightforward: this activity is nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity is nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali today.
