editorial.headline: The Infrastructure That Moves What Roads Cannot
editorial.standfirst: This pipeline-transport activity carries energy, fluids and carbon through dedicated infrastructure—and remains open to foreign investment nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
Pipeline transport is the business of moving substances through fixed pipeline infrastructure: petroleum and natural gas, refined products, liquids, water, slurry, carbon dioxide and other commodities. Its reach also extends to natural gas moving from producers, production-sharing contractors or processing refineries into local distribution systems, as well as carbon transport for injection into geological formations. Increasingly relevant is the inclusion of carbon-free fuels used as energy carriers—hydrogen, ammonia and related compounds—alongside the operation of pumping stations that keep these systems moving.

The distinction is infrastructural as much as commercial. This is not a general label for any delivery of liquids, water or fuel. It concerns transport performed through pipelines, including the specialised movement of carbon for geological injection. The activity is therefore defined by the pipeline system itself: an enduring network capable of carrying conventional energy products, industrial materials, water and emerging low-carbon carriers. That breadth gives the classification a distinctly strategic character, spanning both established oil-and-gas logistics and the physical networks required for carbon-management and alternative-energy flows.

The activity is open at small, medium and large scale. Nationally, it is classified as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, a foreign investor may hold the entire enterprise within the national framework recorded here. There is no lower foreign-equity ceiling to interpret or work around in this activity’s national PMA position.

Bali presents no separate registration block for PMA today. The province’s standing is recorded as acceptable or higher-risk, rather than prohibited under its island-wide moratorium. That moratorium blocks low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities for PMA; this pipeline-transport activity is not blocked by it. At large scale, the OSS risk is recorded as medium-high or high, which is the stated reason it remains outside that moratorium’s block. For founders, the honest reading is straightforward: national foreign ownership can reach 100%, and Bali does not impose a moratorium-based PMA prohibition on this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: Pipeline transport is not blocked for PMA in Bali, while national foreign ownership can reach 100%.

data.judul: Angkutan Laut Dalam Negeri Liner dan Tramper untuk Penumpang
data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup aktivitas transportasi penumpang melalui laut dengan menggunakan kapal laut antarpelabuhan dalam negeri, baik melalui pelayanan angkutan laut yang dilakukan dengan trayek secara tetap dan teratur (liner) dengan berjadwal dan menyebutkan pelabuhan singgah, maupun trayek tidak tetap dan tidak teratur (tramper), termasuk kegiatan kapal penumpang yang dioperasikan pemerintah atau swasta lainnya, serta kegiatan penyewaan angkutan laut berikut operatornya.
Kelompok ini juga mencakup
- angkutan laut dalam negeri pelayaran rakyat untuk penumpang yang menggunakan kapal layar, kapal motor tradisional, dan kapal layar motor dengan ukuran tertentu.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers transporting passengers between Indonesian ports by sea on scheduled liner routes or irregular tramper services, including government or private vessels and renting out ships with crew. It also includes traditional people’s shipping using sailing boats.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, foreign ownership in domestic liner/tramper sea passenger transport is capped at 49% (TERBATAS): a PMA needs an Indonesian majority partner, and domestic shipping additionally runs under Indonesian-flag cabotage rules. In Bali the code is not blocked by the local investment moratorium, but it is flagged as medium-high risk — registration requires careful address verification and the sector operating licences, and will face closer scrutiny from the transport authority.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Angkutan Laut Dalam Negeri Liner dan Tramper untuk Penumpang (50111)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Restricted. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: This is for foreign entrepreneurs planning to run domestic passenger ferry, island-hopping, or charter cruise operations within Indonesian waters, usually through a joint venture or alternative licensing setup.

editorial.headline: Domestic Sea Passenger Transport, on Schedule or by Charter
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers domestic sea passenger transport between Indonesian ports, from scheduled liner services to irregular tramper routes and crewed vessel charter.
editorial.body:
Domestic sea passenger transport is a broad operational category, but its centre of gravity is clear: moving passengers by sea between ports within Indonesia. It includes fixed, regular liner routes with published schedules and stated port calls, as well as tramper services whose routes are neither fixed nor regular. Government-operated and other privately operated passenger vessels fall within the scope, as does the charter of sea transport together with its operator. The category also reaches domestic people’s shipping for passengers using sailing vessels, traditional motor vessels and motor-sailing vessels of the specified size.

The activity is open across the stated business scales: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That matters because the code describes a transport operation rather than a single commercial model. A scheduled inter-port passenger service, an irregular route, a charter arrangement with an operator, and qualifying people’s-shipping passenger transport may all sit inside the same activity description. The practical question is therefore whether the proposed operation genuinely concerns domestic passenger carriage by sea, rather than merely sharing some of its commercial features.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership position is restricted. PMA participation is permitted only up to a 49% foreign-ownership ceiling, so this is not an activity in which foreign investors may hold the entire business. That national limit is the essential starting point for a foreign-backed structure: the activity is available, but the ownership composition must remain within the stated ceiling.

Bali does not add a PMA-registration block for this activity in the record. The province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registrations for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. Here, however, the Large-scale OSS risk is recorded as Medium-High/High, meaning the activity is not blocked by that moratorium. That is a meaningful distinction, not a promise that every operating arrangement will be straightforward: nationally the foreign stake remains capped at 49%, while Bali’s recorded position is that this code is not caught by the Low and Medium-Low risk PMA block.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, foreign participation is possible but capped at 49%; in Bali, the activity is not blocked by the province’s Low and Medium-Low risk PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Pioneer Passenger Shipping: Connecting Indonesia’s Hardest-to-Reach Places
editorial.standfirst: This activity supports scheduled passenger sea links between remote or commercially underserved areas and more developed destinations, with foreign ownership nationally capped at 49%.
editorial.body:
Pioneer domestic passenger shipping is built around connection where ordinary commercial routes have not yet taken hold. The activity covers sea transport for passengers linking remote areas—and areas with potential that remain undeveloped or commercially unprofitable to serve—to places that are already developed. Its purpose is therefore inseparable from the geography of uneven access: putting regular sea links in place where distance, limited development, or weak commercial returns would otherwise leave communities disconnected.

The scope is specifically for pioneer sea transport on fixed, regular liner routes, with vessels positioned to encourage the development of remote areas. It also includes the chartering of sea transport together with its operator. That makes this a defined passenger-shipping activity, centred on scheduled service and the deployment of vessels in support of regional development, rather than a loose description of maritime work.

Registration is open across the full business-scale range in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. For foreign investment, however, the national position is restricted. The maximum foreign ownership is 49%, so a foreign investor cannot hold more than 49% of the business nationally. That ceiling is the national setting for this activity and should be read plainly: foreign participation is permitted, but not at a controlling 100% stake.

Bali presents a more workable picture than the province’s permanent PMA moratorium might initially suggest. That moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA across the island. This activity is not marked as blocked for PMA registration in Bali. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Medium-High or High, placing it outside the risk categories named in the moratorium. The Bali status is therefore recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: the activity is not blocked by that moratorium, while the national 49% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the governing limit for foreign participation.
editorial.pullQuote: Foreign participation is permitted nationally, but the stake cannot exceed 49%, while Bali does not block this activity under its PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Indonesia’s Domestic Sea-Tourism Transport: Open, but Not Fully Foreign-Owned
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers sea-based sightseeing and recreation transport, including passenger submersibles and charter vessels with operators, with foreign ownership nationally limited to 49%.
editorial.body:
This activity is the operating category for domestic sea transport built around tourism, recreation and marine sightseeing. Its scope is practical and distinct: carrying visitors at sea for leisure or tourism, whether the experience is framed as a coastal outing, a marine excursion or a sightseeing voyage. It also expressly includes passenger submersible craft used for viewing underwater scenery, as well as the hire of sightseeing sea transport when an operator is provided with the vessel. The defining feature is not simply a boat on the water, but a transport operation whose purpose is the visitor experience.

Registration is open at the **Menengah** and **Besar** business scales. For foreign investment, however, the national position is restricted: the maximum foreign ownership is **49%**. That ceiling matters because it describes a structure with permitted foreign participation, not a fully foreign-owned operation. The applicable PMA position is recorded as **TERBATAS**, with the stated source being Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. A founder considering this activity should therefore begin with the operating model itself—tourist transport, sightseeing charter, or underwater viewing—and then ensure the ownership structure stays within that national limit.

Bali presents a more workable picture than the island-wide PMA moratorium might initially suggest. The provincial rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities, permanently and across the island. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium because its Bali treatment is medium-high risk. Its Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, meaning it is not barred on the basis of the moratorium; the record nevertheless calls for verification at the particular address. That is an important distinction: Bali does not offer a blanket prohibition here, but neither does the record support treating location review as a formality.

The honest conclusion is therefore measured. Nationally, this is a tourism-transport activity available to medium and large businesses with foreign ownership capped at 49%. In Bali, it is not shut out by the province’s Low and Medium-Low risk PMA restriction, because it falls into the medium-high risk side of the framework. The remaining Bali instruction is specific rather than speculative: verify the position for the intended address before relying on the provincial status.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not impose a blanket PMA prohibition here, but the intended address still needs verification.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers international passenger sea transport between Indonesian and foreign ports, either on fixed scheduled routes (liner) or irregular/charter routes (tramper). It also includes chartering vessels with crew, traditional sailing or motor ships, and other specialized international passenger services like pioneer routes.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this business field is fully open to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, it is not blocked by the general moratorium, but due to its medium-high risk classification, the regency or city authorities will scrutinize the business address and location permit. Entrepreneurs should verify in advance that their intended berthing or office address meets local zoning and safety requirements.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Angkutan Laut Luar Negeri Liner dan Tramper untuk Penumpang (50114)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: This suits a foreign entrepreneur or investor aiming to run a passenger ferry, cruise, island-hopping, or charter yacht service connecting Bali directly to foreign ports.

editorial.headline: International Passenger Sea Transport, on Fixed Routes and Beyond
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers international passenger voyages by sea—scheduled liner services, irregular tramper routes and operator-led charters—with a clear PMA position nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 50114 is the registration home for passenger movement by sea between Indonesian ports and ports abroad. Its scope reaches two distinct operating patterns: liner services that run fixed, regular routes to a schedule, and tramper services whose routes are neither fixed nor regular. The code is framed around the service being provided—transporting passengers by sea—rather than a single route format. It also expressly includes the rental of sea transport together with its operator, bringing that operator-led service model within the activity’s stated boundaries.

The scope is broader than conventional international liner traffic. It includes passenger sea transport operated through pelayaran rakyat, or people’s shipping, using sailing vessels, traditional motor vessels and motor-sailing vessels of specified sizes. Other international passenger sea services, including pioneering transport, are also named within the record. Across the listed business scales—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—the activity remains open. In other words, the defined passenger-transport activity is available across the full scale range recorded here, without the record limiting it to one enterprise size.

Nationally, the PMA position is direct: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. A foreign-owned business may therefore register this activity nationally within that stated ceiling. Bali’s position is likewise not a PMA registration block. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI activities across the island. For this activity, however, the Bali record identifies the OSS risk at the Besar scale as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi and states that it is not blocked by that moratorium.

The Bali picture is not a foreign-ownership prohibition, but a risk-classification question at the Besar scale. That distinction is the useful one for a founder reading the code closely: international passenger sea transport may be structured around scheduled liner operations, irregular tramper routes, operator-led rentals, people’s shipping or pioneering services, while the PMA reading remains nationally open and Bali is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than blocked.
editorial.pullQuote: The Bali picture is not a foreign-ownership prohibition, but a risk-classification question at the Besar scale.

editorial.headline: International Sea Tourism—and Bali’s Clearer Reading
editorial.standfirst: International sea tourism is open to foreign investment through a PMA company; whether Bali's moratorium applies is not yet classifiable pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.
editorial.body:
International tourist travel is the point of this activity, but the route is maritime and cross-border. It covers transporting tourists by sea on tourist vessels from an Indonesian port to a foreign port, or on the reverse journey from abroad to Indonesia. The scope also includes hiring sea transport together with its operator. In plain commercial terms, the activity joins the vessel, its operator and tourists travelling on an international sea route. The departure and arrival pattern is central to how the scope is drawn.

Nationally, the investment reading is direct. PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign share is 100%. A foreign founder is therefore not faced, on the national record, with a foreign-equity cap below full ownership. The activity is open to the Menengah and Besar scales. That scale language should be retained exactly in a registration conversation: it describes who may register this activity, while the service itself remains international sea transport for tourists or a sea-transport charter supplied with an operator. Nationally, its cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Whether Bali's PMA moratorium applies to this activity cannot be determined until its risk tier is established — the earlier reading was based on a risk classification carried over from a different (air-transport) activity and has been removed. National foreign openness remains a separate, unaffected fact. Confirm the current risk tier and any Bali-specific requirement with the Bali Zero team before planning a Bali setup.

That is the distinction founders need to carry into their planning. National openness to foreign investment through a PMA company is a separate part of the record; the Bali conclusion depends on a risk tier that is not yet classifiable, pending re-derivation from the true risk tier for this activity. Confirm current requirements with the Bali Zero team before planning a Bali setup for this international tourist sea-transport activity.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is a separate, unaffected fact; whether Bali's moratorium applies to this activity is not yet classifiable pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers domestic sea freight for general cargo between Indonesian ports, using scheduled (liner) or unscheduled (tramper) vessels. It also includes the leasing of sea transport with an operator.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: In Bali, a foreign-owned company (PMA) can use this KBLI, but foreign shareholding is capped at 49% nationally. Because it's considered medium-high risk, registration is not blocked by moratorium, but location verification is required—your business address must suit maritime zoning and pass local checks.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Angkutan Laut Dalam Negeri untuk Barang Umum (50121)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Restricted. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign shipping or logistics entrepreneurs willing to take a minority stake and partner with an Indonesian majority shareholder to run domestic cargo lines.

editorial.headline: Domestic Cargo Shipping, With a 49% Foreign-Ownership Ceiling
editorial.standfirst: Domestic general-cargo shipping is open across all recorded scales, with foreign ownership capped nationally at 49% and not blocked by Bali’s recorded moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 50121 is the domestic sea-transport activity for general cargo carried between Indonesian ports. It covers the movement of goods by sea in the country’s inter-port network, using sea-going vessels. The scope is broad in operating pattern but precise in geography: the service is domestic, and its cargo is general goods. Within that frame, an operator may sail a fixed and regular liner route according to a schedule, or a tramper route that is neither fixed nor regular. Chartering the sea transport service with its operator also sits inside the stated activity.

This is not an activity defined by one route format. Scheduled liner operations and irregular tramper operations sit side by side in the same scope, so the defining thread is domestic carriage of general cargo by sea. The record also expressly includes charter activity where the operator accompanies the transport. Registration is open at every recorded scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That gives the activity a full scale range without altering the core description of what is being registered.

For foreign investment, the national position is limited. The PMA status is TERBATAS, under the cited Presidential Regulations, and foreign ownership is capped at 49%. That ceiling is the national limit for this activity: foreign participation is possible only within that stated maximum, not on an unrestricted basis. It is the central ownership fact in the record, and it should be read plainly.

Bali is not a simple extension of the national rule, but this record does not show a Bali ban. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. This activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK for Bali because, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—medium-high/high—and it is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. The distinction matters: the 49% national foreign-ownership ceiling remains in place, while Bali’s moratorium does not block this activity on the recorded large-scale risk basis. The record gives no separate Bali ownership percentage or partnership condition, so the Bali position properly stops there.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, the moratorium does not block this activity, but nationally foreign ownership still stops at 49%.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers domestic sea transport of specialized cargo that requires specially designed vessels — from hazardous materials, petroleum, LPG/LNG/CNG, and fish catch to emerging carbon-free energy carriers like hydrogen or ammonia. It’s strictly for moving these goods between ports within Indonesia, not for international shipping.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally this is a TERBATAS code: foreign ownership in domestic sea transport is capped at 49% under the sea-cabotage rule (Perpres 10/2021 positive-investment list), so an Indonesian majority partner is required. Bali does not block this activity. However, because it’s classified as a higher-risk sector, you’ll need additional permits and site-specific verification — the business address and operational base must meet stricter environmental and safety requirements before you can start.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Angkutan Laut Dalam Negeri untuk Barang Khusus (50122)? Nationally this carries PMA status: TERBATAS — capped at 49% foreign ownership. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs with capital, vessels, or clients in the niche domestic logistics of energy, chemicals, or bulk perishables — who can handle heavy compliance and local partnership demands.

editorial.headline: Specialised Domestic Sea Freight, With a 49% Foreign Ownership Ceiling
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 50122 covers specially designed vessels carrying defined cargoes within Indonesia, including energy products, hazardous goods and fisheries support.
editorial.body:
KBLI 50122 is for domestic sea freight carried by vessels purpose-built for a particular kind of cargo. Its scope reaches beyond conventional goods movement: dangerous goods, hazardous and toxic waste, fuel oil, petroleum and processed petroleum products, LPG, LNG and CNG all sit within its stated terrain. So do fish and other aquatic life, alongside the dedicated vessels that move fishing gear and supporting equipment. The common thread is specialisation: the vessel is designed around the cargo it is meant to carry.

That specialisation also extends to newer energy-carrier distribution. The activity includes domestic distribution by sea of carbon-free fuels in gaseous, solid or liquid form, including hydrogen, ammonia and related compounds, when purpose-designed ships are used. In fisheries, it embraces transport from fishing grounds, transport between ports, and sea transport supporting capture-fishing and aquaculture operations. Chartering the vessel together with its operator is included as well. This is therefore a broad operational category for specialised domestic maritime carriage, but its boundaries remain anchored in the defined cargoes and specially designed vessels described in the scope.

The activity is open across the full business-scale range: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. Nationally, however, it is classified as restricted for foreign investment. Foreign ownership is capped at 49%, which means a PMA structure cannot be wholly foreign-owned under this activity. That ceiling is the central ownership fact in the record; it should be read as a limit on the foreign stake, not as a statement about the technical character of the shipping operation.

Bali presents a clearer picture than the province-wide moratorium might initially suggest. The moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities across the island. This activity is not blocked by that rule. At the Large scale, its OSS risk is recorded as medium-high or high, placing it outside the moratorium’s blocked risk bands. A foreign investor can therefore register this activity in Bali within the national 49% foreign-ownership ceiling. Bali does not add a separate ownership percentage or partnership condition in this record; its practical distinction is that the activity remains outside the moratorium rather than being barred by it.

data.judul: Angkutan Laut Dalam Negeri Perintis untuk Barang
data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup aktivitas angkutan laut untuk barang yang menghubungkan daerah-daerah terpencil serta daerah yang potensial namun belum berkembang serta belum menguntungkan untuk dilayari secara komersial ke daerah-daerah yang telah berkembang. Kegiatan angkutan laut perintis ditetapkan dengan trayek tetap dan teratur atau liner serta penempatan kapalnya untuk mendorong pengembangan daerah terpencil, termasuk kegiatan penyewaan angkutan laut berikut operatornya.

editorial.headline: Pioneer Cargo Shipping and the 49% Foreign-Ownership Limit
editorial.standfirst: Pioneer domestic cargo shipping connects remote and developing regions to established ones—but foreign ownership is capped nationally at 49%, while Bali does not block the activity under its moratorium.
editorial.body:
Domestic pioneer cargo shipping is intended to make a connection where commercial shipping has not yet made one. The activity covers sea carriage of goods between remote areas, and between areas with potential that are still undeveloped or commercially unprofitable to serve, and areas that have already developed. It is defined through fixed, regular liner routes and the placement of ships to encourage development in remote areas. Chartering sea-transport services together with their operators is also part of the activity.

That makes the activity more specific than a broad description of cargo movement: its stated purpose is to connect places at very different stages of development, rather than merely to operate a vessel. Its operating pattern is equally material: a fixed, regular route is in the scope, as is positioning vessels to support development in remote areas. Registrants may operate at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, or Besar scale. The record therefore leaves the activity open across all four stated scales, instead of limiting it to a single size of undertaking.

At the national level, foreign investment is TERBATAS. Foreign ownership is capped at 49%, so a foreign investor cannot hold the entire company carrying out this activity. That ceiling is national; it should be read alongside, rather than confused with, the Bali position. Bali’s status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The record says that at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. Consequently, the activity is not blocked by Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium, which applies to Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA. The conclusion is unambiguous: PMA registration for this activity remains available in Bali, subject to the national 49% foreign-ownership ceiling.

Rather than presenting Bali as a separate restriction, the record indicates that the decisive ownership constraint is national. The local outcome is not a Bali-specific ban; it is a status that stays outside the moratorium because of its stated higher risk at the Besar scale. For founders, this is a transport activity whose economic role, eligible scales, foreign-ownership ceiling, and Bali treatment need to be read together.
editorial.pullQuote: PMA registration for this activity remains available in Bali, subject to the national 49% foreign-ownership ceiling.

editorial.headline: Domestic Sea Freight: Foreign Ownership Capped at 49%, Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A domestic sea-freight activity for goods and animals using specified traditional vessel types, including operator-inclusive hire — foreign ownership is capped at 49%.
editorial.body:
**A defined domestic transport operation.** KBLI 50124 covers domestic maritime transport intended to carry goods and/or animals. It names a particular fleet: sailing vessels, traditional motor vessels, and motor-sailing vessels of specified sizes. The scope also includes hiring out that maritime transport with its operator. Read together, those elements identify a live transport activity whose substance is the carriage of goods or animals; the operator-inclusive hire is also expressly within its perimeter. The wording is operational: it tells the reader what is moved, the vessel forms used, and that the transport may be rented with the person operating it.

**Scale is not a narrowing device here.** Registration is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises. That is the full scale range presented in the record, so the activity is not confined to a single business size. The scope stays the same across that range: domestic sea transport for goods and/or animals using the named traditional and sailing vessel forms, alongside operator-inclusive rental. Scale is relevant to how the record frames the Bali risk position, but it does not replace the core activity definition. The essential question is whether the actual operation fits that stated transport-and-hire scope, then the scale at which it will be registered.

**Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%.** Domestic sea carriage of goods and animals by traditional and sailing vessels is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #15, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

**Bali does not add a second obstacle.** The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. This one is recorded at medium-high risk, so the moratorium does not reach it and the company can be registered here. Bali states no percentage of its own and no local partnership requirement; what limits the foreign side is the 49% ceiling, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia.
editorial.pullQuote: The foreign side of the shareholding stops at 49%; what Bali does not do is add a registration block on top of that ceiling.

editorial.headline: Carrying General Cargo Across Indonesia’s International Sea Routes
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers scheduled and chartered general-cargo shipping between Indonesian and overseas ports — foreign ownership is capped at 49% nationwide, and Bali's moratorium does not bar registration.
editorial.body:
General cargo moving between Indonesian ports and ports abroad has its own clear operational frame here: sea transport carried by vessel across international port routes. It includes both the regularity of liner services, operating on fixed and scheduled routes, and the flexibility of tramper services, whose routes and schedules are not fixed. The scope also includes chartered sea transport provided together with its operator. In practical terms, this is an activity for businesses whose work is the organised maritime carriage of goods beyond Indonesia’s borders—not merely the ownership or hire of a vessel in isolation.

Registration is open at **Menengah** and **Besar** scales. That matters because the record positions the activity within operating businesses capable of undertaking international freight movements, whether through predictable scheduled services or less regular charter-based deployment. The distinction between liner and tramper activity is not decorative: it captures two legitimate ways a general-cargo operator may organise its service, while keeping the underlying activity focused on transport by sea between domestic and foreign ports.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. International general-cargo shipping between Indonesian and overseas ports is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #16, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

Bali does not add a second obstacle. The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. This one is recorded at medium-high risk, so the moratorium does not reach it and the company can be registered here. Bali states no percentage of its own and no local partnership requirement; what limits the foreign side is the 49% ceiling, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia.

Angkutan laut khusus dengan menggunakan kapal berbendera Indonesia dengan kondisi dan persyaratan kapalnya disesuaikan dengan jenis kegiatan usaha pokoknya, serta untuk melayani trayek tidak tetap dan tidak teratur antar pelabuhan di Indonesia dengan pelabuhan di luar negeri termasuk usaha persewaan angkutan laut berbendera asing yang diageni oleh perusahaan bukan perusahaan perikanan berikut operatornya.

Surat pernyataan mengenai Pemilik Manfaat, untuk badan hukum c. Pakta integritas dari orang perseorangan atau penanggung jawab badan hukum d. Pas foto orang perseorangan atau penanggung jawab badan hukum terbaru berwarna e. Specimen tanda tangan orang perseorangan atau penanggung jawab badan hukum dan f. editorial.headline: Special-Cargo Shipping Beyond Indonesia’s Waters
editorial.standfirst: This activity governs specialist international sea transport—from hazardous cargo to fish carriers—with a 49% national foreign-ownership ceiling and no Bali moratorium block at Large-scale risk.
editorial.body:
**This is a specialist international maritime-transport activity, not a catch-all freight category.** It covers overseas sea carriage of special cargo, including dangerous goods, hazardous and toxic waste, fish and other aquatic life. Its operating pattern is also specific: it serves non-fixed, irregular or tramp routes between Indonesian ports and ports abroad. The point is not simply that cargo crosses a border, but that vessel, cargo and route are aligned to the specialised character described by the activity.

The scope reaches into emerging energy logistics as well as established fisheries transport. It includes international distribution of carbon-free fuels carried as gases, solids or liquids—energy carriers such as hydrogen, ammonia and related compounds—on specially designed sea vessels, according to storage needs and conditions. It also expressly covers overseas transport of fish on Indonesian-flagged fish-carrier vessels and on foreign-flagged fish-carrier vessels. Chartering a maritime transport service together with its operator sits within the activity too; for foreign-flagged vessels, the scope identifies an agency arrangement by a company that is not a fisheries company, with the operator.

An enterprise entering this activity is therefore registering a particular form of international special-cargo sea transport: one shaped by its cargo, its vessel and irregular international routing. The registration field is open across the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That broad scale availability matters because the record does not reduce the activity to a single company size or a single vessel flag. Instead, it embraces both Indonesian- and foreign-flagged fish-carrier operations, specialised energy-carrier distribution, and chartered transport with an operator.

Foreign participation requires a clear reading of the national and Bali positions. Nationally, the activity is TERBATAS: foreign ownership is capped at 49%, rather than being fully open. In Bali, it is marked OK or higher risk, and PMA registration is not blocked by the island-wide moratorium. The reason is precise: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is medium-high/high, so the moratorium does not block it. Bali’s PMA moratorium covers activities classified low or medium-low risk; this activity’s stated Large-scale risk classification places it outside that block.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, foreign ownership is capped at 49%, while Bali does not block the activity under its PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: People’s Shipping for International Cargo: What 50127 Covers
editorial.standfirst: A maritime freight activity for cargo and animals moving between Indonesian and overseas ports, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
Activity 50127 concerns people’s-shipping maritime transport carrying goods and/or animals between ports in Indonesia and ports abroad. Its working vessels are sailing ships, traditional motor vessels and motor-sailing vessels within the specified size criteria. The scope also includes the rental of that maritime transport together with its operator. In plain terms, this is an operational freight activity: the movement of cargo or animals by sea across an international port-to-port route, as well as operator-inclusive vessel hire.

The activity is open to enterprises at every listed scale: micro, small, medium and large. That breadth matters because the record does not confine the activity to a single business size or operating model. A founder considering the activity should still keep the core distinction clear: the registered business is maritime transport for goods or animals, using the vessel types set out in the scope, rather than a generic shipping label detached from a real transport operation.

Across Indonesia, this activity permits foreign investment with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. There is no lesser national foreign-share cap in the record. For Bali, the more useful question is whether provincial treatment changes that national position. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium: at the large scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Medium-High/High. The Bali status is therefore OK or higher risk, rather than a moratorium exclusion.

That is the honest practical reading of the record. A foreign-owned business may be registered nationally with up to 100% foreign ownership, and the Bali classification does not place this activity behind the stated PMA moratorium. The Bali point is not an invented local ownership limit or special partnership condition; it is the risk-based reason the activity remains outside the provincial block. The defining question remains whether the intended operation genuinely fits the stated international maritime carriage of goods or animals and the associated operator-inclusive charter activity.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign-owned business may be registered nationally with up to 100% foreign ownership, and the Bali classification does not place this activity behind the stated PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Scheduled Ferries Across Provinces, With a Clear Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: This is the large-scale, route-bound public ferry business moving passengers between Indonesian provinces — foreign ownership in it is capped at 49%.
editorial.body:
Interprovincial public ferry passenger transport is the business of carrying passengers from one province to another on ferries operating on established routes. The route-bound character matters: this is public passenger movement organised through a ferry service, rather than an incidental voyage or a loosely defined maritime activity. Its commercial identity is shaped by regular interprovincial connection and the practical work of moving people across provincial boundaries by ferry.

The record opens this activity at the **Besar** scale. That places the code in a large-business setting: an operator registering under it is entering the public ferry transport field at that stated scale, with the focus on passenger carriage across provinces and on services tied to designated routes. The classification does not broaden into a general account of every kind of water transport; its centre of gravity is specific, public, scheduled ferry travel between provinces.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Interprovincial public passenger ferry transport is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #18, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

Bali does not add a second obstacle. The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. This one is recorded at medium-high risk, so the moratorium does not reach it and the company can be registered here. Bali states no percentage of its own and no local partnership requirement; what limits the foreign side is the 49% ceiling, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia.
editorial.pullQuote: For large-scale interprovincial ferry transport, Bali's moratorium is not the constraint — the 49% ceiling on foreign shareholding is.

editorial.headline: The Moving Bridge Between Indonesia’s Cities
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers intercity and inter-regency passenger ferry transport — foreign ownership is capped at 49%, and Bali's moratorium does not block registration.
editorial.body:
Passenger ferry transport is sometimes described as a route across water. This activity is more specific: it covers passenger crossings between designated ferry ports in different regencies or cities, whether across seas, straits or bays. The ferry is understood here as a moving bridge between two particular places, extending a road and/or rail network rather than sitting apart from it. The scope also includes hiring out ferry transport together with its operator.

That definition gives the activity a clear operational centre of gravity. It is for businesses conducting the crossing itself, as well as businesses making ferry transport available with the operator who runs it. The eligible business scale in the record is **Besar**. The focus is therefore not simply on being near a port or serving passengers generally, but on the organised provision of passenger ferry crossings between the specified places and ports.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Public passenger ferry crossings between regencies or cities is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #20, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

For a founder, the distinction is worth holding precisely. The ceiling is the national position and Bali does not soften it; equally, Bali does not stack a registration block on top of it. The practical reading is straightforward: a Besar-scale passenger ferry crossing business, including ferry hire with its operator, can be registered in Bali, with the foreign side of the shareholding stopping at 49% and the rest outside foreign hands.
editorial.pullQuote: A Besar-scale ferry crossing business can be registered in Bali; the foreign side of its shareholding stops at 49%.

editorial.standfirst: A large-scale passenger-ferry activity linking ports within one regency or city — foreign ownership is capped at 49%, and Bali's moratorium does not block it.
editorial.body:

The ferry is conceived as a moving bridge between two specified places, carrying forward a road and/or rail network rather than operating as a detached maritime service. The scope also includes the rental of ferry transport when supplied together with its operator. Put simply, the activity is defined by a local crossing and by the connection it completes within that local network.

That definition gives the code a clear operational shape. The journey is not merely waterborne movement from one port to another: it is a crossing structured around a particular link in the local transport network. Passenger transport is central to the designation, and the geography is bounded inside a regency or city. The record makes the scale equally clear: it is open to businesses classified as Besar. It also encompasses ferry rental when an operator is part of the provision. The commercial identity comes from that combination—public passenger crossings, a defined local corridor, and a large-scale operating frame.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Public passenger ferry crossings within one regency or city is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #22, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

Bali does not add a second obstacle. The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. This one is recorded at medium-high risk, so the moratorium does not reach it and the company can be registered here. Bali states no percentage of its own and no local partnership requirement; what limits the foreign side is the 49% ceiling, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia.

editorial.headline: Pioneer Passenger Ferries Across Provinces: Foreign Ownership Capped at 49%
editorial.standfirst: A large-scale passenger-ferry activity linking remote and not-yet-profitable areas between provinces to developed areas — foreign ownership is capped at 49%, and Bali's moratorium does not block registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 50134 covers passenger ferry transport between provinces across seas, straits and bays. Its stated purpose gives the activity a particular connection role: it links remote areas, and areas that have potential but remain undeveloped and commercially unprofitable to serve, with developed areas. The scope also reaches the chartering of ferry transport when the operator is provided. It combines the transport service and a charter arrangement only where the operator accompanies the ferry. This is passenger crossing transport shaped around connecting the places specified in its scope to more developed destinations. The wording matters because the service is defined by both its inter-provincial route and the places it is meant to connect.

The definition should be read as a whole. It names passenger transport by ferry, the inter-provincial passage across the stated waters, and the connection of remote or not-yet-commercially-profitable areas to developed areas. It does not detach the charter element from the transport service: that element is included when the ferry is chartered with its operator. In a code meant to define an activity, those elements give the operation its precise perimeter.

The registration picture is deliberately narrow on scale. The record lists Besar as the scale open to this activity. For a founder assessing whether the code fits, that is part of the core boundary: the activity is presented here at the large-business scale, alongside ferry crossings, passenger transport, and operator-inclusive chartering. Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Pioneer interprovincial passenger ferry transport is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #19, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

Bali does not add a second obstacle. The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. This one is recorded at medium-high risk, so the moratorium does not reach it and the company can be registered here. Bali states no percentage of its own and no local partnership requirement; what limits the foreign side is the 49% ceiling, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia.
editorial.pullQuote: For this large-scale activity, Bali does not block PMA registration under the moratorium described in the record.

KBLI 50135 covers pioneer passenger-crossing transport over seas, straits and bays between regencies or cities. Its purpose is expressly connective: it brings remote areas, and areas with potential that are still undeveloped or not yet commercially worthwhile to serve, into contact with developed areas. The scope also includes renting this crossing transport with its operator. The wording matters because the service is tied not merely to remote endpoints, but to their link with areas already developed.

The record opens this activity at **Besar** scale. That is therefore the scale at which an enterprise registers this line of business—whether it operates the passenger crossing itself or rents the relevant crossing transport together with an operator. The scale designation is not incidental; it is the record’s stated operating frame for the activity. Its centre of gravity remains passenger-crossing transport on the routes described: a service connecting areas whose commercial and developmental conditions are not the same.

**Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%.** Pioneer passenger-crossing transport between regencies or cities is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #21, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

**Bali does not add a second obstacle.** The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. editorial.headline: Passenger Crossings Connecting Networks at Sea
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers specified passenger sea crossings and vessel hire with an operator, open nationally to large-scale foreign investment and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 50139 concerns passenger crossing transport in seas, straits and bays that is not classified elsewhere. Its defining image is practical rather than abstract: a movable bridge connecting two particular places as a continuation of a road and/or railway network. The scope expressly includes international passenger crossings, as well as the rental of crossing transport together with its operator. It is therefore a category centred on carrying passengers across water-linked routes and on providing that transport with the operating capability attached.

The stated registration scale is **Besar**—Large. That matters because the record does not present this as an activity open across every business scale. The framing is for large-scale participation, where the transport service, the crossing route and the operator are considered together. For an investor or operator assessing the category, the essential question is not simply whether a vessel can be hired, but whether the proposed activity falls within this defined passenger-crossing service and is undertaken at the stated scale.

editorial.headline: Interprovincial Cargo Ferries: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Route-bound ferry freight between provinces is nationally open to PMA up to 100%; at the listed Besar scale, Bali does not block it under its PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 50141 describes a specific interprovincial freight movement:** carrying goods from one province to another on ferry vessels operating on an established route. The detail matters. The activity is not framed simply as moving cargo by water; it is ferry transport, directed to goods, crossing provincial boundaries and tied to a route. Those elements form the useful boundary of the code, making its operating identity clear before ownership or location is considered.

**The declared scale is Besar.** That is the only scale listed as open to the activity. For a business registering this classification, the record therefore places the activity in a large-scale setting rather than presenting a menu of smaller operating categories. It is a concise signal about the registration the record supports: large-scale public interprovincial ferry freight transport on routes. Nothing in the record expands that into a separate licence, capital rule or timetable, so the scale should be read precisely as stated rather than as a proxy for requirements not supplied here.

**At the national level, the PMA picture is open.** The PMA status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%, meaning the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership for this activity. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national position should be kept distinct from Bali's local PMA screen; the two are not competing descriptions of one threshold. One addresses the national foreign-ownership ceiling, while the other records whether Bali's moratorium blocks PMA registration in the activity's relevant risk position.

**In Bali, it is not blocked by the moratorium.** At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Medium-High/High, and the record assigns the Bali status OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. Bali's permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity falls outside that block at the listed large scale. The clear practical conclusion is that a foreign investor can register KBLI 50141 in Bali today: it remains nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali does not bar it under the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can register KBLI 50141 in Bali today: it remains nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali does not bar it under the stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: Goods Carried Across a Moving Bridge
editorial.standfirst: This public goods-ferry activity links ferry ports across seas, straits and bays—and remains open to full foreign ownership nationally and for PMA registration in Bali at the stated scale.
editorial.body:
Goods may cross an island boundary or a narrow stretch of water, yet the commercial logic here remains that of a route. This activity covers public goods ferry transport between regencies or cities, operating across seas, straits and bays between ferry ports. Its defining image is the moving bridge: a crossing that connects two specified places and continues the road network, or the rail network, across water. It is a connective service, arranged around the crossing itself and its role in a wider transport chain.

That wording gives the activity a practical perimeter. The service is the act of carrying goods on a public crossing that joins ports as a continuation of overland travel. It also includes the rental of ferry transport together with its operator. That operator element places rental within the operating service described here, rather than separating it from the crossing itself. For founders, the clearest reading is waterborne goods movement serving a linked road or rail journey between particular points.

The registration profile is specific in one clear respect: the stated scale is Besar. At that scale, the national investment position is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain English, the record permits full foreign ownership nationally for this activity. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national answer sits alongside the activity’s operational description: a public ferry crossing for goods, linking specified places through the continuation of a road or rail network.

Bali does not reverse that answer. Its status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the OSS risk at the Besar scale is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High. Consequently, the activity is not blocked by Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium for PMA registration, which applies to all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. A foreigner can therefore register the activity in Bali today. The national 100% ceiling remains the stated ownership position; Bali’s conclusion follows from the recorded risk status at the stated scale.

editorial.headline: Goods Ferry Crossings Within a Regency or City
editorial.standfirst: A large-scale public-goods ferry activity, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium at its recorded risk level.
editorial.body:
KBLI 50143 concerns public goods ferry transport on routes between ferry ports within a single regency or city. It covers crossings on seas, straits and bays, but its underlying function is more specific than a generic marine journey: the service is a movable bridge joining two designated places. In the record’s framing, that bridge continues the road and/or railway network. The activity also includes renting out ferry transport together with its operator. The essential picture, then, is of a public crossing service for goods, organised as part of a connected transport link.

The registration audience is deliberately narrow. The activity is open to enterprises at the large scale. Nationally, its foreign-investment status is open, with a maximum foreign ownership allowance of 100%. There is no national foreign-equity ceiling below full ownership in the supplied record. For a founder reading the code as a national classification, that is the starting position: this public goods-ferry activity is open to PMA at the listed scale, and a foreign investor may hold up to the stated national maximum.

Bali requires a separate reading, because the provincial rule blocks PMA registration across all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. This activity is not in that blocked result. At the large scale recorded here, the OSS risk is medium-high/high; that places it outside the moratorium’s stated risk bands. Bali’s status is therefore OK or higher risk, rather than a moratorium block. The distinction is important: the province’s constraint is risk-based, not a reversal of the national ownership position shown for this entry.

The honest conclusion is unusually direct. A foreigner can register this activity in Bali today as PMA, provided the registration is for the defined large-scale public goods-ferry crossing activity: routes between ferry ports within a regency or city, including operator-accompanied rental. The national allowance is 100%, and the Bali moratorium does not block the applicable medium-high risk position. That conclusion should not be stretched beyond this code’s defined scope or the large-scale access stated in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: The national allowance is 100%, and the Bali moratorium does not block the applicable medium-high risk position.

editorial.headline: Pioneer Freight Links Across Indonesia’s Provinces
editorial.standfirst: A large-scale interprovincial ferry service for goods, connecting remote or commercially unserved areas with more developed regions.
editorial.body:
This activity covers pioneer interprovincial ferry transport for goods across seas, straits and bays. Its purpose is unusually specific: connecting remote areas, and places with potential that remain undeveloped or commercially unprofitable to serve, with areas that are already developed. It also includes the rental of ferry transport together with its operator. The emphasis is not simply on moving cargo between provinces, but on maintaining a connective route where ordinary commercial shipping has not yet made the service viable.

The activity is open to **Besar** scale businesses. That detail gives the code its practical character. This is a freight transport undertaking framed around substantial operations: vessels, routes and an operating model capable of linking areas separated by water and unequal in their level of development. The inclusion of operator-led rental also makes clear that the activity can be organised around providing the ferry service itself, rather than only carrying goods under a single direct operating arrangement.

For this activity, the national regime is **TERBUKA** to foreign investment and sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at **100%**. In other words, the national setting permits full foreign ownership within the stated ceiling. That openness belongs to this defined activity and its Large-scale setting; the commercial proposition remains the pioneer carriage of goods between provinces, not a generic maritime transport category.

Bali presents a different but not prohibitive reading. This activity is not blocked by the island-wide PMA moratorium because, at **Besar** scale, its OSS risk classification is Medium-High or High. The provincial rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA, but this activity sits outside that blocked band. For a foreign investor considering Bali, the accurate conclusion is therefore neither a blanket warning nor an invented assurance: national ownership may reach 100%, and the Bali moratorium does not block this Large-scale activity on the recorded risk basis.
editorial.pullQuote: National ownership may reach 100%, and the Bali moratorium does not block this Large-scale activity on the recorded risk basis.

editorial.headline: Scheduled Inland Passenger Routes: Foreign Ownership Capped at 49%
editorial.standfirst: This code covers fixed, regular passenger services on Indonesia’s rivers, lakes, canals, swamps and other inland waters.
editorial.body:
This activity is for passenger transport on rivers, canals, lakes, swamps and other inland waters when it operates through a fixed and regular route network with a set timetable. The defining character is scheduled service: passengers are carried on established routes rather than through an ad hoc arrangement. Its scope reaches local services within a regency or city, services between regencies or cities within a province, interprovincial services, and cross-border international inland-water routes.

The registration is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That matters because the activity is not framed as the preserve of only one type of operator. A business can be registered for this scheduled inland passenger-transport activity at any of those scales, provided its actual operation remains within the scope of fixed, regular routes and scheduled passenger services on inland waters.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Scheduled passenger transport on inland waters is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #23, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

Bali does not add a second obstacle. The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. This one is recorded at medium-high risk, so the moratorium does not reach it and the company can be registered here. Bali states no percentage of its own and no local partnership requirement; what limits the foreign side is the 49% ceiling, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity remains available for PMA registration in Bali, up to the national 49% foreign-ownership cap, because it is not marked as blocked by the province’s moratorium.

editorial.headline: Flexible Inland Passenger Transport, With a Clear Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: For non-tourism passenger journeys on Indonesia’s inland waterways, this activity allows flexible routes and no fixed timetable—while Bali’s PMA position turns on risk at the large scale.
editorial.body:
This activity is for carrying passengers across rivers, canals, lakes, swamps and other inland waters where the route is neither fixed nor scheduled. Its defining character is flexibility: the service does not operate on a permanent route or a regular timetable. Just as importantly, the scope expressly excludes tourism. The code therefore describes passenger transport on inland waterways as a transport activity in its own right, rather than a tourism offering.

Registration is open at every stated business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the activity is not framed as the preserve of one particular size of operator. A founder considering this code should begin with the real operating model—passenger carriage on inland waters, without fixed or regular routes—and then identify the scale at which the business will be registered. The activity’s scope is precise about the mode of transport and the irregular nature of its service, which is where the classification’s practical centre of gravity lies.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Unscheduled passenger transport on inland waters is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #24, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

The distinction is worth keeping clean. Bali's position here is not a second ownership cap and not an invented local condition: it is a risk-based reading, and at the large scale the risk assessment places the activity outside the moratorium. For an investor the honest conclusion is straightforward — the activity can be registered in Bali across the listed scales, and the foreign stake in the company that holds it stops at 49%.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity can be registered in Bali; the foreign stake in the company that holds it stops at 49%.

editorial.standfirst: This activity covers tourist passenger journeys on inland waterways — foreign ownership is capped at 49%, and Bali's moratorium does not block registration.
editorial.body:
This activity is about carrying passengers for tourism across Indonesia’s inland waters: rivers, canals, lakes, swamps and other inland waterways. Its scope is deliberately broader than a single type of excursion or customer. It can serve an individual traveller, an organised group, a family, or a social purpose, provided the journey is tourist passenger transport on those waters. The organising idea is not the destination alone, but the movement of visitors by inland water.

A business registering this activity is therefore placing tourist passenger transport at the centre of its operation. The record opens it to Menengah and Besar scales, making scale an explicit part of the registration picture rather than an afterthought. That matters because the activity is defined by both its tourism purpose and its setting: inland waterways, not a generic transport category. The wording also accommodates the different ways tourism is experienced—privately, collectively, with family, or through social activity—without narrowing the activity to only one kind of passenger.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Tourist passenger transport on inland waters is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #25, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

Bali does not add a second obstacle. The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. This one is recorded at medium-high risk, so the moratorium does not reach it and the company can be registered here. Bali states no percentage of its own and no local partnership requirement; what limits the foreign side is the 49% ceiling, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia.

editorial.headline: General Cargo on Indonesia’s Inland Waterways
editorial.standfirst: A clear route for general freight by river, canal, lake, swamp and other inland waters — foreign ownership is capped at 49%, with no Bali moratorium block in this record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 50221 covers the carriage of general goods across Indonesia’s inland waters: rivers, canals, lakes, swamps and other internal waterways. Its focus is freight transport, not a single specialised cargo stream; the goods carried may comprise more than one type. The boundary is equally clear. Hazardous goods, special goods and heavy equipment sit outside the activity described here. The result is a classification for general inland-water freight, defined by both its route and the ordinary character of the cargo.

The activity is open at every listed business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the record does not confine this form of freight transport to a single size of enterprise. A business using this activity is situated in the practical movement of general goods on inland waters, whether the operation is registered at the smallest listed scale or at the largest. The classification’s scope remains consistent across those scales: transporting general freight by river, canal, lake, swamp or another inland waterway, while excluding the specified categories of cargo.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. General freight transport on inland waters is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #26, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

Bali does not add a second obstacle. The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. This one is recorded at medium-high risk, so the moratorium does not reach it and the company can be registered here. Bali states no percentage of its own and no local partnership requirement; what limits the foreign side is the 49% ceiling, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, Bali is therefore not moratorium-blocked for PMA registration, up to the national 49% foreign-ownership cap.

editorial.headline: Specialised Inland Cargo Transport: Foreign Ownership Capped at 49%
editorial.standfirst: This activity is for purpose-modified vessels carrying one specialised cargo type on Indonesia's inland waterways — foreign ownership is capped at 49%, with no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 50222** covers the movement of specialised cargo on rivers, canals, lakes, swamps and other inland waters. It is not a general-cargo description: the vessel or cargo boat is specially modified and carries only one type of goods. The recorded scope includes logs; pipes, steel bars or rails; bulk cargo; liquids; goods requiring refrigeration; plants and live animals; containers; heavy equipment; and other specialised goods. The vessel must meet the technical and seaworthiness requirements appropriate to the particular cargo it carries.

The activity is open across the stated business spectrum: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth does not dilute the defining feature of the code. What matters is the dedicated nature of the transport operation—the craft is adapted to its cargo and operates on inland waters, rather than being described as a vessel for mixed or general freight. For a business selecting this activity, the fit lies in that close relationship between vessel design, cargo type and inland-waterway transport.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Specialised cargo transport on inland waters is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #27, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

The practical reading is deliberately narrow. A company undertaking this specialised inland cargo activity can be registered in Bali, and the foreign shareholding in it stops at 49% — there, and everywhere else in Indonesia. The activity itself remains defined by specialised vessels, a single cargo category and transport across inland waters.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign-owned business may register this specialised inland cargo activity, up to the national 49% foreign-ownership ceiling, and Bali’s cited moratorium does not prevent that registration.
