editorial.headline: Moving Dangerous Cargo Across Indonesia’s Inland Waters
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers hazardous cargo carried by inland waterway — foreign ownership is capped at 49%, and registration in Bali is not blocked by the moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is a specialist inland-water freight operation: carrying dangerous goods on rivers, canals, lakes, swamps and other inland waters, from the loading point through to final unloading. Its stated cargo scope is substantial and specific. It includes hazardous and toxic waste, fuel oil, petroleum, processed petroleum products, and liquefied or compressed gas categories including LPG, LNG and CNG. The work described here is the movement itself across inland waters, with the transport chain running from loading to final discharge.

It is available to businesses registered at micro, small, medium and large scale. That breadth matters because the activity is not framed as a large-operator category alone; the record expressly lists every scale. Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Dangerous-goods transport on inland waters is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #28, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. Foreign shareholders can hold up to that 49% of a PT PMA and no more; the rest of the shares must be held by Indonesian shareholders. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

Bali requires an equally direct reading. The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk, and at the large scale this one is recorded at medium-high risk. It therefore sits outside that restriction: a foreign investor seeking to register this inland-water transport activity in Bali does not face a moratorium block.

The two readings answer different questions. The ceiling answers how much of the company foreign shareholders may hold — 49%, with the rest outside foreign hands. Bali answers whether the company can be registered on the island at all, and here it can. No separate Bali percentage or local-partnership condition is recorded. Taken together: this is a registrable activity for a foreign-invested company, in Bali as elsewhere, provided the foreign side of the shareholding respects the 49% ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: This is a foreign-investment activity capped nationally at 49%, including in Bali, for the inland-water carriage of dangerous cargoes.

data.judul: Angkutan Udara Niaga Berjadwal untuk Penumpang

per_skala.scope_uraian: Angkutan Udara Niaga Berjadwal Dalam Negeri untuk Penumpang atau Penumpang dan Kargo
persyaratan: Dokumen Rencana usaha (business plan) untuk kurun waktu minimal 5 tahun yang akan datang, paling sedikit memuat:
Jenis dan jumlah pesawat udara yang akan dioperasikan (karakteristik dan spesifikasi pesawat, cara perolehan, jumlah kebutuhan pesawat, utilisasi pesawat udara)
Rencana pusat kegiatan operasi penerbangan (operation base) dan rencana rute penerbangan
Rencana kebutuhan SDM yang terdiri dari manajemen, teknisi dan personel pesawat udara. Aspek ekonomi dan keuangan
kewajiban: Melakukan kegiatan angkutan udara secara nyata paling lambat 12 (dua belas) bulan sejak perizinan berusaha diterbitkan dengan mengoperasikan minimal jumlah pesawat udara yang dimiliki dan dikuasai sesuai dengan lingkup usaha atau kegiatannya

Memiliki pesawat udara dengan jumlah paling sedikit 1 (satu) unit dan menguasai paling sedikit 2 (dua) unit dengan jenis yang mendukung kelangsungan operasional penerbangan sesuai dengan rute yang dilayani
Mematuhi ketentuan wajib angkut, penerbangan sipil, dan ketentuan lain sesuai dengan peraturan perundang���undangan
Menutup asuransi tanggung jawab pengangkut dengan nilai pertanggungan sebesar santunan penumpang dan kargo angkutan udara niaga yang dibuktikan dengan perjanjian penutupan asuransi
Melayani calon penumpang secara adil tanpa diskriminasi atas dasar suku, agama, ras, antar-golongan, serta strata ekonomi dan sosial
Menyerahkan laporan kegiatan angkutan udara, termasuk keterlambatan dan pembatalan penerbangan setiap bulan paling lambat tanggal 10 (sepuluh) bulan berikutnya kepada menteri
Menyerahkan laporan kinerja keuangan yang telah diaudit oleh kantor akuntan publik terdaftar yang sekurangkurangnya memuat neraca, laporan rugi laba, arus kas
rincian biaya, setiap tahun paling lambat akhir bulan april tahun berikutnya kepada menteri
Melaporkan apabila terjadi perubahan penanggung jawab atau pemilik badan usaha angkutan udara niaga, domisili badan usaha angkutan udara niaga dan kepemilikan pesawat udara kepada Menteri
Memenuhi standar pelayanan penumpang angkutan udara niaga berjadwal dalam negeri

editorial.headline: Scheduled Commercial Air Transport Is Open to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A fixed-route, regular-schedule passenger air service — foreign shareholding is capped at 49% with a single-majority condition on the national side, and Bali's moratorium does not block registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 51101 is the operating category for commercial air transport provided on fixed routes and regular flight schedules, for a published fare. Its centre of gravity is the scheduled service itself: carrying passengers, or passengers and cargo, by aircraft as part of a repeatable public timetable rather than a one-off flying arrangement. It accommodates both domestic scheduled services and international scheduled services. The code therefore describes an airline-style activity in the plain operational sense—an air service sold against established routes, established schedules and published charges.

Registration is not framed as a preserve of one business size. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises, recognising that the registered scale can sit anywhere from micro through large. That breadth does not change the activity’s defining character. A business registered here is putting forward a scheduled commercial passenger service, with cargo permitted alongside passengers; the fixed-route, regular-schedule and published-fare elements are the boundaries that give the category its shape.

Foreign shareholding in this activity is capped at 49%, and the record carries a second condition the ceiling alone does not express: a national capital owner must retain a single majority. That wording matters when the Indonesian side is split between several holders — whether such a structure satisfies it is a question to settle before incorporation, not after. Both conditions come from Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III, entry #31.

For a founder, the useful distinction is simple but important. This is a code for a scheduled commercial air service, open across the listed enterprise scales, with the foreign side of the shareholding stopping at 49% and a single-majority condition on the national side. In Bali the relevant fact is equally plain: the provincial moratorium does not bar registration, because it reaches only low and medium-low risk lines and this activity sits above that band. The record cites Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 as the source for the national position, and Lampiran III entry #31 as the specific basis.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, the relevant fact is equally plain: PMA registration is not barred by the provincial moratorium on the record’s terms, up to the national 49% foreign-ownership cap.

per_skala.scope_uraian: Angkutan Udara Niaga Tidak Berjadwal Dalam Negeri untuk Penumpang atau Penumpang dan Kargo
persyaratan: Dokumen Rencana usaha (business plan) untuk kurun waktu minimal 5 tahun yang akan datang, paling sedikit memuat:
Jenis dan jumlah pesawat udara yang akan dioperasikan (karakteristik dan spesifikasi pesawat, cara perolehan, jumlah kebutuhan pesawat, utilisasi pesawat udara)
Rencana pusat kegiatan operasi penerbangan (operation base) dan rencana daerah operasi penerbangan
Rencana kebutuhan SDM yang terdiri dari manajemen, teknisi dan personel pesawat udara
Aspek ekonomi dan keuangan
kewajiban: Melakukan kegiatan angkutan udara secara nyata paling lambat 12 (dua belas) bulan sejak perizinan berusaha diterbitkan dengan mengoperasikan minimal jumlah pesawat udara yang dimiliki dan dikuasai sesuai dengan lingkup usaha atau kegiatannya

Memiliki paling sedikit 1 (satu) unit pesawat udara dan pesawat udara yang lainnya dalam bentuk menguasai dengan jenis yang mendukung kelangsungan operasional penerbangan sesuai dengan daerah operasi yang dilayani
Mematuhi ketentuan wajib angkut, penerbangan sipil, dan ketentuan lain sesuai dengan peraturan perundang���undangan
Menutup asuransi tanggung jawab pengangkut dengan nilai pertanggungan sebesar santunan penumpang dan kargo angkutan udara niaga yang dibuktikan dengan perjanjian penutupan asuransi
Melayani calon penumpang secara adil tanpa diskriminasi atas dasar suku, agama, ras, antar-golongan, serta strata ekonomi dan sosial
Menyerahkan laporan kegiatan angkutan udara setiap bulan paling lambat tanggal 10 (sepuluh) bulan berikutnya kepada menteri

Menyerahkan laporan kinerja keuangan yang telah diaudit oleh kantor akuntan publik terdaftar yang sekurangkurangnya memuat neraca, laporan rugi laba, arus kas, dan rincian biaya, setiap tahun paling lambat akhir bulan april tahun berikutnya kepada Menteri
Melaporkan apabila terjadi perubahan penanggung jawab atau pemilik badan usaha angkutan udara niaga, domisili badan usaha angkutan udara niaga dan pemilikan pesawat udara kepada Menteri

editorial.headline: When Passenger Air Travel Does Not Keep a Timetable
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 51102 covers commercial passenger flights built around agreed journeys — foreign shareholding is capped at 49% with a single-majority condition on the national side, and Bali records no moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 51102 is the place for commercial, non-scheduled carriage of passengers—or passengers and cargo—by aircraft when neither route nor flight schedule is fixed or regular. The fare is not a public rate: it is agreed between the air-transport provider and user. That definition gives the activity a particular commercial texture. It embraces charter passenger flights, sightseeing flights, and the hiring of an aircraft with its operator for passenger transport. The stated scope also reaches domestic and international non-scheduled commercial transport, whether the load is passengers alone or passengers and cargo.

This is therefore an activity for operators whose service is formed around an agreed journey rather than a published itinerary. The relevant question is not merely whether the aircraft carries people; it is whether the journey is offered on the non-fixed, non-regular basis described in the record, with a privately agreed tariff. In practice, the code’s own wording keeps the focus on the operating service: the aircraft comes with its operator, and the commercial task is passenger carriage. The entry is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, giving the same defined activity a place across each listed business scale.

Foreign shareholding in this activity is capped at 49%, and the record carries a second condition the ceiling alone does not express: a national capital owner must retain a single majority. That wording matters when the Indonesian side is split between several holders — whether such a structure satisfies it is a question to settle before incorporation, not after. Both conditions come from Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III, entry #30.

Bali requires its own reading rather than an automatic extension of the national result. The provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI island-wide. This record, however, is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and expressly says it is not blocked by that moratorium; at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. A foreign investor can therefore register this activity in Bali today on the record presented here. The decisive point is not a special Bali ownership cap, but the recorded absence of a moratorium block.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can therefore register this activity in Bali today on the record presented here.

editorial.headline: Passenger Space Transport, Open Nationally and Address-Checked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 51103 covers passenger journeys in launch vehicles and operator-inclusive hire, open to foreign investment through a PMA company; whether Bali's PMA moratorium applies is not yet classifiable pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.
editorial.body:
Passenger space transport is the business of carrying people in launch vehicles, across every type of route and launch schedule. The definition is deliberately broad about how the journey is arranged: it covers activity conducted on any routing pattern and at any launch cadence. It also includes the hire of space transport with its operator when the purpose is passenger carriage. Its defining focus is the movement of passengers through space transport.

The code is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. Across Indonesia, its PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. The practical reading is clear: PMA ownership may extend to the full stake in this activity nationally. Scale and ownership are distinct parts of the picture. A registration may sit at any of the four listed business scales, while the stated national foreign-investment position remains fully open.

Bali warrants its own reading rather than an automatic extrapolation from the national figure. Whether Bali's permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium applies here cannot be determined yet: the earlier reading was based on a risk classification carried over from a different activity (code-number collision) and has been removed. Confirm the current risk tier and any Bali-specific requirement with the Bali Zero team before planning a Bali setup.

For a founder assessing a passenger space-transport operation, the record answers three separate questions. The activity can include launch-vehicle journeys on all routes and schedules, as well as an operator-inclusive hire arrangement. It is open at every listed scale, and national PMA ownership can reach 100%. Whether it is caught by Bali's PMA moratorium is not yet classifiable — confirm with the Bali Zero team before planning a Bali setup.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, this activity is open to foreign investment through a PMA company; whether Bali's moratorium applies to this activity is not yet classifiable pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.

Per BPS Tabel Konversi Vol.2 lampiran5 p.193 (image-verified), old-51109 SPLITS into new-51101 (scheduled airline) + new-51103 (space). Its pp28_sources [51103,51108,51104] are all KBLI-2020-vintage AVIATION codes (aircraft operator / AOC / cargo-carrier insurance requirements) — a code-number collision, not the same activity. intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers scheduled air cargo services—transporting goods by plane on fixed routes and published timetables for a set tariff. It specifically excludes unscheduled cargo flights and space or satellite launches.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: This activity is not blocked by Bali's foreign investment moratorium. However, it is classified as medium-high risk, so your PMA and the proposed business address will face closer regulatory scrutiny—you must verify location suitability with the local investment office (DPMPTSP) before assuming approval.

intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Angkutan Udara Niaga Berjadwal Khusus Kargo (51201)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: A foreign logistics entrepreneur ready to launch a scheduled air freight operation, such as an established cargo airline or a freight forwarder expanding a scheduled route into Bali.

editorial.headline: Scheduled Cargo Air Transport, With a Clear Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers commercial air cargo services run on fixed, regular routes and timetables, with published fares.
editorial.body:
This classification is for commercial cargo transport by aircraft where the route and flight schedule are fixed and regular, and the applicable fare is published. Its defining character is therefore not simply the movement of goods by air, but a scheduled service: a cargo operation organised around established routes, recurring flight times and publicly stated tariffs. That combination gives the activity a distinctly structured commercial frame.

It is open at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The classification consequently accommodates the activity across the full scale range identified in the record, while retaining the same essential description of regularly scheduled, tariff-based cargo air transport. The practical question is not whether the activity becomes something different as it grows, but how its operational scale sits within the applicable registration context.

Nationally, the position on foreign investment is uncomplicated. Classified as TERBUKA, the activity carries a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Put simply, the record permits full foreign ownership at the national level. That openness is supported by the cited investment-policy sources, Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021, and there is no lower national foreign-equity cap stated for this activity.

Bali deserves its own, separate reading. This activity is not blocked for PMA registration by the province-wide moratorium, which permanently blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA. The record places the relevant OSS risk at the Besar scale in the Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi range, meaning Medium-High/High, and identifies the Bali outcome as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For a foreign investor considering Bali, the honest conclusion is that the provincial moratorium does not close this activity off; the decisive local context is its higher risk position at the large scale, not a Bali-specific foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali’s moratorium does not close this activity off; its local position rests on the higher risk classification at the large scale.

data.judul: Angkutan Udara Niaga Tidak Berjadwal Khusus Kargo
data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup aktivitas transportasi kargo, termasuk bahan bakar minyak, minyak bumi, hasil olahan, gas minyak cair (LPG), gas alam cair (LNG), dan gas alam termampat (CNG) dengan pesawat udara pada rute dan jadwal penerbangan yang tidak tetap dan tidak teratur dengan membayar tarif yang merupakan kesepakatan antara penyedia jasa dan pengguna jasa angkutan udara dan tidak dipublikasikan.
Subgolongan ini juga mencakup
- penyewaan transportasi udara dengan operatornya untuk keperluan transportasi barang.
Kelompok ini tidak mencakup
- transportasi barang melalui udara dengan rute dan jadwal tetap, lihat kelompok 51201;
- peluncuran satelit dan wahana antariksa, lihat kelompok 51203;
- transportasi antariksa untuk penumpang, lihat kelompok 51103.

per_skala.scope_uraian: Angkutan Udara Niaga Tidak Berjadwal dalam Negeri untuk Kargo
persyaratan: Dokumen Rencana usaha (business plan) untuk kurun waktu minimal 5 tahun yang akan datang, paling sedikit memuat:
Jenis dan jumlah pesawat udara yang akan dioperasikan (karakteristik dan spesifikasi pesawat, cara perolehan, jumlah kebutuhan pesawat, utilisasi pesawat udara)
Rencana pusat kegiatan operasi penerbangan (operation base) dan rencana daerah operasi penerbangan.
Rencana kebutuhan SDM yang terdiri dari manajemen, teknisi dan personel pesawat udara
Aspek ekonomi dan keuangan
kewajiban: Melakukan kegiatan angkutan udara secara nyata paling lambat 12 (dua belas) bulan sejak perizinan berusaha diterbitkan dengan mengoperasikan minimal jumlah pesawat udara yang dimiliki dan dikuasai sesuai dengan lingkup usaha atau kegiatannya

Memiliki paling sedikit 1 (satu) unit pesawat udara dan pesawat udara yang lainnya dalam bentuk menguasai dengan jenis yang mendukung kelangsungan operasional penerbangan sesuai dengan daerah operasi yang dilayani
Mematuhi ketentuan wajib angkut, penerbangan sipil, dan ketentuan lain sesuai dengan peraturan perundang���undangan
Menutup asuransi tanggungjawab pengangkut dengan nilai pertanggungan sebesar santunan kargo angkutan udara niaga yang dibuktikan dengan perjanjian penutupan asuransi
Menyerahkan laporan kegiatan angkutan udara, termasuk keterlambatan dan pembatalan penerbangan setiap bulan paling lambat tanggal 10 (sepuluh) bulan berikutnya kepada menteri

Menyerahkan laporan kinerja keuangan yang telah diaudit oleh kantor akuntan publik terdaftar yang sekurangkurangnya memuat neraca, laporan rugi laba, arus kas, dan rincian biaya, setiap tahun paling lambat akhir bulan april tahun berikutnya kepada Menteri
Melaporkan apabila terjadi perubahan penanggung jawab atau pemilik badan usaha angkutan udara niaga, domisili badan usaha angkutan udara niaga dan kepemilikan pesawat udara kepada Menteri

editorial.headline: Cargo Charter Flights, and Bali’s PMA Registration Reality
editorial.standfirst: A commercial cargo-air service built around negotiated charter operations—open to full foreign ownership nationally and not barred for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is a commercial air-cargo activity for flights that do not follow a timetable. It covers cargo carried by aircraft on routes and flight schedules that are neither fixed nor regular, with charges agreed between operator and customer rather than published. The cargo may include fuel oil, petroleum, processed products, LPG, LNG and CNG, but the defining feature is the bespoke carriage arrangement: an air service configured around a particular movement, customer and agreed price.

That makes the category appropriate for operators whose business is moving goods under negotiated, non-public tariffs rather than operating a regular schedule. It also expressly includes the leasing of air transport with its operator for goods transport. Both domestic and international non-scheduled commercial cargo carriage sit within the activity. Entry is not reserved for one business size: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all open scales, so the code describes the activity without confining it to one end of the enterprise spectrum.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. A foreign investor may therefore hold the full ownership interest nationally. That is a material feature of the code: the business model may be specialised and operationally exacting, but the foreign-ownership setting does not impose a national equity cap below full ownership.

In Bali, the result is also clear, and the reason matters. This activity is not blocked by the moratorium. The record identifies its OSS risk at the Besar scale as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, while the island-wide permanent rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. A PMA registration for this activity in Bali is therefore not barred by that moratorium. National openness and the Bali outcome point in the same direction here: this is an activity that remains open to PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: A PMA registration for this activity in Bali is therefore not barred by that moratorium.

editorial.headline: Cargo Beyond the Atmosphere: Open Nationally, Address-Checked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers launch-vehicle cargo transport, satellite launches and operator-led space transport—open nationwide to full foreign ownership; whether Bali's PMA moratorium applies is not yet classifiable pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.
editorial.body:
Activity code 51203 is the classification for moving freight or cargo by launch vehicle, whatever the route and whatever the launch schedule. Its scope is deliberately wider than a single launch event: it includes the launch of satellites and other spacecraft, as well as the hire of space transport with its operator when the purpose is moving goods. The boundary is equally clear. This is a cargo activity; passenger space transport is expressly outside its scope. The subject, then, is a defined transport activity centred on goods and the vehicle that carries them.

Registration is open to the full set of stated business scales—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the record does not reserve this activity to a single scale: a business registering it may be classified at any of those four stated levels. The activities covered retain the same core: transport of cargo using launch vehicles, including satellite and spacecraft launches and operator-led rental for goods transport. The inclusion of an operator keeps the rental provision within the definition of goods transport.

At national level, this is an open PMA activity, or TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign ownership may reach full ownership nationwide. The record attributes that national position to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The stated national maximum is complete. That national position, however, should be kept distinct from Bali’s own treatment, which is recorded through a different status and an address-specific instruction.

Whether Bali's province-wide PMA moratorium applies to this activity cannot be determined until its risk tier is established — the earlier reading was based on a risk classification carried over from a different activity (code-number collision) and has been removed. This activity remains open to foreign investment through a PMA company nationally, a separate and unaffected fact. Confirm with the Bali Zero team before planning a Bali setup.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity is open to foreign investment through a PMA company nationally; whether Bali's moratorium applies to this activity is not yet classifiable pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.

editorial.headline: Warehouse Receipts Need a Warehouse System, Not Just Storage
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the management of warehouse-receipt-system facilities, from safeguarding goods to issuing the receipts that represent them.
editorial.body:
This activity is for operators of warehouses within Indonesia’s warehouse receipt system. Its work is not limited to keeping goods under a roof: it includes storing and maintaining goods placed in a system warehouse, then issuing warehouse receipts for goods deposited by their owners or by other parties. The defining feature is therefore the warehouse-receipt system itself, with the operator responsible for the facility and the receipts issued against goods held there.

The scope extends across several practical settings. It includes operating warehouse-receipt-system facilities in free-trade zones, cold-storage warehouses operating through that system, and physical commodity storage locations using it. A business registering this activity is positioning itself as the manager of such a warehouse operation—not merely as the owner of stored inventory. The code is open to micro, small, medium and large business scales, giving the activity a broad formal entry point across the stated scale categories.

Nationally, the position for foreign investment is straightforward: the activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That does not turn warehouse-receipt operations into a generic logistics proposition; the commercial identity remains tied to the storage, care and receipt issuance described in the scope. But it does mean that the national investment setting does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity.

Bali’s position is also materially clear. This activity is not blocked for PMA registration under the province-wide rule that blocks low- and medium-low-risk activities. At the large-business scale, however, its OSS risk classification is medium-high or high. The practical Bali reading is therefore not a moratorium barrier, but an activity whose large-scale operation sits in a higher-risk category. For a foreign founder, the honest conclusion is clean: the activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and is not barred from PMA registration in Bali by that moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The practical Bali reading is not a moratorium barrier, but an activity whose large-scale operation sits in a higher-risk category.

editorial.headline: Cold Storage: Fully Foreign-Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Cold-storage operations may accept full foreign ownership nationally, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration there.
editorial.body:
Cold-storage activity is the business of operating paid, contract-based storage for goods needing refrigeration during a defined preservation period before they are sent to their final destination. Its commercial centre of gravity is the storage service itself: holding physical commodities under cooling or freezing conditions for someone else, rather than owning the goods or arranging their final delivery. The paid-service basis matters: a fee or contract governs the preservation period. The scope also reaches cold stores in bonded zones and rapid-freezing facilities, including blast-freezing operations.

This is therefore a category for warehouse operators whose offering is controlled-temperature capacity. It can be registered at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, or Besar scale. The scope recognises routine refrigerated storage, frozen storage, and blast freezing within the same operational frame. Each belongs here when the operator stores goods for compensation or under a contract before final dispatch. The practical purpose is clear: preserve goods under cold conditions for the agreed period, then release them onward to their destination.

At national level, the position is straightforward. This activity is TERBUKA to PMA, and its foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In ordinary terms, a foreign investor can own the business in full under the national position; the record states no lower foreign-stake cap. That nationally open setting applies to the activity as described, including the operational forms expressly included in its scope. The important qualification is geographic rather than a national restriction on ownership.

For Bali, the answer changes decisively. Today, Bali does not permit a foreign investor to register this activity. At the Besar scale, OSS marks every scope as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah, placing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The record identifies this moratorium as applying in May 2026. Bali’s status is Blocked (risk class): the issue is not a reduction from the national 100% ceiling, but a block on PMA registration under Bali’s risk-based rule.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the ceiling is 100%; in Bali, the issue is not the stake but whether PMA can register at all.

editorial.headline: Bonded Warehousing: Open Nationally, Registrable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Bonded warehousing operates physical commodity storage in bonded areas, with foreign ownership open nationally and a Bali route that survives the province’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Bonded warehouse activity is a narrowly defined storage operation inside the customs territory that receives special treatment as though it were outside that territory. In practical terms, the activity is the operation of places that store physical commodities within a bonded area. The point is the warehouse function itself: holding tangible goods in a specially treated customs setting. That definition gives the code its centre of gravity, rooted in the status of the storage area and the physical commodities kept there.

Registration is open across the full listed business-scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. This matters because the activity is not confined in the record to one end of the enterprise spectrum. A micro operator and a large operator appear within the same availability frame, provided each is registering this bonded-warehouse activity. The scale list establishes who may register the activity at each listed scale, while the operating scope remains the storage of physical commodities in a bonded area.

Nationally, the PMA position is TERBUKA: foreign investment is open, and the maximum foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In Bali, the reading requires more precision. The record does not mark PMA registration as blocked; it describes the Bali status as open on the higher-risk track. The provincial moratorium is permanent and island-wide for PMA entries falling into Low and Medium-Low risk. Yet the record places the Besar scale at Menengah Tinggi and states that it survives that moratorium. On that stated basis, a PT PMA may register this activity in Bali.

The result is neither a blanket Bali prohibition nor an assumption that national openness alone answers the provincial question. The national position is fully open to foreign ownership; the Bali outcome is likewise registrable because the activity’s recorded risk position is not within the moratorium’s blocked bands. The activity remains what its scope says it is—operation of physical-commodity storage in a bonded area—so both the ownership position and the Bali conclusion should stay tied to that exact activity.
editorial.pullQuote: The national position is fully open to foreign ownership; the Bali outcome is likewise registrable because the activity’s recorded risk position is not within the moratorium’s blocked bands.

editorial.headline: Energy Storage, With Bali’s Risk Line in View
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, and Bali does not block its PMA registration under the stated moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the storage infrastructure behind petroleum and natural gas: receiving, collecting, holding and releasing petroleum, petroleum fuels, gas fuels and/or processed products. The storage location may be above ground, below ground or on the water’s surface. The scope is specific about those storage functions, and extends to operations in free-trade zones, physical commodity storage sites, storage run through a warehouse-receipt system, and cold warehouses used for oil and natural-gas storage.

The brief also reaches beyond conventional hydrocarbons. It includes carbon-free fuels used as energy carriers—hydrogen, ammonia and other compounds—stored in geological formations, through gas compression, in solid or liquid form, or in other forms. In other words, the classification follows the practical cycle of receipt, accumulation, containment and release across a broad range of energy-storage formats. For this activity, however, the record states that the OSS risk at large scale is Medium-High/High, so it is not blocked by that moratorium.

That distinction is the essential one. The national position permits full foreign ownership, while the Bali position does not introduce a separate foreign-ownership figure or partnership condition in the record. Its status is recorded as “OK_or_HIGHER_RISK,” reflecting the stated large-scale risk position. editorial.headline: Hazardous-Goods Storage: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this specialised storage activity is unavailable for PMA registration at a Bali address under the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 52105 covers the storage of hazardous and toxic goods: inventory that requires a storage place suited to the material’s particular properties and characteristics. Its scope extends to cold warehouses for hazardous and toxic goods, storage in free-trade zones, warehouse-receipt-system storage, and places holding physical hazardous and toxic commodities. The central fact is not simply that goods are being kept somewhere, but that their hazardous and toxic nature determines the kind of storage operation being run.

This is consequently a category for operators of the relevant warehouse or storage facility. It is open at every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That gives the activity a wide national scale range, while keeping its purpose specific. A company using this code is registering the operation of specialised storage for hazardous and toxic goods, not a broad commercial description detached from the facility and the goods it is designed to hold.

At national level, the position is straightforward. The activity is TERBUKA, and foreign ownership is permitted up to 100%. In national terms, full foreign ownership is available. Bali, however, changes the practical answer completely for a PMA applicant. KBLI 52105 cannot be registered by PMA at a Bali address today. The Bali status is a moratorium closure, and the stated reason places the Besar scale in the Medium-Low risk band. Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration.

The distinction is important because it is not a reduced Bali foreign-ownership percentage. The national ceiling remains 100%; the Bali rule closes the PMA registration route for this activity at a Bali address. The moratorium is island-wide and permanent. For a founder assessing this code, the honest conclusion is therefore two-layered: nationally, a foreign-owned company may hold the activity in full; in Bali, PMA registration for the same activity is barred under the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, full foreign ownership is available; in Bali, PMA registration for the same activity is barred under the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Ionising-Radiation Storage Is Open—Nationally and in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A specialist storage activity that is fully open to foreign ownership nationally and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Storage is the core of this activity, but the scope is deliberately specific: it concerns ionising-radiation sources—radioactive substances and ionising-radiation generators. It covers facilities that store those sources, including operations run through a warehouse-receipt system, refrigerated warehousing, storage in a free-trade zone, and the storage of physical commodities comprising those sources. These are not loose examples around a general warehouse description; each sits within the same specialist storage activity. Together, they define a facility category centred on holding ionising-radiation sources in clearly identified operating settings.

The classification is open to Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises. That range matters because it places the same stated activity across small, medium and large business scales, rather than reserving it in the record to one end of the market. A founder should read the scale field as a direct statement of who may enter this activity: businesses operating at any of the three listed scales. The commercial form may vary by scale, but the defining subject remains the operation of storage for ionising-radiation sources.

At the national level, PMA status remains TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. For a foreign investor, that is a clear national position: full foreign ownership is open for this activity. The distinction matters because national openness can still be tested by a separate Bali assessment. Here, the national position is not merely a broad signal; it is the starting point for a Bali reading that remains consistent with it.

Bali does not alter that conclusion. The Bali assessment is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the activity is not flagged as blocked. At the Besar scale, OSS records its risk as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium applies to Low and Medium-Low risk activities; this activity is explicitly not blocked by it. That is the decisive island-level fact. The national opening carries through to Bali because the activity is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium. A foreign investor can therefore read the record without a concealed Bali contradiction: it is open nationally at a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling and remains unblocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The national opening carries through to Bali because the activity is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Radioactive By-Mineral Storage: Nationally Open, Carefully Defined in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers specialised storage of naturally occurring radioactive materials and radioactive by-minerals, open nationally to foreign investment across small, medium and large business scales.
editorial.body:
KBLI 52107 covers the storage of naturally occurring radioactive material (NORM) and radioactive by-minerals arising from activities such as oil and gas processing and the handling of phosphate, tin, zircon and comparable materials. Its focus is storage: the custodial infrastructure required for these materials, rather than their extraction or processing. The scope includes warehouse-receipt operations, cold-storage warehousing, storage in free-trade zones, and facilities used to store physical commodities of radioactive by-minerals. It does not extend to facilities for storing ionising radiation sources.

The activity is open to businesses at the **Kecil**, **Menengah**, and **Besar** scales. That breadth matters because the code is not confined to a single warehouse format or commercial setting. It accommodates conventional storage arrangements as well as warehouse-receipt systems, refrigerated facilities, free-trade-zone operations, and locations holding physical commodity stocks. In each case, the defining subject remains radioactive by-minerals or NORM originating in the stated industrial and mining-related streams.

At the national level, the PMA position is straightforward: the activity is **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. Foreign investment is therefore permitted nationally up to full ownership. The applicable national basis recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. This is an openness finding for the activity itself; it should not be mistaken for a description of operating requirements beyond the storage scope recorded here.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for activity codes assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk, island-wide. For this activity, however, the recorded Bali assessment is that OSS risk at the **Besar** scale is Medium-High or High, meaning it is not blocked by that moratorium. The practical picture is consequently clear: KBLI 52107 remains available for PMA registration in Bali under the recorded risk treatment, while its large-scale classification carries the Medium-High/High risk character stated in the Bali record.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers running general warehouses, silos, tank farms, and container depots—basically any non-specialized storage facility where goods are held before delivery. editorial.headline: Warehousing Beyond the Standard Categories
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans general warehousing, container depots and selected storage services—nationally open to full foreign ownership, with a scope-sensitive PMA route in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 52109 covers the practical infrastructure of holding goods before they reach their final destination. It includes the management or operation of enclosed warehouses, silos and tanks, alongside other storage facilities. The scope also reaches container depots that store or stack containers and may offer additional facilities; warehousing used for electronic-trade activities; tanks for liquid and gaseous products such as water and liquefied gas; and physical-commodity storage not classified elsewhere. In other words, it is a broad operational category for storage activity, provided the proposed business fits one of those stated functions.

The code is open to businesses at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That breadth matters because the activity is defined by what the facility does—holding goods, containers or specified products before onward movement—rather than by one fixed building type. The registered activity should therefore be described with care: the applicable scope is not decorative wording, but the detail that determines how the business is understood in the OSS process.

Nationally, the position is clear. The activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. A foreign investor can therefore hold the full permitted stake nationally, subject to the activity falling within this code’s stated scope. The national basis recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali requires a more exact reading. This is not recorded as an outright PMA block, but as Blocked (scope-dependent): the result depends on the declared scope and its OSS risk treatment. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. For this code, some Besar-scale scopes are assessed as low risk, while others carry a higher risk. PMA registration in Bali is possible only where the business declares the higher-risk scope; the exact activity must be checked live in OSS. The sensible conclusion is neither blanket permission nor blanket refusal: the national 100% ceiling remains the national position, while Bali registration turns on the precise scope selected and its current OSS classification.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% ceiling remains the national position, while Bali registration turns on the precise scope selected and its current OSS classification.

editorial.headline: Land Terminal Operations: Open Nationally, Bali Position Blocked Pending Verification
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the running of land terminals; nationally foreign ownership is open, but no verified OSS licensing rows exist for this code, so the Bali position is blocked pending case-by-case verification.
editorial.body:
This code's Bali registration path is blocked pending verification — no reliable OSS licensing rows are currently on file for it — even though its national foreign-investment setting is open. It covers the operation of land terminals: parking services for transport vehicles, departure scheduling for public transport, and passenger boarding and alighting services. The focus is the terminal as an operating place, where vehicle movements, passenger access and departure timing are organised. In practical terms, it is the work that keeps a land terminal functioning for both vehicles and passengers.

At the national level, foreign investment is permitted in this activity, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. No verified OSS licensing-scale rows are currently on file for this code, so which scales it opens to is undetermined pending verification. Independently of that gap, the official scope reads narrowly: the code is a fit for an operator whose actual business is the operation of a land terminal and the services integral to that operation, rather than a loose description for any transport-related venture. The national position is recorded under Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021; at that level, foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership.

Bali's position for this code cannot currently be stated. The catalogue holds no verified licensing rows for it — the scale data once shown here belonged to a different licensing regime entirely (a port cargo-tally agent block, not land-terminal operations) and has since been set aside — so its Bali risk tier is unknown and the code is treated as blocked until verified case by case. A nationally open foreign-ownership setting does not by itself establish a Bali registration route; what is missing is verification of this specific code's own licensing rows, not the national ownership ceiling. The record also notes Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, cited to a Governor’s letter — whether that moratorium reaches this code depends on a risk tier this record does not yet have.

The distinction is consequential. The national figure is an ownership ceiling, not a guarantee that every province offers a usable PMA registration path. For a founder assessing a Bali setup, the honest answer is that this code is blocked pending verification, not settled closed — confirm the current position case by case with Bali Zero before proceeding. The activity itself remains clearly defined by terminal operation; no verified scale data is currently on file for it.

editorial.headline: Railway Infrastructure Operations: Open Nationally and Unblocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This railway-infrastructure activity spans the systems that keep rail networks moving, and it remains open to PMA nationally and unblocked by Bali’s moratorium.
editorial.body:
Railway infrastructure is the physical operating system of a rail network, and this activity concerns its provision and operation. The recorded scope embraces railway lines and stations, as well as the supporting facilities that make them work: signalling, telecommunications and electrical systems. It is therefore concerned not merely with a single asset but with the infrastructure environment through which rail movements are organised. The scope expressly includes switching and shunting, the practical movements that position rail vehicles within that environment. It also records public railway-infrastructure development and the provision of public railway infrastructure.

The registration field is directed at medium and large enterprises. That framing suits the character of the activity: the record is about providing and operating infrastructure rather than a narrow, isolated service. It covers interconnected assets—track, stations, signals, telecommunications and electricity—together with movement-management work such as switching and shunting. For a founder, the important reading is to keep the business description anchored to this infrastructure-and-operations remit, including its public-infrastructure elements.

**National position.** The activity is recorded as open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. A PMA company may therefore be wholly foreign-owned within the national classification recorded here. The stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is a clear ownership position, to be read alongside the defined activity scope and the medium and large enterprise scales to which the record opens it.

**Bali position.** Bali is also not a blocked PMA case on this record. The province’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registrations for activities rated Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity does not fall into that blocked position: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, and the record states that it is not blocked by the moratorium. The clean conclusion is that a foreigner can register this activity in Bali today under the recorded Bali treatment, while the national foreign-ownership ceiling remains 100%.

A foreign investor cannot register this toll-road activity as PMA in Bali today, despite a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. KBLI 52213 concerns the business of organizing and operating toll roads or toll bridges, including the traffic services through which vehicles use them. That includes running the undertaking itself and serving vehicle traffic in either road or bridge form. Its boundary is deliberately operational: construction and maintenance of a toll road or bridge are outside this activity.

At the national level, the activity is TERBUKA to PMA. The record opens it at the Besar scale only, giving the classification a clear commercial frame without stretching it beyond the evidence. The 100% ceiling means foreign ownership may reach full ownership nationally, under the cited Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. In classification terms, the registrant is the enterprise that organizes and operates the toll-road or toll-bridge business and its vehicle-traffic service; construction or maintenance does not become part of the activity. The scale requirement also matters because Besar is the only scale listed as open.

Bali produces the more consequential reading. For this activity at Besar scale, the OSS risk assessment is Low or Medium-Low across every scope in the record. Bali’s moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities throughout the province, permanently. The present classification is therefore Blocked (risk class): a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali. This is expressly island-wide rather than limited to a particular locality, and it is a bar on PMA registration arising from the moratorium referenced to May 2026.

The national and Bali positions are different rather than inconsistent. Nationally, the activity permits up to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, the risk-based provincial rule prevents its PMA registration. The reading begins with the actual scope—operations and vehicle traffic service—and ends with the location-specific outcome. A national opening is not, in this case, a route to PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: On-Street Parking: Nationally Open, Including in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 52214 covers the operation of parking on the roadway itself, open to every business scale and to full foreign ownership nationally.
editorial.body:
On-street parking is a specific urban service: the organisation of parking conducted on the roadway itself. KBLI 52214 is therefore about managing the use of street space for vehicles, rather than treating parking as an abstract add-on to another activity. Its focus is clear and bounded—parking that takes place on the road body.

The activity is available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That breadth matters because it lets the same defined activity be registered across the full range of business sizes recognised in the record. The national position is equally direct: it is TERBUKA for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the record places no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity.

Bali does not reverse that national openness. A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today; it is not blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium. The moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA across the island, permanently, but this activity is recorded as outside that block. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—which is why the moratorium does not prevent its registration.

That distinction is the essential reading of the code. National openness is real, and Bali remains available rather than merely theoretically possible. The Bali position does not introduce a separate foreign-ownership percentage or partnership condition in this record. Instead, it turns on the stated risk treatment at the Besar scale: the activity sits beyond the category captured by the island-wide moratorium. For a founder considering an on-street parking operation, the regulatory picture presented here is therefore unusually plain: full foreign ownership is permitted nationally, and Bali does not block PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: Full foreign ownership is permitted nationally, and Bali does not block PMA registration for this activity.

Off-street parking is a practical urban service with a defined setting: parking provided away from the roadway itself. This activity covers the operation of parking buildings, parking areas within office buildings, shopping centres and hospitals, as well as other off-street parking services. The focus is the managed parking facility—the place where vehicles are accommodated outside the road corridor.

Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all included among the activity's listed business scales. That breadth matters because the code describes an operating activity rather than a particular type of premises. A parking service may be organised within a dedicated structure or as part of a larger built environment, provided that the service remains off street and falls within the stated scope.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. This means the national record permits full foreign ownership for this activity. That is the operative national position, supported by the PMA source recorded for the code.

Bali does not reverse that position. Its status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and it is not blocked for PMA registration under the province-wide moratorium described in the record. The reason is specific: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so the activity is outside the moratorium’s block on Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. For an off-street parking operator considering Bali, the point is not a hidden local prohibition but a clear risk-based distinction: this activity is not blocked by the stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: Land Transport Support Services: Open Nationally, Address-Checked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A national PMA opening applies to towing, transport gas liquefaction, toll collection and truck-cargo surveys, but Bali’s record calls for an address-by-address check.
editorial.body:
KBLI 52219 deals with the service work that sits around land transport rather than the transport movement itself. Its stated scope is practical and specific: towing assistance; gas liquefaction for transport purposes; operation of toll-collection facilities; and surveying of truck cargo. It is a residual grouping for land-transport services not classified elsewhere, which gives it a clear operational character. The point is not a broad transport label, but the defined supporting activities that make a road-based movement possible, measurable, or recoverable when something goes wrong.

Registration is available across the full scale range in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In plain terms, the classification is not confined to a single enterprise size. What anchors the activity is the service being delivered. An operator using it should be able to recognise its own work in one of the stated functions—towing, gas liquefaction for transport, toll-collection facilities, or truck-cargo surveys—rather than relying only on the broad phrase “related to land transport.” The scope itself supplies the useful perimeter: a defined set of supporting services, not an undifferentiated transport category.

Nationally, the PMA position is TERBUKA and the recorded maximum foreign ownership is 100%. On those terms, a PMA structure may be fully foreign-owned for this activity at the national level. The listed source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower foreign-ownership ceiling in the record: the national position is a full 100% ceiling, stated plainly rather than implied through a general openness label.

Bali needs a separate reading, but the record does not call this activity blocked. It places the activity at medium-high risk and says it is not caught by the moratorium, while asking that the position be verified for the specific address. The provincial moratorium is described as permanent and island-wide for PMA activities at Low and Medium-Low risk. Accordingly, foreign PMA registration for this activity is not barred by that moratorium in Bali. A national 100% ceiling is real, but in Bali the proposed address still needs checking. The record supplies no separate Bali foreign-ownership percentage; its Bali qualification is the risk-based, address-specific one.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% ceiling is real, but in Bali the proposed address still needs checking.

editorial.headline: Sea-Port Services: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Sea-port services are nationally open to PMA up to 100%, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity today.
editorial.body:
Today, a foreign investor cannot register this sea-port service activity in Bali. That is the operative local conclusion even though activity 52221 is nationally classified as open to PMA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The Bali record marks it blocked by risk class: at the Besar scale, every stated scope is assessed in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk. Those risk levels trigger Bali’s moratorium, recorded as an island-wide, permanent block on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. The moratorium date given is May 13, 2026.

At its core, this activity concerns the service infrastructure that makes maritime port movement function. Its stated scope reaches port services connected with water transport for passengers, animals, and goods. That includes operating terminal facilities such as ports and wharves, as well as marine navigation operations. It also encompasses port-based handling arrangements around vessel movement: navigation services, berthing activity, mooring, pilotage, and towing. The scope further covers dangerous-goods storage when it forms part of sea-port services, alongside the inspection of cargo and containers using ionising-radiation sources.

The classification is open across the full stated business-scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth matters because the activity is not described as a narrow terminal-only function. It is a port-service field spanning facilities, navigation, vessel arrival and departure support, and specified cargo-control operations. Still, the Bali result turns on the record’s risk assessment at the Besar scale, where every listed scope is Low or Medium-Low risk in OSS. The practical issue is therefore not whether the activity has a nationally open PMA status, but how Bali applies its local moratorium to that recorded risk position.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, under the stated PMA source. In Bali, however, that national opening does not produce a registrable PMA route for this activity today. The local rule recorded here blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities, and this activity falls within that block at the stated scale. For founders, the distinction should be held plainly: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remain part of the record, while Bali’s current, permanent moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity on the island.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remain part of the record, while Bali’s current, permanent moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity on the island.

editorial.headline: Inland Port Operations, and Bali’s Clearer PMA Line
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the working infrastructure of inland-water ports—and remains nationally open to full foreign ownership, without a Bali PMA moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Indonesia’s inland-water transport network depends on more than vessels. This activity covers the operation of ports serving rivers, canals, lakes, swamps and other inland waters in connection with passenger, animal or goods transport. Nationally, it is open to foreign investment with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, the record does not mark the activity as blocked for PMA registration under the province-wide moratorium.

The practical subject here is port operation: running terminal facilities such as ports and docks; operating river and lake navigation; and providing the services that make a vessel’s arrival, movement and departure work in practice. That includes sailing and berthing activities, mooring, pilotage and towing. The scope also includes inspecting cargo in freight and/or containers using ionising-radiation sources. It is therefore an operational category for the inland-water port environment itself, rather than a catch-all description for every service that may occur around a waterfront.

It is available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the Bali reading turns on the risk signal recorded at the Besar scale: OSS classifies it as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. Since this activity carries the higher risk classification at that scale, the record identifies it as not blocked by that moratorium.

The national and Bali positions should be read together, not as competing answers. At national level, foreign ownership may reach 100% under the cited PMA basis. In Bali, the relevant question is not whether foreign ownership is nationally available, but whether the activity falls within the province’s blocked risk bands. On this record, it does not. For an operator considering an inland-water port business, that produces a straightforward conclusion: full foreign ownership is nationally available, and Bali’s PMA moratorium does not itself bar registration of this activity today.
editorial.pullQuote: Full foreign ownership is nationally available, and Bali’s PMA moratorium does not itself bar registration of this activity today.

editorial.headline: The Operational Spine of Indonesia’s Ferry Ports
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the working infrastructure of ferry and coastal ports—from terminals and navigation to berthing, pilotage and towing—open nationally to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
Ferry and coastal ports are more than arrival points. This activity covers the operation of crossing or coastal ports connected with water transport for passengers, animals and goods: the practical systems that let vessels arrive, berth, move safely and depart. It includes terminal facilities such as ports and jetties, ferry-navigation operations, shipping services and berthing activity, alongside mooring, pilotage and towing services. It also includes inspecting cargo and/or containers using ionising-radiation sources, whether radioactive substances or ionising-radiation generators.

The boundary matters. The activity is about running the port-side service environment, not simply the movement of freight through it. Cargo loading and unloading sit outside this scope, as do marina jetties intended for tourism or recreation. What remains is a substantial operational category: the facilities, navigation and vessel-support functions that make ferry and coastal water transport work as an organised service.

Registration is open across every listed enterprise scale: **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah** and **Besar**. Nationally, its PMA status is **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. In plain terms, the record places no foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity at the national level. That openness is especially significant for an operation whose scope can combine infrastructure, vessel movement and specialised port services within one defined activity.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. For this activity, the record states that at the **Besar** scale the OSS risk level is Medium-High/High, so it is not blocked by that moratorium. The Bali status is therefore **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**: foreign investors can register this activity in Bali, while recognising that the record identifies a higher risk classification at the large-enterprise scale. The honest reading is neither an automatic Bali exclusion nor a made-up local restriction; it is a nationally open activity that remains available for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: The Working Port Behind the Fishing Fleet
editorial.standfirst: Fishing-port operations are open to foreign investment nationwide and remain outside Bali’s PMA moratorium, despite higher risk at large scale.
editorial.body:
Fishing-port activity is the operational backbone where fisheries water transport meets shore. It covers providing port services to fishing vessels: operating fishing-port facilities and wharves, arranging berthing and anchorage, pilotage, and unloading fish. The defined scope also includes inspecting cargo in holds and/or containers with ionising-radiation sources. This is a port-service activity tied specifically to fishing vessels and fisheries transport, rather than a broad label for every waterfront operation.

The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale. Its scope is defined by the service being provided: operating fishing-port facilities or wharves, serving the arrival and departure of fishing vessels, or handling the unloading of fish. It does not extend to general cargo loading and unloading, nor to marina-pier operations for tourism or recreation. The distinction matters because the code is built around the working requirements of a fishing port: vessels, berths, pilotage, port infrastructure, and fish landing services.

Nationally, the investment position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. There is therefore no national foreign-share cap below full ownership in the record. The stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned enterprise considering this activity, the national position is not conditional in the data provided: the activity is open, across the stated business scales, and may be wholly foreign-owned.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the activity is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium. At Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; the record expressly notes that this leaves it outside the moratorium’s block. So a foreigner may register this activity in Bali today: its national openness does not disappear at the provincial level. The important qualification is one of risk classification at the large scale, not a Bali-specific foreign-ownership restriction or partnership condition.
editorial.pullQuote: So a foreigner may register this activity in Bali today: its national openness does not disappear at the provincial level.

editorial.headline: The Technical Work Behind a Managed Ship
editorial.standfirst: A ship-management activity spanning upkeep, docking preparation, crewing and maritime administration, open nationally to full foreign ownership and unblocked by Bali’s stated moratorium.
editorial.body:
Ship management is not simply the administrative afterlife of a vessel. This activity covers technical ship-management services: maintenance; preparing a ship for docking; arranging spare parts and provisions; crewing; and handling insurance and marine-certification administration. Together, those duties describe a practical operating function—keeping the technical and documentary sides of a vessel’s management in order. The breadth matters. The scope is defined by work around the ship itself, from physical upkeep and docking preparation to the arrangements that support its crew, supplies, insurance and maritime certification.

It is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That is useful not because it turns technical management into a generic business, but because it makes clear that the classification is available across the stated scale range. A registrant should therefore be offering the listed management services, rather than treating the category as a catch-all description for any maritime venture. The detail in the scope points to a service business organised around maintenance, docking preparation, spares, provisions, crewing, insurance administration and maritime-certification administration.

Nationally, the PMA status is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain terms, foreign participation is permitted nationally up to full ownership under the record’s national PMA position. That clarity should not be confused with a claim about operations beyond the stated services: the national reading applies to this particular technical ship-management activity and to the scale options recorded for it. The relevant point for a foreign-owned business is direct: nationally, the activity is open, with a ceiling of 100% foreign ownership.

Bali requires a separate reading, but not a pessimistic one. This activity is not blocked for PMA registration there by the provincial moratorium. The record identifies the reason: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, rather than a Low or Medium-Low category. The moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali on a permanent, island-wide basis; this activity falls outside that stated block. Bali’s status is therefore OK or Higher Risk: it remains unblocked under the moratorium, while the recorded risk observation at the Besar scale explains why. That is the honest local position—open nationally and not barred in Bali by this moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the activity is open to full foreign ownership, and Bali does not block it under the stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: When a Maritime Emergency Becomes a Business Activity
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 52226 covers the specialist work of finding, rescuing and recovering vessels or cargo in danger on Indonesian waters.
editorial.body:
KBLI 52226 is the classification for maritime salvage in its most practical and demanding form: searching for, rescuing, diving on, moving or lifting a vessel and its cargo after an accident or while it remains in danger at sea. Its scope reaches beyond ordinary wreck recovery. It also includes work involving vessels or cargo with cultural-heritage status, suspected cultural-heritage status, and objects outside that category. The defining thread is the emergency or distressed condition of the vessel or load, and the specialised intervention required to recover it.

This is an activity for operators equipped to work where marine risk, technical recovery and the physical handling of a compromised vessel meet. For businesses at every stated scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—registration is open. That breadth matters because salvage is not framed here as the preserve of one size of enterprise; the classification accommodates businesses from the smallest scale through large operators, provided their actual activity falls within the stated recovery scope.

Nationally, the position is clear. The activity is **TERBUKA** for PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of **100%** under the cited national source. In plain terms, foreign investment may hold the full permitted stake nationally. The record does not turn that national openness into a vague promise: it states both the PMA status and the ownership maximum, allowing the foreign-investment position to be read directly rather than inferred from the nature of the work.

Bali requires a more exact reading, but not a contradictory one. This activity is not blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium identified in the record, which applies to all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, placing this activity outside that moratorium's blocked risk bands. Its Bali status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: not a blanket prohibition, but a classification whose operating context carries medium-high or high risk at the large scale. For a founder, the honest conclusion is straightforward: national PMA openness remains meaningful in Bali because this activity is not blocked by that moratorium; the relevant Bali distinction is its risk profile at scale, not an invented foreign-ownership restriction.
editorial.pullQuote: National PMA openness remains meaningful in Bali because this activity is not blocked by the province-wide moratorium.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This KBLI covers the operation of small vessels (tenders, crew boats, or launches) that shuttle passengers, crew, or goods between docks, ships, and offshore structures within a port area—essentially the ‘last mile’ harbor transport that connects undeveloped jetties to larger vessels or installations.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Foreign ownership (PMA) is permitted up to 100% nationally, and this activity is not blocked under the current Bali moratorium. editorial.headline: Port Water Transport: The Link Between Quay and Ship
editorial.standfirst: This port-water transport activity connects passengers and cargo between quays, vessels and offshore installations, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
Port water transport is the connective work of a harbour: moving passengers or cargo by sea or along the coast where port facilities are not yet fully complete. It uses rede transport to bridge the practical gaps between quay and ship, from a main vessel to another vessel in port waters, or between a quay or vessel and a building or installation at sea. The activity explicitly includes domestic port-water transport for both passengers and goods. Its subject is therefore not open-sea shipping in the abstract, but the short, essential movements that make a working port function.

The activity is open to businesses at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That range reflects the character of the work itself, which can serve passengers or cargo while connecting the physical points through which port activity takes place. The defining question is not simply whether water moves through a harbour, but how it connects the quay, vessel and installation.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In other words, the national record does not place a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That clarity matters because the operating scope is precise: it is the transfer function within port waters and between port-side or vessel-side points, for passengers as well as goods.

Bali requires its own reading, but the outcome is not a PMA block. The provincial moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. This activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK in Bali, and the record explains that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. It is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. For a foreign investor considering this activity in Bali, the honest picture is that national foreign ownership can reach 100%, while the Bali record places the activity outside the province-wide PMA prohibition because of its stated risk position at the large scale.
