intel_2026.whatItMeans: Two-Star Hotels — commercial accommodation businesses that rent out furnished rooms or suites on a short-term basis. This classification covers entire or partial buildings equipped with dedicated front desk customer service, daily housekeeping, and food/beverage services. It strictly applies to standardized hotel operations and excludes standard residential villas or unclassified homestays.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
PP28 data inherited from KBLI 2020 code 55110 (star hotels, precursor to today's tiered star-hotel codes). Three distinct licensing tiers exist: **Tier 1 — Kecil/Menengah/Besar**: Medium-Low risk (Menengah Rendah). NIB + Standard Certificate issued **automatically** (Otomatis). Self-Assessment document covering Hotel Star standards (Sarana, Organisasi, SDM, Pelayanan, Produk, Manajemen). Health Feasibility Certificate required. Authority: Bupati/Walikota. **Tier 2 — Kecil/Menengah/Besar**: Medium-High risk (Menengah Tinggi). NIB + Standard Certificate within **14 days**. Self-Assessment required. Must obtain LSPr-certified Tourism Business Standard. Health Feasibility Certificate. TKA documentation required if employing foreign workers. Authority: Gubernur. **Tier 3 — Mikro/Kecil**: Medium-High risk (Menengah Tinggi). NIB + Standard Certificate within **14 days**. Same LSPr certification and Health Certificate requirements. Authority: Gubernur. **Important:** Even Mikro-scale hotels carry Medium-High risk under Tier 3 — there is NO low-risk path for any hotel operation regardless of size. **Post-issuance obligations across all tiers:**
- Obtain a Health Feasibility Certificate (Sertifikat Laik Sehat)
- Obtain an Alcohol Direct Sales Certificate (SKPL A, B, or C) if serving alcohol
- Submit Self-Assessment Document (Dokumen Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar usaha Hotel Bintang) **PMA Status:** Fully open (Terbuka) — 100% foreign ownership. **Source Regulation:** PP 28/2025, Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Renumbered from KBLI 2020. Your OSS registration may need updating to the new code. This code has been renumbered and split from the older KBLI 2020 code 55110 (Hotel Bintang) to specifically isolate two-star hotel classifications.
intel_2026.baliContext: Two-star hotels in Bali frequently take the shape of premium surf camps, digital nomad lodges, or boutique budget stays in hotspots like Batu Bolong, Padang Padang, and central Ubud. Setting up a formal hotel requires robust zoning compliance; your land must be located in a commercial or tourism zone (Kawasan Pariwisata). Unlike a simple villa, a two-star hotel involves 24/7 operational overheads, staff facilities, and heavy scrutiny over commercial building permits (PBG). Expect construction costs for a typical 20-room lodge in a secondary location to start around IDR 5-8 billion, plus a hefty land lease (Hak Sewa) running IDR 15-25 million per are per year. Navigating local banjar relations is essential if you plan to secure an alcohol permit (SKPL) for your pool bar.

editorial.headline: Two-Star Hotels: Nationally Open, Bali Depends on the Declared Scope
editorial.standfirst: For two-star hotel stays, nationwide foreign ownership may reach 100%; in Bali, PMA registration rests on the exact scope and its live OSS risk treatment.
editorial.body:
KBLI 55104 is the operating category for two-star hotels that provide short-stay accommodation, usually by the day or week, using part or all of a building. It concerns a stay of limited duration. The accommodation can include furnishings in living areas and suites. The scope also permits a broader service layer: daily cleaning and bed-making, food and beverage service, laundry, and conference or convention facilities may be provided. Direct, on-site customer service is identified as the characteristic way the activity is generally delivered. The record expressly covers both buildings of up to 6,000 square metres and buildings above that area. Whether the whole building or only part is used, the short-stay hotel activity remains within the stated scope.

The registration field is open to Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. All three appear in the record as permitted scales for this activity. The scope can therefore be read alongside a registration opening that reaches small, medium and large scales. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. That is the national ownership position recorded for the activity, and the record attributes it to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It is an unambiguous national position for a foreign-owned project. The Bali layer is different: the provincial rule permanently blocks PMA registration across the island for all KBLI activities assessed as low or medium-low risk.

In Bali, however, the record does not treat this activity as an unconditional block. Its status is scope-dependent, and at Besar scale the OSS risk is low for some scope declarations and higher for others. PMA registration is possible only when the higher-risk scope is declared, with live OSS verification required for the precise activity. This is the central practical distinction: the national 100% ceiling does not automatically produce a registrable PMA outcome in Bali; a low- or medium-low-risk declaration remains inside the island-wide block. Nor does the Bali record state a universally closed result, because a higher-risk scope may be registrable. The exact scope declaration and its live OSS risk treatment therefore determine the Bali answer. Live verification is expressly tied to the exact activity, not a broad category.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% ceiling does not automatically produce a registrable PMA outcome in Bali.

data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan penyediaan akomodasi yang biasanya berbasis harian atau mingguan, untuk tinggal dalam jangka waktu yang singkat, memenuhi ketentuan sebagai hotel bintang satu, serta menggunakan sebagian atau seluruh bangunan.
Kelompok ini mencakup penyediaan akomodasi yang dilengkapi dengan perabot di ruang tamu dan suite. Berbagai layanan tambahan dapat disediakan seperti pembersihan dan merapikan tempat tidur harian, layanan makanan dan minuman, layanan binatu, serta fasilitas konferensi dan konvensi. Aktivitas di kelompok ini secara umum ditandai dengan penyediaan layanan pelanggan/customer service secara langsung di tempat.

persyaratan: Dokumen penilaian mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar

Dokumen Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar
Silakan kirim semua dokumen yang diminta dalam satu file.
1. Unduh dan lengkapi formulir Penilaian Mandiri.
2. Dokumentasi Standar Pelaksanaan Kegiatan Usaha.
Lampirkan 6 dokumen Sarana
  1. Petunjuk identitas/nama usaha dengan tulisan yang terbaca.
  2. Ruang kantor/area administrasi yang dilengkapi peralatan dan perlengkapan kerja.
  3. Peralatan Pertolongan Pertama pada Kecalakaan (P3K) dan Alat Pemadam Api Ringan (APAR) yang berfungsi dengan baik.
  4. Ketersediaan air bersih yang tidak berwarna, tidak berbau, tidak berasa, dan jernih.
  5. Ketersediaan gudang atau tempat penyimpanan barang yang aman.
  6. Status kepemilikan kantor/tempat usaha yang jelas.
Lampirkan 1 dokumen Sumber Daya Manusia
Perlindungan asuransi kesehatan dan/atau kecelakaan bagi karyawan tersedia dan berlaku.
Lampirkan 1 dokumen Ketentuan Produksi
Pelayanan kesehatan, seperti informasi tentang dokter, rumah sakit, atau klinik terdekat terdokumentasi.
Lampirkan 3 dokumen Sistem Manajemen Usaha
  1. Struktur organisasi dan uraian tugas setiap jabatan jalas dan terdokumentasi.
  2. rencana bisnis (business plan) masih berlaku dan terdokumentasi.
  3. S0P dan/atau petunjuk teknis pelaksanaan karja masih berlaku dan terdokumentasi.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: One-Star Hotels — budget accommodations providing short-term stays in basic furnished rooms. It includes daily bed-making, cleaning, minimal food and beverage options, and direct customer service. This is a step up from a simple homestay, operating as a fully structured commercial hospitality business under a formal star-rating.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Small, Medium, Large**: Ranges from Medium-Low (Menengah Rendah) processed automatically (Otomatis), to Medium-High (Menengah Tinggi) taking 14 days (14 Hari). No Micro scale tier exists for this code. **License Type:** NIB + Standard Certificate (Sertifikat Standar). **Post-issuance obligations:**
- Obtain a Health Feasibility Certificate (Sertifikat Laik Sehat)
- Submit a Self-Assessment Document for Hotel Standards (Dokumen Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar usaha Hotel Bintang)
- Obtain a Tourism Business Standard Certificate from an independent agency (Sertifikat Standar Usaha Pariwisata dari LSPr) for higher risks
- Obtain an Alcohol Direct Sales Certificate (Surat Keterangan Penjualan Langsung Minuman Beralkohol / SKPL A, B, C) if applicable **Authority:** Regent/Mayor (Bupati/Walikota) for Medium-Low; Governor (Gubernur) for Medium-High. **PMA Status:** Allocated to Koperasi and UMKM (Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II) — foreign ownership 0%, so a PT PMA cannot register this activity. **Source Regulation:** Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, PP 28/2025.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Renumbered from KBLI 2020. Your OSS registration may need updating to the new code. Renumbered from the KBLI 2020 code 55110 (Hotel Bintang) to create a specific track for one-star establishments in the 2025 system.
intel_2026.baliContext: In the Bali ecosystem, a one-star hotel is often the legal classification used for high-end backpacker hostels, upscale guesthouses, or 'kos-kosan elit' (elite boarding houses) that transition into daily tourist rentals. It is a highly profitable, high-turnover model in dense areas like Legian, Tuban, and central Denpasar. While cheaper to build than a 2-star property, it still requires formal LSPr (Tourism Certification Body) audits. A common trap for foreign investors is treating this like a small homestay; the OSS system views it as a formal commercial hotel, meaning your environmental documents (SPPL/UKL-UPL) and wastewater management (IPAL) will be strictly monitored by the local environmental agency (DLHK).
intel_2026.youllAlsoNeed:
- 55201 — Homestay/Pondok Wisata (an alternative if your scale is much smaller and you live on-site)
- 56304 — Beverage Shops (for a small coffee/juice stand in the lobby)
- 79901 — Tourism Information Services (if running a tour booking desk)
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Opening an upscale hostel or large guesthouse? KBLI 55105 covers formal one-star hotels, but don't underestimate the commercial wastewater and environmental compliance involved.

editorial.headline: A One-Star Hotel, With Bali’s Scope Test
editorial.standfirst: This short-stay hotel activity is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM, which sets foreign ownership at 0% nationwide — so the Bali scope-and-risk question that used to decide a PMA registration no longer arises.
editorial.body:
One-star hotels are a deceptively specific accommodation business. This activity covers short-stay accommodation, generally offered daily or weekly, that meets one-star hotel requirements and uses part or all of a building. It expressly includes buildings of up to 6,000 square metres and those above that size. Rooms and suites may be furnished, while the operating model remains recognisably hotel-led: direct customer service on site, with possible daily cleaning and bed-making, food and beverage service, laundry, and conference or convention facilities. The business is not simply providing a room; it is providing serviced, short-term hotel accommodation.

Registration is open to small, medium and large businesses. That range gives the activity room to operate at different scales without changing its essential identity: a one-star hotel serving short-stay guests directly. The two building-size bands reinforce the point. The scope is not confined to a single physical footprint, but it does remain tied to accommodation that qualifies as a one-star hotel.

Nationally, the position is closed to foreign ownership. The record allocates this bidang usaha to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 10/2021 as amended by 49/2021 (Lampiran II, the *dialokasikan* column), which sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 0%. A PT PMA cannot hold this activity anywhere in Indonesia, at any business scale.

Bali’s own assessment is more granular, and it is now moot for a foreign investor. The record does not categorically block PMA registration there: at the large-business scale some scopes carry low OSS risk and others higher, so a Bali route would have depended on the scope declared in OSS. But there is no national opening for that path to rest on: with the bidang usaha allocated to Koperasi and UMKM, no declared scope makes this activity available to a PT PMA.
editorial.pullQuote: There is no national ceiling to fall back on: the allocation to Koperasi and UMKM sets foreign ownership at 0%, so the Bali scope test no longer decides whether a PT PMA can register.

l4_bali.reason: Closed to new PMA licensing in Bali: the Bali Provincial Government closed OSS to foreign-owned companies for 18 business fields from the third week of May 2026, until further policy, with the approval of the Minister of Investment/BKPM (press release, 24 Jul 2026). This code descends from KBLI 2020 55110 (Hotel Bintang (<6.000 m²)) on that list (BPS KBLI 2020→2025 conversion table). The list limits it to buildings under 6,000 m².

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices
moratorium.virtual_office: requested in letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP; application not confirmed

l4_bali.rule: per-scala-Besar (OSS risk at scale Besar; PMA is Besar by law)

closure.approval: with the approval of the Minister of Investment/BKPM (persetujuan dari Menteri Investasi dan Hilirisasi/Kepala BKPM Republik Indonesia)

data.pma_kondisi: Bidang usaha dialokasikan untuk Koperasi dan UMKM (Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II) — foreign ownership 0%

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Non-star hotels — budget accommodation that meets hotel standards but hasn't been classified into the star system. Losmen, guesthouses operating as hotels, basic but commercial short-stay accommodation in a dedicated building. You run it commercially, it looks like a hotel, but it doesn't carry a star rating.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
Multiple licensing paths inherited from merged PP28 sources (KBLI 2020 codes 55199, 55110, and 55130):

**Micro + Small + Medium**: Medium-Low risk, NIB + Standard Certificate **automatically**. Health cert and periodic reports required.

**Small / Medium / Large**: Two tiers — automatic (Medium-Low with Self-Assessment + health cert) or 14-day (Medium-High with LSPr certification).

**PMA:** Closed — allocated to Koperasi and UMKM (Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II p.15, entry 48, sub-row "Hotel Melati", ex-KBLI 2020 55120); foreign ownership 0% nationwide. Bali also lists the non-star hotel among the 18 business fields it closed to new PMA licensing in 2026.
intel_2026.whatChanged: This code aggregated multiple KBLI 2020 categories: data merged from KBLI 2020 code 55199 (other accommodation), KBLI 2020 code 55110 (star hotels — for the non-star subset), and KBLI 2020 code 55130 (pondok wisata/tourist lodges). If you were using any of those old codes for a non-star hotel operation, you are now under 55106. That is a case of multiple old codes folded into one (aggregated mapping).
intel_2026.baliContext: Non-star hotels are everywhere in Bali — the backbone of budget tourism. Kuta's gang (alley) guesthouses, Ubud's family-run places, Amed's beachfront losmen. This code is for smaller operators who want hotel-level licensing without the investment of star classification — and, under Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II, for Indonesian cooperatives and MSMEs only: a foreign-owned company cannot register 55106, in Bali or anywhere else, and Bali also lists the non-star hotel (ex-Hotel Melati) among the 18 fields it closed to new PMA licensing in 2026. If you're running a 5-15 room place in a quieter area like Sidemen, Munduk, or Lovina, this is likely your code.
intel_2026.youllAlsoNeed:
- 56101 — If you serve food to guests
- 55201 — If the owner lives in the same building (might be homestay instead)
- 96230 — If you offer basic spa services
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Running a budget hotel or guesthouse in Bali? 55106 covers non-star hotels — a Koperasi-and-UMKM activity under Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II, so it is not a PT PMA code. Here is what the record says.

editorial.headline: Non-Star Hotels Are Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM — Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 55106 covers commercially managed non-star accommodation for daily or weekly stays; Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II allocates the Hotel Melati class to Indonesian cooperatives and MSMEs, so a foreign-owned company cannot register it anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
KBLI 55106 is the commercial provision of non-star hotel accommodation, ordinarily offered on a daily or weekly basis. It applies where an operator manages all or part of a building that meets the requirements for a non-star hotel. The scope expressly accommodates both building-area bands: premises above 6,000 m² and premises at or below 6,000 m². The point is not a particular style of hospitality, but commercially managed short-stay accommodation within that non-star hotel framework.

The activity is open to small, medium and large businesses. That matters because the code does not reserve the field for a single operating scale: a modest accommodation business and a larger hotel operation can each sit within the stated scope, provided the actual activity fits it.

The ownership position is set by Perpres 10/2021, as amended by Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran II (p.15, entry 48, sub-row "Hotel Melati", ex-KBLI 2020 55120): non-star hotel operation is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM. A foreign investor can be neither a cooperative nor a UMKM, so the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for non-star hotels is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this code anywhere in Indonesia.

Bali adds a second, independent closure: the provincial government lists the non-star hotel among the 18 business fields it closed to new foreign-owned licensing on OSS from May 2026. For a founder the conclusion is precise rather than scope-dependent: this is not a question to be resolved by the declared scope in OSS; the code is not available to a foreign-owned company at either level.
editorial.pullQuote: Non-star hotels belong to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 49/2021 Lampiran II — the PT PMA route is closed nationwide, and Bali closes it a second time.

editorial.headline: The Homestay Business Is Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM — Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: This is owner-occupied, short-stay accommodation built around daily contact between travellers and the household—but a nationwide Koperasi/UMKM allocation closes it to PMA.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the defining fact is plain: this homestay activity cannot be registered through a PT PMA anywhere in Indonesia. The closure comes from a specific national instrument, not a missing OSS business-scale row: Perpres 49/2021’s Lampiran II lists the *Pondok Wisata* sub-row — carrying the pre-2025 code KBLI 55130, now this activity’s 55201 — as *dialokasikan* (allocated) to Koperasi and UMKM. That allocation is what closes the bidang usaha to a PT PMA nationwide, not only in Bali.

The activity itself is more specific than generic holiday accommodation. It covers short-term lodging offered to the public, paid daily or weekly, by an individual using an owner-occupied residential house. Part of that home is made available for rent, and the arrangement gives travellers the opportunity to take part in everyday life alongside the homeowner. The commercial proposition, in other words, is not simply a room for the night: it is accommodation situated within a lived-in home and shaped by interaction with the household.

The registration scales recorded for this activity are **Mikro**, **Kecil** and **Menengah**. Those scale rows describe the activity’s licensing track, not its ownership eligibility, and they are not what closes this bidang usaha to a PT PMA. The closure comes from a more specific source: Perpres 49/2021’s Lampiran II allocates this bidang usaha to Koperasi/UMKM, and that allocation is national in scope — it closes the activity to PT PMA registration everywhere in Indonesia, not just in Bali.

Bali also has a separate, island-wide, permanent policy blocking PMA for all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI activities, but that provincial rule is not what governs this code. The record does not assign an ownership percentage or partnership condition to this homestay activity, so none should be inferred. The closure that matters here is the recorded one: Perpres 49/2021’s Lampiran II allocates this bidang usaha — via the *Pondok Wisata* sub-row for KBLI 55130 — to Koperasi/UMKM, a national annex entry that prevents a PT PMA from registering the activity anywhere in Indonesia. Founders should treat that nationwide allocation, not a Bali-only rule, as the operative barrier for a PMA setup.
editorial.pullQuote: A national foreign-ownership allowance is not, by itself, a promise of a usable registration path once a Perpres annex allocates the activity to Koperasi/UMKM.

editorial.headline: Youth Hostels: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This short-stay tourism accommodation is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali provides no PT PMA registration path.
editorial.body:
At its practical core, this activity is short-term accommodation for tourism. It covers rooms available for overnight stays, either shared with other guests or occupied individually. The stated purposes of that travel are recreation, broadening knowledge or experience, and the journey itself. The scope also expressly includes youth-lodging and youth-lodge activity. Read together, those elements describe an accommodation offer shaped by the way travellers stay: a guest can take a place in a shared room or stay alone, but the setting remains oriented to short-term tourism. The activity is therefore the provision of youth-hostel accommodation within that defined travel context.

The registration scales named for the activity are Micro, Small and Medium. This is a meaningful part of its regulatory identity, rather than an incidental business description. The Bali record turns precisely on the absence of another scale row in OSS, so the listed scales are central to the available registration picture. For operators, the category sits in an accommodation model serving overnight visitors while being framed at these stated business scales. No additional scale should be assumed beyond what the record identifies.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is unambiguous: it is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical ownership terms, the national rule permits the activity to be fully foreign-owned. That national position answers the ownership question, but it does not erase the separate Bali registration result recorded here. Keeping the two layers apart is essential. A national ceiling of 100% describes what foreign ownership may reach nationally; it is not, by itself, confirmation that a PT PMA can register the activity in Bali.

In Bali, a foreigner cannot register this activity through a PT PMA today. The block is provincial, not sectoral: Bali's island-wide moratorium suspends PMA registration for every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, and youth-hostel accommodation is classified Medium-Low risk. Nothing in the national ownership rules closes this activity to a foreign investor. The Bali status is therefore closed to PMA in the absence of a Large Business scale. Separately, the record identifies a permanent, island-wide provincial block on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The conclusion does not need embellishment: the national rule is open and allows 100% foreign ownership, while Bali supplies no PT PMA registration path for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: A national ceiling of 100% describes what foreign ownership may reach nationally; it is not, by itself, confirmation that a PT PMA can register the activity in Bali.

intel_2026.baliContext:
**🏝 The Bali Villa Market (Reality Check)**
- Villas ARE Bali's tourism identity: Seminyak, Canggu, Ubud, Uluwatu, Sanur — every area has its scene
- **Oversupply warning:** Canggu and Seminyak have thousands of villas competing for the same guests; occupancy rates have dropped significantly since 2022
- **Better ROI areas (2025):** Tabanan, Sidemen (Karangasem), Amed, north coast — lower land prices, growing demand

**💸 Real Costs to Budget**
- Land lease (Hak Sewa, 25 years, Canggu): IDR 1.5–4B per are (100m²)
- Villa construction (mid-range): IDR 8–15M per m²
- TDUP + permits + PBG: IDR 5–15M total
- Monthly operational (staff, maintenance, pool, gardener): IDR 15–40M depending on size

**⚠ Common Mistakes That Kill the Business**
- **Operating without TDUP** — Dinas Pariwisata enforcement intensified in 2023–2024; fines and closure orders have been executed in Canggu, Pererenan, and Seminyak
- **Building before PBG** — IMB/PBG crackdowns since 2024 have resulted in actual demolition orders in Bali
- **Skipping Sertifikat Laik Sehat** — required for legal operation; without it your NIB is valid but your villa is not
- **Ignoring the banjar** — local village council approval is not a government permit but is socially and operationally essential; no banjar consent = neighbor problems, access issues, staff walkouts
- **Nominee land ownership** — still common, still illegal; BPN and PPATK have increased scrutiny on nominee arrangements since 2023

persyaratan: Dokumen Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar

Dokumen Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar
Silakan kirim semua dokumen yang diminta dalam satu file.
1. Unduh dan lengkapi formulir Penilaian Mandiri.
2. Dokumentasi Standar Pelaksanaan Kegiatan Usaha.
Lampirkan 6 dokumen Sarana
  1. Petunjuk identitas/nama usaha dengan tulisan yang terbaca.
  2. Ruang kantor/area administrasi yang dilengkapi peralatan dan perlengkapan kerja.
  3. Peralatan Pertolongan Pertama pada Kecalakaan (P3K) dan Alat Pemadam Api Ringan (APAR) yang berfungsi dengan baik.
  4. Ketersediaan air bersih yang tidak berwarna, tidak berbau, tidak berasa, dan jernih.
  5. Ketersediaan gudang atau tempat penyimpanan barang yang aman.
  6. Status kepemilikan kantor/tempat usaha yang jelas.
Lampirkan 1 dokumen Sumber Daya Manusia
Perlindungan asuransi kesehatan dan/atau kecelakaan bagi karyawan tersedia dan berlaku.
Lampirkan 1 dokumen Ketentuan Produksi
Pelayanan kesehatan, seperti informasi tentang dokter, rumah sakit, atau klinik terdekat terdokumentasi.
Lampirkan 3 dokumen Sistem Manajemen Usaha
  1. Struktur organisasi dan uraian tugas setiap jabatan jalas dan terdokumentasi.
  2. rencana bisnis (business plan) masih berlaku dan terdokumentasi.
  3. S0P dan/atau petunjuk teknis pelaksanaan karja masih berlaku dan terdokumentasi.
kewajiban: Memiliki Sertifikat laik sehat

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Serviced apartments — apartments managed and operated as hotels for short-term stays, with payment calculated per-night or per-period. Think aparthotel (apartel) or condotel (kondotel). The unit is an apartment by design, but it functions as a hotel room: housekeeping, front desk, daily rates. This is *not* a long-term residential lease — it's hospitality accommodation in apartment form.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Micro + Small**: Medium-High risk (Menengah Tinggi). NIB + Sertifikat Standar, but requires a **Self-Assessment Readiness Document** (Dokumen Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar). Processing: 14 days (Jangka Waktu: 14 Hari).

Post-issuance obligations:
- Obtain a Health Feasibility Certificate (Sertifikat Laik Sehat)
- Obtain a tourism business standard certificate from an accredited LSPr (Sertifikat Standar Usaha Pariwisata dari Lembaga Sertifikasi Profesi)

**Authority:** Governor (Gubernur) — provincial level, not Bupati/Walikota. This signals a higher regulatory bar than villas or homestays.

**PMA:** Fully open (Terbuka) — 100% foreign ownership.

Note: Renumbered from KBLI 2020 code 55194 (Apartemen Hotel), same licensing substance.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Renumbered from KBLI 2020 code 55194 to 55204 in KBLI 2025 (a straight renumbering). The PP28 licensing data comes from the old KBLI 2020 code 55194 entry with a perfect 100% match. Same business, new code number. The key difference from villas (55203): aparthotels carry **Medium-High** risk, require Governor-level approval, and need LSPr certification — villas are Medium-Low with automatic issuance.
intel_2026.baliContext: Aparthotels are growing fast in Bali, especially in Seminyak, Kuta, and the Canggu-Berawa corridor. The model is popular with developers: build apartment units, sell them to individual investors, then manage the entire building as a hotel — the owner gets rental income, the operator runs it like a hotel. Condotels in Bali have been controversial (many buyers felt misled about returns), but the model persists because it works for both parties when managed well. Regulatory scrutiny is increasing — the Governor-level licensing reflects this. Occupancy can be excellent in prime locations (70-85% in peak season), but the per-night rate is typically lower than equivalent star-rated hotels. The sweet spot is lifestyle travelers who want a kitchen, washing machine, and living space but still want hotel services. Canggu and Uluwatu are seeing the newest developments in this category.
intel_2026.youllAlsoNeed:
- 56101 — Restaurant or food service (if you offer breakfast/dining)
- 55101-55106 — If any units are classified as star-rated hotel rooms
- 68112 — For the underlying property lease/rental structure
- 96230 — If you offer spa or wellness services
- 93116 — If you include gym/fitness facilities
- 55400 — If you list on OTAs (accommodation intermediary activity)

editorial.headline: Apartment Hotels in Bali: Open Nationally, Clear of the Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: This classification covers public short-stay apartment hotels, open to PMA nationwide and not barred by Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
Apartment hotel activity is the business of providing short-term accommodation to the public by managing and operating apartments as hotels for temporary stays. It puts the emphasis on the service delivered to guests: accommodation is offered to the public, but through a hotel function within apartment units. The record makes that operational character central. An apartment becomes part of this activity when it is managed and made to function as a hotel for temporary residents, rather than being regarded solely by its property form. The temporary-stay element is expressly part of the description, placing guests rather than long-term occupants at the centre of the accommodation.

That definition leaves a useful boundary in plain sight. The scope speaks of payment being calculated under the applicable arrangements and gives hotel apartments and condominium hotels—often known as apartel or condotel—as its examples. The classification follows the operating model: apartments are managed and functioned as hotel lodging for temporary stays. For an operator, that is the critical description to carry through every conversation about the business: not simply apartments, but apartments placed into hotel operation for the public. It is this service-led use that identifies the activity.

Registration is open to businesses at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That full-range treatment gives the classification a notably broad place in hotel accommodation. No one of these listed scales is set apart as the sole entry point; all four appear in the record as open. The practical reading is that the same defined hotel-apartment activity has a recognised place from Mikro through Besar, while the scope itself remains constant: public short-term accommodation operated in the manner of a hotel. That breadth relates to the scale range, not to a different activity.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali does not undo that national position. The Bali entry is not blocked and classifies the position as OK or higher risk. Its stated reason is specific: at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—meaning this activity is not blocked by the moratorium. The distinction matters because Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. The conclusion here is therefore not a Bali-side prohibition. On the facts in the record, foreign investors may register this activity in Bali through PMA; the record places it outside the moratorium’s blocked risk range.
editorial.pullQuote: The classification follows the operating model: apartments are managed and functioned as hotel lodging for temporary stays.

editorial.headline: Short-Stay Stays, Nationally Open but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers a broad range of short-stay accommodation, yet Bali’s registration structure prevents a foreign-owned company from registering it there today.
editorial.body:
This activity is the home for short-stay accommodation that sits outside the more specifically defined accommodation categories. Its practical territory is varied: bungalows, cottages without daily housekeeping, mountain lodges and huts, hostels, bed-and-breakfast units, capsule hotels, tree houses, cabins and glamping all fall within its stated scope. The common thread is not a particular building style but the provision of a short stay, whether that stay is deliberately simple, nature-facing, communal or highly compact.

The registration scales open to it are Mikro, Kecil and Menengah. That matters because the category is framed around businesses operating at micro, small and medium scale, rather than as a generic container for every accommodation venture. An operator should therefore read the scope and the available scales together: the description identifies the kind of stay being provided, while the scale setting identifies the business band in which the activity is open for registration.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. The activity is TERBUKA to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In national terms, that is full foreign ownership rather than a capped minority or majority stake. Bali is the material exception—and it is not a cosmetic qualification. Two separate rules narrow it there. Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 5(5) reserves only the specifically named 'Guest House' sub-activity within this code to Koperasi/UMKM, not the whole code — so whether a given concept falls inside that reserved slice depends on the exact activity and has to be checked case by case.

Separately, and more decisively for this activity, Bali’s provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for every Low and Medium-Low risk classification island-wide, and this activity sits at Medium-Low risk — so registration in Bali is closed today regardless of how the Guest House scope question resolves. A founder may see a nationally open, fully foreign-ownable activity and reasonably expect that position to travel unchanged. Here it does not. The national ceiling remains 100%, but in Bali the moratorium — not the national cap, and not the code's scale structure — is what currently closes the registration path.
editorial.pullQuote: The national ceiling remains 100%, but in Bali the moratorium — not the national cap, and not the code's scale structure — is what currently closes the registration path.

l4_bali.reason: Reserved to Koperasi/UMKM only as to a NAMED sub-activity — Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 5(5) scopes a Lampiran II reservation to the activity named in the Bidang Usaha column, not to the whole KBLI code. Lampiran II p.15, entry 48 sub-row *Guest House*, KBLI 55199 — scoped by Perpres 10/2021 **Pasal 5(5)** to "Guest House" only, not the residual code The rest of the code is not reserved; the answer depends on the scope actually declared. [Perpres annex]

data.mapping_note: PP28 uses KBLI 2020 code 55192 (Bumi Perkemahan, Persinggahan ...). Match: 95%

l4_bali.reason: No foreign-ownership reservation or cap for this activity was located in Perpres 10/2021 as amended by Perpres 49/2021 (Lampiran I, II, III) or in its closed list — so this is not a national 0% finding. OSS currently publishes licensing rows for this code only at Mikro, Kecil and Menengah scale, while a PT PMA is by law an Usaha Besar that must invest more than IDR 10 billion per KBLI per location (Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 7(1); Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 26(1)–(2)): whether OSS will license this code for a PT PMA must be confirmed in OSS; a scale missing from the licensing rules does not by itself restrict the activity (Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 8(6)). In Bali we flag this code as blocked as a precaution, not because a closure naming it was located. The Governor of Bali asked BKPM (letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, 28 Jan 2026) to close OSS to PT PMA in the Rendah and Menengah Rendah risk tiers, which include this code (Menengah Rendah). The provincial government reports that the closure applied from the third week of May 2026 covers 18 listed KBLI, and under the official BPS KBLI 2020→2025 crosswalk this code is not among them. Confirm the current OSS status in Bali before relying on this flag either way.

editorial.headline: Camping and Caravan Accommodation: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Outdoor accommodation for travellers with their own tents or caravans is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but a PT PMA cannot register the activity in Bali.
editorial.body:
Camping, caravan stopovers and caravan parks form an accommodation activity centred on the open air. It covers places where travellers lodge in their own tents or caravans—trailers brought by the traveller and used as a place to live. The scope reaches short-stay accommodation at recreational campgrounds, including camps for fishing and hunting, and the land and facilities that make a caravan stopover possible. It also includes accommodation furnished through shelters or basic bivouac facilities. The common thread is provision: an operator supplies somewhere to stay and the setting that supports that stay.

The activity is available at the micro, small and medium business scales. That makes scale part of the legal description, not a decorative label. For a registrant, the central role is that of the accommodation provider: the party making a campsite, caravan area or simple shelter available to visitors. The relevant offer is temporary lodging in the open air or beside a caravan, with the area and facilities expressly included in the stated scope. The record specifically calls out short-stay accommodation, anchoring the activity in the provision of a traveller’s stop rather than in the land alone.

Nationally, the activity is listed as open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. At national level, the permitted stake can therefore be entirely foreign-held. The local answer in Bali is nevertheless decisive for a prospective PT PMA. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali record categorises it as closed to PMA because of the provincial moratorium: since 13 May 2026 the island-wide block covers every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, and campsite and caravan-park operation is classified Medium-Low risk. The activity itself carries no foreign-ownership restriction we could locate. This is a structural registration barrier, not a Bali-specific foreign-share ceiling.

The provincial setting reinforces why national and Bali conclusions must be kept separate. The Bali rule recorded for this activity blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, permanently and island-wide. The record does supply a risk classification for this activity — Menengah Rendah (Medium-Low) — and that is precisely what places it inside the blocked band, since the moratorium operates on the risk tier and names no codes at all. The practical conclusion remains stark: national openness does not provide a Bali PMA registration route.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not provide a Bali PMA registration route.

editorial.headline: Accommodation Intermediation: Fully Foreign-Open, Including in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A business of matching guests with accommodation providers, this activity is open to full foreign ownership nationally and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Accommodation intermediation is the business of bringing a client together with an accommodation provider for a fee or commission. The match may happen on a digital platform or through non-digital channels, including telephone or post. Commission may be paid by either the client or the provider, while revenue may also include advertising-space sales. The activity also covers accommodation booking services and time-share exchange services. Its centre of gravity is the arrangement itself: creating the connection between demand and accommodation supply.

The permitted registrant base is broad. The record expressly includes non-exempt operators of electronic-commerce systems and intermediary facilities established both within Indonesia and outside the country’s legal jurisdiction when conducting electronic-commerce business in Indonesia. It also identifies businesses beyond those electronic-commerce and intermediary operators. Registration is open at every listed scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the activity is defined by the intermediary function, rather than by one particular channel through which the booking or introduction is made.

Nationally, the position is direct: the activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Full foreign ownership is therefore permitted at the national level. Bali requires a separate reading, and the answer is equally clear. A foreign-owned company can register this activity in Bali today because it is not blocked by the province’s PMA moratorium. That permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. For this activity, however, the OSS risk noted at the Large scale is Medium-High/High, which is why the record identifies it as not blocked by the moratorium.

The Bali position is more useful than a generic label of openness. It does not introduce a separate Bali ownership percentage, local partnership requirement, or other condition in the record. Its significance is narrower and decisive: the moratorium does not close the PMA-registration route for this accommodation-intermediation activity. Founders should assess the business against its actual role in connecting clients and providers, then apply the recorded national and Bali positions without adding restrictions that the record does not state.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign-owned company can register this activity in Bali today because it is not blocked by the province’s PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Managing Accommodation, Not Owning It
editorial.standfirst: This is the business of running accommodation for an owner—fully foreign-open nationally, yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali today.
editorial.body:
Accommodation-management services occupy the space between ownership and advice. The activity is performed by a third-party manager that takes responsibility for an accommodation business’s overall commercial and operational performance. That responsibility is practical, not ornamental: it includes direct involvement in daily operations and managerial decision-making. The manager acts for the property owner and receives a management fee. Put plainly, this is a mandate to manage the operation, rather than to own and directly operate the accommodation property, or to provide general management advice without direct operational control.

The appropriate registrant is therefore the third-party manager acting for the owner, with a real operating role rather than a purely advisory one. The activity is open at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. Its defining feature is the degree of responsibility assumed by the manager: overall business and operational performance, day-to-day involvement, and managerial decisions made on the owner’s behalf. The final reference to hotel-management services confirms the practical character of the activity without changing that wider accommodation-management frame.

At the national level, this open activity permits foreign investment up to a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. That national position must not be mistaken for a Bali registration route. In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity today. The Bali status is blocked on risk classification: at the Besar scale, OSS risk across every scope is Low or Medium-Low, and the province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA. The stated trigger is the Bali moratorium of May 2026. National openness remains the national position; Bali’s block is the local result for PMA registration.

That distinction matters because the formal subject here is a management service, not ownership of the property being managed. The national position reaches every listed business scale and permits full foreign ownership. Yet the Bali assessment resolves differently for PMA because of the stated risk-class rule, not because the national foreign-ownership ceiling is lower. For a founder considering a Bali base, the reading is uncompromising: national foreign openness describes the activity, while the island-wide moratorium prevents PMA registration there today.

editorial.headline: Temporary Accommodation, Open Nationally but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 55909 spans boarding houses, worker and student dormitories, sleeping-car operations and co-living—open nationally, but blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today. Nationally, it is open to PMA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%; in Bali, however, PMA registration is blocked under the province’s island-wide, permanent rule for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. That contrast is the decisive fact for anyone considering this accommodation business: a national opening is not a Bali registration pathway.

This is a category for temporary places to stay, whether meals are provided or not and whether the arrangement uses private rooms, shared rooms or dormitory space. It includes worker dormitories, boarding houses, student accommodation provided for less than a year, sleeping cars operated independently of a railway company, and communal living, or co-living. The form can therefore include a room of one’s own, a shared room or a dormitory, with or without meals; it is defined by how temporary accommodation is supplied, not by one property type. The common thread is a stay designed for a limited period, rather than accommodation of a year or more. The category therefore accommodates several living formats, but holds them within one clear frame: temporary lodging for students, seasonal workers and other individuals.

Registration is available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The list does not confine the activity to only one end of the business-size range. It covers the stated temporary-accommodation activity across those four scales, provided the operation remains within its defined scope. For PMA nationally, the status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In national terms, then, the ownership position is direct: foreign participation may reach the full ceiling shown for this activity.

Bali introduces a separate conclusion. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is recorded as Low or Medium-Low on every scope, which brings the activity within the Bali moratorium. Bali’s rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration across the island, permanently; the recorded block is tied to the moratorium of May 13, 2026. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class). This is not a reduction of the national 100% ceiling or a special partnership condition: it is a block on PMA registration in Bali, despite the national openness.
editorial.pullQuote: A national opening is not a Bali registration pathway when PMA registration is blocked at the provincial level.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This is your classic restaurant code — any place that serves food in a permanent building. Sit-down restaurants, warungs with concrete walls, fast food joints, food courts inside malls, even hotel restaurants. If people walk in, sit down, and eat food you cooked in a fixed building, this is the code.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Micro scale** (smallest operations): Medium-Low risk. You get your NIB + Standard Certificate automatically — no waiting. You'll need a Hygiene Sanitation Label (HSP) and must submit periodic activity reports.

**Small / Medium / Large scale**: Medium-High risk. NIB + Standard Certificate issued within **14 working days**. You'll need a Self-Assessment of Standard Readiness, a certified standard from an LSPr (certification body), and a Hygiene Sanitation Feasibility Certificate (SLHS).

**PMA (foreign investment):** Fully open — 100% foreign ownership allowed.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Correction (2026-07-18): this code's merge list was fixed. The 2025 code 56101 (permanent-building restaurants) absorbs KBLI 2020 code 56102 (Rumah/Warung Makan — home-style eateries) and KBLI 2020 code 56109 (other fixed-building food) — that's it. If you previously operated under KBLI 2020 code 56103 (food stalls/tents) or 56104 (self-service/cafeteria restaurants), those are non-permanent-structure food activities and now fall under KBLI 2025 code 56102 ('Aktivitas Penyediaan Makanan di Bangunan Tidak Tetap'), not this code — check that page instead.
intel_2026.baliContext: This is the single most common business code for foreigners in Bali. Seminyak, Canggu, and Ubud are saturated — the competition is fierce and landlords know it. Sanur and Uluwatu still have room. Keep in mind: Bali's health department (Dinas Kesehatan) does actual inspections for your SLHS, and they check kitchen hygiene, water quality, and food storage. Budget 2-4 weeks for the inspection alone. Also, most Bali restaurants need a separate liquor license if they serve alcohol — 56101 alone doesn't cover that.
intel_2026.youllAlsoNeed:
- 56301 — If you serve alcohol (bar license, required for cocktails and spirits)
- 56303 — If you also operate as a café/coffee shop
- 47221 — If you sell retail beverages (bottled drinks to go)

editorial.headline: A Fixed-Premises Food Business, Fully Foreign-Open Nationally
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 56101 covers food-service operations from permanent premises, with a clear national opening to foreign investment and no Bali moratorium block at Large scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 56101 is the framework for providing food to customers from a fixed, permanent building: a place that is not designed to be dismantled, moved or operated as a travelling venue. It encompasses table service where dishes are cooked to order, as well as counter and buffet formats where customers take, or are served, food already on display. Meals may be eaten on the premises, taken away, or delivered to the customer’s home. In practical terms, this is the home of restaurants, eating houses, canteens and cafeterias, fast-food restaurants, and take-away restaurants.

Its reach is deliberately broader than the classic street-facing dining room. A separately operated restaurant inside a hotel belongs here when it is not part of the hotel business itself. The same separate-unit principle applies to restaurants in transport facilities and aboard transport, as well as a take-away restaurant inside a supermarket. Catering restaurants and ice-cream or yoghurt outlets are also within the stated scope. The constant is not the menu or service style; it is an independently operated food-service business based in a fixed setting.

Businesses may register at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. The activity is TERBUKA to foreign investment nationally, subject to a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a straightforward national position: a foreign investor can hold the entire permitted stake, rather than needing to infer a lower limit from the nature of a food business or from the way it serves customers.

Bali requires a more precise reading, but not a more pessimistic one. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This activity is not blocked by that rule: at Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, and the Bali assessment is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For a foreign founder considering a fixed-premises food operation in Bali, the record therefore does not present a Bali moratorium prohibition. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the relevant ownership position, while the Bali result is expressly one of no moratorium block at the stated risk profile.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign founder considering a fixed-premises food operation in Bali, the record does not present a Bali moratorium prohibition.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Mobile Food Service Meets Bali’s PMA Boundary
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 56102 groups temporary food stalls, carts, food trucks and food stands into one activity—nationally open to full foreign ownership, but unavailable to PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today through a PT PMA. That local answer is not a judgement on the food concept; it follows the registration structure recorded for the activity. Bali's island-wide moratorium suspends PMA registration for every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, and this activity sits in the Medium-Low band. What closes this registration route in Bali is the provincial moratorium on the Low and Medium-Low risk tiers, not anything about the activity itself. The record also notes a permanent, island-wide Bali PMA moratorium for the Low and Medium-Low risk categories it covers; the decisive result for this activity is the structural bar just described.

KBLI 56102 is about providing food to customers from a non-fixed or non-permanent structure. The setting may be capable of moving, dismantling and reassembly, or it may remain in place without those capabilities. What matters is its non-permanent character, rather than a fixed restaurant premises. The scope embraces tented food stalls, travelling food sellers using motorised or non-motorised vehicles, pushcarts, food trucks and food stands. It also includes eating stalls within this temporary-place framework. The code therefore captures food service whose commercial setting is deliberately portable, provisional or otherwise outside a permanent building.

Its listed operating scales are Mikro and Kecil. That is an important part of the activity’s identity: the registration record places this kind of food provision within micro and small enterprise scale, while Bali’s PMA result turns on the province-wide moratorium over the Low and Medium-Low risk tiers. For an operator, the practical reading is straightforward. The business model can be recognisable and familiar—a tent stall, cart, truck or stand—yet the applicable registration route is defined by its scale and structure, not by how polished or ambitious the food concept may be.

Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Put simply, the national record allows this activity to be entirely foreign-owned. Bali does not replace that national ceiling with a different percentage; instead, it closes the PMA registration path through the local scale structure. National openness and Bali registrability are therefore separate questions here. A prospective foreign owner should hold both truths at once: the national ownership position is fully open, while a PT PMA cannot register this activity in Bali under the recorded local conditions.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and Bali registrability are therefore separate questions here.

l4_bali.reason: No foreign-ownership reservation or cap for this activity was located in Perpres 10/2021 as amended by Perpres 49/2021 (Lampiran I, II, III) or in its closed list — so this is not a national 0% finding. OSS currently publishes licensing rows for this code only at Mikro and Kecil scale, while a PT PMA is by law an Usaha Besar that must invest more than IDR 10 billion per KBLI per location (Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 7(1); Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 26(1)–(2)): whether OSS will license this code for a PT PMA must be confirmed in OSS; a scale missing from the licensing rules does not by itself restrict the activity (Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 8(6)). The applicable tourism standard (Permenpar 6/2025) sets a Sertifikat Standar and hygiene requirement with no scale gating, and for food and beverage services the PMA investment threshold is counted per 2-digit KBLI per regency/city (Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 26). In Bali we flag this code as blocked as a precaution, not because a closure naming it was located. The Governor of Bali asked BKPM (letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, 28 Jan 2026) to close OSS to PT PMA in the Rendah and Menengah Rendah risk tiers, which include this code (Menengah Rendah). The provincial government reports that the closure applied from the third week of May 2026 covers 18 listed KBLI, and under the official BPS KBLI 2020→2025 crosswalk this code is not among them. Confirm the current OSS status in Bali before relying on this flag either way.

editorial.headline: Event Catering: Contract Food Service, Delivered to the Occasion
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers contracted, ready-to-eat food service for specified events—nationally open to foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Event catering is the business of preparing and supplying food under a contract with a client, at a location chosen by that client, for a particular occasion. Its centre of gravity is the event itself: an office gathering, celebration, party, seminar, meeting, or a comparable occasion. The food is ready to consume, commonly delivered to the workplace or event venue, and the service can extend beyond delivery to include waitstaff serving guests or participants while the occasion is under way.

That definition matters because the activity is structured around an agreed event engagement rather than an undifferentiated food operation. The client identifies the occasion and location; the operator prepares and provides the food accordingly. In practical terms, the work joins preparation, delivery and, where required, on-site service into one contracted offering. It is a category for businesses whose commercial proposition is feeding a defined gathering with food ready for guests, rather than merely producing food for onward sale.

The registration field is broad. The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale, so the record does not confine it to one end of the business spectrum. At the national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA and foreign ownership may reach 100%. That is the straightforward national position: foreign ownership is permitted up to full ownership for this activity.

Bali does not reverse that position. The provincial rule blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently, but this activity is recorded as not blocked by that moratorium. At Besar scale, the OSS risk position is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which is why the record places it outside the moratorium block. The Bali status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: the activity remains available for PMA registration in Bali, while the record specifically signals its higher-risk treatment at the Besar end of the scale range. For a founder, that distinction is the essential one—national openness is real here, and Bali does not impose the moratorium barrier on this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real here, and Bali does not impose the moratorium barrier on this activity.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Contract catering — providing food services under agreement for specific periods. Covers: food contractors for transport companies, long-term catering at oil drilling sites/mines/hospitals/transport; sports facility/cafeteria catering on concession basis (factories, offices, hospitals, schools); household catering; nutritious meal provision and distribution; cloud kitchen contractor services. Does NOT cover manufacturing perishable food for retail sale.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Dual-tier risk.** Mikro/Kecil: Medium-Low, automatic. Needs HSP (Hygiene label) and SLHS. Menengah/Besar: Medium-High, needs verified standard from LSPr.

**PMA:** Fully open — 100% foreign ownership allowed.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Unchanged from KBLI 2020. Same code, same scope.
intel_2026.baliContext: B2B catering is a stable, unglamorous business in Bali. Hotels outsource banquet catering, tech coworking spaces need daily lunch programs, international schools contract meal providers. Cloud kitchen operations for food delivery apps also fall here. Less location-sensitive than consumer venues — can operate from industrial/mixed zones. Lower community friction (no noise, no tourist crowds). For PMA investors, the IDR 10B minimum makes this viable only at scale — think corporate catering serving 5+ clients, not a single kitchen.

editorial.headline: Contract Catering, With Bali’s Large-Scale Risk Line
editorial.standfirst: Contracted food provision can be fully foreign-owned nationally and is open for PMA in Bali, where a Besar-scale operation sits in the higher OSS risk band.
editorial.body:
KBLI 56290 covers the contractual provision of meals over an agreed period, rather than a one-off service. The work can be organised where the client needs it or prepared from a central unit. Its practical terrain is broad: long-term catering at oil-drilling sites, mining locations, hospitals and transport services; contracted catering at sports facilities; concession-run canteens or cafeterias for factories, offices, hospitals and schools; household catering; and nutritious-food provision and distribution to target groups. It also reaches food-service contractors working for transport companies and restaurant or cloud-kitchen operations.

That breadth is held together by one central idea: a business takes responsibility for ongoing food provision under an agreement with its customer. It may serve a defined client site, a remote operation, an institution or a household, but the contractual period is integral to the activity’s character. All four listed business scales—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—are eligible for registration. The code therefore accommodates operators from smaller contracted providers through to substantial institutional catering businesses, provided the activity remains within that agreed food-service role.

Nationally, the activity is classified as TERBUKA for PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. Foreign investors may therefore hold the entire permitted foreign stake under the national ceiling recorded for this activity. The important point is not merely that meals are supplied, but that the enterprise is established to perform a continuing contractual food-service commitment for its client.

In Bali, the recorded position is OK or higher risk, and the activity is open for PMA registration rather than blocked by the provincial moratorium. At Besar scale, its OSS risk is expressly medium-high/high. That classification places it outside Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium for low and medium-low risk activities. The Bali distinction is consequently clear: there is no Bali-specific foreign-ownership figure or partnership condition in this record, but a large-scale operation sits in the stated higher OSS risk band.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Indonesia’s Bar Activity: Nationally Open, Outside Bali’s PMA Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 56301 covers businesses principally serving drinks, from bars and drink-led beach clubs to separately operated bars on trains or ships.
editorial.body:
KBLI 56301 is the activity code for businesses whose principal work is serving beverages. That includes alcoholic drinks—such as spirits, beer, wine and whisky—as well as non-alcoholic drinks. Its scope also expressly reaches beach clubs primarily organised around beverage service, and bar operations on transport such as trains or ships when those operations are run by a separate unit. The defining question is therefore straightforward: is the business principally there to serve drinks?

The code is open at the *Menengah* and *Besar* scales. That matters because the registered activity is framed around the service itself, rather than a particular style of venue or drink menu. A drink-led beach club belongs within the stated scope; so does a conventional bar, provided serving beverages is its principal activity. The record also recognises a bar operating aboard a train or ship, but only where it is conducted by a separate unit. These are not decorative examples—they draw the practical edges of the activity as recorded.

At the national level, PMA is open, and foreign ownership may reach 100%. In practical terms, the national record permits this activity to be entirely foreign-owned. There is no lower national ceiling stated here, and no additional national condition recorded alongside that percentage. For a founder assessing the activity at the national level, the position is consequently direct: the code is open to PMA and may be held up to the stated full foreign-ownership limit.

Bali requires its own reading, but the result remains clear. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The record explains why: at the *Besar* scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High or High, placing it outside the moratorium’s stated Low and Medium-Low risk categories. Bali’s recorded status is therefore `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`: not a claim that every operating question disappears, but a precise indication that the island-wide PMA moratorium does not block this activity on the risk basis recorded. For a foreign founder, that distinction is the essential one—national openness is matched here by a Bali position that is outside the moratorium, rather than contradicted by it.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign founder, the essential point is that Bali does not block this activity under its PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: When a Nightclub Is First and Foremost a Drinking Venue
editorial.standfirst: For medium and large operators, KBLI 56302 defines a nightclub or discotheque centred on drinking service—nationally foreign-open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 56302 covers the operation of a nightclub or discotheque in which drinking service is the principal activity. Its core is the provision of drinks, while the venue and facilities for dancing form part of the setting. Live music and light-show attractions belong to the additional service, together with hostesses. That hierarchy matters: beverage service sits at the centre, with the dance-floor environment and accompanying entertainment forming the surrounding offer.

Registration is open at the Menengah and Besar scales. That confines the activity to operators whose plan belongs at one of those two stated scales; no other scale is identified in the record. The PMA status is TERBUKA nationwide, with foreign ownership allowed up to 100%. In plain terms, a foreign investor can hold the full permitted stake nationally for this activity. The recorded national ceiling does not reduce foreign ownership below full ownership.

Bali requires its own reading because the provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. For this activity, however, the Bali record marks it as OK or higher risk and says that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High. The recorded outcome is clear: it is not blocked by the moratorium. In Bali, the deciding fact is not the national 100% ceiling but the record’s finding that this activity falls outside the moratorium’s PMA block. A foreign investor can therefore register it in Bali under the position recorded here.

The practical reading deserves precision. The business must be framed around its principal offering—drink service—while the dance facilities, live music, light attractions and hostesses are part of the accompanying service picture described in the scope. The scale must be Menengah or Besar. And the Bali conclusion is simply the stated conclusion for this activity: the relevant provincial moratorium does not block PMA registration. For founders, that is the usable boundary: full national foreign ownership and a Bali position recorded as not blocked.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Café Activity That Bali Will Not Register for PMA
editorial.standfirst: Although nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this café activity cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 56303 concerns a café or drinking-house activity built around drinks consumed where they are served. Its principal offer is hot or cold beverages for on-site consumption, rather than a particular menu, décor or service style. The premises may occupy either part or all of a permanent building. They may be fitted with equipment and facilities for preparing and storing drinks, or operate without those arrangements. What anchors the classification is specific: the principal provision of beverages, consumed at the business premises, within a permanent-building setting.

That definition speaks to the businesses registering the activity: operators whose main undertaking is providing those drinks for people to consume on the premises. The recorded scale availability is broad, spanning Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Each is expressly open in the record, so scale does not narrow the national description of the activity. A business should nevertheless keep the classification’s centre of gravity in view. The code is framed around the provision of hot or cold drinks on the premises and the physical setting in which that provision takes place; those elements give the activity its identity.

At national level, foreign-investment treatment is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100%, cited to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Put plainly, the national record permits full foreign ownership for this activity. That matters because it makes the Bali position a separate geographic constraint, not a qualification of the national ownership ceiling. There is no lower national stake stated here: nationally, the listed ceiling remains 100%.

In Bali, the answer changes from ownership capacity to registrability. In Bali today, a foreigner cannot register this activity for PMA. The Bali entry is a risk-class block: at the Besar scale, OSS places every scope at Low or Medium-Low risk, and the entry says this is blocked by the Bali moratorium of May thirteenth, two thousand twenty-six. The governing provincial rule is island-wide and permanent, blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. It should not be read as a Bali-side reduction in the 100% ceiling; the Bali record supplies no alternative percentage, but a categorical registration block. A nationally open, fully foreign-ownable activity is nevertheless unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under that moratorium.
