editorial.headline: A Beverage Stall’s National Opening, and Bali’s PMA Barrier
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers made-to-order drink stalls, but Bali’s registration structure closes the route to a foreign-owned company.
editorial.body:
A beverage stall is a modest-format hospitality business with a very specific working character: it serves drinks prepared for immediate consumption from a fixed site that can itself be moved or dismantled. The record points to the familiar examples of coffee and juice stalls, often operating with a tent. The emphasis is not merely on selling a drink, but on providing a drink-service operation in which preparation happens on site and the product is ready to consume.

The activity is open to micro and small enterprises. That scale definition matters because it describes the businesses for which the registration row is available: compact, service-led drink outlets rather than an undefined broader category of food-and-beverage trade. For a founder, the practical identity of the activity lies in the combination of service, on-site preparation, immediate consumption, and a stall format that may be movable or demountable.

Nationally, the activity is marked open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national position: foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership in the record. But national openness does not produce an automatic registration path everywhere. In Bali, a foreigner cannot register this activity through a PMA company today. The reason is provincial: Bali's moratorium suspends PMA registration island-wide for every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, and a drink stall is classified Medium-Low risk. The sectoral standard itself imposes no scale gating and no ownership limit.

Bali’s policy setting reinforces the need to read the local position precisely. The province blocks all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. The record’s decisive finding for this activity, however, is the Bali moratorium: despite a nationally open, 100% foreign-ownership position, the Bali PMA route is closed while the block on the Low and Medium-Low risk tiers stands. The distinction is worth keeping intact. National investment openness describes the ceiling; Bali’s registration structure determines whether a PT PMA can use this activity there.
editorial.pullQuote: Despite national openness to 100% foreign ownership, Bali’s registration structure closes this activity to a PT PMA.

The applicable tourism standard (Permenpar 6/2025) sets a Sertifikat Standar and hygiene requirement with no scale gating, and for food and beverage services the PMA investment threshold is counted per 2-digit KBLI per regency/city (Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 26). In Bali we flag this code as blocked as a precaution, not because a closure naming it was located. The Governor of Bali asked BKPM (letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, 28 Jan 2026) to close OSS to PT PMA in the Rendah and Menengah Rendah risk tiers, which include this code (Menengah Rendah). The provincial government reports that the closure applied from the third week of May 2026 covers 18 listed KBLI, and under the official BPS KBLI 2020→2025 crosswalk this code is not among them. editorial.headline: A Clear National Opening, but No PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers jamu houses and stalls serving herbal drinks, nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
A natural-medicine drink house or jamu stall is, at its core, a public-facing place to sell and serve herbal drinks or beverages made from natural medicinal ingredients. The activity may occupy part or all of a permanent building, whether or not it has equipment for making and storing the drinks. Its scope also reaches drink-service businesses preparing ready-to-consume jamu at a fixed site that can be moved or dismantled, commonly in a tented format. The practical point is the service of the drink to the public on the business premises: this is not merely a retail description, but an activity built around preparation and serving.

The registration field is broad on business scale. Micro, small, medium and large enterprises are all open to this activity. Nationally, it is classified as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a full national opening: a foreign-owned company may hold the activity within the national PMA framework, subject only to the information stated for this code. For founders, the scale options matter because the activity can describe anything from a modest jamu counter to a larger operation, while the code’s national investment position remains fully open.

Bali changes the conclusion sharply. Today, a foreigner is unable to register this activity for PMA in Bali. At the large-business scale, the OSS risk classification is low or medium-low across every scope of the activity. Bali’s moratorium blocks all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities from PMA registration across the island, permanently; this code is therefore blocked under that rule. The record identifies the moratorium as taking effect in May 2026. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling is real, but it does not override Bali’s registration block for this activity.

That distinction deserves to be read plainly. National openness answers the ownership question for Indonesia at large; Bali’s moratorium answers whether the PMA registration can proceed on the island. Here, those answers point in different directions. The activity is nationally open across every listed scale, yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali because its large-scale OSS risk treatment falls within the island-wide moratorium. For a founder considering a Bali-based jamu house or stall, the decisive current fact is not the national ownership ceiling but the Bali block.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling is real, but it does not override Bali’s registration block for this activity.

editorial.headline: A Mobile Drinks Trade That Is Open Nationally but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This prepared-drink activity permits full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali’s registration structure prevents a PT PMA from registering it today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 56306 concerns a particular kind of beverage service: drinks are made before sale, served ready to drink, and ordinarily sold while the provider moves from place to place. The scope explicitly captures mobile sellers of ice doger, ice cincau and jamu. That combination is important: preparation and immediate service belong to the activity, alongside mobility. It is defined both by the beverage’s ready-to-drink condition and by the absence of a fixed selling place.

The scale setting is equally specific. The record opens the activity to Mikro and Kecil businesses. That makes the scale classification more than an administrative footnote: it is the frame through which this mobile prepared-drink activity is made available for registration. Founders should read scope and scale together: what is being offered is an on-the-move service for drinks made for consumption, and its stated registration scales are Mikro and Kecil. The stated scales define the registration boundary as given; neither the ready-to-drink nature of the product nor the mobile method of sale removes it.

At the national level, the position is clear. PMA status is TERBUKA and the permitted foreign ownership ceiling is 100%, so the national listing allows full foreign ownership. For someone assessing investment nationally, the point is unambiguous: foreign participation is not merely permitted in part; the stated ceiling reaches the whole capital position. It is a national statement, however—not a promise that every provincial registration path remains available.

Bali changes the conclusion decisively. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today through a PT PMA. The Bali record marks it closed in Bali under the 2026 moratorium: the island-wide block covers every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, and this activity is classified Medium-Low risk. The record also identifies a permanent, island-wide provincial PMA block for low and medium-low risk KBLI. This is a structural restriction, not an editorial caveat: it determines whether an applicant can use the PT PMA form at all. Whether the national listing is fully open is therefore not the practical answer on the island; the local registration structure blocks the PT PMA route outright.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open at 100% foreign ownership does not make the PT PMA registration route available in Bali.

editorial.headline: Selling the Introduction, Not the Meal
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 56400 is for businesses connecting clients with food-and-beverage providers—open nationally to full foreign ownership and not barred for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Food and drink intermediaries sell the connection, not the meal. KBLI 56400 covers businesses that bring clients together with food-and-beverage providers for a fee or commission, while the intermediary itself supplies neither food nor drink. That can mean a restaurant reservation service or a broader matching operation conducted through a digital platform, face to face, by telephone, by post, or through other non-digital channels. Income may come from the client, the provider, or other sources such as advertising. The defining boundary is straightforward: this is an activity of arranging access to providers, not of supplying food and drink.

That distinction gives the activity a clear commercial shape. A business registered here acts as the bridge between demand and the provider that fulfils it; it may facilitate the introduction, reservation, or transaction without becoming the food-and-beverage provider itself. The scope expressly includes restaurant reservation services. It also makes clear that an online platform allowing people to order food-delivery services falls outside this activity. Registration is open at the Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, giving the code room for a modest reservation operation as well as a larger intermediation business.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In practical terms, a foreign-owned business may register this intermediary activity nationally with full foreign ownership. That openness belongs to the intermediary service described here: connecting clients and food-and-beverage providers for remuneration or commission, rather than operating as the provider of the food and drink.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The record places the OSS risk at the Besar scale in the Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi range and states that the activity is not blocked by the island-wide, permanent Bali moratorium. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For a foreign investor considering this particular activity in Bali, the honest conclusion is therefore clean: PMA registration is not prohibited there, and the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the stated position.
editorial.pullQuote: The intermediary sells the connection, not the meal—and Bali does not bar PMA registration for that activity.

editorial.headline: Book Publishing: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Book publishing can be fully foreign-owned nationally, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity across the island.
editorial.body:
Book publishing covers the act of bringing books into publication in its many possible forms. Its scope includes books, brochures and similar publications; dictionaries and encyclopaedias; atlases, maps and charts; electronic books and audiobooks; and comic books and graphic novels. The definition is deliberately format-neutral: print, electronic, digital, analogue and other forms of book publication all sit within the activity. For an enterprise built around publishing books rather than a single delivery format, this is the relevant frame.

The activity is open to businesses at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scale. Nationally, it is open to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That makes the national position unusually direct: a foreign investor may hold the full permitted stake in a book-publishing business under this activity. The record identifies the national basis as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali is the decisive exception. In Bali today, this activity cannot be registered as PMA by a foreigner. At the Large scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope within the activity, placing it inside Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. For book publishing, the result is not a reduced foreign-ownership ceiling or a local-partnership condition: it is a block on PMA registration in Bali.

That distinction matters because the national permission remains real, but it does not override the Bali position. A founder considering this activity therefore has to read the two layers together: national rules allow up to full foreign ownership, while Bali’s risk-based moratorium prevents a PMA registration for the activity on the island. The commercial shape of the publishing business—whether centred on printed books, e-books, audio editions, reference works, maps or graphic novels—does not change the stated Bali outcome, because the record applies the Low or Medium-Low classification across every scope.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, book publishing is open to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, PMA registration is blocked across the island.

editorial.headline: Newspaper Publishing: One Activity, Many Formats
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to PMA at 100%, and Bali’s large-scale risk assessment leaves it outside the province’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Newspaper publishing here is defined by the act of publishing a newspaper, not by a single delivery format. It includes advertising newspapers and accommodates newspaper publishing in print, electronic, digital, analog and other possible forms. That breadth matters: the activity can retain its essential publishing character while appearing in the formats through which newspapers are made available.

The registration is open across the full scale range recorded for this activity: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The scale labels establish that the activity is not confined to one size of enterprise. editorial.headline: The Periodical Publisher’s Clearer Route into Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 58130 covers publishing journals, periodicals and broadcast schedules across formats, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 58130 is the publishing home for journals and other periodicals, as well as for the publication of radio and television broadcast schedules. The medium is not the test: the activity may be carried out in print, electronically, digitally, in analogue form or through another publishing format. That makes the code about publishing a recurring editorial or schedule-led product, rather than the technology used to distribute it. Its boundaries are equally useful: independent journalism, independent photojournalism and the production of television or video news programmes sit outside the stated scope.

The registration is open at every scale named in the record—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. In practical terms, the activity can be registered by a business operating at any of those scales, provided its work is genuinely the publishing described here. The scale list signals availability across the spectrum; it does not change the core description of the activity.

At national level, the foreign-investment position is direct. The activity is listed as TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. A foreign investor can therefore hold the activity in full under the national ceiling recorded here. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lesser national cap in this record, so the salient point is not a partial foreign stake but an open activity with a full-ownership ceiling.

In Bali, this is not a case where national openness runs into a provincial PMA-registration ban. The Bali result is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and marked not blocked. The reason is specific: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, placing the activity beyond the provincial moratorium’s target. That moratorium blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, island-wide and permanently. On the record supplied, 58130 is consequently available for PMA registration in Bali rather than stopped by that rule. The national 100% ceiling remains the national foreign-ownership figure, while Bali’s result here is a risk-based absence of a moratorium block.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, national foreign openness is not undone by Bali’s PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Publishing Beyond Books: KBLI 58190 and Bali’s PMA Position
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 58190 covers a wide publishing field, from directories and catalogues to datasets, with a fully open national PMA position and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 58190 is the publishing category for material that sits beyond the conventional book or periodical. It covers publishing in print, electronic, digital, analogue, and other forms: directories, mailing lists and telephone books; compilations such as legal or pharmaceutical reference collections; catalogues; photographs, engravings and postcards; calendars; forms; posters; art reproductions; unbound leaflets and advertising materials; statistics and other information. It also includes datasets or databases where no related data-processing service is provided.

The practical thread running through that broad list is publication. A business registering this activity is placing defined informational, visual, reference, promotional, or data-based material into a published form. The scope is deliberately wide enough to accommodate both physical and electronic formats, while retaining that central publishing character. It is open across every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That makes the code usable for a modest specialist publisher as well as a larger operation, provided the activity remains within the listed publishing scope.

For foreign investment, the national position is unusually direct. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign ownership may reach the full 100% nationally for this activity. The cited PMA basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower national foreign-ownership cap in the record to read around or qualify: the stated ceiling is the full amount.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion. Its permanent island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, but this activity is not blocked. The Bali record classifies it as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and explains why: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. For a founder considering a PMA registration in Bali, that distinction is material. This is an activity that remains available for PMA registration in Bali, rather than being caught by the province’s low-risk and medium-low-risk moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: This is an activity that remains available for PMA registration in Bali, rather than being caught by the province’s low-risk and medium-low-risk moratorium.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity covers publishing ready-to-play online video games for any operating system or device. It includes offering games through subscriptions, managing in-game and in-app purchases, and providing intermediation services for game publishers.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is 100% open to foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines, and some scopes of this KBLI fall in that band — but at least one large-scale (Besar) scope carries a higher risk class, so the code remains registrable as a PMA in Bali on that scope.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: code renumbered.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Penerbitan Perangkat Lunak Video Gim dalam Jaringan (Game Online) (58211)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign gaming entrepreneurs who want to publish online games or act as an intermediation platform for game publishing.

editorial.headline: Online Game Publishing: Nationally Open, Conditional in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Online game software publishing is open to full foreign ownership nationally, but in Bali the PMA route turns on the exact scope’s OSS risk classification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 58211 is for publishing online video-game software ready to operate across operating-system platforms and devices. It includes a publisher’s provision of online games to every type of user, including subscribers, and expressly encompasses in-game and in-app purchases. It also covers intermediation services connected to the publishing of online game software. The unifying activity is the online publication and provision of a game across the platforms and users named in the scope.

The activity is not confined to one business size. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises, giving the category a broad formal scale range. Across that range, the stated activity remains online game publishing, game provision by the publisher, and the defined intermediation services. The scope is expansive in its platform and user reach, yet specific in its focus on online video-game software publishing.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The activity carries TERBUKA status, allowing foreign ownership up to the 100% ceiling. In plain terms, a PMA structure may be fully foreign owned nationally for this activity; the record does not set a lower national equity cap. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. For a founder assessing the national position alone, this is an open category at the stated ownership percentage.

Bali is a conditional, rather than blanket, answer. The record does not mark the activity as categorically blocked for PMA there—its Bali blocked flag is false—but its Bali status depends on scope. The province’s permanent island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for low and medium-low risk KBLI. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is low for some scopes and higher for others. The Bali PMA route is described as registrable only by declaring the higher-risk scope, and the exact activity must be verified live in OSS. National openness at 100% should therefore not be mistaken for an automatic Bali registration outcome: in Bali, the declared scope’s OSS risk remains decisive.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, 100% foreign ownership is open; in Bali, registration still turns on the declared scope’s OSS risk.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is fully open to 100% foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines, and some scopes of this KBLI fall in that band — but at least one large-scale (Besar) scope carries a higher risk class, so the code remains registrable as a PMA in Bali on that scope.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: code renumbered.

editorial.headline: Video-Game Publishing: Open Nationally, Conditional in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers ready-to-run video-game software publishing and its stated intermediary services, open to full foreign ownership nationally but conditional on scope and live OSS treatment in Bali.
editorial.body:
Video-game publishing looks simple only from a distance. This activity covers the publication of other ready-to-run video-game software for every operating-system platform and device. It also covers intermediary services for publishing that software. Its perimeter expressly includes games used outside a network, so offline video games belong within the activity rather than sitting at its edge. The record does not make a network connection its dividing line: an offline video game remains expressly inside the described publishing activity. It should be read from that practical centre: ready-to-operate games and the services that intermediate their publication.

Who can use it is expressed through activity and scale, not a separate category of person. It is the activity description for the publisher or intermediary the record describes, and registration is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That range is significant because it does not reserve the activity for one end of the market. Still, scale does not expand the scope. The registration should track publication of video-game software that is ready to operate and, where relevant, the listed intermediary role. The code’s reach is broad in platform and device terms, while remaining specific about the software and publishing function at its core.

Nationally, the position is direct: PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a national ownership position, not a shortcut around Bali’s local treatment. In Bali, the status is scope-dependent, not an outright PMA block. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide. For this activity, however, OSS risk at the Besar scale is low for some scopes and higher for others. A PMA registration in Bali is registrable only by declaring the higher-risk scope; the exact activity must be verified live in OSS. That qualification is central, rather than a footnote to the national rule.

The consequence is an editorially simple but operationally important distinction. A national ceiling of 100% confirms full foreign ownership in the national record; it does not, by itself, resolve a Bali registration. Nor is the Bali answer a flat refusal: the recorded treatment changes with the declared scope and its risk reading. For a founder or company whose work genuinely fits the stated publishing or intermediary activity, the reliable reading is two-part—open nationally, conditional in Bali, and dependent on a live OSS check for the exact activity. Precision in the declaration is what keeps those two positions aligned.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: The Publishing Business Behind Ready-Made Software
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers publishers of ready-made software—from operating systems to AI tools—open to foreign investment nationally, while Bali registration turns on the precise scope declared and its OSS risk.
editorial.body:
This activity is about publishing ready-made software rather than software produced to order. Its territory is wide: operating systems, business applications, financial-technology and distributed-ledger software, cybersecurity tools, modelling, design and multimedia software, Internet of Things software, and artificial-intelligence software all sit within the stated scope. It also includes marketplaces for software downloads, intermediation services for publishing software other than video games, and software made or produced by the publisher itself.

The defining idea is publication: bringing a ready-to-use software product into the market. That can mean a publisher whose product is a foundational operating system, a specialist security tool, a business application, or software built around AI or connected devices. It can also mean a publisher operating the route through which software is made available for download, or an intermediary supporting publication outside the video-game field. The record makes room for publishers that create their own software as well as those whose work is centred on publishing it.

Across Indonesia, foreign investment is permitted for this activity, subject to a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. It is available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. In practical terms, the national position is unambiguous: a foreign investor can hold the full permitted stake in a company carrying out this publishing activity. The operative source listed for that foreign-investment position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali requires a more exact reading. This is not recorded as an outright PMA block, but as a position that depends on scope. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is low for some scopes and higher for others; PMA registration in Bali is possible only where the higher-risk scope is declared for the exact activity. That distinction is consequential because Bali permanently blocks PMA registration island-wide for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. A publisher therefore cannot treat the national 100% ceiling as an automatic Bali outcome: the declared scope and its live OSS classification determine whether the activity can be registered there as PMA.
editorial.pullQuote: A publisher cannot treat the national 100% ceiling as an automatic Bali outcome: the declared scope and its live OSS classification determine whether the activity can be registered there as PMA.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Government Film and Video Production: Closed to Foreign Ownership
editorial.standfirst: A government-managed screen-production activity spanning film, video and television work, open across business scales but closed to foreign ownership nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors are unable to register this activity in Bali today. The Bali entry is marked **TERTUTUP**, and the national position is equally clear: foreign ownership is closed, with a ceiling of **0%**. That makes the central issue less about the commercial appeal of screen production than about the activity’s defined institutional setting: it is production managed by government on a remunerated basis.

Its scope is broad within that setting. It covers the making of moving images, including films, videos and audiovisual works such as 2D animation, 3D animation, stop-motion animation and combinations of animation techniques. It also includes television programmes, television commercials, television news programmes, vlogs and video podcasts. Government-managed sports-media content made as film, video or television programming belongs within the same activity, as do films made for television exhibition, film-delivery services and film booking-agency services when managed by government.

The classification is open across the stated business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That scale availability should be read precisely. It describes the scales listed for the activity; it does not alter the national foreign-ownership ceiling. A foreign stake is not available under this code, regardless of the scale at which the activity might otherwise be organised. The scope also draws a practical boundary around production itself: duplicating films or reproducing audio or video recordings onto CD, DVD or other physical media from a master copy is outside it, as is animation post-production.

Bali’s record adds an important distinction without softening the result. At the Besar scale, the recorded OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so this activity is not caught by Bali’s island-wide permanent PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. Yet the Bali status remains **TERTUTUP**. In other words, the moratorium is not the operative barrier described here; the conclusion for foreign ownership remains unchanged in both the national and Bali entries.
editorial.pullQuote: The moratorium is not the operative barrier described here; foreign ownership remains closed nationally and in Bali.

editorial.headline: Private Screen Production: Open Nationally, Scope-Dependent in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A broad private production activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali PMA registration turns on the exact declared scope and its OSS risk.
editorial.body:
Private film, video and television production is the paid, privately managed making of moving-image work. The scope is deliberately broad: films, videos and audiovisual works—including 2D, 3D and stop-motion animation, or combinations of those techniques—sit beside television programmes, moving television advertisements and television news programmes. It also expressly includes vlogs and video podcasts produced under private management for remuneration. Sports-media content made as film, video or TV, films produced for television screening, film-delivery services and film booking-agency work are all part of the same stated activity.

Its edges matter. The record separates this production activity from duplicating films or reproducing audio or video recordings from a master onto CDs, DVDs or other physical media. It also excludes animation post-production. In practical terms, the classification follows the creation and production of moving-image material, alongside the specified delivery and booking services; it should not be stretched to claim the distinct physical-copying or animation-post-production work outside its stated boundary.

This activity is available to businesses at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. Nationally, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with maximum foreign ownership of 100%. This is a national foreign-ownership ceiling, not a partial one: a foreign investor may hold the full stake permitted by that ceiling in a business confined to this scope. It is the cleanest part of the picture, grounded in the listed national source. The scale list establishes who may register; it does not turn every individual element of the production scope into the same Bali registration outcome.

Bali is where precision becomes decisive. The record does not mark the activity as universally blocked for PMA; its Bali status is scope-dependent. At Besar scale, OSS treats some stated scopes as low risk and others as higher risk. Bali permanently blocks PMA registration island-wide for all low- and medium-low-risk activities. The activity can be registered as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope. A founder should therefore verify the exact activity live in OSS before treating the national 100% ceiling as a Bali registration result. No separate Bali ownership percentage or partnership condition is stated here; Bali’s distinction is the declared scope’s risk position.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity can be registered as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope.

editorial.headline: The Public-Sector Engine Room of Screen Post-Production
editorial.standfirst: Government-managed screen finishing, preservation and delivery work sits in a field closed to foreign investment nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 59121 covers the government-managed work that happens after a film, video, audiovisual work or television programme has been made. Its practical territory includes editing and cutting; dubbing; titles and film credits; closed captioning; animation and special effects; transfers from film or tape; and conversion into video-streaming formats. It also encompasses film studios and specialist animation studios that develop and process film, reproduce it for cinema distribution, and document film recordings or other moving-image stock footage on a fee basis. This is the finishing, preservation and delivery layer of screen production, administered within a government-managed setting.

The remit extends beyond conventional post-production. It includes government-managed post-production involving sports-media content, as well as censorship of films, videos and television programmes when undertaken by a government-managed business entity or business operator as part of the post-production process. That institutional character is central to the activity’s definition. The record places it across Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales, while consistently locating the underlying work in government management. Scale describes the available business classifications; it does not detach the activity from that public-sector context.

Nationally, foreign investment is closed, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 0%. There is therefore no room for a partial foreign stake within this activity’s national foreign-investment position. The relevant national basis cited in the record is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. For a founder assessing a foreign-investment structure, the conclusion is direct: this is not an activity open to foreign ownership at the national level.

Bali reaches the same operational conclusion for PMA registration: the activity is listed as closed, and a foreigner cannot register it in Bali today. The detail matters, however. At the Large scale, the OSS risk is recorded as Medium-High/High, meaning this activity is not blocked by Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk PMA activities. That does not create an opening. It simply distinguishes the moratorium from the separate Bali status recorded for this activity: closed.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali’s moratorium does not apply here, but that does not turn a closed activity into an opening for foreign investment.

editorial.headline: Post-Production’s Open National Market, and Bali’s Scope Test
editorial.standfirst: This private post-production activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but in Bali the exact scope declared in OSS determines whether PMA registration is possible.
editorial.body:
Film, video, audiovisual works and television programmes reach their finished form in post-production. This private-sector activity covers the work that happens after production: editing and cutting; dubbing; titles and film credits; closed captioning; animation and special effects; film or tape transfer; and conversion into video-streaming formats. It also includes film studios and specialist animation-film studios that develop and process films, reproduce them for cinema distribution, and manage paid documentation or stock-footage services.

The scope extends to privately managed post-production involving sports-media content, as well as film, video and television censorship performed by a business entity or business actor as part of the post-production process. In practical terms, this is a broad operational category for the businesses responsible for shaping, adapting, processing and preparing moving-image material for its intended distribution. The record also carries a specific qualifier concerning animation, so the exact activity declared matters as much as the general post-production description.

Nationally, the position is straightforward: the activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is available across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That national openness, however, should not be mistaken for an automatic Bali registration outcome. Bali’s permanent province-wide rule blocks all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI activities from PMA registration. For this activity at the Besar scale, the OSS risk result is low for some scopes and higher for others.

That distinction is the whole Bali story. The activity is not recorded as outright blocked, but PMA registration in Bali is possible only when the declaration uses the higher-risk scope. A founder cannot safely rely on the national 100% ceiling alone, nor on the generic label of post-production. The exact activity must be checked in live OSS before registration, because the Bali result depends on the scope selected rather than on a blanket provincial approval or refusal.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is not a Bali registration answer: eligibility turns on the exact scope declared in OSS.

editorial.headline: Government Film Distribution: No PMA Route in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This government-managed distribution activity spans films, video, television programmes and audiovisual rights, but it is closed to foreign ownership nationally and cannot be registered as PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
**This activity concerns the government-managed distribution of screen work, rather than its production.** It covers distributing films, videos, television programmes and comparable audiovisual works to cinemas and feature-film theatres, television networks and stations, and exhibition organisers, where the activity is managed by government for remuneration. The remit also reaches government-managed distribution of film, video and television programming carrying sports-media content. Just as importantly, it includes the government-managed acquisition of distribution rights in films, videos, audiovisual works and similar products. editorial.headline: Private Film Distribution: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This paid private distribution activity spans cinema, television, exhibitors and distribution rights—nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Private film, video and television-programme distribution is, at its core, the paid circulation of moving-image work. The activity covers distributing films, videos and comparable audiovisual productions to motion-picture cinemas or big-screen theatres, television networks and stations, and exhibitors, where the work is privately managed on a fee basis. It also expressly includes distribution of sports-media content in film, video and television programmes. The scope therefore reaches the channels named in the record: cinema, television and exhibition.

The definition also reaches the acquisition of distribution rights to moving pictures, including films, videos, audiovisual works and similar productions, when privately managed. That places both the distribution of content and the acquisition of the rights to distribute it within the activity’s stated terrain. The code is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises, placing it across the full range of scales identified in the record. The registrant is a private operator engaged in that paid distribution activity or in obtaining those distribution rights.

Nationally, the position on foreign investment is unambiguous. The activity is TERBUKA—open—and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. A foreign investor therefore encounters a nationally open classification with full foreign ownership permitted. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national position applies to the distribution activity described here, including its cinema, television, exhibitor and sports-media distribution elements, as well as the stated acquisition of distribution rights.

Bali changes the outcome for PMA registration. Its Bali status is Blocked (risk class): blocked by risk class. At the Besar scale, every scope carries an OSS risk of Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for activities with Low and Medium-Low risk. Since this activity is caught by that rule, a foreigner cannot register it in Bali today. The block is not a reduction of the national 100% ceiling; it is a Bali registration prohibition under the moratorium introduced in May 2026.

editorial.headline: Film Exhibition: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Film and audiovisual screenings are nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering Bali, the central fact about KBLI 59140 is stark: it cannot be registered there through PMA today. This activity covers the exhibition of films and other audiovisual works for audiences in cinemas, outdoor settings, and other screening venues. It also includes film screenings presented as part of film festivals, whether those festivals are managed by government or private organisers. The defining subject is public screening: the moment when a film or audiovisual work is brought before viewers, whether as a regular venue programme or a festival event.

Nationally, the record places the activity in the open category for foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar business scales. That national position is meaningful: the activity is not subject to a national foreign-ownership cap below full ownership. The scope is also broad enough to encompass different presentation settings, from cinemas to open-air screenings and festival programmes, while remaining anchored in the activity of showing films or audiovisual works to an audience.

Bali presents a different and decisive picture for PMA registration. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Low or Medium-Low for every scope of this activity. That risk position places it within Bali’s province-wide rule blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk activities from PMA registration. The record identifies this as a permanent, island-wide moratorium, referenced to May 2026. The Bali status is therefore not a reduced foreign-ownership allowance or a conditional local ceiling: it is a block on the PMA registration route.

The distinction is important because both statements remain true at once. Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%. In Bali, however, the activity is blocked for PMA registration under the province’s risk-based moratorium. For founders, the national openness describes the activity’s general investment position; the Bali classification determines the current local outcome. A full national foreign-ownership ceiling does not create a Bali PMA registration path where the provincial moratorium blocks it.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, but it does not translate into a PMA registration route in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Sound Recording: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Sound-recording work is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium means a foreign investor cannot register it on the island today.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the business of making sound permanent and usable. It includes the creation of original master sound recordings, recording services, and the production of pre-recorded radio programmes rather than live broadcasts. Its territory also reaches audio podcasts, sound made for film, television, books and other media, and the conversion of recorded material into audio-streaming formats. The listed examples prevent the activity from being reduced to music alone: spoken programmes and media-bound audio are expressly within its field. Nor is it confined to capture at the microphone; converting recordings for audio streaming is also part of the defined work.

This can be a very small operation or a large one. Registration is open across the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so the category does not reserve sound-recording work for a single type of studio or producer. A compact specialist setup can sit within the same formal activity as a larger production operation, provided the work remains within the defined field: original masters, recording services, pre-recorded audio programming, audio for media, and conversion to streaming format. The stated scale range makes room for the same activity to be carried out at distinctly different commercial sizes.

The national position is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In national terms, foreign investment is open up to full ownership. A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not override Bali’s island-wide PMA restriction. That distinction matters because a national entry position and a provincial registration outcome can point in different directions.

For Bali, the outcome today is direct: a foreign investor cannot register this activity for PMA. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, which places it within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The moratorium dates from May 2026. This block is tied to the recorded risk position at the Besar scale, not to any reduction in the national ownership ceiling. Nationally, the activity remains open to full foreign ownership; in Bali, its present PMA registration position is blocked.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not override Bali’s island-wide PMA restriction.

editorial.body:
Nationally, this activity is open to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. Yet the immediate Bali answer is firmer: a PMA business cannot register this activity there today. The difference is not a matter of how a business frames its catalogue or distributes music; it follows the Bali entry attached to the activity, whose stated risk position brings it within the province-wide moratorium. A sound decision has to hold both facts at once: national openness exists, but Bali PMA registration is blocked.

At its core, the activity concerns the publishing life of a musical composition. It covers obtaining and registering copyright for musical compositions, then promoting, licensing and enabling their use. The permitted uses expressly extend across recordings, radio, television, film, live performance, print, podcasts and other media. The scope also includes cooperation in publishing and distributing sound recordings, whether the route is through wholesalers, retailers, direct supply to the public, streaming platforms or digital downloads. Music books and sheet-music books are included as well. It is an activity built around the circulation of musical works and related published material across both traditional and digital channels.

The record makes the activity available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That range accommodates businesses that publish compositions, manage their use, collaborate on sound-recording publication and distribution, or publish music and score books. It does not reserve the activity for one distribution model: circulation may be physical, direct to the public, streamed or downloaded, provided it remains within the publishing and distribution work described here. For a prospective registrant, the central issue is whether the business is carrying out that rights, publishing, licensing, use and distribution work.

The Bali restriction turns on the record’s stated OSS risk outcome: at the Besar scale, every scope is Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. The reason recorded for this activity therefore places it inside that moratorium, dated May 2026. The national 100% ceiling remains the national foreign-ownership position; it does not override the Bali PMA registration block. The practical conclusion is straightforward: foreign investment may be nationally open for this activity, but a PMA entity cannot register it in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% ceiling remains the national foreign-ownership position; it does not override the Bali PMA registration block.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Analog Radio Broadcasting: Nationally Open, With Bali Address Checks
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers analogue radio broadcasting and is nationally open to foreign investment, while Bali’s moratorium does not block it.
editorial.body:
Analog radio broadcasting is the operation of a radio broadcasting service using analogue signals: the studio work and the facilities that transmit audio to the public, affiliates, and subscribers through terrestrial, cable, or satellite channels. Its centre of gravity is the live broadcasting service and its transmission capability—not digital-signal radio, on-demand audio distribution or streaming, or the production of non-live radio content and audio recordings.

The activity is open across the full business-scale spectrum recorded here: micro, small, medium, and large enterprises. That matters because the classification does not reserve the activity for a particular size of operator. A broadcaster may therefore be registered at any of those scales, provided the registered activity genuinely reflects analogue radio transmission from a broadcasting studio and through the relevant delivery facilities.

At the national level, the position is unambiguous: the activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the record does not impose a national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. The important distinction is that this is a statement about the national PMA position for analogue radio broadcasting itself; it should be read as the ownership framework for the activity described, rather than as a claim about adjacent media or audio businesses.

Bali requires a more local reading, but not a pessimistic one. The province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks activities classified as low or medium-low risk. This activity is recorded as medium-high or high risk, so it is not blocked by that moratorium. The Bali position is therefore not a prohibition on PMA registration for this activity. Still, the record expressly calls for verification by address: the proposed location should be checked before treating the local position as settled. That is a location-specific diligence point, not a Bali-side foreign-ownership cap or an additional condition stated for the activity.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali’s moratorium does not block this activity, but the proposed address should still be verified.

  4. Stasiun pemancar dan peta lokasi stasiun pemancar, serta gambar peta wilayah jangkauan siaran dan wilayah layanan siarannya; dan

  3. Sanggup memenuhi persyaratan hak labuh dan/atau izin penggunaan spektrum frekuensi radio sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang- undangan;
  4. Sanggup memenuhi ketentuan penyelenggaraan penyiaran sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;

editorial.headline: Digital Radio Broadcasting: Open Nationally, Viable in Bali at Scale
editorial.standfirst: Digital radio broadcasting is open to full foreign ownership nationally and is not caught by Bali’s PMA moratorium when operating at the stated higher-risk large scale.
editorial.body:
Digital radio broadcasting is the business of bringing radio programming to listeners through digital signals: from the broadcasting studio and transmission facilities to the public, affiliates or subscribers, delivered by terrestrial transmission, cable or satellite. It also includes linear radio broadcasting over the internet—programming transmitted as a scheduled stream rather than selected by a user on demand. The essential character is broadcasting: a continuous service designed to reach an audience, not a catalogue of audio available for individual selection.

The activity is open across every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the code describes an operating activity rather than a narrow format or distribution channel. A registrant may run the technical and editorial infrastructure of digital radio broadcasting, provided the activity remains within that defined broadcast model. Its scope reaches public-facing transmission as well as services directed to affiliates or subscribers, while retaining the common thread of digital radio signals and linear delivery.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% under the stated national basis. There is therefore no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership in this record. For founders assessing the activity at the national level, the ownership position is not qualified by a partial stake: the record states full foreign ownership may be held.

Bali requires the more specific reading. The province permanently blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; Bali records its status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. In practical terms, a foreign investor cannot treat the Bali rule as irrelevant, but neither should they mistake it for a blanket prohibition here. At the stated large scale, this digital-radio activity sits outside the moratorium’s blocked Low and Medium-Low risk categories.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali’s PMA moratorium is real, but this digital-radio activity is not blocked by it at the stated large scale.

editorial.headline: On-Demand Audio Has a Clear Place in Indonesia’s Business Map
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 60103 covers the businesses bringing music, podcasts, audiobooks and other digital audio to listeners on demand.
editorial.body:
Audio on demand is now a distribution business in its own right, and KBLI 60103 gives it a precise home. It covers the operation of services that deliver audio when the listener chooses: music streaming, audio podcasts, audiobooks, digital downloads and digital audio distribution. The catalogue may belong to third parties or be original material produced by the operator. The commercial model is equally broad within the stated scope, accommodating subscription-based delivery as well as advertising-funded services. The defining feature is the organised provision of digital audio on demand.

The activity is open at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth is significant because the code does not reserve this field for a particular size of operator. A small team curating a focused audio catalogue and a larger platform managing extensive distribution can each sit within the same activity description, provided the business being registered is the delivery and distribution of on-demand digital audio. The code recognises both the service layer and the commercial infrastructure behind it.

Nationally, the position for foreign investment is direct. The activity is listed as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the national record permits this activity to be wholly foreign-owned. That openness is grounded in the stated PMA source, rather than an informal reading of the market. For founders considering a foreign-owned structure, this is the central national fact: the activity is open, and the recorded ceiling is complete foreign ownership.

Bali requires a more local reading, but the record does not present a moratorium block here. Bali’s standing moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the province on a permanent, island-wide basis. This activity is recorded in the medium-high/high risk range and is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. Its Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`; the remaining caution is practical and specific rather than a general prohibition: the address must be verified. The honest conclusion is that this activity remains open for PMA in Bali on the record provided, with address-level verification still part of the Bali picture.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, KBLI 60103 permits full foreign ownership, while Bali does not block it under its PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Analog Television Broadcasting: Nationally Open, Address-Specific in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Analog television broadcasting is open to foreign ownership nationally, while Bali does not block it under its moratorium but requires address-level verification.
editorial.body:
For analog television broadcasting and programming, the national position is clear: foreign ownership may reach 100%. In Bali, the activity is not blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium. Its medium-high/high-risk position nevertheless makes address-level verification part of the practical picture.

This activity covers the operation of television broadcasting and programming services using analogue signals. It encompasses work carried out through a television broadcasting studio and the facilities used to transmit video to the public, affiliates, and/or subscribers. Those transmissions may travel through terrestrial networks, cable, or satellite. The emphasis is on the broadcasting operation itself: a service that brings scheduled television programming from studio and transmission infrastructure to its intended audience.

The record leaves the activity open across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth matters because the classification does not confine analogue television broadcasting to a single size of operator. A business registering this activity may therefore sit at any of those scales, while the national PMA position permits foreign ownership up to the stated ceiling of 100%.

Bali requires a more precise reading, not a more pessimistic one. The provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk activities across the island, but this record is marked medium-high/high risk and is expressly not blocked by that moratorium. The remaining instruction is practical rather than prohibitive: verify the position for the specific address. For a founder assessing Bali, that distinction is the essential one—this is not an activity shut out by the moratorium, yet its local treatment should be checked where the operation will be based.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, analogue television broadcasting is not shut out by the moratorium, but its position should be verified for the specific address.

Mencantumkan uraian tentang proyeksi pendapatan (revenue) dari iklan dan/atau pendapatan lain yang sah yang terkait dengan penyelenggaraan penyiaran c. Daftar modal yang ditempatkan dan disetor, serta kepemilikan saham d. Mencantumkan kepemilikan saham pada lembaga penyiaran swasta jasa penyiaran televisi yang sudah dimiliki oleh pemegang saham e. Mencantumkan daftar media cetak, lembaga penyiaran swasta jasa penyiaran radio, lembaga penyiaran swasta jasa penyiaran televisi dan/atau lembaga penyiaran berlangganan yang sudah dimiliki oleh Pelaku Usaha f. Peta wilayah jangkauan siaran g. Sarana dan prasarana penyiaran mencakup kantor, spesifikasi perangkat, dan konfigurasi teknis sistem penyiaran
Menyampaikan daftar susunan pengurus untuk membuktikan bahwa direksi dan komisaris badan hukum Pelaku Usaha tidak ditetapkan dalam daftar hitam penyelenggara

Menyampaikan surat pernyataan: a. Sanggup membayar biaya izin penyelenggaraan penyiaran sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan b. Sanggup memenuhi dokumen kerja sama dengan penyelenggara layanan multipleksing c. Sanggup memenuhi persyaratan izin penggunaan spektrum frekuensi radio sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang- undangan d. Sanggup memenuhi ketentuan penyelenggaraan penyiaran sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang- undangan e. Sanggup memenuhi ketentuan terkait isi siaran sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan f. Sanggup membangun dan/atau menyediakan sarana dan prasarana penyiaran berdasarkan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan sebelum mengajukan permohonan uji laik operasi penyiaran g. Sanggup menyampaikan dokumen yang valid dan benar

Dalam hal penyelenggaraan layanan program siaran dan/atau layanan tambahan jasa penyiaran televisi digital melalui media terestrial, wajib melampirkan dokumen kerja sama dengan penyelenggara layanan multipleksing
Mengajukan permohonan uji laik operasi penyiaran setelah membangun dan/atau menyediakan sarana dan prasarana penyiaran berdasarkan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan
Memperoleh surat keterangan laik operasi penyiaran berdasarkan pelaksanaan uji laik operasi penyiaran sesuai standar kegiatan usaha
Membayar biaya izin penyelenggaraan penyiaran dalam jangka waktu 15 (lima belas) hari kerja sejak surat perintah pembayaran diterbitkan

Pelaku[I-2] Usaha yang telah memperoleh Perizinan Berusaha penyelenggaraan penyiaran dapat memperpanjang Perizinan Berusaha penyelenggaraan penyiaran setelah dilakukan evaluasi pada bulan ke 6 (enam) sampai dengan bulan ke 5 (lima) sebelum masa laku Perizinan Berusaha penyelenggaraan penyiaran berakhir, dengan persyaratan sebagai berikut: a. Pengajuan perpanjangan Perizinan Berusaha penyelenggaraan penyiaran paling cepat 4 (empat) bulan dan paling lambat 3 (tiga) bulan sebelum berakhirnya Perizinan Berusaha penyelenggaraan penyiaran dan memenuhi catatan hasil evaluasi atau dinyatakan layak b. Tidak memiliki kewajiban Penerimaan Negara Bukan Pajak yang terhutang kepada kementerian yang menyelenggarakan urusan pemerintahan di bidang komunikasi dan informatika c. Dalam hal menggunakan spektrum frekuensi radio, wajib menyampaikan izin penggunaan spektrum frekuensi radio (ISR) yang masih berlaku d. Dalam hal menggunakan slot multi-pleksing, wajib menyampaikan dokumen kerja sama dengan penyelenggara layanan multipleksing sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan e. Membayar biaya izin penyelenggaraan penyiaran dalam jangka waktu 2 (dua) bulan sejak surat perintah pembayaran diterbitkan f. Bagi lembaga penyiaran swasta penyelenggara penyiaran layanan multipleksing dapat memperpanjang Perizinan Berusaha penyelenggaraan penyiaran setelah dilakukan evaluasi terhadap: a. data penyelenggaraan penyiaran b. laporan tahunan kinerja operasional
kewajiban: Tidak melanggar ketentuan larangan berupa siaran iklan niaga yang dilakukan dengan: a. Promosi yang dihubungkan dengan ajaran suatu agama, ideologi, pribadi dan/atau kelompok, yang menyinggung perasaan dan/atau merendahkan martabat agama lain, ideologi lain, pribadi lain, atau kelompok lain b. Promosi minuman keras atau sejenisnya dan bahan atau zat adiktif c. Promosi rokok yang memperagakan wujud rokok d. Hal Hal yang bertentangan dengan kesusilaan masyarakat dan nilainilai agama dan/atau e. Eksploitasi anak di bawah umur 18 (delapan belas) tahun
Menyampaikan laporan penyelenggaraan penyiaran kepada Menteri yang menyelenggarakan urusan pemerintahan di bidang komunikasi dan informatika
Isi siaran sesuai dengan perlindungan hak cipta dan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan
Memenuhi ketentuan rencana dasar teknik penyiaran dan persyaratan teknis perangkat penyiaran
Dilarang memindahtangankan Perizinan Berusaha penyelenggaraan penyiaran kepada pihak lain
Membayar biaya izin penyelenggaraan penyiaran berdasarkan zona sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang- undangan
Tidak melanggar ketentuan larangan tidak melakukan siaran lebih dari 3 (tiga) bulan secara akumulatif tanpa pemberitahuan berdasarkan alasan yang sah

Bagi lembaga penyiaran swasta yang menyelenggarakan layanan multipleksing wajib: a. Melaksanakan pembangunan dan/atau penyediaan multipleksing sesuai dengan komitmen dalam Perizinan Berusaha yang diperolehnya dan/atau ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan b. Menyediakan set top box sesuai dengan komitmen dalam Perizinan Berusaha yang diperolehnya dan/atau ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan c. Melakukan kerja sama penggunaan slot multipleksing kepada lembaga penyiaran publik, lembaga penyiaran swasta, dan/atau lembaga penyiaran komunitas yang menyediakan layanan program siaran penyelenggaraan siaran digital d. Menetapkan tarif sewa multipleksing sesuai dengan formula tarif dan hasil evaluasi yang ditetapkan oleh Menteri yang menyelenggarakan urusan pemerintahan di bidang komunikasi dan informatika
Memenuhi ketentuan isi siaran sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan dan
Melaksanakan kewajiban penyelenggaraan penyiaran sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan
Memperoleh PB UMKU izin Stasiun Radio dalam hal menggunakan spektrum frekuensi radio
