editorial.headline: Sharia Banking Beyond the Payments Rail
editorial.standfirst: This activity is open to full foreign ownership nationally and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali, where its large-scale risk classification places it outside the moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 64124 covers forms of sharia banking that sit outside the general banking system. Its work has two connected sides: gathering money from the public as deposits and/or investments, then distributing it to the public as financing and/or other sharia-based forms. The boundary is important. This activity does not provide payment-traffic services, including fund-transfer services. It is therefore banking based on sharia principles that channels public funds into financing, without operating a payments-transfer function.

The scope expressly includes the model of a Bank Perekonomian Rakyat Syariah, including Bank Perkreditan Rakyat Syariah. What matters is the underlying activity: receiving public deposits or investments and extending sharia-based financing or other sharia-based forms to the public. The record opens that activity at every listed business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar—so the classification is not confined to one size of enterprise.

At the national level, the PMA position remains TERBUKA and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. The national ceiling is 100%, so foreign ownership can reach full ownership nationally. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-backed registration, that is the central national fact: this code is open, and the record gives no national foreign-share cap below full ownership.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion on the supplied record. The activity is not blocked for PMA registration under the island-wide, permanent Bali moratorium and is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The specific reason is its OSS risk classification at the Besar scale: Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, or Medium-High/High. That classification is given as the reason the activity is not blocked by the moratorium. The Bali record states no separate Bali foreign-ownership percentage, local-partnership requirement, or other Bali-side condition for this activity. On these facts, the Bali position is genuinely open rather than an apparent opening concealing a registration block.
editorial.pullQuote: The national ceiling is 100%, so foreign ownership can reach full ownership nationally.

It includes primary savings and loan cooperatives, secondary cooperatives, and savings and loan business units of cooperatives.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is 100% open to foreign ownership (PMA). In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.

editorial.headline: Conventional Cooperative Credit, Designed Around Its Members
editorial.standfirst: A conventional cooperative lending activity built on member deposits, member credit and an open national foreign-ownership position.
editorial.body:
This activity covers conventional cooperative credit: collecting deposits from members and extending loans back to those members to support their economic welfare. Returns may be agreed through profit-sharing arrangements or reasonable interest. Its practical forms include primary savings-and-loan cooperatives, secondary savings-and-loan cooperatives, and savings-and-loan business units within cooperatives. The recorded scope also reaches the service networks of cash offices and auxiliary branch offices for primary savings-and-loan cooperatives.

The defining feature is the member relationship. This is an activity conducted through a cooperative structure, with deposits and credit circulating within its membership rather than being described as a general retail lending business. It is open across the recorded business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the activity can be registered from micro through large scale without changing the underlying purpose set out in the scope: financing the economic welfare of cooperative members through conventional savings and lending.

Nationally, the activity is open to PMA registration, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali does not block it for PMA registration. The province’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis; this activity sits outside that block in the supplied Bali assessment. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which is why the moratorium does not prevent registration. The Bali position is therefore genuinely open on this record, rather than a national permission undone by a provincial restriction.

That distinction gives the activity a clear regulatory reading. A founder considering a conventional cooperative credit operation should begin with the cooperative’s member-centred model, then place the intended operation at the appropriate recorded scale. The national PMA position permits full foreign ownership, while the Bali assessment confirms that the province’s stated moratorium does not close this activity to PMA. The result is a straightforward framework: conventional member deposits and lending, open across all listed scales, nationally open to PMA, and not blocked in Bali by the cited risk-based moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not block this member-centred cooperative credit activity for PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Sharia Cooperative Lending: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali at Large Scale
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 64192 covers member-funded, member-focused sharia lending through cooperative structures, with full national foreign ownership and no Bali moratorium block at large scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 64192 concerns sharia-based cooperative lending: the gathering of savings from members and the extension of loans or credit back to those members, directed toward their economic welfare. Its centre of gravity is therefore a member-facing financial activity conducted through cooperative structures under sharia principles, rather than lending to an undefined public market. The scope includes primary savings-and-loan cooperatives, secondary savings-and-loan cooperatives, and cooperative savings-and-loan business units operated on sharia principles. It also expressly includes the cash-office and sub-branch service networks of primary KSPPS operations.

The activity is open across the full recorded scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the code is not confined to a small cooperative format; the record recognises it from micro through large scale. In practical terms, the commercial identity remains consistent across those scales: members place savings with the cooperative, and members receive credit from it under sharia principles. The code’s purpose is tied explicitly to the economic welfare of those members.

Nationally, the investment position is straightforward. At the national level, the activity holds TERBUKA status, and foreign ownership may reach 100%. The applicable PMA source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower foreign-ownership cap to qualify: at the national level, the recorded ceiling is full foreign ownership.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The province’s moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. For this activity, however, the record states that the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by that moratorium. The Bali status is therefore not a prohibition: for a large-scale registration, this code sits outside the moratorium’s blocked risk bands. The honest conclusion is clean—this activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali does not block its PMA registration on the stated moratorium basis at Besar scale.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali does not block its PMA registration on the stated moratorium basis at Besar scale.

editorial.headline: Microfinance With a Community Mandate
editorial.standfirst: Conventional non-bank microfinance supports small enterprise and community empowerment—open nationally to 100% foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Conventional non-bank microfinance is finance with a wider social purpose. This activity covers microfinance conducted on a conventional basis, combining lending for micro-scale businesses with enterprise-development services and community empowerment. It may serve members and the public through loans, savings management, and advisory services for business development. The defining point is that the institution is not organised solely to seek profit: finance sits alongside practical support for local economic activity.

The scope describes an institutional field rooted in community finance. It includes conventional microfinance institutions such as village banks, village granaries, market banks, employee banks, and rural credit bodies, as well as similar institutions. The activity is open across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That breadth matters because the essential character does not change with scale: lending, savings management, business-development assistance, and community empowerment remain part of the same conventional non-bank microfinance proposition.

Nationally, the PMA position is TERBUKA. The foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, under the cited Presidential Regulations. In plain terms, a foreign investor may hold the full permitted ownership interest nationally in this activity. There is no lower national foreign-share cap recorded for it, so the national position is straightforward: conventional non-bank microfinance is open to PMA at up to 100% foreign ownership.

Bali does not reverse that position. The provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities, but this activity is not blocked by that rule. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Medium-High or High, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For founders considering a Bali registration, that is the decisive distinction: PMA registration is not blocked by the Bali moratorium for this activity. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the relevant ownership figure, while the Bali record adds no separate foreign-ownership percentage or partnership condition.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling is meaningful here because Bali’s moratorium does not block the activity.

editorial.headline: Sharia Microfinance, with a Wider Mandate Than Lending
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers non-bank sharia microfinance that combines micro-scale funding, savings management, business development and community empowerment.
editorial.body:
This is a non-bank sharia microfinance activity whose remit is deliberately broader than financing alone. Every part of the operation is conducted on sharia principles, spanning business-development services and community empowerment alongside micro-scale financing for members and the wider community. It can also include savings management and business-development consulting. The defining idea is a financial institution serving practical enterprise and community needs through a fully sharia-based model, rather than a business organised solely to seek profit.

The category is for sharia microfinance institutions carrying out that combined role. The record identifies examples such as Bank Wakaf Mikro, Baitul Maal wa Tamwil and Baitul Tamwil Muhammaddiyah, as well as similar institutions. That is useful context for the activity’s character: financing sits beside advisory work, savings management, enterprise development and social empowerment. An applicant should therefore understand the classification as describing the institution’s whole operating purpose, not merely a single financing service.

At the national level, foreign investment is permitted for this activity up to 100% foreign ownership. It is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. In Bali, the picture remains open on the record provided. The provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities across the island, but this activity is recorded as not blocked by that moratorium: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. Bali’s status is therefore recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, rather than as a prohibition on PMA registration.

That distinction matters because the Bali result is not a separate ownership cap or an implied local-partnership requirement. The national ceiling remains 100%, while the Bali note explains why the provincial low- and medium-low-risk moratorium does not block this activity at the stated large-scale risk level. The classification should be read in full: a sharia microfinance institution with a community-development mandate, open nationally across the listed business scales and not blocked in Bali by the moratorium described here.
editorial.pullQuote: This is sharia microfinance with a community-development mandate, not financing in isolation.

editorial.headline: KBLI 64199: Other Monetary Intermediation, Clearly Framed
editorial.standfirst: A deposit-taking and lending activity open to every business scale nationally, with up to 100% foreign ownership and no Bali moratorium block at Large scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 64199 covers monetary intermediation that does not sit elsewhere in the classification: receiving deposits or similar deposit-like funds, then extending credit or other forms of lending. The scope is broad enough to include support for credit in forms such as loans, secured loans, mortgage lending and consumer credit cards. It is generally carried out by financial institutions other than the central bank, including postal giro and savings activities, specialised deposit-taking institutions authorised to lend, and payment-order activities. The defining thread is straightforward: accepting funds and providing credit or loans within this particular residual category of monetary intermediation.

The activity is open at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the record does not confine it to a narrow size of operator; its stated availability runs from micro through large enterprise. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100. In plain terms, the national record permits a foreign stake of up to 100% for this activity. That is the ownership ceiling stated here, rather than an implication drawn from the activity’s financial character or from any adjacent classification.

Bali does not reverse that national position for this record. The province’s island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium applies where OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low. For KBLI 64199, however, the record says that OSS risk at the Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. Its Bali status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and it is explicitly not blocked by the moratorium. There is no separate Bali foreign-ownership percentage or partnership condition recorded here. The honest reading is consequently clean: this activity is nationally open to up to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali does not block its PMA registration under the stated moratorium because of its Large-scale OSS risk position.

That does not turn the classification into a generic label for every financial service. Its scope is anchored in deposit acceptance and the provision of credit or other loans, with examples that show how varied credit support can be. For founders, the useful discipline is to keep the proposed business aligned to that stated core, then read the national ownership position and Bali treatment exactly as the record sets them out. The record supports openness across the listed scales and a non-blocked Bali outcome; it does not add further conditions beyond those facts.
editorial.pullQuote: The record supports up to 100% foreign ownership nationally and a non-blocked Bali outcome for this activity.

editorial.headline: A Holding Company’s Narrow Mandate Meets Bali’s PMA Stop
editorial.standfirst: A holding company may own and consolidate subsidiaries; national foreign ownership is open, but Bali blocks its PMA registration under a permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is for the parent at the top of a corporate group: a company that holds and manages equity interests in one or more subsidiaries and bears responsibility as their owner. Its role is ownership, not the daily command of the businesses beneath it. It may exercise control, consolidate financials and take responsibility for subsidiary activity, but the record draws a firm line at active management. Strategic planning, decision-making and head-office administration are not the work described here; neither are own-account financial-market trading or asset management performed for a fee or under contract.

This makes it an appropriate registration for a group structure where the parent’s essential task is to own the subsidiaries, rather than to sell management services back to them. A company with equity stakes may sit above a single subsidiary or several, but it cannot use this activity as a broad mandate to run their operations. The activity is open across Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. That breadth speaks to the size at which the activity may be registered, while the defining test remains its narrow ownership function.

At the national level, the position is straightforward: PMA status is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. For a foreign-owned parent that otherwise belongs within this ownership-only role, the supplied record sets no lower foreign-stake cap. But Bali requires a separate, more exact reading. In Bali today, this activity cannot be registered as a PMA by a foreigner. At the Large scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope, which brings it within Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registrations for every Low and Medium-Low risk activity, recorded in May 2026.

The distinction is not a technical footnote. It determines whether a founder is choosing a holding-company format for ownership and financial consolidation, or assuming that national openness automatically translates into a Bali registration route. Here it does not. The activity remains precisely bounded by what the parent does not do—no services to the subsidiaries it owns and no active management of them—and its Bali PMA outcome is plainly blocked by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali today, this activity cannot be registered as a PMA by a foreigner.

editorial.headline: Conduit Financing: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A group funding vehicle may be nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet the Bali PMA route is closed by the province’s permanent moratorium.
editorial.body:
Conduit financing is a tightly defined group funding function. A unit formed within a financial or non-financial group gathers or borrows funds—mainly from open markets—and sends them onward to a parent company or another entity in the same corporate group. The code’s focus is the conduit itself: a dedicated vehicle through which a group raises or collects money before directing it within its own structure. It describes the flow of funds as an internal group arrangement, with the unit serving as the channel between the funding source and related group entities.

That can take more than one corporate form. The scope expressly includes captive financial institutions engaged in loans between entities in the same group. It also includes brass plate companies involved in gathering funds and channelling them to their parent company. These may be directly or indirectly owned by non-resident units; most of their balance sheets can consist of claims and liabilities with non-resident units, while they may have few or no employees and little or no physical presence in the jurisdiction where the company sits. The code thus accommodates a corporate funding vehicle whether it is embedded in a financial group or a non-financial one.

At the national level, the registration position is unambiguous. The activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Its permitted scale listing spans Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That means the national record does not reserve the activity to a single size of undertaking; it records access across each of those four scales. For the group establishing the vehicle, the central test is whether its actual role matches the stated conduit function: raising or borrowing funds and routing them to a parent or another group entity. The cited PMA source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

That national openness does not translate to a Bali address. The activity is marked Closed (Bali moratorium) and blocked for PMA registration. The stated reason is that its Besar scale is Low risk, which brings it within the provincial PMA moratorium: all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI are blocked for a Bali address, island-wide and permanently. A national 100% ownership ceiling is not, in itself, permission to register the activity as PMA in Bali. For this activity, the practical conclusion is direct: a foreigner cannot register it as PMA in Bali today. The national entry remains open, but the Bali PMA route is closed by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% ownership ceiling is not, in itself, permission to register the activity as PMA in Bali.

editorial.headline: Money Market Funds: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Money market fund activity can be wholly foreign-owned nationally; whether Bali's PMA moratorium applies to this activity is unresolved, pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.
editorial.body:
Whether a foreign investor can register money market fund activity as PMA at a Bali address is unresolved today — the earlier ‘blocked’ verdict was based on a risk classification carried over from a different activity (code-number collision) and has been detached, so it is unresolved rather than lifted. That question sits beside—not against—the national position: KBLI 64310 is TERBUKA nationally, open to foreign investment through a PMA company. The divergence is the essential fact for a founder considering this classification. National openness establishes the permitted ownership ceiling; Bali’s rule determines whether PMA registration is available at all in the province. Each part of the record must be read in its own jurisdictional setting.

KBLI 64310 covers money market fund activity. Its core is a collective investment scheme that gathers money from the public by issuing shares or units, then invests the proceeds primarily in short-term assets. The record identifies assets with a maturity of one year or less as the example of this short duration. The units can be regarded as substitutes similar to deposits. These details give the activity its shape: public capital is pooled, participation is represented through shares or units, and the investment focus is primarily short term. The classification is framed around that collective scheme and the uses to which its proceeds are put.

As to scale, the activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Those are the four business-scale labels expressly listed, from Mikro through Besar. In the national PMA setting, the TERBUKA designation is paired with maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In direct terms, a foreign stake may reach 100% nationally. The scale listing and the foreign-ownership ceiling are complementary facts: the first sets out the listed scales open to the activity, while the second conveys the national limit on foreign participation.

Bali's earlier verdict here was that PMA registration is blocked, on the stated reason that the activity carried a specific risk classification at the Besar scale bringing it within Bali's PMA moratorium. That risk classification was carried over from a different activity (code-number collision) and has been detached, so the block is unresolved rather than lifted: whether the moratorium applies cannot be determined until the true risk tier is established. Treat a Bali setup as unconfirmed and verify with the Bali Zero team first, notwithstanding national openness to foreign investment through a PMA company.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness establishes the permitted ownership ceiling; Bali’s rule determines whether PMA registration is available at all in the province.

editorial.headline: Investment Funds Beyond the Money Market: Open Nationally, Closed in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to foreign investment, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium prevents registration at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA at a Bali address today. That conclusion does not diminish its national position; it clarifies the geographical divide built into the record. Nationally, this activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%; Bali’s status marks it closed under the PMA moratorium. For a founder, the address is therefore not an administrative afterthought but the fact that changes the practical outcome.

The code concerns non-money-market investment funds: collective investment schemes that gather money from the public by issuing shares or units. It then follows the destination of that pool. The proceeds are invested chiefly in financial assets other than short-term assets and in non-financial assets—typically real estate. Its shares or units are not intended as deposit-like substitutes. The defining picture, therefore, is of a public-facing pooled fund whose capital is directed into the stated financial or non-financial asset base.

Registration is open to enterprises carrying out this fund activity at every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The scale field gives the classification a broad national range, but it does not erase the separate Bali test. At national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national classification permits full foreign ownership up to that ceiling. The national basis recorded for this position is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. It is the national framework, not a Bali registration clearance.

The Bali limitation is specific and dispositive. The record marks the activity Closed (Bali moratorium) because its Besar scale is classified as Rendah. Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium applies to the Low and Medium-Low risk bands stated in the record; this activity falls into the blocking side through that Low designation. As a result, a Bali address cannot be used for its PMA registration today. The national 100% ceiling does not contradict this conclusion: it describes the national ownership position, while the Bali moratorium closes the local registration route.

editorial.headline: Trusts, Estates and Agency: Nationally Open, Closed to Bali PMA
editorial.standfirst: This activity can be wholly foreign-owned nationally, yet a foreign investor cannot register it at a Bali address under the province-wide PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register KBLI 64330 at a Bali address today. That conclusion sits beside—not against—its national position: the activity is nationally open to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In Bali, the record identifies the large-scale activity as low risk and therefore caught by the island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium for all low and medium-low risk activities. The national ownership ceiling describes what is possible nationally; it does not secure a Bali registration.

At its centre, this is an activity for legal entities that assemble securities, estates and other financial assets for shareholders or beneficiaries, without managing those assets as a collective-investment scheme. The portfolio may be shaped toward a particular investment character—such as diversification, risk, return or price volatility—but the entity acts in the name of those with an interest in the assets. Its work can arise under the terms of a trust agreement, a will or an agency agreement. The scope also includes trusts, estates and similar financial entities, as well as family trusts that hold financial assets for individuals and families.

The activity has a deliberately particular economic profile. These entities receive interest, dividends and other property income, while having little or even no employment and no receipts from selling services. The scope also reaches shareholding companies that do not own or control equity, and venture companies funded solely through shares that do not charge fees. It is therefore a holding and beneficiary-facing structure, not a fee-driven operating business. Where income is earned by selling goods or services, that does not fit this activity’s stated scope.

Nationally, registration is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth should not obscure the Bali result. For a PMA applicant seeking a Bali address, the record’s status is blocked because the large-scale classification falls within the provincial moratorium’s low-risk coverage. The practical reading is crisp: national openness and full foreign ownership remain real features of this activity, but they do not override Bali’s island-wide PMA restriction.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and full foreign ownership do not override Bali’s island-wide PMA restriction.

editorial.headline: Financial Leasing: Asset Finance With Bali’s PMA Door Open
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers finance-led leasing of client-selected assets, with national foreign ownership open to 100% and no Bali PMA moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Financial leasing is finance for the acquisition of assets in a client’s or customer’s name. The financier or lessor remains the legal owner, while the client or lessee carries the risk throughout the period of use—usually one that reflects the asset’s expected useful life—and receives the full benefit of using it. The model includes leasing arrangements with an option to purchase durable goods, such as vehicles. Its centre of gravity is therefore not simple rental, but the financing structure behind an asset’s use and eventual option rights.

The scope also accommodates conventional financing companies whose business covers the financing of goods and/or services: investment finance, working-capital finance, multipurpose finance, and other financing activities approved by the Financial Services Authority. Alongside those activities, such a company may conduct operating leases and/or fee-based activities, provided these do not conflict with financial-services law. The distinction matters: operating leasing without an option to purchase is not itself included in this activity’s defined scope, even though conventional financing companies in the group may undertake operating leases within the stated regulatory boundary.

Registration is open across every stated business scale, from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah and Besar. At the national level, the activity is TERBUKA to foreign investment and carries a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the record permits full foreign ownership at the national level; there is no lower foreign-equity cap to infer or work around from this entry.

For Bali, the position remains open rather than provisional. The province’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide. This activity is not blocked by that rule: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk classification is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, placing it outside the moratorium’s blocked risk bands. A foreign investor can therefore register this activity in Bali today, with the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling intact and no Bali-specific ownership reduction or partnership condition stated in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can therefore register this activity in Bali today, with the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling intact.

editorial.headline: International Trade Finance: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: International trade finance permits up to 100% foreign ownership nationally, yet foreign investors cannot register this activity at a Bali address under the island-wide PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the Bali answer is unambiguous: this activity cannot be registered there today through a foreign-investment (PMA) vehicle. That result does not recast the activity itself; it reflects Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. The record identifies the Besar form of this activity as Low risk, so the moratorium blocks a PMA registration using a Bali address. The decisive distinction is geographical: the national position is open, while Bali prevents the foreign-investment registration.

At its centre, this is international trade finance: providing financial support, often with additional services, to help entities send goods to and receive goods from around the world. It concentrates on the financial underpinning of international goods flows. The stated scope expressly includes Indonesia’s export-financing institution, giving the category a clear institutional reference as well as its wider commercial purpose. The relevant activity is therefore the support that enables cross-border trade, including accompanying services where they are combined with that financial support. It should be read as a scope for a provider of that support, rather than as a description of the goods-moving operation itself.

Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA—open to PMA—with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. A foreign investor may therefore hold the full permitted interest at the national level. The entry is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, placing the stated scope within the record’s full range of business sizes rather than confining it to one tier. Those scales answer the question of who can register by size: a business operating at any of the four listed scales. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 is the record’s cited national source for that open status and ownership ceiling.

Bali changes the conclusion without changing those national facts. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities from PMA registration, island-wide and permanently. For this activity, the record ties the block to the Besar scale’s Low-risk designation and cites gubernatorial letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, issued in May 2026. The operative Bali fact is the block, not an alternative local ownership ceiling. At a Bali address, the PMA route is closed for this activity, even though the national framework otherwise permits up to 100% foreign ownership.
editorial.pullQuote: At a Bali address, the PMA route is closed for this activity, even though national rules permit up to 100% foreign ownership.

editorial.headline: Factoring: Buying the Claim, Not Lending Against It
editorial.standfirst: Factoring is the purchase of trade receivables at a discount, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Factoring begins with the purchase of a third party’s trade receivables—such as invoices—at an agreed discount or return. The defining transaction is the acquisition of the receivable itself, rather than debt financing that merely takes receivables as collateral. That distinction establishes the activity’s centre of gravity: a business acquires claims arising from trade, on terms that include a specified discount or return. The scope also expressly includes conventional finance companies that finance goods and/or services through investment financing, working-capital financing, multipurpose financing, or other financing business approved by the Financial Services Authority. Those conventional companies may also undertake operating leases and fee-based activities where these do not conflict with financial-services law.

The registration is open at Micro, Small, Medium, and Large scales. Scale is therefore a clear part of the picture, while a single commercial definition remains at the centre. Across those scales, the activity is anchored in buying trade receivables from third parties at a specified discount or return. For conventional finance companies, the description is broader in operational form but still bounded: financing of goods and/or services may take the stated investment, working-capital, multipurpose, or other Authority-approved forms. Operating leases and fee-based work are additional possibilities in that setting, subject to their consistency with financial-services legislation. The record thus describes both a focused transaction—buying receivables—and the conventional finance-company operations included within this activity.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain terms, the national position permits a foreign stake up to full ownership. Bali does not block this activity for PMA registration. Its provincial status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is precise: at the Large scale, the OSS risk designation is Medium-High/High, so the activity is not blocked by the moratorium. That matters because Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA rule blocks every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The Bali position is therefore specific rather than assumed: this activity has no Bali PMA block, while its Large-scale classification sits outside the moratorium’s Low and Medium-Low reach.
editorial.pullQuote: In plain terms, the national position permits a foreign stake up to full ownership.

editorial.headline: Securitisation Is Open Nationally, but Not for Bali PMA Registration
editorial.standfirst: Securitisation is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium stops registration at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
At a Bali address, a foreigner cannot register KBLI 64940 for PMA today. That is the decisive local position, even though the activity is nationally open to PMA and carries a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The two propositions are not competing descriptions. One states the national setting for foreign investment; the other determines whether that PMA registration can be placed at a Bali address.

The activity is securitisation in the exact sense recorded here: issuing debt securities whose coupon payments and principal repayments are guaranteed by payments from particular assets, or by future revenue streams that do not originate with the issuing unit. The scope expressly includes the securitisation of mortgage credit by a secondary housing finance company, and the securitisation of business credit. Coupon and principal obligations are therefore connected to those identified payment streams. The record makes clear that future income is relevant only when it does not originate with the issuing unit. Both stated inclusions sit within that same definition of debt payments guaranteed by the specified source of payments or income.

For registration purposes, it is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. A business using this code is therefore registering the described securitisation activity across that full scale range. This is a national registration proposition stated with all four named scales. The included forms matter: mortgage-credit securitisation is identified in connection with a secondary housing finance company, while business-credit securitisation is also within the stated scope. That national scale range makes the activity available at each of the four stated business sizes; it does not override Bali’s separate PMA position.

Bali’s restriction is tied in the record to the Besar scale being classed as “Rendah”, which brings the activity within the Bali PMA moratorium. The provincial rule is expressed as an island-wide, permanent block on PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. Its practical result here is direct: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a PMA registration route for this activity at a Bali address. For a foreign founder, the address question comes first, because the activity is locally closed to PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a PMA registration route for this activity at a Bali address.

editorial.headline: Infrastructure Finance, Open Nationally and Clear of Bali’s PMA Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: Conventional infrastructure finance is nationally open to full foreign ownership, and its higher-risk Large-scale profile keeps it outside Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Conventional infrastructure finance is the business of putting capital behind infrastructure projects: direct lending, refinancing infrastructure previously financed by another party, and subordinated loans connected to infrastructure funding. It is a defined financing activity rather than a general advisory mandate. The enterprise at its centre is an infrastructure-finance company operating on a conventional basis, with the work anchored in the provision of funds to infrastructure projects.

Its scope can extend beyond the core loan book. In support of that business, an infrastructure-finance company may provide credit enhancement, advisory services, equity investment, and assistance in finding a swap market connected to infrastructure financing. It may also provide other related activities or facilities, but those require approval from the Financial Services Authority. That distinction matters: the record presents these as supporting capabilities of the infrastructure-finance business, not as a free-standing promise that every associated service is automatically available.

Registration is open across the full scale range: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. At the national level, the activity is open to foreign investment, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain terms, the national position allows full foreign ownership for this activity. The scale range also makes clear that the classification is not confined to a single size of operator, even though the substance of the activity remains infrastructure financing.

Bali’s position is also comparatively direct. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk across the island. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium: at the Large scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High or High. A foreign investor can therefore register this activity in Bali today; the Bali record does not impose a separate foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition. The useful reading is not that Bali creates a special exception, but that this activity sits outside the moratorium’s Low and Medium-Low risk boundary.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today because its Large-scale risk profile sits outside the provincial PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Islamic Infrastructure Finance Is Open Nationally—and in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers sharia-compliant funding for infrastructure projects, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali PMA block on the record provided.
editorial.body:
This activity is the business of financing infrastructure entirely under sharia principles. Its core work is to provide funds to infrastructure projects: through direct lending, refinancing infrastructure that another party has already financed, or subordinated loans connected to infrastructure finance. The defining feature is not simply that money is being raised or lent, but that the financing activity is conducted wholly within sharia principles and directed at infrastructure.

The registrant contemplated here is a sharia infrastructure-finance company. Beyond the principal financing work, the record allows supporting functions including credit enhancement, advisory services, equity investment, efforts to locate a swap market related to infrastructure finance, and other facilities connected with infrastructure financing. Those additional activities are not automatic: the record places them after approval from the Financial Services Authority under sharia principles. The activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar business scales, making its formal scope broader than a large-project-only reading might suggest.

Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. Put simply, the national record allows foreign investors to own the business in full. Bali does not reverse that position. The Bali assessment is not blocked for PMA registration, and its stated reason is that OSS risk at the Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi or Tinggi. That places the activity outside Bali’s permanent province-wide PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. A foreign investor can therefore register this activity in Bali on the record provided; there is no Bali-specific foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition stated here.

The practical distinction matters because this is a specialised finance activity with a defined infrastructure purpose, not a generic funding category. Its national openness and Bali status align in this record: full foreign ownership is available nationally, while Bali’s moratorium does not block the activity. The operative boundary remains the sharia basis of the business and, for its additional supporting functions, the approval condition stated by the record.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali on the record provided; there is no Bali-specific foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition stated here.

editorial.headline: Conventional Pawn Activity: Nationally Open, Bali’s Risk Line
editorial.standfirst: Conventional secured lending, custody and valuation services are open nationally to foreign investment and available at every business scale.
editorial.body:
Conventional pawn activity is a financial-service business built around secured lending. It includes advancing cash against collateral under pawn law, as well as lending secured by fiduciary collateral. Its scope also reaches the safekeeping of valuable goods and valuation services—two functions that place custody and assessment alongside the loan itself. Other commission-based activities that do not conflict with financial-services law may also form part of the business, as can other activities approved by the Financial Services Authority.

The activity is open to micro, small, medium and large enterprises. That breadth matters because the code is not framed as a niche service reserved for one size of operator: it describes a conventional pawn business whose core work can combine secured lending, valuables custody and appraisal. The common thread is conventional operation. The record does not present this as a purely lending-only category; the handling, safekeeping and assessment of pledged valuables are expressly within its stated scope.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is direct: the activity is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In other words, foreign investment is permitted nationally at the full stated ceiling. That national position should be read together with the activity’s full-scale availability, rather than as a shorthand for any particular operating model beyond the services set out in the scope.

Bali does not block PMA registration for this activity under its island-wide moratorium on low- and medium-low-risk KBLI. The Bali record places the activity, at the large-enterprise scale, in the medium-high/high risk range; that is why it is not caught by that moratorium. For a founder considering Bali, the honest conclusion is neither a special Bali ownership cap nor a prohibition: national foreign ownership may reach 100%, and the Bali moratorium does not block this code. The practical distinction is the risk profile recorded for the large scale, not an invented local restriction.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%, and Bali’s moratorium does not block this activity.

editorial.headline: Sharia Pawn Activity, With a Clear National and Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 64954 covers sharia-based pawn activity, from secured lending and valuation to the safekeeping of valuables, and is open to foreign investment nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 64954 is the category for pawn activity conducted wholly under sharia principles. Its scope is broader than the simple image of an item exchanged for cash: it includes lending secured under pawn law, lending secured by fiduciary collateral, the safekeeping of valuable goods, and appraisal services. The defining feature is not one particular item or customer, but that the entire activity is organised on sharia principles.

The category also describes a sharia pawn business whose core work includes those same forms of secured lending, custody and valuation. It can encompass commission-based activities that are unrelated to pawn operations where they do not conflict with financial-services laws and regulations, as well as other business activities with the approval of the Financial Services Authority. That makes the classification precise about its centre of gravity: secured finance, valuables handling and appraisal, all within a sharia operating model.

The activity is open at every listed business scale: micro, small, medium and large. Nationally, it is marked open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the record presents no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. The stated national basis is Presidential Regulation 10/2021 and 49/2021.

Bali does not change that result into a prohibition. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk across the island, but this activity is recorded as not blocked by that moratorium. At the large-business scale, its OSS risk classification is Medium-High/High, which is why the Bali record places it in the “OK_or_HIGHER_RISK” position rather than treating it as moratorium-blocked. For a foreign investor considering sharia pawn activity in Bali, the honest reading is straightforward: the code is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not barred from PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium rule.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign investor considering sharia pawn activity in Bali, the code is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not barred by the stated moratorium rule.

editorial.headline: Tapera Fund Management: Open Nationally, Address-Checked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity manages public housing savings funds, with national foreign ownership open to 100% and Bali access not blocked by the moratorium, subject to address verification.
editorial.body:
Managing public housing savings is a distinct fund-management activity, centred on Tapera and focused on the fund itself. The scope covers handling public housing savings funds from mobilisation, through accumulation, to utilisation. It is a continuous mandate rather than a single moment in the fund’s life: the record allows these functions to be performed separately or together. The activity can be carried out conventionally or under sharia principles, both expressly within its defined scope.

The record makes it available at every listed business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That span matters because the core description does not change with scale. In each case, the formal activity remains the management of Tapera funds, structured around mobilisation, accumulation and/or utilisation. Nor does the record split conventional and sharia operation into separate activities here: both are recognised ways in which the same fund-management activity may be carried out. For a reader weighing the fit of the category, that fund-management focus is the decisive feature.

Nationally, the investment position is direct. The PMA status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. That full ceiling means the national ownership field permits a foreign investor to hold the entire equity stake; it does not impose a lower foreign cap. The basis given in the record is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Read together, those fields make the national position clear: foreign investment is open for this activity, including at the stated maximum of 100%.

Bali calls for a more exact reading, but not a pessimistic one. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and its note identifies the activity as medium-high/high risk. It is therefore not blocked by the province’s island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium. The note nevertheless requires verification per address. Bali does not shut this activity out under that moratorium, yet a PMA registration must still be checked against the specific address.

data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan pemberian kredit lainnya yang tidak dicakup di tempat lain, seperti pembiayaan investasi, pembiayaan modal kerja, dan pembiayaan multiguna, yang diselenggarakan secara konvensional atau berdasarkan prinsip syariah. Kelompok ini juga mencakup kegiatan rentenir.

per_skala.scope_uraian: Usaha perusahaan pembiayaan yang diselenggarakan secara konvensional, dengan kegiatan usaha meliputi pembiayaan barang dan/atau jasa, yaitu: pembiayaan investasi; pembiayaan modal kerja; pembiayaan multiguna; dan/atau kegiatan usaha pembiayaan lain berdasarkan persetujuan Otoritas Jasa Keuangan. Selain kegiatan usaha tersebut, perusahaan pembiayaan konvensional dalam kelompok ini dapat melakukan sewa operasi (operating lease) dan/atau kegiatan berbasis imbal jasa sepanjang tidak bertentangan dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di sektor jasa keuangan.

editorial.headline: Credit Beyond the Usual Categories: KBLI 64959
editorial.standfirst: A broad credit-activity classification spanning conventional and sharia financing, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 64959 covers other credit-granting activities not classified elsewhere. Its practical territory includes investment financing, working-capital financing and multipurpose financing, whether conducted conventionally or under sharia principles. The scope also expressly includes moneylending. This is therefore a classification with a wide financing remit, but one defined by the forms of credit activity set out in its scope rather than by a single product or customer segment.

The classification also accommodates financing companies operating on a conventional basis. Their activities may include financing goods and/or services through investment, working-capital and multipurpose financing, as well as other financing activities approved by the Financial Services Authority. Within the stated scope, a conventional financing company may also undertake operating leases and fee-based activities, provided these do not conflict with financial-services laws and regulations. A company whose entire business is sharia financing may undertake sale-and-purchase financing, investment financing and service financing.

The registration field is broad in terms of business scale: micro, small, medium and large enterprises are all listed as open to this activity. For a foreign investor, the national position is straightforward: ownership may reach 100%. That national ceiling is supported by the stated Presidential Regulation sources, and it means the record does not describe a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity at the national level.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk, island-wide. This activity is not marked as blocked: at the large-enterprise scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High or High, placing it outside that moratorium’s stated reach. Bali’s status is therefore recorded as OK or Higher Risk—not as a prohibition. The distinction matters: national openness is real here, and the Bali record does not impose a separate foreign-ownership figure or partnership condition; it identifies the risk classification as the reason the moratorium does not block PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign investor, the national position is straightforward: ownership may reach 100%.

data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup aktivtias pembiayaan melalui penyertaan modal dan/atau pembiayaan untuk jangka waktu tertentu dalam rangka pengembangan usaha pasangan usaha atau debitur, pengelolaan dana ventura, dan kegiatan usaha lain yang diselenggarakan secara konvensional.

per_skala.scope_uraian: Usaha modal ventura yang diselenggarakan secara konvensional, dengan kegiatan usaha meliputi: penyertaan saham (equity participation); penyertaan melalui pembelian obligasi konversi (quasi equity participation); pembiayaan melalui pembelian surat utang yang diterbitkan pasangan usaha pada tahap rintisan awal (start-up) dan/atau pengembangan usaha; dan/atau pembiayaan usaha produktif. Dalam melakukan usaha modal ventura, perusahaan modal ventura dapat mengelola dana ventura. Selain usaha modal ventura, perusahaan modal ventura dapat menyelenggarakan kegiatan usaha lain yaitu kegiatan jasa berbasis fee dan/atau kegiatan usaha lain dengan persetujuan Otoritas Jasa Keuangan. Kegiatan usaha modal ventura dapat disertai dengan pendampingan kepada pasangan usaha dan/atau debitur.

editorial.headline: Conventional Venture Capital: Open Nationally, Not Moratorium-Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers conventional venture financing and fund management, with a 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Conventional venture capital, as defined here, is a financing activity for developing partner businesses or debtors through equity participation and/or financing for a defined period. Its toolkit is specific: shareholdings; quasi-equity through convertible bonds; purchases of debt securities issued by a partner business at its early start-up and/or development stage; and financing for productive business. A venture capital company may also manage venture funds and accompany partner businesses and/or debtors. The through-line is structured financing in support of a business’s formation or development.

The scope also recognises fee-based services and other business activities undertaken with Financial Services Authority approval. Registration is open at every stated business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the record does not reserve the activity for the largest financial institutions; it places the same conventional venture-capital category within the available registration scales.

Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign shareholding is not capped below full ownership for this activity at the national level. The cited PMA basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is the point to keep clear: the national position is fully open on the ownership percentage recorded here, while the operational scope remains the defined venture-financing and fund-management activity rather than an undefined financial-services mandate.

Bali does not reverse that national position through its permanent island-wide PMA moratorium. The Bali status is recorded as OK or higher risk, and the record states that, at the Large scale, the OSS risk is Medium-High/High; the activity is therefore not blocked by the moratorium. That moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the province, but it is not the barrier for this activity. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, the honest reading is straightforward: the recorded national 100% ceiling remains relevant, and this activity is not moratorium-blocked in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is defined by structured financing in support of a business’s formation or development.

editorial.headline: Sharia Venture Capital, With Bali’s Risk Line in View
editorial.standfirst: A fully Sharia-based venture-capital activity, open nationally to foreign investment at every listed scale and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Sharia venture capital is not simply capital with a faith-based label. This activity covers venture-capital operations, venture-fund management and related business carried out wholly under Sharia principles. Its practical field includes equity participation and time-bound financing for the development of partner businesses at the early start-up or business-development stage, as well as profit-sharing finance, services and other approved activities. The underlying idea is developmental capital for an operating partner business, structured within Sharia principles rather than outside them.

The investment toolkit is defined with useful precision. It can include equity participation, the purchase of sukuk or convertible Sharia bonds, and the purchase of sukuk or Sharia bonds issued by a partner business at an early start-up or development stage. Profit-sharing financing and services also sit within the activity. It is a regulated business form: the enterprise undertaking these Sharia venture-capital, fund-management and related activities does so with the approval of the Financial Services Authority, and its other activities likewise require that authority’s approval.

The registration picture is broad at the national level. The activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, and it is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth should not obscure the character of the activity itself: this is a business built around Sharia-compliant investment, finance and fund management, rather than a generic commercial-services registration.

Bali does not turn that national opening into a prohibition. The province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks activities assessed at Low and Medium-Low risk. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. Bali’s status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, meaning the relevant local picture is not a PMA ban but a higher-risk classification at that scale. For a foreign investor considering Bali, the honest conclusion is straightforward: this activity remains registrable for PMA there, while its large-scale risk position must be read as part of the registration context.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This activity involves acting as a central middleman in financial trades, where you legally become the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer to guarantee settlement. It covers clearing and settlement services across stock markets, commodity futures, crypto and digital assets, money markets, forex, and other financial markets—essentially you step in to eliminate the risk that one party defaults.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is fully open to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: KBLI 2020→2025 mapping: code renumbered.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Aktivitas Counterparty untuk Kliring dan Setelmen Transaksi (64993)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: This suits a foreign entrepreneur aiming to operate a regulated financial clearing house or central counterparty (e.g., for crypto or securities settlement), but currently you must look at jurisdictions outside of Bali.

editorial.headline: Clearing’s Counterparty: KBLI 64993 and Bali’s PMA Position
editorial.standfirst: A financial-market counterparty activity open to foreign ownership nationally and not blocked from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 64993 covers the activity of a party that places itself between participants in financial transactions: buyer to the seller, and seller to the buyer. Its terrain is the machinery of clearing and settlement across capital markets, commodity futures, digital financial assets including crypto assets, money markets, foreign-exchange markets, and other financial markets. It also includes the provision of clearing services and guarantees for exchange transactions to be completed in an orderly, fair and efficient manner; PT Kliring Penjaminan Efek Indonesia is expressly included within the stated scope.

This is therefore not merely an administrative description of post-trade processing. The activity is defined by an intermediary position at the centre of a transaction, taking on the role of counterparty on both sides while supporting its clearing and settlement. The record makes the breadth of the remit clear: it reaches established market venues as well as financial markets involving digital assets, without reducing the activity to any one asset class or trading environment.

Registration is open across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. At the national level, PMA is classified TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling stands at 100%. Put simply, the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. That openness is grounded in Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021, the sources identified in the record.

Bali’s position is equally important, and more favourable than a blanket reading of the province’s PMA moratorium might suggest. Bali permanently blocks PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities island-wide. KBLI 64993 is not blocked by that moratorium: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, and the Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For an investor considering Bali, the honest conclusion is straightforward: this activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not barred from PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium rule.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not barred from PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium rule.

editorial.headline: Own-Account Market Trading, With a Clear Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers proprietary financial-market trading across instruments, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the own-account side of financial-market trading. It covers a trader buying, selling, investing and taking positions in financial instruments and financial assets for its own account, generally in pursuit of short-term gain. The range is deliberately broad: shares, foreign exchange, commodity contracts, crypto assets and their related liabilities, bullion, receivables, swaps, options, money-market derivatives and foreign-exchange money-market derivatives all sit within the stated scope. What gives the activity its coherence is not any one instrument, but the capacity in which it is undertaken: the trader acts for itself, carrying the position and its consequences rather than transacting as an intermediary for someone else. This is not a generic label for participation in markets; it is an account-of-record description.

That distinction makes this a classification for businesses whose trading or investment operations are conducted in their own name. The record expressly embraces own-name investment and trading, own-name receivables trading, and dealers in securities and derivatives operating for themselves. It is open at every recorded business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—so the description does not reserve the activity for only a large institution. Scale identifies the range of businesses that may register the activity; the defining commercial fact remains that the dealing is proprietary.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. For a foreign investor, that is a straightforward national position: full foreign ownership is permitted for this activity. The record attributes this entry to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It is a statement about the permitted ownership ceiling for this activity, not a reason to blur the own-account boundary at its centre.

Bali does not reverse that picture. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA for activities assessed at Low and Medium-Low risk, island-wide. This activity is recorded in Bali as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the reason explains that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High. It is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. The honest Bali conclusion is clear: a foreign investor is not prevented from registering this activity in Bali on the record’s stated moratorium rule. Bali’s relevant distinction is the higher-risk classification.
editorial.pullQuote: National foreign openness and Bali’s higher-risk treatment point in the same direction: this activity is not blocked for PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Carbon-Unit Trading, on the Trader’s Own Account
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers proprietary trading in carbon units—rights connected to emissions or emissions removal—with national foreign ownership open to 100%.
editorial.body:
This activity is the proprietary trading of carbon units: rights connected to the release of emissions or to emissions removal. The defining feature is who acts in the transaction. The trader acts in its own name and on its own account, taking the commercial position itself rather than carrying out a transaction for somebody else. It is therefore a focused activity classification for a business whose role is the trading of those units, not the operation of a marketplace or the measurement and verification work behind them.

For registration purposes, the record gives the activity a clear commercial identity but does not list any `scales_open_to` categories. That absence should be read carefully: it does not create a scale threshold or a special entitlement. It simply means the slim record does not specify which business scales are open to this activity. What is explicit is the own-account character of the enterprise. A registrant should be able to describe its business accordingly, with the carbon-unit trading position held and undertaken by the company itself.

At the national level, the position is unusually direct. The activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership level of **100%** under the cited Presidential Regulations. In plain English, national rules allow full foreign ownership for this activity. There is no lower foreign-ownership ceiling in the record to qualify that conclusion, and no added national condition is stated here.

Bali requires a more location-conscious reading, but not a false alarm. The activity is not blocked by Bali’s moratorium: its stated risk position is medium-high or high, while the province’s permanent island-wide PMA block applies to Low and Medium-Low risk activities. The Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the record expressly calls for verification by address. That is not a Bali-specific foreign-ownership cap or partnership requirement; none is stated. The honest position is that the activity remains open rather than moratorium-blocked in Bali, while the proposed address should be checked as part of the registration assessment.

editorial.headline: Conventional Bullion Banking Is Nationally Open—But Not for Bali PMA
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers conventional deposit-taking and lending in precious metals, nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
Today, a foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali. That is the practical starting point, even though conventional bullion banking is nationally classified as open to foreign investment with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The Bali position is not a qualification to be solved through presentation or structuring: the province’s PMA moratorium blocks activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk for a Bali address, island-wide and permanently. For this activity, the Large scale is recorded as Low risk, placing it within that restriction.

The underlying business is conventional bullion banking: principally receiving deposits of precious metals—such as gold or silver—in bar or currency form, then extending loans of those precious metals. It is a banking activity built around metal deposits and metal lending, rather than the physical storage of bullion or its sale. Its perimeter also matters. Sharia bullion banking, bullion trading for one’s own account, brokerage carried out for another party, and bullion custody or storage are outside the scope described here.

Nationally, the picture is unequivocal. The activity is marked TERBUKA and open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, with the foreign stake permitted up to 100%. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That openness establishes the national investment position; it does not override the Bali address rule. A founder considering a Bali-based PMA should therefore read the two layers together: the national regime permits full foreign ownership, while the provincial moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity in Bali.

The distinction is consequential because it separates the business definition from the place of registration. The activity itself remains clearly framed around conventional precious-metal deposit-taking and lending, and the national classification admits it at every listed scale. Yet Bali’s moratorium changes the immediate answer for a PMA using a Bali address. The relevant gubernatorial letter is dated May 13, 2026, with the record also noting an update of June 28, 2026. For Bali, the honest conclusion is simple: national openness does not translate into a currently registrable PMA activity on the island.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness establishes the investment position, but it does not override Bali’s PMA moratorium for a Bali address.

editorial.standfirst: This sharia-based bullion banking activity permits full foreign ownership nationally, yet PMA registration at a Bali address is blocked by the province-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
**A foreign investor cannot register this activity at a Bali address today.** Nationally, the activity is open to PMA and carries a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In Bali, however, the recorded outcome is a block under the province-wide PMA moratorium. That contrast is not a minor qualification to an otherwise open classification; it is the decisive fact for an operator considering where to place the registration.

At its centre, this is sharia bullion banking. The activity primarily accepts deposits of precious metals, including gold or silver, held as bars or currency, and channels loans of those precious metals. The same asset sits on both sides of the banking activity: bullion is deposited and bullion is lent. Everything is conducted according to sharia principles, which the scope places within the definition of the activity itself. This is therefore a precise banking classification rooted in precious-metal deposits and lending, rather than a broad label for any business associated with gold or silver.

At national level, the slim record makes the activity available at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. It does not confine registration to a single size of enterprise. For a PMA registration nationally, the status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign stake is 100%, allowing full foreign ownership within the national position recorded here. The stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Those facts establish the national frame clearly: an open PMA status, a full foreign-ownership ceiling, and availability across the four named scales.

Bali requires a different conclusion. Its status is recorded as Closed (Bali moratorium), and the activity is explicitly blocked for PMA. The stated reason is that the Besar scale is classified as Low risk, bringing it within Bali’s PMA moratorium. That moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA throughout the province, on a permanent and island-wide basis. The cited governor’s letter is from May 2026, with the record also noting June 2026. For a Bali address, the moratorium—not national openness—decides the result.

editorial.headline: A Clear Bali Route for Specialist Financial Services
editorial.standfirst: Specialist financial services—from hedging to own-name digital assets—are nationally open to PMA, and the stated Large-scale risk position leaves the activity outside Bali’s moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 64999 is a deliberately wide home for specialist financial-services work not classified elsewhere. Its stated scope includes financial vehicle corporations other than securitisation; the writing of swaps and options; and other hedging arrangements. It also covers transactions that securitise assets other than loans by issuing financial instruments. A further strand is the issuance, in a business’s own name, of digital financial assets and their associated liabilities—crypto assets are the example given. The scope then reaches other financial services not otherwise covered and financial-sector technology innovation.

The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses. This is meaningful breadth, but it should be read as a scale position rather than as a promise about any particular financial product or operating model. A company belongs within the activity where its actual work fits the recorded scope: a financial vehicle corporation, hedging arrangements, the stated asset transactions, own-name digital assets and their liabilities, or financial-sector technology innovation. For founders, that makes the description a practical boundary: its range is broad, yet its subject matter is specific.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, a foreign investor can hold all of the ownership permitted under this classification at national level. The national result is not qualified in the record by a lower foreign-equity cap. That clarity matters before turning to the province: national foreign ownership and Bali’s local registration treatment are separate parts of the picture, and each must be read from its own recorded field.

In Bali, the honest answer is still open, not blocked. The province’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. For this activity, OSS places the Besar scale at Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—so the moratorium does not block it. Bali’s status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. A foreign-owned company can therefore register this activity in Bali today, while the national 100% ceiling remains the foreign-ownership limit stated in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign-owned company can therefore register this activity in Bali today, while the national 100% ceiling remains the foreign-ownership limit stated in the record.
