editorial.headline: Conventional Life Insurance: Capped at 80% Nationally, Open in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers conventional life insurance, capped at 80% foreign ownership nationally under PP 14/2018, and not blocked from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Conventional life insurance, under this code, is the business of providing protection against life-related risk through a conventional insurance arrangement. Its promise is a defined payment mechanism: a policyholder, insured person or another entitled party may receive payment when the insured dies or remains alive. The activity also includes payments due at a time specified in the agreement. The amount may be fixed and/or based on the results of fund management. This is therefore a code for operating the risk-management service itself, with policy terms determining the persons entitled to receive the stated payment.

The registrant is a business undertaking conventional life-insurance services: the organisation of risk protection and the payments prescribed by its policies. The record opens the activity at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That gives the code a wide scale range without changing its central proposition: the service exists to make the agreed payment when the insured dies or remains alive, or at another contractually specified time. The recipient remains the policyholder, insured person or another party with the contractual right to it.

Nationally, the PMA setting is capped: the foreign-ownership ceiling is 80% of paid-up capital, not the residual-open default the Perpres would otherwise apply. This is a sector-law cap under PP 14/2018 Pasal 5(1), amended by PP 3/2020 — Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 11(2) carves financial and banking bidang usaha out to their own sector regulations, so the residual-open default cannot ground an ownership verdict here. Listed insurers (perseroan terbuka) are exempt from the cap, and foreign holdings that already exceeded 80% before PP 14/2018 took effect are grandfathered without a further increase. That is the national position to use; the fact that life-insurance payments may draw on fund-management results does not alter the ownership percentage given in the record.

Bali does not add a further restriction on top of that national cap. The provincial moratorium is a permanent, island-wide block on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This code is not marked as blocked. The record's reason is specific: at Besar scale, OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so the activity is not caught by the moratorium. Bali's status is therefore that PMA registration proceeds under the same 80% national ceiling — the moratorium adds no lower cap of its own.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali adds no further restriction on top of the national 80% ownership cap — PMA registration proceeds at that ceiling, not a lower one.

editorial.headline: Sharia Life Insurance: Capped at 80% Nationally, Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A sharia-based life-insurance activity open from Mikro to Besar scale, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 80% under PP 14/2018 and no block under Bali’s stated moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is sharia life insurance conducted entirely under sharia principles. It concerns the management of risk on those principles for mutual assistance and protection. The arrangements provide payments tied to a participant’s death or survival, as well as other payments to a participant or another entitled party at a time set out in the agreement. The amount may be fixed and/or based on the result of fund management. Its commercial centre of gravity is therefore clear: a life-insurance undertaking whose risk management and benefit payments are framed by sharia principles.

The record opens the activity at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That range is useful in its simplicity: scale is not used here to exclude a business from the activity. A prospective operator can read the category as available from micro through large enterprise, while keeping the focus on the defined insurance operation rather than treating the title as a loose label. The scope is specific about the mutual-help and protection purpose, the events that can support a payment, and the possibility that fund-management results affect the amount.

Nationally, the PMA setting is TERBATAS and the stated foreign-ownership ceiling is 80% of paid-up capital. In plain terms, the national record allows foreign ownership up to that figure, not more, for this activity. This is a sector-law cap under PP 14/2018 Pasal 5(1), amended by PP 3/2020 — Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 11(2) carves financial and banking bidang usaha out to their own sector regulations, so the residual-open default cannot ground an ownership verdict here. Listed insurers (perseroan terbuka) are exempt, and foreign holdings that already exceeded 80% before PP 14/2018 took effect are grandfathered without a further increase. For founders, the essential reading is straightforward: the recorded national ceiling is 80% of paid-up capital, not full ownership.

Bali does not add a further restriction on top of that national cap. The province’s rule is island-wide and permanent for PMA registrations in all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK in Bali, and its reason states that, at the Large scale, OSS risk is Medium-High/High. That is why it is not blocked by the moratorium. The Bali conclusion is precise: a foreign-owned registration for this activity proceeds under the same 80% national ceiling, which the moratorium does not lower further.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali adds no further restriction: this activity is not blocked by the stated provincial moratorium, and the 80% national ceiling stands.

editorial.headline: Conventional General Insurance, Clearly Defined
editorial.standfirst: A conventional general-insurance activity open across all recorded scales, with an 80% national PMA ownership cap under PP 14/2018 and no Bali moratorium block on this record.
editorial.body:
Conventional general insurance is the business of covering risk other than life insurance. Under this activity, an insurer provides compensation to an insured person or policyholder for loss, damage, expenses incurred, lost profits, or third-party legal liability when an uncertain event occurs. It is a defined insurance service built around the financial consequences of risk: the damage itself, the cost it creates, income forgone, or liability to another party.

The recorded scale range runs from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah to Besar. That breadth does not alter the activity’s centre of gravity. The business remains conventional general insurance, providing risk-cover services and compensation within the categories set out in its scope. For a founder reading the classification closely, the important distinction is that this is insurance other than life insurance, with the scope expressly focused on losses and liabilities arising from uncertain events.

At the national level, PMA is capped: the foreign-ownership ceiling is 80% of paid-up capital. Put plainly, the national record sets a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity — a sector-law figure, not the Perpres's residual-open default. The basis is PP 14/2018 Pasal 5(1), amended by PP 3/2020: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 11(2) carves financial and banking bidang usaha out to their own sector regulations, so the residual-open default cannot ground an ownership verdict here. Listed insurers (perseroan terbuka) are exempt, and foreign holdings that already exceeded 80% before PP 14/2018 took effect are grandfathered without a further increase. That is the national position; it says something material about foreign participation, but it should not be mistaken for a substitute for the activity’s own operational definition, which remains anchored in conventional general-insurance risk coverage.

Bali’s position is also clear on the record, though it turns on risk classification rather than a blanket exemption. This activity is not marked as blocked for PMA registration in Bali. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk classification is Medium-High/High, placing it outside Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium for PMA activities classified Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s restriction exists, but this activity is identified as not blocked by it. The distinction is specific and useful: the national foreign-ownership position is capped at 80%, while the Bali record confirms that the moratorium adds no further bar on top of that cap for this activity.

editorial.headline: Sharia General Insurance: Capped at 80% Nationally, Unblocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A Sharia-based general-insurance activity capped at 80% foreign ownership nationally under PP 14/2018, and not blocked by Bali's province-wide PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Sharia general insurance is the business of managing risk under Sharia principles to enable mutual help and protection. It is not life insurance. Its purpose is to provide compensation to participants or policyholders after an uncertain event causes loss, damage, costs incurred, lost profits, or legal liability to a third party. That scope matters: this is an activity defined around the collective management of non-life risk and the resulting protection of participants or policyholders, rather than a loose label for any service described as Islamic finance. The stated consequences are deliberately broad, extending beyond physical damage to expenses, lost profit and third-party liability.

KBLI 65123 concerns financial protection for customer funds held in banks and for policy claims arising from insurance products. The protection is funded through periodic contributions paid by the financial institutions involved. Its subject is therefore clearly defined: safeguarding deposited customer funds and insurance-policy claims through a contribution-backed protection arrangement. The record provides no further operational subdivision, so the boundary should remain exactly there—financial protection for those deposits and claims, supported by recurring institutional contributions.

The record does not name a particular legal form of registrant. It does, however, make financial institutions materially visible because they pay the periodic contributions that fund the protection. No eligible business scale is listed in `scales_open_to`. That absence should be read as an absence of stated scale information, rather than turned into an unstated permission or restriction. editorial.headline: Conventional Guarantees: Financial Commitments, Clearly Defined
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers conventional guarantees for financial obligations, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Conventional guarantee activity is about standing behind a financial obligation: a guarantor assures the beneficiary that the guaranteed party’s obligation will be met. Its scope reaches credit and financing extended by financial institutions, loans channelled by savings-and-loan cooperatives to their members, and credit or loan partnership programmes distributed by state-owned enterprises. The work is therefore not merely a promise in the abstract; it concerns identifiable financial commitments and the arrangements through which they are supported.

The remit is deliberately broad within that conventional-guarantee frame. It includes guarantees over debt instruments, instalment purchases, trade transactions, procurement of goods or services through surety bonds, bank guarantees through counter-guarantees, domestic documentary credits, letters of credit, customs bonds and excise guarantees. It also includes management-consulting services connected with guarantee operations, alongside other guarantee activities. The common thread is the provision of a conventional guarantee for the fulfilment of a financial obligation.

The activity is open at every recorded business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the record does not confine the classification to a single size of operator. A business registering this activity should be able to describe its actual guarantee function with care—whether the underlying obligation concerns credit, financing, a cooperative loan, a trade transaction or a procurement commitment—while remaining inside the conventional-guarantee scope set out here.

Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali does not overturn that position through its permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium for low and medium-low risk activities. The Bali record places large-scale OSS risk at Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi and states that the activity is not blocked by that moratorium. In practical terms, a foreign investor is not barred from registering this activity in Bali today on the basis of that moratorium; the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the relevant ownership figure in this record.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor is not barred from registering this activity in Bali today on the basis of the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Sharia Guarantees: Open Nationally, Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers sharia-based guarantees of financial obligations, open to foreign investment nationally and not blocked by Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium at the recorded large-business risk level.
editorial.body:
KBLI 65132 is the business of providing guarantees, wholly on sharia principles, for a guaranteed party’s financial obligations to a beneficiary. Its terrain is broad but coherent: it includes guarantees for sharia financing provided by financial institutions; loans or financing extended by savings-and-loan cooperatives to their members; and partnership-program financing distributed by state-owned enterprises under sharia principles. The common thread is not lending itself, but standing behind the fulfilment of a financial obligation within a sharia-based guarantee arrangement.

The stated scope also reaches into the practical instruments through which guarantees are used in commerce and finance. These include debt instruments, instalment purchases of goods, trade transactions, procurement of goods and services through surety bonds, bank guarantees and counter-guarantees, domestic documentary credits, letters of credit, customs bonds and excise guarantees. Management-consulting services connected to guarantee business are included as well, alongside other sharia-based guarantee activities. In editorial terms, this is a specialist financial-guarantee activity whose identity rests on sharia principles across the whole undertaking.

The code is open at every recorded business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Nationally, its investment status is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is the clean national position in the record: foreign investment may hold the full permitted stake. The applicable policy source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the record adds a separate national cap, timeline or administrative condition, so none should be inferred from the activity description alone.

Bali requires a more exact reading, but not a more pessimistic one. The province permanently blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, island-wide. This activity is not marked as blocked: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, placing it outside that moratorium’s stated reach. Its Bali status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, the honest conclusion is that this code is not barred by the provincial PMA moratorium on the facts supplied; the relevant distinction is its recorded higher risk at the large-business scale, not a Bali-specific foreign-ownership cap or partnership requirement.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, this code is not barred by the provincial PMA moratorium on the facts supplied.

editorial.headline: Conventional Reinsurance: Capped at 80% Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: For conventional reinsurance, the national ceiling caps foreign ownership at 80% under PP 14/2018, and Bali’s risk treatment leaves the activity outside its PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Conventional reinsurance is the provision of repeat risk cover for risks faced by insurance companies, guarantee companies and other reinsurance companies. Its scope is precise: it concerns conventional reinsurance services, not a generic financial-services label. The activity sits where an existing risk exposure faced by one of those named companies is itself given reinsurance protection. The same core description appears twice in the record, once as the group scope and again as the conventional reinsurance business, underscoring that re-covering risk is the defining work.

A business may register this activity at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. That range matters because the record expressly opens the classification across all four listed scales rather than naming only one. The scale list describes who may enter the classification; it does not add a capital, licensing, tax or timing rule, and none should be inferred from it. What remains constant across those scales is the focus of the activity: providing reinsurance services connected to risk faced by the specified industry counterparties.

On national foreign investment, the answer is direct. The activity is marked TERBATAS for PMA, and the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 80% of paid-up capital — a sector-law cap under PP 14/2018 Pasal 5(1), amended by PP 3/2020. UU 40/2014 Pasal 1 angka 14 names 'perusahaan reasuransi' explicitly among the entities the law calls a Perusahaan Perasuransian, so this activity sits squarely inside the same regime as direct insurers; Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 11(2) carves financial and banking bidang usaha out to their own sector regulations, so the residual-open default cannot ground an ownership verdict here. Listed reinsurers (perseroan terbuka) are exempt, and foreign holdings that already exceeded 80% before PP 14/2018 took effect are grandfathered without a further increase. A foreign investor is therefore constrained to that 80% ceiling recorded here, not a minority stake and not full ownership.

Bali does not add a further restriction on top of that national cap. Its status is OK or higher risk, and the activity is not marked as blocked for PMA. The province's permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA for low- and medium-low-risk activities. For conventional reinsurance, the record's specific reasoning is that, at the Large scale, OSS risk is Medium-High/High; it is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. The decisive Bali fact is straightforward: a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, up to the same 80% national ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: The decisive Bali fact is straightforward: a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, within the national 80% foreign-ownership ceiling.

editorial.headline: Sharia Reinsurance: Capped at 80% Nationally, Still Defined by Risk
editorial.standfirst: This activity manages risk under sharia principles for insurers, guarantee companies and fellow reinsurance businesses, with an 80% national ownership cap under PP 14/2018 and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Sharia reinsurance is the business of managing, under sharia principles, risks carried by sharia insurance companies, sharia guarantee companies and other sharia reinsurance companies. It is a specialised risk-management activity rather than a general insurance proposition: its subject is the exposure already faced by those financial institutions, and its operating premise is expressly sharia-based. The scope also includes sharia units within conventional reinsurance companies, provided the reinsurance business is conducted wholly according to sharia principles.

The record makes the activity available at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the code is not framed as an activity reserved for only one size of enterprise. Its commercial identity remains consistent across those scales: managing institutional risk within the sharia insurance, guarantee and reinsurance sphere. The distinguishing boundary is therefore the kind of risk relationship and the sharia basis on which it is managed, not a separate retail-facing description.

Nationally, the PMA position is direct. The activity is TERBATAS and carries a foreign-ownership ceiling of 80% of paid-up capital — a sector-law cap under PP 14/2018 Pasal 5(1), amended by PP 3/2020. UU 40/2014 Pasal 1 angka 14 names 'perusahaan reasuransi syariah' explicitly among the entities the law calls a Perusahaan Perasuransian, so this activity sits inside the same regime as direct sharia insurers; Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 11(2) carves financial and banking bidang usaha out to their own sector regulations, so the residual-open default cannot ground an ownership verdict here. Listed reinsurers (perseroan terbuka) are exempt, and foreign holdings that already exceeded 80% before PP 14/2018 took effect are grandfathered without a further increase. That is the national picture to begin with, rather than an implication drawn from the activity's financial character or the scale at which it is undertaken.

Bali does not add a further restriction for this activity. The provincial moratorium blocks PMA for activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk, island-wide and permanently. Here, however, the record identifies the Besar-scale OSS risk as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—and expressly says the activity is not blocked by the moratorium. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, the honest reading is therefore that this activity is not barred by the moratorium; it proceeds under the same 80% national ceiling because of the recorded higher-risk classification at the Besar scale.
editorial.pullQuote: Foreign investment is capped at 80% ownership nationally under PP 14/2018, and Bali's moratorium does not block this recorded higher-risk activity.

editorial.headline: Conventional Re-Guaranteeing: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A precise guarantee activity, open to full foreign ownership nationally and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium, centred on guarantee companies’ financial obligations.
editorial.body:
Conventional re-guaranteeing is a specialised financial-guarantee activity. It consists of providing guarantees for the fulfilment of guarantee companies’ financial obligations, undertaken through conventional arrangements. That is the centre of this classification: a re-guarantee business conducted conventionally, with its guarantee directed to the financial obligations of guarantee companies. The scope gives the activity both a precise commercial subject and a precise obligation. It is best understood from that stated relationship, rather than by treating the word “guarantee” as a catch-all. In registration terms, the description points to the guarantee operation itself and to the companies whose financial commitments it addresses.

Who can register it is unusually broad on scale. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises—micro, small, medium and large. The scale field therefore does not confine this activity to one end of the business-size spectrum. Yet scale is not a substitute for scope: whether the enterprise is micro or large, the recorded activity remains conventional re-guaranteeing, and the recorded service remains a guarantee for meeting guarantee companies’ financial obligations. Reading the two fields together keeps the registration question grounded: broad scale eligibility, but a tightly stated business function.

Nationally, the foreign-investment stance is clear-cut. The activity is marked TERBUKA, or open, and its maximum foreign ownership is 100 percent. For a foreign investor, that records a national path to full ownership of an enterprise carrying out this stated activity. There is no need to dilute that point: the maximum shown in the record is 100 percent. The listed scale availability and the foreign-ownership ceiling answer different questions, but together they establish a clear national position for this defined conventional re-guaranteeing business.

Bali calls for an equally exact reading. The provincial status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says the activity is not blocked by the moratorium. Its stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi: medium-high/high. The Bali rule cited in the record permanently blocks PMA registration, island-wide, for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity is not placed in that blocked group. The honest Bali conclusion is clean: a foreign investor is not barred from registering this activity in Bali by that moratorium. That conclusion does not alter the national ownership figure; it confirms that Bali’s recorded treatment introduces no separate block here.
editorial.pullQuote: Open to full foreign ownership nationally, this activity is also not barred in Bali by the recorded moratorium.

editorial.headline: Employer Pension Funds: A Clear PMA Position in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This conventional employer pension-fund activity is nationally open to PMA and is not blocked by Bali’s risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 65301 covers the conventional management of an employer pension fund. It is an activity established by a person or entity that employs staff, acting as the founder, to run a pension programme for some or all of its employees. The programme may be a defined-benefit pension programme or a defined-contribution pension programme. The essential structure is employer-founded and employee-facing: the fund exists for participating employees and creates an obligation for the employer.

The people or entities registering under it are therefore employers setting up and managing the conventional fund they have formed. The record opens the activity at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. Those labels span the full scale range stated for the activity, while its purpose remains precise: serving some or all of the founder’s employees through either a defined-benefit or defined-contribution arrangement. Whether participation covers part of the workforce or all employees is built into the stated scope.

At the national level, this activity has TERBUKA PMA status and a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. Bali does not reverse that conclusion. Its entry is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record notes that, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Medium-High/High; the activity is therefore not blocked by Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, and in Bali it is not blocked by the island-wide moratorium.

The distinction between the national allowance and Bali treatment should remain intact. The 100% ceiling is the national PMA figure. Bali’s entry gives a risk-based reason for the absence of a moratorium block at Besar scale, rather than a separate ownership percentage or partnership condition. The appropriate reading is direct: conventional employer pension-fund management is nationally open to PMA, and Bali’s permanent Low and Medium-Low risk PMA moratorium does not block this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, the activity is open to PMA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, and in Bali it is not blocked by the island-wide moratorium.

editorial.headline: The Employer-Founded Logic of Sharia Pension Funds
editorial.standfirst: An employer-founded sharia pension fund is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and, on its recorded risk position, is not blocked from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the management of an Islamic employer pension fund established by a person or entity that employs staff. The employer is the founder; employees—in whole or in part—are the participants. The fund runs either a defined-benefit pension programme or a defined-contribution programme, and its operation creates an obligation for the employer. The language fixes the relationship at the heart of the activity: founder, employees, and employer obligation. It is a workplace pension arrangement conducted under sharia principles. The scope explicitly spans both programme types and allows the participant group to comprise either some or all employees. In each case, the obligation sits with the employer, not the participants.

That origin also explains who it serves. It is a fund established by a person or body that employs workers, while some or all of those employees participate in the pension programme. Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises can all operate under this record. Those scale labels do not dilute the core model. Whether participation is drawn from part of a workforce or the whole workforce, the fund remains employer-founded and carries an obligation for that employer. The wording keeps the employment relationship in view at every point: it identifies the founder, identifies the participant group, and states the employer obligation. That is the activity’s institutional shape.

Nationally, PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That is full foreign ownership on the national reading supplied here, grounded in Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For an overseas founder, the stated maximum means the foreign stake can equal the entire ownership, rather than stop at a partial cap. TERBUKA is the national PMA status stated for the activity, while the percentage supplies its ownership limit. Reading those fields together avoids a false distinction between formal openness and actual ownership capacity: the record places the ceiling at 100%. The national position is consequently clear, but it is not a substitute for reading Bali’s separate moratorium rule.

Bali gives the answer more sharply than a generic regional caveat. The province blocks PMA for every low- and medium-low-risk KBLI on an island-wide, permanent basis. The rule is attributed to Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. This activity is nevertheless recorded as not blocked: at Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—medium-high/high—which places it outside the stated moratorium. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. A foreigner can therefore register this activity in Bali today: the recorded outcome is not blocked by the provincial moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreigner can therefore register this activity in Bali today: the recorded outcome is not blocked by the provincial moratorium.

editorial.headline: Conventional Financial-Institution Pension Funds: Open Nationally, Viable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity manages conventional defined-contribution pension programmes for individuals, from employees to independent workers, with a clear national opening for foreign investment.
editorial.body:
This activity is the conventional management of pension funds established by financial institutions. Its practical focus is a defined-contribution pension programme for individuals: employees as well as independent workers. The programme sits separately from the employer pension fund maintained for employees of the relevant bank or life-insurance company. That separation is central to the activity’s character. It is not simply a general savings arrangement, but the administration of an individual pension programme within the conventional financial-institution pension-fund model.

The code is open to businesses at every stated scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the record does not confine the activity to one end of the business spectrum. The same defined-contribution pension-fund activity is therefore presented as available across those four scales, while retaining the specific institutional setting described in its scope: conventional pension-fund management by a financial institution, for individual participants whose arrangement is separate from the employer fund of the associated bank or life-insurance company.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is unambiguous. The activity is open to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain terms, the record places no foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity nationally. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. That national position should be read for what it says: a conventional financial-institution pension-fund activity may be foreign-owned up to the stated ceiling, rather than being described as nationally reserved or restricted by a lower percentage in this record.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion. The province’s standing is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the activity is not blocked by Bali’s moratorium. The reason is risk classification at the Large scale: it is Medium-High/High risk, rather than within the Low or Medium-Low risk categories covered by the island-wide permanent PMA moratorium. The relevant Bali rule blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities; this activity falls outside that block on the record provided. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, the honest reading is therefore neither a special Bali ownership cap nor a moratorium prohibition, but an activity recorded as not blocked because its Large-scale OSS risk position is Medium-High/High.

editorial.headline: A Sharia Pension Activity That Remains Open in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity administers Sharia-based defined-contribution pension programmes for individuals, from employees to independent workers.
editorial.body:
This is the administration of Sharia-based pension funds operated through financial institutions. Its focus is a defined-contribution pension programme for individuals: employees as well as independent workers. The programme is distinct from the employer pension fund maintained for employees of the relevant bank or life-insurance company. In practical terms, the activity concerns the stewardship of an individual pension arrangement structured around Sharia principles, rather than an employer’s own pension fund.

The record places the activity within every stated business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the scope is not framed as a narrow institutional back-office function. It is an activity directed at individual participants, including people whose working lives sit inside conventional employment and those working independently, while preserving separation from the employer pension arrangement associated with the bank or life-insurance company concerned.

At the national level, foreign investment is allowed for this activity and foreign ownership may reach 100%. That is an unqualified national ownership ceiling in the record, not a partial foreign-investment allowance. A foreign-owned business considering this activity therefore has a clear national reading: the activity is open and the stated ceiling is full foreign ownership.

Bali’s position is also open on the record before us. The provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk across the island. For this activity, however, the Bali assessment states that its OSS risk at the Large scale is Medium-High or High, so it is not blocked by that moratorium. The distinction is important: Bali’s result is not an exception invented around the national rule, but a direct consequence of the recorded risk treatment. On the available record, a foreigner can register this activity in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this activity is also not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.

intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally, this KBLI is fully open to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, the island-wide moratorium (in force since 13 May 2026) only halts PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk lines — this KBLI's large-scale (Besar) risk class is higher, so it is not caught: PMA registration in Bali remains possible.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct 1:1 match from KBLI 2020 — code and scope unchanged.
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Looking into Penyelenggaraan Sistem Perdagangan Efek (66111)? Nationally this carries PMA status: Open. Let me walk you through what it means for a foreign-owned setup.
intel_2026.whoThisIsFor: Foreign entrepreneurs who want to build or operate a licensed securities exchange, carbon trading platform, or alternative trading system—though not in a Bali-based entity under current rules.

editorial.headline: The Market Infrastructure Behind Securities Trading
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 66111 covers the systems that bring securities buyers and sellers together, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block at Large scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66111 is the infrastructure of a securities market: the business of operating and providing the systems or facilities through which separate parties can meet to offer, buy and sell securities. Its scope includes securities trading involving carbon units, whether transactions take place through an exchange or through an alternative trading system. The defining work is not the ownership of the securities being traded, but the organisation of the venue, mechanism or infrastructure that allows other parties’ offers to meet.

That remit also reaches business entities that provide systems or facilities for matching other parties’ buy and sell offers. It explicitly includes an electronic system that continuously brings together service users’ transactions in debt securities and/or sukuk outside a securities exchange. In practical terms, this is a code for the operator of the trading environment: the party making the market’s meeting place function, rather than simply participating in a transaction conducted there.

This activity is available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That is a clean national position: foreign investment may hold the full permitted stake in a business registered under this activity. The record cites Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as the source for that national setting.

Bali does not reverse that position with a PMA registration block today. The province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, but this activity is not blocked by that rule. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which is why its Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For a founder, the important distinction is precise: national foreign openness remains intact, and Bali is not closed to PMA registration under the stated moratorium; the relevant Bali reading is instead the activity’s higher risk at Large scale.
editorial.pullQuote: This is the business of making the trading environment function, rather than simply taking part in the trades conducted there.

editorial.headline: Futures Exchanges: A Clear National and Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the systems and venues that organise commodity trading through futures and derivative contracts, with a full national foreign-ownership ceiling and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
**Bursa Berjangka** concerns the organised setting for commodity trading through contracts. It covers the operation and provision of systems and facilities for buying and selling commodities under futures contracts, sharia derivative contracts and other derivative contracts. The activity includes operating a futures exchange in either physical or electronic form. Its centre of gravity is therefore the exchange infrastructure itself: the systems and means through which contract-based commodity trading is arranged.

The classification is open at every stated business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That range gives the activity a broad formal reach, while its scope remains specific. The record describes an organiser and provider of trading systems or facilities for contract markets, rather than the commodity transaction in isolation. For a founder, that distinction places the business in the architecture of futures and derivatives trading—whether the exchange is conducted through a physical venue or an electronic one.

Nationally, the activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The Bali position does not reverse that national openness. Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk; this activity is not blocked by that moratorium. At the Large scale, its recorded OSS risk is Medium-High/High, which is why the Bali record places it outside the moratorium’s prohibition.

The practical reading is direct. A nationally open activity remains available for PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium framework, rather than becoming locally prohibited merely because it operates on the island. Bali’s record is not a separate ownership cap or partnership condition: it is a status of no moratorium block, with the Large-scale risk classification explicitly noted. The result is a category whose national foreign-investment position and Bali treatment point in the same direction, while still recognising the recorded higher-risk status at the Large scale.
editorial.pullQuote: A nationally open activity remains available for PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium framework.

editorial.headline: Digital Asset Exchange Operations: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 66113 covers the systems, facilities and reporting behind digital-financial-asset trading, with national foreign openness that does not extend to PMA registration at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
Digital financial asset exchange operations are the subject of KBLI 66113. Its scope covers operating and providing systems and/or facilities that facilitate activities connected with trading digital financial assets, expressly including crypto assets. It also includes providing reports on that trading. In practical terms, the activity is defined by the market infrastructure around digital-financial-asset trading: the systems and facilities that enable it, and the reporting that records it.

The activity is open across every stated business scale: micro, small, medium and large. At the national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling stands at 100%. That is a full national opening to foreign ownership within the record’s stated ceiling, rather than a partial foreign stake. The national position is sourced to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. For a business whose actual operations fall within the stated scope, the national record is therefore direct: digital-financial-asset trading infrastructure and trading reports may be carried out at any of the listed scales, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%.

Bali, however, is a separate and decisive constraint for PMA registration. A foreigner cannot register this activity at a Bali address today. Although the code is nationally open, the record states that its large scale is classified as Menengah Rendah. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI at a Bali address. The cited basis is Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, referred to in the record’s Bali reason in May 2026.

The distinction matters because a national foreign-ownership ceiling is not the same thing as local PMA registration availability. Here, 100% foreign ownership is available nationally, yet Bali’s moratorium prevents PMA registration for the activity at a Bali address. The activity remains clearly defined—digital-financial-asset trading systems, facilities and reports—and nationally open across micro through large scales. But for a foreign-owned setup seeking a Bali address, the local moratorium controls the immediate outcome.
editorial.pullQuote: Here, 100% foreign ownership is available nationally, yet Bali’s moratorium prevents PMA registration for the activity at a Bali address.

editorial.headline: Alternative-Market Derivatives Trading: Nationally Open, Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: An own-account alternative-market derivatives activity that is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66114 is a tightly bounded own-account trading activity within an alternative trading system. Its scope is the purchase and sale of derivative contracts other than futures and sharia derivative contracts, carried out in the operator’s own name. Product, capacity and trading mechanism are joined in the definition; each matters. The words “for and on its own behalf” are not decoration: they place the activity with the party conducting its own transactions, rather than describing a general-purpose market role. It is a defined market activity, not merely a broad description of financial dealing. That clarity is useful precisely because the title is specialised.

At registration, the code is open at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. Those labels establish a broad scale range for the same carefully delimited activity, not a broader statement of commercial scope. The scale question and the activity question should be kept separate: the record gives access across those scale labels but retains the same scope wording. At any of those scales, the entry still describes purchase and sale of the specified derivative contracts through the stated alternative trading-system mechanism and on the operator’s own behalf. The record provides no additional operational threshold, licence or timetable, so none should be read into this otherwise direct scale position.

Nationally, the PMA entry is unequivocal: TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In ordinary terms, the national record allows the activity to sit in a wholly foreign-owned PMA structure. There is no national ownership ceiling below full foreign ownership stated in the supplied record. That ownership result belongs to the national entry: it is neither a projection nor a Bali-specific condition, and it should be read alongside the activity’s narrow own-account trading definition.

Bali is not a hidden reversal of that national position. Its province-wide, permanent PMA moratorium blocks every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. This entry, however, is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK; the stated reason is that OSS risk at the Large scale is Medium-High/High. It is therefore not blocked by the moratorium. The record states neither a separate Bali foreign-ownership percentage nor a local partnership condition. The honest local reading is consequently simple: Bali does not block PMA registration for this activity under the stated moratorium rule, while 100% remains the only ownership ceiling supplied.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not block PMA registration for this activity under the stated moratorium rule.

editorial.headline: The Infrastructure Behind Rupiah Market Transactions
editorial.standfirst: This code covers the systems and facilities that enable rupiah money-market and foreign-exchange transactions, with full national foreign ownership and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66115 concerns the operation, provision or use of systems through which financial transactions are conducted in the money market and foreign-exchange market involving rupiah. It is the transactional infrastructure itself: the facilities and systems that allow those markets to function, rather than a generic technology label. Its scope expressly includes electronic trading-platform providers, systematic internalisers, exchange operators and other transaction-facility operators. It also includes businesses that provide technology and operate facilities for rupiah money-market and foreign-exchange transactions, including money-market and foreign-exchange brokerage companies.

The registering business is therefore one that operates transaction facilities or provides the technology and means through which these market transactions are carried out. The activity is open at every listed business scale: micro, small, medium and large. That breadth does not dilute the definition. The common thread is the organisation and operation of a system or facility for transactions in the specified rupiah markets, whether the business is providing an electronic platform, acting as a market broker, or operating another form of transaction venue.

Nationally, the activity is classified as open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. Put simply, the national record allows this activity to be fully foreign-owned. The relevant PMA source is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. There is no lower foreign-ownership ceiling in the record to qualify that national position.

Bali’s position is also clear for this code. Bali does not block PMA registration for this activity under its moratorium. The province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium applies to Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA; the Bali assessment for this activity states that OSS risk at the Large scale is Medium-High/High. It is therefore not blocked by the moratorium. A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, subject to the record’s stated Bali status of OK_or_HIGHER_RISK rather than a moratorium exclusion.

editorial.headline: Financial Oversight: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A nationally open activity covering financial-sector oversight, but one that Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66116 covers the work behind regulation, supervision, inspection and investigation in financial services outside insurance and pension funds. Its scope reaches banking; capital markets, derivatives and carbon exchanges; financing institutions, venture-capital firms, microfinance institutions and other financial-services industries; commodity-contract trading; and financial-sector technology innovation, digital financial assets and crypto-assets. It also encompasses the conduct of financial-services businesses, consumer education and protection, and oversight of the financial sector as an integrated whole.

Nationally, the activity is classified as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is open across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the record places the activity across both the institutional mechanics of finance and the public-facing work of consumer protection. The national position is therefore direct: this is an activity open to foreign ownership up to the full stated ceiling, rather than one restricted to a particular scale of enterprise.

Bali changes the outcome decisively. A foreign investor cannot register this activity at a Bali address today. The record identifies the Besar scale as Menengah Rendah, or medium-low risk, and Bali’s rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the province on a permanent basis. This is not a Bali-specific reduction in the foreign-ownership percentage. The stated result is a block: despite the national TERBUKA classification and 100% ceiling, the Bali status is Closed (Bali moratorium). The record ties that result to the Bali PMA moratorium cited in the gubernatorial letter dated May 13, 2026.

The distinction is consequential and should be read exactly as it stands. editorial.headline: The Institutions That Keep Indonesia’s Financial Markets in Order
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 66117 covers self-regulatory, central-custody and settlement functions in financial markets—open to PMA nationally and not blocked by Bali’s stated moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66117 is the classification for self-regulatory activity in Indonesia’s financial markets: institutions that make rules and supervise the conduct of transactions for their members, so those transactions are safe, orderly and consistent with financial-market policy. It also covers the operating side of central custody and exchange-transaction settlement. The scope places these functions in one institutional frame: oversight of a member market’s transaction rules, alongside custody and settlement carried out in an orderly, fair and efficient way. Its subject is not the financial market in the abstract, but the organisations and operating functions that sustain its transaction architecture. It expressly includes PT Kustodian Sentral Efek Indonesia (KSEI).

The party registering it is therefore the party performing one of those defined roles. It may be a self-regulatory organisation serving its members through rule-making and supervision; it may instead be the party that operates central custody for custodian banks, securities companies and other parties, and handles the stated exchange settlement. The description combines regulatory and operational functions, yet both are specific: one concerns rules and oversight, the other custody and settlement. It is not a broad label for every participant around a financial-market transaction. Registration is open at every stated business scale—Micro, Small, Medium and Large.

Nationally, the investment position is unambiguous. The activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Full foreign ownership is therefore allowed nationally under the record’s cited PMA basis. That openness attaches to the work actually described: market rule-making and supervision for members, or central custody and the orderly, fair and efficient settlement of exchange transactions. It should be read as the ownership position for this defined activity, rather than as a claim about an undefined wider financial-services field.

Bali needs a separate reading, because its provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI across the island. This activity, however, is recorded as not blocked by that moratorium. At the Large scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, which is why the Bali record places it at “OK or higher risk” rather than under a moratorium prohibition. For a foreign investor, the practical conclusion is clean: this activity can be registered as PMA in Bali today under the information given, rather than being shut out by the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The national position is full foreign ownership, and Bali does not block PMA registration under its stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: The Operating System Behind the Market
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 66119 covers the administration and infrastructure that support financial, commodity futures, money and rupiah foreign-exchange market transactions.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66119 concerns the administrative architecture behind financial markets, commodity futures markets and similar markets not otherwise classified. It covers business entities or institutions that provide and organise infrastructure for capital-market transactions, as well as infrastructure operators for money-market and rupiah foreign-exchange transactions not otherwise classified. Its subject is market infrastructure itself: the institutional and operational framework identified in the scope, rather than a generic back-office service.

The remit is broad, but the record is precise about its functions. It includes providing transaction facilities; clearing and risk management; settlement; transaction administration, recording and reporting; securities valuation to establish a fair market price; operating and managing investor-protection funds; financing securities transactions; and providing, managing and operating open electronic-network securities-offering services through which issuers sell securities directly to investors. Together, these functions describe the practical systems through which the listed market transactions can be organised and administered.

Registration is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That position is expressly stated for this activity: the foreign-ownership ceiling is not something to infer from the character of the market infrastructure or the scale at which it operates.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for activities carrying Low or Medium-Low risk, island-wide. Here, however, the Bali assessment records OSS risk at the Besar scale as Medium-High/High and expressly states that the activity is not blocked by the moratorium. In practical terms, a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The Bali record sets out no separate local ownership cap or partnership condition; the scale-specific risk assessment is the reason the provincial moratorium does not interrupt the national opening.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, Bali aligns with the national opening because its recorded risk position does not trigger the provincial PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Securities Brokerage in Bali: Open to Foreign Investment
editorial.standfirst: A securities-brokerage activity with a national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling and no Bali moratorium block for PMA registration.
editorial.body:
This activity is securities brokerage other than carbon units: carrying out securities transactions for another party or client, including the work of a securities broker-dealer intermediary established specifically within a province. It also encompasses a party transacting in securities for its own interest and for others, marketing securities for another securities company, and other activities determined or approved by the Financial Services Authority (OJK). In practical terms, it is a regulated intermediary role in the securities market, rather than a generic trading business.

The activity is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Its provincial formulation is particularly specific. A securities company holding an OJK business licence may operate as a broker-dealer intermediary that administers customers’ securities accounts and is established specifically within a provincial area. That licence is not a decorative detail; it is part of the activity’s stated character and places the business within the OJK-regulated securities-company framework.

Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That means foreign investment is permitted up to full ownership under the cited national basis. The record does not present a lower national cap, a partnership condition, or a separate ownership threshold for this activity. Its openness is therefore direct, while its operational identity remains tied to the stated OJK licensing and securities-account administration role.

Bali does not reverse that national position. A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today: it is not blocked by the province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk position is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which is why the activity sits outside that moratorium block. This is an important distinction: the Bali result is not an exemption invented around a foreign-ownership cap, but a recorded conclusion that the activity is not blocked by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today because it is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium.

Surat pernyataan tertulis di atas materai mengenai:

  1. Kesanggupan memenuhi aspek keselamatan, kesehatan kerja dan pengelolaan lingkungan hidup;
  2. Kesanggupan memenuhi kewajiban badan usaha;
  3. Kesediaan dilakukan audit kepatuhan terhadap ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
  4. Kesanggupan badan usaha menjamin dan bertanggung jawab bahwa sarana dan fasilitas yang dimiliki/dikuasai layak beroperasi dan mampu dijalankan sesuai dengan kaidah keteknikan yang baik selama masa operasi;
  5. Badan usaha bebas dari konflik atau permasalahan hukum lainnya dengan pihak lain;
  6. Dokumen persyaratan dan keterangan/ pernyataan yang diberikan adalah benar adanya dan apabila dikemudian hari terbukti tidak benar akan dicabut izin usahanya sesuai dengan peraturan perundangan-undangan;
  7. Kesanggupan menerima penunjukan dan penugasan dari Menteri untuk melaksanakan penyimpanan dalam rangka penyediaan cadangan penyangga energi dan pemenuhan kebutuhan minyak bumi di dalam negeri pada fasilitas dan sarana penyimpanan miliknya (untuk kegiatan usaha niaga minyak bumi);
  8. Kesanggupan menerima penunjukan dan penugasan dari Menteri untuk melaksanakan penyimpanan dalam rangka penyediaan cadangan penyangga energi dan pemenuhan kebutuhan bahan bakar minyak di dalam negeri pada fasilitas dan sarana penyimpanan miliknya (untuk kegiatan usaha niaga bahan bakar minyak);
  9. Surat pernyataan tertulis di atas materai mengenai kesanggupan badan usaha menerima penugasan dari Menteri untuk pemanfaatan secara bersama dengan pihak lain atas fasilitas yang dimiliki (untuk kegiatan usaha niaga gas bumi yang memiliki fasilitas jaringan distribusi);
  10. Kesanggupan badan usaha menyediakan cadangan LPG minimum sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan yang besarnya dihitung dari rencana volume penjualan harian rata-rata (untuk kegiatan usaha niaga LPG);
  11. Kesanggupan badan usaha menerima penugasan dari Menteri untuk penyediaan dan pendistribusian LPG (untuk kegiatan usaha niaga LPG);
  12. Kesanggupan badan usaha menerima penugasan dari Menteri untuk pemanfaatan secara bersama dengan pihak lain atas fasilitas penyimpanan dan/atau pengangkutan LPG yang dimiliki dan/atau dikuasai termasuk penyalurnya secara bersama dengan pihak lain (untuk kegiatan usaha niaga LPG); dan/atau
  13. Kesanggupan badan usaha menyediakan cadangan operasional LPG sesuai ketentuan peraturan yang berlaku (untuk kegiatan usaha niaga LPG).

Jaminan kecukupan pendanaan, yang dibuktikan dengan:

  1. Dokumen jaminan kecukupan pendanaan sendiri yang dibuktikan dengan laporan keuangan 3 (tiga) tahun terakhir yang telah diaudit oleh akuntan publik yang terdaftar sesuai dengan Peraturan Perundang-undangan bagi Badan Usaha yang telah berdiri lebih dari 3 (tiga) tahun;
  2. Dokumen kesepakatan dengan pihak lain yang menyatakan jaminan kecukupan pendanaan yang dikeluarkan oleh pihak lain yang nilainya sesuai dengan rencana usaha dalam analisis kelayakan usaha; atau
  3. Surat keterangan dari bank umum yang berkedudukan di Indonesia, yang menerangkan bahwa Badan Usaha memiliki kemampuan pendanaan untuk melakukan kegiatan usahanya dengan nominal yang sesuai dengan rencana usaha dalam analisis kelayakan usaha

editorial.headline: Commodity Futures Brokerage, Open Nationally and in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers client-mandated commodity futures and derivatives trading, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Commodity futures brokerage is the business of carrying out client-ordered purchases and sales of commodities through futures contracts, sharia derivatives, and other derivatives. The broker receives a specified amount of money and/or securities as margin to secure the transaction. The activity is defined not by owning or producing commodities, but by acting on a client mandate within contract-based commodity trading. Its scope also expressly includes futures-broker representatives, the opening of branch offices, forwarding mandates abroad to overseas futures exchanges, and participation in an alternative trading system.

Registration is open across every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. For foreign investment at the national level, the status is TERBUKA and the permitted foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In practical terms, the national position in this record does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership. The stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali’s position is equally direct, but it should be read beside the provincial moratorium. That rule blocks PMA registration across Bali for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This activity is not marked as blocked. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, and the record identifies it as not blocked by the moratorium. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: the activity is open in Bali rather than excluded, with its large-scale risk classification explaining why the moratorium does not close it to PMA.

Client mandates remain the connecting thread across the scope. Whether an order is executed through futures, sharia derivatives, or another derivative contract; forwarded to an overseas futures exchange; or connected to an alternative trading system, the activity remains commodity trading performed for a client and supported by margin in money and/or securities. It also accommodates representation and branch-office presence. That is the complete picture in this record: a nationally open, 100-percent foreign-ownership activity whose Bali treatment is not blocked by the province’s lower-risk PMA moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: That is the complete picture in this record: a nationally open, 100-percent foreign-ownership activity whose Bali treatment is not blocked by the province’s lower-risk PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Digital Financial Asset Brokerage: Open Nationally, Closed to Bali PMA
editorial.standfirst: Digital financial asset brokerage permits full foreign ownership nationally, but PMA registration at a Bali address is blocked by the province’s permanent moratorium.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity through PMA at a Bali address today. That conclusion belongs at the beginning, because its national availability can otherwise sound more decisive than it is. Bali blocks PMA registration for this activity under an island-wide, permanent moratorium on low- and medium-low-risk activities. The record’s stated reason identifies the Large scale as medium-low risk, placing the activity within the Bali block when the registration address is in the province.

Nationally, however, the activity is open to PMA and permits foreign ownership of up to 100%. Its national footing is identified as Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. This is a fully open foreign-ownership ceiling at the national level, not a partial one. Yet national openness does not make a Bali address available for PMA registration. The national setting and the Bali registration condition have different effects, and that distinction is the central planning fact for this activity.

Digital financial asset brokerage means facilitating trades in financial assets represented digitally, including crypto. Its scope is precise: transactions are carried out on a digital financial asset exchange in the name of another party or customer. The registered business is therefore defined by its role in enabling those customer-side exchange transactions. The record opens the activity at every listed scale—micro, small, medium, and large—although the stated Bali restriction catches the Large scale because it is classified as medium-low risk.

For Bali, the result is unambiguous for PMA registration: closed under the permanent, island-wide moratorium. The provincial rule applies to all low- and medium-low-risk activities, and the record places this activity’s Large scale within that condition. There is no inconsistency in saying both that the activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and that a Bali PMA registration cannot proceed today; each statement describes a different layer of the record.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not make a Bali address available for PMA registration.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Brokerage Activity, With Bali Registration Blocked
editorial.standfirst: Money and foreign-exchange market brokerage is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet PMA registration at a Bali address is blocked by the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register KBLI 66124 through a PMA with a Bali address today. That result sits in deliberate tension with the national position: the activity is TERBUKA—open—and its national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. The code is nevertheless closed for Bali PMA registration under the province’s moratorium. The national allowance remains real, but it does not displace the rule applied to a Bali address.

At its centre, this is an intermediary activity. KBLI 66124 covers a party that acts for customers transacting in the money market and foreign-exchange market. Its subject is the concrete role of standing between customers and their transactions in those two markets. Both the money market and the foreign-exchange market are expressly named; neither can be edited out of the description. That narrow wording directs attention to the customer-facing brokerage function set out in the record.

The national record is broad on eligible business scale. It lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar as open, corresponding to micro, small, medium and large. No one of those listed scales is presented as the sole national route to the activity; each appears in the open-to field. This is a scale statement, not a different statement of scope: every eligible scale leads back to the same intermediary role. Read alongside the TERBUKA status and the 100% ceiling, the national entry describes an activity available to PMA without a foreign-shareholding cap below full ownership.

Bali changes the practical registration answer rather than the definition of the work. The record identifies the Besar scale as Menengah Rendah, or medium-low, and records an island-wide, permanent Bali PMA moratorium for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI at a Bali address. In this instance, the local status is Closed (Bali moratorium) and the activity is marked blocked. The clear conclusion is therefore no PMA registration in Bali for this activity today. A founder considering this code needs to hold both propositions at once: national foreign ownership may reach 100%, while Bali’s address-based moratorium stops the PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: National foreign ownership may reach 100%, while Bali’s address-based moratorium stops the PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Money Changing: Nationally Open, and Not Barred in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers foreign-banknote exchange and travellers’ cheque purchases; it is nationally open to full foreign ownership and is not barred from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66125 concerns the exchange counter itself: the buying and selling of foreign banknotes, alongside the purchase of travellers’ cheques. The scope is deliberately transactional. It identifies the two dealings that make up the activity, placing foreign paper currency at its centre and expressly retaining travellers’ cheque purchases within it. For a founder, that matters more than a broad label: the registration is anchored in those stated exchange and purchase transactions. It is a clear definition of what the business is being registered to do.

Registration is open at every stated scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. A founder can therefore place the activity at a micro, small, medium or large business scale; none of the four listed scales is left outside the activity. That range is relevant to its Bali reading, because the record singles out the Besar scale for its OSS risk treatment. Scale does not displace the national ownership result, but it becomes important when the provincial moratorium is applied.

At national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA and foreign ownership may reach 100%. That means a company registering this activity can be entirely foreign-owned under the national entry; the record does not set a lower foreign-ownership cap. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The national conclusion is straightforward, but it cannot by itself answer the Bali question, which turns on that province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.

Bali’s result is more favourable than a simple reference to the moratorium might suggest. The activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and is expressly not blocked by the moratorium. The stated reason is specific: at Besar scale, OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—medium-high/high. Because the province’s rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, that higher risk treatment places this activity outside the moratorium. A foreigner can register it in Bali today, with the national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. This is a direct Bali finding, not an assumption drawn from the national open status.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not block this activity for PMA: at the Besar scale, its medium-high/high OSS risk places it outside the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Securities Crowdfunding: The Operator Behind the Open Electronic Offer
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 66126 covers the provision, management and operation of securities offerings that connect issuers directly with investors through an open electronic system.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66126 concerns the party that provides, manages and operates a securities offering in which an issuer reaches investors directly through an open electronic-system network. Its subject is not the issuer’s business in the abstract, but the organisation of the offering itself: the infrastructure and operation through which securities are presented by issuers to investors in an open electronic environment. In practical terms, the activity sits at the point where an issuer’s offer meets a digitally connected investing public.

The record opens this activity to every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the code describes an operational role rather than reserving it to one size of enterprise. The relevant registrant is the party providing, managing and operating the securities-offering arrangement. The defining feature is the direct route from issuer to investor through the open electronic network, not a narrower description of either participant on its own.

At the national level, foreign investment in this activity is **TERBUKA**, with foreign ownership permitted up to **100%**. That is a clean national position: foreign participation is open up to the stated ceiling. It should nevertheless be read as a statement about this specific activity and its stated investment position, not as a substitute for details the record does not supply. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali does not add a foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition in this record. Its position is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the stated reason is specific: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so the activity is not blocked by the moratorium. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently; this activity is recorded as outside that block. For a foreign investor considering Bali, the honest reading is therefore straightforward: the activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked by Bali’s stated moratorium on the record provided.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked by Bali’s stated moratorium on the record provided.

editorial.headline: Carbon-Unit Brokerage: A Clear PMA Position in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers carbon-unit transactions conducted as an intermediary for clients, with full national foreign ownership permitted and no Bali moratorium block at Large scale.
editorial.body:
Carbon-unit brokerage is an intermediary activity: the business conducts transactions in carbon units for another party or for its clients. Its defining role is not simply participation in a transaction, but acting between the market and the client whose interest it serves. That makes the scope specific. The activity is framed around carrying out carbon-unit transactions for others, placing the broker’s relationship with its client at the centre of the business.

The record opens this activity to enterprises at **Mikro, Kecil, Menengah,** and **Besar** scales. It also sets out a broader securities-facing operational scope: transactions in securities may be undertaken for the firm’s own interest and for other parties, securities may be marketed for another securities firm, and further activities may be determined or approved by the Financial Services Authority. For a business choosing this activity, the practical point is to keep its registered operation aligned with the stated intermediary function and the authorities contemplated in the record.

Nationally, the PMA position is unambiguous: the activity is **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. In plain terms, a foreign investor may hold the entire business nationally under this activity. Bali does not overturn that position. The province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks activities carrying Low or Medium-Low risk. Here, however, the record states that the OSS risk at **Besar** scale is Medium-High or High. As a result, the activity is not blocked by that moratorium in Bali.
