editorial.headline: Re-Guarantee Brokerage: A Fully Open Activity With a Clear Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 66226 covers advisory and brokerage work in re-guarantee provision and related claim settlement, acting for and on behalf of the guaranteed party.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66226 is a specialist intermediary activity: it covers providing advisory and/or brokerage services in the provision of re-guarantees, together with handling the settlement of related claims. The work is performed for and on behalf of the guaranteed party. Its centre of gravity is therefore representation and intermediation within a re-guarantee arrangement—not merely the administration of a claim, nor a general consulting label detached from that arrangement.

The code is available across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That matters because the activity is not presented as one reserved for a single class of operator. A business registering under this code may do so at any of those scales, provided its actual work remains within the defined scope: advice or brokerage in providing re-guarantees, and the handling of their claim settlements on behalf of the guaranteed party.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the record permits full foreign ownership at the national level; there is no lower foreign-share cap stated for this activity. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For founders, the useful discipline is to keep that national position separate from the operating scope itself: foreign ownership may be fully open, but the registered activity must still be the defined advisory, brokerage, and claims-settlement work connected to re-guarantees.

Bali does not add a block here. The province’s standing moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA, island-wide and permanently. This activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and at the Besar scale its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; the record therefore states that it is not blocked by that moratorium. The Bali conclusion is unusually clean: a PMA registration is not prevented there by the stated moratorium, while the national foreign-ownership ceiling remains 100%.
editorial.pullQuote: The Bali conclusion is unusually clean: a PMA registration is not prevented there by the stated moratorium, while the national foreign-ownership ceiling remains 100%.

editorial.headline: Actuarial Advice: Pricing Life Insurance Through Mathematics
editorial.standfirst: This activity applies mathematical principles and statistical data to design life-insurance programmes and determine premium rates.
editorial.body:
Actuarial advisory activity is the disciplined work of turning statistical data into the probabilities that underpin life-insurance programmes. Its scope is expressly mathematical: applying actuarial principles to determine or calculate possible outcomes from statistical information, then using that work to prepare or design different forms of life-insurance programme and establish premium rates. It is not a broad label for insurance activity; its centre of gravity is the calculation behind programme design and pricing.

An actuarial business may carry out this activity at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That range matters because the record does not reserve the activity for one particular size of enterprise. Whether organised at a micro, small, medium or large scale, the described business remains anchored in the same substantive work: mathematical analysis of likelihoods derived from statistical data, applied to life-insurance programmes and premium determination.

At the national level, PMA participation is TERBUKA, and foreign ownership may reach 100%. In Bali, it is not blocked for PMA registration. The provincial moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA across the island, permanently; this activity sits outside that block because, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. The practical Bali reading is therefore straightforward: the activity remains open rather than being caught by the moratorium, while its risk position at the large scale is explicitly higher than the categories the moratorium blocks.

That distinction is worth keeping clear. The national position establishes full foreign ownership for the activity, and the Bali position does not reverse it through the province-wide moratorium. The record’s Bali classification is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`: open in that sense, but explicitly associated at the Besar scale with Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi OSS risk. For founders, the useful precision lies in recognising both facts at once—full national PMA openness and a Bali status that remains available because it is not within the permanently blocked Low or Medium-Low risk band.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity remains open in Bali because it is not within the permanently blocked Low or Medium-Low risk band.

editorial.headline: Insurance Oversight: Nationally Open, Bali PMA Closed
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers financial oversight in insurance, guarantee and pension funds—open nationally to full foreign ownership, but unavailable for PMA registration at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66292 is defined by oversight work in financial services, not by a retail or product description. It covers four stated functions—regulation, supervision, examination and investigation—directed at activity in insurance, guarantee and pension funds. Those functions and sectors are the activity’s whole frame in the record. In clear terms, the code concerns work that regulates, supervises, examines and investigates financial-services activity within those named areas. It is a functional definition, built from what is done and the sectors to which it is applied.

The boundary is equally deliberate. The scope excludes supervisory financial-services activity beyond insurance and pension funds. That exclusion keeps the reading disciplined, while guarantee activity remains explicit in the main description. The remit therefore has two inseparable parts: the functions—regulation, supervision, examination and investigation—and the named insurance, guarantee and pension-fund sectors. For this record, both parts together form the definition.

Nationally, the position is open. The record marks the activity TERBUKA, makes it available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, and gives a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Foreign ownership may therefore reach 100% nationally. These facts belong together: the code is not confined in the record to a single business scale, and the stated foreign-ownership ceiling is full ownership. The national basis cited for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali demands a separate conclusion. Although the national position is open, a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA at a Bali address today. The record gives Bali a closed-under-moratorium status and identifies the Besar scale as Menengah Rendah. That classification places it inside Bali’s PMA moratorium: the island-wide, permanent rule blocks PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk classifications. National openness does not turn into a right to register a PMA at a Bali address. The Governor’s letter cited in the record is the local source for that moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not turn into a right to register a PMA at a Bali address.

editorial.headline: Nationally Open, but PMA-Closed in Bali: Insurance Support Activity
editorial.standfirst: This activity supports insurance, guarantee and pension-fund work, with national PMA openness that does not extend to a Bali address.
editorial.body:
KBLI 66299 covers supporting work closely connected to insurance, guarantees and pension funds. Its practical territory includes the administration of salvage and consultancy for insurance and pension funds. It is an ancillary-services category: the work sits alongside those sectors rather than being financial intermediation, claims adjustment or insurance-agent activity. The emphasis is therefore on the operational and advisory functions that help these fields function.

The activity is open across the recorded Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because it allows the category to accommodate an enterprise whose principal business is this specialist support work, whether it begins at a smaller scale or operates at a larger one. The record does not attach a narrower scale condition to the national opening. Its scope remains defined by the nature of the service: support, administration and consultancy closely related to insurance, guarantees and pension funds.

Nationally, the PMA position is clear: it is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign ownership may reach the full national ceiling for this activity. But that national position is not the whole answer for a founder choosing where to register. **A national opening is not, by itself, a Bali registration result.** The distinction is especially important here because the Bali outcome is determined by the province’s PMA moratorium rather than by the national ownership ceiling.

For a Bali address, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA today. The Bali status is Closed (Bali moratorium). The record explains that the Besar scale is classified as Menengah Rendah, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA block for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This is not a reduction of the national 100% ceiling; it is a separate Bali registration barrier. A founder assessing this activity should therefore keep the two conclusions distinct: nationally, it is open to PMA at up to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, PMA registration is blocked under the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: A national opening is not, by itself, a Bali registration result.

editorial.headline: Conventional Investment Management: Open Nationally, Not Barred in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers conventional management of securities and investment portfolios for clients, with full foreign ownership available nationally and no Bali moratorium block stated.
editorial.body:
Conventional investment management in the financial market is, at its core, the professional management of other people’s investments. The activity covers the management of securities portfolios, collective investments and other investment portfolios for either a group of clients or an individual client, conducted on a conventional basis. It is not a broad label for every institution that holds or deploys capital: the stated scope excludes insurance companies, pension funds and banks carrying out their own business activities under the applicable rules.

That distinction gives the activity its proper centre of gravity. editorial.headline: Sharia Investment Management: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers sharia-based portfolio management for individual or collective clients, open to foreign investment nationally and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Sharia investment management in financial markets is the business of managing securities portfolios, collective investments and other investment portfolios for either a group of clients or an individual client, according to sharia principles. It also encompasses an investment manager whose constitutional documents state that its business activities, management methods and services are conducted under sharia principles in the capital market. The code is therefore defined by both the work itself—portfolio management—and the principles on which that work is conducted.

The activity is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Its national investment position is equally direct. It is classified as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. For a foreign investor, that means the national framework permits full foreign ownership of this activity; there is no lower national ceiling to read into the record.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The province’s standing moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities across the island, on a permanent basis. This activity is not blocked by that rule. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which places it outside the moratorium’s stated reach. Bali’s status is consequently OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: viable for PMA registration under the record’s Bali test, while carrying the higher-risk classification noted for the large-business scale.

That distinction matters because the national and Bali readings reach the same practical conclusion here, but for different recorded reasons. Nationally, the activity is open to up to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, it is not exempted by a special foreign-ownership figure; rather, it is not among the Low or Medium-Low risk activities caught by the province-wide PMA moratorium. The result is a clear position: a sharia-based investment-management business within this defined scope is nationally open and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

editorial.headline: Commodity Futures Investment Management: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers pooled-fund management for commodity futures contracts, with national foreign ownership open to 100% and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Commodity futures investment management is the business of gathering and managing money from individuals or groups of individuals for investment in futures contracts. Its scope also includes parties acting as representative managers of a futures fund centre. In practical terms, the activity is defined by the stewardship of pooled investment funds directed into commodity futures—not simply by an interest in the market itself.

The registration field is available across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the record does not confine the activity to one size of operator. It recognises a continuum from micro through large-scale enterprise, while keeping the central identity of the activity constant: collecting and managing investor funds for futures-contract investment. The scope also specifically names the representative-manager function, while distinguishing the wider activity group from that role.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. At the national level, this activity remains TERBUKA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. That means foreign participation is fully open at the national level; there is no lower foreign-equity cap stated in this record. The cited PMA basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For founders assessing structure, the useful conclusion is precise: the national record permits full foreign ownership for this activity, rather than presenting a partial-access arrangement.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The provincial record marks the activity as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and confirms that it is not blocked by the moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—medium-high/high—which is why the moratorium does not apply. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA restriction covers Low and Medium-Low risk activities; this activity sits outside that blocked category on the stated risk basis. There is no Bali-specific foreign-ownership percentage or partnership condition recorded here, so none should be inferred. The honest reading is therefore clear: foreign ownership can reach 100% nationally, and PMA registration for this activity is not blocked in Bali by the recorded moratorium.

The mutual-fund example gives the activity a clear financial-management character, while the wording also preserves its stated boundary around funds other than investment funds and pension funds not otherwise covered by the group.

Nationally, the PMA position is open. The foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, meaning the record states no foreign-capital cap below full ownership for this activity. intel_2026.whatItMeans: Developing and selling residential real estate — buying, selling, and developing houses, apartments, flats, and residential land. This covers the full property development cycle: acquire land, build residential buildings, and sell or lease them. Mobile home park development for residential use also falls here.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**All scales (Micro through Large)**: Medium-Low risk (Menengah Rendah). NIB + Standard Certificate (Sertifikat Standar) issued **automatically** (Otomatis).

**Key obligations:**
- **KKPR** (Kesesuaian Kegiatan Pemanfaatan Ruang) — spatial conformity permit for housing development, issued by ATR/BPN
- **Persyaratan Dasar** — basic business licensing requirements for smaller scales
- **MBR housing** (Masyarakat Berpenghasilan Rendah) — additional specific development requirements if building low-income housing
- **SK Pengesahan** from Pemda — master plan, land parcel split plans, management separation plans
- **Audited financials** — laporan keuangan audited by public accountant, with debt-to-equity ratios

**Authority chain:**
- **National:** Kementerian ATR/BPN (for KKPR), BKPM/OSS (for NIB)
- **Provincial:** Governor / DPMPTSP Provinsi
- **Local:** Bupati/Walikota — PP28 designates this level as primary licensing authority

**PMA:** Fully open (Terbuka) — 100% foreign ownership.

**⚠️ BALI GOVERNOR ALERT (Jan 2026):** The Governor of Bali has formally requested BKPM to CLOSE OSS registration for PMA companies operating Medium-Low risk (Menengah Rendah) activities in Bali — which directly includes 68111. This code is listed as the #1 most abused PMA code in Bali (Surat Gubernur B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, 28 January 2026). If BKPM grants this request, new PMA companies will be UNABLE to register 68111 for Bali operations. Existing NIBs are expected to remain valid. Monitor OSS for changes.

**Source Regulation:** PP 28/2025, Perpres 10/2021.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Unchanged from KBLI 2020 — direct match. Residential real estate development stays the same.
intel_2026.baliContext:
**The Governor's numbers (Surat Gubernur, Jan 2026):**
- **19,262** PMA businesses registered in Bali (2021–2025) — that's 40% of all PMA nationally
- **55,458** projects across those PMA companies
- **47.55%** are low-risk requiring only NIB — nearly half face zero substantive oversight
- The letter also requests closure of PMA at **virtual office addresses** in Bali
- **68111** is cited as the single most abused PMA code in the province

---

**Bali real estate reality:**
- Land prices in south Bali (Canggu, Seminyak, Jimbaran) have **tripled in the last decade**
- **KKPR** (spatial conformity) is critical — Bali has strict zoning near temples, rice terraces, and waterways
- Foreigners **cannot own land freehold** (Hak Milik) — must use PT PMA
- Typical structure: **HGB** (Hak Guna Bangunan — building rights, 30 years + 20 year extension) held by the PT PMA

---

**Common client mistakes:**
- **Virtual office** for a real estate company — the Governor's letter specifically targets this, DPMPTSP Bali is actively flagging it
- **"Holding code" abuse** — registering 68111 with no actual development project is exactly the pattern cited in the Surat Gubernur
- **Hak Milik → HGB conversion** — assuming it's quick; in Bali, BPN processing can take 6–12 months
- **Ignoring the banjar** (local village council) — no government permits will save you if the banjar objects
- **Building first, permitting later** — IMB/PBG enforcement has intensified since 2024, with demolition orders actually executed in Canggu and Pererenan

editorial.headline: Residential Development in Indonesia: Open Nationally, Watched Closely in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 68111 covers the business of developing, trading, leasing and operating residential property, from homes and flats to apartments and projects built for sale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 68111 is the activity code for residential building and land development. Its scope reaches beyond construction in the narrow sense: it includes the purchase and sale of residential buildings, including apartment buildings and homes; the development of houses, flats and apartments, furnished or unfurnished, for more permanent or year-round use; residential mobile-home sites intended as a main home; and residential building projects developed for sale. It also encompasses the purchase, sale, leasing and operation of housing that is either owned or rented, including residential or mixed-residential housing development.

This is therefore a code for the commercial life of housing as well as its creation. A business registered under it may be concerned with bringing a residential project to market, holding and operating housing, or arranging the ownership and rental activity surrounding it. The classification is open to Micro, Small, Medium and Large enterprises, placing it across the full stated range of business scales rather than reserving the activity for a particular size of operator.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is direct: the activity is **open** to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership of **100%**. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In practical editorial terms, the national record does not present a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity.

Bali requires a more careful reading. The record does not mark KBLI 68111 as currently blocked for PMA registration in Bali. Its Bali status is instead recorded as a proposed closure, with the stated reason that real estate is proposed for PMA closure in Bali. Alongside that proposal sits a permanent, island-wide provincial moratorium blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, under the cited Governor's letter. That rule identifies risk categories, while this slim record provides no risk classification for KBLI 68111. The honest position is consequently neither a claim of a current Bali block nor an assurance that the national openness settles the Bali question: nationally the activity is open to 100% foreign ownership, while Bali's record signals a real-estate closure proposal and a separate standing PMA moratorium rule.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, residential development is open to 100% foreign ownership, while Bali's record signals a proposed real-estate closure and a separate standing PMA moratorium rule.

This code descends from KBLI 2020 68111 (Real Estate yang dimiliki sendiri atau disewa) on that list (BPS KBLI 2020→2025 conversion table).

editorial.headline: Residential Leasing: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 68112 covers leasing and operating self-owned or rented residential real estate—open to foreign investment nationally, while its Bali PMA availability remains unclassifiable pending re-derivation of the true risk tier.
editorial.body:
KBLI 68112 is the business of leasing and operating residential real estate that the operator owns or itself rents. In practical terms, its focus is the ongoing provision and operation of homes and residential property through a rental model. The wording matters: the scope joins two linked functions—leasing and operating—and applies whether the residential real estate is self-owned or rented by the business. That is the full activity described in the record, and it is the right boundary for deciding whether the code fits a proposed venture.

The record opens the activity to Micro, Small, Medium and Large enterprises. It does not reserve the scope for a single business size. At national level, it is marked open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national position: a PMA structure may hold up to the stated ceiling for this activity. The source recorded for that national treatment is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Those facts make the national rule unusually straightforward, provided the business remains within residential leasing and operation as stated.

Bali's earlier verdict here was that a foreign investor could not register this activity through a PMA company at a Bali address. That reading depended on a risk tier the record no longer supports: the classification behind it was carried over from a different activity through a code-number collision, and has been detached. The earlier ‘blocked under the Bali moratorium’ verdict was based on that same carried-over risk classification, so it is unresolved rather than lifted — whether the moratorium applies cannot be determined until the true risk tier is established. Treat a Bali setup as unconfirmed and verify with the Bali Zero team first.

editorial.headline: Organising a Tourism District
editorial.standfirst: This activity organises the land, development units and administration of a tourism area, with full national foreign ownership and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Tourism-area management begins with land, but its remit is the organisation of an entire tourism precinct. The activity covers laying out and further dividing land into defined nodes or neighbourhoods; building or leasing those units for businesses that will develop the tourism facilities and infrastructure the area requires. It also includes carrying out and/or supervising tourism-business development under the existing requirements, and building or providing space for business administration within the area. It is an area-wide role.

The code is available to medium and large enterprises. That scale setting fits the work described: it is an operating mandate for a managed tourism area, rather than a single facility inside one. A registrant may be responsible for arranging the land, making development units available, overseeing the tourism development that follows, and ensuring that administration has a place within the managed area. The individual units can be built or leased, but their purpose is fixed: to accommodate businesses developing the tourism support required in the district. The activity also keeps the administrative needs of those businesses within the perimeter of the managed area.

Nationally, the PMA position is open and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. Put plainly, the national record permits full foreign ownership for this activity; it does not set a lower foreign-equity ceiling. The stated national PMA source underpins that position. For a founder assessing the activity on its own terms, that is the starting position: PMA is open nationally, at the stated 100% ceiling. It is an activity-specific national position, not a general conclusion about tourism investment.

Bali changes neither that national ownership figure nor the basic registration conclusion recorded here. The province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA for activities assessed at Low or Medium-Low risk. At the large-enterprise scale for this activity, however, the OSS risk is Medium-High or High. The record therefore says it is not blocked by the moratorium and gives its Bali status as OK or Higher Risk. The honest local reading is straightforward: a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today; the Bali result is not a hidden closure, but a route outside the moratorium’s Low and Medium-Low risk block.

editorial.headline: Industrial Estate Management: Open Nationally and Available in Bali
editorial.standfirst: At Besar scale, this activity manages integrated industrial-estate land and infrastructure, with 100% foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Industrial-estate management under KBLI 68122 concerns a single, continuous expanse of land made into an industrial estate: a place where industrial activity is concentrated and supported by facilities and infrastructure. The work is the management of that estate land and of its supporting elements, which are developed and managed by the estate manager. In practical terms, the activity is defined by stewardship of an integrated industrial setting, not by a disconnected site-by-site arrangement.

The record opens the activity only at the Besar scale. That makes the estate manager—the party developing and managing the supporting facilities and infrastructure—the central registrant in view. The scale is substantive, not incidental: it is the only scale listed as open. A founder considering the activity should therefore frame it around management of a fully formed industrial area, with land in one expanse and the support infrastructure that enables the concentration of industrial activity.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is marked TERBUKA for PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. There is consequently no foreign-equity cap below full ownership in the national figure supplied for this activity. The national reference recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That openness belongs to industrial-estate management as described here and to the Besar scale stated in the record; it does not need embellishment with unprovided requirements or thresholds.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion. Its standing is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—so the activity is not blocked by the provincial moratorium. The provincial moratorium is described as island-wide and permanent, with Low and Medium-Low OSS risk as its stated trigger. At Besar scale, this activity sits outside that block. The honest result is clear: a foreign investor may register this activity in Bali at Besar scale, with the same 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling, because it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: At Besar scale, industrial-estate management is open nationally to full foreign ownership and is not blocked for PMA in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Running a Special Economic Zone: Indonesia’s Management Code
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 68123 covers the companies that build, manage and service special economic-zone land—open nationally to full foreign ownership and not caught by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 68123 concerns the operating ground beneath a Special Economic Zone, not simply a piece of land in isolation. It covers managing land that forms a designated concentration of business activity, where supporting facilities and infrastructure sit within the zone. Its scope runs through the practical life of that area: development, management and leasing, as well as building the area or providing its services to the businesses that operate there. In plain terms, this is the activity of making an economic zone function as an organised place of business.

The registrants described here are development enterprises and management enterprises serving business actors inside the zone. The distinction matters because the record speaks to the business that develops and manages the area, rather than defining the businesses located within it. Registration is open at medium and large scale. That puts the focus squarely on an operator with responsibility for the zone’s land, facilities, infrastructure, leasing and services—the connective work that enables the area to be developed and managed.

At national level, the position is direct: the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is full foreign ownership, not a partial allowance. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign investor, the central point is therefore straightforward: the national classification opens the ownership question fully for this economic-zone management activity.

Bali requires a more local reading, but not a manufactured prohibition. The provincial rule blocks every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. This activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK—medium-high/high risk—and is expressly not blocked by that moratorium. A foreign-owned operator can therefore register it in Bali; the record still calls for verification for the specific address. That is the operative Bali condition: open to PMA at this risk level, with address-level checking rather than a blanket moratorium bar.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign-owned operator can therefore register it in Bali; the record still calls for verification for the specific address.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open MICE Venue Business That Bali Will Not Register
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the timed rental of event venues and facilities—open nationally to full foreign ownership, but blocked for PMA registration across Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is for the rental of places and facilities used to stage meetings, incentive travel, conventions, exhibitions and special events. Its subject is the venue itself: a convention centre, exhibition centre, special venue or multipurpose venue made available for a defined period. That period can encompass preparation, the event’s operation and dismantling afterwards. In practical terms, the activity describes the business of providing the setting in which an event happens, rather than the event as an abstract occasion.

The classification is open across the full business-scale range: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. Nationally, it is also open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That is a clear national position. A foreign-owned operator seeking to rent out a convention centre, exhibition space or special-event venue therefore has an activity that is nationally available on fully foreign-owned terms.

Bali changes the immediate answer. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali status is blocked on risk-class grounds: at the Large scale, every scope is recorded in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for all activities in those two risk bands. The block is not a suggestion to reconsider the commercial model, nor a partial opening subject to a stated local condition; it is a registration barrier for PMA in the province.

That contrast matters because the national foreign-ownership ceiling and the Bali registration outcome describe different layers of the same decision. Nationally, the activity is open and may be held by foreign investors up to 100%. In Bali, however, the provincial moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity because of its recorded risk classification. For founders, the accurate reading is therefore straightforward: the venue-rental business is nationally foreign-open at every scale, yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under the standing moratorium announced in May 2026.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness to 100% foreign ownership does not overcome Bali’s permanent PMA block for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Running the Commercial Destination
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership; in Bali it is not blocked by the moratorium, though the address must be verified.
editorial.body:
KBLI 68125 concerns the business of creating and running defined commercial areas: places arranged for the trade of goods or services rather than a single shop or tenant operation. Its scope includes developing, buying, selling, leasing and operating such areas. Malls, plazas, rest areas and food centres are all examples named within that scope. The common thread is the commercial destination as a managed whole—an area assembled, made available and kept in operation for trading activity.

The activity is open to businesses operating at the `Menengah` and `Besar` scales. That matters because the code describes a broad commercial-area role, encompassing both the transactions around the area and its continuing operation. A registrant may be involved in developing the site, acquiring or disposing of it, leasing its spaces, operating it, or a combination of those functions. The scope is intentionally practical: it follows the commercial area through the work of putting it into use and keeping it available for goods and service trade.

Nationally, the PMA position is `TERBUKA`, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the activity is open to full foreign ownership at the national level. There is no partial foreign-ownership ceiling in this record to soften or reinterpret: the stated national maximum is complete ownership by foreign investors.

Bali requires its own reading. The record places the activity in an `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK` position and states that medium-high or high risk is not blocked by the provincial moratorium, with verification required for the particular address. Bali's island-wide, permanent rule blocks PMA for low and medium-low risk activities; this recorded position sits outside that block. At the national level, full foreign ownership is permitted; in Bali, the activity is not blocked by the moratorium but its address still needs verification. The national 100% ceiling remains the relevant ownership figure here.
editorial.pullQuote: At the national level, full foreign ownership is permitted; in Bali, the activity is not blocked by the moratorium but its address still needs verification.

editorial.headline: Storage Space, With the Bali Address Question
editorial.standfirst: Warehouse and self-storage rental is nationally open to full foreign ownership; in Bali, it is not caught by the moratorium, though every address still needs verification.
editorial.body:
This activity is the business of renting warehouse space and self-storage facilities for keeping goods. It also includes the rental of lockers equipped with security features. Its commercial centre is therefore the provision of space for storage: premises and lockers made available to customers who need somewhere for goods to be kept. The scope is practical and legible, covering both larger storage space and the more contained format of secure lockers.

Registration is open at the Menengah and Besar scales. The record offers no narrower category of applicant or additional description of who may register, so the disciplined reading is to stay with those stated scales. For a founder, that makes the early question one of fit: whether the planned enterprise belongs at the medium or large level identified in the record, and whether the activity being registered is genuinely the rental of storage space and facilities described here.

Nationally, the position is clear. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain English, the national foreign-ownership ceiling permits full foreign ownership. The applicable PMA reference in the record is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is the national setting from which an investment case begins: an open status, a stated ceiling of full ownership, and no need to imply restrictions that the record does not contain.

Bali does not turn that national openness into a prohibition in this record. Its status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason places it in the medium-high/high risk range, meaning it is not blocked by the moratorium. The provincial rule permanently blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island; this activity is outside that blocked class. One practical qualification remains explicit: the position must be verified for the specific address. Bali is therefore not a blanket bar here, but address-by-address verification remains part of an honest reading.

editorial.headline: Office Buildings: Foreign-Open Nationally, With a Bali Proposal in View
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers developing, leasing and operating office buildings and flexible workspaces, open nationally to large-scale foreign investment while Bali records a proposal for PMA closure.
editorial.body:
Office property, in this definition, is not just the finished shell of a commercial building. The activity covers developing, leasing and operating office buildings, coworking spaces and individual office rooms. Its centre of gravity is the continuing life of work premises: bringing them to market, making them available to users and keeping the setting in operation. Conventional offices and shared work environments sit within the same stated scope, a useful reminder that the activity is drawn around the management and use of professional workspace rather than a single building format.

The registration frame is deliberately large-scale. The record opens the activity only to a Besar business scale, so the relevant operator is a substantial office-property or workspace business rather than a small-scale venture. That single scale signal deserves to be read plainly: it defines who the record names as eligible, without supplying extra thresholds, capital figures or operational conditions.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the record supports a fully foreign-owned PMA structure for this large-scale activity nationally. That clarity is important because it comes directly from the national position; it should not be weakened by importing local conditions that are not actually stated for the activity.

Bali calls for a more qualified reading. The supplied record does not mark the activity as currently blocked for PMA registration. It does, however, classify real estate as proposed for PMA closure in Bali. A proposal is a policy direction, not a completed prohibition, so the Bali record here is neither a clean local green light nor evidence that foreign registration has already been shut. The accompanying provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI across the island, but this slim record gives no risk classification for this activity. It cannot therefore establish that the moratorium applies here—or that it does not. The firm conclusion is narrower: national openness is explicit; Bali records a proposed closure, while no current Bali block is shown.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is explicit; Bali records a proposed closure, while no current Bali block is shown.

editorial.headline: Non-Residential Real Estate, With a Bali Warning Flag
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 68129 covers non-residential property operation and development, nationally open to full foreign ownership while Bali is marked for a proposed PMA closure.
editorial.body:
KBLI 68129 concerns the business of making non-residential real estate available, operating it, or developing it. Its scope reaches buildings held in ownership or lease, including other non-residential premises and data centres. It also embraces the development of non-residential building projects, whether the developer intends to operate them directly or sell them. Factory leasing belongs within the activity too, whether machinery and equipment are included or not. Even the rental of non-residential rooftops—for example, for solar-panel installations—sits within the stated scope.

The practical thread is property as an operating asset or development project, rather than a single type of tenant or building. A business may be earning from the use of premises it owns or leases, bringing a new non-residential project into operation, preparing it for sale, or leasing industrial space and associated equipment. The activity is open across the full recorded scale range: micro, small, medium, and large enterprises. That breadth matters because the code describes the nature of the real-estate activity, not a narrow company size or one fixed commercial format.

Nationally, the PMA position is open, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the record permits a fully foreign-owned structure at the national level for this activity. Bali requires a more careful reading. The code is not marked as blocked for PMA registration in Bali today, but its Bali status is recorded as a proposed closure for PMA in the real-estate field. That is a serious directional signal, not the same thing as a current block.

The record also notes a permanent, island-wide Bali moratorium on PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. It does not state this activity's risk classification or identify that moratorium as the present basis for blocking this code. The honest position is therefore precise: nationally the activity is fully open to foreign ownership; in Bali, it is not presently marked blocked in this record, yet it carries a proposed-PMA-closure status that should not be treated as a settled invitation.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the activity is fully open to foreign ownership; in Bali, it is not presently marked blocked but carries a proposed-PMA-closure status.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Real estate agents and brokers — intermediating the buying, selling, and renting of property. You connect buyers with sellers or tenants with landlords, earning a fee or commission. This can be done on digital platforms or the traditional way. You don't own the property; you facilitate the deal.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**All scales (Micro through Large)**: Medium-High risk. NIB + Standard Certificate within **3 working days**. Strict requirements:
- Must be a legal entity (badan hukum) registered in Indonesia
- All brokers must be certified property professionals
- Broker supervisors and back-office staff must be certified
- Written agreements with every client

**PMA:** Fully open — 100% foreign ownership.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct match from KBLI 2020, but the PP28 source code is 68200 — the old general real estate services code. The licensing requirements are substantial for this intermediation role.
intel_2026.baliContext: Bali's property agent market is a Wild West. Hundreds of 'agents' operate without proper licensing, especially in the expat market. Licensed agents are actually the minority. If you want to do this properly as a PT PMA, the broker certification requirement is real — your staff need certified property broker qualifications (from AREBI or equivalent bodies). The 3-day turnaround for the certificate is fast, but getting your brokers certified takes longer. This code covers the booming online property listing businesses too — Bali villa rental platforms, property marketplaces, and the like.
intel_2026.youllAlsoNeed:
- 68111 — If you also develop property (not just broker)
- 68112 — If you manage rental properties directly
- 62199 — If you're building a property platform/app
- 68291 — If you also do property appraisals

editorial.headline: The Business of Bringing Property Deals Together
editorial.standfirst: From listings to deal-making, this activity turns introductions into fees and commissions—and is nationally open to full foreign ownership, with Bali not blocked by its PMA moratorium at the recorded Large-scale risk.
editorial.body:
Real-estate intermediation is the work of making a property transaction connect: bringing clients together with sellers or service providers for the purchase, sale or rental of real estate. The consideration can be a fee or commission paid by the client, the seller, or the property-service provider. The activity is not confined to a traditional office. It may be conducted through a digital platform or through non-digital channels—face-to-face, including door to door, by telephone, by letter and similar routes. The scope also reaches real-estate listing services and may include third-party advertising-space revenue alongside intermediary income.

The record expressly places real-estate agents and independent agents inside the activity, where they provide intermediation on a fee or contract basis. It separately addresses non-exempt PPMSE and PSP based either inside Indonesia or outside it when they conduct PMSE business in Indonesia. Registration is open at every recorded scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth follows the function of the business—connecting parties and earning an agreed intermediary return—rather than limiting the work to one channel or one size of enterprise.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward: status TERBUKA with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain English, the record sets no foreign-equity ceiling below full foreign ownership for this activity at the national level. Its cited PMA basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is the recorded position for the defined intermediation activity, whose revenue may arise from fees, commissions and the specified sale of advertising space to third parties.

In Bali, the record is equally clear, although it must be read through risk: its status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and it is not marked as blocked. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—which means the activity is not blocked by the island-wide permanent moratorium described in the record. That moratorium blocks PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI in Bali. The practical conclusion is clean: Bali is not a registration dead end for PMA under this record; the decisive recorded fact is its Large-scale Medium-High/High risk classification.
editorial.pullQuote: At the Large scale, Bali’s Medium-High/High risk classification keeps this activity outside the island-wide PMA moratorium.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. intel_2026.whatItMeans: Property valuation and appraisal services — assessing the market value of real estate assets.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Medium/Large.** MEDIUM-HIGH RISK. NIB + full License (Izin). **14-day processing.** Standard certifications. Authority: Minister/Agency Head.

**PMA:** Fully open — 100% foreign ownership allowed.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Renumbered from KBLI 2020 code 68200 (previously a broad 'fee-based real estate' code). Now carved out specifically for valuation/appraisal.
intel_2026.baliContext: Property appraisal in Indonesia is regulated by MAPPI (Masyarakat Profesi Penilai Indonesia) and requires certified appraisers (KJPP). For PMA investors, entering the appraisal market means competing with established local firms and requiring MAPPI-certified staff. This is a professional services play — revenue comes from fees per valuation. The growing foreign property investment in Bali increases demand for appraisals, particularly for lending purposes (bank collateral valuations). However, the Indonesian appraiser certification requirements create a barrier for purely foreign-staffed operations.

- 68292 — Property Management (for ongoing property services)
- 69201 — Accounting (for financial due diligence)

editorial.headline: Real-Estate Appraisal: Open Nationally, Not Barred in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Real-estate appraisal is open to PMA nationally, with full foreign ownership permitted; in Bali, its higher-risk large-scale profile leaves it outside the permanent PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Real-estate appraisal is the business of providing services to assess the value of real-estate property. That is the centre of gravity of this activity: not property ownership, but the service of establishing a property’s value. The category is therefore best read from the work being offered. Where a business’s stated activity is the appraisal of real-estate value, this is the classification that describes that work. Its plain scope is useful precisely because it keeps the commercial proposition focused on valuation services.

The record opens the activity to micro, small, medium and large enterprises. In classification terms, that breadth matters: the stated scale options extend from Mikro through Besar, so the activity is not limited in the record to one size of undertaking. The national investment position is equally direct. Its PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In plain English, the national foreign-ownership ceiling permits complete foreign ownership for this activity. The cited national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali is where an otherwise simple reading requires a more exact sentence. The province has a permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. Yet this activity is not recorded as blocked in Bali. The reason given is specific: at the large scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, placing it outside that moratorium. The local outcome is therefore non-blocking, rather than a Bali-specific ban.

The result is a clean national-versus-Bali conclusion, without pretending the two layers are the same question. Nationally, PMA is open with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In Bali, this activity is not blocked under the province’s permanent rule because of the stated large-scale risk position. A foreign investor considering a real-estate appraisal business can read the record plainly: it is available across every listed scale and remains registrable for PMA in Bali under the rule described here.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, this activity is not blocked under the permanent PMA moratorium because its large-scale OSS risk is Medium-High/High.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

moratorium.rule: Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields (KBLI 2020 numbering), not for every low/medium-low risk activity
moratorium.source: Bali Provincial Government press release, 24 Jul 2026
moratorium.request: Governor letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP (28 Jan 2026), a request covering all low/medium-low risk PMA and virtual offices

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Residential Estate Management: Open Nationally, Viable in Bali at Larger Scale
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the contracted management of residential property, from operations and repairs to budgets, charges and resident rules.
editorial.body:
Residential real-estate management under a fee or contract is the work of keeping a housing estate functioning as an organised whole. Its scope includes supervising and coordinating daily operations, maintenance and repairs; preparing and collecting residential charges; setting management budgets and income-and-expenditure plans; and drafting and enforcing residential rules. In practical terms, this is not the ownership or sale of homes, but the professional administration of the residential environment after the homes are in use.

The activity is open at micro, small, medium and large scale. That breadth matters because the code describes a management function rather than a single physical format of housing. A modest operation may coordinate routine upkeep and resident contributions, while a larger one may carry the fuller responsibility of operational oversight, planned maintenance, budget preparation and the enforcement of estate rules. Across those scales, the defining feature remains the same: management is delivered for a fee or under contract.

Nationally, this activity is open to foreign investment, up to a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The national position is therefore direct: a foreign-owned PMA business may enter this activity within that ceiling. There is no need to read a lower foreign-share cap into the record; the stated national maximum is full foreign ownership.

Bali requires a more precise reading, but it is not a prohibition. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for activities assessed at Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium: at the large scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High or High. Bali’s recorded status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, meaning the activity sits outside the moratorium’s blocked risk band rather than being barred for PMA registration. For founders, the useful conclusion is clear: national openness is matched by a Bali position that does not trigger the island-wide moratorium, with the stated risk treatment at large scale explaining why.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Fee-Based Real-Estate Services, Open Nationally and Unblocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: From rent collection to non-residential property management and transaction advice, this fee- or contract-based real-estate activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 68299 covers real-estate services supplied for a fee or under another contractual arrangement. Its scope includes rent-collection agencies; the management of non-residential real estate, including jointly owned non-residential property; and paid consulting connected with the purchase, sale and leasing of real estate. It also reaches other forms of real-estate provision delivered on a fee or contract basis. The common thread is service work around real estate carried out for remuneration or contract: collecting rent, managing non-residential property, advising on purchase, sale and leasing, or providing another included real-estate service.

That framing matters when deciding whether this is the right activity to register. The record makes it available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. It presents the same scope alongside all four scales. For a registrant, the activity description turns on the work actually being carried out—rent collection, non-residential real-estate management, consulting around transactions or leasing, or another fee- or contract-based real-estate service within the stated scope.

Nationally, the PMA position is plain in the record: status TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In ownership terms, that permits full foreign ownership for this activity. The national PMA source cited is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national position sits alongside the broad scale availability, from Mikro through Besar, without changing the defined service scope.

Bali is also clear, though for a different reason. The Bali assessment gives the status OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and does not mark the activity as blocked. At Besar scale, the stated OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—which is why the activity is not caught by the moratorium. The applicable Bali rule is island-wide and permanent and blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This activity falls outside that prohibition in the supplied assessment. For a foreign investor, the candid conclusion is simple: the national 100% ceiling carries into a Bali position that is not blocked by this moratorium.

editorial.headline: Legal Practice: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Legal practice is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
**For a foreign investor in Bali, the operative fact is straightforward:** this activity cannot be registered through PMA there today. Nationally, the record marks it as open and permits foreign ownership up to 100 per cent. Bali reaches the opposite result: the activity is blocked for PMA registration under the provincial risk-class rule and moratorium. The national opening therefore does not carry across to an island registration.

This is the work of a law office: lawyers and legal advisers, legal-aid institutions, and other legal-service providers giving advice and representation in civil, criminal, state-administrative and employment disputes. The stated scope also takes in legal audits and other legal work, legal mediation, and appointments as a legal guardian. It brings several legal functions into one professional scope, from advice and representation to mediation. Its boundary is equally clear: it is not the activity of a judicial body, and it does not provide residential care or accommodation.

Across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, the activity remains open. That is a wide national scale range, but it should not be read as an override to the Bali position. Nor does the 100 per cent national foreign-ownership ceiling settle where a PMA registration can proceed. The scale list establishes the national range of registration, while the Bali classification determines the local PMA outcome. For a foreign-owned registration, those two levels must be read together rather than treated as interchangeable.

The stated Bali pathway is specific: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk rating is Low or Medium-Low for every scope. The province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium makes the relevant Low and Medium-Low risk classifications unavailable for PMA registration. The record dates that moratorium to May 2026 and identifies a Gubernur letter as its source. For this activity, the national permission is real, but Bali’s block is equally real—and it is the deciding condition for a PMA registration on the island.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor cannot register this activity through PMA in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Legal Consulting: Nationally Open, but Off-Limits to Foreign Nationals in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans company-formation documents and legal instruments, yet Bali’s professional rule closes the registration path to foreign nationals.
editorial.body:
Legal consulting under this activity is document-centred work with real consequences for how organisations are formed and governed. Its scope includes preparing legal documents, documents for legal entities, cooperation agreements and similar instruments connected with company formation. It also reaches the preparation of notarial deeds, wills, trusts and related materials, alongside other legal-document work. The record further identifies the activity with a law office: this is a professional legal-services setting, not merely administrative support around paperwork.

The activity is open nationally across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. At the national level it is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the national investment classification does not impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. That national position is important, but it is not the whole answer for a founder choosing Bali as the place of registration.

In Bali, the answer is direct: a foreign national cannot register this activity for PMA today. The Bali status is TERTUTUP because legal services are reserved for advocates licensed in Indonesia. Although the national KBLI catalogue records the code as open, the profession itself is off-limits to foreign nationals under the rule cited in the record. This is not a minor local qualification on an otherwise usable foreign-investment route; it determines whether the activity can be registered by a foreigner in Bali.

Bali also maintains a permanent, island-wide block on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, as set out in the Governor’s letter cited in the record. That province-wide rule forms part of the wider Bali setting, while this activity’s stated closure rests specifically on the Indonesian-licensed-advocate requirement. Founders should therefore read the national 100% ceiling accurately: it describes the national classification, not a permission to bypass the professional restriction that closes this activity to foreign nationals in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not override Bali’s closure of legal services to foreign nationals.

l4_bali.reason: Legal services are reserved for Indonesian-licensed advocates (UU 18/2003 on Advocates). The KBLI catalogue lists the code as TERBUKA, but the profession itself is closed to foreign nationals.

editorial.headline: Intellectual-Property Consultancy, and Bali’s PMA Divide
editorial.standfirst: This activity handles intellectual-property applications across a wide range of rights; it is nationally open to foreign ownership up to 100%, but PMA registration is blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 69103 covers the professional work of submitting and handling intellectual-property applications, together with related activity in the same field. Its scope reaches across patents, copyright, trademarks, geographical indications, industrial designs, integrated-circuit layout designs, trade secrets and other intellectual-property matters. The record also places intellectual-property consultancy offices and law offices within the activity. This is therefore a broad rights-administration practice, concerned with moving applications and related matters through their proper course.

The activity is open at every scale listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That range suits a field that can be carried out through an intellectual-property consultancy office or a law office, while still encompassing a substantial spread of intellectual-property subject matter. The scale categories establish that the activity is not confined to one size of operation; they do not alter what the activity itself covers, which remains the submission, handling and related work associated with intellectual-property matters.

Nationally, the position is straightforward. This activity is marked TERBUKA under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national record permits PMA registration with foreign ownership up to that full ceiling. There is no national foreign-ownership cap below 100% to qualify in this case. That openness is material, but it is not the whole answer for a founder intending to establish the activity in Bali.

In Bali, the conclusion changes decisively: a foreign investor cannot register this activity through PMA today. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class). At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low on every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium of May 13, 2026. The provincial rule blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, island-wide and permanently. The national ceiling of 100% remains the national figure; it does not override Bali’s PMA block. For a Bali proposal, the honest answer is a present bar on PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: The national ceiling of 100% remains the national figure; it does not override Bali’s PMA block.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.
