editorial.headline: Technical Testing, With a Clear Bali Route for Foreign Capital
editorial.standfirst: A bounded technical-testing activity open at every listed scale, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
This activity is a deliberately bounded home for technical testing and analysis. It covers work that is neither certification, inspection, verification nor validation, and that is not otherwise placed in a separately classified technical-testing activity. “Other” does not mean unlimited: the record sets clear edges around the category. Testing involving ionising radiation, the organisation of interlaboratory proficiency testing, and the development of technical standards used as testing references all sit outside it. Laboratory security-and-order operation is also outside the scope when it is separate from the testing activity itself.

The activity is available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That is broad access, but it does not dilute the definition. The relevant business is one undertaking the specified technical testing and analysis; the registration should follow the work actually performed rather than absorb adjacent functions that the record distinguishes. For founders, the useful reading is precise rather than expansive: start with the nature of the technical testing or analysis, then keep it within the stated boundary.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. The activity is marked TERBUKA and has a maximum foreign ownership of 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national record imposes no foreign-share ceiling below full ownership for this activity. That conclusion applies to this defined technical-testing and analysis activity, at the scales named in the record. It is a clear opening, not an invitation to treat every laboratory-adjacent undertaking as the same registered activity.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: The Business of Systematic Natural-Science Research
editorial.standfirst: This activity code frames research and development in the natural sciences as a registered business, open nationally to foreign investment and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity covers regular, systematic research and development in the natural sciences. Its field is deliberately broad: mathematics, physics, biology, chemistry, astronomy, geology, botany and zoology all sit within its stated scope. It also expressly includes work in life sciences, chemical sciences, computer and information science, earth and environmental science, mathematics and physics. The common thread is not a single discipline, but an organised research-and-development activity rooted in natural science.

That makes the code suitable where research is the activity being registered rather than an incidental feature of another operation. The record describes work undertaken regularly and systematically, a useful distinction for founders whose enterprise is built around sustained investigation and development across one or more of the listed scientific fields. It is open to small, medium and large business scales, so the classification does not reserve this activity for only the largest institutional research settings.

At the national level, the position is clear: the activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the record places no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That openness rests on the cited investment framework, while the underlying business description remains anchored in research and development rather than a broader claim about every possible scientific or commercial undertaking.

Bali requires the more local reading. The record classifies the Bali position as OK or higher risk and says the activity is medium-high risk; it is therefore not blocked by the provincial moratorium. That moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk activities across the island, but this activity is outside that blocked category on the supplied record. The remaining instruction is address-specific verification: Bali is not presented as closed to this activity, yet the relevant address should still be checked before relying on the local position. The honest conclusion is that the activity is nationally foreign-open and, in Bali, not barred by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is nationally foreign-open and, in Bali, not barred by the moratorium.

editorial.headline: Engineering Research in Bali: Open Nationally, Dependent on Scope
editorial.standfirst: This engineering and technology R&D activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali eligibility turns on the risk level of the exact scope declared in OSS.
editorial.body:
KBLI 72102 covers regular, systematic research and development in engineering and technology. It embraces engineering and technology research itself, including interdisciplinary work centred principally on natural science and engineering. Its technical territory is expansive: civil and chemical engineering; electrical and electronic systems; environmental, materials and mechanical work; medical, agricultural and instrumentation engineering; and research involving resources, extractive metallurgy and granular mechanics. It also includes nanotechnology, hydrogen, oil and gas, minerals and coal, electricity, and engineering and technology related to meteorology, climatology and geophysics.

The classification is for businesses whose recurring activity is that research and development work. It is open at every stated business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. Nationally, the activity is marked open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That is a clear national position for a business conducting the engineering-and-technology R&D described in this scope, rather than a general statement about every activity that may sit around a technical project.

Bali requires a more exact reading. The record does not treat this activity as universally blocked for PMA registration; its Bali status depends on scope. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI activities across the island. At the Large scale, however, OSS risk may be low for some scopes and higher for others. For this activity, PMA registration in Bali is available only by declaring the higher-risk scope.

The practical conclusion is precise rather than pessimistic. Nationally, foreign ownership is open across the listed scales, with a 100% ceiling. In Bali, that national position does not by itself determine whether a proposed registration can proceed. The exact activity must be verified live in OSS, because the declared scope and its risk treatment decide the local PMA outcome. For an engineering R&D business, that distinction belongs at the beginning of the registration analysis, not after the business model has already been framed.

editorial.headline: Medical and Health Research: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Systematic medical, life-science and health research is open to foreign investment nationally and is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium, subject to address verification.
editorial.body:
Medical and health research under this activity is not a loose label for anything adjacent to care. It is the regular, systematic conduct of research and development in medical science, life science and health, and health science. The definition extends from basic and clinical medical science to health science and medical biotechnology. It also expressly reaches other medical and health disciplines, including art therapy, audiology, chiropractic, music therapy, naturopathy, occupational therapy, orthoptics, physiotherapy, podiatry, prosthetics and orthotics, speech pathology, and traditional and integrative medicine. The organising idea is disciplined inquiry: a business registered here is built around sustained research and development across that specified medical-and-health terrain.

Registration is open at small, medium, and large scales. The record therefore does not reserve the activity for a single size of operation; its scale availability begins with small and continues through medium to large. In practical terms, an applicant should frame the business around the systematic research work described in the scope, rather than let a broad health label obscure the actual R&D activity. The code’s precision lies in the work being undertaken—medical, life-science and health research and development—while the permitted scale range remains broad.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is open, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. That means the activity can be fully foreign-owned at the national level. The point is consequential because the ceiling is not merely an indication that foreign capital may participate; it states the full extent of foreign ownership available for this activity nationally. The national position is therefore straightforward: foreign participation is open, and the stated ceiling does not require a reduction below full ownership.

Bali changes the setting, but not the result. The activity is marked as medium-high risk and is not blocked by the province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium, which applies to Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. For this activity, the result is clear: a foreign investor is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium today, although the precise address must still be verified. That address check is part of the Bali position recorded here, and it should be completed before treating the local registration path as settled.

editorial.headline: Biotechnology R&D: Nationally Open, Unblocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 72104 covers systematic biotechnology research and development, open from Mikro to Besar scale and to 100% foreign ownership nationally, with no block from Bali’s stated PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 72104 concerns systematic biotechnology research and development carried out on a regular basis. The activity includes research and development in environmental biotechnology, industrial biotechnology, and applications of biotechnology that do not involve genetic modification. These are expressly named fields within the scope. The organising idea is regular, systematic R&D related to biotechnology, with environmental, industrial and non-genetically-modified applications as its stated areas of work.

Who may register is equally clear on scale. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses, so the stated eligibility runs from the smallest named scale to the largest. It does not confine this biotechnology R&D activity to one particular size of organisation. Each of the four scales is expressly included. The scale range and the activity description should be read together: the registration covers the systematic biotechnology research and development set out in the scope, across every listed scale.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. That makes the national position straightforward: a foreign investor may hold the entire ownership interest permitted by the record for this activity. The cited PMA source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder considering ownership before location, the national answer is direct: this activity is open to PMA, and the stated national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%.

Location changes the question in Bali, but not into a prohibition here. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for activities classified Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity is expressly recorded as not blocked by that moratorium. The reason is specific: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, translated as Medium-High/High. Its Bali position is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The honest reading is clean: this systematic biotechnology R&D activity is nationally open to PMA at 100% foreign ownership, and Bali does not block it through the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: This biotechnology R&D activity is nationally open to PMA and is not blocked in Bali by the stated moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Research at the Root of Agriculture and Animal Health
editorial.standfirst: A systematic R&D activity spanning agriculture, fisheries, forestry, marine fields and veterinary science, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s stated moratorium.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity is systematic research and development for the knowledge systems that support agriculture and animal health. It reaches through agricultural science, animal husbandry, forestry, fisheries, marine affairs and veterinary medicine. Its stated scope includes agricultural biotechnology; agricultural, fisheries and forestry sciences; animal and dairy science; veterinary science; fertiliser research; and research into sustainable agricultural development. That breadth spans land- and sea-based sectors as well as the veterinary dimension of animal health. Environmental research is excluded from the activity’s stated remit.

This classification is for businesses undertaking that regular, systematic R&D. Registration is open at small, medium and large scale, putting a modest specialist research operation and a larger research organisation on the same stated footing as to scale. Being small, medium or large speaks to permitted scale, while the defined subject remains the R&D scope itself. The subject does not narrow to one discipline: biotechnology, dairy science, fertiliser work and sustainable agricultural development sit alongside the wider agricultural, forestry, fisheries, marine and veterinary fields. The unifying thread is research conducted regularly enough to be systematic.

For foreign ownership at the national level, the position is direct. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign participation of 100%. In practical terms, a foreign investor may hold up to 100% of the business carrying out this activity nationally. That is a full foreign-ownership ceiling, not a partial cap, and it belongs to the national position set out for this activity. Bali, however, has its own registration context and must be read on its own terms.

Bali’s separate reading is not a block. The activity is listed as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record expressly says that it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium. The reason lies in its medium-high or high-risk character: Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk activities, categories not assigned here. The Bali position should nevertheless be verified for the relevant address, exactly as the record directs. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, the honest position is clear: the activity is nationally open to up to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked by the stated moratorium, while address-specific verification remains part of the Bali picture.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is nationally open to up to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked by Bali’s stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: Nuclear R&D: Nationally Open, Conditionally Registrable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A systematic nuclear-technology R&D activity with 100% national PMA openness—but a scope-sensitive Bali registration route.
editorial.body:
KBLI 72106 is for systematic, ongoing research and development connected to the use of nuclear technology, including research and development for the use of ionising radiation sources. It is a research activity, defined by the regularity and method of the work as much as by its technical subject. The stated scope excludes research-and-development service businesses connected with electric-power installations. For founders, that boundary matters: the registration should describe the nuclear-technology research and development actually undertaken, rather than allowing the code’s broad scientific language to carry work it does not state.

Registration is open to small, medium and large businesses. At the national level, the activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national position; it does not turn the technical scope into a general authorisation for work beyond the stated activity. The company’s operating description still has to stay within systematic research and development related to nuclear technology and, where relevant, the stated use of ionising-radiation sources. The cited national instruments provide the source for that opening, while the scope remains the measure of what the activity is.

Bali demands a more granular reading. This activity is not marked as categorically blocked for PMA registration there. Yet Bali’s status depends on scope because OSS assigns low risk at the large-business scale to some scopes and a higher risk to others. Under the Bali rule, low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities are blocked for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. Accordingly, a PMA applicant can register this activity in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope; the exact activity must be verified in live OSS. That is not a Bali-side foreign-ownership cap. It is a scope-and-risk condition on whether PMA registration is available at all.

The practical question is therefore not whether national foreign ownership is open—it is—but whether the particular declared Bali scope lands inside the higher-risk route. Live OSS verification for the exact activity is expressly called for, and that caution is material rather than merely procedural. A national ownership ceiling and a Bali risk filter answer different questions: one concerns the permitted foreign stake; the other determines whether PMA registration is available in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: A national ownership ceiling and a Bali risk filter answer different questions: one concerns the permitted foreign stake; the other determines whether PMA registration is available in Bali.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Research Activity, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Systematic experimental research in uncategorised technology and engineering—from biological-process DNA sequencing to space research—is open nationally at every business scale, but blocked for PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity covers regular, systematic experimental research and development in technology and engineering that is not classified elsewhere. Its range is deliberately broad but still technically defined: it includes DNA sequencing undertaken for general research into biological processes, as well as research and development in the field of space. The common thread is not a particular commercial output, but an organised research effort directed at scientific and engineering questions beyond the more specifically classified fields.

The activity is open to enterprises at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That matters because the code does not reserve this research work for a single size of operator: a small specialist undertaking and a large research organisation may each fall within the stated scale range, provided their work remains within the activity’s scope. Nationally, it is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% under the cited presidential regulations.

Bali is where the national opening stops being the practical answer. A foreign national is unable to register this activity for PMA in Bali today. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, and Bali’s moratorium blocks the activity on that basis. The provincial rule is island-wide and permanent: PMA is blocked for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This is not a qualification of the national foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a separate Bali registration barrier arising from the code’s risk classification at scale Besar.

For founders, the distinction requires a clean reading. At national level, the activity is open to full foreign ownership. In Bali, the same activity is blocked for PMA registration because of the provincial moratorium. The decisive issue is therefore not whether the research concerns DNA sequencing, space research, or another technology and engineering programme within the stated scope. It is that the activity’s relevant OSS risk treatment at the Besar scale falls inside Bali’s permanent PMA restriction.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, the activity is open to full foreign ownership; in Bali, it is blocked for PMA registration.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Social-Science Research: Nationally Open, With a Bali Address Check
editorial.standfirst: This systematic social-science research activity is fully foreign-open nationally and unblocked by Bali’s moratorium, though the record calls for address-level verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 72201 covers regular, systematic research and development connected with the social sciences. The recorded scope embraces work in economics and business administration, psychology and cognitive science, education, sociology, anthropology, law, political science, government, trade, media and communication, and customs and traditions. It also reaches social and economic geography, criminology, demography, development studies, gender studies, policy and administration, social work, and other social-science research. The record specifically identifies research and development in economics and business, education, media and communication, political science, psychology and cognitive science, and sociology alongside that broader field list. Its scope is broad in discipline, while remaining anchored in regular, systematic research and development.

That breadth matters when describing the registrant. The record’s investment setting is a PMA one: nationally it is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. A PMA company can therefore be fully foreign-owned for this activity under the national position recorded here. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The scale field supplies an empty list of open business scales. Consequently, this source provides no listed scale-specific qualification, whether permissive or restrictive, to add to the national ownership position.

Bali is where an otherwise straightforward national reading must remain specific. The province’s stated moratorium blocks PMA across all Low and Medium-Low risk activities, island-wide and permanently. This entry, however, is listed as OK or higher risk; its stated reason places it in a medium-high/high-risk setting and says it is not blocked by the moratorium. The plain Bali conclusion is that a foreign investor is not barred from PMA registration for this activity today on that moratorium ground.

That does not turn Bali into an automatic address-level answer. The Bali record expressly says to verify per address. Its message is precise: the province-wide Low and Medium-Low risk moratorium is not the barrier for this activity, while the particular address still needs verification. National openness at 100% and Bali’s unblocked status can therefore be stated together without confusing one for the other.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness at 100% and Bali’s unblocked status can therefore be stated together without confusing one for the other.

editorial.headline: Humanities Research in Indonesia, With a Clear Bali Boundary
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers systematic humanities research and development, open to full foreign ownership nationally while requiring address-specific verification in Bali.
editorial.body:
Humanities research is often treated as an academic afterthought in business planning. This activity gives it a defined commercial home: systematic research and development in language and literature, religion, the arts, psychology and cognition, history, archaeology, and cultural heritage. It also embraces work across visual art, art history, performing arts and music, as well as philosophy, ethics and religion. The common thread is organised, regular inquiry—not a one-off cultural project or an informal intellectual pursuit.

The scope is broad enough for a research-led organisation whose work moves between cultural analysis, historical investigation, linguistic study and the development of ideas in the humanities. It is framed around research and development, so the centre of gravity is the sustained production of knowledge: studying, testing, documenting and advancing understanding in these fields. The record does not state which business scales are open to this activity, so its scale eligibility should not be assumed from the breadth of the subject matter.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is listed as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That means the national record does not impose a local equity share through the stated ownership limit. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned research venture, that openness is meaningful—but it is only the national side of the picture.

Bali carries a more location-sensitive reading. This activity is not blocked by Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. The Bali record instead places it in a medium-high or high-risk context and says it is not blocked by that moratorium. Its Bali status is therefore not a blanket prohibition; it is an address-specific matter that should be verified for the proposed location. The practical conclusion is measured: nationally open to full foreign ownership, and not moratorium-blocked in Bali, but not something to treat as location-neutral before the address is checked.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is clear, while Bali requires an address-specific reading rather than a blanket assumption.

editorial.headline: Advertising in Indonesia: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans campaign-making, media placement and brand work; it is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali blocks PMA registration under its permanent risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
Advertising in this classification is more than buying media space. It covers the creation and execution of advertising campaigns, advertising placement, brand-identity creation and brand development, campaign management, and the development of creative advertising materials. That work may appear in periodicals and newspapers, radio and television, on the internet and digital media, or through other media, for sports content as well as other fields. It also includes the design of display-location structures, connecting the creative message with the environment in which it is encountered.

The scope is deliberately broad in its practical expression. It encompasses advertising in print, broadcast, online and outdoor formats; media representation through the sale of advertising space and time; aerial advertising; distribution of advertising materials or samples; and the provision of billboard space and similar sites. It also reaches exhibition stands and other advertising locations, alongside marketing campaigns intended to attract and retain customers. Product promotion, point-of-sale marketing and direct mail sit within that same commercial terrain. Advertising agencies and media representatives are the providers generally associated with the activity.

The registration field is open across the full enterprise spectrum: micro, small, medium and large businesses. Nationally, the foreign-investment position is equally clear. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In plain terms, a foreign investor may hold the entire business at the national level. The record grounds that position in Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021; it does not attach a lower foreign-equity ceiling or an additional national condition.

editorial.standfirst: This activity spans structured market and opinion research across every business scale, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium overrides its nationally open position.
editorial.body:
Market research under this activity is not merely a survey function. It encompasses studies of awareness, evaluation and use of goods and services; work on product development and pricing; investigation of media use; and research into advertising recall and impact. It also covers scientific market research and opinion research conducted with qualitative and quantitative methodological guidance. The working methods are broad: reactive and non-reactive survey procedures, plus research data collected through interviews, observation, measurement and counting, whether face to face, by post or by telephone. In practical terms, the activity is the disciplined gathering and interpretation of evidence about markets, audiences, products, media and advertising.

That breadth matters to the profile of the registrant. The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so the classification does not reserve market-research work for only one size of enterprise. A small operator conducting interviews or observations, and a larger organisation running structured research programmes, both sit within the recorded range of scales. The defining thread is the research task itself: using stated qualitative or quantitative methods to examine market views, behaviour, use, recall or impact, and collecting relevant information through the listed survey and fieldwork procedures.

At the national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national opening: foreign participation may reach the full ceiling recorded for this activity. Bali, however, is not a softer local variation of that result. This is therefore a classification that rewards a clean reading of jurisdiction. National openness answers whether foreign ownership is permitted under the recorded national position; it does not override Bali’s specific PMA block. Founders considering work that falls within market studies, opinion research, survey design or the listed data-collection methods should distinguish the activity’s substantive scope from the place in which PMA registration is sought. editorial.headline: Public Opinion Polling: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Research into public views and voting behaviour is open nationally to full foreign ownership, but PMA registration is blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
Public-opinion polling is a research activity concerned with how people describe their lives, choices and public orientation. The stated scope covers studies of quality of life and lifestyle; social and political participants; party preference; and voting behaviour. It is consequently defined by investigation of opinion across both everyday and political questions. These subjects sit within one activity: research into the views people hold and the choices they make, from lifestyle questions through to participation, party preference and voting.

Registration is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. The record therefore makes the activity available at each of the four listed business scales. Nationally, it is TERBUKA to PMA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no national foreign-share limitation below full ownership in the supplied record. That national position is supported by Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign-owned company considering this activity nationally, the position is direct: it is open to PMA registration with up to full foreign ownership.

That national openness is not the answer for PMA registration in Bali. This activity cannot currently be registered in Bali by a foreign investor. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class). At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, placing the activity within Bali’s relevant prohibition. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. This is not a lower Bali foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a block on PMA registration arising from the local risk-class moratorium, notwithstanding the national 100% ceiling.

The distinction is decisive. The 100% ceiling describes the national foreign-ownership position; it does not override Bali’s permanent risk-class moratorium. The record’s Bali outcome follows the local rule that blocks PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. Thus, while the activity remains nationally open at the listed scales, the current Bali conclusion for a PMA applicant is unequivocal: registration is blocked. That is the operative Bali result for this activity, based on its stated risk treatment and the provincial moratorium.

editorial.headline: Public Relations: Nationally Open, but No PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A public-relations activity open to 100% foreign ownership nationally, but unavailable to PT PMA registration in Bali today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the decisive fact is Balinese: a PT PMA cannot register this activity in Bali today. That local outcome sits beside a nationally open classification, so this is not a universally closed activity. The distinction matters because the stated national ownership ceiling and the local registration result point in different directions.

The activity itself is public-relations work in the practical sense. It covers advice, guidance and operational assistance given to companies and other organisations on public relations and communications. It also covers lobbying, together with sales-representation activity undertaken for promotional purposes. Read as a whole, the scope describes a communications-facing service that can combine counsel with hands-on support and promotional representation. It is work concerned with the relationship between an organisation, its communications, and its external representation. It is not merely a title for public messaging: the recorded scope deliberately reaches operational assistance as well as advice.

At the national level, the PMA status is **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. The registration scales listed for the activity are Mikro, Kecil and Menengah. Those two facts need to be read together without smoothing away the distinction: the national investment setting is open, while the available scale rows named in the record stop at Menengah. The record names no Usaha Besar row among those listed scales, and supplies no further conditions for this activity.

Bali changes the practical conclusion. Its stated status is **Closed in Bali (2026 moratorium)**: the province-wide block covers every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, and public relations is classified **Low risk**. The two licensing annexes that mention it disagree with each other on scale, and neither is an ownership rule. This is the structural reason given in the record, rather than a qualification to the national ownership ceiling. In addition, the province has a permanent, island-wide rule blocking PMA registration for activities classed as Low or Medium-Low risk. Neither the national 100% ceiling nor the open national status creates a Bali registration path for a PT PMA under the recorded position. Founders should therefore treat the national and Bali readings as distinct: open nationally, but closed to PMA registration in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: Founders should therefore treat the national and Bali readings as distinct: open nationally, but closed to PMA registration in Bali today.

l4_bali.reason: No foreign-ownership reservation or cap for this activity was located in Perpres 10/2021 as amended by Perpres 49/2021 (Lampiran I, II, III) or in its closed list — so this is not a national 0% finding. OSS currently publishes licensing rows for this code only at Mikro, Kecil and Menengah scale, while a PT PMA is by law an Usaha Besar that must invest more than IDR 10 billion per KBLI per location (Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 7(1); Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 26(1)–(2)): whether OSS will license this code for a PT PMA must be confirmed in OSS; a scale missing from the licensing rules does not by itself restrict the activity (Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 8(6)). Two instruments disagree on scale: PP 28/2025 Lampiran I.P lists Mikro/Kecil/Menengah only, while Permen Ekraf 7/2025 lists Usaha Besar too. In Bali we flag this code as blocked as a precaution, not because a closure naming it was located. The Governor of Bali asked BKPM (letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, 28 Jan 2026) to close OSS to PT PMA in the Rendah and Menengah Rendah risk tiers, which include this code (Rendah). The provincial government reports that the closure applied from the third week of May 2026 covers 18 listed KBLI, and under the official BPS KBLI 2020→2025 crosswalk this code is not among them. Confirm the current OSS status in Bali before relying on this flag either way.

editorial.headline: Transport and Machinery Design: Nationally Open, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Industrial design for vehicles, machinery and their components is open to foreign investment nationally, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium means it cannot be registered there today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the defining fact is geographic: this activity can be foreign-owned nationally, but it cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. Bali blocks it under its island-wide, permanent moratorium on Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA. In this case, OSS places every scope of the activity in those risk bands at the Besar, or large-business, scale. The Bali restriction is therefore direct, even though the national position is open.

The activity is industrial design for products, production-support equipment and components used in transport equipment and machinery. Its brief is unusually broad: designs may concern bicycles and animal-drawn vehicles; handcarts, pushcarts, prams, wheelchairs and stretchers; rail vehicles; chairlifts and ski lifts; elevators and lifting equipment; and motor vehicles, ships, aircraft and spacecraft. It also includes the design of tyres, anti-slip chains, vehicle components and accessories, as well as machines, pumps, compressors, agricultural and construction machinery, and textile machinery. The design work may also be carried out using specialised software.

This is a registration space for industrial-design businesses working across those product categories, and it is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, so the record does not impose a foreign-equity reduction for this activity. That national openness is the relevant answer for an investor considering the activity in Indonesia as a whole; it is not, however, an answer that transfers automatically to Bali.

Bali’s position is more definite. The provincial moratorium cited in the record, dated May 13, 2026, blocks PMA registration where the applicable risk class is Low or Medium-Low, and it applies island-wide on a permanent basis. For this activity, that condition is met across every scope at the large scale. The practical reading is clear: national policy permits full foreign ownership, while Bali does not permit a foreign-owned registration for the activity today.
editorial.pullQuote: National policy permits full foreign ownership, while Bali does not permit a foreign-owned registration for the activity today.

editorial.headline: Designing the Domestic Objects That Shape Everyday Life
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet a Bali-wide PMA moratorium prevents registration there for the activity’s recorded risk class.
editorial.body:
This activity covers industrial design for household equipment and furniture: the practical and decorative objects that populate kitchens, bedrooms, dining spaces and living areas. Its scope reaches from glassware, tableware, cooking, serving and food-storage products to fireplace accessories, beds, tables, chairs and storage furniture. It also includes mirrors and frames, clothes hangers, curtains and blinds, wall and table ornaments, vases and pots, medals and belts, flags and festival decorations, and artificial flowers, fruit and plants. The design work may be carried out using specialised software.

The breadth matters. This is not a narrow label for one furniture type or one decorative object; it is an activity category for designing a wide field of domestic and furnishing products. A registered business can operate at Micro, Small, Medium or Large scale. That gives the category room for practices whose work ranges across functional household goods and furniture, while keeping the defining activity clear: industrial design for the products specified in the scope.

Nationally, the position is direct. Foreign investment is permitted for the activity, and foreign ownership may reach 100%. Put plainly, the national record allows this activity to be wholly foreign-owned. That is the national setting founders should begin with, but it is not the complete location-specific answer for Bali.

In Bali, a foreign-owned registration cannot be made for this activity today. The Bali record classifies it as blocked by risk class: at the Large scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every listed scope, and the activity is therefore caught by Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. The distinction is consequential rather than technical: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remain part of the record, while Bali’s local moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity there.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not override Bali’s island-wide PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.

editorial.headline: Textile and Fashion Design: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A broad design activity spanning textiles, garments, accessories and jewellery, open nationally to full foreign ownership but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the industrial design of textile, fashion and garment products, including work carried out through specialised software. Its practical canvas is wide: fabric and woven goods, crocheted products, clothing and underwear, headwear, footwear, socks, stockings and laces all sit within it. So do designs for bags, suitcases and cases; ties, shawls, scarves and handkerchiefs; gloves, umbrellas, walking sticks and fans; ribbons, hair ties, clothing accessories and other adornments; and jewellery. The common thread is design: the activity concerns creating the product design rather than describing a particular retail or manufacturing operation.

It is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Nationally, the position is straightforward. The activity is TERBUKA to foreign investment, and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In other words, the national record permits full foreign ownership for this activity; there is no lower foreign-ownership ceiling stated in the record.

Bali changes that answer decisively for a foreign-owned registration. Bali does not presently permit a foreign investor to register this activity. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Low or Medium-Low across every part of the stated scope. That places the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, introduced on May 13, 2026. The restriction is therefore not a reduced ownership percentage or a local-partnership condition: it is a block on PMA registration in Bali under the province’s risk-based moratorium.

That distinction matters. The national setting remains open to 100% foreign ownership, but it does not override Bali’s separate provincial position. For a founder considering this activity, the honest reading is two-layered: the activity is nationally available to foreign investment at every listed scale, while Bali’s recorded risk classification makes PMA registration unavailable on the island. The national openness is real; so is the Bali block.
editorial.pullQuote: The national setting remains open to 100% foreign ownership, but it does not override Bali’s separate provincial position.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Strategic and Defence Design: Nationally Open, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Industrial design for defence, security and disaster-response products is open to full foreign ownership nationally, but blocked from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
**Foreign investors cannot register this activity in Bali today.** That is the decisive local fact for Strategic and Defence Industrial Design Activities. National rules permit foreign investment in the activity up to a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, however, PMA registration is blocked under the province’s risk-class moratorium. The national openness is real; so is the island-wide restriction. The divergence is categorical, rather than a minor adjustment to the national ownership position.

The activity is industrial design created to produce strategic and defence products. Its stated remit includes design for national-defence products, military products, weapons, security and police products, and products for emergency disaster response. Those specified end uses give the activity its perimeter: it is concerned with the creation of industrial designs for these particular product areas. The scope also expressly says that the design work is carried out through specialised software, placing that digital design process within the stated activity.

Businesses can register the activity at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, or Besar scale. The record gives the same activity description across those scale labels and sets out no additional threshold, permit, capital figure, or operating timetable. The scale listing should therefore be read for what it says: the activity is available across the four named scales. Its local investment position, however, cannot be inferred from scale alone, because Bali’s record supplies a specific risk-based restriction.

The Bali block is explicitly tied to risk classification. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, with the stated trigger on May 13, 2026. This is a registration block, not a separate Bali foreign-ownership percentage. The result is stark but precise: national policy allows 100% foreign ownership for the activity, while Bali presently does not allow its PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: The national openness is real; so is the island-wide restriction.

editorial.headline: Electronic Design: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This industrial-design activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s PMA moratorium blocks its registration there today.
editorial.body:
**The Bali conclusion comes first:** a foreign investor cannot register this activity through a PMA company in Bali today. That is not a judgment on the design work itself or on its national investment status. At the Large scale, OSS classifies every scope in the activity as Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, resulting in the recorded Bali status of being blocked by risk class. The restriction is tied to a Governor’s letter and is recorded as applying from May 2026. For a founder considering a Bali vehicle, that practical registration outcome needs to lead the discussion.

This is an industrial-design activity focused on developing products that carry, process, store, power and control electronic functions. Its scope includes design for information-technology products, communication and control equipment, sound- or image-recording products, data-storage products, power-generation and motor-drive products, power-storage and power-amplification products, and products for electricity distribution and control. It also covers the design of cooling machinery, washing machines, and drying and cleaning machines. The record adds an important working detail: this design activity is also undertaken through specialised software. In plain terms, the classification concerns the product-design layer—the development of a design solution for equipment—rather than a generic label for the wider electronics economy.

Registration is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar business scales. That breadth makes the activity relevant to a range of design practices, from compact studios to substantial product-development organisations. Scale is not merely background in the Bali assessment, however. The record explicitly places the risk finding at the Besar scale, where every listed scope is Low or Medium-Low. It is a reason to read the activity’s scope and local PMA treatment together, rather than treating national openness as a local registration clearance.

Nationally, the position is open: foreign ownership may reach 100%, under the cited Presidential Regulations. That national ceiling is clear, and it should not be quietly recast as a Bali permission. Bali’s restriction rests on the recorded risk classification and the provincial PMA moratorium, not on a lower stated foreign-ownership ceiling. The result is a precise distinction: the activity remains nationally open to PMA at full foreign ownership; for PMA registration in Bali, the recorded moratorium blocks it.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness to full foreign ownership is not a Bali registration clearance.

editorial.headline: Designing Sport and Play, With a Bali PMA Barrier
editorial.standfirst: This code covers industrial design for sports, play and outdoor equipment—nationally open to full foreign ownership, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Industrial design sits upstream of the finished object: it is the work of creating the product before it reaches a factory, shop floor or playing field. This activity covers industrial design for sports and games equipment, including toys and entertainment products, sports equipment, and tents and outdoor equipment. The design work may also be carried out using specialist software. Its subject is the creation of the product design itself, across play, sport and outdoor use.

The activity is open at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Nationally, it is classified as open to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In practical terms, the national position permits full foreign ownership for this activity; there is no foreign-equity cap below that ceiling in the record. The stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali requires a distinctly different reading. A foreign investor is unable to register this activity as PMA in Bali today. At the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk. That places the activity within Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The restriction is not a partial limitation on ownership: it blocks PMA registration on the island for this activity.

That makes the distinction unusually clear. National openness answers the question of whether foreign ownership is permitted for the activity in Indonesia; for this code, the answer is fully open up to 100%. Bali’s risk-based moratorium answers a separate, local registration question. Because the activity falls within the Low and Medium-Low risk category at the Besar scale across every scope, the Bali route is closed to PMA despite the national foreign-ownership position. Founders considering sports, games or outdoor-equipment design should therefore treat the national permission and the Bali registration outcome as two different facts, both essential and neither interchangeable.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this activity is nevertheless blocked from PMA registration in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Designing the Health and Beauty Products People Depend On
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers specialist product design across medical, laboratory, cosmetic and beauty-equipment fields—open nationally to foreign investment, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali today.
editorial.body:
This activity is the design and development of products used in health, cosmetics and laboratory settings. Its scope reaches from medical equipment, materials and hospital products to medical devices and prosthetics; from pharmaceutical and cosmetic products to cosmetic packaging and containers. It also includes the design of beauty-salon and toilet accessories, wigs and similar products. The work is not confined to sketches or physical prototypes: specialised software is expressly part of how these design activities are carried out.

The registration is available to businesses operating at micro, small, medium and large scale. That breadth matters because the code describes a professional design activity rather than a single finished product. A studio developing a prosthetic concept, a team shaping laboratory equipment, or a practice creating cosmetic containers can all sit within the same activity, provided the work is genuinely product design and development within the stated health, cosmetic or laboratory scope.

Across Indonesia, the activity permits foreign investment up to a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In other words, the national position allows full foreign ownership for this activity. That clarity should not be mistaken for a universal location result, however. Bali’s position is different: a foreign-owned company cannot register this activity there today. The Bali classification records it as blocked for PMA registration under the province’s risk-class rule.

The reason is specific. At large scale, OSS assigns every scope within this activity a Low or Medium-Low risk classification. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities from PMA registration. The block is tied to that Bali rule, announced in May 2026, rather than to a reduction in the national foreign-ownership ceiling. For founders, the practical reading is straightforward: the activity remains nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali is presently closed to PMA registration for it.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity remains nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali is presently closed to PMA registration for it.

editorial.headline: Packaging Design Is Nationally Open, but Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This industrial-design activity covers packaging forms from bottles to pallets, nationally open to full foreign ownership yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Packaging design is a distinct industrial-design activity focused on producing packaging products. KBLI 74118 covers designs for bottles, tubes and containers; receptacles for rubbish or scrap; cans, drums, storage barrels and boxes; and closures, baskets, wooden crates, pallets, bags and capsules. The scope therefore runs from familiar containers to storage and transport forms, while remaining centred on the design of the package. It does not describe a single material or object: the listed output includes rigid containers, closures and carrying or storage formats. The design work may also be carried out using specialised software, making that toolset an express part of the activity.

The registration picture is broad in scale. The activity is open to enterprises at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Those are the record's complete stated scale range, so packaging-design work is not confined to one size of enterprise. An undertaking at any of those scales remains within the same activity when its work concerns the listed packaging products. The important continuity is the purpose of the work: industrial design that produces packaging-product designs. Scale identifies the available registration range, while the defined subject of the work remains packaging design.

Nationally, the foreign-investment stance is clear. The record marks the activity TERBUKA and gives a national PMA maximum foreign share of 100%. For national registration, a foreign-owned business may be held to that full ceiling; the stated national limit does not stop below full foreign ownership. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This national conclusion follows the PMA status and national maximum given in the record. It speaks to the activity's position nationally, rather than resolving the separate Bali position.

Bali changes the answer decisively. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): a foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, every scope falls within Low or Medium-Low OSS risk. That puts the activity inside Bali's island-wide, permanent moratorium, which blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration. The record ties this block to a moratorium in May 2026. editorial.headline: Industrial Design, Nationally Open but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 74119 spans industrial design for a broad range of products, open nationally to full foreign ownership yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 74119 covers industrial design activity for products across a broad range of practical uses. Its scope includes design for timekeeping, measuring and office equipment; brushing products; tools and hardware; photographic, cinematographic and optical equipment; musical equipment; office stationery; sales and advertising equipment; and hunting and fishing equipment. It also reaches products for fluid distribution, ventilation, air-conditioning and heating, solid fuels, lighting, construction elements, firefighting, animal care, food, tobacco and cigarettes, and crafts. The record expressly includes this design activity when it is carried out through specialist software.

For businesses, the record admits this activity at the Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. That gives the category a wide organisational reach, from smaller design operations to large enterprises, while keeping the subject of registration clear: industrial design for the listed product fields. The range is functional: it moves from office and measuring equipment to climate-control, lighting, construction, firefighting, food, tobacco and craft products. A timekeeping device, an optical tool, a lighting product or a firefighting product may sit far apart in the market, but each illustrates the same through-line in this record: the design of an industrial product.

For PMA at the national level, the position is just as clear. The activity is marked open, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%, referenced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. A foreign investor therefore encounters no national foreign-ownership cap below full ownership in the supplied record. That national reading matters, but it is not the final answer for a Bali registration.

Bali’s position is different and decisive. Today, a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali as a PMA. The record marks it blocked by risk class because OSS risk at the Large scale is Low or Medium-Low on every scope; Bali’s moratorium of May 2026 blocks PMA registration for all KBLI carrying those risk levels. The provincial rule is island-wide and permanent. National openness does not override Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA block for the risk classes recorded here. This is not a Bali-specific reduction of the 100% national ceiling. It is a territorial bar on PMA registration in Bali, even though the activity remains nationally open.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not override Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA block for the risk classes recorded here.

intel_2026.whatChanged: Completely new code in KBLI 2025. In the 2020 classification, interior design was bundled into broader design categories. The 2025 overhaul created specific codes for each design discipline: industrial design (74111-74119), interior design (74191), graphic design (74192), film/video design (74193), game design (74194), and others. Interior design finally has its own dedicated code.
intel_2026.baliContext: Bali has a thriving interior design scene — driven by the constant pipeline of new villas, hotels, restaurants, and boutique spaces. The 'Bali style' (tropical modern, open-air, natural materials) is exported worldwide. Many international interior designers have set up studios in Bali, particularly in Seminyak and Canggu. The market ranges from budget villa fit-outs (IDR 200-500M) to ultra-luxury resort interiors (billions). Since this is a code new in KBLI 2025 with no PP28 data yet, licensing requirements are minimal for now — just NIB. Local craftsmen (stone carvers, woodworkers, furniture makers in Gianyar and Klungkung) are a major resource that makes Bali competitive for interior design globally.

editorial.headline: Interior Design With Room for Full Foreign Ownership
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 74191 frames interior design as a full professional service—shaping spaces around use, safety, health, comfort, accessibility and atmosphere, from study to supervision.
editorial.body:
KBLI 74191 treats interior design as the disciplined shaping of the inside of a building around the way people use it. The work begins with planning and designing rooms and interiors to suit human activity and the function of the space, but it seeks a particular atmosphere as well as an orderly plan. Safety, health, security, comfort, disability support and aesthetic considerations all sit within the stated scope. The activity therefore works at the point where a space must feel coherent while also responding to the practical demands placed on it. Rather than ending at a concept, it is defined by a considered interior response to use, function and atmosphere.

The category gives that proposition a broad professional envelope. It includes the design-consulting service itself, alongside survey work, feasibility studies, drafting, artistic-impression design, supervision of building interiors, price estimation/QS and project management within the construction planning of an interior-design project. It reaches interiors in buildings as well as other civil structures. In registration terms, the activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. The business being registered is thus one that supplies interior-design consulting and design services, whether its role remains in planning or includes the supporting work specified for an interior-design project.

Nationally, the PMA status is open, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a full foreign-ownership position for this activity, not a ceiling below complete ownership. Its cited PMA basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The national position sits over the whole stated scope: planning and designing interiors, and the related survey, feasibility, drafting, artistic-impression, supervision, estimation and project-management services. It is a national setting that reflects the category’s comprehensive account of interior-design work.

Bali calls for a separate reading, and the result remains open on the facts given. The island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA activity classified at Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity is expressly not blocked by that moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—which places it in Bali’s OK-or-higher-risk position. The distinction matters because the national openness is not cancelled in Bali by the rule supplied here. The honest conclusion is straightforward: a foreign investor may register this interior-design activity in Bali today, with national foreign ownership open up to 100% and its large-scale risk classification outside the stated PMA moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The honest conclusion is straightforward: a foreign investor may register this interior-design activity in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Graphic Design’s National Opening—and Bali’s Closed PMA Door
editorial.standfirst: Graphic and visual communication design is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but a foreigner cannot register it through a PMA company in Bali today.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the professional work of giving information, identity and persuasion a visual form. It encompasses visual-communication and graphic-design services performed manually or digitally; in static, moving or interactive formats; and across printed, screen-based, offline, online and virtual media. The work can appear on phones, television, computers and LED displays as readily as on print. Its subject matter is equally recognisable: brand identities, logos, advertising designs, infographics and stationery all sit within the activity’s stated terrain.

That terrain extends beyond a single logo or campaign. The scope includes communications materials such as posters, brochures, books and other printed matter, together with work for profiles, websites, applications, social media, reports, presentations and promotional materials. It also reaches packaging design—particularly the surface of a package—and environmental graphic design for exhibitions and events, product displays, billboards, wayfinding, signage and building or retail markers. Brand-identity work is expressly part of the picture, from research and brand strategy to the visual identity, logo-use standards, lettering, typeface design and illustration that make a system coherent.

Who may operate in this field is broad in scale: the record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises. At the national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In practical terms, the national record does not set a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. It is a broad professional-design category, spanning the strategic foundations of a visual identity and the applied materials through which that identity is seen.

Bali is the decisive exception. A foreigner cannot register this activity through a PMA company in Bali today. The block comes from Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. For this activity, the cited OSS risk at the Besar scale is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, triggering that moratorium. The provincial reason is therefore not a reduced Bali ownership percentage: it is a registration block. National openness does not create a Bali registration pathway for a PMA company under this activity today.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not create a Bali registration pathway for a PMA company under this activity today.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates.
