editorial.headline: Designing the World Before the Screen Comes Alive
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the specialist creative planning that gives film, video, television, animation and comics their narrative, visual and production shape.
editorial.body:
This activity is about the design work that happens before a screen project takes its final form. It covers specialist creative planning for films, videos, television programmes, animation and comics: shaping stories, designing characters and casting choices, setting artistic and visual direction, planning production’s technical design, and identifying supporting requirements. The work is formative rather than merely decorative; it provides the creative and practical framework through which a production can be imagined, organised and realised.

That scope makes it a natural home for studios, creative teams and specialist practitioners whose contribution lies in conceiving a project’s narrative, visual and technical language. It is open at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The breadth matters. A small creative practice and a larger production-design operation may both undertake this planning work, provided the activity remains within the stated scope. The classification does not extend to the creation of comics itself, or to the planning and production of computer animation.

Nationally, the position is clear: the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In other words, the record permits full foreign ownership at the national level. That national openness should not, however, be mistaken for an automatic route to a Bali PMA registration. Bali’s position is materially different, and it is the distinction founders need to read first rather than last.

In Bali, this activity is Blocked (risk class) for PMA registration. At the Besar scale, every scope is recorded in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, bringing the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The recorded block is tied to that moratorium as of 13 May 2026. The practical conclusion is direct: although foreign ownership can reach 100% nationally, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness to 100% foreign ownership does not create a Bali PMA registration route for this activity today.

editorial.headline: The Work Behind a Game’s Content
editorial.standfirst: Game content design shapes mechanics, stories, visual worlds, interfaces and levels; it is nationally open to full foreign ownership at every scale, yet PMA registration is blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
Game content design is the disciplined planning work that gives a game its playable and expressive shape. Under this activity, it includes devising game-mechanics logic and story, directing the artistic design of characters, visual interfaces and levels, and resolving technical design connected with the technology used. It also includes preparing design documents, conducting research and development, and carrying out other supporting activity. The focus is the creative and technical blueprint: the connected decisions through which a game’s content is conceived, articulated and developed. Its components run from play logic and narrative through visual and technical decisions to the documents and research that support them.

Registration is open to businesses at micro, small, medium and large scale. Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment and permits a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. No separate scale is excluded in the record: each of the four stated scales is open. The range of listed work explains the breadth of that national position: a business may work across narrative planning, mechanics, artistic direction, interface and level design, technical design, documentation and research, rather than being confined to one creative discipline. The scope holds these strands together as content-design activity.

Bali alters the immediate conclusion. A foreign investor cannot register this activity there today. At the large scale, every scope within the activity is classified by OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium applies to the Low and Medium-Low risk classifications recorded here; this activity is therefore blocked for PMA registration. The moratorium identified in the record dates from the thirteenth of May, two thousand and twenty-six. It is not a narrower condition attached to a single design element: every scope is in those risk classes at the large scale.

The distinction is decisive rather than technical. The national record addresses foreign ownership and allows the full 100% ceiling; the Bali rule addresses whether PMA registration is available in the province. For founders, the result is a clean split: every listed business scale is nationally open, yet Bali does not presently provide a PMA registration route for this activity. National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not make PMA registration available in Bali. The record gives the local registration block its own rule.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not make PMA registration available in Bali.

editorial.headline: Special Design Work, and the Bali Registration Divide
editorial.standfirst: This special-design planning activity is nationally open to foreign ownership, but its Bali registration position is decisively narrower.
editorial.body:
This activity is a home for special-design planning that does not sit elsewhere in the stated classification. It also includes planning for other creative content not otherwise covered by that scope. The practical thread is planning: shaping a design or creative-content direction where the work is specialised but cannot be placed in a more specific activity. It is therefore a deliberately broad category, defined by the nature of the planning work and by what remains unclassified within the stated scope.

The permitted business scales are Mikro and Kecil. That matters because scale is not decorative metadata here; it frames who can enter the activity through the available registration structure. A founder should not assume that a broad description of creative or design work automatically creates a broad corporate-registration route: the licensing annexes set the scales for the permit, and in Bali it is the moratorium that decides registrability, by risk tier.

Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national record does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership. That is the national investment position, supported in the record by Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. But a national foreign-ownership setting is not the final answer for a business intending to register in Bali: the local registration architecture still determines whether a PT PMA can enter the activity there.

In Bali, the answer is clear: a foreigner cannot register this activity through a PT PMA today. The Bali status is closed because of the provincial moratorium, which since 13 May 2026 blocks every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI island-wide; this activity is classified Low risk. No ownership restriction on the activity itself was located. National openness does not overcome the local registration architecture that keeps a PT PMA out of this activity in Bali. The provincial backdrop is also permanent and island-wide: Bali blocks all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI from PMA registration. For this activity, however, the immediate recorded obstacle is structural—the absence of the large-enterprise registration row required for a PT PMA.

editorial.headline: Aerial Photography Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Aerial photography is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks its PMA registration today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 74201 is about making photographs from the air: images captured with aircraft, unmanned aircraft and comparable aerial means. It follows the production of an image from an aerial viewpoint, whether the platform is manned or remote. The scope is centred on the photographic activity, not merely the fact that something flies. It expressly leaves out air transport undertaken for sightseeing, drawing a useful boundary between selling an aerial image and selling a scenic flight. For registration purposes, the activity is aerial photography itself.

The listed access is broad in scale, running from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah to Besar. That makes the record relevant to a small operator as well as a larger enterprise, provided the activity remains inside that photographic scope. At the national level, PMA status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. This is the straightforward national position: a foreign investor can register this activity under PMA up to the full stated ceiling; it is not a partial-ownership category. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali changes that conclusion rather than softening it. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class), and the record expressly identifies PMA registration as blocked. There is no separate Bali foreign-ownership percentage in the record. Instead, the stated OSS risk result at the Besar scale is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah across every scope. Under the province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium, Low and Medium-Low risk classifications are blocked for PMA. The record dates that moratorium to 13 May 2026.

The practical reading must therefore keep the national and Bali positions apart. Nationally, the activity permits 100% foreign ownership and is open across every listed scale. In Bali, however, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA today because of the applicable risk-class outcome. The Bali block does not redefine the activity: it remains aerial photographic work from aircraft, drones or similar means, while sightseeing air transport stays outside its stated scope. Both the national opening and Bali’s registration block are necessary parts of the same answer.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, aerial photography is nevertheless blocked from PMA registration in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Other Photography Activities: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This broad photography activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks its registration there today.
editorial.body:
Photography is often treated as a simple service, but this activity has a broad working perimeter. It covers still photography and photo shoots for individuals and business purposes: passport, school and wedding work, alongside commercial, publication, fashion, real-estate and tourism photography. It also includes underwater photography and video recording for events such as weddings and meetings. The common thread is commissioned image-making for a person, an event or a commercial use—not a narrow studio-only practice.

The scope continues after the shutter. It includes processing and printing clients’ film or cine-film negatives, including washing, printing and enlarging; film-processing laboratories; and one-hour photo shops, provided these are not part of a camera store. Slide mounting, duplication, restoration and minor alteration of transparencies also sit within the activity. So do photojournalism, the creation of document microfilm, 3D-object scanning, and processing or converting photographs into digital formats before uploading them to cloud storage. It is therefore a practical category spanning capture, image handling and digital delivery.

Nationally, the activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is available across micro, small, medium and large business scales. That national position matters: it confirms that foreign participation is permitted for the activity as such, rather than limiting the work to a particular business size. A founder considering this category should nevertheless separate national openness from the place where the PMA registration is to be made.

In Bali, that distinction is decisive. A foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA there today. At the large scale, OSS assigns a Low or Medium-Low risk level across every scope within the activity, placing it inside Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The block is tied to the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026. Nationally open therefore does not mean PMA-registrable in Bali: for this activity, the provincial restriction controls the practical outcome on the island.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not translate into PMA registrability in Bali: this activity is blocked there today.

editorial.standfirst: This code gives translation and interpreting a national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, while Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium currently stops PMA registration there.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this translation and interpreting activity in Bali today. That is the decisive local fact, even though the activity is nationally open to foreign investment with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The contrast is not cosmetic: national openness defines the position across Indonesia, while Bali’s PMA restriction determines whether this activity can be registered on the island.

The activity itself is the professional work of translating and interpreting across languages, including sign language, whether delivered orally or in writing. Its substance is not merely replacing one word with another. The recorded scope expressly reaches translation from a source language into a target language with attention to equivalent terminology, sense of language and culture. In practice, that framing places linguistic judgment at the centre of the activity: the registered business is concerned with carrying meaning accurately between languages and communicative contexts.

The code is open across the full recorded range of business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. It therefore accommodates a translation or interpreting business at any of those scales under the national position. For PMA, the national ceiling is 100%, and the status is TERBUKA. There is no national foreign-share cap below full ownership in this record. A business considering registration should nevertheless distinguish that national setting from the place where it intends to operate, because the Bali position is separately and explicitly restrictive.

In Bali, the record marks the activity as Blocked (risk class) and confirms that it is blocked for PMA registration. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk classification is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope; Bali’s moratorium blocks PMA for those risk categories. The moratorium is island-wide and permanent, and the record dates the applicable block to May 2026. The result is straightforward: national rules allow foreign ownership up to 100% for this activity, but Bali does not presently permit PMA registration for it. For a founder, that is the line that matters before treating national openness as a Bali operating route.

editorial.headline: KBLI 74910: Where Intellectual Property Rights Meet the Market
editorial.standfirst: A nationally open activity for patent brokering and intellectual-property rights management, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 74910 covers the commercial work that helps intellectual-property rights move, generate income, and remain properly managed. Its core activity is patent brokerage and marketing services, including arranging the purchase and sale of patent rights. The remit also reaches the management of copyright and the income it produces, the administration of industrial-property rights such as patents, licences, trademarks and franchises, and the work of collective rights-management bodies or organisations. It is an activity centred on managing and connecting rights, rather than exploiting those rights on one’s own account.

That boundary matters. The activity does not include renting intellectual property or similar products, nor does it include buying and selling patents or comparable intellectual-property rights in one’s own name. Within its stated scope, however, the category is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. It therefore accommodates both smaller specialist operators and larger organisations whose work involves brokering, administering, or managing rights and the revenues connected to them.

editorial.headline: Weather Services: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Meteorological analysis, forecasting and specified weather-modification services are nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali currently blocks PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
This activity concerns professional meteorological analysis of the atmosphere and the forecasting of weather processes and conditions. Forecasting is its most familiar expression, but the scope is wider: it also includes weather-modification services performed from the air, using aircraft, unmanned aircraft systems, balloons and other airborne vehicles. It further covers services using generators and other ground-based weather-modification equipment. The centre of gravity is technical and operational—the provision of meteorological analysis, forecasts and specified weather-modification services. Meteorological research and development sits outside this activity’s boundary.

For the business carrying out this work, the permitted registration scales run from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah to Besar. Nationally, the foreign-investment setting is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national position: foreign capital may take the full permitted stake in a company registered for this activity. The stated PMA source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The key word, however, is nationally. A national ownership ceiling does not itself determine whether PMA registration is available in a particular province.

In Bali, the answer is stark. This activity is marked Blocked (risk class): at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Low/Medium-Low across every scope. That brings it within Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium, recorded in May 2026. The practical consequence is a registration block: a foreigner cannot register this activity for PMA in Bali today. The national 100% ceiling remains the national ceiling, but it does not override Bali’s registration barrier for this activity.

For a founder, that distinction belongs at the front of the decision, not in the footnotes. The work may be nationally open to full foreign ownership and available across all four listed scales, yet Bali turns on a separate factual question: whether PMA registration is allowed there. On this record, it is not. The responsible reading is therefore two-part and simultaneous—nationally open at up to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, blocked for PMA registration because the applicable OSS risk classification at Besar triggers the provincial moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% ceiling remains the national ceiling, but it does not override Bali’s registration barrier for this activity.

editorial.headline: Professional Expertise, Broadly Applied
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 74999 covers a wide field of client-facing professional, scientific and technical services, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 74999 is the broad professional-services category for work that calls on specialist professional, scientific or technical skill, usually delivered to commercial clients. Its scope is deliberately wide: it can encompass business brokerage for small and medium-sized businesses and professional practices; valuations of antiques, jewellery and similar items outside real estate and insurance; freight-bill and tariff-information audits; security, workplace-safety, agronomy, environmental and energy-saving advice; and other technical consultancy. It also reaches construction economics, non-architectural, non-engineering and non-management consultancy, and the development of technical standards used as references for testing and analysis.

The activity is equally attentive to specialist representation and advisory work. It includes agents and agencies acting for individuals in connection with films, theatre, entertainment, sport, books, games, artworks and photography, placing those works or people with publishers, producers and others. Supervisory-board activity is also within the stated scope. The common thread is not a single industry but the provision of defined expertise or representation: a business should be able to identify its actual service clearly within that wide perimeter, rather than treating the category as a substitute for an ongoing routine operation.

Registration is open at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In practical terms, the record permits full foreign ownership for this activity at the national level. That is the central ownership position; it does not need to be softened by conditions that do not appear in the record.

Bali does not reverse that position for this code. The province-wide PMA moratorium blocks low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently, but this activity is not blocked by that moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. Bali’s status is therefore OK or higher risk: the activity remains outside the moratorium’s blocked category, while the applicable large-scale risk classification should be treated as part of the registration picture.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not block this activity for PMA registration because it falls outside the province-wide moratorium’s low- and medium-low-risk category.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Independent Veterinary Practice, With a Clear Bali PMA Route
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers independent veterinary health services across livestock, pets, aquatic animals and wildlife, with PMA registration available in Bali.
editorial.body:
Independent veterinary health work is a practical, clinical activity: the provision of veterinary medical services through personal practices or independent individual practitioners. Its scope runs from supervision, care and examinations to treatment, diagnosis and consultation on animal health. The work may concern livestock, companion animals, aquatic animals and wildlife, and it also includes ambulatory animal services. In other words, the activity is defined by professional animal-health service, whether delivered in a practice setting or through mobile care.

The people named within that work are equally specific. It may be carried out by veterinarians and paramedics; by reproductive-technology assistants working under a veterinarian’s supervision; and by animal chiropractors and animal nutrition specialists working with horses, aquatic animals or wildlife. The code is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the activity is not framed as a narrow specialist category: it accommodates independent practice across the full stated range of business scales while retaining its professional veterinary-health character.

At the national level, the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. There is therefore no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership in the record. The Bali position is also affirmative: a PT PMA can register the activity in Bali. The record notes that the Besar scale is classified as Menengah Tinggi, placing it outside Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA block for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.

That does not make Bali a footnote. Its status is Open in Bali (high-risk track): open in Bali, but marked for the higher-risk track. The practical reading is precise. National openness and full foreign ownership remain available, and Bali registration survives the province’s PMA moratorium because the relevant Besar-scale classification is not among the risk levels the moratorium blocks. For an independent veterinary-health business, Bali is not a closed door; it is an available route whose eligibility rests on the stated risk distinction.
editorial.pullQuote: For an independent veterinary-health business, Bali is not a closed door; it is an available route whose eligibility rests on the stated risk distinction.

editorial.headline: Veterinary Health Facilities: Nationally Open, Registrable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers business-managed veterinary health facilities, open to foreign ownership nationally and registrable by PT PMA in Bali at the stated Besar scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 75002 covers the management of animal-health facilities providing veterinary medical services. Its remit is practical and broad: animal care, examinations, treatment, diagnosis and health consultation for farm animals, companion animals, aquatic animals and managed wildlife. The record places these activities within business-managed veterinary clinics, animal hospitals, animal-health centres, animal ambulatory services, animal laboratories and animal shelters that include animal-health care. It brings these service settings within one activity description.

The activity is open at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. The record expressly recognises a span from micro through large operations, while keeping the defining thread clear: veterinary health services delivered through the listed facility settings. Those services may include care, examination, treatment, diagnosis or consultation for one or more of the animal groups named in the scope. A clinic or hospital environment, a centre or ambulatory service, and laboratory or shelter operations all sit within the description when accompanied by animal-health services.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. A PT PMA route is therefore available nationally under the cited Presidential Regulations. Bali calls for a more exact reading, but the result remains open. The provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. This activity’s Bali record states that the Besar scale is Menengah Tinggi; on that basis, it survives the moratorium and is registrable in Bali by a PT PMA.

That distinction is the essential one. Bali does not block this activity for PMA registration: its status is open on the higher-risk track. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the reference point, while the Bali outcome rests on the stated Besar-scale classification of Menengah Tinggi rather than the risk bands named in the moratorium. For a veterinary-health-facility business within this scope, the record supports a straightforward conclusion: it is nationally foreign-open and remains registrable by PT PMA in Bali.

editorial.headline: Animal Health’s Specialist Support Services
editorial.standfirst: A defined home for the banks, transport, optical work and specialist support that sit behind animal health services.
editorial.body:
KBLI 75009 covers the supporting infrastructure that allows animal health services to function beyond a conventional clinical encounter: animal blood-transfusion units and blood banks; eye banks; companion-animal sperm banks; organ-transplant, cell and tissue banks; animal optical services; animal ambulances; and other supporting animal-health services. Its centre of gravity is not a single treatment, but the systems, storage, movement and specialist support that make animal care possible. The wording also leaves room for other supporting animal-health services, while its examples consistently point to specialised support functions.

Registration is open at every listed scale—Micro, Small, Medium and Large—so the record does not confine this activity to one size of operator. That breadth does not widen the activity’s subject matter: the enterprise must still be built around the defined animal-health support functions. Nationally, it is marked TERBUKA, or open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. On this record, foreign capital can therefore hold the entire permitted ownership interest; the stated basis is Presidential Regulations 10/2021 and 49/2021.

In Bali, a PT PMA can register this activity because its medium-high classification sits outside the permanent moratorium for low and medium-low risk activities. That is the decisive local point: the provincial rule is island-wide and permanent, but it blocks PMA registration only in the lower-risk categories named in that rule. The Bali record expressly says this activity survives the moratorium and is registrable by a PT PMA. Its local position is therefore the recorded consequence of its classification under the risk rule.

The national and Bali conclusions need to be read together. Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%, and Bali does not reverse that result for this activity: it remains registrable there by a PT PMA. The relevant Bali explanation is the activity’s placement outside the moratorium’s low and medium-low risk boundary. For founders, the practical reading is clear: an animal-health support business within this defined scope can be structured with foreign investment nationally and registered in Bali under the stated classification.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, a PT PMA can register this activity because its medium-high classification sits outside the permanent moratorium for low and medium-low risk activities.

editorial.headline: Vehicle Rental: Open Nationally, Bali’s Proposed Closure
editorial.standfirst: A driverless vehicle-rental and operational-leasing activity that is fully foreign-open nationally, while Bali records a proposed closure for rentals rather than a current PMA block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 77100 concerns the rental and operational leasing—without a purchase option—of motor vehicles used for land transport. Its terrain runs from driverless passenger cars to trucks, motor caravans, trailers and recreational vehicles, and it also takes in driverless private cars and motorcycles. The decisive boundary is control of the vehicle: this is provision of the vehicle itself, not a land-transport service supplied with an operator. The category is broad in the kinds of land vehicles it admits, but exact about the form of leasing involved. Its coverage expressly includes operational leasing of driverless private cars and motorcycles.

Registration is open to micro, small, medium and large enterprises. Each is expressly listed as open, so the record does not reserve the activity for a particular scale of enterprise. At national level, the PMA status is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national entry permits full foreign ownership for the activity. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a business model built around a fleet or the operational leasing of vehicles, that national reading is direct: the activity is not presented as a partial foreign-investment category.

Bali requires a more measured reading. The Bali entry is labelled as a proposed closure for rentals, but the record does not mark the activity as currently blocked for PMA registration. It would therefore be wrong to turn the proposal into a present prohibition, just as it would be wrong to treat the national 100% ceiling as an automatic assurance detached from Bali’s own entry. The status signals a restrictive proposal, not a Bali-side ownership percentage or a stated partnership condition.

The record separately notes an island-wide, permanent Bali rule that blocks PMA for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. Yet it provides no risk classification for this activity. On this record alone, that general rule cannot be translated into a current Bali block for 77100. The honest reading is consequently twofold: fully foreign-open nationally, and in Bali not presently marked as blocked, while carrying a proposed-closure status for rentals. For a registration decision, that distinction is worth keeping intact rather than smoothing away.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, the activity is fully foreign-open; in Bali, the record shows a proposed closure, not a current PMA block.

editorial.headline: Recreational Equipment Rental: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A broad rental activity for leisure and sports equipment, open to foreign investment nationally but blocked for PMA registration throughout Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign-owned company cannot register this activity in Bali today. The provincial position is not limited to one type of equipment: every scope in this activity is assessed in OSS at the Besar scale as Low or Medium-Low risk, placing it within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA for those risk classes. The record identifies the block with the Bali moratorium of 13 May 2026. That result sits alongside the national position: nationally, the activity is open to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%.

Nationally, this is an activity for renting and operational leasing recreation and sports equipment without an option to buy. Its practical range is deliberately broad: recreational boats, canoes, sailboats and yachts supplied without an operator; bicycles, including electric bicycles; beach chairs and umbrellas; and other sporting equipment, including ski equipment. The boundaries are equally important. It does not cover boat hire with crew, water transport equipment hired for passengers or goods, media and other personal or household goods, or equipment rental that is an integrated part of a recreational facility.

At the national level, this activity is available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That wide national scale availability should not be read as a Bali PMA pathway. In Bali, the large-scale OSS risk assessment applies across every scope of this activity, and the provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI on an island-wide, permanent basis. The restriction therefore reaches the activity as a whole rather than only a particular item of equipment.

For founders, the distinction is straightforward but consequential: the national foreign-ownership ceiling describes what is permitted nationally, while Bali’s moratorium determines whether PMA registration can proceed there. A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not make PMA registration available in Bali. This activity remains nationally open, but Bali is not presently a place where a foreign-owned company can register it.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not make PMA registration available in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Event Hire: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This event-equipment rental activity carries a 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling, yet PMA registration in Bali is blocked by the province’s permanent risk-class moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the rental and leasing, without an option to purchase, of goods used to stage an event. Its inventory may include tents, guest chairs, bridal seating, decorations, costumes, and dining and serving equipment. The scope is deliberately broad: it concerns the practical furnishings, visual elements and serviceware required for an event, rather than one particular format of occasion or a single type of rental item.

Registration is open across the full recorded business-scale range: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. It can therefore serve an operator working at any of those scales, provided the business activity is the supply of event equipment and accessories on a rental or leasing basis. Nationally, the PMA status is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In national terms, a foreign investor may hold the full permitted stake in a company registered for this activity.

Bali changes the practical answer decisively. At present in Bali, a foreigner is unable to register this activity as PMA. The provincial status is blocked by risk class, with a recorded reason that is specific to the activity: at the Large scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium bars PMA registration where the risk assessment is Low or Medium-Low. This is not a reduction of the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, nor a separate Bali ownership cap; it is a block on PMA registration in the province under that moratorium.

For founders, the distinction should remain sharp. National openness answers the question of the maximum foreign stake for this event-rental activity. It does not create a PMA registration route in Bali while the province’s risk-class moratorium applies. The activity itself remains defined by the rental and leasing of the equipment and accessories that make events possible, across every listed scale. But for PMA, location is decisive: the national position is fully open, while Bali’s present position is blocked.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not create a PMA registration route in Bali while the province’s risk-class moratorium applies.

A foreigner cannot register this activity as a PMA in Bali today, even though it is nationally open to PMA. KBLI 77292 covers the rental and operational leasing, without an option to buy, of musical equipment. Guitars, drums, organs and gamelan sit inside that frame. In clear terms, it is the activity of making musical equipment available through rental or an operational lease that carries no purchase option. That distinction is central to the stated scope: the arrangement is defined by rental or lease use, while the right to purchase is absent.

The national position is therefore straightforward: a PMA investor may hold up to 100% foreign ownership in this activity. It is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. The stated reference for that national PMA position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Taken together, these fields describe a nationally foreign-open activity across the listed business scales.

Bali is a separate and decisive question. Its status is Blocked (risk class). At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within the stated Bali moratorium. That moratorium, dated 13 May 2026, is island-wide and permanent: it blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The relevant Bali setting is therefore not a locally adjusted foreign-ownership percentage or partnership condition; it is a block on PMA registration. The cited provincial basis is Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.

The two layers must be kept distinct. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA up to 100% foreign ownership and across the listed scales. In Bali, that national ceiling does not create a PMA registration pathway because the province-level status is a block. The precise conclusion is that national openness remains in place, but PMA registration for this activity in Bali is unavailable today.

editorial.headline: The Rental Business Behind Books, Discs and Recorded Media
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
KBLI 77293 concerns a particular kind of access business: renting and operational leasing, without an option to purchase, goods produced through printing and publishing. In everyday terms, it is the commercial circulation of books, magazines, comics, video games, cassettes, video discs and recordings on a rental basis. The distinction matters because the activity is framed around temporary use, not transfer of ownership. It therefore speaks to an operator maintaining a rentable catalogue of printed, published or recorded material and making it available again and again through rental or non-option operational lease arrangements. The record expressly includes rentals of video cassettes, CDs, VCDs/DVDs and similar media, placing older and newer recorded formats within the same stated activity.

Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA: it is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national position; there is no lesser foreign stake shown in the record. It is also open at every listed business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—rather than being described as a large-company-only activity. For a founder, that combination matters: the code is about the rental model itself, while the permitted scale range embraces the smallest listed enterprise through the largest.

Bali is the decisive exception, and it should be read without euphemism. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali record marks it Blocked (risk class) and states that, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every stated scope. Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration island-wide and permanently; the cited block is tied to the moratorium of May 2026. So the national 100% ceiling remains the national ceiling, but it is not a route to PMA registration for this activity in Bali. This is not a narrower ownership cap or a condition that a foreign founder can solve by choosing a different participation level: it is a Bali PMA-registration block founded on the stated risk-class moratorium. The responsible reading is simple: national openness describes the code’s position in Indonesia, while Bali’s current status prevents PMA registration there.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Household Rental, Nationally Open but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A wide rental category for household and personal goods, open nationally to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Personal and household rental is often mistaken for a narrow shopfront business. This activity is broader: it covers the rental and operational leasing, without an option to buy, of personal and household goods not otherwise specified within its stated scope. The practical inventory can include textiles, ready-made clothing and footwear—curtains and shoes are named examples—alongside jewellery, household furniture, pottery and glassware, kitchen equipment and electrical appliances. Recreational and sports equipment sit outside the stated activity. It also reaches the rental of ornamental fish with aquariums, where care and cleaning services may accompany the aquarium.

That breadth matters because the registration is framed by the activity being carried on, not by a single product line. A provider whose offer moves between home furnishings, kitchen items and personal goods can still be understood through this defined rental-and-operational-leasing scope, provided the goods remain within it and the arrangement has no purchase option. The activity is open at every listed business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. This gives the category a broad operating frame, from a focused rental inventory to a larger service handling many kinds of eligible goods, including the distinctive aquarium-and-ornamental-fish offering.

At the national level, the ownership reading is straightforward. The record marks the activity as open to foreign investment and sets the maximum foreign ownership at 100%. In national terms, foreign ownership may therefore reach the full 100% ceiling. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is the national investment position for the activity, and it must be read separately from the provincial registration position in Bali.

Bali changes the immediate answer. A foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today: the Bali status is Blocked (risk class), and the record marks it blocked for PMA registration. The reason is not a Bali-specific ownership percentage. Rather, the OSS risk at the Large scale is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule is island-wide and permanent for this risk classification; the record dates the cited moratorium to May 2026. Nationally, foreign ownership can reach 100%, but Bali’s moratorium prevents PMA registration today.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, foreign ownership can reach 100%, but Bali’s moratorium prevents PMA registration today.

editorial.headline: Rail and Caravan Leasing: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Operator-free leasing of rail equipment and non-motorised caravans is nationally open to PMA, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for the activity.
editorial.body:
**This is an equipment-leasing activity, not a transport service.** It covers the rental and operational leasing, without an option to purchase and without an operator, of non-motorised land-transport equipment. The stated examples place rail equipment at its centre: railway trains, electric trains and monorail trains. Non-motorised caravans are also within the activity. The wording identifies both the relevant asset and the leasing format: qualifying equipment is made available for use, but operation is not supplied alongside it. That is the core of the activity’s commercial identity.

That formulation is more exact than a broad reference to transport assets. The activity is limited both by the equipment and by the way it is offered. It does not extend to motorised land vehicles, nor to land-transport equipment provided with an operator. To read the scope accurately, both limits matter: the equipment must be non-motorised, and the arrangement must be operator-free; operational leasing is also without an option to purchase. A business registering here is therefore describing an operator-free rental or operational-leasing proposition for the stated equipment. The category accommodates the named rail examples and non-motorised caravans while preserving that distinction.

At the national level, the PMA position is open, and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In plain terms, the record permits full foreign ownership at the national level for this activity. It is also open to enterprises at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. Those fields establish national availability across each listed business scale, rather than confining the activity to one end of the enterprise spectrum. For a founder, the national position is clear. Yet it is not the complete answer where the proposed registration is in Bali.

In Bali, the answer changes sharply. A foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA there today. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. That places the activity inside Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The moratorium is recorded from May 2026. This is not a revision of the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a Bali-specific registration block. The two positions can be true at once: nationally the activity is open to PMA, while Bali’s current moratorium prevents PMA registration for it.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally the activity is open to PMA, but Bali’s permanent moratorium prevents PMA registration for it today.

editorial.headline: Watercraft Leasing Is Nationally Open—but Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: The national PMA position permits full foreign ownership of operator-free commercial watercraft leasing, yet Bali blocks PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
**The business at the centre of the code.** Watercraft is not treated as a generic category here. This activity covers rental and operational leasing, without a purchase option, of water transport equipment supplied without an operator. The examples given are commercial ships and boats. The asset, not an operated transport service, is the subject. Water transport rented with an operator sits outside the scope; so does the rental of boats for sport and recreation, including recreational boats, canoes, sailboats, and yachts. The code therefore has a precise commercial centre: water-transport equipment made available without an operator.

**Who can register it.** The record lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar as the scales open to this activity. That full spread is worth noticing: it is not confined in the record to a single scale of business. Nationally, PMA status is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national setting permits the full ownership stake stated in the record. It is a national position, however, not a Bali registration clearance. The same slim record contains a separate provincial finding for Bali, which changes the practical answer for a foreign investor there.

**What changes in Bali.** For a foreigner seeking to register this activity in Bali today, the answer is no. Its Bali status is Blocked (risk class). The stated reason is specific: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope. Bali blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI through an island-wide, permanent moratorium; the record links this block to that Bali moratorium in May 2026. Under the stated provincial rule, that risk finding puts this activity behind a Bali PMA block.

That contrast is the decisive planning fact. Read only nationally, the activity is open and can carry the stated 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. Read in the Bali setting supplied here, the location changes the outcome: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not overcome Bali’s block on PMA registration. The scope remains the same—operator-free rental and operational leasing of commercial water transport equipment—but a foreign investor cannot register it for PMA in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not overcome Bali’s block on PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Aircraft Leasing Is Nationally Open, but Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This operator-free aircraft, balloon and helicopter leasing activity is open to full foreign ownership nationally, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
Air-transport equipment can be rented in ways that look similar on the surface but are treated differently by the scope of this activity. This one is limited to the rental and operational leasing, without an option to buy, of air-transport equipment supplied without an operator. Aircraft, balloons and helicopters are expressly within the described equipment. The operating model is consequently equipment-only: the asset is provided without the person who operates it. Where an aircraft is rented with an operator, it falls outside this activity. That boundary defines what the registration is for.

The stated scale availability is wide. The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale, so the classification is not limited to one size of enterprise. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA and its maximum foreign ownership is 100%. Read plainly, the national record permits full foreign ownership; it does not state a lower foreign-share cap. This national position is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder assessing the activity at national level, the equipment-only scope and the 100% ceiling are the starting frame.

Bali changes the practical result decisively. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. That places the activity within the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026. The stated provincial rule blocks PMA registration for every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activity; it is island-wide and permanent. The record therefore treats this as a Bali risk-class block and flags PMA registration as blocked.

The contrast needs no softening. A national ceiling of 100% does not change the fact that this activity cannot be registered as PMA in Bali today. The block follows the permanent, island-wide moratorium triggered by the risk classification at the Besar scale, not a national foreign-ownership ceiling. The practical reading is therefore two-part: nationally TERBUKA up to 100%; in Bali, blocked for PMA. Staying inside the scope matters just as much: the activity is the operator-free rental or operational leasing of the listed air-transport equipment.
editorial.pullQuote: A national ceiling of 100% does not change the fact that this activity cannot be registered as PMA in Bali today.

This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Industrial Machinery Leasing: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers operational leasing of industrial capital equipment without an operator—open nationally to all business scales, but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering a Bali registration, the decisive fact comes first: this activity cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today. That local result sits beside—not inside—the national classification. Nationally, it is listed as open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for every KBLI assessed Low or Medium-Low risk. For this activity, the OSS risk at the Besar scale is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, so the Bali block applies.

At its core, the activity is operational leasing: renting and leasing industrial machinery and equipment without an option right, and without an operator. The equipment is of the kind generally used as business capital goods. The recorded examples give the category its practical texture: textile machinery; machinery for processing or working metal and wood; printing machinery; electric welding machines; and machine tools. The absence of an operator is central to the stated scope. So is the absence of an option right, which keeps the activity within operational leasing as described in the record.

The registration range is broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses are all included. A registrant may therefore fall within any one of the four named scales while carrying the same stated activity: leasing industrial machinery or equipment without an operator, generally for use as capital goods. That national scale availability, however, does not override the location-specific PMA result. The Bali moratorium applies to PMA registration on the basis of the recorded risk treatment, including the Besar-scale assessment across every scope.

Both parts of the picture are true at once. Under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, the national PMA position is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Yet a national ownership ceiling is not a Bali registration clearance. In Bali, the block follows the activity’s risk-class treatment and the moratorium recorded for May 2026; it does not reduce the national foreign-ownership percentage. The clear reading is national openness, but no PMA registration in Bali for this industrial machinery leasing activity.
editorial.pullQuote: A national ownership ceiling is not a Bali registration clearance.

editorial.headline: Farm Machinery Leasing: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity permits full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration there today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 77392 concerns the rental and operational leasing—without an option to purchase—of agricultural and forestry machinery, equipment and their accessories, supplied without an operator. It includes working equipment used in those fields, with agricultural tractors given as a concrete example. The defining commercial proposition is access to the machinery itself: the activity is the provision of equipment for use, rather than the supply of an operator alongside it. That keeps the scope centered on machines, equipment and their accessories under an operational-lease arrangement that carries no purchase option.

That scope is open to registrants across every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. In practical terms, it gives the activity a full stated scale range, rather than reserving it for one end of the market. The record supplies no narrower profile of a particular legal form, customer class or equipment specialization. What it does establish is clear: a business whose stated activity is renting or operationally leasing agricultural and forestry machinery without an operator may be registered at any of those four recorded scales.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is unambiguous. The activity is marked TERBUKA and its national maximum foreign ownership is 100%. A foreign-owned setup can therefore be registered nationally within that ceiling, which is full foreign ownership rather than a capped foreign stake. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. This national position is a fact about the activity at the national level; it is not a promise that provincial treatment will mirror it.

In Bali, the answer changes decisively. A foreigner is unable to register this activity as PMA in Bali today. The Bali record marks it Blocked (risk class) and says that, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. That classification triggers Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, recorded in connection with 13 May 2026. The key planning point is not a tension in the national ceiling—it remains 100%—but a separate Bali registration block. For a founder considering Bali, the location determines the immediate answer: national foreign openness does not override the island-wide PMA moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: National foreign openness does not override Bali’s island-wide PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Construction Equipment Leasing: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers operator-free leasing of construction and civil-engineering equipment—nationally open to full foreign ownership, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Today, a foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali. That is the practical starting point, even though the national position is notably more open: the activity is classified as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. For founders assessing a leasing business across Indonesia, the distinction is decisive. National openness does not override Bali’s separate island-wide restriction on PMA registration for the relevant risk classes.

The activity concerns the rental and operational leasing, without an option to purchase, of machinery and equipment used in construction and civil engineering. It includes the associated equipment supplied without an operator: crane lorries, scaffolding and work platforms are clear examples. The boundary is equally important. This is an equipment-leasing activity, not the provision of machinery with personnel; it also excludes the installation and piling of scaffolding and work platforms. editorial.headline: Office Equipment Leasing: Nationally Open, Bali Barred to PMA
editorial.standfirst: An operator-free office-equipment leasing activity, open to full foreign ownership nationally but barred from PMA registration in Bali under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 77394 covers the operator-free rental and operational leasing—leasing without an option—of office machinery and equipment. Its scope is broad but coherent: typewriters, accounting machines, counting equipment such as cash registers and electronic calculators, data-processing machines, photocopiers, office furniture, and computers with their equipment. The defining commercial fact is that the equipment is made available without an operator and under an operational-leasing arrangement. It is a category for supplying the working apparatus of an office rather than the people to run it.

Registration is open to enterprises at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That breadth does not change what is being registered from one scale to another. In every case, the activity remains the provision of office machinery, equipment, or furnishings on an operator-free rental or operational-leasing basis. The wording expressly includes computers and their related equipment, provided they too are supplied without an operator. A registrant’s actual business should therefore centre on making these office assets available under that defined arrangement.

Nationally, the PMA position is unambiguous. The status is TERBUKA, with a stated foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the national record permits full foreign ownership of this activity. Its cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no national foreign-ownership ceiling below full ownership in this record, so the activity should be understood as genuinely open to foreign investment at the national level.

Bali is the decisive exception, and it is not a percentage adjustment. The Bali status is a risk-class block: at the Besar scale, every scope is assessed as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. Bali blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI island-wide on a permanent basis. The record ties this application to the Bali moratorium of May 13, 2026, cited to Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. Consequently, even though an investor may own 100% nationally, a foreign-owned company cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. For a Bali-facing plan, that is the controlling fact: not a diminished foreign stake, but an outright registration block.
editorial.pullQuote: Even though an investor may own 100% nationally, a foreign-owned company cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Mining Equipment Leasing: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This equipment-leasing activity permits full foreign ownership nationally, but PMA registration for it is blocked in Bali today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 77395 covers the rental and operational lease of mining and excavation machinery and equipment, supplied without an operator. It is a capital-equipment activity: the company makes machinery available for business use rather than providing people to operate it. The stated range is broad but specific, taking in power-generation machinery—including engines or steam machinery and turbines—mining and petroleum equipment, and professional radio and communications equipment. The leasing model is equally defined: it is an operational lease without an option right. That distinction keeps the focus on access to the equipment itself.

The record opens this activity to enterprises at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. This makes the code available to a leasing business at each of the listed sizes, while preserving one central boundary: the rented machinery and equipment come without an operator. A registration under this activity therefore rests on the equipment-leasing function set out in the scope, whether the assets are mining-related, petroleum-related, power-generating or professional communications equipment. The scale list is wide; the defined activity remains exact.

At the national level, the foreign-investment reading is clear. The activity is TERBUKA and carries a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In other words, the national record permits a PMA company to hold the activity with full foreign ownership. This is not a partial-equity opening: the cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The result is a clean national position for the particular leasing activity described here, rather than a separate claim about operations beyond its stated equipment scope.

Bali changes the answer entirely. A foreigner cannot register this activity through PMA in Bali today: its Bali status is blocked by risk classification. The reason is expressly risk-based. At the Besar scale, OSS treats every scope here as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA registration for activities in the Low and Medium-Low risk classes, so the restriction follows from the classification rather than a lower foreign-ownership ceiling. The moratorium is recorded as applying from May 2026. Founders should keep the two conclusions separate—100% foreign ownership nationally, but no PMA registration for this activity in Bali under the applicable risk moratorium.

editorial.body:
KBLI 77396 is the commercial activity of making specialised communications and multimedia equipment available under rental or operational-leasing arrangements without an option to purchase. Its communications side covers radio, television and professional communications machinery and equipment, expressly including walkie-talkies. Its multimedia side reaches the equipment behind creative-content production: image and sound recording tools such as cameras, CCTV cameras, microphones, recording media and lighting, alongside digital-media processing equipment including render farms, motion-capture equipment and three-dimensional scanners. The scope is therefore broad in equipment type but specific in the commercial form: rental or operational leasing.

The register is open to Micro, Small, Medium and Large enterprises. That breadth is important: the activity is not confined in the record to one business scale. The registrant is the business carrying out the rental or operational leasing of this defined range of equipment. A single code can therefore encompass communications gear and the practical tools used for recording, lighting and digital-media processing, provided the activity remains within the stated rental and lease-without-option model.

At national level, the position is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The cited basis is Presidential Regulations 10/2021 and 49/2021. In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity for PMA today. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently; the record dates the cited moratorium trigger to May 13, 2026. The stated sphere is broad enough to include equipment deployed in industrial processes, construction and other applications. A useful concrete example in the record is baggage-scanning equipment that uses an ionising-radiation source. The category therefore describes a way of supplying specialised equipment for work: the provider rents or operationally leases the machine or radiation equipment, while ownership does not pass through an option to purchase. That distinction is the backbone of the activity’s stated scope.

Who can register it? The scope is open to businesses at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That is a wide stated range, but it does not alter what the activity is: the same rental or no-option operational-leasing work, focused on machinery and radiation equipment used in the described settings. The scale list is significant because it places the activity in reach of enterprises from Mikro through Besar, rather than assigning it to one size of operator. For a founder reading the classification, the clean takeaway is to keep the commercial description aligned with the recorded activity—providing access to this equipment through rental or operational leasing without a purchase option.

Nationally, the position is open. The record marks foreign investment as TERBUKA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%, citing Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In the national framework recorded here, a PMA business can therefore participate in this activity with full foreign ownership. It is important to read that statement for exactly what it says: 100% is the national foreign-ownership ceiling, and the national status is open. This is a clear national position for the leasing activity described in the record.

Bali produces a different outcome. The Bali status is a moratorium closure, and the record is direct: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA at a Bali address today. The stated reason is that the Besar scale is classified as Low risk, bringing it within Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA block for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. National openness therefore does not produce a Bali PMA registration route for this activity. This is not a Bali-specific reduction of the foreign-ownership ceiling. Bali blocks the registration itself under its PMA moratorium, notwithstanding the national permission for up to 100% foreign ownership.

editorial.headline: Operational Leasing, Nationally Open but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This broad rental activity permits full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium prevents its registration on the island.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is an operational-leasing activity: the rental or lease, without an option to purchase, of machinery, equipment and other tangible goods not classified elsewhere within its rental grouping. The stated examples show how broad the activity can be: containers used for homes or offices, pallets and comparable equipment for lifting containers, plus the rental of livestock and racehorses. Those examples should be read together, not as a closed inventory. They show an activity framed by the rental or operational-lease arrangement and tangible assets, rather than by one particular machine, customer setting or end use.

This is also an activity available to a full range of business scales. Registration is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises. At the national level it is TERBUKA for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%; the record cites Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as its PMA source. In national terms, that is a complete foreign-ownership opening, and it applies alongside the stated availability from micro through large scale. The national position answers the ownership question nationally, but it does not itself decide whether a foreign-owned company may register the activity in Bali.

On Bali, the answer changes decisively. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): registration by PMA is blocked under an island-wide, permanent Bali moratorium covering all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The record identifies the reason for this activity with unusual specificity: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low on every scope, and it is therefore blocked by the Bali moratorium recorded on May 13, 2026. The result is plain: a foreign-owned company cannot register this activity in Bali today.

This is a registration block, not a reduced Bali ownership percentage beside the national ceiling. The 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the national fact, while Bali’s local rule determines the island outcome. The distinction matters particularly for an activity whose stated scope is intentionally wide—from containers and lifting equipment to livestock and racehorses—because the breadth of its tangible assets does not override the local risk-based moratorium. Nationally it is open across every stated scale; in Bali it is unavailable for PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: The result is plain: a foreign-owned company cannot register this activity in Bali today.
