editorial.headline: Public Kindergarten Education, Reserved for Government Provision
editorial.standfirst: Government-run general kindergarten education for children aged four to six is closed to foreign investment nationally and unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is government-run general kindergarten education for children aged four to six, with priority given to those aged five and six. Its purpose is broad childhood development, not early specialisation: children’s potential is to be developed as a whole, alongside general religious education that is not taught in depth through any one faith. The institutional setting is equally important. The record places the activity with government providers, including public kindergartens and public special-kindergartens.

That makes the registrant question unusually direct. This is not a private operator category recast in public language; it is an activity organised by government. The record identifies no business scale as open to it. For founders, that absence should be read together with the scope, not filled with assumptions about a small, medium or large route: none is supplied. Within that frame, the named examples matter: a public kindergarten and a public special kindergarten are both illustrations of the government-run form. The education remains general kindergarten education, with a whole-child emphasis and religious learning that is not pursued in depth within a particular faith.

At national level, foreign investment is closed. The foreign-ownership ceiling is 0%, under the cited Presidential Regulations, so a foreign-owned PMA vehicle is not available for this activity. This conclusion does not turn on a partial stake, a commercial structure or a different scale; the record provides a closed PMA status and no foreign share. The clearest reading is therefore that the activity sits within public provision, rather than an opening through which foreign capital may be registered.

Bali reaches the same practical result: a foreigner cannot register this activity there today. It is recorded as closed for PMA registration in Bali. The Bali note says the activity is medium-high/high risk and is not blocked by the province-wide moratorium; the specified address should be verified. That distinction is useful, because the moratorium applies island-wide and permanently to Low and Medium-Low risk activities, while this activity’s Bali closure is recorded separately. The prudent conclusion is simple: government-run kindergarten education remains closed to foreign investment nationally and, in Bali, unavailable for PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Private Kindergartens: Nationally Open, and Not Barred in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A private kindergarten activity spanning early childhood education is open to full foreign ownership nationally and is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity covers privately run general kindergartens for children aged four to six, with particular priority given to five- and six-year-olds. Its purpose is broad early development: helping children develop their potential as a whole, while providing general religious education without concentrating deeply on any one faith. The scope includes private kindergartens, private special kindergartens, and kindergartens established through cooperation with foreign educational institutions.

The defining feature is private operation. The activity is designed for education delivered by private providers, while the underlying early-childhood programme serves children in the four-to-six age range. It is not a narrow tuition category or a specialist religious instruction activity; the record places the emphasis on general kindergarten education, child development, and a broad educational setting. Registration is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, allowing the activity to sit within a small local operator as well as a larger educational organisation.

Nationally, the PMA position is clear: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, foreign investment is permitted nationally without a stated local equity requirement in this record. That national openness matters, but it should not be treated as an abstract answer to a Bali decision. Bali applies a permanent, island-wide restriction to PMA registrations for activities classified as Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity is not marked as blocked under that rule.

The Bali outcome is therefore genuinely workable on the record provided. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which places it outside the risk categories caught by Bali’s moratorium. Bali’s status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: a foreign investor is not barred from registering this activity there today, but the larger-scale risk classification remains part of the operating picture. The honest conclusion is neither a blanket warning nor a casual assumption of openness: national PMA access is full, and Bali does not block this activity through its stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: Islamic Preschool Education: Open Nationally, Address-Checked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers Islamic preschool education for children aged four to six, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85103 covers preschool education for children aged four to six, where preparation for primary education is integrated with Islamic values. The curriculum described in the record combines early learning with an introduction to worship practices, memorising prayers and understanding the Qur’an. It includes settings identified as Qur’an early-childhood education (PAUD Al-Qur’an), raudhatul athfal (RA), and bustanul athfal (BA). This is a defined preschool educational activity in which Islamic formation is part of the preparation for basic education.

At the national level, the activity is open to PMA and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. A foreign investor may therefore hold the full permitted stake nationally. The record does not specify eligible business scales. It would be inaccurate to infer a micro, small, medium or large-business qualification from that omission. For registration planning, the national ownership position is clear, while the supplied record does not attach the activity to a named scale.

Bali is neither an automatic green light nor a blanket PMA prohibition. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk activities, island-wide. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. Its Bali assessment is medium-high/high risk and expressly calls for verification per address. The distinction matters: national openness does not remove the need to test the actual Bali address, yet the island-wide moratorium identified in the record is not the obstacle for this activity.

That produces a sober planning position. The educational scope is specific: Islamic preschool preparation before basic education, with named devotional and Qur’anic elements. Nationally, foreign ownership may reach the full 100% ceiling. In Bali, the pathway is not described as blocked, but it carries an address-level verification instruction associated with its medium-high/high-risk assessment. A registration decision should retain both truths at once: full national PMA openness, and a Bali position that requires verification for the particular address.

editorial.headline: Faith-Based Preschooling, With a Clear Bali Address Test
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 85104 covers faith-integrated preschool education for children aged four to six, nationally open to full foreign ownership, with Bali eligibility turning on the specific address.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85104 covers preschool education for children aged four to six, integrating Protestant, Catholic, Hindu, Buddhist or Confucian values into preparation for primary schooling. Its examples—seminary kindergartens, pratama widyalaya, pratama widya pasraman and nava dhamamasekha—clarify the activity’s character: early learning shaped by one of those religious traditions. The focus is the educational programme itself, preparing young children for the next level while embedding the stated religious values in learning.

At national level, the PMA status is open and foreign ownership is permitted up to 100%. That is a full foreign-ownership ceiling. The slim record names no business scales as open to this activity, so it provides no basis for attaching a micro, small, medium or large-business label. Nor does it supply a separate list of institutional forms or registrations. The reliable reading is narrower: an operator establishing the described religious preschool activity has an open national PMA position, with foreign ownership allowed to the stated ceiling.

Bali calls for a more address-conscious reading. The provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for every low- and medium-low-risk KBLI, permanently and island-wide. This activity is marked medium-high/high risk in the Bali record and is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. Bali’s status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, but the record also says to verify per address. That does not reduce the national 100% ceiling or create a Bali-side foreign-ownership cap; it means the Bali result is not a blanket approval disconnected from location.

The distinction matters because the national and Bali entries answer different questions. The national entry concerns PMA openness and its ownership ceiling. The Bali entry concerns the effect of a province-wide moratorium tied to risk categories, then requires an address check for this medium-high/high-risk activity. Read together, they support a disciplined conclusion: the code is nationally open at the stated ceiling; in Bali it is outside the moratorium’s barred risk range, while its place-specific status still needs verification.

editorial.headline: Private Primary Education, Open Nationally and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This private primary-education activity spans general learning for children aged seven to twelve, with a fully open national foreign-ownership ceiling and no Bali PMA moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
This activity concerns privately provided primary education for pupils aged seven to twelve, along with related equivalency education. Its centre of gravity is general knowledge and practical skills: the foundational work associated with private primary schools, private primary special-education schools, and private Paket A provision. The scope also includes formal primary-level education delivered through cooperation between a foreign educational institution accredited or recognised in its home country and an Indonesian educational institution, within the applicable legal framework.

It is a broad private-education category in terms of business scale. The record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises, placing small providers and larger educational operators within the same activity classification. That breadth matters because the subject is not a narrow specialist service; it is the private delivery and management of general primary education, including forms designed for learners requiring special education and recognised equivalency routes.

Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. In plain terms, the record does not place a national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That is a material point for founders assessing whether a foreign-owned education operator can sit within the national investment framework, rather than assuming that primary education is closed merely because it is socially consequential.

Bali requires its own reading. The provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the island. Yet this activity is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and is not marked as blocked: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which places it outside that moratorium block. Nationally open does not erase Bali’s screen, but here the record says that screen does not block PMA registration. On the record’s terms, a foreign-owned operator is therefore not barred from registering this activity in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open does not erase Bali’s screen, but here the record says that screen does not block PMA registration.

editorial.headline: Islamic Primary Education: A Clearer Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: An Indonesian primary Islamic education activity that is nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium, with address verification still required.
editorial.body:
This activity covers primary-level Islamic education for learners aged seven to twelve, alongside related equivalency education. Its centre of gravity is Islamic scholarship: Qur’anic studies, hadith, fiqh, Islamic history and Arabic are all within scope. Yet the definition is not narrow or devotional-only. It also includes the teaching of general knowledge and practical skills, placing religious learning within a broader primary education setting.

The scope names several established forms through which that education may be delivered: madrasah ibtidaiyah, ula-level muadalah education, formal diniyah ula education, and ula-level pesantren teaching centred on the study of classical Islamic texts. It also includes equivalency education at salafiyah Islamic boarding schools at the same level. In other words, this is an activity defined by a distinct primary educational stage and a recognisably Islamic curriculum, while retaining general learning as part of the educational offer. The slim record does not list business-scale categories open to this activity.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is marked open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That means the national entry permits full foreign ownership; there is no lower foreign-share cap stated in the record. The relevant national reference is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder assessing the activity at the national level, the classification presents an open route rather than a restricted one.

Bali calls for a closer reading, without warranting pessimism. This activity is marked `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK` and is classified as medium-high or high risk, so it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium. That moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk activities across the province; this entry sits outside that bar. For Bali, the decisive point is that the activity is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium, although the address still needs verification. The record’s instruction to verify by address should therefore be treated as part of the registration check, not as evidence of a Bali-wide prohibition.

editorial.headline: Religious Primary Education, With Bali’s Address-Level Check
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers primary religious schooling that teaches faith traditions while retaining general knowledge and skills in the curriculum.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85204 covers primary religious education for pupils aged seven to twelve, together with related equivalent education. Its focus is Protestant, Catholic, Hindu, Buddhist, or Confucian religious learning, but it is not confined to devotional instruction. The scope includes scripture, religious law and worship practices, classical religious languages, and the history of religious civilisation and figures, while continuing to teach general knowledge and skills. It encompasses formats such as Christian theology primary schools, Catholic religious primary schools, adi widyalaya, adi widya pasraman, and mula dhammasekha.

In practical terms, this is an activity for organisers and providers of primary-level religious schools with that combined curriculum: serious instruction in a faith tradition alongside general education. The slim record does not identify a particular business scale as open to registration. Nationally, however, the activity is classified as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national position: foreign capital may hold the activity in full, within the scope described.

Bali’s position is also clear, though it needs to be read accurately. This activity is not blocked for PMA registration by the provincial moratorium. The Bali record places it in the medium-high/high-risk range and marks it for verification by address. The province’s permanent, island-wide restriction applies to low- and medium-low-risk activities; this activity is expressly described as outside that blocked category. A foreign investor therefore does not face a moratorium block for this activity in Bali today, but the address-specific verification stated in the record remains part of the picture.

The distinction matters because the activity is educational in purpose and religious in orientation, yet its investment reading is not defined by a blanket Bali prohibition. Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In Bali, it is treated as an activity that is not moratorium-blocked, with its risk position and address requiring attention. editorial.headline: Public Junior Secondary Education: Closed to PMA Nationally and in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Government-run junior secondary education is nationally closed to PMA and cannot be registered by a foreign investor in Bali, despite a specific distinction on the provincial moratorium.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this government general junior-secondary education activity in Bali today. The Bali record marks it closed to PMA registration, while the national record is also closed. That makes the starting point clear before the educational description is considered: this is not an available foreign-investment route in Bali.

The activity is public provision of general junior secondary education for learners aged thirteen to fifteen, along with related equivalency education. Its instructional orientation is towards scientific knowledge and general skills. The scope specifically embraces state junior secondary schools, state special junior secondary schools, and state-operated Paket B provision. Read together, those examples keep the activity grounded in education administered by government, rather than a loosely defined education-service label. The focus is a particular public stage of schooling and its stated equivalency pathway.

That government character is decisive when considering who may carry out the activity. The record says it is organised by government and gives no scale category open to it. There is therefore no listed small, medium, or large-business entry point to present. The important distinction is simple: the record defines a government-run educational function, and it does not identify an open business scale for investors or operators. It should be read from that stated institutional setting, not stretched into a generic registration category.

At the national level, the PMA status is TERTUTUP and the maximum foreign ownership is 0%. There is no foreign equity space disclosed for this activity. Bali reaches the same closed PMA outcome: the Bali status is TERTUTUP and the record flags the activity as blocked. Its reason, however, adds a useful boundary. It places the activity in the medium-high/high risk range and says that it is not blocked by Bali’s island-wide moratorium; verification remains address-specific. The cited moratorium is permanent and applies to the low and medium-low risk band. It is not the stated basis for this activity’s Bali result, and the record provides no separate Bali ownership percentage or partnership condition to add. The practical conclusion does not change: a foreigner cannot register this PMA activity in Bali under this record.

editorial.standfirst: A private junior secondary education activity open to full foreign ownership nationally, with Bali’s moratorium not blocking it at large-scale risk.
editorial.body:
This activity covers privately run general junior secondary education for learners aged 13 to 15, together with related equivalency education. Its centre of gravity is broad learning in science and general skills: the familiar work of a private junior secondary school, but also private special-needs junior secondary education and private Paket B provision. The scope also accommodates formal educational cooperation between an accredited or recognised foreign educational institution and an Indonesian educational institution, provided it operates within the applicable formal-education framework.

The registrant is, in practical terms, the private education provider establishing or managing the junior secondary unit. The activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the record does not confine it to a single size of operator. That breadth matters because this is an education activity defined by the institution and the learning it provides, rather than by a narrow delivery format. A provider may be operating a conventional private school, a specialised junior secondary school, an equivalency programme, or a formal cross-border educational collaboration within the stated scope.

Nationally, the PMA position is clear: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, it is not blocked by the province-wide moratorium. The record places the OSS risk at Besar scale in the Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi range, rather than the Low or Medium-Low categories covered by that moratorium. Bali’s status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: a foreign-owned registration is not shut out by the island-wide rule, while the record expressly signals the higher-risk profile at large scale.

That distinction is the useful one for founders. This is not an activity whose national openness disappears on arrival in Bali. It remains foreign-open nationally at the stated ceiling, and Bali does not block it under the moratorium described in the record. The operational question is instead whether the intended institution genuinely fits this private junior-secondary educational scope, including its age group, general-learning orientation, and—where relevant—the formal structure of cooperation with an overseas educational institution.

editorial.headline: Islamic Junior Secondary Education: Nationally Open, Bali Address by Address
editorial.standfirst: This classification covers Islamic-oriented junior secondary education and equivalent programmes—open to foreign investment nationally and not barred by Bali’s moratorium, with address-level verification still required.
editorial.body:
At its centre, this classification is for junior-secondary education for learners aged 13–15, and related equivalent educational pathways rooted in Islamic studies. Its curriculum can encompass the Qur'an, hadith, fiqh, Islamic history and Arabic while continuing to include general knowledge and skills. The scope explicitly reaches Madrasah Tsanawiyah (MTs), wustha muadalah education, formal diniyah wustha education, wustha-level pesantren centred on kitab kuning study, and equivalent wustha-level education in salafiyah pesantren. It is a defined educational field whose religious orientation sits alongside general learning rather than replacing it. These details give the category its working identity.

editorial.standfirst: This religious junior-secondary education activity is open to 100% foreign ownership nationally and is not moratorium-blocked in Bali, subject to verification for the specific address.

Its curriculum reaches beyond general religious instruction: sacred texts, worship law and practice, classical religious languages, and the history of religious civilisation and figures all sit within its stated scope. At the same time, it retains general knowledge and skills learning. The examples named in the record range from Christian theology and Catholic religious junior-secondary schools to madyama widyalaya, madyama widya pasraman and muda dhammasekha.

This is therefore the activity for an operator delivering a defined form of faith-oriented junior-secondary schooling, rather than a narrow class in a single tradition. The scope is specific about the learning offered and the age group served, while still recognising related equivalency education. It is equally specific that religious learning does not displace general knowledge and skills. The record does not list any business-scale categories as open to the activity. No scale designation should be assumed beyond that absence.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is open. The stated foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, meaning the activity may be fully foreign-owned at the national level. That is the central ownership fact: there is no lower national cap stated for this code. The record identifies Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 as its PMA source, anchoring the national position without adding conditions that are not supplied here.

Bali requires a more location-conscious reading, but not a false alarm. The Bali status is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. This is not a field in which a foreign investor may take a minority position; the national ceiling leaves no foreign stake. The classification is instead organised by government, a boundary that matters before any question of operating format arises.

At its centre is education for pupils aged sixteen to eighteen, alongside related equality education. Its stated orientation is learning in science and general skills: the core substance of general senior secondary education. The scope identifies its institutional setting with precision through state general senior secondary schools, state upper-secondary special schools, and state Paket C provision. These are not loose illustrations; they show the government-delivered settings included within the activity. The result is a defined public education activity, rather than a broad label for education at a similar level.

The question of scale provides no alternative route. The record identifies government as the organiser and lists no scales as open. That absence is meaningful rather than an invitation to guess: no open scale category is supplied for this activity, and the national PMA position remains closed. Read together, the fields place this activity on the government-operated side of the classification and outside foreign-owned registration.

editorial.headline: Private Upper-Secondary Education: Nationally Open, Bali Risk-Led
editorial.standfirst: This code covers private upper-secondary and equivalent education, including formal collaborations between recognised foreign and Indonesian education institutions.
editorial.body:
Private upper-secondary education sits at the centre of this activity: education for learners aged 16 to 18, alongside related equivalency education, delivered by private providers and focused on general knowledge and skills. Its scope includes private senior high schools, private special senior high schools, and private Paket C programmes. It also includes a primary school resulting from cooperation with a foreign education institution, where that arrangement falls within the stated activity scope.

The code is designed for private education providers operating across every listed business scale: micro, small, medium and large. It also expressly accommodates formal education units established or managed through cooperation between a foreign education institution—accredited or recognised in its home country—and an Indonesian education institution. That collaboration must operate on the appropriate formal-education pathway and within the applicable legal framework. The common thread is private provision of structured education, whether delivered through a conventional school, a specialist upper-secondary setting, an equivalency programme or a qualifying institutional partnership.

Nationally, the position is open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That matters because the activity is not framed merely as a domestic private-school category: the scope itself recognises formal cooperation involving foreign education institutions and Indonesian counterparts. The national setting therefore permits full foreign ownership within this activity, while the practical shape of the provider remains defined by the private, formal and education-focused character set out in the scope.

Bali requires a more exact reading, rather than a generic assumption about foreign investment on the island. The provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk activities, island-wide and permanently. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium: at the large scale, its OSS risk is medium-high or high. Bali’s recorded status is therefore OK or higher risk, not a prohibition. For a founder considering private upper-secondary education in Bali, the decisive point is straightforward: the activity remains open nationally with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, and Bali does not block it under the low- and medium-low-risk moratorium because of its stated higher-risk treatment at the large scale.

editorial.headline: Islamic Upper-Secondary Education: The National and Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers Islamic-oriented upper-secondary and equivalency education, with national foreign ownership open to 100% and no Bali moratorium block on the record’s risk reading.
editorial.body:
Islamic religious upper-secondary education is, in this record, an education activity for learners aged 16 to 18, together with related equivalency education. Its centre of gravity is Islamic scholarship: Qur’anic studies, hadith, fiqh, Islamic history and Arabic sit within the curriculum, while general knowledge and skills remain part of the educational offer. It is therefore upper-secondary schooling oriented towards the Islamic sciences, rather than instruction detached from general learning.

The scope embraces the institutional forms named in the record: madrasah aliyah (MA), ulya-level muadalah education, formal diniyah ulya education, and ulya-level pesantren based on kitab kuning study. It also includes equivalency education at salafiyah Islamic boarding schools at the ulya level. These examples give the activity its educational setting and level with useful precision. The record does not, however, designate a particular registrant type; it defines the activity without identifying a specified kind of founder or institution that must register it.

On national foreign ownership, the position is clear: it is listed as TERBUKA, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The cited source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is the national PMA reading for the activity and should remain distinct from the Bali assessment. The slim record gives no entries under scales_open_to, so it does not support a claim that the activity is limited to, or excludes, any named business scale. That silence is meaningful: an empty scale field is not evidence for an invented threshold.

For Bali, the honest answer is not a prohibition. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record places the activity at medium-high or high risk: it is not blocked by the moratorium, though the address should be verified. The stated provincial rule blocks PMA for all low- and medium-low-risk activities island-wide and permanently. This activity sits outside that blocked group on the record’s risk reading. A foreign investor is therefore not blocked from registering it in Bali on the stated moratorium basis; address-specific verification remains part of the Bali picture, without any stated Bali ownership cap or wider ban.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor is therefore not blocked from registering it in Bali on the stated moratorium basis.

editorial.headline: Faith-Based Senior Secondary Education, With a Clear Bali Route
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers religious senior secondary education for students aged 16–18, combining doctrinal study with general knowledge and practical skills.
editorial.body:
This activity covers senior secondary education for learners aged 16 to 18, together with related equivalency education, centred on Protestant, Catholic, Hindu, Buddhist or Confucian religious studies. Its curriculum may include sacred texts, religious law and worship practice, classical religious languages, and the history of religious civilisations and figures. The scope is not confined to doctrine: it also retains general science and skills learning. The examples named in the classification range across Christian theological secondary schools, Catholic religious senior secondary schools, and Hindu and Buddhist institutions.

At the national level, foreign investment is permitted in this activity, up to 100% foreign ownership. That makes the national position unusually direct: the record does not set a lower foreign-share cap for this activity. Its scale field, however, contains no stated scale categories. In practical reading, the classification defines the educational and religious character of the activity clearly, while providing no scale-specific opening to cite from this record.

Bali does not close this activity to PMA registration under the province-wide moratorium. The Bali assessment places it in the medium-high or high-risk range, rather than among the low and medium-low risk activities caught by the permanent island-wide block. The local position is therefore open in principle, but address-level verification remains expressly required. For a founder, that distinction matters: national foreign openness is real, and Bali is not subject to the moratorium for this activity, yet the proposed address still needs to be checked before treating registration as settled.

The result is a measured route for a foreign-owned religious senior secondary education venture: a nationally open ownership position, a Bali status that is not blocked by the moratorium, and a final local verification point tied to the address. The activity should be understood through its full educational character—religious scholarship alongside general learning—rather than as a narrow instructional category.

editorial.headline: Public Vocational Secondary Education: A Government-Run Field
editorial.standfirst: A government-run field of vocational secondary education, nationally closed to foreign ownership and marked closed for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity covers government-provided vocational secondary education: learning in both knowledge and practical skills across a wide vocational curriculum. Its setting includes public vocational secondary schools, with study areas ranging from tourism, culinary work, management and office administration to hospitality, engineering, pharmacy, beauty and hair, and agriculture—including marine and fisheries subjects. It also encompasses public special schools at secondary level for learners with special needs. The unifying feature is not one profession, but a public secondary-school framework built around vocational preparation.

The record places the activity across every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Yet its substantive identity remains firmly governmental. It is education organised by government, directed at secondary-level students and structured around different vocational fields rather than a single specialist trade. That breadth matters. Tourism and hospitality appear alongside technical, agricultural, pharmaceutical and administrative studies, while provision for learners with special needs is expressly part of the same secondary-education scope.

Nationally, the position is closed to foreign investment. The foreign-ownership ceiling is **0%**, meaning foreign ownership is not available under this activity. This is not a field where a foreign investor can enter at a reduced stake: the record’s national status is TERTUTUP, supported by the cited presidential regulations. For founders assessing an education proposition, the distinction is therefore fundamental: the activity describes public vocational secondary education, but it does not offer a foreign-owned registration route.

In Bali, the record is likewise marked TERTUTUP, and a foreigner cannot register this activity for PMA today. The stated Bali explanation is nuanced: it is identified as medium-high/high risk and is **not** blocked by the province-wide, permanent moratorium that applies to all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. Its position must instead be verified for the specific address. That address-level verification does not alter the recorded Bali status; it explains why the closure is not simply an island-wide moratorium outcome. The practical reading is clear: Bali is closed for PMA registration, while the applicable reason must be checked against the proposed location.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is broad in its public educational scope, but it offers no foreign-owned registration route nationally or in Bali.

editorial.headline: Private Vocational Schools: Nationally Open, Unblocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Private secondary vocational education is open to full foreign ownership nationally, and Bali does not place it within its PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Private secondary vocational education is an institutional activity, centred on a privately organised vocational high school rather than on a single trade. It includes private vocational schools and private special schools at the secondary level for students with special educational needs. The curriculum may range across tourism, culinary arts, management, office work, hospitality, engineering, pharmacy, beauty and hair, and agriculture. The scope also expressly includes a vocational school formed through cooperation with a foreign education institution, provided that institution is accredited or recognised in its own country and works with an Indonesian education institution on the formal education pathway. It remains a secondary education category, with vocational study delivered in a school setting. The common thread is the private delivery and management of secondary vocational schooling, whether the programme has a conventional specialist focus or is shaped through formal international educational collaboration.

The entity described here is the private party that organises or manages the vocational-school unit. That can include a private provider operating an ordinary vocational secondary school, a private special school at that level, or an Indonesian education institution involved in the specified formal cooperation. The listed scale range is broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all open to the activity. The scale entries establish the coverage available in the record, from Mikro through Besar without narrowing it to a particular school subject. Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The activity is open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100%. In practical terms, the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership; it is not a partial-equity category. This national position is the starting point for assessing the Bali position.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The provincial moratorium is permanent and island-wide, and it blocks PMA registration for activities classified Low or Medium-Low risk. Yet this activity is not marked as blocked in Bali. The Bali record places its OSS risk at the Besar scale in the Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi range—Medium-High/High—and expressly says that it is not blocked by the moratorium. The result is a clean but important distinction: Bali’s restriction exists, but its stated trigger does not catch this activity. A foreign investor is therefore not barred from PMA registration in Bali by that moratorium, while the national ownership ceiling remains 100%. The Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, an affirmative position that still reflects the stated risk description at the Besar scale.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali’s restriction exists, but its stated trigger does not catch this activity.

editorial.body:
This activity covers Islamic vocational secondary education: programmes that develop vocational knowledge and practical skills while integrating Islamic values and teaching. Its educational remit can include study of sacred texts, worship practice and law, classical religious languages, and the history of religious civilisation and figures. The vocational side is equally concrete, spanning fields such as multimedia, animation, administration, accounting, pharmacy, tourism, shipping, mechanical engineering, culinary arts and electrical work.

The setting may be a vocational madrasah aliyah, but the scope also reaches equivalency schools and specialised Islamic religious schools serving secondary-level learners with special needs. What unifies these forms is not a single course catalogue, but the combination of vocational preparation and Islamic religious education at the secondary level. An operator registering this activity is therefore establishing an educational offer with both professional and religious substance, rather than simply adding religious content to a general training programme.

Each business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—is covered by the opening. At the national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Put simply, the record allows full foreign ownership at the national level. That openness matters, but it should be read alongside the location-specific position rather than mistaken for a universal answer to every address.

In Bali, the record places the activity in the OK_or_HIGHER_RISK position and says it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium, subject to verification for the particular address. The moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk activities across the province; this activity is recorded as medium-high risk instead. Bali is therefore not presented as closed to PMA registration for this activity, but the address remains material and should be checked before relying on the classification. The honest conclusion is measured: the national framework allows full foreign ownership, and Bali does not block this activity through its stated moratorium, yet the final local position depends on address-level verification.

editorial.headline: Postsecondary Learning Beyond the Tertiary Boundary
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers general and vocational education after secondary school that remains outside tertiary education, with a nationally open foreign-ownership setting and no Bali moratorium block recorded.
editorial.body:
Postsecondary education does not automatically mean tertiary education. This activity covers the provision of general or vocational learning after secondary school where the programme remains outside the tertiary category. Its scope includes postsecondary non-tertiary education and training through both general and vocational pathways. It can also include additional postsecondary programmes that prepare learners for higher education, as well as vocational education and training at the same non-tertiary level. The defining point is therefore both the stage of learning and the classification of the programme: it follows secondary education, but it is not tertiary education.

The record opens this activity to micro, small, medium, and large scales. That matters because the classification is framed around the educational provision itself, rather than reserving the activity for one size of operator. Within its stated boundary, the activity can encompass general programmes, vocational programmes, and additional preparatory education for learners moving towards higher education. It also expressly accommodates non-tertiary postsecondary vocational education and training, keeping the vocational route within the same overall educational level.

Nationally, the activity is recorded as open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. In practical terms, the record presents a fully open national ownership setting for this activity: foreign participation may reach the stated 100% ceiling. That national position should be read alongside the actual scope of the activity, which remains confined to postsecondary programmes that do not fall within tertiary education.

Bali does not add a moratorium block for this activity in the record. Its Bali status is recorded as OK or higher risk, with the reason identifying the activity as medium-high risk and therefore not blocked by the moratorium; verification remains necessary for the specific address. The Bali moratorium described in the record applies island-wide and permanently to low- and medium-low-risk PMA activities. For this activity, the honest position is more straightforward: it is nationally open, and it is not recorded as blocked for PMA registration in Bali under that moratorium, subject to address-specific verification.
editorial.pullQuote: It is nationally open, and it is not recorded as blocked for PMA registration in Bali under that moratorium, subject to address-specific verification.

editorial.headline: Public Higher Education Is a Government-Run Academic Mandate
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers government-delivered higher education, from diploma study to doctoral and professional programmes, but it is closed to foreign investment nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
Public higher education, in this classification, is government-delivered study across diploma, undergraduate, master’s and doctoral levels, alongside comparable academic, professional and vocational education. Its purpose is broad rather than narrowly commercial: developing knowledge, technology, the arts and the humanities on a universal footing. The institutional setting is equally clear. The activity is carried out by government through universities, institutes and higher-education schools.

The scope is therefore defined by both provider and level. It embraces the full progression of higher learning, from diploma education through advanced postgraduate study, while also including equivalent academic, professional and vocational programmes. The record lists the activity as open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That scale listing describes the activity’s recognised business-scale range; it does not alter the defining fact that the education itself is organised by government institutions.

For foreign investment, the national position is unequivocal. The PMA status is TERTUTUP, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 0%. There is no national foreign stake available within this activity. That conclusion should be read as part of the classification itself, not as a question of whether a particular university, institute or school might appear attractive as an operating proposition: the national PMA setting is closed.

Bali reaches the same practical result for PMA registration today: a foreigner cannot register this activity there. Bali’s status is TERTUTUP and the record marks it as blocked. The stated Bali rationale places it in the medium-high/high-risk range and says it is not blocked by the province-wide moratorium, with verification required for the specific address. That distinction matters. Bali’s permanent island-wide moratorium applies to Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA, whereas this activity’s Bali outcome is recorded as closed despite not being blocked by that moratorium. The honest position is therefore simple: foreign ownership is unavailable nationally, and Bali is also closed for PMA registration, while address-level verification remains expressly noted in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: Foreign ownership is unavailable nationally, and Bali is also closed for PMA registration.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Private universities and higher education institutions — degree-granting institutions operated by private foundations or corporations. This covers undergraduate, postgraduate, and doctoral programs. The institution must be accredited by BAN-PT (National Higher Education Accreditation Board) and approved by Kemendikbud (Ministry of Education, Culture, Research and Technology).
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**All scales: High Risk (Tinggi)**
This is one of the heaviest licensing paths in the entire KBLI system. NIB + Izin (permit-based licensing). You need full Kemendikbud accreditation, which involves institutional review, faculty qualifications, curriculum approval, and facility inspections. The approval process can take 12-24 months.

**PMA:** Fully open — 100% foreign ownership allowed. But in practice, foreign universities typically partner with Indonesian foundations (yayasan) to navigate the regulatory landscape.

High risk at ALL scales — there is no “easy” entry point here.

editorial.headline: Private Higher Education: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This private higher-education activity spans diploma to doctoral institutions and remains open to PMA nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
Private higher education under this activity is institutional rather than incidental: it covers privately run education at diploma, undergraduate, master’s, and doctoral levels, alongside comparable academic, professional, and vocational programmes. Its stated educational orientation is expansive—the universal development of science, technology, art, and the humanities. The category is designed for private universities, institutes, and higher schools, placing the emphasis on an organised higher-education institution rather than a single subject, course, or faculty. It embraces the spectrum from formal academic learning through professional and vocational equivalents while retaining that broad, universal intellectual orientation. The scope also expressly includes establishing private academic higher-education institutions both within special economic zones and outside them.

The prospective registrant is therefore the private operator establishing that kind of institution. The permitted business-scale range is equally broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all listed. This is an unusually useful point of clarity in the record: each named scale is included, while the category continues to be defined by the character and level of the education provided. A diploma-level provider and a doctoral-level institution can each fall within the stated scope, as can the academic, professional, and vocational forms identified there. For a founder, the disciplined reading is to keep the activity anchored to private higher education and to the institution types expressly named—university, institute, or higher school.

Nationally, the PMA position is clear. The activity is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100%. In plain terms, the national record sets the ceiling at full foreign ownership rather than a partial foreign-share cap. The wording matters: this is not an inference from the educational subject matter, the institution type, or its scale. The record explicitly marks the activity open to PMA and separately gives its 100% maximum foreign-ownership figure. Those two details establish the national position directly and leave no lesser foreign-ownership limit to infer from the data. For an operator reviewing the activity at national level, that is the complete ownership message supplied by the record.

Bali does not reverse that conclusion. The provincial status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and the record says it is not blocked by the moratorium. The island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. Here, the OSS risk at the Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—medium-high/high—which the record expressly identifies as outside that moratorium block. A foreign-owned operator can therefore register this private higher-education activity in Bali today; the stated national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. The honest Bali picture is not a hidden prohibition, but an activity that remains open for PMA registration, with its Bali treatment explained by the stated higher risk classification at the Besar scale.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this private higher-education activity is not caught by Bali’s PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: The Public Mandate of Religious Higher Education
editorial.standfirst: Government-run religious higher education spans diplomas through doctorates—but national foreign ownership is closed, and Bali reaches the same result.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 85403** is government-run religious higher education. It covers diploma, undergraduate, master's and doctoral study, as well as equivalent academic, professional and vocational programmes. The defining educational approach joins general knowledge with religious values, while allowing focused study in Islamic, Protestant, Catholic, Hindu, Buddhist and Confucian disciplines. Its institutional setting is equally specific: government provision at universities, institutes and schools of higher education. Rather than describing a generic teaching service, the scope names a public higher-education function in which the institution, level, and integration of knowledge and religious values are all part of the activity itself.

The description locates the activity in the full architecture of higher learning rather than in one degree or one religious tradition. A programme may be broad in curriculum, integrating general scholarship and religious values, or focused on a particular religious discipline; both sit within the stated scope when delivered by government. It therefore reaches from initial higher-education qualifications through advanced degrees, including the stated academic, professional and vocational equivalents. The record lists registration scale across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That all-scale listing does not displace the activity's central character: it is higher education organised by government.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is not ambiguous. The status is TERTUTUP, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 0%. In practical registration terms, there is no foreign stake to structure within this activity. It should not be read as a partial foreign-ownership allowance: 0% is a closed position. Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 provides the cited basis for that national position. The clarity matters because the scope can be expansive in academic level and religious discipline while remaining closed in its foreign-ownership setting.

Bali does not create an alternative route. Its status is also TERTUTUP and the Bali record marks the activity blocked: a foreigner cannot register it in Bali today. The reason provided classifies it as medium-high/high risk and says it is not blocked by Bali's moratorium; that standing is instead subject to verification for the address concerned. The province's permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, but this record expressly separates this activity from that rationale. No Bali-specific ownership percentage or partnership condition is stated in the record, and the address check remains part of reading the Bali position.
editorial.pullQuote: The scope can be expansive in academic level and religious discipline while remaining closed in its foreign-ownership setting.

editorial.headline: Private Religious Higher Education, Open Nationally and Clearer in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Private religious higher education is nationally open to PMA, while Bali’s risk-based treatment keeps it outside the provincial moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85404 frames private religious higher education: provision at diploma, bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral levels, alongside equivalent academic, professional and vocational programmes. Its defining thread is not religious study in isolation. The stated scope combines general knowledge and religious values, while also providing specialised courses centred on religious disciplines. It is therefore an education activity with room for both wide academic study and focused religious scholarship.

The record names private universities, institutes, higher schools and *ma’had aly* as its institutional forms. Its examples include Islamic universities, theology colleges and seminary colleges. These indicate the range of private higher-education settings contemplated by the activity, without narrowing it to a single religious tradition or academic format. It is open at every recorded business scale: micro, small, medium and large. That broad scale access does not change the essential character of the activity, which remains higher education integrating general scholarship with religious values.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct. The PMA status is open, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. A foreign investor may therefore hold the full foreign stake permitted nationally for this activity. The record identifies Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as its PMA source. The central point for founders is straightforward: religious higher education in this private institutional form is not presented here as a nationally closed PMA activity.

Bali requires an exact reading rather than a dramatic one. Its recorded status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK; the reason classifies the activity as medium-high/high risk and says it is not blocked by the moratorium, subject to verification by address. Bali’s permanent island-wide PMA moratorium applies to all low and medium-low risk KBLI activities. As recorded, this activity sits outside that blocked set. It should not be described as barred to PMA registration in Bali today, but address-level verification remains part of the locally stated picture.
editorial.pullQuote: As recorded, this activity sits outside Bali’s blocked set.

intel_2026.baliContext: This is the holy grail code for Bali's massive wellness and surf industries. editorial.headline: Sport and Recreation Training, With a Clear Bali PMA Route
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers structured sports and recreation instruction—from camps to online coaching—open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is for organised instruction in sport and recreation: the kind of teaching that gives participants a deliberate learning structure, an instructor relationship and a defined programme. It can be delivered through a camp, a school-style setting, a training facility belonging to either organiser or client, an educational institution, or online. Day and overnight sports camps sit comfortably within the scope, as do programmes in team sports, gymnastics, riding, swimming, climbing, surfing, martial arts, yoga, card and board games, and esports.

The essential character is educational rather than merely recreational. A professional instructor, teacher, coach or assistant coach may provide the training, but the activity is designed around learning. It does not, however, award a formal qualification in the preschool-to-tertiary education system. For a founder, that distinction keeps the focus on a structured teaching offer: a curriculum, coaching relationship and purposeful participant development, whether delivered in person, digitally or through a camp format.

Registration is open at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Across Indonesia, the PMA status is TERBUKA, allowing foreign ownership up to the full 100%. In practical terms, a foreign investor may hold the entire business nationally. That clarity matters for operators building a sports academy, specialist coaching practice, camp programme or recreation-learning platform: foreign ownership is not limited below full ownership by the national position in this record.

Bali presents a similarly direct result, with an important risk context rather than a prohibition. Its status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and at the Besar scale the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. The activity is not blocked by Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium, which applies to Low and Medium-Low risk activities. A PMA sports and recreation training business can therefore register in Bali today under this activity, while recognising that a Large-scale operation falls within the stated higher-risk OSS classification.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign-owned sports-training business, the distinction is clear: nationally fully open, and in Bali not swept into the PMA moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. editorial.headline: Cultural Education Is Open Nationally—and Not Barred in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 85520 covers structured, non-credential cultural training, with national foreign ownership open to 100% and no Bali moratorium block on the recorded position.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85520 is the home for structured cultural education: teaching in music, visual arts, dance, drama, fine art, performing arts and photography, delivered through schools, studios, classes or similar settings. What gives the activity its shape is not simply the subject matter but the learning format. It is organised training, built around deliberate interaction between participant and instructor, and designed to support the training process. Its natural purposes are hobby, recreation and personal development. It does not confer qualifications within basic-to-tertiary education—a boundary that keeps the category focused on non-credential cultural learning rather than formal educational attainment. That distinction matters for a founder defining the offer. A music studio, dance class, art workshop or photography course belongs here when it is structured learning for those purposes, with a teacher and participants at the centre of the experience. The code is about teaching as a service—an arrangement in which lessons, instruction and practice have an intentional place.

Registration is open across the full scale spectrum recorded for this activity: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth is a practical clue to the code's reach. The same core proposition can be organised as a modest class-based practice or as a larger education business; the description remains anchored in structured cultural training rather than in the size or setting of the operator. The scales are not a grading of the teaching itself. They show stated registration openness from Micro through Large, while the core activity remains the same. Nationally, the investment position is unambiguous in the record: the activity is open to foreign investment, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Put plainly, a foreign investor is not nationally required by this code to give up an ownership share merely because the activity is cultural education.

Bali is where the regional rule must be read without euphemism. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI, island-wide. Yet this activity is not marked as blocked by that moratorium. The record identifies the OSS risk at the Large scale as Medium-High/High and expressly says that it is not blocked by the moratorium. For a foreign investor examining KBLI 85520 in Bali today, the practical conclusion is clear: the regional restriction does not bar the activity on the record presented. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the relevant ceiling. The evidence is specific to the recorded risk position at Large scale; it should not be turned into a claim that Bali's moratorium has disappeared or that every cultural-training proposal is treated alike. It means that, for this activity as recorded, the regional restriction does not prevent PMA registration.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. editorial.headline: The Business of Teaching People to Drive—and More
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans private driving instruction, selected non-commercial transport training, and qualifying nonformal education partnerships.
editorial.body:
This activity is broader than a driving-school sign might suggest. At its most familiar, it covers instruction for private, non-commercial drivers: the practical teaching that prepares people to drive for themselves rather than for a commercial occupation. It also reaches educational programmes run by aviation, nautical and shipping schools when those programmes do not issue commercial certificates or licences. A further strand concerns nonformal education units jointly organised and managed by an accredited or recognised foreign education institution and an Indonesian nonformal education institution, within the applicable legal framework.

The activity is open to enterprises at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because the scope is defined by the education being delivered, not by a single classroom format or a narrowly fixed type of learner. A business may be centred on private driving lessons, while another may operate relevant non-commercial instruction in aviation, maritime or shipping settings. The common thread is educational provision within the stated boundaries, including the distinction between training and the issuance of commercial certification or licensing.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership position is direct: the activity is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. Accordingly, the national record allows foreign investors to hold 100% ownership of this activity. That is the national ceiling, and it should be read alongside the scope itself: foreign openness does not expand what the activity covers beyond the education described here.

Bali presents a different operational reading, but not a prohibition. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the island. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which places it outside the moratorium's stated reach. Bali's status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: a PMA applicant is not barred by the island-wide moratorium, while the risk classification at the large scale remains central to the Bali picture.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not bar PMA registration for this activity because its large-scale OSS risk sits outside the moratorium's reach.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Other Nonformal Pesantren Education: Bali’s Registration Picture
editorial.standfirst: This nonformal pesantren activity is open to foreign investment nationally and is not blocked by Bali’s moratorium, with a higher OSS risk profile recorded at Large scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85541 concerns other pesantren education delivered through the nonformal education pathway, whether arranged in levels or delivered without a graded sequence. The record frames it as an “other” category for pesantren educational units within that pathway. It expressly includes Pesantren Takhassus Al-Qur’an and other Pesantren Takhassus. The word *nonformal* is significant here: it defines the route of provision and accommodates both sequential and non-sequential forms of delivery.

Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all permitted operating scales for this activity. Its scope also identifies a cross-border institutional form: a nonformal education unit may be organised and managed through cooperation between a foreign educational institution accredited or recognised in its home country and an Indonesian educational institution. That cooperation sits within the nonformal pathway and is described as operating in accordance with applicable legal provisions. The relevant enterprise is therefore a nonformal pesantren educational unit, including one established through this stated institutional cooperation.

Nationally, the PMA status is recorded as TERBUKA, with maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain English, the record presents the activity as fully open to foreign ownership at the national level: no foreign-share ceiling below full ownership is stated. That national position should be read alongside the Bali entry, which addresses whether the provincial moratorium closes the PMA registration route.

Bali requires a more exact reading, but it is not a shutdown message. The provincial rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. This record, however, is not marked as blocked. Its Bali reason states that, at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Medium-High/High; consequently, the moratorium does not block this activity. The record therefore supports a clear conclusion: it is nationally open with 100% foreign ownership and is not barred by Bali’s stated moratorium. No separate Bali ownership cap or partnership condition is supplied, so none should be inferred.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is nationally open with 100% foreign ownership and is not barred by Bali’s stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: A Nonformal Home for Islamic Religious Learning
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers nonformal Islamic religious education, from staged learning units to Qur’an education, with a nationally open PMA position and no stated Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
This activity is the nonformal education setting for Islamic religious learning. It covers education units delivered either through a sequence of levels or without levels, including madrasah diniyah takmiliyah at ula, wustha, ulya, and jami'ah levels. Its remit also includes Qur’an education such as TKQ, TPA, TQA, and Rumah Tahfidz Al-Qur’an. The common thread is not a single teaching format, but the operation of Islamic religious education on the nonformal pathway.

For registration purposes, the activity is anchored to the organiser of those nonformal education units. The record places it at every stated business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. It also includes nonformal education units operated and managed through cooperation between a foreign educational institution that is accredited or recognised in its home country and an Indonesian educational institution, provided the arrangement follows the nonformal pathway under applicable regulations. That makes the collaborative model part of the defined scope, rather than an afterthought to it.

Nationally, the PMA position is open, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. For a founder assessing the national setting, that is a full foreign-ownership ceiling rather than a partial cap. The relevant source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The practical editorial point is straightforward: the activity remains defined by nonformal Islamic religious education even where it is organised through recognised foreign-and-Indonesian institutional cooperation.

Bali requires its own reading. The provincial indicator is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`, and the activity is expressly not marked as blocked. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. editorial.headline: Religious Education Beyond the Formal Track
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 85549 covers non-formal religious education other than Islamic education: nationally open to foreign investment, with Bali’s PMA position shaped by its risk-based moratorium screen.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85549 describes a distinct non-formal education activity: religious education units other than Islamic religious education. Its subject is not a general school category, but education provided on the non-formal pathway, whether organised in levels or without levels. That distinction is central. The activity concerns the delivery of such non-formal religious education itself, framing the code as a setting for organised learning rather than as a broad label for every faith-related undertaking. The scope also expressly includes non-formal education units created and managed through cooperation between a foreign educational institution accredited or recognised in its home country and an Indonesian educational institution, provided they operate on the non-formal pathway in line with applicable legislation.

Registration is open at every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That wide scale availability sits alongside an activity that may be arranged with or without educational levels, while remaining within a defined non-formal route. For an operator approaching Indonesia through a foreign-investment structure, the national position is direct: the status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no national foreign-share cap below full ownership stated for this activity. The national reference recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali calls for a careful reading, not an invented warning. The provincial rule in the record permanently blocks PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the island. KBLI 85549 is not marked as blocked by that moratorium. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated explanation is that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi — Medium-High/High — which is why the moratorium does not block it. Nationally, then, the activity is open to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, the record does not present a PMA-registration block under the permanent Low and Medium-Low risk moratorium. This is not a basis for adding conditions the record does not give. The useful conclusion is narrower: the Bali screen does not close this activity on the moratorium ground identified here.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, the record does not show a PMA-registration block for this activity under the permanent Low and Medium-Low risk moratorium.
