editorial.headline: Teaching the Skills Behind Craft and Industry
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 85597 covers private education in practical craft and industry skills, from batik and weaving to cooking, sewing and woodworking.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85597 is the classification for privately delivered education in craft and industrial skills: the kind of teaching that turns practical knowledge into a learnable trade. Its scope reaches from weaving, embroidery, batik, sewing and fashion to woodcarving, furniture, woodworking, screen printing, cooking, home-industry skills and other courses in making and craftsmanship. This is education with its hands in the material world—structured instruction rather than the production or sale of the resulting goods.

The activity is available across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the classification accommodates both intimate skills courses and larger private education operations without changing the essential character of the activity. What binds the examples together is the provision of education or courses in practical craft and industry capabilities, whether the subject is a traditional technique, a household-enterprise skill or a more formal vocational craft.

At the national level, the activity is TERBUKA to PMA and its foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. Put another way, the record authorizes full foreign ownership at the national level. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no lower foreign-ownership cap in this record to obscure the position: for this activity, the national ceiling is complete foreign ownership.

Bali does not reverse that result. The provincial moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis, but this activity is not blocked by that moratorium. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The record adds an important operational distinction at the Besar scale: the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. That is not a prohibition; it is the reason the activity sits outside the moratorium’s blocked category. For a foreign investor considering a Bali-based private craft or industrial education business, the honest reading is therefore clear: PMA registration is not blocked here, while a Besar-scale operation carries the stated higher OSS risk classification.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign investor considering a Bali-based private craft or industrial education business, PMA registration is not blocked here.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Private Education Beyond the Usual Curriculum
editorial.standfirst: This broad private-education activity is open to full foreign ownership nationally and is not blocked by Bali’s provincial PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
A foreign-owned provider can register this activity in Bali today: nationally it is open to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali does not block it under the province-wide PMA moratorium. That clarity matters because the activity is deliberately broad. It is the home for privately run education and training that sits beyond the specifically defined education groupings, allowing a provider to frame a serious non-formal learning business around a distinct subject, professional capability, or practical skill.

Its reach extends from teacher and education-personnel competence development to professional-exam review courses, speed-reading instruction, safety-guard training, survival training, and public-speaking tuition. The scope also expressly includes courses in agribusiness, animation and film, broadcasting, journalism, maritime work, tourism and hospitality, agriculture, fisheries, livestock, public relations, entertainment, modelling, law, business law, tax law, and a range of cargo, travel, shipping, and hazardous-goods subjects. Education outside the school system connected with nuclear-energy topics is included as well.

This is therefore a category for private organisers whose offering is educational but does not need to be confined to a single narrow discipline. It also encompasses non-formal education units organised and managed through cooperation between an accredited or recognised foreign education institution and an Indonesian education institution, where that cooperation follows the applicable legal framework. Companies conducting training for personnel who respond to pollution in waters and ports also fall within its stated scope. The permitted business scales run from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah and Besar, giving the classification room for both a modest specialist course provider and a larger training operation.

The Bali position is unusually direct. Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk activities. For this activity, however, the OSS risk at the Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi or Tinggi, so it is not blocked by that moratorium. The result is not a Bali-side foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition hidden behind the national position: the record states a national ceiling of 100%, while Bali’s relevant conclusion is that the moratorium does not prevent PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, this activity is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium, while nationally it is open to 100% foreign ownership.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Course and Tutor Intermediation, Properly Understood
editorial.standfirst: This is the business of making the match—not teaching the class—and it is nationally open to foreign investment while remaining unblocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is about arranging learning, rather than providing it. It covers intermediaries that bring clients together with course providers or tutors, facilitating the transaction without delivering the training or guidance themselves. That distinction is central: the value lies in the connection, whether it is made through a digital platform or through a more traditional channel—face-to-face contact, door-to-door activity, telephone, letters, or another non-digital route. Revenue may come as a fee or commission from either the client or the training provider, and can also include advertising income.

The scope is deliberately broad in the kinds of intermediaries it reaches. It includes non-exempt electronic-commerce operators and intermediary-facility operators established within Indonesia, as well as those established outside Indonesia that conduct electronic-commerce activity in the country. It also extends beyond those operator categories. The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, reflecting a model that can range from a modest matching operation to a larger intermediary business.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is direct: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the national framework allows a foreign investor to hold the full ownership interest recorded for this activity. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national openness belongs to the intermediary activity itself; it does not alter the defining boundary that the intermediary facilitates access to courses or tutoring rather than teaching or tutoring directly.

Bali does not place a moratorium block on this activity. The province’s standing rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities, island-wide and permanently. Here, however, the Bali record is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and specifically notes that, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. That is why it is not blocked by the moratorium. The Bali position is therefore not a separate foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition: it is a risk-based conclusion that leaves this activity outside the stated moratorium block.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity is about arranging learning, rather than providing it.

l4_bali.reason: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium

editorial.headline: Certifying Your Own Talent: KBLI 85691
editorial.standfirst: A foreign-open activity for organisations assessing and certifying the professional competence of their own employees or students.
editorial.body:
Professional certification can be an important part of how an organisation recognises capability within its own ranks. This activity covers the assessment and certification of employees’ or students’ work and professional competencies by the organisation responsible for them. In the record’s terms, it is a first-party professional-certification activity: the focus is on measuring and certifying the competence of the organisation’s own people.

That scope gives the activity a clear institutional character. It speaks to an employer assessing its own workforce, or to an education and training organisation certifying its own students. The slim record does not specify any business scales open to this activity, so it does not support a claim that it is reserved for, or limited to, a particular size of organisation. What it does establish is the national PMA position: the activity is **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. Nationally, a foreign investor may therefore hold the full foreign-owned stake permitted for this activity.

Bali calls for a more precise reading, without inviting pessimism. The province applies an island-wide, permanent moratorium to PMA activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity is recorded instead as medium-high/high risk, and it is explicitly marked as not blocked by that moratorium. Bali is therefore open to PMA registration for this activity today, subject to verification for the specific address.

That distinction matters because the provincial result is not merely a restatement of the national position. National openness establishes the 100% foreign-ownership ceiling; Bali’s record addresses whether the provincial moratorium blocks registration. Here, it does not. A founder considering this activity in Bali should read the position plainly: the activity is foreign-open nationally, it is not barred by Bali’s Low and Medium-Low risk moratorium, and the address remains part of the verification required for the Bali registration picture.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali is therefore open to PMA registration for this activity today, subject to verification for the specific address.

editorial.headline: Professional Certification for Partner Networks: The Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers professional competence certification for partners and suppliers, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s stated PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85692 concerns professional certification undertaken for the interests of partners and their suppliers. Its focus is the certification of the work or professional competence of human resources: an activity the record expressly places in the territory of second-party professional certification. The centre of gravity is therefore clear. This is not a broad description of education or training itself, but of the certification function applied to competence within a defined partner-and-supplier relationship.

The people and relationships identified in the record matter. Human resources are the subjects whose work or professional competence is certified, while partners and suppliers are the interests served by that certification. Beyond this, the slim record does not specify a registrant category or name any business scale open to the activity; its scales field is empty. That absence should be read plainly rather than filled with assumptions: the record establishes the certification scope and its partner-and-supplier setting, but does not add a scale-based distinction.

Nationally, the investment position is direct. The activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership level of **100%**. In practical ownership terms, the record sets no foreign-share ceiling below full ownership for this activity at the national level. That is the national position to begin with: professional competence certification for partners and suppliers is open to foreign investment on the stated maximum-ownership basis.

Bali does not reverse that position through the stated PMA moratorium. The Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, and the record describes the activity as medium-high or high risk; for that reason, it is not blocked by the moratorium. The Bali moratorium itself is permanent and island-wide, but the record’s conclusion for this activity is explicit: PMA registration is not blocked on that basis. The remaining instruction is equally specific—verify the position for the relevant address. This is not a Bali-specific foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition; none is stated. It is an activity that remains open in Bali under the record’s risk reading, subject to that address-level verification.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, Bali does not reverse the national openness to full foreign ownership; it requires address-level verification, not an invented prohibition.

editorial.headline: Professional Certification by Associations: A Clear Route Into Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 85693 covers association-led professional certification, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Professional certification has a particular institutional role: it measures competence, then gives that competence formal recognition. KBLI 85693 covers certification activities conducted collectively by industry associations or professional associations to assess and certify the work or professional competence of workers and professionals within their respective industrial sectors. The scope expressly includes third-party professional-certification activity. It also distinguishes construction-services professional certification bodies within the stated scope.

This is therefore an activity for associations operating as a collective professional standard-setter within their field, rather than an individual practitioner offering a personal service. The work lies in establishing and carrying out a process of assessment and certification for the relevant workforce or professional community. For registration purposes, every stated business scale remains open: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the classification does not reserve the activity only for large institutions; the record places it within the available scale range from micro through large enterprise.

At national level, the foreign-investment position is direct. The activity is **TERBUKA** to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%** under the cited Presidential Regulations. In practical terms, foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership by the national position recorded here. That conclusion should be kept distinct from the operational character of the activity itself: the relevant entity still needs to be an association undertaking collective competence measurement and certification in its industrial sector.

Bali does not add a PMA-registration block for this activity. The province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, but this record is assessed as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK** rather than blocked. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk classification is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which places it outside that moratorium block. For a foreign-owned association considering professional certification activity in Bali, the honest reading is straightforward: the national position permits up to 100% foreign ownership, and the Bali assessment does not mark the activity as blocked by the province’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: For a foreign-owned association considering professional certification activity in Bali, the record does not mark this activity as blocked by the province’s PMA moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Independent Professional Certification: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 85694 covers independent, impartial certification of individual competence—open to full foreign ownership nationally and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Independent Professional Certification is a business activity built around a narrow proposition: judging an individual’s competence through competency testing, then providing certification on an independent and impartial basis. The emphasis on independence matters: the scope distinguishes this service from professional certification conducted by associations. It is an assessment-based service centred on a person’s competence. Its stated scope reaches independent professional certification in sport and services certifying the competence of technical electricity workers. That combination makes the activity specific in method while allowing application across the areas named in its scope.

The record opens this activity to Micro, Small, Medium and Large business scales. The relevant registrant is therefore an operator actually delivering the defined certification service, rather than simply participating in the professional field being assessed. At every permitted scale, the essential character remains the same: competence is tested, certification is delivered, and the process is independent and impartial. The scale range gives the activity room to be organised from a smaller enterprise through to a large operation without loosening that central definition.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA: open. The foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, meaning the record permits full foreign ownership of this activity at the national level. This is not a partial foreign-share allowance disguised as an open category; the stated ceiling is the full 100%. The national PMA basis cited in the record is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a foreign investor reading the classification carefully, the national position is direct: independent professional certification under this scope is open to PMA up to full ownership.

Bali’s position is also clear, though it turns on the stated risk treatment. The record says the activity is not blocked by the provincial moratorium because, at Large scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High. That places it outside Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium rule for PMA registrations in Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. Its Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The honest conclusion is straightforward: this activity is nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership and remains registrable for PMA in Bali, rather than being barred by the moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity is nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership and remains registrable for PMA in Bali, rather than being barred by the moratorium.

Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Education Support, with a Crucial Bali Scope Test
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the services around education itself—and remains nationally open to foreign ownership, subject to a decisive Bali risk-and-scope assessment.
editorial.body:
Education is not only delivered in classrooms. This activity covers the supporting work that helps education systems function: education consulting; vocational, career and academic guidance; educational evaluation and testing; student-exchange programmes; curriculum development; and specialist or rehabilitative work assessing learning ability. It also includes operational advice and assistance for the education sector. Within the non-formal route, it encompasses institutions run through cooperation between an accredited or recognised foreign educational institution and an Indonesian educational institution, in accordance with applicable requirements.

The registration can therefore suit organisations whose role is advisory, evaluative, developmental or programme-based rather than conventional teaching. It is open across the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, giving the activity a broad practical range—from a small specialist guidance practice to a larger organisation administering educational services or exchange programmes. The scope matters: a business should describe the actual service it intends to provide with care, because the code brings together several forms of non-teaching educational support.

Nationally, the position is clear. The activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali is more exacting. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide. For this activity, the Bali outcome depends on the precise scope declared: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is low for some scopes and higher for others. PMA registration in Bali is available only where the business declares the applicable higher-risk scope, and the exact activity should be verified in live OSS before proceeding.

That distinction is not a technical footnote. A national foreign-ownership position does not, by itself, settle the Bali registration outcome. The practical question is whether the real educational-support activity falls within the higher-risk scope required for PMA registration there. Founders should treat the scope declaration as the central regulatory description of the business, not as an administrative afterthought.
editorial.pullQuote: A national foreign-ownership position does not, by itself, settle the Bali registration outcome.

editorial.headline: Government Hospital Activity: Closed to PMA, Including in Bali
editorial.standfirst: For substantial government-run hospital operations, this activity is closed to PMA nationally and remains closed to PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this government-hospital activity in Bali today. That conclusion is not merely a provincial nuance: the national PMA position is closed, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 0%, and Bali is likewise marked closed for PMA registration. This is not an entry route for a foreign-owned hospital operator. The point holds across the clinical settings named in the record, whether attention is on outpatient treatment, admitted patients, or a combination of the two.

KBLI 86101 concerns healthcare and physical-treatment activity carried out by hospitals managed by the government. Its scope encompasses government-run general hospitals, maternity hospitals, and specialist institutions, including sanatoria and leprosy hospitals. It covers treatment delivered to outpatients as well as treatment provided during inpatient admission. The record identifies two hospital-capacity bands: more than 250 beds, and 201 to 250 beds. These descriptors locate the activity in actual hospital care under government management, with substantial bed capacity expressly within scope.

The relevant registration scale is Besar. At that scale, the record assigns a Medium-High/High risk classification. Those facts should be read for what they are: statements of scale and risk, not a reopening of the ownership position. The ownership conclusion is separately and plainly national—TERTUTUP for PMA, with no foreign share allowed. The stated source for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. A large-scale classification does not override that closed PMA status.

Bali's status needs one precise distinction. The province has a permanent, island-wide moratorium that blocks PMA in all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. This activity, at Besar scale, is classified Medium-High/High; the Bali reason therefore expressly says it is not blocked by that moratorium. Yet Bali still records the activity as TERTUTUP and flags it as blocked for PMA. The practical reading is simple: no PMA registration in Bali for this government-hospital activity. The closure is real, but it must not be misdescribed as an outcome of the Low and Medium-Low risk moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: The practical reading is simple: no PMA registration in Bali for this government-hospital activity.

editorial.headline: Puskesmas: Nationally Open, Restricted in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This first-level community health activity is open to foreign investment nationally, while Bali records a more limited local ownership position.
editorial.body:
KBLI 86102 covers the work of a community health centre: first-level public-health and individual-health services delivered within its service area, with priority given to health promotion and prevention. The emphasis matters. This is not defined simply as treatment after illness arises; the activity joins population-facing health efforts with first-contact care for individual patients. Its scope is broad enough to include the centre’s public-health role while remaining anchored in first-level services.

The record distinguishes two operating forms. A non-inpatient puskesmas may provide outpatient care, home care and emergency services; it may also provide inpatient care for normal childbirth. An inpatient puskesmas, with beds, adds inpatient provision for normal childbirth and other inpatient health services. The distinction is practical rather than decorative: it describes the service configuration contained in the activity’s stated scope. The code is open across Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales, giving it a national scale range rather than confining it to a single enterprise size.

At national level, the PMA status is open, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a straightforward national opening for foreign investment, not a substitute for the Bali position. Bali records the activity as restricted. Its local condition states that, for clinics, foreign nationals may hold no more than 67%. The record therefore presents a more limited Bali-side ownership picture than the national ceiling; the two figures describe different levels of the framework and should not be collapsed into one.

Bali’s record also notes a permanent, island-wide rule blocking all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI activities from PMA registration. Yet this activity is not marked as blocked in the Bali field. With no risk level supplied here, the responsible reading is not to assign it to the moratorium’s categories. The clear conclusion is narrower: 86102 is nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership, while Bali classifies it as restricted and records a 67% foreign-national limit for clinics. Any registration analysis must keep those statements separate.

editorial.headline: Private Hospitals: Foreign-Open Nationally and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A large-scale private hospital activity that is nationally open to full foreign ownership and, because of its stated risk category, not blocked from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Private hospital care is the essential subject of this activity. It covers health care and physical treatment delivered by private general hospitals, private maternity hospitals and private specialist hospitals. The work may be outpatient care, or inpatient care in which the patient is admitted. This is not a loose label for health services generally: the record fixes the setting as a private hospital and the service as care and physical treatment carried out there. The definition is concerned with where and how care occurs, not merely the broad subject of health. It also identifies two bed-count bands—private hospitals with more than 250 beds, and those with 201 to 250 beds—placing those institutions squarely within the stated scope.

For registration, the scale explicitly open is Besar. That is the whole scale signal supplied by the record, and it matters: the activity is framed around large-scale private hospital provision rather than an undifferentiated health-care venture. The code therefore speaks to the private institution that delivers the specified care through a general hospital, maternity hospital or specialist hospital, across outpatient and admitted-patient treatment. Both outpatient and inpatient care remain inside that same hospital frame. Its scope is concise but not casual; it ties the registered activity to the hospital setting, the forms of care, and the listed bed ranges.

At national level, the position is unequivocal. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. Put plainly, the national ceiling allows full foreign ownership of this activity; it is a ceiling, rather than a partial foreign stake. That conclusion belongs to this activity’s own record and does not depend on a wider reading of the health sector. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, but the practical point is already clear in the entry itself: foreign capital is nationally open up to the stated 100% ceiling.

Bali does not overturn that national openness. Its local assessment is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK because OSS places the activity, at Besar scale, in the Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi risk category. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks every Low and Medium-Low risk activity; this one is expressly not blocked by that moratorium. There is no separate Bali-side foreign-ownership percentage or partnership condition in the reason given, so none should be inferred. The honest local conclusion is clean: a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, because its stated risk position sits outside the activities that the moratorium blocks.

editorial.headline: Government Clinics, With No PMA Route in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 86104 covers comprehensive government clinic care, from primary to further services and outpatient to inpatient settings, and is closed to foreign ownership nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register KBLI 86104 in Bali today. The activity is the classification for government clinic activity: comprehensive health-care and physical-treatment services that provide primary care and/or further health services. Its defining feature is the public organiser. Services may be run by the central government—through ministries or institutions, the police, or the armed forces—or by regional government. The scope also distinguishes clinics by service capability, identifying Klinik Pratama and Klinik Utama, with either outpatient or inpatient arrangements. It includes special government health clinics for athletes.

Every government Klinik Pratama and Klinik Utama is expressly included. The record makes the activity available across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Those scale labels tell us the breadth of the classification, while the named public bodies tell us who may organise the service. The classification goes beyond one level of clinic and beyond one mode of attendance. By naming both Pratama and Utama clinics and both outpatient and inpatient formats, the scope preserves the distinctions that frame the services, without departing from government organisation. It is a precise description of the government-clinic field set out in the record, rather than a general label for health care.

Nationally, the foreign-ownership position is decisive. The PMA status is TERTUTUP and maximum foreign ownership is 0%. There is no foreign equity available under this record, and no PMA registration route for the activity in Indonesia. The national source cited is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The fact that the activity is listed across four scales does not change that result: scale coverage identifies the listed scales, whereas the PMA field states the foreign-ownership ceiling.

Bali carries the same PMA conclusion: TERTUTUP, with the activity marked blocked. But the record makes an important distinction about the provincial moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; it is therefore not blocked by Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk PMA activities. That absence of a moratorium block is not an opening. Bali’s status remains closed, exactly as the national 0% ceiling leaves no foreign ownership. The honest reading is uncomplicated: this government-clinic activity cannot be registered as PMA in Bali today.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Private clinics — smaller medical facilities that provide outpatient care, consultations, and basic medical procedures. Unlike hospitals (86103), clinics typically don't offer inpatient stays or full surgical suites. This covers general practice clinics, specialty clinics, and polyclinics operated by private entities.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**All scales: Medium-High risk (Menengah Tinggi)**
NIB + Sertifikat Standar within **14 working days**. You need SIP (Surat Izin Praktik) for the clinic and STR (Surat Tanda Registrasi) for all practicing medical staff. Compliance with Ministry of Health facility standards is mandatory.

**PMA:** Fully open — 100% foreign ownership.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Direct match from KBLI 2020. Private clinics have maintained the same classification. The licensing requirements remain stable.
intel_2026.baliContext: Bali's medical tourism market is driving demand for private clinics — especially in aesthetic medicine, dermatology, dental care, and wellness. Clinics in Seminyak, Kuta, and Sanur cater to tourists and expats. The growth area is integrative medicine: combining Western medical practice with wellness services (IV drip clinics, hormone optimization, longevity medicine). These hybrid clinics attract the health-conscious digital nomad demographic. Licensing is significantly lighter than hospitals — no KARS accreditation needed, just MOH facility standards and local health department approval.
intel_2026.youllAlsoNeed:
- 86201 — If your clinic houses general practitioners
- 86202 — If you have specialist doctors
- 86991 — If you offer paramedical services (physio, nursing)
- 86992 — If you integrate traditional health practices
intel_2026.zantaraOpener: Opening a private clinic in Bali? 86105 is Medium-High risk, fully PMA-open — lighter than a hospital but still needs proper medical licensing.

editorial.headline: Private Clinics: Open Nationally, Unblocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers private clinical care from primary services to specialist settings, with full foreign-ownership capacity nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Private Clinic Activities covers the provision of primary and/or advanced health services through outpatient and/or inpatient care. It is framed as a privately organised activity, whether run by an individual or a business entity. The scope is broad within clinical practice: it includes primary and main clinics, occupational health clinics serving workers in support of workplace health efforts, and private health clinics specifically for athletes. It also identifies a PMA-supporting primary-clinic activity.

The code is open to businesses at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. At the national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain terms, the record does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity at the national level. That openness applies to an activity defined by the delivery of clinical services, not merely by the building or brand through which those services are offered.

Bali requires its own reading, because the province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This code, however, is not marked as blocked. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk classification is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; the record expressly concludes that it is therefore not blocked by the moratorium. Bali’s status is consequently not a contradiction of the national position: the national field sets the foreign-ownership ceiling, while the Bali field confirms that this code is not stopped by the province-wide PMA moratorium.

For a founder, the useful conclusion is precise rather than dramatic. A private clinic undertaking that genuinely fits this stated clinical scope may be structured across the listed business scales, with full foreign ownership available nationally. In Bali, the activity is not blocked for PMA registration by the moratorium. The large-scale OSS risk position explains that Bali outcome; it does not alter the underlying clinical scope, which remains centred on outpatient or inpatient primary and advanced care, including the occupational-health and athlete-clinic settings expressly named in the record.
editorial.pullQuote: The key distinction is simple: this code is fully foreign-open nationally and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Other Hospital Services: Nationally Open, Address-Sensitive in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This hospital-services activity is open to full foreign ownership nationally and is not blocked by Bali’s moratorium, though the proposed address still requires verification.
editorial.body:
### A residual hospital-services category

This activity sits within hospital services as the category for other health-care and physical-treatment work not included in the specifically enumerated hospital activities. That restrained wording matters. It is not a broad label for every venture with a clinical dimension; its centre of gravity remains hospital activity. The classification provides room for the remaining health-care and physical-treatment activity described by its scope, so the real question is whether the proposed care or treatment belongs within that hospital-services setting.

On scale, the record gives one clear answer: **Besar**. It is the only scale open to this activity. That makes the registration profile unusually focused: the classification is available to operators registering at the large scale stated in the record, rather than across a range of business scales. Nothing in the record adds a separate applicant type, licence pathway, capital threshold, or timetable, so those should not be inferred from the activity title alone.

For foreign investment at the national level, the position is direct. The activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In practical terms, the national classification permits full foreign ownership. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. There is no lesser foreign-share ceiling recorded here, and no partnership condition is attached to the national PMA position in this slim record.

Bali calls for a closer reading, without warranting pessimism. The Bali status is recorded as **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**, with the activity described as medium-high/high risk and therefore not blocked by the provincial moratorium. That moratorium blocks low and medium-low risk KBLI activities for PMA across the province; this activity is outside that blocked category on the record presented. The important qualification is geographical rather than numerical: the record says to verify the position for the proposed address. The honest conclusion is that a foreign investor is not shut out of Bali by this moratorium, while the address-specific check remains part of a careful registration assessment.

editorial.headline: A Doctor’s Independent Practice, and a Nationwide PMA Boundary
editorial.standfirst: Independent general medical care may be nationally foreign-open, but a foreign doctor cannot register a solo practice anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
For a foreign doctor, the conclusion comes first: this activity cannot be registered as an independent solo practice. Under Kemenkes health law, an independent medical practice is TERTUTUP — closed to foreign nationals — and that closure holds nationwide, not only in Bali. Our records do not support a foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity: the practice is closed to WNA outright, not restricted by percentage. A foreign doctor seeking a company structure instead should look at code 86103 (klinik), which our records show open to PMA at a foreign-ownership ceiling of 67%.

The activity is a focused professional practice. It covers general care and treatment for diseases, delivered independently by a doctor. In clear English, it is the independent practice of a doctor providing general medical care. The word “independently” does important work here: the care and treatment within scope are carried out by the doctor as an independent practitioner. That gives the activity a defined clinical character rather than making it a broad label for health-related enterprise.

Nationally, the record makes the activity available at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. That is a notably broad range of business scales, while the centre of the activity remains the same: a doctor independently providing general care and treatment. The record does not supply further detail on facilities, credentials, permits or operating steps, and those should not be inferred from either the ownership status or the scale categories.

This closure is not a Bali peculiarity. The stated rationale is Kemenkes health law: a foreign doctor cannot open a solo practice, and that rule reaches foreign nationals nationwide, not only in Bali. Read together, these facts establish a firm boundary grounded in national health regulation, not a technical footnote or a local carve-out. For a founder assessing this route, the honest answer is therefore no registration of this independent practice by a foreigner anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national ceiling allows full foreign ownership nationally; it does not create a registration route for this solo practice.

editorial.headline: Specialist Medical Practice: Open Nationally, Closed to Solo PMA Practice
editorial.standfirst: An independent specialist practice is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet a foreign specialist cannot register a solo practice under this code.
editorial.body:
A foreign specialist cannot register a solo specialist practice anywhere in Indonesia, not only in Bali. That nationwide restriction — TERTUTUP to foreign nationals under Kemenkes health law — is the essential fact about an activity centred on independent specialist physicians providing care and treatment for particular diseases and conditions. Its field includes eye care, ear, nose and throat medicine, internal medicine, and dermatology and venereology. The focus is not general medical service, but the individual specialist’s independent professional practice. It is clinical work rendered by the specialist on an independent basis, with both care and treatment at the heart of its stated scope.

Nationally, the picture is the opposite of an open default: the activity is TERTUTUP to foreign nationals under Kemenkes health law, so a PT PMA cannot register a solo specialist practice under this code. Our records do show a route for a foreign-backed specialist-medicine business: KBLI 86103 (klinik) permits PMA ownership up to a TERBATAS ceiling of 67%. That is a different registration — a clinic structure, not an individual specialist's independent practice — and it does not reopen this code to foreign ownership.

This is not a Bali peculiarity: the closure is nationwide, and the stated health-law position is direct — a foreign specialist cannot open a solo practice anywhere in the country. This should be read as a registration outcome that applies across Indonesia, not an administrative inconvenience confined to one province. Under Kemenkes health law, TERTUTUP status attaches to this activity nationally; there is no more permissive setting to find by registering it elsewhere.

There is no national-versus-Bali split to reconcile here: because the restriction comes from national health-sector law rather than a regional rule, the same closed outcome holds wherever in Indonesia the practice might be registered. For founders, the honest reading is not location-specific — a foreign specialist cannot register a solo specialist practice under this code anywhere in the country. The alternative noted above, the TERBATAS klinik code 86103, remains the route for PMA into specialist-adjacent care; this code itself does not open up regionally.
editorial.pullQuote: A national PMA ceiling of 100% does not create a pathway where Kemenkes health law closes solo foreign-specialist practice.

editorial.headline: Independent Dental Practice: Open Nationally, Address-Checked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers independent dental care and treatment by dentists, open across every listed business scale with full national foreign-ownership access.
editorial.body:
Independent dental practice is defined here with useful precision: it is the provision of dental health-care and treatment services carried out independently by dentists. The centre of gravity is the professional activity itself—dental care and treatment delivered by a dentist in independent practice. That focus keeps the classification clear: this is not a broad description of health services, but a specific activity rooted in the independent work of dentists.

The code is open at every listed scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That range matters because the record does not reserve the activity for one business size. Its commercial frame can therefore sit across the full stated scale spectrum, while the underlying activity remains the same: independent dental care and treatment undertaken by dentists. The scale classification describes the available range; the scope describes the work that gives the code its identity.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is open, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain terms, the record places no foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity at the national level. For a foreign-owned structure, that is the governing national position supplied by the record: the activity is open and may carry up to 100% foreign ownership. The relevant source is the cited Presidential Regulations, rather than an inferred rule drawn from adjacent activities or general assumptions about health-related practice.

Bali requires a more exact reading, but not a dramatic one. The Bali classification is recorded as medium-high risk and is not blocked by the province-wide moratorium. A foreign investor is therefore not shut out from registering this activity in Bali by that moratorium. The record nevertheless calls for verification by address. That is an important distinction: national openness and Bali's absence of a moratorium block support the activity's availability, while the address remains a stated point to verify. The accurate conclusion is neither a blanket Bali prohibition nor an unconditional promise. It is an activity open nationally to full foreign ownership and not moratorium-blocked in Bali, subject to the record's address-specific verification.

data.judul: Aktivitas Jasa Intermediasi untuk Kesehatan Medis, Kedokteran Gigi, dan Pelayanan Kesehatan Manusia Lainnya
data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup jasa intermediasi medis, kedokteran gigi, dan layanan kesehatan manusia lainnya, dengan mempertemukan klien dan penyedia layanan dengan imbalan biaya atau komisi, tanpa penyediaan layanan medis, kedokteran gigi, dan kesehatan manusia lainnya yang dimediasi oleh perantara. Aktivitas intermediasi ini dapat dilakukan melalui platform digital atau saluran nondigital (tatap muka, termasuk door-to-door, telepon, surat, dll.), misalnya layanan telemedisin. Biaya atau komisi dapat diterima dari klien atau penyedia layanan medis, gigi dan kesehatan manusia lainnya. Pendapatan untuk kegiatan intermediasi dapat mencakup sumber pendapatan lain, seperti pendapatan dari iklan. Kelompok ini juga mencakup
- reservasi janji temu untuk kunjungan medis.
Kelompok ini tidak mencakup
- jasa intermediasi untuk aktivitas perawatan berbasis residensial, lihat subgolongan 8791.

editorial.headline: The Business of Connecting Patients and Providers
editorial.standfirst: This code covers health-service intermediation—not the delivery of medical care—and gives Bali a scope-dependent PMA answer.
editorial.body:
KBLI 86910 is not the provision of medical, dental, or other human-health services. It is the business of bringing clients together with those providers for a fee or commission, while the intermediary does not itself deliver the service being arranged. The activity can operate through a digital platform or through non-digital channels: face-to-face contact, door-to-door work, telephone, letters, and similar routes. Telemedicine is among the examples given. Booking appointments for medical visits is expressly within the group. Income may come from clients or providers, and may also include sources such as advertising revenue. Intermediation for residential care is outside this activity.

The code is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses. Its scope specifically addresses non-exempt PPMSE and Penyelenggara Sarana Perantara operators established within Indonesia, as well as non-exempt operators established outside Indonesia that conduct PMSE business in Indonesia. It also extends beyond those operator categories. The practical centre of gravity is therefore the intermediary role: organising the connection between a client and a health-service provider, rather than becoming the provider of care.

At the national level, PMA is TERBUKA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. That makes this an activity with full foreign ownership available at the national level under the cited presidential regulations. The ceiling matters because it describes the national PMA position for this activity; it does not, by itself, answer whether a particular declaration can be registered in Bali.

Bali’s position is conditional on scope rather than simply blocked. The provincial rule permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI island-wide. For this activity, the record says that OSS risk at the Besar scale is low for some scopes and higher for others. PMA registration in Bali is available only by declaring the higher-risk scope, with PPMSE for platform-trade codes given as an example, and the exact activity must be checked in live OSS. A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not, on its own, settle the Bali registration question.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not, on its own, settle the Bali registration question.

editorial.headline: The Wider Health Workforce, Clearly Classified
editorial.standfirst: Health services beyond doctors and dentists are nationally open to full foreign ownership, with Bali remaining unblocked under its risk-based moratorium reading.
editorial.body:
Health-service work does not begin and end with a doctor’s consultation. This activity covers the delivery of health services by health personnel other than doctors and dentists. Its stated scope is deliberately broad: nursing, midwifery, pharmacy, public-health and environmental-health work sit alongside nutrition, physical therapy, medical technical work and biomedical engineering. It also names traditional-health personnel, clinical psychologists, physiotherapists and other health workers. The distinction matters because the scope is framed around the health personnel who provide the service, while explicitly excluding doctors and dentists from that provider description.

Traditional health is not an afterthought in this definition. The scope expressly includes traditional health services delivered by traditional health personnel, and by others with traditional-health competence, in traditional health-service facilities. Griya Sehat is identified as part of that setting and described as a Type 1 Traditional Health Clinic. In editorial terms, this makes it a broad service category with a specific place for traditional-health practice, rather than a label confined to one conventional profession. The record preserves that connection between the traditional service and the facility it names.

For a registration, the category is open across Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. That breadth does not alter its subject: health services performed by the non-doctor, non-dentist health personnel set out in the scope. Nationally, the PMA status is open, with maximum foreign ownership of 100%. The national position is therefore direct: foreign ownership may reach full ownership. The record does not confine the activity to one business size or set a foreign-shareholding ceiling below full ownership.

Bali calls for a scale-aware reading, but not a false note of prohibition. The provincial moratorium blocks PMA for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. For this activity, however, the OSS risk at the Large scale is Medium-High/High; the Bali assessment consequently records it as not blocked by the moratorium. The activity is nationally open to a 100% foreign stake, and the Bali record does not block it under the provincial moratorium. That is the honest Bali result on the supplied record.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is nationally open to a 100% foreign stake, and the Bali record does not block it under the provincial moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.baliContext: This is where traditional Bali meets the modern wellness economy. Balian (traditional Balinese healers) are cultural treasures — some have been treating locals and tourists for decades. The wellness tourism trend has created a market for 'authentic healing experiences': Balinese massage with spiritual components, jamu preparations, sound healing, energy work. Ubud is the epicenter — it's practically become a global wellness pilgrimage destination. The business opportunity: packaging traditional Balinese wellness for international audiences, combining Balian wisdom with modern health standards. Be respectful — this sits at the intersection of business and Balinese Hindu culture. Working with local healers as partners rather than employees is culturally appropriate.

editorial.headline: Traditional Health Care, Defined by Prevention
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 86992 frames traditional health services around promotion and prevention, with a clear national opening and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 86992 covers traditional health services whose centre of gravity is promotive and preventive care. The work is delivered by traditional health practitioners through skills-based methods and/or preparations, in a *Panti Sehat*—also described as a Type 2 traditional health clinic. Its scope embraces practices such as health massage, reflexology, acupressure, Indonesian herbal preparations, hypnotherapy, bone-setting, dry cupping, sinse practice and energy therapy. The unifying idea is not a single technique, but a traditional-health service organised around supporting health through those recognised forms of care.

The activity is open at every stated business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. Nationally, it is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is the straightforward national position recorded for this activity: foreign participation is not capped below full ownership. The applicable source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali requires a more specific reading, but it does not reverse that national openness. The province’s standing rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. This activity is not marked as blocked by that moratorium. The record identifies the relevant reason at the Large scale: its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, placing it outside the moratorium’s blocked Low and Medium-Low categories. Bali’s status is therefore recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, rather than as a prohibition. For a foreign-owned registration, the honest conclusion is that this activity can be registered in Bali today; the Bali moratorium does not block it on the stated risk basis.

That distinction matters because the national foreign-investment position and Bali’s island-wide moratorium operate on different terms. Here, the national ceiling remains 100%, while the Bali assessment turns on the activity’s recorded risk treatment at Large scale. The result is neither a hidden Bali cap nor a special local partnership condition: the record states neither. It instead gives a clean, bounded answer—traditional health services under this activity are nationally open to foreign investment and are not blocked for PMA registration in Bali by the provincial moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Health Support Services: Nationally Open, Bali Dependent on Scope
editorial.standfirst: This broad health-support activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but in Bali its PMA route turns on the precise service and risk level declared in OSS.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the less visible infrastructure that enables modern health care to function: blood-management units, medical and public-health laboratories, optometry providers, diagnostic centres and other medical-support services. Its scope also reaches specialised facilities, including stem-cell and cell-processing laboratories, eye and plasma banks, cell or tissue banks, biobanks, biorepositories, precision-medicine and genetic-testing facilities, hearing-aid centres, and optical services. It is a wide professional field, spanning both clinical support and the systems that preserve, analyse or make health-related material available.

The record places these services in the hands of operators managed by either government or private institutions. Registration is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the activity is not one uniform operational model: a diagnostic centre, a genetic-analysis laboratory and a bank for biological material all sit within the same defined field, while performing distinctly different health-support functions. The registration choice must therefore follow the exact service being declared, rather than relying on the category’s broad title alone.

Across Indonesia, the PMA position remains open, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That is a clear national signal, but it does not make the Bali position automatic. Bali’s status is scope-dependent: at the Besar scale, some included scopes are low risk while others carry a higher risk level. The provincial rule permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI across the island. For this activity, PMA registration in Bali is available only when the applicant declares the higher-risk scope; the precise activity should be verified in live OSS.

The result is a category where the headline national openness is real, but not sufficient on its own for a Bali decision. A founder considering Bali must read the activity at service level: what is being operated, how it is classified for risk, and what is actually declared in OSS. The national ceiling remains 100%, while the local PMA route depends on that exact scope assessment.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not settle the Bali question: there, the precise health-support scope and its risk level decide whether PMA registration is available.

editorial.headline: Medical Evacuation: Nationally Open, Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A domestic medical-evacuation transport activity open to PMA nationally and not blocked from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Medical evacuation is a specialised transport activity for moving people who are ill when particular circumstances call for it. The scope expressly names aircraft and ambulances as examples, and places the destination in cities or provinces within Indonesia. That domestic orientation is important: this is a category for special carriage of sick people in a defined situation, not a broad label attached merely because a journey has a health context. The record calls the activity medical evacuation and keeps the focus on the transport itself.

Who may register it? The classification is open to enterprises at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That is a wide formal range, but the scope supplies the common thread across it: the special transportation of sick people, using examples that range from an ambulance to an aircraft, when the relevant circumstances arise. The record does not reduce the activity to one vehicle or one business size; it anchors it in a particular kind of passenger transport with domestic city- or province-bound destinations.

Nationally, foreign investment is explicitly open. The maximum foreign ownership is 100%, so there is no national foreign-equity ceiling below full ownership recorded for the activity. Its stated legal source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder weighing a PMA structure, the national conclusion is direct: a foreign-owned medical-evacuation transport business can be registered, and that openness sits alongside every listed enterprise scale.

Bali's result is also favourable, but it should be read with the province's stated screen in view. The Bali moratorium permanently blocks PMA for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI island-wide. This activity is not blocked: at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, and the Bali record marks it OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. In plain terms, a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today; its treatment at the Besar scale sits outside the moratorium's blocked risk bands.
editorial.pullQuote: Medical-evacuation transport is open nationally and is not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Traditional Massage Houses: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This small-scale traditional therapy and massage activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but a PT PMA cannot register it in Bali today.
editorial.body:
A massage house under this activity is a place for alternative therapy and Indonesian traditional massage, designed to provide comfortable, safe and beneficial services. Its scope reaches beyond conventional massage to include healing practitioners, hypnotherapy practitioners, reflexology, shiatsu, tuina qigong and Thai massage. The activity is framed around professional ethics, and may also include food and drink provision as an accompanying element.

The intended operating scale is telling: this activity is open to micro and small businesses. That places the emphasis on a locally grounded, service-led establishment rather than a large-format operation. The scope is broad enough to accommodate several traditional and alternative therapeutic practices under one roof, but it remains defined by the provision of premises and facilities for those services. Professional conduct is not incidental to the description; it is part of the activity’s stated character.

Nationally, the investment position is open, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. On that basis, the national classification does not itself impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership. Bali presents a different and decisive registration outcome. A foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali through a PT PMA today, because the province-wide moratorium blocks every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI and this one is classified Medium-Low risk. The Bali block is provincial and applies to the whole Medium-Low risk tier, rather than being a discretionary judgment about this business.

Bali’s position sits within a permanent, island-wide moratorium that blocks PMA for all low- and medium-low-risk activities. For this activity, however, the immediate result is already clear from the scale structure: Bali is closed to PMA registration. The national openness remains real, but it does not override the local registration barrier. Founders should therefore read the national 100% ceiling as a statement of foreign-ownership allowance, not as confirmation that a PT PMA can be registered for this activity in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness remains real, but it does not override Bali’s local registration barrier.

l4_bali.reason: No foreign-ownership reservation or cap for this activity was located in Perpres 10/2021 as amended by Perpres 49/2021 (Lampiran I, II, III) or in its closed list — so this is not a national 0% finding. OSS currently publishes licensing rows for this code only at Mikro and Kecil scale, while a PT PMA is by law an Usaha Besar that must invest more than IDR 10 billion per KBLI per location (Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 7(1); Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 26(1)–(2)): whether OSS will license this code for a PT PMA must be confirmed in OSS; a scale missing from the licensing rules does not by itself restrict the activity (Permen Investasi/BKPM 5/2025 Pasal 8(6)). The Permenkes 14/2021 standard for this activity has not been read from its annex. In Bali we flag this code as blocked as a precaution, not because a closure naming it was located. The Governor of Bali asked BKPM (letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, 28 Jan 2026) to close OSS to PT PMA in the Rendah and Menengah Rendah risk tiers, which include this code (Menengah Rendah). The provincial government reports that the closure applied from the third week of May 2026 covers 18 listed KBLI, and under the official BPS KBLI 2020→2025 crosswalk this code is not among them. Confirm the current OSS status in Bali before relying on this flag either way.

The care model combines nursing with personal care, delivered by a permanent core team of registered or licensed practising nurses alongside other staff.

The operational substance is clinical as well as custodial. Services can include administering medication, making medical diagnoses and treating wounds. Bali does not impose the province-wide PMA moratorium block on this activity. The Bali record places it in the medium-high or high-risk range and identifies its status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The permanent island-wide rule blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA, but this activity is expressly described as not blocked by that moratorium. Its scope is deliberately broad within that setting. That management model is central to who carries out the activity. The record identifies it as a government-operated service and does not list any business scale as open to registration.
