Its practical character is institutional and continuing: the work encompasses the living environment as well as the support offered within it.

Nationally, the PMA status is **TERTUTUP**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **0%**. In plain terms, foreign ownership is not available for this activity. editorial.headline: Residential Social Care for Older People and Physical Disabilities
editorial.standfirst: A social-welfare institution may provide residential personal care nationally with up to 100% foreign ownership, while Bali requires address-level verification.
editorial.body:
This activity is residential social care delivered by a social-welfare institution for older people or people with physical disabilities who cannot manage their own care and do not wish to live independently. It is not merely a place to stay. The scope describes a managed setting in which personal care is joined by rooms, meals, supervision, day-to-day safeguarding and household-style support. Nursing services may also sometimes be provided to patients in a separate location.

The defining operator is a social-welfare institution: the care is organised through that institutional setting, rather than framed as an informal arrangement between individuals. The intended residents are equally specific. They are older people or people with physical disabilities whose needs make independent self-care impractical, and whose preference is not to live on their own. The record lists no business-scale entry, so it does not identify a particular scale of enterprise as open for this activity.

At the national level, the activity is marked **TERBUKA** for foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of **100%**. In plain terms, the national record permits full foreign ownership. Its cited basis is *Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021*. That national position matters because the activity concerns a form of care where accommodation, daily living support and personal assistance are integral to the service described—not incidental additions.

Bali presents a more location-sensitive picture, but not a blanket bar. The provincial moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for all low and medium-low risk activities across the island. This activity is identified as medium-high or high risk, so it is not blocked by that moratorium. Its Bali status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK**. That is not a substitute for checking the actual site: the record expressly says the position must be verified for the address in question. For a foreign-owned social-welfare institution considering Bali, the honest conclusion is therefore open nationally, not blocked by the provincial moratorium, and still subject to address-level verification in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not block this activity through its PMA moratorium, but the proposed address still needs to be verified.

editorial.headline: Senior Living Is Nationally Open, but Not for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Commercial senior-living accommodation is open to foreign investment nationally, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks its PMA registration today.
editorial.body:
Senior living under this activity means the commercial management of accommodation designed for older residents. It is not simply housing with an older demographic: the accommodation is conceived with supporting facilities, professional caregivers and other professional staff, and with attention to the different activities and limitations an older person may experience. The stated scope also includes senior or elderly tourist accommodation, placing the activity within a broad accommodation-management setting shaped around later-life needs.

The activity is open across the full stated business spectrum: micro, small, medium and large enterprises. That matters because the description is operational rather than merely property-based. Its centre of gravity is the management of a commercially run living environment, supported by people with professional caregiving roles and by facilities calibrated to residents’ needs. Whether the operation is organised at a smaller or larger business scale, the record frames the same essential undertaking: managed accommodation for older people, delivered with professional support.

At the national level, the position is straightforward. The activity is open to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign investment may hold the full permitted ownership interest nationally. The national opening is grounded in the cited Presidential Regulations, and there is no lower national foreign-ownership cap in this record to qualify that 100% ceiling.

Bali changes the practical answer completely. Today, Bali does not permit a foreign investor to register this activity. At the large-business scale, every stated scope carries a Low or Medium-Low OSS risk classification; Bali’s moratorium, effective from May 2026, blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities across the island on a permanent basis. The national permission is real, but it does not override Bali’s island-wide PMA moratorium. For a senior-living project intended for Bali, the decisive fact is therefore the provincial block, not the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: The national permission is real, but it does not override Bali’s island-wide PMA moratorium.

editorial.headline: Residential Care Intermediation: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers paid matchmaking between clients and residential-care providers, online or offline; it is fully open to foreign investment nationally and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Residential-care intermediation is the business of bringing together people seeking residential-care services and the providers able to deliver them. The intermediary is paid a fee or commission, which may come from either the client or the provider. It is a matching and access function, rather than the provision of care itself: the business can earn from commissions and may also draw revenue from sources such as advertising.

The activity is deliberately channel-neutral. It can be operated through a digital platform, but it does not depend on one. Face-to-face introductions, door-to-door activity, telephone and correspondence all fall within the stated scope. That makes this a practical category for businesses whose value lies in organising demand, presenting providers, and facilitating the connection between the two. Intermediation involving medical, dental and other human-health services is outside this activity’s scope.

The registration picture is broad. The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale, and its scope expressly addresses non-exempt electronic-trading organisers and intermediary-facility organisers, whether established within Indonesia’s legal territory or established abroad while conducting electronic-trading activity in Indonesia. It also extends beyond those organisers to other businesses undertaking the activity. Nationally, foreign investment is TERBUKA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. In plain terms, the record sets no foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity at the national level.

Bali does not reverse that national opening. Its status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record explains that, at Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. As a result, the activity is not blocked by the island-wide, permanent Bali moratorium that applies to PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities. A foreign investor can therefore approach registration in Bali on the same essential premise as nationally: the activity is open, with full foreign ownership permitted, and it is not caught by that moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: For this activity, Bali does not reverse the national position: full foreign ownership is permitted and the PMA moratorium does not block registration.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Residential Child Welfare Services: Nationally Open, Bali Site Check Required
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers residential social care and child protection, nationally open to foreign investment but requiring an address-specific check in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity concerns residential social services and care for children delivered by child social-welfare institutions. Its practical setting is continuous support: temporary accommodation and round-the-clock social accompaniment for children needing special protection, where healthcare and education are not the principal services. Orphanages, children’s hostels and temporary shelters sit within that frame, alongside other residential institutions offering protection and family support.

The scope also reaches residential social rehabilitation for people experiencing social dysfunction, as well as work that supports their social reintegration. The defining thread is not merely a building in which people stay, but organised welfare provision with residential care at its centre. It is an activity associated in the record with child social-welfare institutions, and with institutions that organise child welfare. No business scale is listed in the record as open to this activity, so the scale question should not be filled in by assumption.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is clear: the activity is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That makes the national setting unusually direct in the record’s own terms. It does not, however, remove the need to read Bali as a separate operating context. Bali’s status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the activity is not blocked by the province-wide moratorium described in the record.

That distinction matters because Bali’s permanent island-wide rule blocks all low- and medium-low-risk activities from PMA registration. This activity is instead described as medium-high or high risk, placing it outside that stated block. The record nevertheless calls for verification by address. For a founder, the honest conclusion is therefore neither a blanket warning nor an automatic green light: foreign investment is nationally open at 100%, Bali does not block this activity through the stated moratorium, and the proposed address still needs to be checked before treating the provincial position as settled.
editorial.pullQuote: Foreign investment is nationally open at 100%, while Bali requires an address-specific check rather than imposing the stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: Residential Care and Legal Support for Children in the Justice System
editorial.standfirst: This residential social-services activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership and, in Bali, sits outside the PMA moratorium—subject to verifying the specific address.
editorial.body:
KBLI 87992 covers residential social services that combine care, support and legal assistance for children involved with the justice system. Its remit spans three positions a child may occupy: perpetrator, victim or witness. The scope also includes rehabilitation group homes for people with social and personal problems, rehabilitation group homes for people with criminal tendencies, and social-protection homes. It is, in essence, a residential setting in which social care and legal support are part of the same mandate.

Both government and private parties may undertake this activity. The record does not list any business-scale category as open to it, so no scale-based entitlement should be implied. That absence is worth treating with discipline: the category identifies the type of provider and the nature of the service, but it does not supply a scale range to be filled in by assumption. For an operator, the defining features are residential provision, care and assistance, and children who require support in connection with the justice system.

Nationally, the activity is marked TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In practical terms, a foreign investor may hold the full ownership interest allowed by the national record. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is a clear national position: the activity is open to PMA at the recorded foreign-ownership ceiling.

Bali does not reverse that position through its provincial PMA moratorium. The activity is classified as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and described as medium-high/high risk, meaning it is not among the low and medium-low risk activities blocked island-wide and permanently for PMA. Bali has therefore not barred PMA registration for this activity. The remaining local instruction is specific rather than abstract: verify the position for the intended address. The honest reading is that the activity is nationally open and not blocked by Bali's moratorium, while the address remains a necessary point of confirmation.

editorial.headline: Public Social Care Without Accommodation: The 88101 Position

editorial.body:
KBLI 88101 is a public-service activity centred on social assistance for older persons and persons with disabilities, delivered without accommodation. The record places its services at home or elsewhere and identifies the government as the organiser. Its work may include social services, counselling, welfare support, referrals and comparable assistance. In practical terms, the scope runs from visits and day-care to services that help people carry out activities of daily living. It also reaches social rehabilitation, habilitation and vocational work for people with disabilities, while limiting the educational component. Caregiving and home nursing, where it forms part of home-care services, are within the stated scope.

That definition matters because it makes this neither an accommodation activity nor a general-purpose service label. The subject is direct support—care, connection and assistance—aimed at a specifically identified population in a public-service setting. The official description gives no separate business scales open to the activity: the scales field is empty. The only stated organiser is government, so an applicant should read the code as a defined government-organised social-service activity rather than stretch its wording to cover services not listed.

At the national level, the PMA position is clear: it is open, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. That is the national ceiling supplied for this activity, with Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 listed as its PMA source. The point is not to infer further operating requirements from an ownership setting; the slim record supplies none. It does, however, establish the national foreign-investment position plainly.

Bali’s picture is also more permissive than a blanket warning suggests. The record gives the activity the status "OK_or_HIGHER_RISK" and says it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium because it is medium-high/high risk. Registration for PMA is therefore not shown as blocked in Bali. The record still says to verify per address: that is a location-specific check, not a stated new ownership cap or condition. The honest conclusion is narrow but useful: national foreign ownership may reach 100%, and Bali does not show a moratorium block for this activity, provided the address is verified.

editorial.headline: Care Without Residence: The Scope of KBLI 88102
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 88102 is a nonprofit social-care activity for older people and people with disabilities, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium, subject to address verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 88102 concerns social care provided without accommodation for older people and people with disabilities. Its work can take place in a person’s home or another setting, bringing together social services, counselling, welfare support, referrals and related assistance. The scope is practical as well as relational: visits, day-care, help with activities of daily living, social rehabilitation, habilitation and vocational work for people with disabilities all sit within it. The educational component of that vocational work is expressly limited. It also includes care activities and home nursing when delivered as part of home-care services.

The activity is organised by a nonprofit Social Welfare Institution. That institutional character matters because the scope describes a continuing care function rather than a single, isolated service. It reaches into the ordinary routines that can determine whether an older person or a person with a disability can remain supported at home or participate more fully in daily life. The record does not list business-scale categories open to this activity, so it offers no separate scale-based position to add to the definition.

Nationally, the picture is open. With PMA status marked TERBUKA, the foreign-ownership ceiling stands at 100%. In plain terms, the national record allows full foreign ownership rather than imposing a partial foreign-equity cap. That clarity should not be diluted by assumptions about service format: the activity remains defined by nonprofit social-welfare provision for the specified people and by the services set out in its scope.

Bali presents a different, but not prohibitive, reading. The record places the activity at medium-high/high risk and says it is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium. It is therefore not accurate to say that a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today on that moratorium basis. Nor is this an address-free conclusion: the record calls for verification for the proposed address. The honest position is straightforward—national foreign ownership is open up to 100%, and Bali does not presently block this activity under the moratorium, while the specific location still needs to be checked.

editorial.headline: Playgroup Education: Nationally Open, Not Blocked by Bali’s Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers playgroup and preschool education for young children, including formal collaborations between recognised foreign and Indonesian educational institutions.
editorial.body:
Playgroup education is an early-childhood activity for children aged two to six, with particular priority given to ages three and four. Its scope includes playgroups run by government or the community, as well as preschool provision that combines educational and child-welfare programmes from birth to age six, prioritising children aged two to four. The category is therefore not merely a place for supervised activity: it describes a defined early-years educational setting.

The activity can be managed by government or by the community. It is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, giving the category a broad operating range rather than confining it to one size of provider. Its stated scope also includes playgroups created through cooperation with foreign educational institutions. Where that cooperation forms a formal educational pathway, the record describes a playgroup educational unit organised or managed through collaboration between an accredited or recognised foreign educational institution and an Indonesian educational institution.

Nationally, the investment position is clear. The activity is TERBUKA for PMA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign ownership may reach the full permitted ceiling nationally. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That openness sits alongside the activity’s educational character: the record frames the work around early-childhood education, community or government management, and—in the collaboration case—a structured relationship between foreign and Indonesian educational institutions.

Bali requires its own reading, but the outcome here is also direct. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The record identifies its OSS risk at the Besar scale as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, and marks the Bali position as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. Accordingly, a PMA registration for this activity is not barred in Bali by the stated moratorium. The distinction matters: national openness is real, and the Bali rule does not reverse it for this activity on the facts provided.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Child Day-Care Education: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 88907 covers early-childhood education through child day-care services, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 88907 covers early-childhood education for children from birth to six years old, with priority given to those from birth to four. It includes provision organised by government or by the community, and expressly includes child day-care centres as well as centres established in cooperation with foreign educational institutions. The activity is therefore defined by its educational purpose and its focus on the earliest years of a child’s development.

Founders may register at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. That range does not dilute the core remit: the work remains education for the birth-to-six cohort, with the stated priority for children up to age four. A founder should read the scope as one centred on an early-years educational programme delivered through a child day-care setting. The record also recognises that this may be organised publicly or by the community, and that cooperation with a foreign educational institution can form part of the day-care model.

Nationally, the PMA status is open and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain terms, the national position permits the foreign stake in this activity to reach full ownership. That conclusion applies alongside the stated availability across every listed business scale. It is a clear national opening for the defined educational activity: early-childhood education through child day-care provision, rather than a generic label detached from the children, age range and educational purpose set out in the record.

Bali requires an equally direct reading. The provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities across the island on a permanent basis. This entry, however, is not blocked by that rule. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, placing it outside the Low and Medium-Low risk group caught by the moratorium. The practical conclusion is straightforward: a foreign investor can register this child day-care education activity in Bali today. Bali’s result is affirmative because the record places the activity at the relevant higher-risk classification, not because the national foreign-ownership ceiling is being assumed to override the provincial rule.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can register this child day-care education activity in Bali today.

editorial.standfirst: This activity spans literary and technical writing nationwide, yet Bali’s PMA moratorium closes the registration route for a Bali address.
editorial.body:
**Activity 90111 is the professional home of the written work itself.** It covers writing and editing undertaken by individual writers, whether the work is credited to them or prepared for someone else, and whether it is fiction or nonfiction, printed or digital. Short stories and novels sit comfortably within that remit, as do scripts for film, television, radio, computer games and animation. Independent blogging, technical writing, poetry and comparable literary creation are included too. The focus is authorship and editorial craft: creating the words, shaping the text and developing the written work.

That focus matters because it draws a practical boundary around the activity. It is not the production, reproduction or distribution of books and music, nor translation for book editing, nor the work of independent musicians and actors in video or audiovisual content. For founders, the relevant question is therefore whether the business being registered is centred on writing, editing and literary creation. For this activity, every one of the listed business scales remains open: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. It can accommodate a solo author or editor as readily as a larger writing-led operation, provided the registered activity remains within that written-works remit.

Nationally, the PMA position is unequivocally open. The status is **TERBUKA**, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In other words, the national entry does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. But Bali changes the registration reality sharply. A foreigner cannot register this activity as PMA at a Bali address today. The Bali record identifies the Besar scale as low risk, and the provincial PMA moratorium blocks all low- and medium-low-risk activities for a Bali address. The restriction is island-wide and permanent under the stated Bali rule.

This is not a contradiction in the national record; it is a location-specific constraint on PMA registration. The national framework remains open to full foreign ownership, while the Bali position is recorded as **Closed (Bali moratorium)**. For a writing, editing or literary-creation venture, that distinction is the central fact: the activity is nationally open, but a Bali-address PMA registration is blocked by the moratorium. editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali currently blocks its PMA registration under a permanent, island-wide risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
**The work here is the creation of music.** This activity covers making musical compositions, whether the person doing it is a songwriter, composer or music arranger. It also expressly includes composition work done in another person’s name. That detail prevents an overly narrow reading: the defined activity reaches both work carried out under the creator’s own name and work created for another name. Its subject is the act of composing and arranging music, as the scope puts it.

**The registration range is broad in scale, but specific in subject.** It is open at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. The record identifies the people carrying out its core work — songwriters, composers and music arrangers — and makes clear that another person’s name does not take the work outside this activity. The listed scales do not alter that stated centre: from Micro through Large, the activity remains the creation of musical compositions.

**At national level, the foreign-investment position is open.** The recorded PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. The relevant national PMA references are Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. That ceiling is national, while the Bali status is supplied separately in the record. **Independent news journalism begins with the individual reporter.** This activity covers the gathering of news by individuals as information material, followed by self-publication through either print or digital media. The definition is important because it describes a practical editorial act: finding news, shaping it for public information, and publishing it through one’s own channel. It is not framed here as a general media operation, but as independent news work undertaken and published by the person doing it.

**The record identifies individuals as the operative participants.** It does not list any business-scale categories in `scales_open_to`, so no scale classification should be read into the activity from this record. What is clear is the personal character of the work: the journalist gathers the news and publishes it independently. For founders and practitioners, that makes the scope worth reading closely. The activity is defined by both the source of the reporting and the fact of self-publication, whether the final outlet is print or digital.

**Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling.** The record marks its PMA status as open and identifies the applicable source as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain terms, the national record does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That national position should be kept distinct from the local operating picture: national openness establishes the foreign-investment setting, while Bali’s treatment is recorded separately.

**In Bali, this activity is not marked as blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium.** Its Bali status is recorded as `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`, with a medium-high/high-risk designation and an instruction to verify the position for the specific address. The stated reason is that it is not blocked by the moratorium. That matters because Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities; this activity is not placed in that blocked category. editorial.headline: Visual Art Creation, and Bali’s PMA Stop
editorial.standfirst: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this visual-art activity is nevertheless blocked from PMA registration across Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity concerns the creation and production of visual artworks through varied media and methods, whether the resulting work is tangible or intangible. Its natural inhabitants are independent makers: sculptors, painters, cartoonists, calligraphers, carvers, sketch artists and craft artists. It also expressly reaches digital visual art and artworks made with light installations. A studio practice, a solo artist’s output or a production-led art business can all fit the description when the central act is making the visual work. The unifying fact is not the medium but authorship and production of the artwork itself.

The boundary is deliberately narrow. The record keeps this category with original visual-art creation rather than the broader orbit of creative, presentation, commercial, technical, conservation or event activity that may surround a work of art. That distinction matters for registration. A business does not enter this activity merely because it works near the arts; its activity must be the creation and production of the artwork. In that sense the code gives independent artists and art-making enterprises a common, precise home, without stretching the definition into a catch-all label for culture.

All four stated business scales—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—are open to it. Nationally, its PMA status is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. For a foreign investor, that is an unequivocal national position: full foreign ownership is permitted within this activity’s national classification. It is an important starting point for an art practice or company, but it is not the end of the location analysis. The Bali position must be read separately, on its own stated terms.

Bali changes the result decisively. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. At the Besar scale, the record assigns every scope an OSS risk of Low or Medium-Low; those risk levels place it within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration. The Bali record marks the activity as blocked by risk class and attributes the block to the moratorium in force since May 2026. National openness has not disappeared, but it does not overrule the Bali restriction: in Bali, the 100% national ceiling cannot be used to secure a PMA registration for this activity.

editorial.headline: When Creative Work Is Nationally Open but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity embraces conceptual art, choreography and fashion styling, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium makes PMA registration unavailable there.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, this is not a Bali registration today. Nationally, however, the activity is open to PMA with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100 per cent. That creates a clear distinction that matters before the creative description is even considered: the national position permits full foreign ownership, while Bali’s province-wide rule blocks PMA registration for this activity. The contrast is not a matter of interpretation or a small procedural hurdle; it determines whether the activity can be registered in Bali by a foreign-owned business now.

At its centre, the activity is about making art: creating conceptual works, developing choreography and working as a fashion stylist, alongside other art-creation work within the stated scope. It is framed for performing-arts creative practitioners, artists and other creative workers whose contribution is the making of the work itself. The boundary is important. The stated scope keeps restoration and conservation work outside it, including furniture restoration other than museum restoration, stained-glass restoration, renovation or restoration of buildings and historic sites, museum operation, and restoration of artworks, textiles, embroidery, decorated interiors, furnace tiles and decorative painting. The description focuses attention on original creative production rather than those listed restoration or institutional activities.

That creative orientation does not confine the activity to one company size. The stated scale range runs from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah to Besar. Its availability is therefore expressed across all four stated scales, rather than being limited in the record to a single size band. The category’s own language brings together performing-arts creative practitioners with other art and creative workers, while its named examples give it a practical centre of gravity: concept-led art, choreography and fashion styling. These are the recorded expressions of the activity’s creative remit.

In Bali, the answer changes completely. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns every scope in this activity a Low or Medium-Low risk classification. Bali’s moratorium, in force from the thirteenth of May 2026, blocks PMA registration for all KBLI in those two risk bands, island-wide and permanently. The record therefore marks this activity as blocked in Bali on risk-class grounds. A national ceiling of 100 per cent remains the national position, but it does not override the Bali moratorium: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Performance Arts: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Performance arts are nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
**A foreign investor cannot register this performance-arts activity as PMA in Bali today.** That is the practical conclusion, even though the activity is nationally open and permits up to 100% foreign ownership. In Bali, the OSS risk assessment at the Besar scale is Low or Medium-Low across every scope in this activity. That brings it within the island-wide, permanent Bali moratorium barring PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities, recorded here as taking effect on May thirteen, twenty twenty-six.

The activity itself is broad, but coherent: it is the presentation of artistic and stage entertainment by individuals or groups. It encompasses drama and theatre, music performances and concerts, opera, pantomime, dance, and regional art performances including wayang orang and lenong. It also covers groups such as circuses, orchestras and bands; individual performers including actors, stand-up comedians, dancers, singers, musicians, backing singers and conductors; and wayang performances led by a dalang. Monologues, dramatic readings and poetry set to music sit within the same field.

The scope also recognises the contemporary working lives of performance practitioners. Photo models, influencers, content creators and YouTubers appearing in vlogs or other content are included, as are independent musicians and actors visible across video and audiovisual content. A group may operate an arts facility for its own artistic group. Registration is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so the national classification accommodates both individual creative practice and larger organised performance operations.

That national openness should not be mistaken for Bali availability. A 100% foreign-ownership ceiling nationally does not displace the Bali restriction: the decisive local fact is the Low or Medium-Low OSS risk profile at the Besar scale, and the moratorium applies island-wide and permanently. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, the current answer is therefore not conditional or procedural; this activity is blocked.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not displace Bali’s permanent bar on PMA registration for this activity.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Arts-Venue Activity, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Operating cultural centres, auditoriums and live-music venues is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity through PMA today, even though nationally it is open to 100% foreign ownership. The activity concerns the operation of places in which art is made, shown and heard: concert and theatre auditoriums, cultural centres and cultural parks, facilities that support the creation of visual art, and other arts facilities. It also covers the operation of live-music venues, music clubs and comparable facilities where artists perform. The focus is operational—the running of the venue or facility that accommodates artistic creation or live performance.

The national registration picture is broad in scale. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses, covering the full range of enterprise categories stated in the record. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. For an investor considering the operating side of a cultural centre, auditorium or live-performance location, those are clear national settings. Yet the national ownership ceiling answers only the position at national level; it does not determine whether a PMA registration can be made in a particular region.

In Bali, the position is direct. The Bali designation is Blocked (risk class), and the record expressly identifies the activity as blocked. Its stated basis is the OSS risk profile at the Besar scale, where every scope is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah. Bali’s stated rule is island-wide and permanent: it blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The recorded moratorium was issued on the thirteenth of May, twenty twenty-six, under the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.

That distinction is the essential planning fact. A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling means full foreign ownership is available nationally for this activity, but it is not a Bali-side entitlement. Here, the Bali result is a registration block under a risk-based moratorium. The practical reading is therefore clear: this is a nationally open activity that may operate across the listed scales, while a PMA route in Bali is closed.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling is not a Bali-side entitlement when PMA registration is blocked.

editorial.headline: Producing the Stage: Indonesia’s Live Arts and Culture Activity
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the organisation and production of live arts and cultural events, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 90391 is the operational home for bringing arts and culture events into being. It covers the management and staging of cultural and entertainment performances in the arts, spanning performing and visual arts as well as film, musical, music and dance festivals. Its scope also reaches the practical machinery behind a live event: technical planning; the provision, arrangement and operation of audiovisual equipment; and special effects used in a live arts setting. Producers and live-event entrepreneurs fall within the activity, whether they operate with facilities of their own or without them.

This is therefore not merely a label for a performance itself. It is for the party that assembles, administers and delivers the event around it: the producer shaping a live programme, the organiser coordinating its presentation, or the operator responsible for its audiovisual and special-effects execution. The record does not specify any scale categories open to this activity. Its emphasis is instead on the character of the work—organising, producing and operating live arts and cultural events.

Nationally, the position is direct: the activity is open to PMA registration, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That ceiling is the national one, drawn from the stated PMA source. For a foreign-owned business, the important distinction is that full foreign ownership is permitted for this activity at the national level; the record does not attach a lower foreign-ownership cap.

Bali requires a more exact reading, but it is not a prohibition. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This activity is recorded as Medium-High or High risk, so it is not blocked by that moratorium. Its Bali status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with one practical instruction retained from the record: verify the position for the specific address. The honest conclusion is not that Bali closes this activity to foreign investment, but that it remains outside the stated island-wide moratorium while address-specific verification still matters.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not close this activity to foreign investment; it sits outside the stated island-wide moratorium, subject to address-specific verification.

editorial.headline: The Unseen Work Behind a Live Performance
editorial.standfirst: This activity gathers the producing, technical, artistic and critical work that makes live arts happen—and reveals a sharp divide between national openness and Bali registration.
editorial.body:
A live performance is never only the person in the spotlight. This activity covers the supporting work involved in producing and staging live arts and stage entertainment: drama and theatre, music performances and concerts, opera, plays, pantomime, dance, regional arts performances, bands and orchestras. It describes the operational and creative framework that lets a performance move from an idea to a functioning event.

Its cast of professionals is broad. Producers, stage managers and arts managers sit alongside stage-set designers, scenographers and stage visual artists; scene-shifters, lighting engineers and sound-system specialists carry the practical work of presentation. The scope also includes directors, dramaturgs, artistic directors, film promoters, programme makers and supervisors, as well as curators and literary or visual-art critics. It is therefore an activity for those whose work shapes, organises, presents, interprets or supports an artistic programme, rather than only those appearing before an audience.

The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. At the national level, PMA is classified as TERBUKA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. In plain terms, the national record does not set the foreign stake below full ownership for this activity. That is an important part of the picture, but it is not the whole of it: national openness does not itself determine whether a PMA registration can proceed in Bali.

In Bali, the position is decisive: a PMA investor cannot register this activity there today. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registrations for all Low and Medium-Low-risk KBLI. The result is a Bali-specific registration block, not a reduction of the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. For founders, the distinction matters precisely because both statements are true at once: the activity is nationally open to PMA, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and a Bali PMA registration block can both be true for the same activity.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Government Libraries: A Public-Service Activity, Not a PMA Entry Point
editorial.standfirst: This code covers the stewardship of government libraries, from cataloguing collections to retrieving information, but it is closed to foreign investment nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
Government library activity is the public work of managing, maintaining, preserving and appraising libraries run by national, regional or local government institutions. It applies where those institutions sit outside an educational body or another cultural institution. The scope is broad in the practical sense: it includes documentation and information services across government libraries, including digital libraries, reading rooms, listening rooms and viewing rooms. It also reaches the organisation and cataloguing of collections, as well as the lending and storage of books, maps, periodicals, films, recordings, tapes and artworks.

At its centre, this is an information-access function. Government institutions operating such libraries may organise specialised or general collections and retrieve documents to meet information needs. The activity therefore describes an institutional public service rather than a private commercial format: a library’s collection is kept intelligible, preserved and available through the systems that make its materials findable and usable. The slim record identifies government institutions at national, regional and local level as the relevant operators, and lists no business scales as open to this activity.

For foreign investors, the national position is decisive: the activity is closed to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 0%. Bali records the activity as closed and blocked for PMA registration, so a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali entry characterises the matter as medium-high/high risk, states that it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium, and says the position should be verified for the specific address. That address-level verification does not alter the recorded conclusion: Bali’s status for PMA registration is closed.
editorial.pullQuote: A government library may be a vital public information service, but it is not an entry point for foreign investment.

editorial.headline: Private Libraries: Nationally Open, but Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Private library work can be wholly foreign-owned nationally, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium prevents registration there today.
editorial.body:
Private Library Activities is a private-sector library practice in the full sense, not merely a room of books. It covers the management, maintenance, preservation and appraisal of libraries operated by individuals, organisations, companies, foundations and other private bodies, provided they are not under an educational institution or another cultural institution. The scope includes private libraries of many kinds—including digital libraries—as well as reading, listening and viewing rooms. Its work also reaches documentation and information services: organising collections, cataloguing them, and retrieving documents to answer information needs.

The collection itself may be broad. Books, maps, periodicals, films, recordings, tapes, works of art and other materials can be stored or lent through a private library. Private archive management is included too. The activity is therefore defined by stewardship as much as access: maintaining a collection, giving it order and description, keeping it available, and making information retrievable. An individual, organisation, company, foundation or another private institution can carry out this work within those boundaries.

For registration, the activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Nationally, its PMA status is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That means a foreign investor may hold the activity entirely at the national level. It is a clear national position, but it should not be mistaken for a Bali registration outcome.

In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity under PMA today. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope recorded here, placing it within Bali’s moratorium in May 2026. The provincial rule blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide and permanently. This is not a lower Bali foreign-ownership ceiling: despite the national 100% position, PMA registration for this activity is blocked in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not override Bali’s permanent block on PMA registration for this activity.

editorial.headline: Government Archiving Is a Public Institutional Function
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers government institutions that build, preserve, classify and communicate physical and digital archives—and it is closed to foreign investment nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
Government archiving is the public work of making a record durable, intelligible and available. This activity covers archiving services carried out by government institutions to build, store and classify collections of physical or digital archives, then communicate them to the general public or to defined user groups. Its centre of gravity is not merely storage: it is the ordered stewardship of documents and collections so they can be found, understood and used.

The scope is broad within that public institutional setting. It includes public archive services for general users and particular communities such as students, scientists, staff and members, as well as the operation of government archives. It reaches from acquiring or collecting archives through identifying, inventorying, describing and classifying them. It also includes safeguarding collections: monitoring sanitary and climate conditions, maintaining security and safety, and undertaking rehabilitation. Archives may be communicated on site or remotely, alongside related cultural and educational activities that bring their value to wider attention. The record expressly includes the archiving of documents in paper and electronic form.

The registration picture is direct. The activity is described as one performed by government institutions, and the record identifies no business scale as open to it. Nationally, it is **TERTUTUP** for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 0%. There is therefore no foreign-investment route to register this activity under the national position recorded here. That conclusion follows from the stated PMA status and ceiling, rather than from an assumed operational requirement or threshold.

Bali is also recorded as **TERTUTUP**, so a foreigner cannot register this activity there today. The Bali position is not attributed to the province-wide PMA moratorium for low- and medium-low-risk activities: the record places this activity at medium-high or high risk and says it is not blocked by that moratorium. Its Bali treatment must instead be verified for the particular address. That address-specific verification does not soften the recorded Bali status; it explains why the moratorium itself is not the basis for the closure.
editorial.pullQuote: Government archiving is the public work of making a record durable, intelligible and available.

editorial.headline: Private Archiving: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Private archiving is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but a foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today under the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register private archiving in Bali today. That is the practical starting point, even though the activity is nationally open to foreign ownership of up to 100%. In Bali, every scope at the large-business scale is classified as Low or Medium-Low risk, placing the activity within the province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for those risk classes. The distinction matters: national openness does not overcome the Bali-specific block.

This is a broad information-stewardship activity rather than a narrow document-storage service. It covers archival services undertaken by non-government individuals, organisations, companies, foundations and other private institutions to build, store and classify physical or digital archive collections, then make them accessible to the public or defined groups of users. The work may serve the general public or specific users such as students, researchers, staff or members, and includes the operation of archives themselves.

Its scope reaches across the life of an archive. That includes acquiring or collecting material; identifying, inventorying, describing and classifying it; and maintaining collections through sanitation and climate-condition monitoring, security and safety measures, and rehabilitation. It also includes communicating archives on site or remotely, alongside cultural and educational activities connected to their wider use and appreciation. Archiving paper or electronic documents sits within the same activity, as do privately managed archives and private library activities.

The code is open across Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales, so its national frame accommodates a wide range of private operators. For PMA, however, Bali is not a matter of selecting a smaller scale or relying on the national ownership ceiling: the record identifies Low and Medium-Low risk across every scope at the Large scale and states that the Bali moratorium blocks all such KBLI for PMA, permanently and island-wide. Founders should therefore read the national position as an ownership rule, and the Bali position as a current registration barrier for foreign investment.

editorial.headline: Government-Managed Museums, Closed to Foreign Ownership
editorial.standfirst: Museum management under public stewardship has an educational and preservation remit—and no foreign ownership pathway nationally or in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity concerns the government management of museums as places and facilities: caring for and presenting cultural heritage, art objects, collections and replicas. Its programme includes exhibitions and is intended to serve education, recreation and research, while supporting tourism development. The operative balance matters. The record describes a profit-seeking purpose, but places that purpose within government management and a duty to respect preservation values. This is therefore an activity shaped as much by stewardship of the collection as by the public-facing museum experience.

That definition also answers who is positioned to operate it. The title and scope locate management with government, rather than presenting the activity as a general private museum category. The record lists no business scale as open to it. For a founder deciding whether an operating plan belongs here, the decisive questions are practical and curatorial at once: are the premises and facilities being managed as a museum, and do exhibitions of heritage, art, collections or replicas perform the stated educational, recreational and research roles while preserving their values? Tourism support is part of the stated purpose, but not a substitute for the museum function itself.

The national foreign-investment position is unequivocal: it is closed, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 0%. That is not a situation in which a foreign shareholder may participate up to a reduced cap; it leaves no foreign ownership available under this activity. The result deserves to be read plainly. A foreign investor cannot use it as the basis for a PMA registration nationally. The government-managed character in the scope and the closed national PMA status point in the same direction, without any need to infer additional permits or compliance conditions.

For Bali, the outcome is equally direct: the record marks PMA registration as closed and blocked, so a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The stated reason says the activity is medium-high/high risk and is not blocked by Bali's permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium, whose stated reach is Low and Medium-Low risk activities; it nevertheless calls for verification by address. That distinction is useful rather than reassuring: the moratorium is not the basis stated for the block, and the closed Bali result remains the one a prospective applicant must take seriously. Address verification is explicitly required by the record, but it does not alter the national 0% foreign-ownership ceiling.

editorial.headline: Private Museums: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Private museum operations are open to 100% foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks their registration at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
**A foreign investor cannot register a privately managed museum at a Bali address today.** KBLI 91212 is the activity of operating museums managed by private parties. In clear English, it covers the running of a privately managed museum: the stated scope identifies both museum activities and private management. The category centres the operating museum and its private management, which is the defined activity in the record. A museum can be small or large, but its scale does not change that defined subject.

The record makes this activity available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That range answers the question of who can register by size: a private museum operator may sit at any of those listed scales. At the national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA. The national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, so the national position permits full foreign ownership of the activity within the stated code. Its national source is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

The Bali result is unambiguous. Despite the national TERBUKA status, the record states that the Besar scale is classified as Rendah, or Low. Bali’s provincial moratorium blocks PMA for every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI at a Bali address; the record describes this rule as island-wide and permanent. This code is therefore blocked for PMA registration in Bali, even though the national entry is open and allows 100% foreign ownership.

The two positions must be held together, not averaged into a softer conclusion. A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not produce a Bali registration route where the Bali moratorium has blocked PMA. Nor does the national TERBUKA status displace the Bali address result. Outside Bali, the national record is open across the listed scales; for a Bali address, the operative fact in this record is the PMA block. The Bali source named is the Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national ceiling does not create a Bali PMA registration route where the moratorium blocks it.

editorial.headline: Public Stewardship of Indonesia’s Historic Sites and Monuments
editorial.standfirst: This government-led activity safeguards historic places, monuments and visitor-accessible archaeological sites of cultural, scientific and religious significance.
editorial.body:
This activity is the public stewardship of historic places and monuments: the operation and preservation of heritage created through human intervention in the environment, whether landscapes, parks, buildings or sites. Its remit embraces built cultural heritage and natural heritage whose importance lies in history, science and culture, as well as places valued for education and religion. Temples, saints’ tombs and historic mosques illustrate the kind of places contemplated by the record, but the underlying purpose is broader: keeping significant heritage places operational, protected and meaningful to the public.

The work is explicitly governmental. It includes operating and conserving historic sites and buildings, alongside archaeological sites open to visitors. That framing matters. This is not merely the maintenance of an old structure or the presentation of an attraction; it is public responsibility for places whose significance is judged across historical, scientific, educational, religious and cultural dimensions. The slim record lists no business-scale categories open to registration, reinforcing the activity’s institutional character.

Nationally, the position for foreign investment is closed. The foreign-ownership ceiling is zero, so a foreign investor cannot hold a stake in an entity registered for this activity under the national PMA position recorded here. The cited basis is Presidential Regulation 10/2021 and 49/2021. For a founder assessing the code, that is the decisive national answer: the activity is reserved from PMA participation, not simply subject to a reduced foreign share.

Bali reaches the same practical conclusion for PMA registration: the activity is marked closed and blocked today. The Bali record also makes an important distinction about why. Its medium-high or high-risk treatment means it is not blocked by Bali’s island-wide moratorium, which applies to low and medium-low risk KBLI activities; the applicable classification should nevertheless be verified for the specific address. In other words, the Bali outcome is closed, but it should not be casually attributed to the moratorium. The clean conclusion is that foreign investors cannot register this activity in Bali today, while government stewardship remains at the centre of what the code describes.

editorial.standfirst: Private stewardship of heritage places is open across all business scales nationally, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium prevents foreign-owned registration at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
At its heart, this is a stewardship activity. It covers private operation and preservation of places whose significance lies in history, science, education, religion, or culture: human-shaped landscapes and gardens, buildings, and heritage sites, whether built cultural heritage or natural heritage. Temples, saints’ tombs, and historic mosques are named examples, but the principle is broader: keeping a meaningful place operating and cared for. It also embraces historic sites and buildings, and archaeological sites that visitors can enter. The emphasis is the continuing life and preservation of the site, not simply the existence of an old structure.

That distinction matters in practice. The code is for private operators entrusted with a site’s ongoing operation and preservation. It does not extend to the construction-side work of renovating or restoring historical places, to architectural rehabilitation or restoration work, to archaeological excavation, or to the restoration and preventive conservation of museum artworks and collections performed outside a unit of this type. In other words, it describes the private steward of a heritage place and of visitor access to an archaeological site; it is not a catch-all label for every specialist intervention that may occur around heritage.

The national investment position is unambiguous: the activity is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. Registration is stated to be available for Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar enterprises, so the classification is not reserved for a particular business scale. Those national facts make this a clear route for a private heritage operator outside the Bali-specific constraint. They do not, however, translate automatically into a Bali registration for a foreign-owned company.

On a Bali address, the position is closed today for PMA registration. The record identifies the Besar scale as Menengah Rendah and says that this triggers Bali’s PMA moratorium, which blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide on a permanent basis. The cited Governor’s letter dates from May 2026. The result must be stated plainly: a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today, notwithstanding the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. editorial.headline: Keeping Cultural Heritage Intact, in Physical and Digital Form
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the careful preservation, restoration and digital continuity of cultural heritage—and remains open to full foreign ownership nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is about preserving cultural heritage before loss becomes irreversible. It includes preventive conservation, curative conservation and restoration, together with consultancy that considers both the tangible and intangible significance of heritage and its sustainability. The scope is deliberately broad across materials and surfaces: movable and immovable archaeological assets, leather, archival documents, graphic and printed documents, wooden panels, art objects, ceramic tiles, goldsmith work, canvas and mural paintings, photography, sculpture, textiles and embroidery, stained glass, and scientific and industrial objects all sit within it.

It also recognises that preservation now has a digital dimension. Digitising movable and immovable heritage, gathering data, managing collections, creating virtual replicas and using other digital means to secure heritage preservation are all part of the activity. A business registering here is therefore framed around the stewardship of cultural material and its continuity, whether the work concerns a physical object, a collection, or its durable digital record. The slim record does not state any enterprise-scale categories open to this activity, so it provides no basis for assigning it to a particular business scale.

At the national level, the position is straightforward: foreign investment is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That means the national record does not impose a reduced foreign share for this activity. The practical significance is clear: an investor may structure a PMA registration around cultural-heritage conservation, restoration and its supporting digital work without a national foreign-equity cap below full ownership.

Bali requires its own reading, but the current record is not a prohibition. Its status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with the activity described as medium-high or high risk and therefore not blocked by the provincial moratorium; the address must still be verified. The Bali moratorium permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities across the island, under the cited Governor’s letter. This activity is recorded outside that blocked risk band, so a foreign investor can register it in Bali today, subject to address-specific verification rather than an island-wide moratorium bar.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not block this activity under its PMA moratorium, but the business address still needs verification.

editorial.headline: A Living Institution for Conservation, Learning and Recreation
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the operators of botanical gardens, zoos and aquariums—open to full foreign ownership nationally and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This is an operational activity: it covers the day-to-day running of botanical gardens and zoos, including those where children interact directly with animals, together with aquariums. Its centre of gravity reaches further into conservation: ex situ areas for breeding or rescuing plants and animals outside their natural habitat, while preserving the integrity of their species. These institutions are used for education, display, research, scientific development and recreation. The scope embraces wildlife parks and specialised animal parks, specialist animal training centres, botanical gardens, herbaria, zoological museums and specialist plant gardens. It is the operation of a public-interest conservation institution, not simply an attraction.

The code is open to operators at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. It therefore accommodates institutions across all four stated business scales. The registrant is the operator: the party running a garden, zoo, aquarium, animal park, herbarium or other named conservation institution. Across those settings, the common thread is a managed place where plants or animals are conserved, displayed and used for learning, research and recreation.

Nationally, the investment position is direct. The record classifies the activity as TERBUKA, with PMA maximum foreign ownership of 100%. Foreign capital may therefore own the activity in full at the national level. This is the ceiling stated by the record, supported by Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In this activity’s own terms, both the operational scope and national ownership position are explicit.

The Bali picture is also clear, but it must be read through the provincial moratorium. Bali permanently blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI across the island. This activity is nevertheless recorded as not blocked. The stated reason is that, at Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For PMA registration, this activity remains open in Bali and is not a moratorium exclusion. That conclusion follows precisely from the Bali record supplied.
editorial.pullQuote: For PMA registration, this activity remains open in Bali and is not a moratorium exclusion.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.
