editorial.headline: Wildlife Sanctuaries: Conservation Management with a Clear PMA Route
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the stewardship of wildlife sanctuaries where species, habitats and ecosystems are protected and allowed to develop naturally.
editorial.body:
A wildlife sanctuary is not simply a place where animals are present. This activity concerns managing a nature-reserve area distinguished by the diversity or uniqueness of its animal life, while supporting the habitat on which that life depends. Its setting may also be defined by distinctive plants, fauna and ecosystems, or by a particular protected ecosystem whose development proceeds naturally. The scope is therefore conservation management in its fullest sense: protecting the character of the area while maintaining the conditions that sustain it.

The record frames the activity around the management of the sanctuary itself, rather than around a separate commercial service or a particular type of operator. It does not specify any business-scale tier open to the activity. That absence matters: the record supports a reading of the conservation function and its ownership position, but it does not assign the activity to a listed scale category.

At the national level, the PMA position is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, foreign ownership may reach the full shareholding limit nationally for this activity. That is the starting point, but it is not a substitute for reading the Bali position on its own terms. Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium applies island-wide to all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This activity is identified in Bali as Medium-High or High risk, so it is not blocked by that moratorium.

That makes the Bali conclusion more direct than a blanket warning, but not casual. The record calls for verification by address. A foreign investor considering a wildlife-sanctuary activity in Bali therefore has an open national PMA route and no moratorium block on the stated risk basis, while the proposed location still requires address-specific confirmation. The governing distinction is not whether conservation activity sounds sensitive in the abstract, but the status and risk treatment recorded for this particular activity.

editorial.standfirst: National-park management with nature-tourism facilities in utilization zones is nationally foreign-open to 100%; in Bali it is not blocked by the PMA moratorium, with address verification specified.
editorial.body:
National-park management is a rare activity where conservation stewardship and visitor infrastructure meet. The classification covers managing nature-conservation areas with original ecosystems, organized through zoning, so that nature-tourism facilities can be provided in the designated utilization zone. Its stated purpose is to increase the use of natural phenomena, uniqueness and natural beauty. The examples cited include Gunung Gede Pangrango, Gunung Leuser, Kelimutu, Komodo, Gunung Palung and Bromo Tengger Semeru. The common thread is clear: this is management of a conservation landscape, with tourism facilities situated in its utilization zone—not an undifferentiated tourism proposition.

The national foreign-investment position is equally clear. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. For a foreign investor, the national record therefore permits full foreign ownership of a company registered for this activity; there is no lower national foreign cap to read into it. The entry is also precise about what it does not classify. Its scales_open_to field lists no business-scale categories. The record makes no stated distinction among scales, so it should not be stretched into a scale-based entitlement or exclusion that is not actually provided.

Bali presents a more nuanced picture, but not a closed one. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK; the record places the activity in the medium-high or high-risk range and states that it is not blocked by the provincial PMA moratorium. That moratorium applies island-wide and permanently to Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA, a category this record does not assign here. The local instruction is narrower and more practical: verify the position for the particular address.

National openness is real, Bali’s non-blocking status is real, and location verification is the final fact the record insists upon. The Bali entry does not state a different foreign-ownership ceiling, a partnership condition or an additional approval requirement. The clean reading for a founder is therefore straightforward: the activity may be fully foreign owned at the national ceiling, is not barred in Bali by the stated moratorium, and still calls for address-specific verification.

editorial.headline: Protected Forests: A Public Stewardship Activity
editorial.standfirst: Government-managed protected forest areas are nationally open to foreign investment up to 100%, and Bali does not block their PMA registration under its risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
Protected Forests describes the government’s management and use of forest areas whose function is to safeguard ecosystems, water systems, soil fertility and protection against erosion. This is not a broad description of woodland in general, but of a forest area defined by its protective role. The record points to Bukit Daun Protected Forest in Bengkulu as an example of that function in practice: stewardship is inseparable from maintaining the ecological and hydrological services the forest provides.

The government is expressly named as the actor carrying out the management and use of these protected forest areas. Nationally, the PMA position is **open**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. That is the national investment position recorded for the activity. The supplied record does not list any business-scale categories under `scales_open_to`, so it provides no basis for attaching a scale-specific eligibility claim to this activity.

In Bali, the position is also clear, though it remains address-specific. The activity is not marked as blocked for PMA registration. Its Bali status is recorded as **OK or higher risk**, with the accompanying assessment placing it at medium-high or high risk and stating that it is not blocked by the moratorium; verification is required for the particular address. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium applies to low and medium-low risk activities. On the record supplied here, this protected-forest activity sits outside that moratorium treatment.

The honest reading is therefore two-layered but not conflicted: national policy records the activity as open to foreign ownership up to the full 100% ceiling, while Bali does not impose a moratorium block on it at the stated risk level. That does not remove the need to verify the address in Bali; it is the specific qualification given by the record. The national PMA basis cited for the activity is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021, while the Bali position is tied to the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, the activity is not barred by the PMA moratorium, but its medium-high or high-risk treatment must be verified for the particular address.

editorial.headline: Nature Tourism in Conserved Landscapes
editorial.standfirst: A conservation-area tourism activity that is nationally open to full foreign ownership, with its Bali position blocked pending case-by-case verification rather than settled either way.
editorial.body:
KBLI 91424 concerns the management of nature-conservation areas for tourism and nature-based recreation. Its scope includes providing facilities within utilisation blocks and operating nature-tourism services in a protected setting. The emphasis is therefore twofold: maintaining the setting in which conservation tourism takes place, and making the facilities and visitor services available for tourism and recreation. The record illustrates this kind of activity through named nature tourism parks in several Indonesian regions.

This code's own scale categorisation is not established in our sources: the catalogue carries no confirmed licensing rows for it, so no scale-based requirement can be stated here. The obstacle we located is not an ownership rule and a PT PMA can satisfy it: UU 5/1990 Pasal 34, as replaced by UU 32/2024, makes managing a nature tourism park a State function, with private parties entering by permit or concession over the utilisation zone — and PP 36/2010 Pasal 8(3) names badan usaha among those who may hold one. That local structural position does not by itself decide the outcome for a foreign-investment company: whether a PT PMA can register this activity in Bali is a separate question this record cannot settle, because the catalogue holds no licensing rows for this code at all.

Nationally, the position is clear. The activity is marked TERBUKA for PMA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In other words, the national record does not impose a foreign stake below full ownership for this activity. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For an investor considering the activity at the national level, that is the relevant starting point: it is open to PMA and can accommodate full foreign ownership.

Bali produces a different practical outcome. This record cannot say which way that outcome goes — not because Bali sets a separate foreign-ownership percentage, but because the evidence needed to say either way is not something we have on file. What is missing is our own evidence: we hold no verified licensing rows for the code, so its Bali risk tier is unknown and the position cannot be stated. It is treated as blocked until verified case by case — unproven rather than closed, and what a private party would actually hold is a permit or concession over the utilisation zone. The record also states that Bali permanently blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island under the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. For this activity, national openness does not settle the Bali question — that stays blocked pending case-by-case verification, not resolved either way.

editorial.standfirst: This activity supports nature-tourism facilities within forest parks, open nationally to full foreign ownership but unavailable for PMA registration at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this Taman Hutan Raya activity as a PMA business at a Bali address today. That is the practical starting point, despite a nationally open position and a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The distinction matters because the activity is not a generic tourism proposition: it concerns nature-conservation areas maintained for collections of plants and/or animals—natural or cultivated, native or non-native—and the provision of nature-tourism facilities within their designated utilisation blocks.

In plain terms, the activity sits where conservation stewardship meets visitor infrastructure. A forest park may hold botanical and wildlife collections while providing the facilities through which visitors experience the area as nature tourism. The scope expressly includes such facilities in utilisation blocks, and identifies Tahura Ngurah Rai in Bali among the examples. Registration is open across the full business-scale range: micro, small, medium, and large. That breadth speaks to who may participate nationally; it does not remove the Bali-specific PMA restriction.

Nationally, the activity is classified as open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. For a PMA structure outside the Bali restriction, that is a clear national ceiling rather than a partial foreign-share allowance. In Bali, however, the large-scale classification is recorded as low risk. The province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities for a Bali address. The result is categorical: the national opening does not translate into an available PMA registration route in Bali for this activity.

Founders should therefore read the activity in two layers. Its national treatment permits complete foreign ownership, and its scope accommodates businesses operating at every listed scale. Yet a Bali address changes the answer decisively: PMA registration is blocked under the provincial moratorium. The relevant commercial question is not whether the activity is nationally foreign-open, but whether the proposed registration address is in Bali. For this activity, the national rule and the Bali outcome are both true—and they lead to different registration realities.

editorial.headline: A Protected Sea, Open to PMA Nationally and in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This marine-park activity joins recreation with habitat preservation and sustainable ecosystems—and is open to full foreign ownership nationally, without Bali’s PMA moratorium blocking it.
editorial.body:
Marine park activity begins with a protected stretch of sea: a place that may be used for recreation, or reserved solely to conserve a particular habitat and sustain the ecosystem on which organisms there depend. The scope is deliberately broader than a single visitor experience or a single conservation purpose. It describes a protected marine area whose public and ecological roles may coexist, or whose preservation role may stand on its own. The reference points named in the record—Pahawang Marine Park in Lampung, Raja Ampat Marine Park in West Papua, and Gili Matra Marine Park in NTB—make the setting concrete without narrowing the activity to any one of them.

Nationally, the activity is open to PMA registration. Foreign ownership may reach 100%, under the source cited as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This is a clear national ownership position: there is no lower foreign-ownership ceiling in the record for this activity. Nor does the record’s list of open business scales identify a particular scale. That absence should be kept intact; the record establishes a national PMA opening, but does not supply a scale-based distinction for registration.

Bali changes neither the national ceiling nor the nature of the activity. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide. This activity is marked OK_or_HIGHER_RISK in Bali and described as medium-high/high risk, so it is not blocked by that moratorium. The honest local conclusion is straightforward: a foreigner can register this activity in Bali today, not merely elsewhere in Indonesia. The record nevertheless calls for verification at the address in question.

The resulting picture is precise. A marine park is not defined only by leisure or only by preservation; it can serve a protected area’s recreational use, habitat conservation, and sustainable ecosystem aim. Full foreign ownership is available nationally. In Bali, the stated moratorium does not close the activity because its recorded risk placement sits outside the two blocked bands. Address-level verification remains the local point carried by the record.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, the stated moratorium does not close the activity because its recorded risk placement sits outside the two blocked bands.

editorial.headline: Conservation-area enterprise, read through the practical work it permits
editorial.standfirst: A conservation-area activity spanning water-based nature tourism, aquaculture infrastructure and other permanent operations, open at every business scale and to full foreign ownership nationally.
editorial.body:
KBLI 91429 concerns the management, maintenance and use of other natural-reserve areas. Its scope is operational rather than merely descriptive: the business-licensing framework covers water-based nature-tourism infrastructure; related facilities, equipment rental and services; the placement of aquaculture infrastructure; and other permanent activities in conservation areas. It is therefore a category for enterprises making an enduring, practical intervention in a conservation setting through visitor infrastructure, supporting services, fisheries-cultivation infrastructure or another fixed activity within the stated scope.

The activity is open to micro, small, medium and large businesses. That breadth means the code does not confine its underlying work to one size of operator. At the same time, its scope has a clear internal logic: it brings together stewardship functions—management and maintenance—with specified forms of use. Water-based nature tourism, associated facilities and equipment, aquaculture infrastructure, and other permanent conservation-area activities are all named as parts of that operational picture.

Nationally, foreign investment is open. The foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, so the record sets no foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. The stated basis is Presidential Regulation 10/2021 and 49/2021. This is a direct national position on ownership, while the conservation-area scope gives that position its particular commercial and operational setting.

Bali does not reverse that result. The province’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. For this activity, the Bali record states that OSS risk at the large (Besar) scale is medium-high/high; it is therefore not blocked by that moratorium, and Bali is marked as OK or higher risk. The distinction matters because Bali’s rule is broad: a national 100% ceiling does not by itself resolve every Bali question, but this record indicates no moratorium block. A foreign investor can treat the activity as open nationally and not barred from PMA registration in Bali on that moratorium ground.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor can treat the activity as open nationally and not barred from PMA registration in Bali on that moratorium ground.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: KBLI 92000: Gambling and Betting, Closed to Foreign Investment
editorial.standfirst: This broad gambling and betting activity is closed to foreign investment nationally and recorded as closed for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 92000 covers gambling and betting as an operating activity, not merely the social act of playing a game. Its scope runs from bookmaking and other betting facilities to off-track betting, casinos—including floating casinos—lottery-ticket sales, coin-operated gambling machines, subscription quiz applications offering prizes, sports betting, and card games operated as wagering activities. The boundary matters: ordinary card-game clubs, such as trumps or bridge clubs, sit outside this activity where gambling is not the organising purpose.

For an investor considering the formal business category, the national position is decisive. The record classifies the activity as **TERTUTUP** for PMA and sets the maximum foreign ownership at **0%**. There are also no business scales listed as open. In practical terms, this is not a category presented in the record as available for foreign-investment registration at any scale; the issue is not selecting a smaller or larger enterprise format, but the national closure itself.

Bali does not soften that conclusion. Its local status is likewise **TERTUTUP**, and the record explicitly marks the activity as blocked for PMA registration. A foreigner cannot, therefore, register this activity in Bali today. That conclusion should not be confused with Bali’s province-wide permanent rule affecting all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities for PMA. This activity is described instead as medium-high/high risk and as not blocked by that moratorium.

That distinction is worth preserving because it keeps the analysis honest. The Bali outcome remains closed, yet the record does not attribute that result to the island-wide low- and medium-low-risk moratorium. It also calls for verification by address. For founders and advisers, the responsible reading is narrow and clear: the category’s stated national PMA closure already precludes foreign ownership, Bali records it as closed and blocked for PMA, and any address-specific review belongs to confirming the local position rather than inventing an opening the record does not provide.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreigner cannot, therefore, register this activity in Bali today.

editorial.headline: Stadium Facilities: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Stadium facilities and self-run sports schools are nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium leaves no registration route at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the Bali position is blunt: Stadium Facilities cannot be registered as PMA at a Bali address today. Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment and permits up to 100 percent foreign ownership; in Bali, however, the record marks it closed under the province-wide PMA moratorium. This is not a marginal qualification to an otherwise open activity. The national setting and the Bali address rule lead to different outcomes, and a proposal that is available to fully foreign-owned investment nationally has no currently registrable PMA route in Bali.

Stadium Facilities is a venue-and-facilities activity, defined by the provision of places and infrastructure for sport as the principal business. The stated sports are football, hockey, cricket, baseball, jai-alai and athletics. The athletics scope expressly embraces running, throwing, jumping and related events, keeping the description anchored in the practical provision of a sporting setting. It also reaches self-managed schools or sports education in those same disciplines. In other words, the record places both the facilities and independently operated training or school activity for its named sports within this single field, provided they are managed by the operator itself.

Registration is open across the small, medium and large scales listed in the record. At the national level, “open” carries a concrete ownership consequence: the ceiling for foreign ownership is 100 percent, under the Presidential Regulations cited in the record. A foreign investor considering the activity outside the Bali restriction can therefore read the national setting plainly: full foreign ownership is permitted at that level. editorial.headline: Circuit Facilities: Nationally Open, Address-Specific in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A competition circuit for motor, horse or dog racing is nationally open to full foreign ownership, while Bali requires an address-specific check.
editorial.body:
**Fasilitas Sirkuit** is a circuit-facility activity: the provision of sports venues and facilities formed as a looping or circular road. Its subject is not racing in the abstract but the place in which it happens—a repeated course made available for competition. The stated competitive uses are motor-racing events, horse races and dog races, and they are not incidental examples: the record places them within the activity’s principal purpose. In plain English, this is the business of providing a circuit-shaped venue and the facilities that support its core use for those races.

The classification is open at Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, which establishes the business sizes identified in the record. At national level it is TERBUKA for PMA, and its maximum foreign ownership is 100%. Put plainly, the national position permits a wholly foreign-owned registration for this activity; the ceiling is not a minority or joint-ownership limit. That national reading rests on Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021, the source named in the record. Those are the stated national facts—scope, eligible scale and ownership ceiling—and they should be kept distinct from Bali’s local treatment.

Bali’s result is less absolute than a simple open-or-closed label. The province has a permanent island-wide rule blocking PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. This activity does not fall into that stated moratorium treatment: its Bali status is `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK`, and the reason records a medium-high risk position. Accordingly, it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The same reason adds an important geographic qualification: the position must be verified per address. That is the relevant local check, rather than evidence of a Bali-specific foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition; neither appears in this record.

For a founder, the clean editorial conclusion is measured. Nationally, the activity is fully open to foreign ownership and can be registered at the three stated scales. In Bali, it is not barred by the permanent PMA moratorium that applies to lower-risk activities, but the applicable position has to be confirmed at the proposed address. The practical story is therefore a circuit facility with a clear core purpose, a 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling, and a Bali assessment that remains address-specific.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, it is not barred by the permanent PMA moratorium that applies to lower-risk activities, but the applicable position has to be confirmed at the proposed address.

editorial.headline: The Arena as a Business: KBLI 93113
editorial.standfirst: A broad sports-facilities activity, nationally open to full foreign ownership and not caught by Bali’s PMA moratorium—though each Bali address still needs verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 93113 is about providing the venue and facility itself for sport: an indoor or outdoor setting for land, water and air activities. Its scope is intentionally wide, reaching from facilities for swimming and bowling to arenas for ice hockey, bungee jumping and winter sports. It also expressly includes arenas for slingshot activities, paragliding and hang gliding. The point of connection is not a single sporting discipline; it is the management of the place and the facilities in which those activities occur. That makes this a classification with an unusually broad physical canvas, spanning water, ground and air, while remaining centred on the operation of an arena or facility.

For a business choosing this activity, its principal activity is the provision and management of those sports venues and facilities. The examples help give the term arena its working shape: it can be a swimming venue, a bowling arena, an ice-hockey arena, a bungee-jumping facility, a winter-sports venue, or a site for paragliding or hang gliding. The record opens the activity to Menengah and Besar scales. In editorial terms, this is a category defined by the operating facility—not by an abstract association with sport. The facility is the business’s centre of gravity, and its management is identified as the principal activity.

At the national level, the position on foreign investment is direct. KBLI 93113 is TERBUKA and its maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In plain English, the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership for this defined activity; there is no national foreign-share cap below full ownership in the record. That clarity applies to the activity as described—providing and managing the listed kinds of sports venues and facilities—and it should not be blurred by the separate provincial lens that applies in Bali.

Bali needs that separate reading. Here this activity is recorded as medium-high risk, and the consequence is material: it is not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium. The provincial rule is described as island-wide and permanent, blocking PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. That description does not extend the block to this activity. But “not blocked” is not the same thing as a generic, location-free conclusion. The Bali note expressly says to verify per address. So the honest Bali position is precise: the moratorium does not bar this medium-high risk activity, while the particular address still requires verification. National openness is real, and Bali’s pathway remains address-specific.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is real, and Bali’s pathway remains address-specific.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: The Business of the Playing Field
editorial.standfirst: A national opening for sports-field facilities, with Bali's registration status scope-dependent and still to be confirmed.
editorial.body:
This activity is the business of providing venues and facilities for sport as its principal undertaking: golf, badminton, volleyball, basketball and tennis. The emphasis is on the place and the facility itself—the operational setting in which these sports are played. That gives the code a practical clarity. It is for an enterprise whose core activity is making those grounds, courts and sporting facilities available, rather than treating sport as a peripheral feature of another business.

The activity is open across the full stated range of business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the commercial form of a sporting facility can vary considerably while remaining anchored in the same central proposition: providing the sporting space. A founder should therefore keep the declared activity faithful to that core. The record describes a facility-provider, not an undefined lifestyle concept; its centre of gravity is the availability of golf, badminton, volleyball, basketball or tennis facilities as the main business activity.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In other words, the record places no national foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. Its stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For an international founder, that is the essential starting point: the activity is nationally open and can sit within a foreign-investment structure at the stated ceiling.

Bali requires a more exact reading, and the record does not settle it either way. The Governor's moratorium request asked Bali to close OSS to PMA registration for low and medium-low risk activities; as applied, Bali closed OSS to new PMA licensing for 18 business fields named in KBLI 2020 numbering, not for every such activity. Golf facilities are recorded at Tinggi risk, outside those tiers, and no Perpres reservation for them was located. The other sports-field scopes — badminton, volleyball, basketball, tennis and similar courts — are recorded at Menengah Rendah risk and are flagged blocked in Bali as a precaution, and whether OSS licenses this code for a PT PMA is not yet confirmed. The national opening is real; the Bali pathway described here is not a settled fact.

editorial.standfirst: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this activity reaches a hard structural stop for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
A martial-arts facility is not simply a room with mats, bags or a ring. This activity covers the provision of dedicated places and facilities for pencak silat training halls, karate dojos, taekwondo dojangs and boxing gyms as the principal business activity. The common thread is the facility itself: a defined setting for martial-arts practice, rather than a loose description of sport or recreation. That clarity matters when the business is being framed for registration, because the code is anchored in providing the place and its sporting facilities.

No verified scale-based licensing rows are on file for this code, so which enterprise sizes it is open to cannot be confirmed here. At the national level, it is classified as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the national position does not impose a lower foreign-share cap on this activity. The relevant national reference is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder assessing the code at national level, that is a clear ownership signal: the activity is open, and full foreign ownership is permitted within the recorded ceiling.

Bali changes the conclusion decisively. A foreign investor cannot yet rely on a Bali registration pathway for this activity through a PMA company, pending case-by-case verification. The obstacle is our own evidence, not an ownership rule: we located no foreign-ownership restriction, and we hold no verified licensing rows for this code, so its Bali risk tier is unknown and no Bali position can be stated. It is treated as blocked until verified case by case. The local status here, `Blocked — pending verification`, records that same gap in the catalogue rather than a reduced foreign-ownership percentage.

The provincial backdrop is also strict. Bali permanently blocks PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities across the island, under the Governor's letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. Whether that rule reaches this specific activity cannot be confirmed either, because no verified risk tier is on file for it; the recorded reason for today's block is the missing licensing record itself, not a determination under the moratorium. The national invitation to 100% foreign ownership is therefore real, yet it cannot open a Bali registration pathway until a verified licensing row is found and the case is reviewed.

editorial.headline: Fitness Centres: Nationally Open, but Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers fitness facilities and independently managed fitness education—open to foreign ownership nationally, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 93116 is the activity for providing places and facilities for fitness and other forms of physical conditioning as the principal business activity. Its scope also includes fitness schools or fitness education operated by the business itself. In plain terms, it is the classification for an enterprise whose core offer is access to a fitness or wellbeing facility, including an independently managed educational fitness operation within that same activity.

The activity is open at Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. That is a clear national position: foreign investment may hold the full ownership ceiling stated for this activity. The applicable national source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder assessing the classification at national level, the essential point is not an implied restriction but the one expressly recorded here: the activity is open to PMA up to that full ceiling.

Bali is the decisive exception. In Bali, this activity is not currently registrable by a foreign investor. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class), and the record identifies the reason precisely: at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. The moratorium cited in the record took effect in May 2026.

That produces a straightforward but consequential split. The national foreign-ownership ceiling remains 100%, yet it does not create a PMA registration path for this activity in Bali while the island-wide risk-based block applies. The issue is therefore not a reduced Bali ownership percentage or an additional local condition stated for this activity; it is a direct block on PMA registration under Bali’s permanent moratorium for the relevant risk classes. Anyone reading the national openness as a Bali registration approval would miss the central fact of this record.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness up to 100% does not create a PMA registration path in Bali while the island-wide risk-based block applies.

editorial.headline: Sport Centres, Nationally Open but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers sports venues, including sport centres, but Bali offers no PMA registration path despite national foreign-investment openness.
editorial.body:
Sports facilities are the core business here: providing a place and the supporting facilities for sport, including a sport centre. The emphasis is on operating the venue itself rather than treating sport as an incidental amenity. In practical terms, this is the activity for a business whose central proposition is the space, infrastructure and setting in which sporting activity takes place.

The registration record opens the activity at the **Mikro** and **Kecil** scales. That matters because scale is not a decorative classification in this case; it frames who can enter the activity through the available registration rows. The national opening is not what is in question here; what closes Bali today is the moratorium over the Low and Medium-Low risk tiers.

At the national level, the activity is **TERBUKA** to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. That is a clear national position: foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership for this activity. But national openness does not itself create a route to register in every locality. In Bali, a foreigner cannot register this activity through a PT PMA today. The Bali record marks it as closed under the **2026 provincial moratorium**, which blocks every Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI island-wide; this activity is classified Low risk, so it sits inside the blocked band.

Bali’s position is reinforced by its permanent, island-wide rule blocking all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities from PMA. The decisive point for this activity, however, is already explicit in its registration structure: there is no large-business row available to a PT PMA. For founders, the honest reading is not that Bali has narrowed an otherwise usable foreign-investment option. It is that the national 100% ceiling and the Bali registration pathway lead to different outcomes: national foreign openness, but no PMA registration route in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not itself create a route to register in Bali.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.standfirst: A golf-club activity can be wholly foreign-owned nationally, yet no verified Bali licensing row exists for this code — until one is found, Bali Zero treats registration here as blocked and reviewed case by case.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, this golf club’s Bali registration position could not be verified against the official 2025 regulation text, and until it is, Bali Zero treats it as blocked rather than open. That is the central practical fact, even though this activity is nationally open to foreign investment with a 100% ownership ceiling. National openness is real, but it does not make Bali registration available for a foreign-owned golf club. The distinction is not cosmetic: it is exactly why this activity’s Bali registration currently sits blocked pending verification, rather than settled either way. Anyone assessing the activity should start with that jurisdictional divide, rather than treating the national ceiling as a Bali outcome.

The activity is broader than a particular course or clubhouse. It covers professional, semi-professional and amateur golf organisations or clubs that give members the opportunity to take part in sporting activity. A club may provide the venue and facilities for the sport, or it may operate without providing them. Membership and participation are the defining thread: the club exists to enable involvement in golf, whether or not it also places physical facilities at members’ disposal. That scope accommodates differing club structures without reducing the activity to a single physical setting.

Nationally, the confirmed fact is the ownership ceiling: Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 name this activity as open to up to 100% foreign investment. A Mikro/Kecil scale row also surfaced during the KBLI 2025 crosswalk build, citing a PP 28/2025 lampiran — but an exhaustive check of that lampiran could not locate the row anywhere in it, so it has been set aside as unverifiable rather than treated as a confirmed OSS scale entry. Bali’s position could not be confirmed. Until a verified source is found, this activity should be treated as blocked for PT PMA registration in Bali pending case-by-case review. A founder should read the national 100% ceiling as the national investment position only, and confirm the current Bali requirement directly with the Bali Zero team before proceeding.

editorial.headline: A Lawn-Tennis Club That Remains Open to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: For professional, semi-professional and amateur lawn-tennis clubs, this activity is open nationally to full foreign ownership and remains registrable by a PT PMA in Bali.
editorial.body:
A tennis club is not necessarily a venue. This activity covers professional, semi-professional and amateur lawn-tennis organisations or clubs that give members the opportunity to take part in sport. It can apply whether the club provides a place and facilities for the sport or operates without them. The governing idea is membership and participation: an organisation built around access to tennis activity. It is equally within scope where the club’s members are professional, semi-professional or amateur participants.

That breadth matters at registration. At Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale, the activity is open. Every stated scale is open, rather than a subset limited to one band. The record is more exact about those permitted scales than about any particular business model. Its stated scope is a lawn-tennis club or organisation giving members an opportunity to participate in sport, with facilities if it provides them and without them if it does not. For a prospective club organiser, the defining elements are tennis, club organisation and member participation.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is plainly open. The record marks the activity TERBUKA and sets the maximum foreign ownership at 100%, so there is no stated national foreign-equity cap below full ownership. The cited national sources are Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. Bali’s status is Open in Bali (high-risk track), and the Besar-scale classification is recorded as Tinggi—high risk. That distinction is decisive because Bali’s permanent provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI across the island.

The practical conclusion is clean: a PT PMA can register this activity in Bali today. It is not a case in which national openness is neutralised by the island-wide moratorium. The reason supplied in the record is specific: its Besar-scale risk position survives because the restriction reaches only Rendah and Menengah Rendah. The record expressly says the activity is registrable by a PT PMA in Bali. For founders, the useful discipline is to read both layers together. Nationally, full foreign ownership is permitted; in Bali, the activity remains registrable because the record places its relevant risk position beyond the moratorium’s blocked bands. That is an affirmative Bali position, while keeping the club’s real-world offer within the stated lawn-tennis membership scope.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, full foreign ownership is permitted; in Bali, the activity remains registrable because its relevant risk position lies beyond the moratorium’s blocked bands.

It does not require a dedicated sporting setting. A club may provide a place and facilities for sport, or may give members that opportunity without providing either. That makes facilities relevant to the possible operating form, but not a prerequisite for falling inside the stated scope. The definition instead holds on to the club’s role: creating the opportunity for its members to take part in sport.

editorial.headline: Fitness Clubs: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This fitness-club activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet a foreigner cannot register it at a Bali address under the province-wide PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
KBLI 93127 covers professional, semi-professional and amateur fitness and bodybuilding clubs organised to give their members the opportunity to take part in sport. The defining activity is the club’s role in enabling participation, rather than a particular level of competition or a single physical format. It includes organisations that provide a place and facilities for sport, as well as those that do not.

The activity is open across small, medium and large business scales. That matters because the classification accommodates a club model at more than one size, while keeping the focus on access for members to sporting activity. A fitness or bodybuilding club may therefore fall within this scope whether its organisation is professional, semi-professional or amateur, provided that its purpose remains the opportunity for members to participate in sport.

At national level, the position is clear: the activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. The national framework cited in the record is Presidential Regulations 10/2021 and 49/2021. In other words, the national classification does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity.

For a Bali address, however, a foreigner cannot register this activity today. Bali treats it as closed under its PMA moratorium because the large-business scale is classified as medium-low risk. The provincial rule blocks all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities from PMA registration across the island, on a permanent basis. This is not a reduction of the national 100% ownership ceiling; it is a Bali-specific bar on PMA registration for the activity, reflected in the Governor’s letter of May 2026.

editorial.headline: A Bowling Club Can Be Nationally Open—Blocked in Bali Pending Verification
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 93128 covers bowling clubs for members at every competitive level. Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%; in Bali, this activity carries no verified licensing basis, so its registration status is treated as blocked pending case-by-case verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 93128 is the category for bowling clubs: professional, semi-professional, and amateur organisations that give their members an opportunity to take part in the sport. Its scope is deliberately broad. A club may provide bowling premises and sporting facilities, or it may organise member activity without supplying either. The defining feature is the club’s sporting role for its members, rather than the particular form of venue it operates.

This code's licensing rows have been detached: an exhaustive search of the pinned PP28 regulatory corpus could not locate the row this code's scale classification was reportedly based on, so no scale tier can currently be confirmed. The activity itself remains club-based sporting organisation, where membership and participation sit at the centre. It is not written as a category for a single style of bowling operation or a single competitive standard: the scope expressly accommodates professional, semi-professional, and amateur clubs alike.

Nationally, the PMA status is **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of **100%**. In plain terms, the national foreign-investment setting permits full foreign ownership. The source stated for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national openness is real, but it is not the end of the registration question for a business intended for Bali.

In Bali, this activity's registration status cannot currently be settled. This code holds no verified licensing rows: the same exhaustive search found no row to classify its risk tier against,. A national 100% ownership ceiling does not by itself establish a Bali registration route while this record carries no licensing basis to classify against. Bali Zero's working posture, pending that verification, is to treat KBLI 93128 as blocked in Bali; confirm the current position case by case with the Bali Zero team or directly at oss.go.id before proceeding.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% ownership ceiling does not establish a Bali registration route while this code's licensing basis remains unverified.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Sports Club Activity Blocked in Bali Pending Verification
editorial.standfirst: Other Sports Clubs can be fully foreign-owned nationally, yet in Bali the registration path is blocked pending verification of this activity's licensing data.
editorial.body:
**In Bali, this activity's registration path for a foreign investor is blocked pending verification.** That is the practical starting point for Other Sports Clubs, even though the activity is nationally open to foreign investment with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The contrast is not a minor footnote: nationally, full foreign ownership is permitted; in Bali, the registration path is blocked pending verification of this activity's licensing data. Reading only the national opening would miss the operational result on the island.

The activity covers professional, semi-professional and amateur sports clubs that give members an opportunity to participate in sport, whether or not the club provides a venue and facilities. Its centre of gravity is the club as an organised membership setting for participation, rather than a definition tied to owning a particular site. The scope expressly includes winter-sports clubs, chess clubs, athletics clubs for running, jumping and throwing, shooting clubs, e-sports clubs, and card-game clubs such as trump or bridge. The examples are varied, but the common thread is clear: members are given a route into sporting activity.

Which scales this activity registers at, and at what risk tier, cannot be confirmed here — we hold no verified licensing rows for this activity. Bali's record therefore states no position at all, and the code is treated as blocked until verified case by case. The unresolved licensing gap is what currently blocks a PT PMA from registering this activity in Bali. This does not alter the national description of the club activity itself; it determines who can use the registration path in Bali.

The record also notes Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA block for low- and medium-low-risk activities, under Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. For this activity, the stated conclusion is narrower: the licensing gap leaves Bali's position unresolved, and the registration path stays blocked here until it is verified case by case. Nationally, it is TERBUKA and may carry foreign ownership up to 100%; in Bali, a PT PMA's registration remains blocked pending verification. The national ceiling describes foreign-ownership capacity, but it does not override Bali’s recorded registration position.

editorial.headline: The Business of Staging Sport
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but a PMA registration at a Bali address is blocked by the province-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
93191 is the operational code for bringing a live sporting event into being. Its scope reaches from technical planning and provision through to the arrangement and operation of audiovisual equipment and special effects. It applies to sports weeks and other multi-event programmes as well as single-event championships. It also includes sports promotion services confined to sport, including esports promotion. In practical terms, this is the activity of managing, organising and running the presentation machinery of sport—not merely appearing within the event.

The code is open across the full stated business-scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the activity can sit with a small organiser as readily as with a larger operator handling technical delivery, event management or specialist promotion. Its PMA status is TERBUKA nationally, and its foreign-ownership ceiling stands at 100%. The national position is therefore unambiguous: foreign investment may hold the full permitted stake under the cited PMA basis.

Bali changes the registration outcome. A foreign investor cannot register this activity at a Bali address today. The record identifies the Besar scale as Menengah Rendah and says that it is blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium. That moratorium applies island-wide and permanently to all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA. The cited governor’s letter is dated May 2026; the record’s later note is dated June 2026. Neither the national openness nor the 100% national ceiling removes that Bali-address restriction.

For founders, this is a case where the activity description and the investment geography must be read together. The national framework permits full foreign ownership for the listed sports-event and sports-promotion work. Yet the Bali rule is decisive for a PMA registration located in the province: the activity is blocked there under the stated moratorium. The honest reading is not that foreign ownership is conditionally reduced in Bali, but that PMA registration at a Bali address is unavailable for this activity under the recorded rule.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this activity is nevertheless unavailable for PMA registration at a Bali address.

editorial.headline: Professional Judges and Referees: Open Nationally, Bali Status Blocked Pending Verification
editorial.standfirst: Nationally, this individual professional activity permits full foreign ownership, yet no verified licensing route lets a PT PMA register it in Bali today — the position stays blocked until checked case by case.
editorial.body:
This activity covers professional judges and referees who act in an individual capacity. The operative idea is personal professional officiating: the code is about the work done by a judge or referee, carried out in that person’s own capacity. That makes the scope deliberately specific. The record identifies a professional role, the two forms of officiating it includes, and the individual basis on which that role is performed. For founders, the useful starting point is therefore the activity itself: professional judging and refereeing, registered on an individual footing.

Scale is meant to define the available registration range for this activity, but the licensing rows this record once carried have since been set aside as unverifiable against the current KBLI 2025 text, so no confirmed scale list can be stated here today. That gap is not a side detail: it is the same reason neither the risk tier nor the Bali position below can be settled from this record alone, and both need case-by-case verification before anyone acts on them.

Nationally, the investment position is unequivocally open. The PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, which means the national record permits full foreign ownership of this activity. That is a meaningful national fact, not a hint at a partial foreign stake: the stated ceiling is complete ownership. But a national ceiling answers only the national ownership question. It does not, on its own, establish that the activity can be registered through every regional route. Bali supplies the qualification — and it is an unresolved one, not a settled one.

In Bali, this record carries no confirmed route today for a PT PMA to register this activity. The Bali position is unstated rather than closed, and the code is treated as blocked until verified case by case. The requirement we located is a personal licence and not an equity rule — UU 11/2022 Pasal 69(1) and Pasal 71 with PP 46/2024 Pasal 103 require a foreign referee or judge to hold a competency certificate, a federation recommendation and a government permit — while the catalogue holds no licensing rows for the code, so its risk tier is unknown. Bali separately runs a permanent, island-wide moratorium blocking PMA registration for confirmed Low and Medium-Low risk activities, but this code’s own risk tier has not been verified, so whether that moratorium even reaches this activity is itself part of what remains unresolved. What is established: 100% national foreign ownership stands, while the Bali route stays blocked pending case-by-case verification — neither confirmed open nor confirmed closed for good.

editorial.headline: Hunting-Area Activity: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the management of recreational and sporting hunting areas, but a Bali address remains unavailable for PMA registration.
editorial.body:
This code covers the management of hunting activity within designated areas that have potential game animals. Those areas may take the form of hunting gardens, hunting parks or hunting grounds intended for recreation or sport. Its scope also includes providing the facilities and infrastructure needed for hunting. In practical terms, the activity is about operating the setting in which hunting takes place: the area itself, its recreational or sporting purpose, and the supporting provision around it.

Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to **100%**. The registration scope is not confined to one business size: it is open at micro, small, medium and large scale. That breadth matters because the classification is framed around the management of a hunting area and its facilities, rather than around a single narrowly defined type of operator. A registrant should therefore describe the actual managed activity with care, keeping the hunting-area function and the provision of hunting facilities clearly within view.

Bali presents a materially different result for a foreign-owned registration. A foreign investor cannot register this activity under PMA for a Bali address today. Although the national position is open, the record identifies the large-scale classification as **Medium-Low** risk for this purpose. Bali’s province-wide, permanent PMA moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for a Bali address. The restriction is therefore not a reduced foreign-ownership allowance or a conditional local arrangement; it is a registration block for PMA in Bali.

That distinction is the essential reading of this code. The national ceiling remains 100% foreign ownership, but it does not override the Bali-specific moratorium. For a business located outside Bali, the national openness and the available scale range define the starting position. For a business seeking a Bali address, the decisive fact is the block: the activity may be nationally open, yet it is closed to PMA registration on the island under Bali’s permanent rule for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not override Bali’s PMA registration block.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: The Organisations Behind Sport’s Rules
editorial.standfirst: Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%, but Bali holds no verified licensing record for this framework — registration here is blocked pending case-by-case confirmation.
editorial.body:
Sport relies not only on competitors, but on the organisations that make competition legible and repeatable. This activity covers disability-sport organisations and other sporting organisations, regulatory bodies, and sports leagues. Their role is to provide the rules for matches or races and to run competition on a regular, tiered basis. The participants may be individuals, groups, or clubs; the format may be a week-long multi-event programme or a single-event sports championship. The defining feature is the structure around the contest: rules, recurrence, and an organised path for competition.

The scale boundary cannot be stated here: the licensing rows this classification's scale tiers were once read from have been removed until a verified source is found. No scale — Mikro, Kecil, or otherwise — is currently confirmed for this activity. Until re-verified, the record is limited to scope: what the organisation does, not the business size at which it may register.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is open. Foreign ownership may reach **100%**, under the source cited in the record, Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That is the national ownership ceiling for the activity. It is important, however, not to mistake a national ceiling for a guarantee that the same registration route exists in every location. The ownership position answers one question; the available scale rows and local registration position answer another.

In Bali, no verified position can currently be given for this activity. The local record identifies a duty to partner, which does not bar foreign ownership: UU 11/2022 Pasal 54(3), hardened by Permenpora 9/2026 Pasal 73(1), obliges a foreign entity organising an international-level championship to partner with the national federation and/or a professional sport organisation. No licensing rows are held for the code, so its Bali risk tier is unknown, the position cannot be stated, and it is treated as blocked until verified case by case. This sits alongside Bali’s island-wide, permanent rule blocking PMA across all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI, cited to the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. The honest reading is therefore straightforward: pending verification, national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not currently confirm a Bali PMA registration path for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not verify a Bali PMA registration route — the Bali record here is unconfirmed.

editorial.headline: Traditional Sport, Cultural Stewardship, and Bali’s PMA Line
editorial.standfirst: This activity organises, manages and regulates traditional sports in service of Indonesia’s living cultural inheritance.
editorial.body:
Traditional sport is treated here as more than an event programme or a recreational sideline. The activity covers the management, organisation and regulation of traditional sports, whether undertaken by an individual or a group, with the stated purpose of preserving tradition and culture. Its scope reaches forms such as pencak silat, Nias stone jumping, Sumba’s pasola, debus and Minang silek: practices whose sporting character is inseparable from the cultural values they carry.

That framing matters for the people registering the activity. The scale-based licensing detail once cited for this code could not be verified against the current regulation text and has since been set aside, so no confirmed scale profile can be stated here. The record does not reduce the work to staging a spectacle. It includes the practical stewardship around traditional sport: its administration, its delivery and the regulation connected to sustaining it.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is open, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That is the national ceiling, and it is an unambiguous one. Bali, however, produces a different operating answer for a PT PMA. The Bali record leaves the activity unclassified rather than closed, and treats it as blocked until verified case by case: the requirement we located is a mandatory business standard with no ownership term anywhere in it — Permenpora 9/2026 Lampiran I, eight cumulative persyaratan and a Sertifikat Standar — and we hold no licensing rows for the code, so its risk tier is unknown. That gap in the licensing record — not a settled scale or ownership rule — is why Bali Zero holds a PT PMA filing for this activity as blocked pending case-by-case verification, not as a closed matter.

The provincial backdrop adds a separate layer: Bali permanently blocks PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities across the island. For this activity, the decisive point is that no verified licensing row exists to confirm which risk category it falls into — not the national foreign-ownership ceiling, and not yet a confirmed moratorium hit either. A founder can therefore read the national position as fully open while recognising that Bali Zero cannot yet confirm this activity as admissible for a PT PMA registration in Bali. In a field built around cultural continuity, the distinction is not a technical footnote; it determines whether the proposed vehicle can be registered on the island at all.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not make this activity registrable by a PT PMA in Bali.

persyaratan: Memiliki Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar

Dokumen Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar
Silakan kirim semua dokumen yang diminta dalam satu file.
1. Unduh dan lengkapi formulir Penilaian Mandiri.
2. Dokumentasi Standar Pelaksanaan Kegiatan Usaha.
Lampirkan 6 dokumen Sarana
  1. Petunjuk identitas/nama usaha dengan tulisan yang terbaca.
  2. Ruang kantor/area administrasi yang dilengkapi peralatan dan perlengkapan kerja.
  3. Peralatan Pertolongan Pertama pada Kecalakaan (P3K) dan Alat Pemadam Api Ringan (APAR) yang berfungsi dengan baik.
  4. Ketersediaan air bersih yang tidak berwarna, tidak berbau, tidak berasa, dan jernih.
  5. Ketersediaan gudang atau tempat penyimpanan barang yang aman.
  6. Status kepemilikan kantor/tempat usaha yang jelas.
Lampirkan 1 dokumen Sumber Daya Manusia
Perlindungan asuransi kesehatan dan/atau kecelakaan bagi karyawan tersedia dan berlaku.
Lampirkan 1 dokumen Ketentuan Produksi
Pelayanan kesehatan, seperti informasi tentang dokter, rumah sakit, atau klinik terdekat terdokumentasi.
Lampirkan 3 dokumen Sistem Manajemen Usaha
  1. Struktur organisasi dan uraian tugas setiap jabatan jalas dan terdokumentasi.
  2. rencana bisnis (business plan) masih berlaku dan terdokumentasi.
  3. S0P dan/atau petunjuk teknis pelaksanaan karja masih berlaku dan terdokumentasi.

Apabila mengoperasikan kapal milik sendiri untuk menunjang kegiatan usaha, maka wajib memiliki izin operasi angkutan laut khusus.

editorial.headline: Where Recreational Fishing Becomes a Managed Business
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the places, waters and supporting services that turn recreational and sport fishing into an organised offering—and it remains open to PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Fishing is the main event here, but the activity is broader than a single pond or shoreline. It covers the operation of places and facilities designed primarily for fishing, across freshwater settings such as rivers, estuaries, lakes, beaches, archipelagic waters and fishing ponds, as well as saltwater settings from shallow onshore waters to offshore sea. The commercial proposition may be recreational fishing or sport fishing; what matters is that the operator is providing the setting in which the activity takes place.

That setting can be practical, social and guided. The scope expressly includes recreational fishing-guide services, alongside supporting services such as food and beverages. In other words, the activity can hold together the physical fishing environment, the visitor experience and the ancillary hospitality that makes a day on the water—or at a managed fishing pond—work as a coherent operation. It is an activity open at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales, allowing the business model to be registered across the full scale range stated in the record.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward: the activity is open, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. There is no lower national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for it. That clarity matters because Bali applies a permanent, island-wide PMA restriction to activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. The local position for this activity, however, does not turn that rule into a prohibition.

For Bali, the record places the decisive point at the Large scale: its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, and it is therefore not blocked by the moratorium. The Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. Put plainly, a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today; the provincial moratorium does not bar it. The national openness and the Bali outcome are aligned here, but the Bali conclusion rests on the recorded risk position at Large scale—not on an invented exemption or a separate ownership condition.
editorial.pullQuote: Put plainly, a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today; the provincial moratorium does not bar it.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.
