editorial.headline: Independent Athletes, and Bali’s PMA Boundary
editorial.standfirst: Independent athletes, including individual e-sports competitors, are nationally open to full foreign ownership — but Bali carries no verified licensing rows for this code, so a PT PMA’s registration route there is blocked pending case-by-case verification.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor should not assume KBLI 93197 is currently registrable through a PT PMA in Bali — the record’s Bali position is unresolved, not a settled closure. That is the practical starting point, even though the activity is nationally open to foreign investment. The activity concerns sportspersons or athletes acting in their own individual capacity, expressly including individual e-sports participants. The wording places the person at the centre: it captures sporting activity carried on in the athlete’s personal capacity. It is a classification built around the independent athlete’s own professional activity—personal, direct and individual in form.

At the registration level, this record carries no verified licensing rows for the activity — no confirmed scale eligibility and no confirmed risk tier. That gap is why Bali states no position here: the code is treated as blocked until verified case by case, not cleared and not ruled out. For founders, that is the practical takeaway — treat any scale or risk-tier claim for this code as unverified until the Bali Zero team confirms it activity by activity.

Across Indonesia, PMA is classified TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In ordinary language, the record makes room for full foreign ownership at national level; it does not impose a reduced foreign stake for this activity. There is no lower foreign ceiling to account for in this national entry. The source identified for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For an independent athlete considering the activity outside Bali, the national reading is therefore straightforward: the ownership ceiling itself does not close the door.

Bali changes the answer entirely. The same gap carries straight through to Bali: with no confirmed licensing pathway, there is nothing here to certify a PT PMA route, so the blocked, verify-case-by-case position above stands. Separately, Bali enforces a permanent, island-wide moratorium blocking PMA registrations across the Low and Medium-Low risk band, under the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP — whether this code falls in that band is itself unverified. Until the licensing gap closes, the practical answer for a PT PMA stays what the record shows: blocked, not cleared, and not something to assume open.
editorial.pullQuote: No verified licensing rows exist for this code in Bali — the position stays blocked until verified case by case, not cleared and not closed by default.

editorial.headline: Sport’s Overlooked Operating Layer Meets Bali’s PMA Barrier
editorial.standfirst: This broad sporting-activities category is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet in Bali a foreign-owned company’s registration is currently blocked pending verification.
editorial.body:
This activity gathers the sporting work that sits beyond the more familiar, purpose-built categories: promoting sports activities; operating racing-horse or racing-dog kennels and similar facilities; individual e-sport participation; mountain guiding; vertical aerodynamic wind tunnels; and training animals for sport or entertainment. It also reaches supporting work for recreational or sporting fishing and hunting. The common thread is not one particular venue or discipline, but the operational infrastructure, specialist participation and support that make sporting and recreational pursuits possible.

This code’s licensing rows — including which business scales it opens at — have been removed until a verified source is found. That matters because its scope is deliberately wide: a business may be rooted in a guided outdoor experience, a specialist facility, animal training, sport promotion, an individual e-sport career, or supporting activity around recreation. The registration question is therefore less about whether an undertaking looks conventionally athletic and more about whether its actual work belongs within this stated field of sports-related activity.

Nationally, the position is clear. The activity is **TERBUKA** to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%** under the cited Presidential Regulations. In national terms, foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership for this activity. That national openness should be read precisely, however: it describes the investment position for the activity; it does not erase the registration structure that applies in a particular place.

In Bali, the answer for a PT PMA is different and immediate. We located no foreign-ownership restriction for this activity, and no verified licensing rows either — so the Bali risk tier is unknown, the position cannot be stated, and the code is treated as blocked until verified case by case. That block rests on missing licensing data, not a settled scale-based exclusion. For a founder considering Bali, the national permission is real, but it is not a route around the Bali registration barrier.

data.judul: Aktivitas Taman Bertema dan Taman Hiburan
data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan taman hiburan dan taman bertema yang dicirikan oleh pengoperasian berbagai atraksi secara permanen dan berbasis lokasi, seperti wahana mekanis, komidi putar, permainan, galeri tembak, pertunjukan, pameran bertema, dan tempat piknik, yang disediakan berdasarkan arahan ekonomi dan operasional dari operator pusat. Taman-taman ini biasanya terletak di area yang dibatasi secara struktural, dan pelanggan harus membayar tiket masuk.
Kelompok ini juga mencakup
- aktivitas taman akuatik/air.
Kelompok ini tidak mencakup
- pengoperasian perjudian dan permainan lotre, lihat subgolongan 9200;
- pengoperasian wahana, permainan, dan pertunjukan mekanis oleh penyedia independen, misalnya di tempat pekan raya, festival rakyat, dan pasar natal, lihat 9329.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Theme Parks and Amusement Parks — operating permanent, location-based attractions such as mechanical rides, water parks, themed exhibitions, and picnic grounds where customers pay an entrance ticket. It explicitly excludes gambling and lottery operations.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
Two licensing tiers, per our PP28 mapping:

**Tier 1 — Menengah/Besar**: High risk (Tinggi). NIB + License (Izin) within **14 days**. Self-Assessment required. LSPr-certified Tourism Business Standard + Health Feasibility Certificate (Sertifikat Laik Sehat). Authority: Menteri/Kepala Badan. **Note:** This tier is flagged as inferred data in our PP28 mapping — the licensing requirements were extrapolated from related theme-park/amusement-park KBLI 2020 source codes, not directly published for 93210. Treat with caution and verify with OSS when KBLI 2025 is fully integrated.

**Tier 2 — Mikro/Kecil/Menengah/Besar**: Medium-Low risk (Menengah Rendah). NIB + Standard Certificate issued **automatically** (Otomatis). Health Feasibility Certificate required. LSPr certification for PMA companies. Self-Assessment document for theme park/amusement standards. Authority: Bupati/Walikota.

**PMA Status:** Fully open (Terbuka) — 100% foreign ownership.

**Source Regulation:** PP 28/2025 (aggregated from related KBLI 2020 theme-park/amusement-park source codes).
intel_2026.whatChanged: This code consolidates multiple KBLI 2020 activities into one. Verify your specific activity maps correctly. Merged and cleaned up from previous KBLI 2020 codes to explicitly consolidate theme parks and water parks into one category.
intel_2026.baliContext: This is the big leagues. If you are building a water park (like Waterbom), a massive cultural park, or a large-scale beach club that operates primarily as an amusement venue with immersive attractions, 93210 is your code. The capital expenditure is astronomical, and so is the red tape. A High-Risk classification means your NIB is virtually useless until you pass rigorous Environmental Impact Assessments (AMDAL or UKL-UPL) and deal directly with Ministerial levels in Jakarta. Water rights (SIPA) for waterparks in Bali are currently highly contested due to the island's dropping water table, meaning securing extraction permits can take over a year. You must also have profound alignment with the local Desa Adat (Customary Village) regarding traffic management.

- 47192 — Non-Food Retail (for the inevitable gift shops and merchandise stores)
- 90200 — Performing Arts (if your theme park features live theatrical or cultural dance performances)

editorial.headline: A Permanent World of Attractions, With a Bali Registration Test
editorial.standfirst: A permanent, ticketed park operation is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but in Bali the PMA route depends on the exact scope declared and its OSS risk level.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity is the business of running a fixed, ticketed world of entertainment. It is defined by a permanent, location-based mix of attractions rather than a single attraction in isolation. Mechanical rides, carousels, games, shooting galleries, shows, themed exhibitions and picnic facilities may all belong within one centrally directed operation; water parks do, too. The physical setting matters: these parks are normally contained within a structurally bounded area, and customers enter against an admission ticket. The scope is concerned with the park as an integrated, place-based operation, joined by the economic and operational direction of a central operator.

The activity is open at Menengah, Besar, Mikro and Kecil scales. That broad scale listing does not dilute its defining shape. Whether organised at a Mikro, Kecil, Menengah or Besar scale, the record centres the same model: a central operator coordinating a permanent site, its attractions and the visitor’s paid entry. It also draws a boundary around the activity. Equipment that needs particular operating expertise, and rides described as extreme-risk, are outside the stated coverage.

Nationally, the foreign-investment position is unambiguous. The activity is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In practical terms, that national ceiling allows a fully foreign-owned registration. The 100% figure is the record’s national ceiling; it is not a separate Bali figure. It is nevertheless an ownership position, not a substitute for the place-specific and scope-specific reading required in Bali. The stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021.

Bali requires more attention. The record does not mark the activity as universally blocked for PMA registration there; it marks it as dependent on scope. Bali’s standing provincial rule blocks PMA for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI, island-wide and permanently. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk level is low for some scopes and higher for others. PMA registration in Bali is available only when the higher-risk scope is declared, so the exact activity must be checked live in OSS. Registration cannot be resolved from the activity title alone in Bali. This is neither a Bali-wide green light nor a categorical prohibition: the result turns on the scope and its risk classification.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, PMA registration is available only when the higher-risk scope is declared.

editorial.headline: When the Dance Floor Is the Main Event
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers venues built around dancing, music and light shows—open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is for operating venues and facilities where dancing is the main attraction: a dance floor animated by music and light-show performances. Food and drink may be served, but they are not the principal activity. The scope expressly includes nightclubs and discotheques, placing the emphasis on the operation of the dancing venue itself rather than on hospitality as the core business.

The registration is open across the full stated business-scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the activity is not confined in the record to a single size of operator. Whether the venture begins at a smaller scale or is structured as a larger operation, the defining commercial character remains the same: a place and facilities organised for dancing, with music and lighting integral to the experience.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain terms, the record permits full foreign ownership at the national level; there is no lower foreign-equity ceiling stated for this activity. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That openness should be read as a fact about this activity’s national PMA classification, not as a substitute for details the record does not provide.

Bali’s position is also materially more favourable than a blanket assumption about island-wide restrictions might suggest. The provincial rule recorded here permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities across the island. This activity, however, is not marked as blocked by that moratorium. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which is why it falls outside the moratorium block. The Bali status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: a foreign-owned operator is not shut out of Bali registration for this activity by the stated moratorium. The honest conclusion is clear—nationally it is fully foreign-open, and in Bali the cited risk position means the island-wide Low and Medium-Low risk PMA block does not stop it.

editorial.headline: Karaoke Facilities: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Providing karaoke venues is nationally open to PMA at every listed scale, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration on the island.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the decisive fact comes first: activity code 93292 cannot be registered as PMA in Bali today. That does not erase its national standing; it marks the difference between a nationwide investment classification and a province-wide registration restriction. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA and carries a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, it is marked as blocked because of its risk class. The national ceiling is therefore not a Bali authorisation: the activity may be nationally open while a PMA registration on the island remains unavailable.

The underlying business is the provision of a place and facilities for karaoke as the principal undertaking. That focus matters: the venue and karaoke facilities form the activity’s core. Food and beverage service may be provided alongside it, but the record describes that as an addition, not the defining business. The code is available at micro, small, medium and large scales. It is consequently framed to accommodate operations at each of those listed scales, without changing the essential description of a karaoke venue business.

Bali’s restriction rests on the risk treatment recorded for the large scale: every scope is assessed in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all KBLI with Low or Medium-Low risk for PMA. The record consequently identifies the activity as blocked in Bali under the risk-class status. This is not a different Bali foreign-ownership percentage; it is a bar on the PMA registration itself. The cited provincial basis is the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, and the record dates the moratorium to May 2026.

For founders, the disciplined reading is simple. The national record says the activity is open to PMA, and 100% is the national foreign-ownership ceiling. The Bali record says a PMA registration cannot be made there because the large-scale OSS risk classification falls within the province’s permanent prohibition. Those statements are not competing answers: they describe two different levels of rule. Any plan built around Bali must treat the island restriction as decisive, rather than treating national openness as a substitute for local registration availability.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is not a Bali authorisation: the island’s PMA registration block is decisive.

editorial.headline: Running a Games Arena: a Clear National and Bali Reading
editorial.standfirst: For arena operators, this classification is open across all business scales, fully foreign-open nationally, and not moratorium-blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Managing a games arena is, at its core, a venue-and-facilities activity. The scope covers the provision of places and facilities for games of skill and/or gaming machines operated with coins or cards as the principal activity. Food and drink service may be added, but it is supplemental rather than the business’s defining purpose. The classification therefore centres on the operator of the arena itself: the setting in which those games and machines are made available, rather than a description of a particular game, product, or hospitality format.

That operator may register at the micro, small, medium, or large scale; all four are expressly open. The breadth matters because it accommodates operations at a range of commercial sizes without changing the record’s stated focus: the physical venue and facilities where the activity takes place. A food-and-drink offering can sit alongside the arena, but the record places it as an addition to the principal activity. The classification thus gives a clean frame for an arena-led business, whether its operating footprint is modest or large.

On foreign ownership, the national position is equally clear. The PMA status is open, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. In plain terms, the national classification allows full foreign ownership. Bali does not convert that national openness into a moratorium block. Its status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is that, at the Large scale, OSS risk is Medium-High/High. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium applies to all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities; this one is expressly recorded as not blocked by that moratorium.

The result is a notably direct reading for a foreign investor considering this activity in Bali. The activity is nationally open to PMA at the 100% ceiling, and Bali’s record does not prohibit PMA registration under its risk-based moratorium. That is not an invitation to recast the business as something else: the centre remains the provision and management of the arena and its facilities, with coin- or card-operated machines and games of skill at its core. Any food and drink service stays an optional accompaniment.
editorial.pullQuote: The activity is nationally open to PMA at the 100% ceiling, and Bali’s record does not prohibit PMA registration under its risk-based moratorium.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: The Bali Test for Cave, Bathing and Adventure Tourism
editorial.standfirst: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, this nature-tourism activity reaches a more conditional answer in Bali, where the precise declared scope and its OSS risk classification matter.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is a place-based nature-tourism and adventure business. It covers operating natural bathing sites and facilities whose principal business uses hot springs or waterfalls; managing cave tourism or cave exploration and traversal as the main activity within a defined area, potentially with guides; and managing tourism based on risk-bearing exploration or travel that calls for special skills and physical effort. Its stated terrain includes paragliding, paramotoring, hang gliding, bungee jumping, gliding, canyoning, orienteering, off-road trips and mountain biking. The defining question is whether these activities form the core managed offering.

Registrants are therefore operators for whom natural bathing, cave experiences or physical adventure tourism is the principal business—not an incidental amenity. Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises may all take up the activity under this record. That breadth allows the business to be registered at the scale actually used, while keeping the declared activity tied to operating and managing the specified visitor experience. It does not turn every nature-connected tourism venture into this activity; its boundaries remain the stated core operations.

Nationally, the PMA position is direct. The activity is TERBUKA and carries a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling under the cited Presidential Regulations. In national terms, a foreign investor can hold the full permitted stake in an enterprise carrying out this activity. There is no lower ceiling in the record to qualify that reading. The practical discipline is to identify the real operating centre: natural bathing facilities, cave tourism and exploration, or the specified high-skill adventure management.

Bali requires a more exact reading. It is not marked as outright blocked, yet its status depends on scope. Bali’s permanent, islandwide moratorium blocks PMA registration where the OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low. For this activity, OSS risk at the Besar scale is low for some scopes and higher for others. A PMA registration in Bali is available only where the exact declared operation is the higher-risk scope, and the record expressly requires live OSS verification for the precise activity. National 100% openness is real, but it is not by itself a Bali registration answer; the declared scope and its OSS risk classification decide the route.

editorial.headline: Beach Tourism: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Beach-centred visitor facilities may be fully foreign-owned nationally, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration at the recorded Large-scale risk assessment.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register a beach-tourism activity under this code in Bali today, even though national policy opens it to PMA with foreign ownership up to 100 per cent. That contrast is the central fact of the record. At the Large scale, every stated scope is rated Low or Medium-Low risk in OSS, and the provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for both risk classes. National foreign openness and Bali PMA registrability are separate results here: Bali’s outcome is a registration block, not a reduction of the national ownership ceiling.

In practical terms, this activity provides a place and facilities for enjoying natural beauty where the beach is the principal attraction. The beach is not incidental scenery; it is the core setting around which the visitor offer is organised. The scope expressly includes the rental of facilities such as bathrooms, lockers and seating. Food and drink services and accommodation may also be provided. Those additions can sit alongside the principal beach-based activity, but they do not displace the beach as the stated centre of the business.

The activity is open at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. The record names all four classifications without attaching a different PMA percentage to any of them. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign holding of 100 per cent under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This means full foreign ownership is permitted nationally for the activity. The breadth of the listed scales answers who may register it in the national framework; it does not alter the stated foreign-ownership ceiling.

Bali requires a separate reading. Its recorded status is Blocked (risk class) because the provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. The Bali reason identifies the Large-scale OSS assessment across every scope as Low or Medium-Low and notes the moratorium of 13 May 2026. The rule is recorded as originating in Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. There is no Bali-specific ownership percentage or partnership condition in the record to soften or replace the national figure. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, the operative answer is block, notwithstanding the 100 per cent national ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100 per cent national foreign-ownership ceiling does not overcome Bali’s permanent PMA registration block.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Agro-Tourism Is Open Nationally, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity turns farms, fisheries and livestock settings into visitor experiences—nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet blocked for PMA registration across Bali.
editorial.body:
Agro-tourism turns agricultural landscapes and practices into the reason to visit. It covers the management of tourism attractions built around food-crop and horticultural cultivation, plantations, fisheries and livestock, where the agricultural setting is the principal visitor draw. The experience may be recreational, educational or participatory: guests might encounter cultivation, agricultural learning, conservation, product processing or the cultural value of local farming communities as part of a tourism offering.

The scope is broad enough to accommodate a carefully composed destination rather than a single activity. It includes production, collection, conservation, cultivation, processing and agricultural education when they support the tourism function. Supporting facilities may include food and beverage services, visitor-interaction areas and places to sell agricultural products. Fruit gardens, plantation visits, coffeenery concepts and winery concepts all sit comfortably within that tourism-led frame. What matters is the developed visitor function: agriculture conducted solely to produce commodities, without that tourism dimension, is outside this activity.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is **TERBUKA** for PMA and carries a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. It is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so the national classification does not itself limit participation to a particular business size. For a founder assessing the activity at national level, the record supports a fully foreign-owned PMA structure.

Bali changes the practical answer completely. A foreign investor has no route to register this activity in Bali today. At the Besar scale, every scope is classified in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, placing it within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The Bali status is **Blocked (risk class)**: this is not a reduction in the national ownership ceiling, but a block on PMA registration in the province. The national openness therefore remains real, while Bali’s current rule prevents a PMA from using this activity there.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness remains real, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity on the island.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup
- aktivitas pengelolaan wisata dengan pemanfaatan sungai-sungai arus deras untuk mengadakan kegiatan arung jeram sebagai kegiatan pokok di kawasan tertentu, seperti Arung Jeram Sobek Bali, Arung Jeram Arus Liar Citarik, termasuk rafting tubing, river boarding, canoeing, kayaking, body rafting experience.
- aktivitas pengelolaan untuk mengadakan kegiatan selam, menyediakan penjualan dan penyewaan serta perbaikan peralatan selam (equipment), mengorganisasikan perjalanan wisata selam, baik skala lokal, nasional, dan internasional, termasuk kegiatan-kegiatan yang terkait dengan tujuan untuk menjaga dan merawat kondisi lingkungan laut dan pesisir (environment), serta kegiatan sejenis lainnya yang mendukung pelestarian lingkungan pada kawasan tertentu sebagai kegiatan pokok, termasuk kegiatan snorkeling, free diving, dan sea walker.
- aktivitas hiburan dan rekreasi yang berkaitan dengan infrastruktur marina;
- aktivitas pengelolaan wisata air seperti selancar angin, paralayar (parasailing) dan motor air (jet ski), perahu motor (motor boating), pelayaran (sailing), selancar ombak (surfing), rakit (rafting), perahu tradisional/naga (traditional/dragon boat race), berpetualang dengan perahu/kapal (boating adventures), pelatihan petualangan berlayar (sail training adventures), kapal selam wisata (submarine experience), dan flying board sebagai kegiatan pokok di suatu kawasan tertentu dan dapat dilengkapi dengan penyediaan berbagai jenis fasilitas, termasuk jasa pelayanan makan dan minum serta berbagai fasilitas pendukung lainnya.

persyaratan: Memiliki Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar

Dokumen Penilaian Mandiri Kesiapan Penerapan Standar
Silakan kirim semua dokumen yang diminta dalam satu file.
1. Unduh dan lengkapi formulir Penilaian Mandiri.
2. Dokumentasi Standar Pelaksanaan Kegiatan Usaha.
Lampirkan 6 dokumen Sarana
  1. Petunjuk identitas/nama usaha dengan tulisan yang terbaca.
  2. Ruang kantor/area administrasi yang dilengkapi peralatan dan perlengkapan kerja.
  3. Peralatan Pertolongan Pertama pada Kecalakaan (P3K) dan Alat Pemadam Api Ringan (APAR) yang berfungsi dengan baik.
  4. Ketersediaan air bersih yang tidak berwarna, tidak berbau, tidak berasa, dan jernih.
  5. Ketersediaan gudang atau tempat penyimpanan barang yang aman.
  6. Status kepemilikan kantor/tempat usaha yang jelas.
Lampirkan 1 dokumen Sumber Daya Manusia
Perlindungan asuransi kesehatan dan/atau kecelakaan bagi karyawan tersedia dan berlaku.
Lampirkan 1 dokumen Ketentuan Produksi
Pelayanan kesehatan, seperti informasi tentang dokter, rumah sakit, atau klinik terdekat terdokumentasi.
Lampirkan 3 dokumen Sistem Manajemen Usaha
  1. Struktur organisasi dan uraian tugas setiap jabatan jalas dan terdokumentasi.
  2. rencana bisnis (business plan) masih berlaku dan terdokumentasi.
  3. S0P dan/atau petunjuk teknis pelaksanaan karja masih berlaku dan terdokumentasi.
kewajiban: Memiliki Sertifikat Standar Usaha Pariwisata yang diterbitkan oleh LSPr

editorial.headline: Water Tourism Across Rivers, Reefs and Open Water
editorial.standfirst: This activity brings managed water-based recreation into one operating category, from rafting and diving to marina entertainment and sailing adventures.
editorial.body:
Water tourism under this activity is organised recreation built around rivers, the sea and related facilities in defined areas. On the river, it includes the management of white-water rafting as a principal activity, alongside rafting tubing, river boarding, canoeing, kayaking and body-rafting experiences. The marine side is equally broad: diving activities, snorkelling, free diving and sea walking sit alongside the sale, rental and repair of diving equipment and the organisation of dive travel at local, national and international scale.

The scope also reaches beyond an individual excursion. Operators may run activities connected with marine and coastal environmental care, as well as comparable work supporting environmental preservation within a particular area. Marina-related entertainment and recreation are included, as are managed water-tourism activities such as windsurfing, parasailing, jet skiing, motor boating, sailing, surfing, rafting, traditional or dragon-boat racing, boating adventures, sail-training adventures, tourist submarine experiences and flying boards. These principal activities may be supported by facilities, including food and beverage services and other supporting amenities.

The registration picture is unusually direct at national level. Foreign investment may hold up to 100% ownership in this activity. It is also open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar business scales. For a founder, that means the category accommodates both a compact specialist operation and a larger managed water-tourism business without changing the stated national ownership ceiling.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The province’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities island-wide. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium because, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi. The practical reading is clear: foreign participation remains nationally open up to 100%, and Bali is not marked as blocked for PMA registration under the stated moratorium test. The decisive distinction is not a separate Bali ownership cap, but the activity’s higher risk position at the Besar scale.
editorial.pullQuote: Foreign participation remains nationally open up to 100%, and Bali is not marked as blocked under the stated moratorium test.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Nationally Open, Blocked in Bali: Recreation at a Regulatory Divide
editorial.standfirst: This broad entertainment-and-recreation activity permits full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali blocks its PMA registration under a permanent moratorium tied to its recorded risk class.
editorial.body:
KBLI 93299 is a deliberately wide berth for entertainment and recreation operations. It includes the operation of ski hills and fairgrounds, recreation-equipment hire inseparable from a facility, and the production of live entertainment or recreation shows outside sport and art. Its scope also reaches independent animators within facilities, computer-game rooms, self-service amusements, airsoft and paintball fields, virtual-reality and geolocation experiences, billiard and bowling venues, escape rooms, laser games, light-and-sound shows, underwater-tour guiding, and fireworks making and displays.

The common thread is operation: running, staging, supplying or managing the experience. That can include mechanical rides and shows run by independent providers at exhibitions, folk festivals and Christmas markets, as well as picnic grounds unrelated to nature conservation. It also covers the technical planning, provision, arrangement and operation of audiovisual and special-effects equipment connected with managing live entertainment and recreation. The activity is open at Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale, giving the category room to accommodate both contained venues and larger operational formats.

Nationally, the record is clear: the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. A founder considering the activity at national level can therefore read the foreign-investment position as fully open. But that ceiling is not a portable answer for Bali. National foreign ownership and the provincial registration result are separate facts in the record; confusing them would overlook the constraint that governs a Bali PMA filing.

In Bali today, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA. At Besar scale, OSS risk is recorded as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every listed scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium. The record places that moratorium in May 2026 and marks the Bali result as Blocked (risk class). The practical conclusion is precise: national foreign ownership may reach 100%, but PMA registration for this activity in Bali is blocked under the stated provincial moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not turn into a Bali PMA registration right.

l4_bali.reason: Not among the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026. The low/medium-low risk tier was named only in the Governor's January 2026 request letter (B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP); check the risk tier and zoning on OSS before filing.

This activity covers membership organisations that are not directly affiliated with political parties and that work on public issues through public education, political influence, fundraising and related means. Its territory is deliberately broad: non-governmental organisations, youth and civic bodies, protest movements and citizen initiatives, environmental movements, groups supporting public or educational facilities, and associations advancing the interests of ethnic or minority groups all sit within its reach. It also extends to patriotic associations, including veterans’ groups.

The category makes room for the everyday infrastructure of collective interests. Consumer and automobile associations belong here, as do social-knowledge associations such as Rotary-style clubs. Youth, student and fraternity groups are included, alongside associations devoted to health promotion, animal protection, and cultural, recreational or hobby pursuits other than sport and games. Poetry, literature, book, history, gardening, photography, music, art, collecting, social and carnival clubs are expressly within the scope. The record also includes assistance provided by membership organisations or other organisations.

Nationally, the activity is open to PMA registration, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. The slim record does not set out which business scales may register under this activity, so it offers no basis for treating a particular scale as either eligible or excluded. What it does establish is a national foreign-investment position: this is not an activity subject to a foreign-share cap below full ownership.

Bali requires a more local reading, but not a dramatic one. The provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk activities across the island. This activity is recorded as medium-high or high risk and is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. Its Bali status is recorded as OK or higher risk, with verification required for the specific address. For a foreign-owned organisation, the honest conclusion is that Bali does not impose the stated island-wide moratorium block here; the address remains material to the registration assessment.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali does not impose the stated island-wide moratorium block here, but the specific address remains material.

editorial.headline: Computer Repair: Nationally Open, PMA-Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wide computer-repair activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium bars PMA registration.
editorial.body:
Computer repair is often treated as a small practical service, but this activity is drawn broadly. It covers the repair and maintenance of desktop computers, laptops, magnetic disk drives, removable and flash drives, printers, monitors, keyboards, mice, joysticks, trackballs, internal and external modems, computer terminals, servers, scanners—including barcode scanners—smart-card readers, virtual-reality headsets, webcams and computer projectors. The perimeter also includes repair and maintenance of non-mechanically operated ATM and point-of-sale terminals, as well as handheld computers, or PDAs. In short, it is a service activity for keeping computer equipment and associated terminals operating.

Registration is not reserved for a particular business size. The record lists the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises. That breadth matters because the classification accommodates repair and maintenance work across the stated range of computer equipment, peripherals and terminals. Its centre of gravity is the service itself: maintaining and repairing the specified computer-related equipment, from everyday devices such as laptops, printers and monitors to servers, scanners, smart-card readers and specialised terminals.

At the national level, the PMA position is unequivocally open. Foreign ownership may reach 100%, which is the stated national foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity. The position is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder considering foreign investment in Indonesian computer repair and maintenance, the national setting is clear: the activity is TERBUKA and the stated PMA ceiling is 100%. The distinction between this national position and Bali’s registration outcome is essential rather than technical.

In Bali, however, a foreign-owned company cannot register this activity as PMA today. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): at the Besar scale, every scope recorded for the activity is assessed in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk, and that result is blocked by the Bali moratorium. The stated provincial rule is island-wide and permanent for PMA registrations in the Low and Medium-Low risk categories. The block is attributed to a Bali moratorium recorded in May 2026, under Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. The national 100% ceiling is real, but it does not overcome Bali’s PMA-registration block.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not overcome Bali’s PMA-registration block.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Communication Repair: Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans the repair and maintenance of communication equipment, with a clear national opening to foreign investment and an equally clear Bali restriction.
editorial.body:
Communication equipment repair is a broad, practical technical activity: restoring and maintaining the devices and systems that move information between people, networks and places. Its scope reaches from wireless telecommunications equipment—mobile phones, RFID devices, tablets, handheld computers, wireless modems and vehicle trackers—to wired equipment such as fax machines, analogue telephones, ADSL/HDSL equipment, PABX systems, modems, routers and bridges.

It also covers repair work on cable-based transmission equipment, including analogue telephone exchanges; radio-transmission equipment such as microwave links, studio-to-transmitter links and troposcatter links; and two-way radio systems, from trunking and conventional radio communications to walkie-talkies. The activity extends further to radio transmitters and receivers: broadcast television transmitters, television and smart-TV sets, broadcast radios, mobile-network transmitting and receiving equipment, and video cameras. In other words, this is an activity defined by the upkeep of communications infrastructure and the devices at its edges, rather than by one narrow class of hardware.

The national position is direct. The activity is open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. It is available across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the record does not confine the work to a specialist workshop, a particular network technology or a single level of enterprise; it frames the activity as a repair-and-maintenance field available from micro through large business scale.

Bali changes the registration picture for PMA entirely. At present in Bali, a foreign investor is unable to register this activity. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is classified as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The restriction has applied under the Bali moratorium since May 2026. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the national rule, but it does not override Bali’s PMA registration block for this activity.
editorial.pullQuote: The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the national rule, but it does not override Bali’s PMA registration block for this activity.

editorial.headline: Nationally Open, but Bali Stops This Consumer-Electronics Repair Activity
editorial.standfirst: This consumer-electronics repair activity is open nationally to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium stops registration there today.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this consumer-electronics repair and maintenance activity through PMA in Bali today. That conclusion is not softened by the national position: the activity is marked TERBUKA nationally, with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The distinction is central for anyone deciding where to place the business. National openness describes the national investment setting; Bali supplies a separate, binding local result for PMA registration. Read together, the two positions give a clear answer: national eligibility does not itself secure a Bali registration.

The activity itself is practical and defined by the equipment it services. It covers repair and maintenance of television and radio receivers, with antenna installation expressly included. Audio and video players are within scope, alongside video cameras made for home users and video-game devices. These are not stray examples: they describe consumer electronics across reception, playback, home recording and gaming. The common thread is the service of repairing and maintaining the stated equipment, with the examples establishing the working perimeter of the activity.

The activity can be registered at the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. The record therefore presents the activity across the full set of listed scales, while preserving its particular Bali risk finding at the Besar scale. For national PMA purposes, foreign ownership may reach the stated 100% ceiling. Its cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain terms, national PMA treatment permits foreign ownership up to that declared ceiling; it does not answer the separate question of whether Bali will register the activity.

Bali is where the answer changes. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class). The stated reason says that, at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah across every scope. That finding places the activity within Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium for PMA registration, recorded as taking effect in May 2026. The practical result is straightforward: a nationally open, fully foreign-ownable consumer-electronics repair business still cannot be registered through PMA in Bali. The national ceiling remains a national fact; it does not displace the Bali block.
editorial.pullQuote: A foreign investor cannot register this consumer-electronics repair and maintenance activity through PMA in Bali today.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Household and Garden Equipment Repair: Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM, and Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans the repair and upkeep of household appliances and home-and-garden equipment, open to all business scales but allocated to Koperasi and UMKM — foreign ownership is 0% nationwide, and PMA registration is separately blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot obtain PMA registration for this activity — and the reason is national, not local. Perpres 10/2021 as amended by 49/2021 allocates this bidang usaha to Koperasi and UMKM in its Lampiran II, which sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 0% and puts the activity out of reach of a PT PMA anywhere in Indonesia. Bali adds a second, independent restriction on top of that, but moving the registration to another province would not lift the first.

The work itself is practical, broad and firmly rooted in the maintenance economy of everyday life. It covers repair and servicing for household equipment including refrigerators, stoves, washing machines, clothes dryers, air conditioners, electric irons, vacuum cleaners and other electrical household goods. It also includes the repair and maintenance of home-and-garden equipment: lawn mowers, edgers, snow and leaf sweepers, trimmers and related equipment. In clear terms, this is the business of restoring the machines and appliances that keep homes and gardens functioning.

The activity is open to Micro, Small, Medium and Large businesses. That range gives the classification room to accommodate a compact repair operation as well as a larger service business, without changing the basic nature of the registered activity: repair and maintenance of household and home-and-garden equipment. Scale, however, does not change the ownership position: a bidang usaha allocated to Koperasi and UMKM is closed to a PT PMA at every scale.

Bali requires a separate reading, and it is additional rather than decisive. Its status is Blocked (risk class) because the relevant OSS risk assessment at the Large scale is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, and Bali’s permanent, province-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. The moratorium was identified in the record in May 2026 and is sourced to the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. The practical conclusion is that two restrictions apply at once: the national allocation to Koperasi and UMKM, which no province can lift, and the Bali moratorium on top of it.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness remains real, while PMA registration for this particular activity is blocked in Bali under the stated moratorium.

editorial.headline: Footwear and Leather Repair: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Although nationally open to 100 per cent foreign ownership, this repair activity cannot be registered under PMA in Bali today.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity under PMA in Bali today, even though the national record opens it to 100 per cent foreign ownership. The activity covers repair and maintenance services for footwear and leather goods. The stated examples make the scope concrete: shoes, boots and sandals on the footwear side, and suitcases and bags among leather goods. Fitting shoe heels is expressly included, while shoe-shining is expressly outside the group. Both inclusions are part of the stated scope. The category is therefore defined by repair and maintenance of the identified goods, with its boundary stated directly rather than left to implication.

The national entry supplies both the scale and foreign-ownership position. It is open to PMA, and its stated foreign-ownership ceiling is 100 per cent. At the national level, a foreign stake may reach that 100 per cent ceiling. The activity is available at every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The national PMA basis given for this position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The record therefore presents national availability across all of its listed scales, with the ceiling stated for the activity.

Bali must be read separately, because the local result is not a revised percentage but a block. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk position is recorded as Low/Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s stated rule is an island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk classifications. The entry is accordingly marked Blocked (risk class). Its stated reason is that the moratorium, recorded in May 2026, blocks the activity. That status carries the key local fact: PMA registration is blocked in Bali.

That produces a clear national-versus-Bali reading. Nationally, this is a PMA-open activity, with a foreign stake that may reach the recorded 100 per cent ceiling and availability across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. In Bali, the same activity cannot be registered under PMA because of the recorded risk-based moratorium. The national opening does not override the local block, and no lower Bali ownership ceiling is supplied instead. National openness cannot be read as permission to register this activity under PMA in Bali; under the recorded Bali position, it remains unavailable there today.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness cannot be read as permission to register this activity under PMA in Bali.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: Furniture Repair: A National Opening, a Bali PMA Bar
editorial.standfirst: Furniture repair and maintenance is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium means a foreign investor cannot register the activity there today.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity is the practical craft of keeping furniture and household fittings in service. It covers repair and maintenance work on furniture and household equipment: coating, finishing, repair and restoration. The scope also reaches office furniture and the assembly of self-standing furniture. Rather than a loose furnishing label, it identifies the interventions that matter: treating a surface, completing a finish, repairing a piece or bringing it back into condition. It is as relevant to a piece’s finish as to its restoration.

Who can register is unusually clear. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises—every scale named in the record. This broad eligibility does not alter the subject of the registration. Across that range, the work remains defined by repair and maintenance, whether it concerns a coating or finishing job, a repair or restoration, office furniture, household equipment or the assembly of self-standing furniture. Scale is an access category here, not a change to the listed activity.

Nationally, no fine print complicates the foreign-investment picture for this code. The activity is TERBUKA and carries a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. For a PMA company, that means full foreign ownership is allowed at the national level; there is no lower stated ceiling to navigate. The national basis recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That ceiling is not a promise about a particular province, yet it is the national benchmark against which a local restriction must be read.

In Bali, the answer is more restrictive and immediate: a foreign investor cannot register this activity there today. Its Bali status is Blocked (risk class). At the Besar scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope; Bali’s island-wide, permanent PMA moratorium blocks PMA registration for every activity classified Low or Medium-Low risk. The reason records the moratorium as of May 13, 2026. The distinction needs to remain crisp: 100% is the national foreign-ownership ceiling, while Bali blocks PMA registration for this activity. This is a jurisdictional bar, not a reduced Bali ownership percentage.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, the ceiling is 100%; in Bali, PMA registration for this activity is blocked.

editorial.headline: Commercial Clothes Alterations: Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM, Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: Commercial clothes alterations are allocated to Koperasi and UMKM, so foreign ownership is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this activity anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
Commercial clothes alteration is a practical service with a precise legal perimeter: altering garments for the general public as a commercial activity. It covers a business that takes in clothing from everyday customers and returns it altered. The emphasis is on the paid public-facing service itself, not a vague label for any work connected with clothing. That clarity gives the activity its useful, modest definition: a commercial alterations desk serving the public.

The record opens registration at the Mikro, Kecil and Menengah scales. These are not background details. They describe the operating sizes available to the activity and help explain its place in the business landscape: it is structured for micro, small and medium enterprise participation. A founder considering this activity should read the scale line together with the scope line. The public-service character and the permitted scales belong to the same picture, setting the terms on which the activity is presented for registration.

At the national level, the answer is not an open one: Perpres 49/2021's Lampiran II allocates this bidang usaha to Koperasi/UMKM in the *dialokasikan* column, so a PT PMA cannot take it. That is a national allocation, not a scale-based inference, and it is the basis carried through the rest of this entry — there is no separate, more open national default sitting underneath it for a Bali venture to inherit.

The restriction is not something that appears only once a venture reaches Bali: a foreign investor cannot register this activity through a PT PMA anywhere in Indonesia. The reason is a specific allocation, not an inference from OSS's scale rows: Perpres 49/2021's Lampiran II lists this activity — page 16, entry 57, sub-row "Vermak pakaian", KBLI 95291 — in its *dialokasikan* column, reserving the bidang usaha for Koperasi and UMKM and barring a PT PMA from taking it. The code number is unchanged from 2020 to 2025, so that allocation carries straight through to the current KBLI. The result is direct rather than nuanced: there is no national opening for a PT PMA that a Bali registration narrows down — the Koperasi/UMKM allocation is the basis recorded, nationwide. An enterprise that wants to serve the public through commercial clothing alterations under a PT PMA structure cannot use this registration anywhere in the country.
editorial.pullQuote: The national position is a Lampiran II allocation to Koperasi and UMKM — 0% foreign ownership — and it does not translate into PT PMA registration anywhere in Indonesia.

editorial.headline: The Repair Trade Nationally Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM
editorial.standfirst: This broad repair activity is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM — foreign ownership is 0% nationwide — and PMA registration in Bali is separately blocked under the province's permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor is unable to register this activity, and the restriction is national before it is local. Perpres 10/2021 as amended by 49/2021 allocates this bidang usaha to Koperasi and UMKM in its Lampiran II, setting the foreign-ownership ceiling at 0% for a PT PMA anywhere in Indonesia. Bali adds a second restriction of its own: every scope at the large-business scale is assessed by OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk, placing the activity within the province-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for those risk bands.

The activity is the practical craft of keeping personal and household possessions in use. Its scope includes repairing and maintaining bicycles, electric bicycles, monowheels, hoverboards and kick scooters; repairing or altering jewellery; and repairing watches, clocks, wall clocks and their components, from straps and cases to movement frames. It also reaches sporting equipment other than sporting guns, books, musical instruments, toys and similar goods, as well as other personal and household articles. Piano tuning and key duplication are expressly within the scope.

It excludes, among other things, metal engraving, repairs to sporting or recreational guns, repairs to powered hand tools, restoration of organs and other historic musical instruments, and repairs to time locks, time-and-date stamps and other time-recording equipment. For a business built around everyday objects rather than industrial equipment, the category is therefore broad in consumer-facing practice while still clearly delimited.

Registration is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar business scales, but scale does not change the ownership position: a bidang usaha allocated to Koperasi and UMKM is closed to a PT PMA at every scale. In Bali the provincial rule adds a further block — all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities are blocked island-wide and permanently, under the Bali moratorium dated May 2026. editorial.headline: Car Repair Is Nationally Open, but Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 95311 covers the practical work of keeping cars, trailers and semitrailers roadworthy—nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. That is the decisive local reality for KBLI 95311, even though the activity is nationally classified as open to PMA with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali’s block follows its permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA activities carrying Low or Medium-Low risk; at the Large scale, every scope in this activity falls within those risk categories. The block is recorded under the Bali risk-class status and tied to the moratorium in force from May 2026.

The activity itself is the broad working life of a vehicle repair shop. It encompasses mechanical and electrical repair, electronic injection-system work, routine servicing, bodywork, component repair, spraying and painting, and the repair of vehicle glass, windows and seating. It also includes diagnosing and repairing mechatronic systems; fitting, replacing or repairing inner and outer tyres; anti-rust treatment; and installing parts and accessories where that installation is not part of a manufacturing process. Cars are central, but trailers and semitrailers are expressly within the scope as well.

Nationally, the activity is available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. That breadth matters because the code is not framed as a narrow specialist trade: it accommodates both routine maintenance and a substantial range of technical, structural and finishing work. Its national PMA position is equally clear. It is TERBUKA, and the stated ceiling permits 100% foreign ownership. There is no need to infer a lower national cap from the operational diversity of the workshop.

Bali changes the practical conclusion without changing the national classification. The province’s rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration, island-wide and permanently. For this activity, the Large-scale OSS risk assessment is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, bringing it within that block. So the accurate reading is not that foreign ownership is nationally restricted; it is that a nationally open, fully foreign-ownable activity cannot presently be registered as PMA in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: A nationally open, fully foreign-ownable activity cannot presently be registered as PMA in Bali.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code.
