editorial.headline: Car Washing and Detailing: Nationally Open, PMA-Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Car washing, polishing and limited non-manufacturing accessory fitting sit inside a nationally open activity—but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
Car washing and car detailing is the whole frame of this activity. It covers the practical work of washing and polishing vehicles, as well as fitting spare parts and accessories where that fitting is not part of a processing or manufacturing operation. The distinction matters: the code describes a customer-facing vehicle-care activity, with a bounded add-on installation element, rather than a manufacturing process. Its centre of gravity is the condition and presentation of the car—cleaning, finishing and compatible ancillary fitting—as expressed in the recorded scope.

The registration audience is not confined to a particular business size. The record lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises as open to the activity, which gives the code a broad formal scale range. At national level, the PMA position is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. For a founder looking only at the national setting, that reads as a fully open foreign-ownership ceiling. It is a national position, however, and it cannot be read in isolation where the operating location is Bali.

For Bali, the conclusion is clear: a foreign investor cannot register this activity there today. The Bali status is blocked for risk class. The record says that, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope; Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration. The stated reason ties the block to the moratorium of May 13, 2026. That is not a reduction of the national 100% ceiling or a local equity cap. It is a Bali-specific prohibition on PMA registration for this activity under the stated risk basis.

The editorially important point is therefore one of jurisdiction, not commercial appeal. This code can describe the familiar work of a car wash and detailing salon with limited non-manufacturing parts and accessory installation, and it is open across the listed enterprise scales nationally. Yet in Bali the national openness does not translate into an available PMA registration path. A local plan should be evaluated against that exact separation: nationally open, but blocked for PMA in Bali under the permanent island-wide rule.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not translate into an available PMA registration path in Bali.

editorial.headline: Motorcycle Care Is Nationally Open, but Bali PMA Registration Is Blocked
editorial.standfirst: This motorcycle repair-and-care activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet PMA registration in Bali is blocked under the island-wide risk moratorium.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity is the repair-and-care side of motorcycle service. It includes repair and maintenance for conventional motorcycles and electric motorcycles alike. Its stated scope also encompasses spraying and painting motorcycles and their equipment, motorcycle-body repair, conversion, washing, polishing, and other care work. These are not presented as isolated add-ons: they are all named parts of the same activity. The result is a definition that covers a motorcycle’s maintenance and repair, its body work, its conversion, its painted finish and equipment, and its washing and polishing. The scope is therefore broad in the literal services it names, while staying focused on motorcycles throughout.

Registration is open at every scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar—micro, small, medium, and large. At the national level, PMA is classified TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In clean ownership terms, that means full foreign ownership is permitted nationally for this activity; the record does not state a ceiling below 100%. The scale field is equally direct: each of the four listed scales is open to this activity. The cited national PMA basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national record alone, the ownership and scale position is clear.

Bali is different, and this is where the registration question becomes decisive. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today: its recorded Bali result is Blocked (risk class). The local restriction is not a Bali-specific foreign-ownership percentage, and it does not lower the national 100% ceiling. Rather, the record says that, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah for every scope of the activity—Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium, recorded in May 2026, blocks PMA registration for that risk classification. That is the stated basis for the block.

This produces a genuine national-versus-Bali split, rather than a qualification that can be read away. The national position remains TERBUKA, with full foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. But Bali’s PMA-registration result remains blocked under the island-wide permanent moratorium. For a founder assessing this motorcycle repair-and-care activity, both statements must remain visible at once: national openness answers the foreign-ownership question; the Bali block answers whether a PMA registration can be made on the island. The record supports no softer reading of that final point. In Bali, the condition is a block, not a reduced stake or a conditional local percentage.
editorial.pullQuote: A national opening to 100% foreign ownership does not make PMA registration available in Bali for this activity.

data.judul: Jasa Intermediasi Reparasi dan Perawatan Komputer, Barang Pribadi dan Rumah Tangga, Mobil, serta Sepeda Motor
data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup jasa intermediasi dalam reparasi dan perawatan komputer, barang pribadi dan rumah tangga, mobil, dan sepeda motor dengan cara mempertemukan pihak pengguna dan penyedia jasa berdasarkan imbalan atau komisi, tanpa intermediator menyediakan jasa yang diintermediasikan. Kegiatan intermediasi dapat dilakukan melalui platform digital atau melalui kanal nondigital (tatap muka, termasuk door-to-door; telepon; surat; dan lainnya). Imbalan atau komisi dapat diterima dari pihak pengguna atau penyedia jasa reparasi. Pendapatan dari kegiatan intermediasi juga dapat mencakup sumber lain, seperti pendapatan dari iklan.

editorial.headline: The Business of Bringing Repairs Together
editorial.standfirst: A fully foreign-open national activity for matching repair customers with providers, with a more conditional PMA path in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 95400 is for the business of making a repair connection, rather than performing the repair itself. It brings users together with providers for the repair and maintenance of computers, personal and household goods, cars, and motorcycles. The intermediary may operate through a digital platform or through non-digital channels, including face-to-face and door-to-door contact, telephone, post, and other routes. Its role ends at the introduction: it does not provide the repair service being arranged. Income may come from a fee or commission paid by either the user or the repair provider, as well as from sources such as advertising.

The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scale. In practical terms, the registrant is the business that creates the connection between demand for repair and the provider able to fulfil it. That is a distinct commercial position: the value lies in arranging access, whether through a platform or a more traditional channel, while the underlying repair remains with the service provider.

Nationally, the PMA position is clear. The activity is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. A foreign investor may therefore hold the business in full at the national level. That openness applies to the intermediation activity described here, not to an invented set of adjacent services or conditions.

Bali requires a more exact reading. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. For this activity, however, the Bali status is scope-dependent rather than an outright block: at the Besar scale, some OSS scopes are low risk while others are higher risk. Registration as PMA in Bali is available only by declaring the higher-risk scope, and the precise activity must be verified live in OSS. In Bali, the decisive step is the higher-risk scope declared in OSS, which must be verified live against the exact activity.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, the decisive step is the higher-risk scope declared in OSS, which must be verified live against the exact activity.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: Washing and Dry Cleaning of Textiles and Fur — covers commercial laundry, dry cleaning, ironing, carpet cleaning, curtain cleaning, and uniform/linen rental services. It applies to services operated mechanically, by hand, or coin-operated, for both the general public and industrial/commercial clients. It explicitly excludes clothing alterations.
intel_2026.whatChanged: This code consolidates multiple KBLI 2020 activities into one. Verify your specific activity maps correctly. Consolidated from multiple fragmented cleaning codes in the previous system into a single comprehensive textile cleaning category.
intel_2026.baliContext: Commercial laundry is one of the most stable, unglamorous, yet highly profitable B2B businesses in Bali. Every villa, hotel, and spa needs reliable daily linen turnaround. However, operating a large-scale laundry business in Bali faces one massive, existential hurdle: water. You cannot simply dump chemical detergent wastewater into the local subak (irrigation) system. Villages (Banjars) and the Environmental Agency (DLHK) will shut you down immediately. You must invest heavily in a proper Wastewater Treatment Plant (IPAL) and secure a Groundwater Extraction Permit (SIPA). Finding industrial-zoned land away from tourist centers (like in Denpasar or Tabanan) is the smartest play to keep costs down.

editorial.headline: Laundry in Indonesia: Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM, Closed to PT PMA
editorial.standfirst: This activity ranges from everyday laundry to linen care and reusable-diaper services — and it is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 49/2021's Lampiran II, which sets foreign ownership at 0% and makes it unregistrable by a PT PMA anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
This activity is the practical infrastructure of clean textiles: washing, dry cleaning and ironing every kind of clothing, including fur, as well as other textiles. It can be performed mechanically, by hand or through coin-operated machines, for the public or for industrial and commercial clients. Its reach also includes collection and delivery, carpet and rug washing, and the cleaning of curtains and drapes, whether at a client’s premises or elsewhere. The scope extends beyond a conventional laundry counter to combined rental-and-care services for items such as linen and work uniforms, and to reusable-diaper provision.

The boundary matters. Clothing repair and alteration are outside this activity, as is clothing rental outside the integrated work-uniform arrangement described in the record. What remains is a service defined by the care, cleaning and circulation of textiles—not by tailoring or a general clothing-hire business. That distinction gives the activity a clear operational centre: maintaining garments, household textiles and work-related linen in usable condition, from individual pieces to recurring commercial volumes.

The scale eligibility is real: this activity is open at Mikro, Kecil and Menengah levels. editorial.headline: Hairdressing Is Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM — Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: Hair and facial-hair services are allocated to Koperasi and UMKM under Perpres 49/2021's Lampiran II, which sets foreign ownership at 0% and puts the activity out of reach of a PT PMA anywhere in Indonesia.
editorial.body:
Code 96210 covers the hands-on work of putting hair and facial hair in order: washing, trimming and cutting hair; styling; colouring, dyeing, perming, straightening and similar treatments. It also includes hair styling in its own right, alongside shaving and tidying beards, moustaches and sideburns. The scope draws an important boundary: wig manufacture is excluded. Taken together, these statements define a grooming and treatment service by the work performed on hair and facial hair. They encompass both services that alter hair and the routine upkeep of cutting, styling and shaving.

The relevant operator is one whose actual activity falls within that stated service perimeter. The record opens the activity to the Mikro, Kecil and Menengah scales. Those are the scale labels supplied for this activity, and they frame the registration picture more precisely than a broad description of appearance or personal care services would. The scope is detailed enough to include hair treatment, styling and facial-hair grooming, while retaining its express exclusion for wig manufacture.

At national level, the position is not simply open. Perpres 49/2021's Lampiran II allocates this bidang usaha — recorded there under the old KBLI code 96111, the *Pangkas rambut/barber shop* sub-row, page 16, entry 57 — to Koperasi and UMKM in its *dialokasikan* column. That allocation sits in a national annex, not a regional variation, and it places the activity outside what a PT PMA may register wherever the Perpres applies. Our records do not carry a separate foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity beyond that allocation.

This is not a Bali-only breakpoint. Perpres 10/2021, as amended by 49/2021, assigns this bidang usaha to Koperasi/UMKM nationwide through Lampiran II's *dialokasikan* column, and a PT PMA cannot register this activity anywhere the Perpres governs, not only in Bali. For a foreign investor, this is not a reduced foreign-ownership ceiling; it is a nationwide bar on PMA registration for this specific bidang usaha, regardless of scale.

editorial.headline: Beauty Beyond the Clinic: Reserved for Koperasi and UMKM, Closed to PT PMA Nationwide
editorial.standfirst: From nail art and brows to makeup and facial massage, this activity is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM — foreign ownership is 0%, and it cannot be registered by a PT PMA anywhere in Indonesia today.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the conclusion comes first: a PT PMA cannot register this activity, and that holds nationwide, not only in Bali. Peraturan Presiden 10/2021, as amended by 49/2021, allocates this beauty-care activity to Koperasi and UMKM in its Lampiran II — naming it, under the old KBLI code 96112, "Salon kecantikan," as dialokasikan — and a business field reserved that way is closed to PT PMA irrespective of scale, whether or not OSS lists a Besar-scale row for it, and irrespective of where in Indonesia the investor is registering. That reservation does not reach spa (96230) or fitness activities. Our records do not support a foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity; the reservation itself is the governing fact.

The activity itself sits firmly in the non-specialist beauty-care world. It covers beauty treatments not performed by specialist doctors, including work by cosmetologists. Its practical range is broad but coherent: nail care and beautification in a nail studio or at a client’s home, including nail art and manicures or pedicures; eyelash services such as extensions, lifts, perming and tinting; brow treatments including eyebrow embroidery, brow bomber and brow lamination; and hair removal in a wax studio or at home. It also includes makeup services by a makeup artist, facial massage and skin tanning.

The boundary is important. This is not a clinical category: plastic surgery or operations performed by specialist doctors fall outside its stated scope. The distinction is not decorative. It defines an activity built around cosmetic care and appearance services, whether delivered from a dedicated studio or through a home visit, rather than specialist medical intervention.

There is no separate national opening to weigh against a local outcome here — the reservation described above is itself the national position, not a regional carve-out from it. Our records do not support a foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity, so there is no percentage for a Bali rule to override. For foreign investors, the point that matters is simple: the activity is reserved to Koperasi and UMKM under a national Perpres annex, wherever in Indonesia that Perpres governs — not a Bali-specific closure sitting behind an open national position.

data.uraian:
Kelompok ini mencakup kegiatan yang menyediakan pelayanan kebugaran dan perawatan dengan memadukan metode tradisional dan modern secara holistik. Aktivitas ini menggunakan air dan pendukung perawatan lainnya berupa pijat menggunakan ramuan, terapi aroma, latihan fisik, terapi warna, terapi musik, makanan dan minuman. Tujuan aktivitas ini menyeimbangkan antara tubuh (body), pikiran (mind), dan jiwa (soul), sehingga terwujud kondisi relaks dan bugar untuk kesehatan yang optimal. Aktivitas ini juga merupakan upaya mempertahankan tradisi dan budaya bangsa.
Kelompok ini mencakup
- aktivitas pemandian Turki, sauna, dan pemandian uap, spa harian, solarium, salon pelangsing dan pengecilan tubuh, dan lainnya.
Subgolongan tidak mencakup
- layanan kesejahteraan fisik sebagai bagian dari aktivitas akomodasi, lihat golongan pokok 55l
- aktivitas terapis pijat medis, lihat subgolongan 8699;
- aktivitas praktisioner di bidang shiatsu, pijat Thailand, watsu, tuina qigong, lihat subgolongan 8699;
- aktivitas klub dan fasilitas kesehatan, kebugaran, dan pembentukan tubuh, lihat subgolongan 9311.

  1. Struktur organisasi dan uraian tugas setiap jabatan jalas dan terdokumentasi.

editorial.headline: Daily Spa, Sauna and Steam-Bath Activities: Bali’s Clear PMA Position
editorial.standfirst: A holistic wellness activity open nationally to full foreign ownership, with Bali’s moratorium not blocking the stated higher-risk large-scale route.
editorial.body:
This activity covers day spas, Turkish baths, saunas and steam baths, alongside solariums and body-slimming salons. Its defining idea is holistic wellbeing: water-based care may be combined with traditional and modern methods such as herbal massage, aroma therapy, physical exercise, colour therapy, music therapy, and food and drink, all directed towards relaxation, fitness and a balance of body, mind and soul. The scope also places this work in the continuing practice of Indonesia’s traditions and culture. A spa operation that has moved into Medical Spa territory is excluded.

The registration field is broad in business scale. It is open to micro, small, medium and large enterprises, which matters because the activity is not framed as a niche reserved for only one type of operator. The commercial proposition may be shaped around a conventional day spa, sauna or steam-bath experience, but the stated scope permits a wider wellness environment where water is one element in an integrated care offering. What remains important is the nature of the activity itself: wellbeing and treatment-oriented services rather than a Medical Spa.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. This activity is open to foreign investment and carries a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a full national opening, not a partial allowance requiring an implied local equity share. For an overseas founder, the point is clear: the national investment setting permits full foreign ownership for this activity.

Bali requires a more exact reading, but it is not a contradiction of the national opening. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium: at the large scale, its OSS risk is stated as Medium-High/High. Bali’s status is therefore not a blanket PMA prohibition, but an indication that the relevant large-scale risk classification sits outside the moratorium’s blocked categories. A founder should read that as a real distinction between a national ownership rule and Bali’s risk-based registration screen, rather than as a reason to dilute the national 100% ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: Bali is not a blanket PMA prohibition here: the stated large-scale risk classification sits outside the moratorium’s blocked categories.

data.pma_official_basis: Perpres 10/2021 Pasal 3(1)(d) + 3(2) (as amended by Perpres 49/2021): the residual category — «Bidang Usaha yang tidak termasuk dalam huruf a, huruf b, dan huruf c» — «dapat diusahakan oleh semua Penanam Modal». Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

intel_2026.whatItMeans: This covers the full range of funeral and burial services: preparing bodies for burial or cremation (embalming, funeral home services), conducting burials or cremations, renting or selling grave plots, and maintaining graves, mausoleums, and burial grounds for the community. It excludes religious funeral ceremonies and gardening in cemeteries.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed: Nationally this business is 100% open to foreign ownership (PMA). However, in Bali, the provincial moratorium blocks all foreign-owned companies from registering KBLI with a risk classification of 'Besar' (large scale) where the actual risk level is low or medium-low. As this activity falls under that blocked risk class, a PMA company cannot obtain this license in Bali at this time.
intel_2026.whatChanged: This code exists in the BPS classification but has no corresponding PP28/2025 licensing data yet. Funeral services have historically been community-managed in Indonesia, and the commercial classification is still catching up.
intel_2026.baliContext: Funeral services in Bali are deeply tied to Hindu religious traditions — the Ngaben (cremation) ceremony is one of the most important cultural practices. Commercial funeral services for the local Balinese population are virtually non-existent as a PMA opportunity; these are managed through Banjar and family structures. The realistic PMA angle is serving the international community: expat memorial services, repatriation logistics for deceased foreigners, and potentially pet cremation services (growing niche). Denpasar has a small number of commercial funeral service providers, mostly serving non-Hindu communities.

editorial.headline: Burial and Cremation Services: Nationally Open, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity embraces burial, cremation and funeral-home services at every business scale—but its 100% national PMA ceiling does not permit foreign registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors cannot register this activity in Bali today. Nationally, it is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali reaches a different result: the activity is blocked for PMA under the province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The record identifies the relevant trigger clearly: at the Large scale, every scope is assessed by OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk, placing it within Bali’s restriction introduced in May 2026.

The activity itself concerns the practical, continuing work around human or animal burial and cremation. It includes preparing a body for burial or cremation, embalming, and funeral-home attendant services; providing burial or cremation services; and renting equipped rooms in a funeral home. Its scope also extends beyond the immediate ceremony to the rental or sale of grave sites and the maintenance of graves, mausoleums, and other matters connected with the burial process in service of the public.

The national registration position is broad in enterprise scale. The record opens the activity to Micro, Small, Medium, and Large businesses, rather than reserving it for a particular size of operator. For PMA, the national position is equally direct: foreign ownership may reach 100%, with Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 cited as the source. That national openness describes the foreign-investment ceiling; it does not override a provincial restriction that applies to the relevant risk class.

A national 100% ceiling does not create a PMA registration route in Bali. For an investor considering this activity elsewhere in Indonesia, the record presents a nationally open PMA position across all listed scales. For Bali, the decisive fact is the provincial block: the activity’s Low or Medium-Low OSS risk classification at the Large scale brings it under the permanent moratorium. The distinction is not cosmetic. It means that, despite national openness, a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% ceiling does not create a PMA registration route in Bali.

data.judul: Aktivitas Jasa Intermediasi untuk Jasa Perorangan
data.uraian: Kelompok ini mencakup jasa intermediasi jasa perorangan yang mempertemukan klien dan penyedia layanan dengan biaya atau komisi, tanpa intermediator yang menyediakan layanan yang diintermediasikan. Kegiatan intermediasi ini dapat dilakukan melalui platform digital maupun melalui saluran nondigital (tatap muka, termasuk door-to-door; telepon; surat). Imbalan atau komisi dapat diterima baik dari klien maupun penyedia layanan pribadi. Pendapatan dari kegiatan intermediasi dapat mencakup sumber pendapatan lain, seperti pendapatan dari iklan. Kelompok ini juga mencakup kegiatan agen penatu dan dry cleaning.

editorial.headline: Personal-Service Intermediation: Open Nationally, Conditional in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers paid matching between clients and personal-service providers, with a fully open national PMA ceiling but a scope-dependent path in Bali.
editorial.body:
Personal-service intermediation is the business of making the connection, rather than delivering the underlying personal service. It brings clients and service providers together for a fee or commission, while the intermediary itself does not provide the service being matched. The model may operate through a digital platform or through non-digital channels: face-to-face contact, including door-to-door activity, telephone, or post. Commission may come from either the client or the personal-service provider, and revenue may also include other sources such as advertising. Laundry and dry-cleaning agency activity is included within the group.

The scope also expressly reaches qualifying electronic-trade system operators and intermediary-facility operators established either within Indonesia’s legal jurisdiction or outside it while conducting electronic-trade business in Indonesia. It separately accommodates businesses outside those operator categories. In practical terms, this is a classification for the intermediary role: organising introductions, transactions, or access between the two sides of a personal-service relationship, and being paid for that position in the chain.

At the national level, foreign investment is allowed for this activity, and foreign investors may hold up to 100% ownership. It is available at Micro, Small, Medium, and Large scale. That national position is clear, but it should not be mistaken for a simple Bali registration outcome. Bali’s provincial rule permanently blocks PMA registration for activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk across the island. For this activity, the Bali result depends on the exact declared scope and its risk level at Large scale: some scopes are low risk, while others carry a higher risk level.

The consequence is precise rather than absolute. Bali does not mark this activity as categorically blocked for PMA, but a PMA registration there is possible only where the declared scope is the higher-risk one. A low-risk scope cannot pass through that route under the province-wide rule. The classification therefore calls for a live OSS check against the exact activity being declared, not an assumption drawn from the national foreign-ownership position alone. The national ceiling remains 100%; the Bali question is whether the precise scope meets the higher-risk condition required for PMA registration.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open does not make Bali automatic: the precise declared scope and its risk level determine whether PMA registration can proceed.

editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Personal-Services Activity, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This broad personal-services activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration today.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 96900** covers an unusually broad field of personal services. At the household end, it includes cooking, washing, cleaning and ironing performed in households. Its social strand includes companion and dating services, speed-networking activities and marriage bureaux, alongside astrology, spiritual activity, genealogy organisations and house-sitting. It also reaches animal-related services: pet boarding, grooming, care, guarding and training; shelters for abandoned animals; and horse whispering. The scope is deliberately expansive rather than centred on one profession, bringing together everyday assistance, personal occasions and specialised small services under one activity.

That breadth continues in its operational examples. Shoe shining, porter work and valet parking sit beside coin-operated personal-service machines, including photo booths, weighing machines, blood-pressure machines and coin-operated lockers. The activity also covers photo booths and printing machines that make photographs from electronic records such as phones, memory cards and flash drives; temporary decorative tattoo work using biological substances such as henna; and private-event organisation other than funerals, including wedding planning, birthday parties, bachelor and bachelorette parties, and annual celebrations. It is an activity defined by the range of personal-facing services it brings together.

At the national level, the status is open and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. At the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, registration remains open. This gives the activity a clear national footing across every scale listed in the record, whether the business is built around household assistance, animal care, personal-service machines or private-event organisation. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nationally, foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership for this activity.

Bali is the decisive exception. A foreign investor is unable to register this activity in Bali today. The record marks it blocked by risk class: at the Besar scale, every scope carries Low or Medium-Low OSS risk, placing it within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. The stated moratorium date is 13 May 2026, with Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP given as the source. National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a PMA registration route for this activity in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a PMA registration route for this activity in Bali.

Derived from the instrument by ABSENCE, not from a row that names this code: over the BPS 2020→2025 crosswalk the code is on no Lampiran I (prioritas), Lampiran II (dialokasikan/kemitraan Koperasi-UMKM) or Lampiran III (persyaratan tertentu, foreign-ownership caps included) row — tested against Lampiran III BOTH by code through the crosswalk AND by activity title, because BPS re-scopes numbers between vintages while a cap attaches to the ACTIVITY the annex names — no body article names it (Pasal 2(2) closed list, Pasal 6(3a) alcohol trade) and no Pasal 11(2) sector-law referral reaches its SECTOR — the article's unit is «Bidang Usaha keuangan dan Bidang Usaha perbankan», so the whole of KBLI divisions 64, 65 and 66 is withheld from this lane, not merely the six codes the carve-out artifact enumerates. No instrument maps the 5-digit code; the residual article IS the locator. Open to all Penanam Modal, max foreign 100%. Scope: this is the Perpres investment axis only — sector statutes OUTSIDE the Perpres were not swept per code, and where that gap is load-bearing (divisions 09, 35, 49-53, 61: migas, ketenagalistrikan, pelayaran, penerbangan, pos, telekomunikasi) the codes are withheld from this lane rather than published under it. Four Pasal 2(2) items close an ACTIVITY and name no code (narkotika golongan I; perjudian/kasino; CITES species and koral; industri senjata kimia and bahan perusak lapisan ozon): they are tested here by the state's OWN per-code markers — the licensing requirement for a «Surat Pernyataan tidak memproduksi senjata kimia … Bahan Perusak Ozon/BPO», plus the hand-held exclusions for the alcohol, tobacco, explosives and CITES chains — and none of them reaches a code in this lot. This basis does not clear a closed ACTIVITY carried on under an open code. The OSS licensing gate (risk tier, scale, zoning, and for a PMA the Pasal 7(1) >Rp10bn Usaha Besar test) is a separate question this basis does not answer.

editorial.headline: When a Household Is the Employer
editorial.standfirst: This classification records the household itself as employer, with a national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling and a Bali status that remains unblocked by the provincial moratorium.
editorial.body:
A household can be an employer in its own right. This activity covers households that employ domestic workers: household assistants, cooks, cleaners, gardeners, personal drivers, house guards, child carers and personal assistants. It also includes teachers where they are employed by the household. The point is not to describe a commercial service business, but to identify the household as the employing unit behind work carried out for that household.

That distinction is central to the classification. It gives domestic workers a way to state their employer’s activity in a census or research setting even when the employer is an individual or a household rather than an organisation. The output of the activity is consumed by the employing household itself. It does not extend to independent or organisational providers supplying cleaning, ironing, cooking, garden care or home-care services to others, whether those providers operate for profit, without profit, publicly or on a self-employed basis.

The slim record identifies no scale categories open to this activity. Its defining feature is therefore the role of the registrant: a household acting as the employer of domestic workers, rather than a provider marketing domestic services. Nationally, the activity is classified as open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That is an unusually direct national position: the record sets no lower foreign-ownership ceiling for this activity.

Bali does not reverse that national position through its province-wide PMA moratorium. The moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA across the island on a permanent basis, but this activity is recorded as medium-high or high risk and is not blocked by that rule. In practical terms, it remains open for PMA registration in Bali today; the record nevertheless says the position must be verified for the relevant address. The honest reading is neither a Bali ban nor a special Bali ownership cap, but an open national classification whose address-specific registration position still merits confirmation.
editorial.pullQuote: A household can be an employer in its own right, without becoming a commercial domestic-services business.

editorial.headline: What a Household Makes for Itself
editorial.standfirst: A self-provisioning household activity is nationally open to PMA at 100%, while Bali records no moratorium block but requires address verification.
editorial.body:
This is a classification for the domestic economy at its most literal: a household making the basic goods it needs for itself. Its scope includes hunting and gathering, agriculture, the provision of shelter and clothing, and other goods produced for the household’s own needs. The unifying idea is not one particular product, but self-provision: a household undertaking a range of goods-producing activities to sustain itself.

That boundary is central to reading the activity accurately. Where a household also takes part in producing goods that are marketed, the record directs that production into the appropriate goods-producing industry. Where its principal activity is the production of particular basic goods, it is likewise directed to the corresponding production industry. This activity therefore describes own-use production, not a catch-all label for everything made at home. The record identifies households as the participants and lists no open-to scale categories, so it offers no basis for assigning the activity to a stated business scale.

At the national level, PMA is open and foreign ownership may reach 100%. That is a straightforward national setting for a foreign-owned registration: the record does not state a reduced foreign stake. But the ownership position does not alter the activity’s defining limit. It remains concerned with goods made by a household for its own needs, while the record preserves a clear distinction for marketed production and for production centred on particular basic goods.

In Bali, the immediate picture is not a blanket bar. The record marks the activity as medium-high/high risk and states that it is not blocked by the moratorium. Its Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. There is nevertheless a specific instruction attached to that result: verify the position for the address. Bali is therefore open in the terms recorded here, with address verification remaining part of the practical reading.
editorial.pullQuote: This activity describes own-use production, not a catch-all label for everything made at home.

editorial.headline: A Household’s Own Services: KBLI 98200 in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A household-only service activity, nationally open to 100% foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium, subject to address-level verification.
editorial.body:
KBLI 98200 concerns a tightly defined form of service production: a household making services for its own needs. The scope reaches into the practical core of domestic life—cooking, teaching or educating, caring for or watching household members, and other services produced by the household for itself. It also covers a household that produces a range of such services to meet its own needs. The point is not the individual task in isolation, but the setting and purpose: services generated within a household, for that household’s needs. The language gathers these varied activities within one domestic purpose, making the boundary of the activity unusually clear.

Who sits inside that description is equally important. The producer is the household itself, and the beneficiary is that same household. The slim record does not identify any business scale as open to the activity, so it supplies no scale-based qualification to infer. Without a stated scale field to work from, it would be inaccurate to attach a business-size label to this activity. Nor should the breadth of examples be mistaken for an open-ended claim over external service work. Cooking, education and care appear as illustrations of essential household services, while the unifying condition is self-provision. For a founder reading the code, that is the discipline: retain both halves of the definition—diverse services, but produced by a household to satisfy its own needs.

Nationally, the PMA setting is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali changes the practical reading without reversing it. The province’s moratorium is island-wide and permanent for PMA activities classified Low or Medium-Low risk; this activity is recorded in Bali as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with a medium-high/high risk reason. It is therefore not blocked by the moratorium. The national allowance and Bali result answer different questions: one states the nationwide foreign-ownership ceiling, while the other addresses whether Bali’s moratorium blocks PMA registration at this risk level. That is not an invitation to ignore location: the Bali record expressly says the position must be verified for the particular address. Nationally open to full foreign ownership, and not moratorium-blocked in Bali, with address-specific verification still part of the Bali picture.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to full foreign ownership, and not moratorium-blocked in Bali, with address-specific verification still part of the Bali picture.

editorial.headline: The KBLI for International and Extra-International Bodies
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the work of foreign-state representatives and international bodies, but it is closed to foreign investment nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the operations of foreign-state representatives and international or regional bodies working from Indonesia under arrangements determined by the host country rather than the country they represent. Its scope reaches from United Nations representations and sub-organisations to bodies such as UNICEF, UNESCO, UNDP, WHO, ILO, ASEAN, IMF, OECD and OPEC, alongside embassies, consulates, military bases and scientific bases. It is therefore an institutional category: a place for the operational presence of public and international bodies whose standing is defined through their official mandate.

The relevant registrants are those bodies and representations themselves—foreign-country representatives, international and regional institutions, international financial and monetary bodies, and the other official presences named in the scope. The record does not list any business scale as open. That absence matters: this is not framed as a conventional commercial activity that becomes available merely by choosing a micro, small, medium, or large operating scale. Its identity lies in the character of the institution and the authority under which it is present.

Nationally, the position is unambiguous. The activity is marked **TERTUTUP** for PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **0%**. Foreign investment is therefore not permitted for this activity. Bali reaches the same practical result: it is marked **TERTUTUP**, and a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The record notes that the restriction is not caused by Bali’s island-wide PMA moratorium for low and medium-low risk activities; instead, its medium-high or high-risk position calls for verification at the specific address. That is a check on the local position, not an opening of foreign ownership.

For founders, the distinction is worth holding clearly. This is an official institutional activity, not a route into ordinary foreign-owned enterprise. Its national closure is decisive, while the Bali entry adds a location-specific verification note without changing the closed outcome. The proper reading is neither optimistic nor speculative: the activity may describe major international presences, but the record does not permit PMA participation in it.
editorial.pullQuote: This is an official institutional activity, not a route into ordinary foreign-owned enterprise.
